First, it has to be admitted that the game had a horrible launch. The devs didn't anticipate the volume of people who bought it and their servers melted down, resulting in thousands of players unable to play or save progress for 3-4 days. I can understand people's anger about this, and I won't absolve the devs of their responsibility, but I know they were incredibly upset about it and they worked their asses off to make things right. Sadly, the reviews tanked, partly due to gameplay critiques but mostly because of the botched launch. Everything is working fine now, though!
That said, for gameplay, I love it. It's not a polished game by any means, and the controls can feel a bit clunky, but there's more depth to the game that initially meets the eye. Yes, Jason is incredibly strong, but not "unbeatable." People complain about his Shift grab, but it's jukeable. Jason can be evaded, tricked and outsmarted. Part of what makes counselors successful is understanding the psychology of what other players want to accomplish. Cooperation with other counselors can result in success or failure, depending on how they behave. A group can save each other and keep Jason stunned, or it can lead to them being discovered more easily and dispatched. Stealth and evasion seems like the most rewarding way to play, but fighting can work, too.
The game has a ton of tension and thrills, and it's a blast to play with a big group of friends that coordinate. Jason is fun and terrorizing people on voice chat can be hilarious. There's a lot of moments where you feel like you're really in a Friday film.
I do think there are some problems with the game, like making Vanessa the default starting character. She's the loudest in the game and attracts Jasons like flies on poop, which means a lot of newbie players are going to get stomped and not understand why. Mechanics like Stealth and Composure aren't understood immediately until you have a chance to play with more counselors. A counselor's Fear stat is communicated more by facial expressions, stumbles and HUD interference, but many players don't know that makes them light up in red to Jason. Expanded tutorials, maybe with videos, would maybe be more helpful. The game could also use more maps and more differentiation between them.
I recommend this to anyone who's a fan of the Friday The 13th series and survival horror fans in general. It's not a triple A quality game but it is a lot of fun and the devs said they'll keep working on it in the future.

I highly recommend this game to anyone who loves Survival games, Sandbox games and/or Dinosaurs and other creatures!
There are two game modes:
Sandbox; Where you choose a dinosaur and play as it. If you die than you can either choose that dinosaur again or choose a different dinosaur and choose the skin you want.
Progression; Where you start from the bottom tier (lowest stats, damage, etc) and choose a path to go down collecting points that you save up to get to the next tier of dinosaurs.
(Progression is not finished yet and it takes a long time to get to the next tier so I recommend choosing Sandbox.)
Also the developers are working on Humans, Tribals and Cannibals.
They are also working on aquatic creatures and are working on aerial creatures like the pteranodon, Quetzalcoatlus and more.
They are also working on nesting for dinosaurs and weapons for Humans, Tribals and Cannibals
The developers are currently working on Mod support which I can't wait for as players will be able to create their own content and add it to the game such as:
•New creatures
•Maps
•Skins
•Game Modes
And a lot more!
(I will edit this every now and then when more stuff is added to the game.)

A good story set in an evocative world with a great backstory and lore. Told through well fleshed out and somewhat unique characters.
The story is more straightforward than Bastion and Transistor and focuses more on the actual plot and character development than it does worldbuilding through narration. Though there's also more worldbuilding than in Bastion and Transistor combined.
The world is much heavier on the fantasy elements, and the deeper worldbuilding lets you really get a feel for it. Unlike Bastion where all you get is a good idea of concepts for each of the areas and groups, and unlike Transistor where it's all politics, the world of Pyre offers a good glimpse into the politics of the Commonwealth you're exiled from, the world surrounding you in the Downside purgatory you're exiled to, the ancient history of the setting. And of course the people living in it.
The visuals can be a bit busy at times on the world map, but it doesn't really make it hard to navigate or get your bearings in any way. You also get used to it over time and start separating out details more easily.
Other than that the artstyle is great, placing itself somewhat midway between Bastion's high-quality cartoon characters and Transistors graphic-novel-realism-style, with exagerrated yet proportional and real-enough looking characters.
The music is excelent as you'd expect from Darren Korb, and more to the point, in several parts it is dynamic, layers of the music will fade out when you go into your wagon, and variants of themes might play in important rites. Not to mention that every major character in this large ensamble cast has their own theme. Every area has it's own theme as well.
Speaking of the Rites... While a large portion of the gameplay is visual-novel or RPG-style dialogue boxes interspersed by point-to-point travel and accompanying events. The focus of the game (and the story) are the "Rites".
The Rites are in essence a one player 3-on-3 MOBA/Hero arena style duel.
It looks like a sportsball affair, and can be easy to dismiss as such. But the impactful character-unique abilities, the fast paced gameplay focused around "killing" the enemy heroes and pressuring the objective while the enemy is waiting to respawn. Plays much more like a MOBA in miniature.
This form of ritualized combat is surprisingly deep for such a simple concept, with almost every class archetype having a unique playstyle, and with a good amount of variety within the small skill trees, leading to even further variety within each character's role.
There's also a bunch more depth in the equippable items. Though each character can only have one item at a time, this allows the late-game or fully developed items to be rather powerful, absurdly so in some cases.
Your teamcomp also has a great deal to say in how any given match plays out.
In short, the core gameplay has a ton of depth, even if the first few matches might not display it very well.
On difficulty, the game can be a bit easy depending on your own general skill level and how quickly you grasp the game. Thankfully you can freely switch difficulty at any point in the game through the options menu, and eventually you'll unlock this game's self-challenger tools (akin to the Idols from Bastion or Limiters from Transistor) here called the Titan stars, you'll eventually be able to pick these before the start of every match, giving your enemies advantages ranging from pure extra stats, to increasing the starting health of their pyre (or decreasing the health of yours!), to instantly ressing them if they all go down at the same time.
While on the easy side it can feel a bit shallow, if you crank the difficulty up it will get really tense, just like you'd expect from a hero-arena style action game.
One of the really great things about the game is how the game interleaves the narratively focused parts of the game, and the gameplay driven parts.
You have a level up system in place, and only your highest level characters will be eligible to go free. So you will undoubtedly loose some of your most relied upon players. This, along with unused characters getting a "rested" state (or inspired in the game's own terms) earning bonus exp after sitting out a match, encourages you to switch things up every now and then.
In that small way, the gameplay naturally informs the details of the story, it becomes important to the ultimate goal of freedom who has been your most used characters in the gameplay itself. (if those two paragraphs were a bit disjointed I apolgize)
It's also a good touch that a loss doesn't lead to any form of game over and that the story continues on regardless. It's better to win of course, but in some situations, you might even decide to let your adversaries win, if only because you feel they deserve the win more than you. (It's still a good thing that they included an easy restart rite button though)
Otherwise, the story itself is rather linear, varied yet linear. There's a lot of choice in it, but 80% of it is detail work, although a lot of the conversations you make with party members can have direct benefits or drawbacks in terms of temporary (or some rare times even permanent!) stat boosts or penalties. There's a lot of potential branches in the individual character's narratives of course, some of which will depend on the outcomes of your matches, but the overall plot doesn't change much depending on your actions.
Needless to say any backstory stays the same from playthrough to playthrough :P
The most negative thing about the story though, is probably the details that go unexplained. Though there's not at all many of them,  the identities of a couple of major characters and the truth of their role is left entirely unclear in the end. As is another fairly major point in the backstory. It's not a major deal in the end (the specifics don't impact the plot at all and enough is implied that you can get a good grasp of the characters and events unspoken of, but it might nag you if you don't like those kinds of specific details left up to interpretation). So basically, nitpicks.
The game has a good playthrough variance in both the story (with a lot of branching choices and influence based on gameplay performance) and the gameplay (with a good roster of playable characters, and easy to increase difficulty for repeat playthroughs). Though it's lacking any sort of New Game+. Of course, it doesn't really need one, as any meaningful progression of stats would mess with the progression and structure of the game (unlike Bastion and Transistor you tend to cap out in both exp and items towards the end). It would still be nice to have a softer NG+ only keeping progress in your book of unlockable backstory (some of which can be easily missed if you lose some specific battles) and giving you all the Titan stars at once rather than as a slow escalation (though that would also run kind of counter to the game's theme).
There's not really much more to say. It's a solid title, very different from Supergiant's previous works in a lot of ways, but just as imaginative and with a much more fleshed out world, and a much more unique kind of combat. Featuring the same great music as ever and a wonderous and colorful artstyle to go with the wonderous myths you travel through. Though with a heavier kind of storytelling and a heavier focus on it.

I owned rainbow six siege for PS4 prior to buying it for PC so I've played a lot more hours than my playtime will show.
RB6S is a cool FPS Shooter in the vein of Counter strike and those types of games. Each character has a gimmick or trick they can use that seperates them from the other characters. For example sledge uses a hammer to smash walls and ash uses a grenade launcher to blow open walls, that kind of thing. There are now 2 seasons of characters released but you need to pay more to unlock them. I purchased the 20 dollar starter version because I've played this game lots and I already know I only use a couple operators so now I'm using my operators to unlock the rest. It's almost like a mini game for me since I've already used them all already. I go on daily to grind rep to do unlocks and it makes it more fun because it feels like I need to play to unlock all the characters. Sometimes PvP matches can be rediculous and the gimmicks are a bit wonky in some cases so I'd recommend trying to find the characters you'd like to play if you are buying this cheaper version. Getting stuck with 2 bad operators you dislike will not make the game any easier for a beginner. The player base seems a bit dead/dying and its sometimes hard to find a game but it's a fun game when you are playing. The highlights for me are destructable walls and also being able to rappel up walls is cool. You can put up barricades which are destructable so there is lots of fun to be had and the game makes you think. At the start of multiplayer rounds you throw out a little camera unit that rolls around looking for the objectives and enemies. They actually use these camera devices in real so I thought it was a neat twist, some people might not like it but I think its great. You can also use cameras to detect intruders. There is a lot of fun here and not all of it is just in the direct combat like say counter strike. You really need to pick your operator well and know what they can do to be effective. Every operator uses his own weapons so that is another factor imporant to choosing a character, which weapons they can use. Anyway for 20 dollars I'd totally recommend it because its a really fun game, maybe wait till it goes on sale if you want all the operators.

This is the third game from developer Supergiant Games, and the first game of theirs that I immidiately began playing over again upon completion. I've played all of their games at least twice, but not RIGHT after I got done with my first playthrough. I'm that engrossed with this game. The story, the characters, the gameplay, the music, the art, all of it. This game wasn't actually developed, it was crafted. It's a piece of art. An intricately woven and layered one at that. The story branches off enough to where you will get plenty of character interaction and dialouge that you didn't get the first time through, which is great. It sports BEAUTIFUL hand drawn backgrounds and characters, with fluid animations, and the effects for all the fire and the auras and everything are just straight up eye candy. I love it. In my opinion, the RItes are SUPER fun to play, the mechanics for them are rather in depth, giving you quite a bit of potential strategy and options to defeat your opponents.
I'd like to use this oppurtunity to shamelessly address some of the ridiculous criticisms I've been seeing about this game on Steam lately. I already know this is going to get me called a fanboy, which I could understand seeing that honestly, but I do think this game is a unique case that deserves some defense from some of the criticism it's been receiving. If you just flat out don't enjoy the game for whatever reason born of personal preference, that is absolutely fine. I can totally understand that. Some of the reasons for leaving a negative review I simply DON'T understand are:
It's not like Supergiant's other games - Well... yeah. That would start getting pretty stale. Transistor and Bastion were already rather similar, and I think Supergiant didn't want to get typecast as the devs that make THAT type of game specifically. It would get boring as hell. If you had done ANY research into the game beforehand or paid ANY attention to the developement process, you wouldn't be complaining.
-The Rites aren't good: Ok.... how? This is seriously a complaint I've seen a few times on the internet already, and the ONLY reason I'm even bringing it up is because seriously NOONE has been able to explain why. There's a very good reason for that. They are good. They are damn good. They are Nintendo levels of tight with the mechanics. If you "don't personally find them very fun" that's one thing, but the Rites are an objectively well put together set of gameplay mechanics. That said, the opponent A.I. can be pretty dumb on the lower difficulties. If you want the game to force you to learn all the different ways you can go about to protec and attac the Pyres, while making the opponent A.I. not kill themselves in certain arenas, I'd throw the difficulty above standard.
Too much reading: This brings it back to doing ANY research at all before purchasing a game. If you had done any, you would have known that your character is called...... wait for it.... the READER. So yeah, you'll be doing a bit of reading. This one's pretty subjective, but still, do any research whatsoever. Don't just buy a game because a certain developer made it. THAT'S being a fanboy.
-Not enough of the Rites: There's an entire versus mode where you can do nothing BUT the Rites. Null and void as far as I'm concerned.
-Basically making any definitive judgments on the game when you have .8 hrs on record.
Really the only negative I have about this game that's big enough to consider it a strike is (no spoilers) the story ends pretty abruptly when, earlier in the game, it made it seem like you were going to be doing much more than you actually end up doing. The rest are just minor gripes here and there that I'm sure can be ironed out with some patches over time.
This is, in my opinion, the best game from Supergiant so far. It's by far the most unique game I've personally ever played, and I haven't really been able to put it down since it's release.

*DISCLAIMER* I'm not a fan of the horror genre in general and I haven't played many horror games so I cannot assess the game in terms of its horror mechanics and tropes.
I've been blown away by everything in it. What is even more amazing is that this game doesn't have jump scares. I was trembling with fear at times and the horror was put in me masterfully through visuals, sound (especially sound) and story. The fear and tension were always at the back of my mind (and neck, haha), waiting to overcome me. I respectfully commend the designers for this achievement.
So I finally finished the game. I will not be changing my original review. I will just add a few notes.
If you overcome your fears, you'll find a masterfully crafted game experience - a unique and immersive atmosphere, brilliant sound design, a deep and imaginative sci-fi story that is on par with some great sci-fi works of past times, that can leave you awake at night for hours, contemplating what just transpired. Play this game preferably at night or in a dark room with
the best headphones you have.
I've read in other reviews that the monsters in the game weren't good but for me if it weren't for them, I wouldn't have enjoyed the game as much as I did. Still there are two aspects I didn't like about them. First, they could've been more developed in terms of their character. Each monster has its backstory if you are willing to look for it but it is not obvious and only if you look for it, you will find it. Second, at a certain point you get used to anticipating the next monster and generally the encounters were similar with a slight twist in each of them. However, the first point and a few surprises and unpredictable moments alleviate this issue.
The other and last problem I had with the game is a mild spoiler about the narrative in terms of its structure but I reveal nothing specific about the story.
Finally, I'd like to mention something important that I think people must know before playing this game. Although the main plotline is presented to you through dialogue and in-game cutscenes, a huge amount of the overall story or the lore is hidden, in a way, in the game world. Some things are in data logs, some - in audio logs however the rest are in the game world itself - its sounds, its visuals, the environments, object placements, etc. Some pieces are even not mentioned at all  and you have to figure them out by yourself. For me that was one of the best aspects of this game but I understand that some people may not like this at all. Just keep it in mind.
This is by far one of the best games I've played and an all-time favorite of mine. The narrative issue is there but without it the game wouldn't have been possible. Even all of its flaws cannot take away from this truly unique and amazing experience.

Pyre is a very unique experience.  There is a lot of reading involved, at times it is a bit much.  But the characters you come to know and the story that is presented through this reading... Nothing short of stellar!  The visuals and music are just as you'd expect from SGG- incredible.  There are.. frankly too many potential outcomes (albeit with relatively minor differences) to count.  This ensures that everyone can/will have their own experience.  With how I played through... it felt as if it was specifically scripted, the character reactions and emotions were just so fitting.  If all paths that can be taken provide as much character development and interested as what I did... then I am blown away. (I have no reason to suspect that this is not the case!).
The actual gameplay, as many others have states, is along the lines of a 3v3 mysic basketball.  This feels like an odd way to describe it, but I cannot think of a better way to do so.  The difficulty curve is very nice, it starts off almost too easy and then steadily rises to be quite a challenge.  Your team members will gain different abilities and have unique trinkets that they can equip.  This is yet another mechanism that ensures everyone will have a unique experience!  I personally enjoyed the story and exploration more than the actual rites.  The rites will definitely feel frustrating and unfun for some people... but the rest of the experience made the frustration extremely worth while for me!

Hook is a relatively simple puzzle at heart.  In some ways, it is closer to a maze game than a puzzle.  First you locate which pins can be safely removed at the moment, and then you find the paths that allow (only) their removal.  You repeat until all the pins are removed.
Hook is a relatively slow starter.  The first puzzle is  the menu screen itself.  New elements are added very slowly.  For the majority of the game, there is no penalty for mistakes; it is only around puzzle 30 or 40 (I forget which one) that the game puts a limit on how many times you can pull the wrong pin.  The game never limits how many times you can attempt to pull pins, which means you can take your time getting them one at a time even if several pins can be safely pulled at once.
Hook's saving grace is that it knows it is a simple hour-long distraction, and is priced as such.

I dropped a basketball on my head, my arms flew through the ceiling, I died, then the game crashed.
2/10 GOTY

WHAT I LIKED ABOUT THE GAME:
1) The grungy atmosphere, the choice of using pixel graphics, and the way you are immediately thrown into the game is a lot of fun. I hate long, bumbling tutorials that don't actually involve game play for the sake of learning, but Sheltered doesn't do that. It teaches you while you play, doesn't waste time or cut corners, and it's a great way to dive in head first. Everything, right down to the appearance of the people, shouts the word "apocalypse". Lots of survival games can drop the ball by making things to pretty to fit (such as clothing or hair), but Sheltered is not one of those games.
2) The intensity of survival is something that can be edited based on the desires of the player. There are certain traits that perform better than others, thus making survival easier. There are certain animals that are more useful and take less resources. There is the ability to change the size of the map, the chances of rain, the local factions, etc. I love being able to customize my survival, and Sheltered is one of the games that got it right with making that a choice.
3) I personally enjoyed being able to personalize my entire starting family. The only other game I've played that allowed such customization options was 'This War of Mine'.
4) Loot is randomized well enough that I never really got bored of sending people out on missions. I've played on all difficulties, and even the easiest still had a challenge or two that had me scratching my head. There is a lot of strategy to Sheltered, and because everything is randomized for each save, you are able to replay it plenty of times and never experience the same run through twice.
WHAT I DIDN'T LIKE ABOUT THE GAME:
1) Sheltered is REALLY mind numbing and eventually, it turns bland. After experiencing multiple runs of the game, you kind of experience everything there is to experience. The main goal is: survive. There's not really any story, and if there are quests presented, it's only presented to make a challenge in the game. Most of the game play is spent juggling the needs of those in the shelter and trying not to run out of damn water for expeditions. Even the few Easter Eggs I discovered were boring. Oh, and you'd be surprised at how annoying the generic "run-ins" through the Wastes are. ESPECIALLY WHEN YOUR CHARACTER RANDOMLY IS KILLED OFF. It's like punishment for not wanting to have to go through the silly transitioning screens every 10 seconds!
2) When I play a game that has very little to no plot, I expect the absence to be made up somewhere else. Whether it be through intense questing, a leveling up system, or something similar. Unfortunately, my runs of Sheltered have offered nothing to fill the void of no plot. I worked really hard to completely upgrade my shelter, but got bored halfway through and moved on to playing Stardew Valley instead because I had actual goals and quests presented to me. Of course, not everyone prefers story over upgrade-centric play. However, I am someone who was raised on RPGs and because of my personal history, I just innately prefer games with at least a basic plot to guide me.
3) Characters are expendable. The leveling up system for skills in the game is so easy, and some of the deaths that occur are so ridiculous, I just couldn't bring myself to care if I lost a survivor or two to the Wastelands. All I needed to replace them was a bookshelf, a punching bag, and a few days. Sure, you lose the gear they had, but when you get a good enough flow, you end up replacing it all immediately after the death. In games like State of Decay and This War of Mine, I was cursing the heavens each time I lost someone. In Sheltered, it was almost a game to see how many bodies I could stick in the freezer before someone got too traumatized and snapped.
4) This is a minor annoyance, but the fact that you don't find children wandering the wastes, or that you can't replace your pet should it ever kick the bucket is just silly. The kids offer no skills or benefits to the shelter, all they do is require a toy box to learn, and thus losing them / gaining them is like losing a mannequin arm. Not only that, but even when you eventually are presented the option to move, all that happens is the game gets SLIGHTLY more challenging and you STILL don't get new kids or a new pet. What a lose-lose situation.
Either way, I still like the game, and I still play it when I get bored. However, for the price of 14.99, I don't personally think it was worth it for me. I'm glad I got it on sale, otherwise I'd have returned it, no doubt. If you like games that don't really have a set plot or focuses on upgrading-goals as the general theme, it may be totally worth it for you, and I recommend trying it for yourself if you're unsure. Worst case scenario, just return it. ;)

So what's to say about Shelter? At first, based on screenshots and graphics, I expected it to be, at best, low effort bunker building simulator to appeal to the niche base of post-apocalypse fans. In a nutshell, it is. However, it's not JUST a bunker building game, it's got a surprising layer of complexity to how you can build your shelter up, not a lot of complexity, but it's much more than one may expect based on initial appearances. The game can get fairly redundant in the cycle of 'Build > Low on resources > Expedition > Return > Repeat' however, this is made up for by the relaxing OST and amusing things such as traps for hunting and the later game jukebox. This game is by no means perfect, however, considering how low my expectations for the quality of this game were, I'd rate it about a 7.5 or an 8.0 out of 10.0. 1 being horrible, 5 being average and 10 being perfection. So my rating for this game is 'very good'.
Pros:
Well designed crafting system
Varied ways to layout your shelter to your tastes
Lovely backdrops in the exploration menu
Relatively decent depth of day to day management of your bunker
Cons:
Expeditions can feel very repetetive at times (or quickly, based on how patient you are).
Shooting is bizarelly inaccurate even when you do meet the strength requirements.
Bears are a damn nuisance to fight or flee.
Sometimes it feels like it's just a clickfest with minor interaction.
Good timewaster.

It is a 3rd Person, stealth game with "Sabotage" and "Kill" missions. If you like Splinter Cell and Hitman series, this game may be right for you. But beware: it has its many flaws, but is playable as soon you fix the start crash message asking for Physx drivers. I set Ant-aliasing to "maximum" and the game now works under Win10.
My comments are based on 60% of the game so far (7 missions in 11 hours), playing with a XBOX controller for Windows.
Overall - 8 out 10
Story 10 out 10 - It is a german game based on the 2nd real mission of a French agent, Lieutenant Violette Szabó. This game follows the "Kill some nazis, sabotage and flee" approach. Story is narrated by main character briefing the mission and presenting further objectives while reaching critical checkpoints by showing some (skipable) short cutscenes. After carefull consideration, I decided to give a 10 for being inspired in real events AND I am really planning to read her biography written by her daugther, Tania Szabó:
Level design  & Graphics - 8 out 10 - For a 2009 title, they could be better, but is detailed enough to portrait the WW2 setting. Nothing special so far. At least, few maps have a few different routes to complete a mission. Best part is after reaching a checkpoint, you can go back to collect items, ammo, medkits, etc. So, game is not purely linear.
Game lenght - 6 out 10 - Missions are short and based on "infiltrate, find a key, open a locked door, find a plot item, and continue further to mission's objective. Then, get the hell out there". You can beat a mission in 45 to 90 min. The best part is that you need to be careful and think about the right tactical approach to each mission. Sometimes, you can evade all enemies, sometimes, killing is mandatory. Ammo is rare, so think twice.
Game Features - 10 out 10 - It combines splinter cell and hitman series as I have said before, AND the possibility to "level up" your character in three categories: Stealth, Morphine and Strength. For instance, you can upgrade the morphine's effect duration if you see fit.
1. You gain XP for each completed mission and collectible you may find due to exploration on the map. That means, you need to kill some nazis in most of the maps for safer exploration. However, I have noticed that some kills are not really necessary, but it will take longer to finish that map.
2. Inventory - as a standard feature, nothing special. Weapons, medkit, flashlight, and morphine (used to speed up the time for you, so a targeted enemy will not have enough reflexes to kill you, even if you go running towards him in a frontal attack. You can kill just one enemy at a time, by pressing attack buttom once you get close enough to him).
3. Mission map - very short zoomable maps, 45-90 min length each, with 3-4 checkpoints. Here is one of the most hated feature of the game I read on the players' reviews. The game forces you to think carefully before attemping a movement or an attack. Simple put: do not rush and you going to make it. Additionally, there are 'secret objectives' based on personal interests of the main character. You really need to explore the map to figure out.
4. Collectibles - just to justify your XP points. It could be used for additional XP instead. Additional XP points should be earned by completing a map with no kill, for instance, or for not triggering an alarm. For short, it could be better designed.
5. Controller support and controller customization - Additionally to Mouse and Keyboard, the game can recognizes a gamepad, AND you can change buttom layout as you see fit. IMHO, an interesting feature. I have never seen gamepad customization in any other PC game.
6. Mission briefing. The main character narrates every mission briefing with a combination of pictures and short movies to introduce you you next mission.
7. Stealth - As you enter in a shadowed zone, your silluete turns into purple, and you character becomes invisible to enemies,  similar to splinter cell series. You can turn lights off to avoid being detected. You can drag bodies to hide them.
8. Interaction. Loot corpses, open closets and lockers, insert a bomb, use an uniform as disguise (requires a closet or cabinet to change clothes), use items, use armor vest, change clothes, pick up plot items up, climb fences, change weapons, reload, pick collectibles up, open doors, peek through keyholes, crouch, run/walk, aim guns, crawl into a wall hole, turn radios on/off and whistle to lure enemies, electrify a flooded area to shock enemies, pick up, drag-to-hide bodies, push crates, jump over a gap, climb over a crate, climb a ladder, climb down, jump down a floor hole, use a flahslight, use morphine, disarm electrified fences, shoot explosive/gas barrels, use gas masks, light enemies on fire with a flare gun, perform silent lethal takedowns (my favorite part), listen to footsteps to guess enemy distance and walking path behind doors. Note: When using a german uniform, your footsteps becomes louder due to the high heels. AND as you get too close to an enemy, he will figure out and you disguise will be blown up. So, change clothes wisely whenever possible. Once disguised, there will be a 'proximity bar' indicator to warn you about. The closer (to an enemy), the smaller (the bar).
9. Weapons. Standard: Combat Knife and pistol (silenced Colt) AND rare to find: flare guns to incinerate enemy, loud german pistols, sniper rifle, and shotguns. The bad is you cannot accumulate guns. Every mission starting point you go back to basic weapons (knife and silent Colt pistol). AND ammo is scarse. Meaning, it is not a shooter game. Period.
10. Mission stats - every completed missions presents a summary of number of enemies killed out of maximum possible, collectibles found, XP earned, etc. Nothing special.
Enemy AI - 6 out 10 - The controversial part of the game. AI is dumb, but extremelly lethal and accurate. That means do not try anything rushed or stupid (like crouching or aiming a gun while disguised), otherwise you gonna be killed.
If you want to give it a try, at least buy it on sale.

I love stealth games (especially Thief and Thief 2 which have close to 1000 hours of playtime not counting the time before I bought them a second time on Steam). I have read the stories about Violette Szabo and other SOE agents. So hey, this game must be for me. Well, it turns out I was wrong.
The game is extremely linear. There is usually one way to go through, sometimes 2 or 3. Every now and then you can pick which room you want to go to first. Violette can't step over 20 cm high barbed wire or climb on ~50 cm high boxes to get over them. So forget about creativity for getting through the missions. By the time the second mission began I was getting pretty bored.
You can't save whenever you want. There are some predefined save-points. I hate that. Quite often I messed up right before the next save point and had to repeat the entire sequence again and again until I figured out how to get past a point. The clumsy controls don't help that.
But the worst part are the constant crashes. I first needed help from the forums to get the game started but since it's a sticky the problem was solved fast. But this didn't make a good first impression. Then the crashes began somewhere around the time I found the golden wine bottle. From then on my only suspense came from hoping that I would reach the next save point before the next crash. The scene right before entering the Cathedral crashed over 10 times. I stopped playing for some time because it takes any fun out of the game.
Another thing I still don't get is the stat improvements. For finding collectibles you can improve your stealth speed (haven't tried the other 2 options yet) but it is completely for nothing. Sure, she walks faster now but so do the damn soldiers. They are not speeding up Violette, they are speeding up everything.
I am now nearly 5 hours in the game of which 1.5 probably were repeating sequences thx to crashes. And I probably will not finish this game any time soon because frustration and boredom are fighting against each other. I bought the game for only 1 € but I could have gotten some chocolate instead. If would have gone fast but left me happy. This game doesn't go fast and it definitey doesn't make me happy.

I didn't think I could ever get into puzzle games until I picked this one up.
The Bejeweled franchise is similar to those typical facebook game apps (Candy Crush being a good example), where you must match identical gems next to each other by swapping them across the screen.  However, you can only swap gems that are above, below, and to the left and right of each other.  The game not only challenges your eyesight, but your strategical skills as well.
The main game can keep you entertained for a couple hours, though it offers other gamemodes if it feels too repetitive.  Some require you to work under a time limit, destroying gems to accomplish objectives, and more. You'll find that a couple gamemodes may require you to plan ahead while you play on to guarantee your success.
Obviously, the game is perfect for casual gamers and competitive players alike.  I am a little disappointed that the main game (Classic mode) usually predetermines your outcome for you.  You can find yourself reaching past level 10+, or even lose at the beginning of level 2 - all because of the gem randomizer.  A "NO MORE MOVES" announcement will pop up on the screen, which means...well, there are no more successful gem movements you can make.  This is the only way to get a game over, but it comes out of nowhere and you can't do anything about it.  There may be some kind of strategy to minimize your chances (AKA scoring as many points as possible in single turns to move to the next level), but you are going to lose randomly eventually.
Overall it's still worth a buy with the amount of content provided.  The game has an amazing HD polish, complimented by the clear sound effects.  Go ahead and give it a try!

--- The Ultimate Doom ---
Ultimate Doom was released back in -95 as the definitive Doom experience as they added episode 4, Thy Flesh Consumed, to the games standard 3 episodes. I'm unsure whether they did some behind the scenes stuff to the game itself also, it's not impossible that is the case. In any way, this is not important as this looks, smells, behaves and sweats like the original thing.
One important difference about this version is that they now let you control the Doom Guy with the WASD keys + the ARROW keys. Now this feels really weird by todays standards, but trust me when I say it's way better then the original DOS version's controls which caused serious pain in the wrists after a couple of hours gaming.
The good stuff....
- It's Doom with "better controls" and more levels. What more could you possibly want?
The bad stuff....
- They did slight changes to some levels for reasons unknown, and I like my classics like I remember them back in the days so to me this a negative thing.
- The (awesome) MIDI music sounds a little different from what I remember. The output is lower and some crackling can be heard sometimes.
- Steam overlay doesn't work.
Final verdict....
8/10 - A solid must-buy-game. 1 point removed for the minor neg stuff.

I highly recommend this game.  Yes its a bit buggy and the launch was a fiasco but it doesn't change the fact that this game is quite fun and will tide me over for the summer until some fall bangers come out.  Here's looking at you Destiny 2 ;)

So recently there's been buzz around town for a very tasty lobster dinner, "Pour L'honneur," from the local 5-star restaurant, Subioft. You go to Subioft looking to try it. There it is on the menu, right below the other recently added dish, "Chiens de Garde II" (which, by the way is an excellent entrée, I recommend that to everybody, even though the first rendition of that meal was not so good, they actually improved upon it drastically.) You order the meal and wait for it to come out. About thirty minutes later, the waiter collects it from the kitchen and brings it to you. (He seemed to have had a little trouble balancing it while he was walking it to you, but luckily didn't drop it.) He sets it on the table.
It looks amazing.
But where's the cutlery?
The waiter hands you a plastic, off-white fork that feels and looks like it's part paper or less-sturdy-than-plastic-material. He says it's all the restaurant can afford to give its customers. Wait, what? This is Lobster..? Shouldn't this warrant at least a fork AND a knife??? Metal cutlery, too, perhaps-- isn't this a 5-star restaurant?? (I mean, they don't specialize in seafood, but-- they should technically have had a lobster cracker and special utensils, but apparently this kind of behavior has become expected of Subioft???) The waiter stays silent to these questions. You confusedly shrug it off, and continue to the task at hand-- eating delicious lobster.
You go to grab your napkin and get ready to attempt to chow down with your plastic peer to pe-- I mean cutlery. You realize your napkin is a stark white piece of tissue paper. The waiter brings up a large corkboard that displays an assortment of fine napkins of assorted colors and materials. There's a label on the top of the board; "Premium Napkins." He says you can pay small amounts of money in exchange for exclusive currency called Steel used to purchase and use their premium napkins, otherwise, you'll get a tiny amount Steel earned for eating the dish, which can be used for, say, a used low-rate polyester hankerchief.
Whatever. You don't care. You just want to eat the very tasty lobster dinner. That's what you came for, what you came to eat, came to experience, came to enjoy.
So you try. Some of the experience was rather pleasant, and the dish, itself, was indeed very tasty.
Other times, your fork chipped and snapped and fragmented and broke into the meal, and you would end up tasting that plastic later, or the fork wouldn't properly grab food, or it would just fall apart in your hand. The fact that the restaurant couldn't even provide at least a knife was demeaning. The lack of a proper napkin made it messy at times, and you couldn't help but wonder if paying for a better napkin might've been worth it. Also the seasoning was a little inconsistent, sometimes it'd taste a little salty, other times... was that cheese? That definitely tasted like it. Bleu, perhaps.
In the end, it was a very tasty lobster dinner. But only when you could enjoy the meal itself, and not be bogged down by the lack of real cutlery where there definitely should be, or a proper napkin instead of being prompted to pay even more than 60$ on, say, a silk lavender napkin imported from Japan. And you couldn't help but feel bad for the chef, who clearly made great efforts into the presentation and taste of the dish itself, which would have only been truly realized had the restaurant, Subioft, made any effort to provide better services and emphasis on the quality of the things which accompanied the meal, such as the utensils or the napkins. If you had a nice napkin that came standard, a proper set of cutlery accomodating a crustacean dish, you would have, without a doubt, truly enjoyed the dish.
Later that night, you got on your computer and went on Nudle Chrome and went to Nudle Plus, where you updated your review of the restaurant Subioft, stating that the cooks must be great, but the restaurant itself was not, for it was clearly not the cook that ruined the dish you ate. When you commented about "Pour L'honneur" specifically, however, a random commenter responded,
Yeah, they had a taste test of that dish earlier this month because they had planned to add that to their menu, and we complained to them about the exact same things!!
This made you suddenly feel very uneasy and concerned for the new dish Subioft was pushing to add to their menu soon, "Terres Sauvages." You also wondered why Subioft is even considered a 5-star restaurant at all.

This is the third game from developer Supergiant Games, and the first game of theirs that I immidiately began playing over again upon completion. I've played all of their games at least twice, but not RIGHT after I got done with my first playthrough. I'm that engrossed with this game. The story, the characters, the gameplay, the music, the art, all of it. This game wasn't actually developed, it was crafted. It's a piece of art. An intricately woven and layered one at that. The story branches off enough to where you will get plenty of character interaction and dialouge that you didn't get the first time through, which is great. It sports BEAUTIFUL hand drawn backgrounds and characters, with fluid animations, and the effects for all the fire and the auras and everything are just straight up eye candy. I love it. In my opinion, the RItes are SUPER fun to play, the mechanics for them are rather in depth, giving you quite a bit of potential strategy and options to defeat your opponents.
I'd like to use this oppurtunity to shamelessly address some of the ridiculous criticisms I've been seeing about this game on Steam lately. I already know this is going to get me called a fanboy, which I could understand seeing that honestly, but I do think this game is a unique case that deserves some defense from some of the criticism it's been receiving. If you just flat out don't enjoy the game for whatever reason born of personal preference, that is absolutely fine. I can totally understand that. Some of the reasons for leaving a negative review I simply DON'T understand are:
It's not like Supergiant's other games - Well... yeah. That would start getting pretty stale. Transistor and Bastion were already rather similar, and I think Supergiant didn't want to get typecast as the devs that make THAT type of game specifically. It would get boring as hell. If you had done ANY research into the game beforehand or paid ANY attention to the developement process, you wouldn't be complaining.
-The Rites aren't good: Ok.... how? This is seriously a complaint I've seen a few times on the internet already, and the ONLY reason I'm even bringing it up is because seriously NOONE has been able to explain why. There's a very good reason for that. They are good. They are damn good. They are Nintendo levels of tight with the mechanics. If you "don't personally find them very fun" that's one thing, but the Rites are an objectively well put together set of gameplay mechanics. That said, the opponent A.I. can be pretty dumb on the lower difficulties. If you want the game to force you to learn all the different ways you can go about to protec and attac the Pyres, while making the opponent A.I. not kill themselves in certain arenas, I'd throw the difficulty above standard.
Too much reading: This brings it back to doing ANY research at all before purchasing a game. If you had done any, you would have known that your character is called...... wait for it.... the READER. So yeah, you'll be doing a bit of reading. This one's pretty subjective, but still, do any research whatsoever. Don't just buy a game because a certain developer made it. THAT'S being a fanboy.
-Not enough of the Rites: There's an entire versus mode where you can do nothing BUT the Rites. Null and void as far as I'm concerned.
-Basically making any definitive judgments on the game when you have .8 hrs on record.
Really the only negative I have about this game that's big enough to consider it a strike is (no spoilers) the story ends pretty abruptly when, earlier in the game, it made it seem like you were going to be doing much more than you actually end up doing. The rest are just minor gripes here and there that I'm sure can be ironed out with some patches over time.
This is, in my opinion, the best game from Supergiant so far. It's by far the most unique game I've personally ever played, and I haven't really been able to put it down since it's release.

Pyre is a game in which you play matches of Orb-ball in order to escape from magic Australia.
I enjoyed Pyre, and I definitely recommend it, because it works for the price.  However, I must say that as an overall experience, it might be my least favorite Supergiant game to date.
In depth review of individual categories to follow after the break, but the TLDR version is: The lore feels incredibly rich, but actual gameplay and main storyline didn't, and the soundtrack felt like the weakest of the three games.
______________________________________
Art: Rich and distinctive, when it's not being covered by dialogue boxes or particle effects. It lent itself well to the world's distinct feel, but served primarily as a background rather than something to be interacted with in most cases.
Lore: Along with the characters, easily my favorite aspect of the game. Not only was the world genuinely interesting, its history played a big part in art, gameplay, music, and main story of the game. The use of meta-text in the dialogue and the fact that you unlocked lore based on your interaction with the world and storyline made it feel very organic and immersive to learn as your character learned.
Characters: Genuinely interesting characters I could empathize with. More than once in the game I found myself trying to make decisions based on what was best for my characters, rather than any strategic benefit. You’ll even start to develop strong feelings towards some the groups you’re forced to compete against, rather than just seeing them as color coded factions.
Gameplay: Each match, in the moment, is fun and well-paced.  Over the course of the game though, the act of just playing so many similar matches back to back becomes tedious.  The game itself is aware of this, and does its best to pace the story around that weakness. The only real problem lies in the replayability.  Due to the nature of the choices you have to make in the game, it begs to be played through more than once. The prospect of replaying through another 30 or so fairly similar matches for each new play-through makes me in no hurry to do so.
Main Storyline: Its main strength is that it ties well into the world’s fantastic lore. As a plot itself though, it’s pretty predictable once it gets going and not terribly interesting. The nature of the game means that the ending feels more like an 80’s movie “Where are they now” credits montage than a satisfying ending.
Music: This one is incredibly subjective given it’s based on personal taste, but I just didn’t get nearly the same emotional impact from Pyre’s soundtrack that I did from Transistor or Bastion. And what the hell was up with that piecemeal, dull, and drawn out song over the credits? It’s still a better soundtrack than the average game, but it earns a solid “meh” in comparison to Supergiant’s previous work.

Alpha Prime is a fairly interesting game, it's a sci-fi FPS that takes elements from games such as Doom 3 and Quake 4 (Even the aesthetic of the game will remind you of them) and implements some of its own little things here and there. At first it does seem cliche and it kind of is but players will soon find that there is a very slight supernatural element to the game that affects the psyche of all the people surrounding Alpha Prime, turning them into deranged madmen and making the base's AI go nuts and the Corporation is on clean up duty. Your job is to save your friend who's stranded on Alpha Prime.
Unlike most shooters that take a more old school approach (health packs, hip fire, carrying a full arsenal, etc), on normal difficulty the enemies hit very hard which will require you to take a more tactical approach to combat situations which will encourage you to use the lean function as well as the remote control mechanic, allowing you to hack into devices such as cameras, gun turrets, doors and other electronic devices. So since that little introduction is out of the way, now I'll start the review and first I'll break it down into lists of pros and cons to make this review a lot more straight forward:
Pros:
- Fun and solid gunplay
- Nice visual effects
- Cool art style
- Graphics still look good even today
- No regenerating health, all done with medkits and health stations
- You can fire from the hip (Always good to have)
- Characters have a bit of personality to them
- Level design is pretty good
- The soundtrack is just awesome
- Enemy AI are quite intelligent, always seeking cover, trying to outsmart and outgun you whenever possible and will rush you when they have the chance
- A nice array of weapons to use (A gatling-based assault rifle is pretty awesome)
- The remote control is cool and fun to use, turning gun turrets against your foes is always fun
- Very challenging, will crush gamers who are used to modern FPS and regenerating health
Cons:
- The story could have been really cool but it was fairly bland and the cliffhanger didn't help either
- Bullet time and flamethrower are near enough useless except for the last boss
- Enemy placement can be very cheap at times making the difficulty feel very artificial
- Enemy variety is near enough non-existant, just different guys with different guns and some robots
- Weapons given to the player have pretty poor pacing, it gives you every gun near enough from the get go
- The remote control mechanic is too underutilized, you'll often forget you have it later in the game
- Voice acting can be pretty atrocious sometimes
- The one vehicle segment is just awful, it controls like crap and you can't even run enemies over with it
- Enemies have pinpoint accuracy to the point where it's unfair at times (And you can't even dodge their shots in bullet time, yes it's that useless)
- Some character models look creepy, making the main character look like a plastic action figure
- Cutscenes and dialogue segments go on for WAY too long and when you need to do something, you can't pause them but thankfully they can be skipped
- The game only runs for the best part of 4 hours, for a single player only game that will be far too short for most
The game has a lot of flaws, but it's nowhere near as incompetent like games such as The Stalin Subway and Dusk 12 (Which I did enjoy somewhat). It's not awful by any stretch, some people will love what Black Element did with the game, others may not. It really comes down to a matter of opinion and my opinion is that I really enjoyed it, as short as it was, it was a fun little sci-fi romp with lots of action, somewhat interesting characters and cool aesthetic. It's a shame the remote control was barely ever used and the game was very unbalanced at times but it was a fun game to play as the afternoon or evening just wizzes by.
I do recommend this game to those who enjoyed old school shooters or for those who will enjoy something that makes players take a more tactical approach to their combat strategy, for me the positives outweigh the negatives and since I'm a sap for obscure FPS games, there is a chance I will like it for it's quirk. For those who prefer modern FPS with highly linear levels and the overuse of iron sights and regenerating health then this really isn't for you. But if you like kickass FPS soundtracks then this game is great to have, it has some truly fantastic music in there that just gets you really pumped for the action, big kudos to the composer! I'll wrap this up now though, it's on sale now for £0.59 or your regional equivalent and that will give 4 hours of great sci-fi action. I'd say it's worth picking up.

I personall really enjoyed this game, but I cannot in good conscience recommend it. There were too many things in the game that were grating, unbalanced and unpolished.
Let's start with the positives first:
-As a fan of pixel art, I think the game looks very nice. I enjoyed seeing all the different structures in the base.
-You can customise your base at ANY TIME! Sliding around beds, freezers, traps - everything except the generator can be moved around for as long as there is no intruder in the base.
-A ton of great concepts come together in this game, with a lot of great attention to detail that sets it apart from other similar games.
-Short tutorial which teaches you the basics in seconds!
-A lot of fun little things to discover!
Unfortunately, the negatives heavily outweigh the positives:
-A ton of great concepts come together in this game, and they sadly do not get the attention to detail they deserve. The traits of your people barely seem to matter, and their stats even less. Strength is necessary for wielding weapons, and intelligence lets you craft homemade medicine, but the rest of these stats appear to have as much influence as a fart in a whirlwind.
-AI of your people is clunky. Either you are forced to 'Sims' your way through the game, or your people will sit around and only take care of their basic needs, refusing to clean the shelter, repair vital objects, and enhance their abilities.
-The user interface was terrible. For every thing you do, small menus or options pop up, making sure that every action takes at least 2-5 clicks.  Not for people with RSI sensitivity. ( There is an option to use the controller, but I did not try this. Keyboard and mouse I cannot recommend )
-Selective automation. Everything that is truly important cannot be automated, even though it becomes a chore after only a few times. You manually pick which items your people bring home. For every. single. location. And first you need to approve of them even GOING to the location, even though you planned out your route beforehand - specifically going to that place to loot it!
-Unintuitive mechanics. Did you know you can eat human flesh if you are desperate? Well, only if you have a freezer that is. Cannibalism is A-OK but eating meat that HASN'T been in a FREEZER? Not an option.
-No pause feature. Also very little in the way of managing how time passes. Either it speeds by, or it slows to a barely tolerable crawl. For people with the keyboard, I recommend you don't waste time pressing the small buttons at the top of the screen - use LEFT SHIFT instead.
-Short tutorial fails to mention handy short-cuts that can save your poor wrist from RSI.
-RNG. Though not as obnoxious as it is in other titles, this game definitely suffers from the Random Number Generator. Do you happen to need 1 hinge to make your freezer, so you can finally eat that moose that you trapped a week ago? Well tough luck. Fifteen locations discovered, and none of them had a hinge!
-Lackluster storytelling. While there are quests you can encounter and finish, doing so is rarely worth it and more of a chore than anything else. What appeared like the beginning of a story was oftentimes ... just the entire story.
-Once you find the way to survival ( start out with tons of water-things, make trap, make freezer, survive indefinitely ) the game loses all challenge and stress. Recruits for your shelter are so easy to come by that it's frankly ridiculous. I am not sure if the game ends if your family dies, because I brought one family member from start to finish with me. Guy lost both his kids and his wife, but he's fine. He has a jukebox, see?
I enjoyed this game, but I would only recommend it to people who love the genre. And even then, I'd recommend getting it on a sale. The game is fun, has potential, and a lot of small details to admire, but bad UI and bad game design make for a bothersome experience that is more like a repetitive chore than a true game.
tl;dr It's The Sims with less options and some weird survival DLC attached at the ankle.

A superb entry in the Heroes franchis, Heroes V is exactly what you expect as a heroes fan.  If you've never played Heroes before, I's like to recommend this title to you as an excellent intro to turn-based strategy gaming.
You basically run an empire, determined by the scenario setup, of a few towns, and can recruit army leaders ("heroes") to lead your forces to victory.  The heroes level up, RPG-style, as they win combat encounters and explore the map, and the towns develop in a similar fashion, as you invest in them -- producing larger, more interesting armies as they get better.
Heroes is very much a strategic title, rather than a tactical one -- its true that bad tactics can lose you a battle very easily, but good tactics can't really best a vastly superior force, because the AI simply never plays in a manner to would allow you to overrun it, in a such a manner.  You win the battle before it starts, as it were.

If you're into strategy, and high fantasy, this is a game for your library, plain and simple.

Was a Huge Fan of the first game for years, I played the second one as well when I was younger but never really appreciated it when I beat it. Now that I am older and wiser, I feel I can proudly say I love KOTOR 2....To a point.
First and Formost I am writing this review because I love The Exile and Kreia as characters, but mainly I am here to stop the belief that KOTOR 2 with the content restored mod, is far superior to KOTOR 1 because in the end, KOTOR 2 is still an incomplete game. Putting content that was cut back into the game does not complete it, it just restores some content to an originally content lacking game.
KOTOR 1 did something that 2 did not. It fleshed out your side companions more, it made them feel important. Sure, the supporting cast of characters were interesting, and not as cliche, but they were not as deep and fleshed out in the game as KOTOR 1 companions. Their plotlines, after obtaining their jedi classes reached dead ends which is a shame because I really wanted to get more into characters like Mira, Bao-Dur, and Atton. There were no loyalty missions, or sidequests pertaining to them which was a real shame. I also think the game could have done with more moments where the companions would stop and start to argue or have a conversation with one another, instead they only did that when you were already in a dialogue. Then again, Bioware is highly specialized with making characters feel more deep and complex,  and feeling more important and I don't ever see that in Obsidian's games.
I digress that it is a rushed and incomplete game. I am sure if Obsidian had more time to make the game, they would have included more of these things but alas that is not so. However this game does many things right. It really makes you think and has a much more darker atmosphere and story. The Exile, Meetra Surik is such a mystery to me and that is something that the protagonist from the first game loses once you complete the game. But the character Kreia is the real mystery, so much so that people have made hour and a half long videos looking into her character and her philosophies. The game is thought provoking, has more replayability in a sence and the combat and gameplay feels more fleshed out that the first. Classes feel much better as well and the ability to turn allies into Jedi is a plus.
All in all, KOTOR 2 is a great game, and you should play it. The restored content mod really helps to add more to the game and fix major plot holes. Just keep in mind that when speaking to characters over and over, not much new dialogue will open up no matter what you do because the game was rushed and is incomplete. Still a great game. Gets a 8/10 from me.

I'm sad that I can't recommend this game, because I was really looking forward to it and expecting something good.
On the surface, game is great - superb graphics and art style, supported by glorious symphonic OST makes for epic adventure. Problem is everything else, or rather lack of it.
Gameplay is incredibly weak and this game is yet again another case of indie game being "substance over matter". It should've been called Buttstab, because that's what you will be doing through the course of the game, just put your weapons into enemies butts. Lemmingball Z and Soldat were much more complex and those from what I remember were free. You block, you attack, there is no depth to it at all, because of AI.
The AI in this game amounts to bots from CS 1.6 or Unreal, even though that's an insult to those game. All AI will do most of the time is bunny hop and some of the mini-bosses might even run away from you, so you have to run around like an idiot through entire map, like trying to kill evil wolf, he can even go through the ground just to prolong the game. I guess I shouldn't knoc this game too much, because while playing you can clearly see game was designed for multiplayer from the start.
Story is God of War copy paste with one hilarious electrocutioner twist near the end and that part made the story actually worth it.
In single player this game fails on pretty much every field, because they tried to push it as some kind of lesser Metroid clone without understanding that what made Metroid great, like new powers. You gain new powers, but that's it, you actually rarely or never use them. And the amazing power of no need for lockpicks you get near the end of the game. Wow.
Shame that such great art direction and OST got wasted on meh game. I still thank the Gods that bundles exist, so I didn't get it full or sale price, but for a fraction of it. I advise you to wait for bundle, because it is completely not worth the money.
If you want brainless multiplayer, just get Soldat.

I have zero nostalgia for anything except for Jak II, so most of the positive reviews for older games are kinda offputting for me. It seems like most of the people who like the original DOOM are people who have been playing it since the 90s, so it's tough to gauge how this game might fare for a newcomer.
As someone who is relatively new to FPS's and PC gaming as a whole, I was floored by this game. It's stupid fun and surprisingly fast-paced; like, a lot of people say it's fast, but I always assumed that was compared to other games of its time.
No. You can run a mile a minute, You can outrun your own projectiles. It's crazy fast.
Controls are a bit of a hurdle (arrows instead of mouse to look around), but it's still managable. The inability to look up/down feels weird at first, but the auto-vertical aiming compensates nicely.
There's so much attitude, from the dificulty selection to the "Go ahead & leave. See if I care." There's a lot of nice touches and bits of polish that make the game stand out all the more. It's a great experience all around and I'd especially recommend it to anyone looking to get into older games.

Interesting Greek setting, diverse boss battles, plenty of different weapons and shields, bunch of areas to visit, difficulty is sufficient (I turned on the optional hard mode and only died two or three times, came close a couple other times), decent length (probably 8-12 hours depending on how much you explore),  Gold is useful to find throughout the game since it lets you upgrade gear and I still hadn't fully upgraded everything by game end.  Pretty good map system which points you to your possible/current objectives.  Music is good.
On the downside, combat is pretty clunky.  Game uses a semi-autoaim system that sometimes autoaims at the wrong things or simply aims poorly (hitting the ground instead of the enemy 2 feet in front of you).  Switching weapons and items mid combat can be a hassle, and you'll need to switch weapons periodically since they break after a while.  Certain weapon types can be very annoying to land hits with, as you need to land the hit exactly on the enemy.  Sometimes enemies will run directly on your character as you're swinging and since handles/shafts don't count as hits, you'll miss them quite often.  Other times enemies run away from you, and they can run backwards at the same speed you can run forwards, which makes chasing down archers and flying enemies quite annoying on occasion.
Chests could have been designed better since they almost always contain things you've already discovered anyway and may already have maxed out you inventory on.  By 1/3 of the way through the game, I could usually only get 1-2 of the 3 items out of chests and by 1/2 way through the game I was only able to grab 0-1 of the 3 items out of them.
Some aspects of the game aren't explained sufficiently, but you do learn them over time.
The combat can be annoying at times and does drag the game down a bit, but it's not bad enough to ruin the game.  Good game if you can get past the clunky combat.

This is the third game from developer Supergiant Games, and the first game of theirs that I immidiately began playing over again upon completion. I've played all of their games at least twice, but not RIGHT after I got done with my first playthrough. I'm that engrossed with this game. The story, the characters, the gameplay, the music, the art, all of it. This game wasn't actually developed, it was crafted. It's a piece of art. An intricately woven and layered one at that. The story branches off enough to where you will get plenty of character interaction and dialouge that you didn't get the first time through, which is great. It sports BEAUTIFUL hand drawn backgrounds and characters, with fluid animations, and the effects for all the fire and the auras and everything are just straight up eye candy. I love it. In my opinion, the RItes are SUPER fun to play, the mechanics for them are rather in depth, giving you quite a bit of potential strategy and options to defeat your opponents.
I'd like to use this oppurtunity to shamelessly address some of the ridiculous criticisms I've been seeing about this game on Steam lately. I already know this is going to get me called a fanboy, which I could understand seeing that honestly, but I do think this game is a unique case that deserves some defense from some of the criticism it's been receiving. If you just flat out don't enjoy the game for whatever reason born of personal preference, that is absolutely fine. I can totally understand that. Some of the reasons for leaving a negative review I simply DON'T understand are:
It's not like Supergiant's other games - Well... yeah. That would start getting pretty stale. Transistor and Bastion were already rather similar, and I think Supergiant didn't want to get typecast as the devs that make THAT type of game specifically. It would get boring as hell. If you had done ANY research into the game beforehand or paid ANY attention to the developement process, you wouldn't be complaining.
-The Rites aren't good: Ok.... how? This is seriously a complaint I've seen a few times on the internet already, and the ONLY reason I'm even bringing it up is because seriously NOONE has been able to explain why. There's a very good reason for that. They are good. They are damn good. They are Nintendo levels of tight with the mechanics. If you "don't personally find them very fun" that's one thing, but the Rites are an objectively well put together set of gameplay mechanics. That said, the opponent A.I. can be pretty dumb on the lower difficulties. Pyre is a game in which you play matches of Orb-ball in order to escape from magic Australia.
I enjoyed Pyre, and I definitely recommend it, because it works for the price.  However, I must say that as an overall experience, it might be my least favorite Supergiant game to date.
In depth review of individual categories to follow after the break, but the TLDR version is: The lore feels incredibly rich, but actual gameplay and main storyline didn't, and the soundtrack felt like the weakest of the three games.
______________________________________
Art: Rich and distinctive, when it's not being covered by dialogue boxes or particle effects. It lent itself well to the world's distinct feel, but served primarily as a background rather than something to be interacted with in most cases.
Lore: Along with the characters, easily my favorite aspect of the game. Not only was the world genuinely interesting, its history played a big part in art, gameplay, music, and main story of the game. The use of meta-text in the dialogue and the fact that you unlocked lore based on your interaction with the world and storyline made it feel very organic and immersive to learn as your character learned.
Characters: Genuinely interesting characters I could empathize with. More than once in the game I found myself trying to make decisions based on what was best for my characters, rather than any strategic benefit. You’ll even start to develop strong feelings towards some the groups you’re forced to compete against, rather than just seeing them as color coded factions.
Gameplay: Each match, in the moment, is fun and well-paced.  Over the course of the game though, the act of just playing so many similar matches back to back becomes tedious.  The game itself is aware of this, and does its best to pace the story around that weakness. The only real problem lies in the replayability.  Due to the nature of the choices you have to make in the game, it begs to be played through more than once. The prospect of replaying through another 30 or so fairly similar matches for each new play-through makes me in no hurry to do so.
Main Storyline: Its main strength is that it ties well into the world’s fantastic lore. As a plot itself though, it’s pretty predictable once it gets going and not terribly interesting. The nature of the game means that the ending feels more like an 80’s movie “Where are they now” credits montage than a satisfying ending.
Music: This one is incredibly subjective given it’s based on personal taste, but I just didn’t get nearly the same emotional impact from Pyre’s soundtrack that I did from Transistor or Bastion. And what the hell was up with that piecemeal, dull, and drawn out song over the credits? It’s still a better soundtrack than the average game, but it earns a solid “meh” in comparison to Supergiant’s previous work.

I am not sure if you noticed, but I don't play multiplayer first person shooters at all. With the exception of games like TF2 that I played a long time ago, and that was just goofing around on my computer that barely boot up. I mostly avoid it because I suck at these sorts of games. I have terrible aim, terrible reaction time, terrible eyesight, and add in a pinch of just being plain crap. So why this? And better question, if I am so bad, how can I even possibly do well and recommend this game?
Well I started playing the game because a friend told me to buy it to play with them. Everyday they would ask me to buy the $20 version of the game so I could play with them. Keep in mind this was maybe 5-6 months after the game launched, so I know it had a rough launch and was not well received. Eventually I just caved and bought it so they would not bug me anymore. I played some matches, I was understandably bad, as expected. Sarah being bad at first person shooters is not a new thing, it is just a fact of life. The game still felt really cool and tactical feeling though, so I kept with it until I unlocked some new operators to try out.
After unlocking them, I was also bad with them. I messed up bad, felt embarassed, wanting to hide in a corner and cry for embarassing myself in front of the everyone. But I stuck with it, learned, and was to a lesser degree, a useful member of the team. As long as I got whatever my operator ability was used up, I could experiment without worrying about being useless to the team. I tried things out, practiced more, got better, tried new things.
Where did that put me? Well my aim is still bad, I still miss obvious stuff, and I still cant peek a door and get someone before they get me. But what I did learn was that you can still win with better tactics, instead of always needing more skill. See, I just need an extra half-full second, if I can use spacial positioning or some other way to gain that extra reaction time, I stand a chance. With better tactics, you can usually counter many skilled players. Thats how I can get the success I have had in this game. It feels like it rewards more than just raw aiming/reaction time skill.
The game is good, and has only gotten better. Over time they have ironed out many problems the game had early on, and the new characters are always a treat to use. The only thing that has gotten worse is the community, with all the csgo kids moving over to playing Siege, but that is tolerable at the very least.
As for which game pricing option to get, the $20 one is not a bad choice to check out the game and see if you like it. If you do, you can spend $40 in the in game credits to unlock all the base game operators (thus equalling the normal game purchese price, meaning no net loss for you). It is what I did.
So in other words, I highly recommend it. Coming from someone who does not like multiplayer first person shooters, I think that is saying a lot

I really love this platformer game.  The levels are challenging but not impossible, and makes the right choice to have there be varying rewards based on how well you do, rather than make every level a pass/fail.
One of the best parts of it is that there's no real penalty for dying.  Other players can just shoot you, and you're back.  This means that I can play it with my 5 year old and 7 year old, and we all have fun.  Sure, I'm getting most of the lums, but they're having a blast, too.
I'm not as big a fan of the challenges.  They're repetitive, and I felt like I was grinding out my million lums by the end.  There's also the problem that there are so many cheaters that a platinum result in the challenges is basically impossible, so it makes it an even longer grind.
By far the biggest problem, though, is the lack of multiple saves.  I couldn't play my own game, and then start over again with my kids.  If you want to start over, you need to delete your entire save.  That means multiple people can't really have their own games.  It's a huge flaw, and something the first game didn't do.
Score: 8.5/10
