===Original unedited review===
Krobon, a depressingly little-known Japanese indie developer, along with composer Pepo and illustrator Doromizu, made one of the finest indie games I've ever played: treasure-hunting, exploratory platform game with the showmanship and over-the-top, inventive craziness of the best arcade games. Before I continue praising this game though, I'll have to make a little side-note: those expecting the interconnected worlds of traditional "Metroidvanias" might be disappointed: this game features a more streamlined, stage-based layout. Don't mistake "streamlining" for "hand-holding", though; all the hidden passages and invisible walls are for you to discover; the enemies and platforming for you to defeat, as they can and will kill you if you're not paying attention or using your skills effectively (on that note I recommend playing on Hard mode for the best experience). Krobon offers us some absolutely out-there scenarios presented in a suitably exaggerated way, including (I'll try to make this as non-spoilerish as possible by not giving away the context, though feel free to skip the paragraph if you're bothered by even the most minor of spoilers) **********dodging lasers from outer-space while using a Jojo's Bizarre Adventure-like Stand to beat up crazed Egyptian hotel employees. And you can also get drunk off your♥♥♥♥♥while doing so.***********. Yes, that is a thing that happens.
The gameplay is pretty much as good as this type of game gets; the controls are spotless, the difficulty curve is near-perfect (maybe the first Guardian boss is a LITTLE too hard given what came before, but that's a massive nitpick), the levels are well-designed and nicely varied... and perhaps best of all, the game doesn't let you ruin its challenge by allowing you to mindlessly grind. The ONLY way to build your stats in this game is by exploring the levels and finding hidden items, which is perfect for the tone of the game. The unlocking of skills and thus areas that were inaccessible in the past is gradual, yet just fast enough to make you feel like you're constantly making progress and getting stronger as you go along on your epic adventure. To avoid any hassle, though, I recommend screencapping the mini-map whenever you uncover a dead end that requires a later skill; or, if you're THAT type of player, drawing your own map using pencil and paper. Some might take issue with the car-driving stage and the somewhat trial-and-error way of collecting all the treasure by making blind jumps. Another minor gripe is the lack of a fast-travel system, which I personally would have liked; but, much like this game's other flaws, it is just that: a minor gripe that shouldn't keep you from playing this game (after all, the stage-based setup is kind of like a fast travel system of its own and the levels become easier to navigate as you unlock more skills). Another such minor gripe includes the lack of specific sliders for music and sound; there's just a simple sound volume slider and that's it.
Narratively, Rebirth does a great job for what it is; the dialogue never felt like it was wasting my time, and if YOU feel like it's wasting yours, you can always skip pretty much every cutscene, even if you haven't gone through it before. I don't recommend it, though; the presentation as a whole actually makes you feel like you're really an archeologist, exploring every nook and cranny of a strange yet often surprisingly serious cartoon world. In fact, the juxtaposition of comedic shenanigans with dramatic moments and even little nuggets of brief yet oddly-fitting sociopolitical commentary make the writing a huge treat, somewhat comparable to an Osamu Tezuka story. The translators also did a great job at making the dialogue have a natural flow to it, which is great because the character interaction is charming and often genuinely funny. The Egyptian atmosphere is nicely complemented by Pepo's tunes, which succeed at giving the game a dynamic action-adventure feeling.
Graphically, Pharaoh Rebirth would have been impressive even if it came from a team of hard-working sprite artists. However, if Krobon's own Twitter account is any indication, he's responsible for absolutely every bit of pixel art and animation in the game, with Doromizu only having the job of drawing the non-pixelated character art and portraits. As someone who's obsessively into animation, this is particularly impressive to me because this is one of *THOSE* 2D sprite-based games; the kind that, instead of simply doing its job to serve the gameplay, genuinely takes into account the principles of animation to make controlling your character and fighting enemies feel particularly lively. It's not quite on the level of games like Metal Slug 3 or Super Tempo in terms of feeling like you're playing a wonderfully made cartoon (the use of color could use some work, for example), but it's still pretty up there and Krobon is a very high-level sprite artist. The animation and believable physics (shooting tennis balls underwater makes them float to the top!) makes navigating the levels and fighting enemies feel fluid and fun.
The fact that this game has been out for so long while not being covered at all by the gaming press shows just how little hard work and clever, well-executed ideas matter in the anglosphere's indie gaming scene. Along with Krobon's inability to make connections with indie-clique darlings and journos comes the dreary number of only TWO Metacritic reviews of this game. This unfairness is why I only now decided to point out that there is a shareware, untranslated version of the game out there. Beyond the English script, it lacks the extra stage of the Steam version along with the difficulty settings (and likely other stuff; I only played a tiny bit of the shareware version), but I chose to buy this primarily to support an extremely talented underdog developer who put loads of love, care and effort into creating a charming little adventure that should not be forgotten.
Also, a little hint: there's an item you can ONLY get from right after the first boss battle by doing a specific thing over and over again. Otherwise, say goodbye to 100% completion.
===Edit upon completion===
If you spend a lot of time exploring, you might end up too powerful and the end bosses will be too easy. In order to avoid this, I recommend completing the game and THEN going out of your way to treasure-hunt.

Strawberry Vinegar is a sweet and lighthearted visual novel with yuri elements, featuring 6 endings and depending on your choices it will change the outcome of the story. Developed by ebi-hime and published by Sekai Project. The story is written by Ebi-hime, the creator of Asphyxia and The way we ALL GO.
Sakuraba Rie, aged nine, is a cynical and grumpy girl who cares little for her fellow classmates, and does not have a single friend.
That is, until a self-proclaimed demon named, Licia,  from the deepest, darkest pits of Hell suddenly appears in Rie’s kitchen and steals a tray of cookies Rie just baked! Through some “convincing” Lucia managed to get lodging in Rie’s home for 6-7 days.  “Feed me, or I’ll reap your soul!” – Licia
What will happen between these two young girls? Will friendship blossom between them, or perhaps something more darker?
That is up to the reader to decide – but rest assured, no matter what, there will lots and lots of delicious food!

Let's be honest, I don't really recommend it.
Aside things that have been well done, there are flaws that make my recommandation.
The main issue for me are controls : the game tries to reflects pro/cons of using different weapons, but instead of making some weapons better that others, it makes some weapons worst than others. As an example, adding latency to much bigger weapons also make it much more difficult to use. If in a 1vs1 combat it's ok, but when enemies are many, attacking at the same time, you just can't wait for 1 second for your axe to raise and strike, while unshielded during that time. You just take hits that reset your attack. It becomes unplayable.
Another issue during combats are the stairs : fighting in stairs is just awful. Your character climbs a stair as a priority instead of walking on the ground. When going forward or backward during a combat, to avoid a hit or to do one, it can't be a worst thing than seeing your character climbing up or down. Trying to jump off the stair to go back on ground using Jump + Down direction makes fights really irritating, while your enemy is hitting your unshielded because climbing exposes you character to enemy's hits.
I would have preferred an arcade game that allowed me more progression, rather than this fighting system that tries to be skills based (but that fails, in my opinion), with such ergonomics and controls flaws. At least I could have enjoyed the narration and though "it's ok I didn't pay this game for playing 45min".
There are other design flaws, in my opinion, like the crafting system. Why would I craft a life potion instead of picking it up as a bonus, while I can pick dozen times the ingredients to make it. It's just creating a false game mechanic, that gives no pleasure, but instead is a useless steps I would prefer to not have to do (there is nothing enjoyable in crafting it, nothing enjoyable in collecting ingredients, everything just being a non ergonomic menu navigation manipulation).
I prefer stop playing that game, I know I won't return to it. Too bad.

Strawberry Vinegar follows the story of young Sakuraba Rie, a girl who has her life upturned after a demon shows up that will reap her soul if she doesn't feed this demon food. For the next week (6 days, because weeks don't have 7 days in Hell), Licia will be living with Rie and her family, and yes - there will be lots of food.
Strawberry Vinegar is one of my favourite VN's I've read, despite how hungry it made me. The artwork is extremely charming, and the characters are very likeable. There are 6 endings to aim for in the game, and each is sure to make your mouth water with how much food you are shown. I did find some minor odd spelling issues (such as "parents" in place of "patients"), but they didn't detract from the story too much.
I highly suggest this game to anyone who loves food and/or good stories. There is some hint of female love, especially in some of the endings, but considering for the bulk of the game Rie and Licia are 9, don't expect much.
Disclaimer: I was provided a key by the publisher for review purposes.

Strawberry Vinegar is a lighthearted visual novel, with lots of mouthwatering food and fluffy scenes between two girls and family. I personally really enjoyed this visual novel with its cheerful tone! For those familiar with ebi-hime's previous works, which are generally more dark in tone, this VN may seem quite different in terms of style but I was not disappointed for sure. I'd sum this VN up as silly cuteness, food scenes making me very hungry, and fluffiness that made me melt~
Strawberry Vinegar follows the life of Rie, a young girl that is quite sarcastic, cynical, and sassy as we can see throughout the VN. (At age 9, she's read
, Adler and Kelso, 1958.) One day she finds an intruder in her house stealing her cookies, who is none other than the young demon, Licia. Through some strange circumstances Licia ends up staying with Rie's family for a week, learning about human customs and eating lots of food, described in exquisite detail, accompanied with amazing artwork by Silly Selly.
Rie's parents are a very endearing couple, and we see the four of them (Rie, Licia, Parents) interact in their daily life. Rie and Licia get to know each other better, and depending on Rie's choices during the game, there may be romantic feelings between Rie and Licia. You can even die in this game though, if you anger some other demons... Overall the story is lighthearted and gave me quite a lot of laughs, with some extra cute fluffy scenes, and made me very hungry during the food scenes.
This visual novel features 5 endings (or 6?) with multiple branching storylines - I finished one route and went for another and was pleasantly surprised that they did indeed quite branch out with lots of content I hadn't seem in the other route. Overall this isn't a very long game, about 5 hours for my first route (romance), There are quite a few extras, such as author's notes and music, as well as CGs (FOOD screenshots!)
One thing I think worth mentioning though is that the light coloured font and the also light coloured text box made it a bit difficult to read initially, so I had to take some time to get used to it and it was better after reading for some time.
I enjoyed this visual novel, between the cuteness and food, Strawberry Vinegar brought a smile to my face. For those that came to this game from Ebi-hime's previous works such as Asphyxia, just a heads up though this game is much different in tone. Ebi-hime is an excellent writer, so reading this visual novel was a pleasure and the artwork is gorgeous, perfectly bringing out the personalities of the characters. If you enjoy VNs in general, or lighthearted, cute ones in particular do check this title out.

There is a pure simplicity in the gameplay of Doom. 'Visceral' has become a buzz word in pop culture these days, a shorthand for "gritty", "violent", "intense". In describing Doom, I must reclaim the word visceral: it is something under your skin, something that plays not to the intellect, but to the hardened insctincts buried deep in our brains.
Doom is a game that taps into heart of darkness.
It is the thrill of fighting for your life every step of the way, towards a single goal: the total destruction of everything in your way. With the utmost efficiency of narrative, you push deeper and deeper into the abyssal Hellscape.
On a narrative level, Doom supplies the bare minimum necessary to be engaged. It lacks the mythos of Halo, the literary rabbit-hole of Marathon, or the cosmic transcendence of Half-Life. It is tough-guy male power fantasy distilled to its 100-proof essence. Unlike its successor, Quake, which had too little narrative in its single-player, Doom gives you some compelling reason to keep fighting.
Gameplay is fast-paced, the sound design and music still hold up. Even its sprite graphics have aged well, looking better than many 3D games of the 90s.
Doom is a must for any FPS fan. To play it in 2016 is to boil the FPS experience down to its bare essence, and to see Id Software's influence across two decades. Well worth $4.99.

Supergiant Games has made, if not the best of their current trio, another beautifully drawn, intelligently designed, heart plucking (amazing) mess of a game.
You are cast down from the Commonwealth, and in the Downside, the only way to win your freedom, is to prevent your opponents from taking theirs.
However, there's a catch. Only one of you(r party) may go free at a time. Creating what I believe to be the most emotional/difficult choices in gaming.
And what if you happen to like your opponents? What if... Just maybe what if... You want them to go free?
Each choice you make drastically impacts the end of the game, unlike some others I know, where there are only a couple endings, thsi game has more than I could think of off the top of my head. (And if you played, you would see why.)
The most contreversial thing about this game is, in my opinion, the Rites themselves. Personally, I never had a problem with them. There are many different strategies, and the use of Talismans, whcih are essentially powerups, gave neverending complexity to them. Of course, faster characters are almost always more advantageous, you get the point.
Like Supergiants former games, there are ways to... Make the game more difficult, and in turn, more rewarding.
It gets hard, let me tell you.
All in all, I had a really great first playthrough, and let me tell you, I plan on going again. The characters, the story, The Voice, (And don't even get me started on the soundtrack, Darren Korb's outdone himself again.) and, last but not least, the gameplay, all made up for an amazing experience I likely won't forget.

As I said, this game gets better daily and has a lot of cool features down the line, stick with the game through the long haul and it will improve. With all of the current drawbacks, I still love the game, keep up the good work.

Rayman Legends is a more accessible platformer than its predecessor Rayman Origins with a gradual difficulty scale, easier to find secrets, and slower paced levels.  Does this bother me, no, not really because Rayman legends is still a fun platformer with well-designed levels.
What bothers me is that the creative art design and amazing soundtrack in Rayman Origins was not passed down to its sequel.  Fortunately for Legend owners there is a large collection of Origin levels that can be earned and unlocked, which is a great bonus feature.
Remember the treasure chest speed levels from Origins?  No chests this time, but there are these speed levels that go along to a song and all of them are fun and challenging.

Last thing to note is that I have mixed feelings with the Wii-U touch screen levels where you tell the A.I. to interact with obstacles instead of a touch screen swipe motion, these levels feel a bit awkward IMO.
To sum up Rayman Legends has better pacing, level design, and more content.  Rayman Origins has a better soundtrack, artwork, and harder, faster levels.
Overall Rayman Legends is a must have game for platform gaming fans.

The angst-fueled action junkie's dream game: a first-person shooter where you're one part Scarface and one part Satan. It's goal is to make you feel like an unstoppable train of supernatural violence and it does so with sadistic glee. A mass of vaporous snakes surround the player that hack enemies to pieces, throw objects to crush or impale them, or drag them away to be executed in grisly fashion. Area-of-effects like insect swarms and black holes are showboatingly overpowered in their ability to rend apart large groups of enemies. Even the standard gunplay, which includes dual-wielded weapons, can be assisted by the Darkness in turning your gunshots into wisps of energy to reduce adversaries to soup. The environments have been simplified a great deal from the original and its stereotypical comic book plot and machismo grit are turned up way past eleven. Other action titles have tried to make you feel like a monstrous force of nature, but none of them are nearly as successful as The Darkness.

Traditional single-player FPS that mixes gunplay with the "Power of the Darkness". Obviously, as the title of the game implies, the darkness is what makes this game what it is. The two demons hanging over your shoulder mix suprisingly Very well with the gunplay aspect. Gunplay is traditional, but handled well, giving the player the choice of Dual-Weilding two different handheld weapons or sticking to one big gun (Shotgun, Assault Rifle, etc.), similar to Max Payne 3. Gameplay is fast paced and brutal, given the fact that your practicaly playing as a demon. Ripping people apart, decapitating, and even pulling someones spine out of their♥♥♥♥♥♥are all part of the disturbing yet oh-so-satisfying executions the player can bring. As far of the story goes, Its simple but gripping. Characters are interesting and are cleverly written, and the voice acting in this game is Outstanding. None of the characters feel out of place and are even humorus at appropriate times, epecially your AI companion, the Darkling. The only real problem with the game is its length. It can be completed in nearly 6-7 hours. There are relics you can collect during missions, but the secret hunting dosent add too much replayability by itself. Overall, the Darkness 2 is a very fun game and definatly not a waste of time. Definatly worth a buy during a sale or even a rent.
OVERALL
(+) Darkness/Gunplay combo works well
(+) Story, Voice acting, Characters (Johnny Powell and the Darkling are probably the best)
(+) Comic book style graphics work well for the games theme
(+) Brutality is handled well
(+) Secrets are interesting, worth finding
(+) Refreshing change of pace from other generic shooters
(-) Too Short
(-) Not much replayability
(-) Not much to do in-between missions
(-) The Ending (It hints toward a third game)
Final Score: 7.5/10

Honestly, it's taken me more than a few days to write something significant about
. It's not enough for me to say that this is a really good game, and that it's a hidden gem well-deserving of your time. I have to write something that goes above and beyond, so that you come away thinking "Wow! This is serious! I must play this game immediately!" This is the difficulty I've run into when writing about games that are really impressive. Aside from having a mediocre vocabulary, I'm too used to discussing what's wrong with games, to really explain what's right with them.
For example, let's start with the controls. When the controls are thoroughly solid, then there's actually nothing to discuss. In this game, moving the anthropomorphic rabbit around is as natural and easy as turning one's palm. The controls are so good, that you won't notice them. They're like an extension of yourself. As the game progresses, Jonathan (the rabbit) acquires new moves and abilities, and the experience continues to be perfectly seamless. Another aspect that goes un-noticed when it's handled properly is the mechanics. The hit-boxes are great, the game doesn't try your patience with cheap hits, and nothing stands out... poorly.
Oft-times with Metroidvanias, there's only so much of an incentive to explore.
strikes a good middle-ground with its plethora of collectible treasures. What makes exploration interesting is that not all of the items are helpful. Some exist solely to fill slots in your collection screen, while others can boost stats or award hidden skills. This adds another layer of mystery to the adventure. Every time you discover a hidden artifact, you gain a sense of anticipation. Whereas in most other similarly-designed games, all you have to look forward to is another heart container, or a slightly larger box to hold more daffodils. When you fight enemies in that other game, are you even using the daffodils? It's a completely meaningless collectible.
The sub-weapons in this game are not only fun to use, but they're also very helpful. While Jonathan's ears are just as deadly as any whip, the sub-weapons allow you to approach situations and bosses in different ways. Some of them can have other uses as well. There's a certain point very late in the game where you're faced with a spike pit. Over this pit is a floor, but most of the sections are false, and you'll fall to your death if you attempt to cross. The first weapon you obtain is a machine-gun... that fires tennis balls. As they bounce across the ground, they'll helpfully point out which sections of the floor are false, so you can safely pass. It reminds me of
.
These days, it seems like every indie title references classic games from the distant past. Thankfully,
sets itself apart by implementing its references in a clever manner. As far as I can tell, the least subtle reference is one of the characters having the name Belmondo. Just from playing through the game, the Konami influences are pretty clear, but you're not going to get hit over the head with them. It also helps that the character-designs are charming and have their own unique look. The soundtrack is thoroughly fantastic as well.
For the most part, the level-design is superb. Since every stage is self-contained, there isn't a need to make sure that each location connects to the others. The stages are well-designed, so that the first play-through is sufficiently enthralling. Also, you're welcome to repeat stages to find all of the hidden treasures. In many cases this is required, since the double-jump isn't available until towards the end. When repeating a previously-cleared stage, the pacing is speedy, and you can even take advantage of a few shortcuts.
But you're probably wondering what I meant when I wrote "For the most part". Well, this game has a vehicle-section. In stage 4, you have to drive a jeep. Actually, you don't drive it so much as time jumps to avoid plummeting to your death. To start things off with a positive I can say this much: It could've been a lot worse. There are visual and audio warnings when a jump is coming, and there are four checkpoints, which is pretty generous for a section that should take less than four minutes.
Still, "driving the jeep" in
is a textbook example of everything that's wrong with vehicle-sections. Several years ago, I actually wrote an opinion-piece on the subject. Looking back at it now, "driving the jeep" covers all of the bases. I played through this game on the normal level of difficulty, and I died more times on the jeep than anywhere else in the game. A sizable number of these deaths can also be attributed to the annoyingly-placed treasures throughout the stage. Also, If I want to 100% complete the game and get all of the achievements, I have to perfect my driving skills. To that I say: No thanks. All that said, the vehicle-section in this game isn't terrible, and it probably won't grind everything to a screeching halt, but I would have gladly traded this section away for a fully-featured stage.
The only other complaint I have is that you can only have one save-game at a time. I suppose this could be worked around by moving the old save-file to a different folder. I'll have to give it a shot sometime, because I'm really curious about the hard difficulty-setting.
Aside from an unfortunate vehicle-section,
is a superb game. It's a reminder that yes, even today there are great 16-bit/32-bit inspired action-platformers getting released. It's a shame I couldn't come up with anything significant to say though. What can I say? Even when I recognize quality, it's tough to put together the words that do it justice.

I've played a lot of these kinds of games. That said, for what it does this feels less like an innovative next step for Bejeweled and more like a finely tuned highly polished, ultimate version of Bejeweled. There are other games like this that are more interesting or change things up, either how it is played or by adding other features, this is as pure and perfect a match 3 game you will probably ever find.
The game is simple enough. You are presented with a grid of colored jewels that you must match three or more to clear, and as you clear them more jewels fall into the grid. Some jewels are power ups that allow you to clear a larger amount of jewels, and some can be hazards out to stop your game. Different modes offer different styles of play and different power ups. There is a really great variety of play modes presented beyond standard and Zen such as Poker; a score based variant that allows you to build points with like matched (match three yellows, to make a card and another three yellows to make a second card for a 'pair'). Quest mode is a fun but easy goal-based game. Lightning, Diamond Mine, and Ice Storm are tense and fast-paced modes meant to keep you moving. There are other modes, all basically variants of the same game with changing rules on how to win but very similar styles of play.
The controls are perfect. It is easy to mess up clicking the wrong match in a hurry but this is all user error and never the result of the game being laggy or unresponsive.
The music and sound are fine, nothing memorable, though some of the sounds seem almost like stock sound effects which can give this game a cheap feeling while playing (the lightning sound, for example, sounds like a cheap cartoon sound effect).
Earning Badges adds a little incentive to play further, though a few of them require grinding, which is a negative in my book. Poker is especially bad about this.
If you enjoy Bejeweled or match 3 you pretty much can't go wrong here.

My internet is about as fast as death by Gangrene, so I'll write another game review. Woohoo!
I only played a little of the base game which is still a solid bit of fun (I have about 12 hours in the game). However, in order to get max enjoyment I reccommend installing the Brutal Doom mod. It takes the game to a higher level of ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.
The gameplay is quick, challenging (I played Super Bad Difficulty), and brutal. Every weapon feels like it packs a HEAVY punch; the good ole' shotgun might be one of my favorite weapons in gaming. The enemies explode like someone packed C4 in a 10 gallon bucket of blood. Sometimes you'll blow half their body off, and they'll wail in agony just before you finish em off with a chainsaw (I'm killing sprites from 1995, I'm not a psycho). Because the combat with this mod is so satisfying I never got bored of killing the same enemy types over and over again.
The 80's thrash metal choice of music also fits the game well. There's a surprising number of tracks that were put into the game, something that might easily be overlooked by someone just tearing through this game. I appreciate it when a game has an appropriate soundtrack that enhances your experience. If you don't like the music in the base game then there are several mods that can be installed.
The level design is also excellent, especially in the first two chapters of the game. I like that I had to search around for secret items in order to keep my health, armor, and ammo stockpools high enough to survive. What makes the level design impressive is that these items are usually spaced out in such a way that keeps the challenge high but not impossible. It's a very hard thing to do when you think about it; something that modern day fps designers don't have to worry about. While I like the maze design of the maps I will call it a double edged sword. If you overlook anything in these complex levels during the chaotic combat, say a door switch, you might not be able to advance. You'll have to trek on back through the level to find that button, and it can take a fairly long time (especially when you consider the pace of the game).
Lastly, the Brutal Doom mod allows for a fair amount of gameplay customization. You play how you want to play. I haven't  looked into many other mods for the game yet, but there are plenty out there that'll keep me coming back to this classic.
Overall, the game is a hell of a lot of fun. It belongs in any fps fan's library. I may have written a long review for a $5 game (cheap af btw), but hey I wanted to say why this game kicks so much♥♥♥♥♥

After playing for a little (and watching some of my friends play), I can say that Friday the 13th is, for sure, worth checking out. Although the game has some issues with dropping players into servers our of their region. While it's cool to see Jason rubberband like you're watching some glitched VHS tape, you'll mostly be annoyed when you're suddenly stabbed from a mile away. However, games will usually be smooth-sailing with really tense and spooky, complete with that great 80s-as-hell atmosphere!
But there are glitches and a lot of them really break the fun. At the time of this writing, the devs have fixed quite a number already, such as trying to get through a window as a Counselor while being hit by Jason, which cancels out the climbing animation and leaves you clipped through the window frame, unable to move while Jason clears your head from your neck. The devs fixed this in, essentially, the second patch, along with a few other exploits and gamebreaking bugs, so, they're quick atleast!
Many players cite the "lack of maps" to be a downside, keep in mind that the game is ultimately about the Curse of Crystal Lake from Part I, II, and III, centering around Camp Crystal Lake. Personally, I feel that it adds more to the isolated atmosphere than, say, running around a Manhattan city-block. However, I think some more randomized layouts for the camp, as items and objectives are already put in random spots, each game.
I feel the game is definitely worth playing. Although riddled with more bugs than Jason could shake a harpoon at, the devs are cracking down on the more awful exploits and animation bugs while staying incredibly faithful to the movies!

A look at Ubisoft's own forums and other sources will show you just how common this problem is.  I meet the requirements, even set everything to low, and yet the game will not work.
In addition, the server problems extend to the single player of the game.  If there is an error, you can be kicked out of the single player experience.  How is this possible?  Why is this acceptable?  For others like myself, the "game" is now a 60+$ digital paperweight that breaks more with every "patch".
This is not a matter of any so called balance.  This is not about the matchmaking system, though that itself is a whole other terrible issue.  This is about how the game itself is fundamentally broken.  I cannot recommend this game at all.  While it may be fun, the amount of time you will spend not actually playing the game and praying you can work through the issues soils the experience.  Ubisoft has a reputation for releasing broken and unfinished games, and it seems that this is yet another "fine in concept, dead on execution" product.
While I am unable to get a refund for this, I am hoping that this review adds some insight into the numerous others.  Do not throw away your money, the issues are not exaggerated.

To start this review off, I've decided to begin with the negative points of the game.
- It is Early Access and so far from completion that core updates are almost painful at times. But come on people, the game states that it is Early Access, so you should know what you are getting into: bugs, bugs, bugs, and more bugs.
- Unbalanced game play. As some one who has managed to reach top tier for both herbivores and predators, I can safely say that game play is heavily leaning towards the carnivores. I'll explain why later, but this makes life difficult for those who just want to play a passive herbivore.
- Toxic Community. Not something I thought I would have to warn interested parties about, but there it is. Between people who are screaming about things they shouldn't be, anti-developer parties, herbivore and predator extremists, people who know nothing about wildlife and use it as their arguement anyway, and general trolls; The Isle suffers from a very poisonous communtity.
Those three things are what make The Isle something to avoid until it is a little more put together.
On to the positives.
+ Beautiful Graphics. Even people who are crowing about wanting their money back should be able to agree that The Isle has fantastic art and graphics for the budget currently available to Dondi and his team. I got this game back when there a total of seven dinosaurs to play and even then I found the game to be gorgeous. It has only improved since then.
+ YOU CAN PLAY AS A DINOSAUR. Do I really need to say more?
+ Even in its unfinished state, The Isle is showing true promise as a hard core survival game.
+ Generally a very neutral in game community. Sensing some contradiction? Well, like any community of a multiplayer game, the community is both the low and high of the game. Herbivores usually are few enough in number that ANY fellow herbivore is a welcome sight and mixed herds are common. Predators who play a more naturalistic game - hunting only when at half hunger or lower - or have decided to carebear are often kind enough to let herbivores get a drink from a lake.
+ Many promising and interesting features are yet to come. From nesting, to humans, to life cycles, to natural distasters and mutant strains (carnivores only as far as I know,) The Isle is certainly going to be a game in which each session is filled with delightful uncertainty and chance as the player strives to survive as their choosen or earned species.
Now then, for the chatter.
As I stated earlier, the game seems to be leaning heavily towards carnivores. Naturally, they do the most damage and bleed, but they also out number herbivores in playable species. As far as I know, carnivores are going to be the only ones that recieve mutant strains while herbivores do not get that extra evolutionary kick. As new carnivores are added, more people abandon the herbivore ranks to test out this creature, leading to a surge in carnivore numbers. Many carnivores are also fairly impossible to kill for an herbivore and any attacks herbivores have do little to ward off a swarm of adult rexes. As it stands, the only really buffer against predators that the herbivores will have are the AI - which are currently in the works, but not fully implemented.
Despite unbalanced gameplay, obvious Early Access problems, and a community that is crying for sandbox mode to return - the progression system is meant to take time, yes, but no one said that you have to play for six hours straight when safelogging allows you to leave andcome back without losing points or your current species - I would still recommend this game to people.
It has a lot of promise despite its current flaws and buying it now at its current price with all of those flaws will probably be a better deal then waiting for the game to be completed and watching the price jump to something a little less affordable.
So be patient and just enjoy what you can! IT WILL GET BETTER!

While the concept has been seen and heard of before, it goes without saying that the premise of this game is intriguing if you're even the least interested in the survival genre of games. On this game's steam page, you're presented with a lot of good-looking images filled with atmosphere and promise of a unique and immersive experience.
But don't... PLEASE don't let yourself be fooled. This is far from an immersive, or even playable, experience. The game is fully released, with no mention of Early Access or Beta, but after playing it for a while one could easily mistake it for still being something more akin to PRE-ALPHA! The game is filled with annoying bugs and design decisions; World objects not having colliders, other objects having too large colliders, game freezing when loading up the server list, weapons not working even though the animation plays, really, REALLY bad hit detection/hit feedback from shooting/hitting enemies... the list goes on and on and on and on.
Oh, I did mention bad design decisions? Well here you go - Options when looking for servers not being saved, safe zones (where you trade and bank your items) being invaded without warning (OK: there's a server message saying there WILL be an invasion, but it doesn't tell you where) so if you're unlucky, you'll get flooded with monsters while you're quietly trading gear and food. Certain, unprepared death with no chance of escape what-so-ever because SUDDENLY COLLISION DETECTION WORKS! Hallelujah!
Also, the animations really suck. And I mean they REALLY suck. At least it looks hilarious, giving you SOME form of entertainment.
No, this game... this game I would not, in any form or way, in any life or in any state, recommend. It's somewhat good-looking, sometimes. It has got potential, that much I can give it, but the execution of it is so poorly done and so poorly optimized that even the mere pricetag of 13,99€ (which is what I bought it for) is too high of a money-waste. We, as customers, are paying for a product that is supposed to be finished and in it's full, playable state... but this game, once again, IS NOT.
I will revisit this game in the future (not likely), and hopefully it has been fixed and turned into the full-fledged realization of the awesome concept and premise it builds upon, and the game I expected to play when I purchased it. Until then, please do not lie to your consumers. Be honest, tell them clearly and visibly that this game still is in development, and you will get so much more out of it in the long run.
That's all from me, thank you for reading. And whatever you do - DON'T BUY THIS SO CALLED GAME.

I have to say, this is a pretty inspired platformer. The controls are simple, power-ups are few, but instead you get treated to some seriously well designed environments. The daily and weekly challenges are a testament to how much gameplay variety the game has. There are enough background touches that replaying a level a few times, you'll notice things that you missed the first time through. The musical stages are a treat for the eyes, and a nice homage to the early auto-play ROM hacks (i.e. SMW Kumikyoku) which would do the same thing. (though you need to jump and fire to the beat, of course)
You don't have a lives counter. When you die, you just start back at some arbitrary checkpoint. You can also just opt to restart at the last checkpoint via the pause menu if you messed up getting some collectible. (lums or teensies) Challenge purists may scoff at this feature but anti-frustration features such as these are long overdue. Some players go for utter perfection and they can still impose that challenge on themselves. Those of us who'd rather not endure dozens of repeats of an entire stage for one difficult section will have things the way they are. Not to mention, anti-frustration features are much more kid friendly. Finally, Ubisoft cycles through challenges every day where you can compete with the world. They have you covered, though they admittedly do a miserable job at managing the hackers.
The game is fairly non-linear, with paths opening up as you collect more teensies and lucky tickets.  Teensies make more standard stages available, and tickets (eventually) open up more of the "Back to Origins" stages.
90% of what I _didn't_ like about this game can be summed up in one word: UPlay. The fact that they're using steam as a conduit to push their redundant DRM system which significantly adds to the startup time is appalling. One thing you better not do is check the box that says "don't tell me again" when you close the window with your key. You won't have the steam overlay available to get it again when it's time to enter the key again, many minutes later. I almost botched my install this way...luckily I hadn't copied something else into my clipboard. This experience alone almost caused me to knee-jerk a negative review in...lucky for them, the game is extremely good.
The rest of what I found irritating were some of the pop-ups after a level. One made it look like an option but literally forced me to stop what I was doing and go play an invasion level. I also kept getting annoying popups to use the tickets even though I'd already responded to one such popup. It's my own damn prerogative if I want to use them all at once. I also don't like the fact that unlocking levels is somewhat RNG based, but I'm guessing that they had the sense to heavily influence the "randomness" of unlocking said levels.
All in all, I guess I recommend it. Hopefully someday Ubisoft will realize they're alienating gamers with their DRM, and...yeah, I'm sticking with Steam. Thanks. That said, the game itself is worth the annoyance.

Humans will spawn in as just about as useless as a dinosaur unless it finds loot, people to cooperate with and more. In this game, If you progress all the way up to the best dinosaur, but you die. You start over as the smallest possible dinosaur again.
In this game you (will, all is not implemented yet) have to look out for volcanos, floods, drought, storms, bigger animals and better players, starvasion, dehydration and much more just for a taste in the game. As a herbivore dinosaur cooperation is the key, same for most carnivores and all humans and tribes.

There are also a lot of negative reviews pointing out toxicity on behalf of the devs and the community... Yes Dondi can seem brash, harsh or even an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but to tell you the truth.. so what. He's not a PR rep, he's not a sales person. Hes a software dev and thats what hes doing.. hes makeing the game. He is honest and sometimes its brutal but he is nothing if not honest and transparent with things he is able to share with the community. When you decide you want to make a game one of the first things you do is make whats called a Game design document. This is a a living roadmap of concepts, methods, ideas and the like. You outline EVERYTHING in the game from beginning to end. Scroll through some of the negative reviews and you will see lots of people upset at the devs for doing things a certain way or adding something when there are still bugs or removing something that they liked. What these people fail to understand is.. ITS A PROCESS and they are doing things in accordance with their roadmap. Some suggestions might be added if they would be a good addition but most ideas submitted via the community wont work or will be implemented in the future.
TLDR: Dont assume you are entitled to anything. Understand what your buying into and take the devs and community with a grain of salt.
Now onto the good stuff!
This game is hands down the best Dinosaur game ive ever played. If you have any interest in Dinosaurs or survival titles then you will enjoy this game. The amount of content that is slated to be added to this game is staggering and really exciting.
Who hasnt wanted to play a game where you were a Raptor or Allosaurus stalking your prey across a giant landscape. Who hasn't wanted to be a giant T-rex crashing through the forest, bursting into a clearing and taking down a Stegosaurus with a thunderous roar. And eventually you can be a member of a tribe, vicious cannibal or modern human trying to eek out an existance on a harsh and unforgiving island.
A word of caution however, this game is unforgiving. Survival is brutal and hardcore. Currently it takes hours of gameplay to reach the higher tier dinosaurs (this is expected to take EVEN LOGNER in the future) and when you die (i didnt say if because it WILL happen) you start all the way back at the bottom of the ladder.
If you can handle bugs, game changes and updates, an ever increasing difficulty level and above all if you love dinosaurs and/or survival games (and you dont have thin skin) then you will REALLY enjoy this game.

Traditional single-player FPS that mixes gunplay with the "Power of the Darkness". Obviously, as the title of the game implies, the darkness is what makes this game what it is. The two demons hanging over your shoulder mix suprisingly Very well with the gunplay aspect. Gunplay is traditional, but handled well, giving the player the choice of Dual-Weilding two different handheld weapons or sticking to one big gun (Shotgun, Assault Rifle, etc.), similar to Max Payne 3. Gameplay is fast paced and brutal, given the fact that your practicaly playing as a demon. Ripping people apart, decapitating, and even pulling someones spine out of their♥♥♥♥♥♥are all part of the disturbing yet oh-so-satisfying executions the player can bring. As far of the story goes, Its simple but gripping. Characters are interesting and are cleverly written, and the voice acting in this game is Outstanding. None of the characters feel out of place and are even humorus at appropriate times, epecially your AI companion, the Darkling. The only real problem with the game is its length. It can be completed in nearly 6-7 hours. There are relics you can collect during missions, but the secret hunting dosent add too much replayability by itself. Overall, the Darkness 2 is a very fun game and definatly not a waste of time. Definatly worth a buy during a sale or even a rent.
OVERALL
(+) Darkness/Gunplay combo works well
(+) Story, Voice acting, Characters (Johnny Powell and the Darkling are probably the best)
(+) Comic book style graphics work well for the games theme
(+) Brutality is handled well
(+) Secrets are interesting, worth finding
(+) Refreshing change of pace from other generic shooters
(-) Too Short
(-) Not much replayability
(-) Not much to do in-between missions
(-) The Ending (It hints toward a third game)
Final Score: 7.5/10

Part Star Wars  movie and part well-rounded RPG.  Loved it.  If you've played the Mass Effect series you'll notice the style similarities.
There are a ton of voiced dialogs and cutscenes in the game, giving it that movie-like feel.  But most of it is interactive, and there is where it shines as an RPG, because your dialog choices make a difference - not only to the gameplay but also to your character.  And, of course, to round out the RPG side: attributes, skills, feats, force powers, and equipment.  There is even a crafting system.
The story was great, and the writing in general was pretty good.  The voice acting was pretty good overall, though some of the characters were a bit weak.  I think it all came together pretty well for an immersive experience.
The character and equipment management was very flexible.  I spent plenty of time arranging equipment and upgrades for my character and my allied NPCs while coordinating skills and attribute increases.  That's fun for me, I guess some folks won't care that much.
You can get up to ten NPCs in your group although you can only take two of them with you when you leave your ship - but most of the time you can swap them on the fly outside of the ship.  Sometimes you can't swap, sometimes you are forced to take a specific character, sometimes you can't take anyone, and sometimes you have to play one of the NPCs as the leader!
There were some hiccups on the technical side, although fairly minor.  Like standing right in front of a container and you can't open it until you move two steps to either side.  Or using a force power in combat and queuing attacks afterward and then the queue self-clears after you finish using the power.  Or setting your target in combat but when your character tries to run over there to attack, he gets partially blocked by enemies (or allies) on the right side (for example) and instead of going around the left side he keeps trying to run through the right side.
The thing that will probably drive most people nuts is the movement control.  WASD on the keyboard (I think I remapped to A and D from other keys...) moved your character in that direction without changing the view on the screen.  So if you're pressing S, your character will be moving forward but like he's trying to get out of the screen.  To actually turn while moving you have to swing the mouse all the way to the edges of the screen.  I.E. the keys select the character's direction of movement while the mouse selects the "forward" view on the screen.  It takes some getting used to and will probably still irk you at the end of the story, but I don't think it took away from my enjoyment of the game.
And, of course, the graphics are dated.  That's to be expected, the game is 12+ years old.  Still, the cutscenes were rather pixelated even for 2005....
Overall, a great experience.  You get lightsabers, you get Jedi, you get Sith, and AFAIK the story doesn't mess with Star Wars canon since it's set 1000 years (I think) before the movies.

Rarely do games I play changed my outlook on life. SOMA is one of those few games. I now lie awake wondering whether or not I'm in a simulation for at least an hour every night before I go to sleep.
This game may not be very fun or extremely scary at times, but boy does the philosophy get to you. I cannot recommend it for everyone and it is certainly quite taxing on your thoughts, but I really enjoyed it.
The pacing is excellent, the level design frankly incredible (I love underwater stuff) and the puzzles are moderately hard, so as to not hinder progress. The payoff at the end is really emotional, and there are many, many moments when you think to yourself "What the ♥♥♥♥ am I anymore?".
There is some serious moral ambiguity and the game neither punishes nor encourages either option. This I like because you actually consider yourself what goes on.
I'm no fan of horror games (and as such I went wuss mode) but this was doable. The monsters are incredibly scary, although often beautiful.
It's only 10 hours long, and its a little bit expensive but I would say the game is worth it.
Right now its $12 on Humble Bundle Monthly, so I would strongly suggest you go buy it!

Alpha Prime (Released: 7 Nov 2007, Acquired: 23 Jan 2014)
Given that I got the game in 2014 (7 YEARS after release), this game still has much kick being put into it. I wouldn't go into the plot since steam already has it.
As an overview, I am going to say that this game has a feel of an old school shooter. Health do not regenerate and health packs are needed, replenishing your oxygen supply is also in order out in martian soil. One is able to carry around 7-8 weapons, going around getting creative on how you want to kill your next enemy. Oh, and sometimes out in martian environment, you get to drive a jeep of some sort. Graphics are as that of the 2000s, not great but bearable, not bad for a 2007 game, but we all seen better. The sound wise, loops and loops of action music played through when you are dealing with enemies, voice acting is OK, although sometimes it can be quite laughable.
Next I am going to list the Pros and the Cons of this game.
old school shooter
challenging (due many factors)
explorable environments and multiple entry points and ways to begin a gunfight
get to play with a lot of weapons
intriguing storyline
no gore (if you do not like gore)
overpowered enemies (contributes to it being challenging)
lack of health packs lying around (you need them due to OP enemies and this contributes to it being challenging)
repetitive gameplay (explore, shoot people, find important plot points, shoot more people!)
linear gameplay (kind of expected in a 2000's game)
loopy music (can  get on your nerves)
no gore (if you LOVE gore)
In conclusion, I would not recommend this game in the current age, although if you are one of those people that would fancy yourself a challenge or you are into that kind of old school shooter style. If you want a relaxing game you can shoot people in the face without really worrying about health, this game is totally not for you.
I may have left out a few pointers here and there, would love some comments and feedback on my reviews so improvements are in order.

Pharaoh Rebirth+ takes the classic Japanese action/platform games from the 16/32-bit era and adds a "metroidvania" flair to it.
The player takes control of Jonathan Banfield, an archaeologist that was cursed and turned into a silly rabbit.
I stumbled upon this game just a few weeks before release and I was baffled by the overall lack of publicity and awareness of its existence. It's really a shame because there's so much care put into this work that might get overshadowed by tons of pointless "retro" platformers which come out every day.
Mechanics-wise, the game is pretty solid. There are various moves that can be executed from the start and others to be unlocked. Overall, combat works as intended and every enemy or boss has a dinstinct pattern that often intersects nicely with the level layouts.
Player progression is not based on elements borrowed from RPG's like experience points or equipment, but instead rewards exploring and collecting the different, unique treasures scattered through the ruins and temples of Egypt.
Instead of presenting itself with one, massive area that blocks your progress whenever you don't possess the right ability to get through, the game has a standard, stage-based structure. This helps in limiting both the backtracking factor and the typical "fake sense of freedom" of the genre.
I found the level design to be quite clever, as it encourages exploration by showing the player unaccessible routes right from the start, but never requires to backtrack to a previous stage to get to the next. This means freedom of choosing  to get on with the story OR to go back and replay a chapter to get all the extra stuff which could come in handy, without being forced to revisit some old areas to get a mandatory powerup.
The classic stage-based structure also makes it easier to carry out more action-oriented set pieces, like a helicopter pursuit or a mine car ride.
Technically speaking, Pharaoh Rebirth+ looks and sounds great. The high-res (640x480) nicely crafted and animated pixel art is matched by an upbeat, memorable soundrack which features an obvious Egyptian vibe. However, digitally painted character portraits that show up during radio chatter fall a bit short, as they look detached from the overall style and don't really match its quality.
I recommend playing the game using its original 4:3 ratio, as stretching 2D art is a crime, especially when it's done so well.
As of today, screen resolution selection and VSync have been fixed, so I don't have anything else to report at this time.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
cinnamon
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy

I am going to say upfront that this game needs some work before I can recommend it but issues aside it is an interesting title and I hope that the kinks get ironed out eventually. I wouldn't pay fifteen dollars for it as is, but on sale or with fixes it would be worth it I think.
Some issues of note in no particular order:
~Character creation, though limited, is fairly standard. Stats can be selected based on templates instead of a point-buy system which streamlines things but perhaps this goes too far? I'd say keep the templates but allow a point-buy system alongside it as a 'custom' template. As for traits, the positive ones are all useful in their own way but it feels like only a few of them are essential while the bad ones are randomly selected and hidden during creation. One playthrough saw me with two pessimists, let's just say that was not a happy family and leave it at that. I think a point-buy system would work well here too, a character gets three or four points to spend with positive traits costing points while negative traits give some back, or even have each trait have positives and negatives, so maybe someone who crafts/repairs faster tends to be more wasteful while doing so or someone who walks faster while exploring tends to eat more. I would like to see additional options in character creation. For instance, the option to start with fewer people, or even just go it alone. Maybe some relationship options instead of being two parents with their two children. Maybe some more age options as well, the ability to have elderly or teens/infants along for the ride. I suppose you could just head-canon it as you play, kinda what I do anyway, but it would be a nice base feature I think.
~Inventory is a huge issue for me as I greatly dislike a slot-based inventory system mostly because a few nails or some medication shouldn't take up the same 'space' as bags of cement to use a game-relevant comparison. This is true for the shelter inventory as well as expedition inventory. Also, it seems that a character's strength has nothing to do with inventory capacity. While this doesn't hurt my high-perception/low-strength character in exploring, it also means that I have no reason to send the strong person out since they carry just as much but don't have the same scav results. I could, of course, send the two together but they don't contribute the same to the expedition's inventory size it seems while doubling its water consumption (or at least close to it). One person can carry six things that aren't equipped while two people can only carry eight I think it was. It certainly wasn't twelve slots, even with both having plastic bags equipped (+2 inventory slots). Speaking of equipment, why can't someone equip something they find while exploring? A character has an open bag slot but can't equip a bag they find while scavving? Same with a weapon? "I found this neat thing I can defend myself with but I'll just leave it in my pockets until I get home and hope I don't meet anyone who wants to take my stuff..."
~Also on inventory, I am finding that items being transferred from an expedition inventory to the shelter inventory are simply disappearing and this was the main purpose of writing a review in the first place. Twice in one playthrough I had cement or its ingredients fail to transfer and in the next playthrough, it was food. That's all I've noticed but I doubt it's all that failed and for a game that hinges on resource collection and management, this is almost game-breaking. Even if it's not very often that's still wasted resources not just to collect the stuff that disappeared but also to deal with any injury or illness due to the expedition and with an inventory size of six to eight, losing two items to the nether is rather costly.
~When characters die in the shelter, their corpse will be left where it fell until you bury them (which requires resources so no shallow, unmarked graves in this wasteland) all the while everyone complains about it. You can 'harvest' them of course unless you don't have a freezer in which case you're SOL.
~It seems to me that some of the stats don't make sense. An example is that intelligence affects recruitment chance instead of charisma and without training (which is gained through trial and error dealings with NPCs) it isn't really possible to have one person who is all-around good with people.
~Lastly, the trading. You only get to trade once and you can only have five items up for trade. I imagine this is to keep you from simply trading nails back and forth over and over again and cheating XP so I understand but it's still too limited. Which reminds me, I love that it seems like trade value is honored both ways and instead of the NPC getting a huge markup you trade as equals. I think this is the first game I've played that featured an equal barter system like that.
~Okay, one more thing but it is the last, I promise. In the game's description, we are told that this is a deep and emotional game. Where is the emotion? Last playthrough dad was in the shelter with little Suzie while everyone else was out exploring. I got a notification that she had radiation sickness but it's okay because mom is coming back with some rad-x, er, whatever it is in this game. No joke, the kid keeled over just moments before the expedition returned. This caused the little girl's father to take some 'trauma' damage sure, but there was zero reaction. They were standing right next to each other after having just eaten and nothing... Where's the emotion?! I was unhappy because 'damn we almost made it' and now I'm down my charismatic trading person but what about him? He watched his little girl die (and she died pretty good, classic drop to the knees and then fall backward in a heap) but no reaction whatsoever. No journal entry either. When some random person joins up, I get an entry about how we're sure they'll fit in well and we're happy to have more help (this person then loots the storage and leaves while everyone just stands around, they also took a hammer to my air filter topside, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) but I get no entry when someone dies?
Anyway, an interesting concept that could end up being a great game but it needs work first. Overall I would say that this title is worth a look, especially if it's on sale like my copy was, and once the bugs are ironed out it would be fine even at full price. Although, even at full price its the same cost as a theater ticket and a small soda, or popcorn. No, you gotta pick one because you can't have both for fifteen bucks, not to mention you don't have the inventory space. Don't eye the candy, that costs more than the rest of it. Oh, you wanted a large popcorn? Do you even finish a large by the end of the movie? No? You know what, just skip the concessions and save five bucks, that's a third of the price of the game right there.

After playing for a little (and watching some of my friends play), I can say that Friday the 13th is, for sure, worth checking out. Although the game has some issues with dropping players into servers our of their region. While it's cool to see Jason rubberband like you're watching some glitched VHS tape, you'll mostly be annoyed when you're suddenly stabbed from a mile away. However, games will usually be smooth-sailing with really tense and spooky, complete with that great 80s-as-hell atmosphere!
But there are glitches and a lot of them really break the fun. At the time of this writing, the devs have fixed quite a number already, such as trying to get through a window as a Counselor while being hit by Jason, which cancels out the climbing animation and leaves you clipped through the window frame, unable to move while Jason clears your head from your neck. The devs fixed this in, essentially, the second patch, along with a few other exploits and gamebreaking bugs, so, they're quick atleast!
Many players cite the "lack of maps" to be a downside, keep in mind that the game is ultimately about the Curse of Crystal Lake from Part I, II, and III, centering around Camp Crystal Lake. Personally, I feel that it adds more to the isolated atmosphere than, say, running around a Manhattan city-block. However, I think some more randomized layouts for the camp, as items and objectives are already put in random spots, each game.
I feel the game is definitely worth playing. Although riddled with more bugs than Jason could shake a harpoon at, the devs are cracking down on the more awful exploits and animation bugs while staying incredibly faithful to the movies!

Like "This War of Mine" but without the dark colors.
The game is still highly focusedon surviving as long as you possible can.  You controll 4 characters at the start that you can customize as you with in apperance, clothing, and skills.  And you can even gain a pet.  The crafting system is deep as you need many more items than you think (Besides just parts, wood, and metal).  You need to pay attention to alot of things like your generator to make sure your oxygen and water filters work and making sure you have enough water to bath in, granted that you have toilers and showers to handle needs.  Combat in the wasteland is turn based as you have certain actions for certain weapons.  Usually you have a melee attack, a ranged attack (If you have guns), a defend option, and a subdue which will take you enemy down in one hit, but has the chance of either being blocked or resisted.  Long story short, the mechiacs are pretty fun for those that like deep survival and doesnt take long to get used to.  If you like survival games that are deep but still fun, play this. Quite a fun Disaster-Survival-Game. Once you figure out the basic tricks of survival, it's not that hard anymore though. later game mainly consists of tracking down rare materials you have had problems finding for a while, leaving behind the stuff you already have tons of.
The occasional running into gangs that happens more often over time does kill off your team-members occasionally, but does not really add to difficulty, since the only way to beat them is hoping for the chance of a first hit and throwing a grenade at them.
Even though it's a complete game, it never looses the feeling of being an unpolished indie-game. Other disaster-survival games, like This War Of Mine manage to provide a better feeling of scarcity of resources and importance of the characters. Characters in Sheltered always seem to be replacable. Not even the starter-family seems to be important. Having a couple extras running around in case a character dies is usually not an issue. Food and water is abundant.
If you can get sheltered at a discount, during steam sales for example, it's a great addition to your library. Figuring out how to survive will keep you busy for a couple hours. But once you figured it out, replayability drops to zero. I'd recommend This War of Mine over Sheltered any day though.

Where Bastion was about choices and Transistor was about strength in the face of adversity, Pyre is about relationships and life, about the places that it takes you, and doing whats right. And here you will truly feel the camaraderie among this ragtag band of exiles, all with their own vastly unique personalities, histories, and agendas, but all ultimately in pursuit of the same singular goal.
STORY
Read every bit of dialogue. Really. It would practically be a sin to not do so, to miss any part of it. Because it is within the words where you will find all of the heart and soul of this game. In essence, the overarching plot is simple. You got kicked into purgatory. You want out, and so does a bunch of others. But everything that happens in between will be where this game truly shines. You will quickly come to know about the band and even your adversaries. And ultimately, you will come to form ties with all of them, especially for those who stay with you longer. So when it comes time to choose who stays in your company and who regains their freedom, you will find it harder and harder to decide.
GAMEPLAY
Magic Basketball was not what I expected to enjoy, but this was so much of a twist on the ball game that I absolutely loved it. There is so much potential here even as a PvP game mode: The team building, the various skills and perks, then resource management, all contribute to some amazing matches where you are sitting on the edge of your seat trying to outmanuever your foes. Sure, some of the AI could use work. And the balance is generally a little off too (seriously, how do you even catch a ranked up Fae or Ti'zo?), but they definitely didn't detract from me thoroughly enjoying the 'rites'. That said, as some detractors noted the gameplay does feel a little disconnected from the rest of the game's style, but I don't think its a big enough point to be a dealbreaker.
MUSIC
I mean, its Supergiant. If you haven't heard any of the music from them, do yourself a favor and go check out any of the soundtrack for their 3 games (they uploaded everything on thir Youtube channel). You're welcome.
BUGS & ISSUES?
Had the game tell me a few times now and then that it couldn't save the game, and it did also crash on me when i tried to load the very last checkpoint (to try and send a different person back at the end), but otherwise it's smooth like butter to me.
CONCLUSION
100% you should play it. Unless you hate reading. Or absolutely abhor ball games. Or you can't handle your heart constantly giving you the feels.

Alpha Prime is a Sci-Fi FPS based on a space station (a mine for a rare, new mineral called habardium.. or something) which has suffered an accident and on which there are only a handful of survivors. You have been sent in at the behest of your ex in order to save their current husband to be from the station.
The game plays somewhat like an inferior Fear, having sci-fi weaponry and the ability to slow down time for a short while, but the guns in the game feel very underpowered. The assault rifle is the only weapon that is of any worth - the sniper rifle, shotgun and pistol doing practically no damage and being inferior in every situation to just tap shooting from the assault rifle. For 10 rounds you can kill an enemy which may take a second or two, but two shotgun blasts will take perhaps double that - and the shotgun is only able to be used at close range, where your health will vanish pretty quickly.
The game is pretty unforgiving in some places with the combat. Your slow motion doesn't recharge on it's own and requires the mineral harbidudmidmm (you know, the mineral that's being mined on the station that you're turning into your own battlezone) and a single enemy, unchecked, can easily kill you. Additionally, ammunition for the assault rifle is pretty hard to find, even though it drops off of the enemies that you kill, meaning that a tight spot might grow tighter.
The game has aged to a far greater degree than Fear, whilst the Unreal 2 engine's physics and lighting standards are still adequete enough, the physics in this game leave much to be desired. Ragdolls seem to go through objects sometimes and get stuck in them, the ground is often littered with random objects which you can easily get snagged on and the lighting seems hardly like a step up on DOOM.
TL;DR it sucks

(Note: I didn't play the first The Darkness game nor do I have experience with The Darkness comic books)
At its best The Darkness II is a very stylish game. The comic book origins of this title really come out in a positive way in that regard. Sadly the gameplay does not live up to the presentation aspect of this title.
At the very best you can call The Darkness II an above average shooter. It does nothing special which might sound weird considering how you basically are a semi-god demon monster with tentacles coming out of you ready to rip enemies and the envinroment alike apart. It's just very basic under the shiny shell. You're not really encouraged to utilize your demonic skills and when you do it just doesn't feel very cool.
Naturally darkness is weak to light which brings us to a very frustrating gameplay mechanic. Remember how everyone loves getting hit by flashbangs in shooters? Me neither. The Darkness II manages to take this to another level. Light makes you incapable of using your demon skills which in practice means whatever plan you had with impaling an enemy with that spear-like object you can forget. The real pain starts when enemies start using light against you. This results in many chaotic moments where you just have no idea where to shoot to regain some level of control over the game. The blinding effect of light is way overdone and will make you feel frustrated. When you being the badass mob leader demon you are have to stop every time coming to a new area to snipe off lightbulbs with your pistol you know something is not done right. To top this off the game has a bug which frequently makes motion blur "reverse". What this means is that everytime the motion blur should be off it's on and vice versa. It's not enough to destroy the experience but it's annoying.
The story is The Darkness II's best part. It's not magnificient but it will keep you interested. Characters are solid with a few really standing out. That said I felt very unsatisfied with the ending. As a stand-alone product it doesn't really work.
After about 7 hours of singleplayer campaign you don't have much to do. You can hunt down relics (with some really interesting descriptions as a reward I have to say!) or try a harder difficulty level. The game also features the "mandatory online element" where four of your friends take on separate missions from main story. With no real story I had absolutely no motivation in trying my hands at those the gameplay being mediocre. If you want a multiplayer co-op shooter I'm sure you can think of better ways of spending your time and money.
After all the complaining you might think I hate the game but this is not the case at all. Beyond the presentation it's just not anything special. Mediocrity is not a crime and I'd say The Darkness is definitely worth it if you can find a great deal. At anywhere close to the full price I wouldn't consider it.
