After playing Knights of the Old Republic, I was blown away by how incredibly amazing that game was. When I began to play the sequel, The Sith Lords, in my mind I thought it would be very good but not as fantastic as KOTOR...
The Sith Lords, after playing it and then replaying it again, is perhaps one of the most utterly amazing games I have ever played, in such a way that it surpasses the original. Obsidian Entertainment has truly created a wonderful game.
The game improved upon everything from KOTOR, from the atmosphere to the character development, to the story and music, and most importantly the complex morals and philosphies introduced in the game that shed new light on the Star Wars interpretation of the Jedi, the Sith, and the Force.
The gameplay is almost identical from the first game, but it gives you new options that can influence companions to become stronger and learn new techniques, whether you are light, dark, or somewhere in between. You can mold your character into whatever playstyle you choose.
So much of this game is incredible, but unfortunetly, there are some technical issues that can decrease your playing experience.
Back in 2004, one year after KOTOR was released, LucasArts pushed Obsidian to release the game in a hurry by the holiday season. So, much of the game was left bugged and with plotholes.
Thankfully, there exists a mod on the Steam Workshop that restores this content and fixes the bugs: The Sith Lords Restored Content Mod. Created by a group of dedicated modders and fans, the mod fixes over 500 bugs and restores much of the content cut from the original release. This mod is a definite must if you want to play and enjoy this game.
In conclusion, The Sith Lords is an underated masterpiece that is truly mind-blowing. In 2015, IGN listed this game as one of the best PC RPGs of all time, and rightly so. I would HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who not only enjoys Star Wars, but also a really wonderful experience.

Pharaoh Rebirth takes the idea of metroidvania style of maps and item acquisition and mashes it up with more high action platformers such as Dust, or Cave Story.
To break the game down simply, you go from stage to stage, searching through the map for new items and skills in order to advance through, until you reach the end boss. Along your journey you have a variety of ways to defend yourself against the game's varied amount of enemies and traps. You have a basic forward attack, an upward swing, and the ever useful, aerial somersault. Each attack will have it's own advantages and disadvantages, for example, the normal attack does a ton of damage but have limited reach and utility. While the aerial somersault is incredibly useful for comboing, protecting yourself from oncoming projectiles, and for control of a given combat scenario, however, it's weaker than your basic attack. You also have a quick dodge / dash that you can use for both maneuverability, as well as bypassing incoming projectiles. Along your travels you'll also come across items of varying degree. Some items will give you passive buffs, while others are active, and can be used to heal, buff, and some are even usable weapons. As you continue through the game you'll find many more skills, items, and weapons. This is essentially the core of what makes up Pharaoh Rebirth.
Pharaoh Rebirth's visuals are well illustrated and animated. The frames are smooth, and the pixel art professional looking. The overall design is rather cutesy, but not so overbearingly so, that you'll be ashamed to play it in public. It's overall aesthetic quality is great, but it is mired by technical limitations. There is no native resolution, no 1080p, or even simply a wide screen mode. If you set the game to "full screen" on the pre-launch menu, you'll be greeted with stretched pixels, and distorted images. Even when set to Windowed mode, the game will launch as a tiny 640 X 640 square, where you'll have to manually stretch the game, doing your best not to stretch the pixels out side of it's originally designed resolution. To say the least, this is not optimal.
The game itself is a very enjoyable romp, that offers a fair challenge to the player, while maintaining a very accessible set of mechanics that most could quickly understand within just a few minutes of play. Though it's simple at first, you'll find yourself dying more than once as you progress. Enemies take off large chunks of life, and there is no health regen except very specifically located check points. Trial and error will be your best teacher. As you would expect from a metroidvania style of game you'll be fighting bad guys, and exploring the map which seems like a fine endeavor, however, there doesn't seem to be any real map makers, compass, minimap, or even... a map at all. The player will be forced to rely on memory, or in my case, pure attrition to make it out of any given stage.
Overall Pharaoh Rebirth is a satisfying, and enjoyable action platformer with some metroidvania style mechanics for good measure. The combat and map design are enjoyable, creative, and just deep enough to keep players entertained, however, what is an otherwise very enjoyable game is mired by technical limitations with it's resolution, and player conveniences such as a map.
Pros:
- Enjoyable combat and boss fights
- Just deep and challenging enough to satisfy
- Simple enough for casual play
- Excellent animation and pixel art
Cons:
- No map (That I could find)
- Terrible resolution options

As a kid, KOTOR 2 always seemed like lesser of the two games. It was less polished & not nearly as complete as the first, more technically demanding/frustrating than the first, and didn't have the lighter-hearted RPG feel of the first. I found the influence system frustrating, the planets a little more boring, and many playthroughs would just end halfway through. But now, a bit over half that lifetime later, I've come to realize how much this game completely obliterates the first in terms of storytelling and philosophy.
KOTOR 2 is a prime example of how well-written characters can make or break a game. There are no real low points in terms of your companions backstories, options, & goals, and the progression system is very much appreciated. It makes every NPC encounter a strategic opportunity, and there'll be times where taking a small hit to your morality is worth it to make a companion more loyal to you, and consequently open up more dialogue & training options.
These points, however, are taken to the extreme with the addition of Kreia, who single-handedly takes the game and carries it on her back, from the very beginning to the very end. In my eyes, she is without a doubt the greatest video game character ever written. As a companion, and more-so as a teacher & mentor, she's both written and voice acted flawlessly. I can think of no other character who's teachings of morality, of perspective, and of the power of words, have transcended beyond the game into others... and real life. She also plays a significant part in what I consider one of the greatest cutscenes in video game history. Overall, I would highly recommend that players both new and experienced listen what she has to say... you might be surprised.
In terms of combat, it's a bit more of a mixed bag. Sentinels have been made much more useful with the addition of destructible loot, and the complete overhaul of the upgrade system. Councilors got a small buff, as force powers are available right from the start (though to a very limited degree), and gradually become powerful as the levels start building up. In my eyes though, Soldiers are much less useful than in the first game, as they have neither the flexibility of Sentinel classes, nor the highly useful crowd control abilities of Councilors, and NPCS can generally be used to fill the role of tanks or cannon fodder.
The level cap has been increased from 20 to around 50 or 60, which you'll never reach without cheats, though it is a welcome addition. Shops can either be incredibly useful or universally unhelpful, as stocks seem to only be generated once, as opposed to being restocked after every planet, like in the first game. Loot drops are more meaningful but sometimes conflict with lore, as multiple "unique" items can be dropped from completely unrelated NPCs. There's also a more RPG-focused resource-management aspect that I like quite a lot, but their is an RNG aspect to it. Exploration can reward lower leveled players with higher tiered rewards (IE getting Jedi armour pre-Telos), or it can screw you over (IE not getting enough lightsaber crystals for your party... or only getting offhand/double-blade lightsabers, when most of your team are spec'd for 1-hand combat).
Combat movement (and subsequent cheesing) can be hit or miss as well; you can gain a single quick followup action after a kill, but at other times NPCs can cancel a halfway executed attack under certain circumstances. The game also has a bad habit of adding in basic attacks when you want to use an item/skill/force power, which gets really annoying when you're trying to kite an enemy and use a medpack to heal (which is made more frustrating by the downgrade of having to click on a character portrait for every item use). Again, a mixed bag; none of these points make/break the game, but will sometimes lead to frustrating encounters, and maybe a checkpoint load or two.
As a fair warning though, this game isn't 100% complete, and at times you'll notice the glaring oddities of certain encounters. Sadly, the development of this game seems to have been rushed at some point or another, so while the core of the game is solid, you'll notice certain aspects that bring down the overall quality and immersion of the world around you. Some areas will feel like empty voids, some characters & encounters will feel odd & out of place, some voice sections will be oddly chopped up, or subtly sound different due to differing recording sessions/environments, and some plot lines will feel a tad rushed or incomplete. The Content Restoration Mod, which I highly recommend getting, does well to fill in some of these gaps. On the other hand though, it does add in some very roughly-edited cutscenes, and a few missions/encounters that, in my eyes, should have stayed cut out.
Exploration can be rewarding, but can also be a bit boring. As mentioned previously, RNG can either give you great items or bad items, and there are definitely some areas that feel like empty wastelands. In contrast to KOTOR 1, which had multiple segments for each planet that were generally well populated and thought out, KOTOR 2 tends to have planets with 3-4 sections each (and maybe a special area or two) that vary in population.
Furthermore, KOTOR 2 doesn't quite capture the joy of exploring each planet as it's predecessor did. In general, the tone of this game is much darker, grittier, and down to earth, which is reflected in the planets and the NPCs that populate them. From a lore perspective, they add more backstory in terms of recent & long-past events, and provide a more realistic look at how the congruent wars have devastated the galaxy & it's citizens. But the tradeoff is a lessened sense of identity for each planet, which ultimately boil down to either an exhausted city, a ravaged forest/jungle, or a dead wasteland. In contrast to KOTOR 1, which had the open, rural plains of Dantooine, the ominous tombs of Korriban, the open desert of Tatooine, the mysterious jungles of Kashyyyk, and the beautiful, utopian oceans of Manaan, KOTOR 2's planets tend to blend together.
In conclusion, KOTOR 2, from a technical point of view, isn't nearly as polished as it's predecessor was. It adds a lot of welcome balance changes, but simultaneously regresses in certain areas with a few dumb combat decisions. Planets are a bit more empty and not quite as full of life as their original counterparts, but add in a bunch of smart lore that the previous ones fell a bit short on. But where this game really shines is in the story, more-so in the characters that tell it, and I can't emphasize enough how much of an impact that has on this game. KOTOR 1 is more of a fun, traditionally-styled RPG, but few games hit me as philosophically hard as KOTOR 2 does, to the point where it's lessons and morals transcend into other games, and into real life. And that, to me, is one of the greatest triumphs a video game can achieve.
Overall 9/10. I'd very much recommend this game to Star Wars fans, or fans of games with great stories to them. A great addition to anyone's collection.

Positives:

The variety in the environments and boss encounters kept the game interesting throughout.
Greek mythology is an underutilised setting in gaming, used to great effect here to create an immersive atmosphere.
The art style is strikingly beautiful, the sound design was much richer than expected, particularly the voice acting.
Negatives:
The game is fairly short, if you don't focus on completing all the side quests and collectables then you won't probably won't get more than a couple of hours of gameplay.
I would love a difficulty setting above Olympian.
Towards the end game it could've used a little more variety in the basic enemies you fight.

The final encounter is a little disappointing in that it does not utilise any of the more complex skills developed or items collected throughout the game.
Other comments/neutral:

Supergiant has done it again. Another amazing game. Beautiful art and music as always. This one is very different from Bastion and Transistor (play those if you haven't.) Pyre has a lot of reading so be prepared for that. The story, lore, and characters are good enough to keep me reading. I became attached to the characters pretty quickly and enjoyed the conversations the group had. There are also a lot of choices along the way. Some are small choices. Some of them are hard ones. There isn't a new game plus like their previous two games, butI feel like there are enough choices to make the single player replayable.
I enjoyed the gameplay as well. Mystical ball sport was an interesting choice for Supergiant and I think they pulled it off. The rites are pretty simple. Get the orb and jump in the pyre. You have to get down all the controls and get used to using three people. The first few matches aren't that hard, but it will be later on. You can always change the difficulty to hard or use the stars that debuff you/buff the enemy for more enlightenment(xp.) There are a bunch of different character types, masteries, and trinkets to change things up. Try to get used to playing all the characters. I haven't played versus yet, but I assume it will be fun challenging my friends.
It's an interesting mix that I really enjoy, but this may not be the game for everyone. I highly recommend playing this though. I know I'm playing it again. 10/10
TL;DR: Amazing art, music, story, characters, and enjoyable gameplay. Yes.

Pure logic. That's all this game requires. "Hook" looks a lot like electrical diagrams, but that's not a coincidence. It's a simple game in premise where you have to remove lines and hooks while making sure that you don't accidentally try to remove ones that are locked by others.
The early levels are incredibly easy but that's to allow you to understand the various symbols and switches and how they work. The later levels are definitely more difficult but each level builds upon what you've learned up to that point. By the time you get level 40+, you'll end up taking way more time analyzing the layout followed by the eventual "Wait ... how was THAT one connected?" when you accidentally activate one item that you didn't intend.
It's a short game - easily less than two hours - but it's simple and fun and can test your grey matter. If you like logic games, then buy it. Don't even wait for a Steam sale. (It's less than a dollar, for crying out loud.) This one is worth it.

I was not really expecting much from that game and it turned out to be a very playable and addictive game at the end.
I gave it 2 good tries, once back a while and more recently in Jan 2017.
You are basically owning a bunker in a desolate and radioactive post apocalyptic world and kinda like the Sims game, you have to take care abour your few inhabitants.
Fatigue, stress, hunger, thirst, hygiene, health and bladder are the main things you need to focus on.
That could be easily boring but the thing is that you start with almost nothing.
So, you'll have to find compromises, take tough decisions and start scooting around.
There is very roughly 50 different kinds of loot in the game and you'll need some of those to start building add-ons in your bunker.
Maybe start with a bed, a tube for a shower and a bucket as the loo ?
But if I let my guys having a shower, the water supply runs dry way too quickly... so maybe I'll accept having dirty survivors in my bunker for a while until a great rain comes in ?
This is the kind of decisions you'll have to make.
And that sweet but glutton family dog we had that keeps begging for some food and getting skinnier by the day... should I really feed him, but what about my kids ?
Then there are the expeditions.
Pick one or 2 of your survivors, have them wear a gas mask if you can't treat them for radiation once back, a backpack if available and a blunt weapon ? Yeah, wasteland is not friendly. Bears and hungry wolves ? Not only ! cannibals, bandits or crazy people will be around too.
If you're charismatic enough, good for you, you might be able to trade with them, that's a win win. Other wise, try out running them if you can't give a good hit.
The funny part of the expedition is that the further away you wander, the more water you'll need, and water is vital in your bunker... so, again, what compromise are you willing to do ?
Then you pick your way and decide to walk through a small town south west or maybe the larger one further away ? Or is just that you want to find an axe and the forest hut is your only goal ?
Anyway, once you're gone, the funny collect and prioritize game starts.
your inventory gets full very quickly and you'll have to focus on your priorities... but then, you stumble on a very rare piece that might be useful to repair the camping car... so... should I leave my pile of 5 food for a car battery ? Again... compromise, priorities...
Some nice extra things:
- The special blue prints you'll stumble upon at the end of the game
-
So I really enjoyed the game and I think I kinda finished it but that's where the cons are kicking in.
Kinda reviewing the time I spend and figuring out that there could have been better or more stuffs.
Here are a few of them:

- Lack of goals. I mistakenly thought the idea was to repair the van and leave... though once repaired, it basically helps a lot your expeditions but you don't really need that any more at that time.
- I don't see the point of recruiting more and more people in your bunker. They will anyway not fight when your bunker gets raided and you don't really need them.
- Overall, the TIER 3-4 construction list is not really that necessary and most of the items come too late in the game to still be really useful.
Anyway, I spent quite some nice time on that game and I recommend it, I just wished there was a proper end or closure and not just stopping to play it when I got tired of it.

Nice though the idea and a lot of this games concepts are, there's no getting around the fact that its about as RNG dependent as a slot machine and involves long periods of sitting around with nothing to do
Like every survival game you need food and water. Water increases whenever the RNG decides to make it rain, which can be a little annoying when it doesn't rain for a week, but is at least fairly realistic. What isn't realistic is the fact that i searched 20 settlements and didn't find a single hinge, as such I couldn't build a freezer, and everyone starved to death, as all my animal traps (the only food source of any note) were rendered useless by my inability to store the meat and you're not allowed to take the meat straight from the animal to the stove (not that i could build a stove of course, that also bafflingly required a hinge).
In my next playthough i did find a Hinge!!!, thank the gods! unfortunately i didn't find any rope, so couldn't build any traps and everyone starved again, so, you know, the more things change, the more they stay the same
I then removed my big boy pants and changed the difficulty down to easy, at which point the first shelter I looted contained all the materials one would need to construct pretty much every upgrade in the game. As such any tension the game previously had ran out the door, and the game basically turned into The Sims with pixel art; just watching people aimlessly wandering about, eating and showering, without the ability to drown them all or burn the house down once boredom inevitably sets it
A degree of randomness in a management game is good as it forces you to come up with a new strategy each time; so much randomness that the game is either unwinnable or wins itself straight off the bat is just obnoxious. On normal difficulty my entire time with this game consisted of not doing a whole lot, just watching, waiting and hoping that the RNG would give the next house a single door to pillage; on easy mode my entire time with the game also consisted of not doing a whole lot, as once you've built the half dozen high level items there's not much else to do.
tl;dr: if you want actual survival management gameplay I can highly recommend Thea: the awakening; if you want gambling and a depressing atmosphere I'd "recommend" Blackpool
<Update>
For what it's worth (ie nothing) I'd like to offer my two cents on how to improve the game, as it does have a lot of the right building blocks, but they've been strewn all over the carpet rather then put together into some kind of structure (hence why I keep coming back to it, despite quitting every couple hours after the bad design has finally worn me down). Having to individually instruct everyone to go drink some water, have a nap, eat something or take a shower is utterly tedious, but having turned on the automation, there's very little minute to minute interaction to be had with the game and you end up just sitting and waiting, whether that's waiting for rain, your expedition to stumble across something, or a trader to turn up bearing hinges.
My solution, make the whole thing turn based instead; pretty much all the individual elements would transfer from real time to turn based without very much alteration and you'd remove a lot of the dead time waiting for the next bit of gameplay. Combine that with a bit less randomness and you'd have something great; as it is, the game just bores and frustrates to the point that I can't really recommend it

I got Nether because I liked the sound of creatures, as opposed to the popular zombie theme, and it was only $3 at th time. In playing the game, I was pleasently surprized that there is a global stash that you can horde things and save them for later. If your character dies, that kinda sucks. Fortunately, you could replace lost items if you had spares in the stash. I frequently find myself going out and scavenging for stuff with only a melee weapon. If i die, no big deal. I gather things and go back to a safezone, save them for later.
You also have to keep in mind that your character needs food. This aspect forces players to constantly roam around and scavenge more.
As for the population, it's a little hit and miss. You migh find a server with relatively nice people who like to chat and stick with the mentality that they won't attack unless someone else attacks first. Then you have your people who hunt and stalk other players just cause they can. they can get frustrating.
I do wish the chat system was a little less out of the way. Sometimes I'd like to say something to someone who worries about whether or not I'm friendly but taking that long, opening the chat window, only leaves you exposed. If the other person decides he doesn't want to trust you, you're already at a disadvantage. The chat window stops you from moving, naturally, so you can type.
Also, the whole map is not available yet. I'm excited to see what will be in store with the coming expansion.
I'd like to see more variation on the creatures as well.

A simple little game about babysitting a group of survivors. I usually like build and stockpile games enjoyable, but I did not find this particularly fun- although possibly I was missing something about the playability?
1) Starting out with high base stats in Int or Chr seems not to matter.
2) Survivors don't seem to do anything exciting, standing around when not working. The pet is somewhat animated, but my people didn't interact with each other. Without cues about this little nuclear family and how they get on, it was very hard to care about whether their metres were full or not.
3) For an inventory management game, the inventory system was dull and extremely unituative. For that matter the click-select between family members was not at all seamless and I frequently had trouble moving things between carried and equiped.
4) The random nature of the salvage means that your base fills up pretty quickly with things you neither need, nor want, while access to vital supplies like food is entirely random with no story telling style seeding- it's not very interesting to have unsolveable problems. Nor is there much enertainment in knowing you have 30 bits of string, pipe, etc.
5) I will never enjoy a game where I need to manually tell someone to defecate. I should not be having to hands-on tell an adult of sound mind to poop, x_x
Just save your money and wait till this game is heavily discounted.

I'm going to start off by saying how great this game is, honestly it's an extremely polished well rounded experience. The 12 hours I got out of it were CRAM PACKED with puzzles, horror, dialogue, beautiful set pieces, and me trying to figure out what the HECK is going on. Having enjoyed previous Frictional Games.. games.. I've only played this one now admittedly because of the price tag. I was apprehensive of shelling out $32CAD for a game much like one I've already played, and seeing my friends clock in 12 hours or so made me question it more. Needless to say I bought the game and to say my fears were very unfounded. Echoing what aforementioned friends say, the game is more about the story and atmosphere than the other elements. Now with that being said the natural assumption is that the other elements are a buffer, well that's a criticism I've seen of this game but I didn't feel that way at any point. The monsters and puzzles both felt like a natural extension of the world and made it just plain fun (if being scared af is fun). I will say that some of the puzzles were stretching the word unintuitive, but most hiccups were a result of me trying to rush and failing to see and take note of queues around me.
Really though this game has one of the freshest stories I've played through in a long time, it's one that allows a lot of freedom of interpretation while still creating moral dilemas that only play out a few ways. This is definitely a game I was glad to play through, I look forward to whatever comes next!

Seeing as I have fnally finished this game twice, once Jedi and once Sith, I will attempt to make my views on it clear.
Firstly, to get my biases out of the way, I'm a huge Star Wars fan, so I started off with a positive view towards this game, as well as a bit of a pair of Nostalgia Goggles from playing the first one badly years ago.
On to the game. The story of this game was certainly very enthralling, and as i have now played through it three different ways, I can confirm that there are indeed consequences to your choices as well as different paths and missions depending on your actions, if only Bioware had kept that idea up and not just made your choices a disappointing visual filter. (We all know what I mean) (***Cough******cough*** mass effect) (gah musta just had something inmy throat). in all seriousness though my first actual and complete playthrough of this game was incredible. I never watched any video or had any plot points spoiled by anyone, and if you can achieve this state, even for such an old game, You will have a much better time of it.
Of course story means nothing if your character is uninteresting. Take modern examples of RPGs, (and yes i mean Mass Effect again, jesus christ Andromeda, or fallout with its bland and uninteresting main character with scripted predetermined lines) for example. KOTOR II takes a different path. The lines of your main character will never be voiced, they will only appear as numbered choices at the bottom of your screen during conversations at the end of other character's voice lines. (Everyone's so nice in this corner of the galaxy, nobody interrupts anyone) The lines you have generally breakdown into a few categories as follows, "Good" morally Jedi type lines, "Good" less Jedi more charity type lines, "lol pay me" bounty hunter lines (just about always there(Also usually work btw)), Generally "Rude" lines that might earn you some dark side points, and straight up "DIE!" lines of psycho-sith dialogue that usually then begin combat (sometimes darkside runs can be fun because these are always an option). While the pattern is somewhat predicatable, with the lines usaully aligning to the place they would move you to on the light/dark scale, with "lol pay me" being morally neutral, the lines are well written and additional more contextual lines appearing when your character has uncovered or recieved. These don't align morally but if you see them, might be best to click them, they usually reveal quests, interesting details, or can turn your loveable group of companions into equally lovable but more useful Jedi, you never know until you click it. (Save often, some of these might backfire).
Speaking of lovable companions, they serve as a decently sized part of the fun of this game. Theorhetically you will eventually get all of your party slots filled, you will always have Atton and Kreia. you cannot avoid recruiting them, so don't try to get rid of them. You wouldnt want to anyway, as these two turn out to be quite interesting. Atton is a scoundrel, basically he's Han Solo for this game, and seeing as you can't fly a ship despite any skills you may develop, you kinda need him. Kreia is a hooded and ominous mother in law... thats basically it. Doesn't matter what you do, you're gonna♥♥♥♥♥♥her off. "Doing too much good is bad" "doing too much bad is also bad" "Walk a middle line only a sith deals in absolutes"... i never listen to her. I deal in absolutes. also, keeping your character "Grey" is really hard, it requires you to swing between benevolent bounty hunter and murderous psychopath within the same mission sometimes. I assume its possible, I just choose between Space Jesus or Space Satan, there are no in betweens. Do or do not, there is no try amiright?
Speeking of the galaxy's highest swamp frog, do you like force powers? cuz you can get some sick force powers. You can bend the minds of the weak or troubled like Obi-wan, and yes that actually does hapen in conversation, you can Shreev it up and arc force lightning from one fool to another as you do 920 kickflips with your body and screech at the top of your lungs while only stabbing with your weapon that literally cuts in all directions(well maybe not but you can imagine it, you're playing an RPG after all). You can also just do what i did, choose Consular, grind your way to lvl 15 specializing in force powers and points and unlocking "Force Wave" and then Proceed to waltz your way across the galaxy massacring hundreds with explosive waves of force that throw your enemies into walls and onto the floor, stunning them and eventually killing them as they are unable to fight back, and still be considered a good guy. You heard me right, I have murdered hundreds of people entirely incapable of fighting back against me, and I'm still te good guy, Huzzah for neutral force powers! Also get heal. idc what kind of jedi you play, get heal. it doesnt matter how many enemies you can force choke or force lightning or just straight up force kill, some spacer is gonna hit your emo crackaddict looking sith rear, and you're gonna want to heal. All of this is just to say that the force powers and possibilities are many and various, and they are quite fun to use.
Combat may seem tedious at times as it is still TECHNICALLY a turn based combat system. Combat is done in rounds, with each character doing one action each round. The animations can be repetitive after you have sunk a good number of hours in, but they are entertaining enough and aren't as stale as watching 2d pixel characters bounce slightly before a slight effect plays over an enemy and some numbers pop up. Make no istake, numbers still pop up, but the ability to break combat and run off to heal can be useful and is honestly how i got through some bosses while lvling to my ultimate form of force wave annihilation. Ironically KOTOR II may be a game where killing everyone may be more tedious than just persuading them otherwise or paying them off. I will not proclaim to fully understand the combat system, but it is basically D&D dice rolls hidden behind spinny animations and lightsabers, not that I'm complaining, its still pretty fun, but i like force spam, so the rolls mean slightly less to me. The combat is not really forced on you, really. there are many cases where you can simply avoid conflict,but it will often come with a consequence or loss of something. I will say no more, but the Good and Evil characters still fight a lot, no matter what alignment you are. (sometimes violence is just the answer ya know)
Progression is fairly good. It can feel quite sluggish as you advance later into the game, but by that time lvling up mostly ceases to be a priority as the story accelerates and the stakes increase, as well as the development of your party and character in the universe. "Powers" "Feats" and "Skills" are all granted to you in the form of points that allow you to specialize your character into anything you want. the general breakdown is this. "Powers" are your force abilities, they range from healing to kill, and yess its just called kill. "Feats" are your general aptitudes for different things, such as the ability to wear heavier forms of armor or use two blades with a much reduced penalty. "Skills" can be best defined as "what your character does well". If your persuade is high you can become a silver tongued smoothtalker, diplomatically cruising your way through a marginally more peaceful run or making more credits haggling at merchants or for better bounties. other skills include Computer Use or Repair, both incredibly useful.
Altogether this game is great, and I have had an amzing time playing it. It has its flaws, sure, but as a game it has entertained me for hours on end, and even if I'm just looking for something to pass the time its a great way to continue my quest to become Space Jesus... Or a sith so evil I'd make the Emperor blush, either way.
By the way, get the restored content pack

First things first: This game is "Early Access". It's not yet ready. More features are constantly added as the development proceeds, but some features are
missing. It appears that most reviews here don't seem to take this into account, so this needed to be said. If a rapid cycle of game update patches and encountering occasional bugs not yet fixed is something you don't want to see, then "Early Access" is not for you. In that case wait until the game is done and officially released.
If this is not a problem for you, then read on.
The Isle is a horror/survival game from the hardcore end of that genre. And when I say "hardcore" I really mean
. The core premise of the game can be summarized as:
If you are expecting a dinosaur simulator game, move on. Play Ark or whatever. The Isle is something else. Oh, it's a multiplayer, shared world, online game where you live the life of a dinosaur, but this game takes that phrase "live the life"
. The Isle puts you on a world that is beyond harsh. Not as an environment but in how the ecology of the players is set up. If you want to survive, you need to eat. If you are a carnivore, that means someone else is going to be your meal. When you realize that this applies to everyone else in the game you start to see the picture...
Survive long enough and you can progress and evolve into more powerful creatures, but understand you are playing a
. There are no saves. There are no backups. You die and the journey ends. Start over. No saves and no backups. This single mechanism solves the big flaw in most MORPGS where everyone just constantly progresses to ever greater heights. Not so in The Isle. Your time as the apex predator at the top of the pyramid is limited. Not by the game but by your ability and by the actions of other players. You stay there at the top until someone outwits you, or you get careless, and you get killed. Which will happen.
Value your life because in this game it truly
something and survive as long as you can but keep in mind that in the end The Isle will always kill you. If you can't take this, this game is not for you. If, on the other hand, this raised your interest, then go ahead and you will see a beautiful game. A harsh one, but beautiful.
Welcome to The Isle. You will get killed.

Heros of Might & Magic V is a classic game of epic strategy. This game combines turn-based, army-oriented combat with RPG-like logistics to grow the various forces. Instead of clicking on a building to query up troops, you must either send out your general out to rally them, or recruit them from you town. It's a refresting, and unique take, on the stregy genre of games.
The graphics of this game havn't aged very well, as with most games published around the same time as this one. Also, it's art style is pretty much a rip-off of the Warhammer Fantasy tabletop game. But that is basically what this game is: "Warhammer: the Campign". And thats not a bad thing.
If the idea of a semi-casual, low-APM, army campign game sounds even mildly interesting, then you'll love this game. Just, try not to look the in-game characters in they eyes during dialoge. The uncanny valley is strong here, after all.

There are also some inconsistencies in the design, as some of the levels have areas that you're just on the cusp on making the jump, only to realize that you just don't have the ability to actually make it. It's no where near a big problem, but it's more of an annoyance that keeps on showing up over and over again, getting a tiny bit more annoying each time. But regardless, it's a good game that's appropriate for it's price point, and is worth your time if you like the genre.

NOTE:
First I want to mention that the overall time you need for a single playthrough is about 10h (at least for my first run). If you want to find every single secret it might be a bit longer 1 -2h (I guess). Other than that there is a multiplayer which is not that great and will most likely not entertain you for more than a few hours.
ABOUT THE GAME:
The game focuses on a mix of melee and ranged gun battles. Your Darkness-powers allow you to smash enemies and execute them in gruesome (and satisfying) ways. While melee combat is rather simple (grab, slice vertically, slice horizontally) the guns have more variety. You have one-handed weapons (2x) and two-handed weapons (1x) which you can have a the same time equipped. There are several different guns, from simple pistols over machine guns to shotguns, though there isn't something exceptional there, so don't hope for "Souleating daggers of death" or anything like that. Also I have to mention, that the gunplay feels a bit week at times, there isn't enough recoil to the guns and so you feel the weight of the gun and your shots.
STORY & CHARACTERS:
The story is nothing too fancy but is rather fresh. Evil in form of "The Darkness" existed since the beginning, god said "it shall be light!" and The Darkness didn't like it. So it now jumps from host to host, since it's powers vanishes when it comes in contact with light. Now our protagonist has The Darkness inside him and runs the Mafia. While he is a rather nice guy, he does not hesitate to rip apart his enemies (literally). You find yourself amongst your family (Mafia) and have to deal with an organisation that wants to steal your Darkness. Also you have to cope with the death of your love Jenny (which died in the predecessor).
The characters you meet are rather interesting, the English voice acting is great throughout the game and you feel like these characters are real. Especially Jonny, the weird expert on magic artefacts is rather intriguing and will entertain you with his neurotic personality.
SHOULD I BUY IT?
Short answer is yes. It is entertaining and even though there are some flaws in the gameplay department, it is still an enjoyable game experience. But since the playtime is rather short I recommend you buy it when it is discounted.

The most outstanding and unique aspect of Apotheon is naturally its ancient Greek art style, which gives a brilliant first impression of the aesthetic appealing. This alone should already worth a recommendation. However, the maker Alientrap still cannot get a firm hold on the control, hit judgement and physical engine. As same as their former game Capsized, the control of Apotheon feels floating, and the hit judgement is very weird, making the combat (which is the predominant part of the game) a pain. The story is quite simple, you just defeat every God on your way, unitl you bring down Zeus and Hera. The level design is decent with enough versatility and creativity.
In addition, there are quite a few technical issues in the game. During my playthrough, the game crashed two or three times and I encountered 3 game breaking bugs (like the upper part of the screen during Poseidon battle is covered by the canvas-like background, and two guards I supposed to defeat are closed off the sealed door, etc, each requiring me to quite to the main menu and continue from the last checkpoint).
The graphics alone does not make it a good game. But if you don't mind the awkward control and the possible technical problems, Apotheon should be in your collections. For hardcore action lovers, you may want to avoid this game. Thus, and for other players, wait for a heavy discount.

Where Bastion was about choices and Transistor was about strength in the face of adversity, Pyre is about relationships and life, about the places that it takes you, and doing whats right. And here you will truly feel the camaraderie among this ragtag band of exiles, all with their own vastly unique personalities, histories, and agendas, but all ultimately in pursuit of the same singular goal.
STORY
Read every bit of dialogue. Really. It would practically be a sin to not do so, to miss any part of it. Because it is within the words where you will find all of the heart and soul of this game. In essence, the overarching plot is simple. You got kicked into purgatory. You want out, and so does a bunch of others. But everything that happens in between will be where this game truly shines. You will quickly come to know about the band and even your adversaries. And ultimately, you will come to form ties with all of them, especially for those who stay with you longer. So when it comes time to choose who stays in your company and who regains their freedom, you will find it harder and harder to decide.
GAMEPLAY
Magic Basketball was not what I expected to enjoy, but this was so much of a twist on the ball game that I absolutely loved it. There is so much potential here even as a PvP game mode: The team building, the various skills and perks, then resource management, all contribute to some amazing matches where you are sitting on the edge of your seat trying to outmanuever your foes. Sure, some of the AI could use work. And the balance is generally a little off too (seriously, how do you even catch a ranked up Fae or Ti'zo?), but they definitely didn't detract from me thoroughly enjoying the 'rites'. That said, as some detractors noted the gameplay does feel a little disconnected from the rest of the game's style, but I don't think its a big enough point to be a dealbreaker.
MUSIC
I mean, its Supergiant. If you haven't heard any of the music from them, do yourself a favor and go check out any of the soundtrack for their 3 games (they uploaded everything on thir Youtube channel). You're welcome.
BUGS & ISSUES?
Had the game tell me a few times now and then that it couldn't save the game, and it did also crash on me when i tried to load the very last checkpoint (to try and send a different person back at the end), but otherwise it's smooth like butter to me.
CONCLUSION
100% you should play it. Unless you hate reading. Or absolutely abhor ball games. Or you can't handle your heart constantly giving you the feels.

Bejeweled 3 is what they call a 'match 3' game, meaning you need to combine three or more of the same items on the game board, which then disappear, to score points. In this case those items are jewels that come in 7 different colors.
You decide how complex you want this basic principle to become by selecting one of the 8 game modes. Some modes are very casual, like 'classic', 'poker' and 'zen'. Others are more intense because they add a timer of some sort to the game board. There is also a 'quest mode' in which you will play all of the game modes in some form, easy versions at first and more difficult with each level. You don't need to finish all of the games of one level in order to play games from the next level, so if there are one or two game modes you don't like, it's no problem to just skip those each time and progress to the next level anyway.
In each mode, the game will explain clearly what the objective is and what the specific 'twists' for that game mode are.
The background music is quite nice but you can switch it off through the Options menu if you want.
There are a lot of Steam Achievements to be had, which adds even more challenges. Some achievements are built up to by simply playing the game, others are specific goals to be reached in one or more of the game modes.
I recommend giving Bejeweled 3 a try if you're at least a bit into puzzle games, and even more so if you can get it on sale.

This is a fabulous little game.  It IS short, but the mechanics are clean, interesting, original, and easy to pick up.
Hook is basically an order-of-precedence puzzle game, which could easily get boring, but the visual design in the game kept me engaged the entire time. I had thought I'd try it out, beat a few levels, and make it something that I'd use to kill a few minutes now and again until I finished it...but I found it so compelling that I couldn't stop and played all 50 levels right in a row.
Depending upon how good you are at spatial relations, order of precedence, and logic puzzles in general, this will most likely take you between 60 and 90 minutes to complete the whole thing (I finished in 68 minutes). The first few levels are essentially training and will only take a few seconds apiece.
The game is only a buck (US), and even though it's short, I got way more than a dollar's worth of enjoyment out of it. Heck, even if I'd finished in an hour, that's less than half of the hourly rate of seeing a movie (even at matinee prices) at the theater, so as far as I'm concerned it's a great value for my money. If you want to find a good way to kill 1-2 hours, you could do a lot worse. Pick this one up.

The Good: Gameplay is fun. Seems to be a decent sized comunity, the gunplay is good, graphics are a little simple but fine, maps are decent in size and variety. I like the customability of your character - not only which weapons, but his appearance and clothes/armour. Haven't really seen that type of rpg stuff in an online twitch shooter before and it works pretty well.
The bad: Needs more game types. There are apperently three right now - though team deathmatch is the only one I've played. It's fun, but we need some more types like capture the flag, etc. Every game I played had everyone running randomly around the map - very little team play. That's may be different in the other game types though... Also needs more weapons types. As far as I could see there are no heavy weapons at all in the store, no rpgs, no melee, just a pretty stock standard line up of auto rifles and subs, bolt action rifles, pistols, and shotguns, which amoung other things limits how you can play the game. In an era with games like Titanfall, Heroes and Generals, even Nosgoth which add some interesting twists like vehicles and asymmetrical classes, I think this really needs to bring more to the table than the standard pvp arena shooter it is now.
The ugly: The ping. Probably better where the servers are located (US, Euro, Russia) but in Australia, the best I can get is around 300 on the Euro server which is close to unplayable. I started on the US, which had me at over 400. Needs an Asia server for all the Pacific countries.
Verdict: It is in early access so who knows what will happen in the future. For Aussies, I would say no, the lag is close to unplayable. For the rest of the world... well, how much do you want to play a post apocalyptic counter strike? If it's the game you've been waiting for your whole life, then yes, give it a go, it's free after all - if not, it won't hurt to wait until it matures a bit more.

A lot can be said about Doom. It started a fascination with first-person shooters that still lingers to this day. It spurred a rise in violent video games that eventually necessitated a ratings system. It pushed the limitations of 3D graphics to breathtaking highs in 1993. It revolutionized LAN play and was the catalyst for internet TCP/IP play.
But by now, you probably all know that. Doom is such a big name that it was even made into a (rather mediocre) film in 2005. It's become part of pop culture and the media conciousness. To try and sum it up is pointless.
What you really want to know is whether or not grabbing the Steam version is worth it. In it's default state, I would say no. The copies on Steam are emulated through DOSBox, which kind of sucks. The games run fine and all, but they have low resolution, choppy sound and some obtuse key bindings.
Still, ID Software also pioneered a new file format when they released Doom; the WAD file. Since this version is basically the same one from the 1995 re-release, it has the WAD file that can be extracted to any numerous source ports available. There is even a method of making ZDoom (one of the most popular ports) work with the Steam overlay.
For that reason, if you don't already own Doom, then go ahead and grab it on Steam. $15 is a great price for 2 classic games and some expansion packs. It doesn't hurt that the fundamental design of Doom is timeless. Even if you have played it before, it remains addictive and ingenius all these years later.
If anything, I think I'll be playing this until I die. I may go years without touching a single WAD, but when the itch comes, I always stick around for a long while. Those source ports can also get you online multiplayer (along with a host of other "enhancements"), so you really cannot go wrong.
As for the game itself, I've always loved the simplicity of Doom's design. The level layouts feel like labyrinths and require some lateral thinking. The enemy design is brilliant; it conveys exactly what you need to know in seconds. Even the sound design helps with it's directional audio and individual sound bytes. This is one of the best examples of retro gaming, bar none.
While I may prefer the sequel for it's faster combat, it's hard to deny how well made each episode in Doom is. The first episode, to be specific, is one of the greatest collections of maps you're bound to ever find. Even the pointless fourth episode (that was a bonus to the "Ultimate" Doom) can be a bit of fun.
The game may not be long, but there is definitely a good reason that it has remained a staple for many PC gamers.

I got The Isle...man, I have no recollection of how long ago, but within the last year. I'd followed it for a long while before that as well. All in all I have found it to be one of the most fun early access games I've played. Feel free to peruse my library, I've played some wonky alpha games that did not work out.
You've probably already seen the 'Mixed' marker for the game, which I usually would use as a metric for a game I'd avoid. In this case it feels a bit like people that have been on board for a while, or had some kind of expectation for the game that isn't panning out for them. Or, and this also seems to be often the case, there's a lot of demanding for things...which when the demands aren't fulfilled become bad reviews.
At the moment I think the game is pretty good, and most problems I have with it are so temporary that it isn't worth the time to really get pushed out of shape about them. For example, one thing I've seen since I started playing is that development is constantly ongoing, almost daily I see a patch, either with balance stuff or suddenly and unexpectedly a new feature or general progression. I like to see that, since it shows that development is indeed continuing, unlike a lot of alphas where you see either no progression, or you here from the devs so infrequently that you're constantly forced to ask what's actually happening behind the scenes.
The game provides a fairly starightforward dinosaur survival system. Most gripes are related to features coming out soon, or frustration that the game isn't completed. It's also functionally the only dino sim available, seeing as how ARK is a 'stand next to oversized dinos and ride them' which is something that in theory will be added to the Isle later...though right now if it were simply a dino survival simulator it would still be good. The only problem I could see people really having when getting into the game is the frustration that comes with loss. Since certain features aren't in yet, it means that survival can be pretty tough, and when you lose, you lose some time trying to get back to where you were. It can be extremely frustrating...but whatever, every few days there's a new thing in the game so it's always something.

Still as good as I remember it. This game, and Neverwinter Nights 2, made me a rabid fan of Obsidian Entertainment. That love echoes still, though I'm not so sure if they are my absolute favorite any more.
The first game was BioWare's rather straightforward good vs evil Star Wars story, this sequel goes to the other direction with shades of grey. It's essentially Chris Avellone's thought provoking, if a little preachy, deconstruction of the Star Wars universe mostly delivered by Kreia, one of the best Star Wars Expanded Universe and video game characters ever, brilliantly voice acted by Sara Kestelman. I also feel that it's a bit more personal story with player gradually learning things about his character's past instead of it all revealed in a big plot twist. I believe this game was the first one to have the influence system, which is quite commonplace in RPGs of today.
There is some flaws too, mostly because the game was originally horribly rushed. You should not play it without The Sith Lords Restored Content Mod (TSLRCM), which is really install now that Steam Workshop is supported. Even with that there is some unpolishedness and gameplay pacing problems, but the story will be much more coherent and the game less buggy. Like the predecessor, the game also suffers for being designed for XBox with simplification and interface design choices my PC gamer soul finds offensive. Likewise the d20 system that was the early 00's RPG system for Star Wars is not best for the setting IMO, but at least it's familiar. These things don't dectract too much from the enjoyment of the game and its story, however.
It's easy to see why this is a cult classic. Much better than any Disney canon. It is good that it is still receiving support. An official remake would be a dream come true.

Oh man this game was heavy! Frictional Games have delivered yet another great story driven puzzle / horror game with SOMA!
Set in a facility under the ocean, you find yourself being guided by the brain-scan of a female scientist towards the ARK, which is mankind’s last hope after a catastrophic event has wiped out most of the human race. The facilities’ helpful AI has been corrupted and uses a number of cybernetic monstrosities to try and stop you from reaching the ARK in a twisted duty to protect it. Like the Amnesia games before it, you are never empowered with weapons, and you must flee and play a painstaking game of cat and mouse with these beasts whenever you encounter them.
The environments and sound design is top notch. If you weren’t already scared when you encounter a monster, then the game makes you scared by playing the loud, fast thumping of your heartbeat and heavy breathing that the player character is experiencing. It’s amazing how well they can control how you feel through the game by doing this.
The story is so enthralling, and numerous times it left me pondering major plot revelations for hours. There’s some really heavy themes at play, and I can’t say that I’ve encountered something like this in recent memory. To explain it would ruin the mystery of the story, but to hint at the themes, I would have to say – If a person’s mind was scanned and made digital, would that still be that person?
Pros
- Amazing and intense story
- Great graphics, environment and sounds
- The developers know how to make you feel scared without doing it cheaply
Cons
- Puzzles might be a bit too easy

SOMA is a heavy emotional adventure that explores the topics of existence, conscience and afterlife, as all hope for a future is taken away. I honestly didn't know how to feel when I finished this game.
You take the role of Simon, a man who has recently been in a car accident, which has left him without a potential significant other and a rather nasty brain condition. His condition is pretty risky as high levels of stress can be fatal to him, and he also has to deal with occassional bleeding from his head. Not everything is lost however, as he gets an invitation to a test treatment, which could improve his condition and lead him back to a healthy life. The treatment would start with a brain scan, the scan would be used to simulate multiple treatment stimuli to help the brain repair itself and eventually the best one would be applied to the real thing.
As you're strapped into the scanner, something seemingly happens or goes wrong, because you're not where you were as you step out. There is no one around. Everything looks strange, foreign and nothing around you makes sense. As you keep looking, you eventually find out that you're no longer in the office building you stepped into, but deep underwater and most confusingly of all, in the future. And this is where the game begins.
When I got to this point, like many (I like to think), I started to hypothesise what could be really going on: Am I really in the future? Is this all still part of the scan? Is this all a representation of Simon's brain as he's trying to heal himself? Is the black slime and clots I keep finding, a representation of his condition growing worse? I kept guessing throughout the game that a lot of what was happening was all a trick of the brain, forcing Simon to buy into it all. But I guess going into the story any further would be spoiling too much.
The game is very nice visually. There were times I think that it was too dark, but overall it represented the art style it was going for. Can't say the same thing about the water though, it felt strangely out of place, which is bad when you're surrounded by it half the time. I was also experiencing glitches and significant slowdown whenever I transitioned from area to area, which you would think wouldn't happen in a game like this. I must compliment the soundtrack, ambience  and generally the sound design of this game though as it really captures the feeling of the areas you're in and keeps you on edge whenever the enemies are prowling around.
The gameplay is very similar to Frictional Games' other titles, such as Amnesia: The Dark Descent. You're generally left helpless with no weapons or ways to defend yourself other than running and hiding, but even that will rarely help. Staring at enemies will only hurt you in the long run, as you'll be getting visual glitches (part of gameplay), they will spot you and will attack you, and while it will not always result in instant death, it will hurt you pretty badly and a second encounter will most likely be your last. Funny enough, you do get a weapon (of sorts) at a later date, but once its function is completed, you'll never see it again.
Like in Amnesia, the environment can be interacted with based on the game's physics. A lot of the objects you will find are just junk to look at, but can also be used to produce noise, either to lure the enemies away or accidentally make yourself heard and subsequently attacked. The enemies usually also have a pattern to them and will slightly differ from each other: some will only attack you if you look at them, others will attack if you make too much noise and so on. Other than that, it's usually just a fetch quest with the characters chiming in every now and then: take this item, use it there, move on, next obstacle.
My biggest annoyance with this game is the main protagonist, Simon. I honestly feel like he's making a conscious effort to be an idiot most of the time. While I feel like I would react in a similar way in some of the situations, I feel like he is way too accepting with how things are, not empathetic or just generally stupid. The other character, Catherine, is similar in some way, but as you learn more about her motivations and character, she makes much more sense in how she reacts or behaves to whatever occurs around them than Simon. I also have to question the light hearted humor that happens in this game, I mean, I know humor is a coping mechanism, but it really takes you out of the game.
Overall, I enjoyed my experience with this game, even with the constantly depressing topics being presented to me, the soul wrenching choices you have to make and the ultimate fate that you have to accept. The ending left me feeling very empty, but I would still recommend this game to anyone who thinks it's wotth a shot.
Just don't expect to come out happy at the end of it all.

What a beautiful game.
The story is immersive, at times you actually feel what Simon (the main character) is feeling. It seems to blur the "fourth wall" where reality and the game are one. The events provoke strong philisophical questions and gray moral choices all while exploring a beautiful undersea world, the whole game is eye-candy, even the creatures. The story didn't follow any pre-ordained path, it actually did provide interesting twists.
The puzzles weren't terribly complex, but I felt they didn't need to be. I felt I was actually trapped in a scenario that is plausible and not overly complicated when these puzzles arrived (I should emphasize that the game seems to be more about story, immerssion and depth of feel).
The horror aspects were about as good as they get, maybe a bit better than similair games. I actually felt legitimate fear on those "scripted" scares, because they did not feel scripted, at least at first. Being alone walking across the abyssal plain definately helped contribute to an ambience that facilitates fearful curiosity, Beautiful sights and monsters were done well here.
For anyone looking for a solid story based horror game, I'll recommend this with all my being, it was that good.

Bejeweled 3 is what they call a 'match 3' game, meaning you need to combine three or more of the same items on the game board, which then disappear, to score points. In this case those items are jewels that come in 7 different colors.
You decide how complex you want this basic principle to become by selecting one of the 8 game modes. Some modes are very casual, like 'classic', 'poker' and 'zen'. Others are more intense because they add a timer of some sort to the game board. There is also a 'quest mode' in which you will play all of the game modes in some form, easy versions at first and more difficult with each level. You don't need to finish all of the games of one level in order to play games from the next level, so if there are one or two game modes you don't like, it's no problem to just skip those each time and progress to the next level anyway.
In each mode, the game will explain clearly what the objective is and what the specific 'twists' for that game mode are.
The background music is quite nice but you can switch it off through the Options menu if you want.
There are a lot of Steam Achievements to be had, which adds even more challenges. Some achievements are built up to by simply playing the game, others are specific goals to be reached in one or more of the game modes.
I recommend giving Bejeweled 3 a try if you're at least a bit into puzzle games, and even more so if you can get it on sale.

I really wanted to like this game. It's got a cool look, a great setting, a nice plot, but the thing that breaks this game are the awful, awful controls and mechanics. The game wants to be dark souls, in that it wants to be a dodge-roll enemy gauntlet with ambrosia instead of estus. Not a bad idea, as other games have done similar things by taking what works and putting their own spin on it. The issue is that, to refil health, you need to switch to it, which means you no longer have your weapon out at all. Which means when fighting bosses, where precision and timing are important, you are often trapped because you can't just use healing; you need to manually switch to your healing, use it, then manually switch back, which results in you taking more damage than needed.
But that is a drop in the bucket compared to the real issue, which is the fact that the game uses an auto-lockon system which will get you killed. As a 2D platformer, fighting enemies on both sides of you is normal. What isn't normal is the fact that the game will often lock onto things that you aren't fighting, or onto things that are even on the screen at all. You'll have an enemy right in front of you trying to kill you, and the game will decide an enemy a hundred yards behind you or the random box sitting on the ground is what you need to be looking at. And because you can't manually turn around when the game locks you onto something, you end up getting stabbed in the back a lot. What makes it worse is that there is no indication when you are suddenly locked onto someone or something. So you'll be running, have an enemy on either side of you, and rather than being able to turn and face one of them, you'll inexplicably be walking backwards and getting stabbed because the game decided it knew what you should look at. You also can't switch targets, which means that the game does; and if you thought 'does this mean the auto target switches randomly in combat' then you would be correct, because it does do that. So when facing multiple targets, as you often do, expect the game to frequently move between targets without any rhyme or reason, making the game more frustrating than it needs to be.
And I hate that this is the case, because it's a great looking game, with great atmosphere and a decently intriguing story. But the game itself isn't fun to play; it's actively a chore to get through, and after completing the intro stage and moving on to early stages of the game, it's clear the problems get worse, not better.
As an idea, it's great. As a game, it's mechanically broken, and that's awful when talking about a 2D platformer. Soft pass.

I have been waiting for Supergiant to release another game for a while now, and when I heard of Pyre, I was very much hyped about it. Although going into the game I thought it was something else, I still fell in love with it.
Firstly, the game is not a group based RPG as many know the term. The game focuses on a group of people that are outcast and exiled from their home country into a hellish landscape with many dangers. In this place there is only one way to escape. This is through "Rites;" rites make up the main gameplay as you vie for control of an orb and try to put it into the opponent's pyre. This is where the term "group based RPG" confused me and probably others. The actual gameplay is like magical soccer. But more on that underneath.
What I loved:
o Amazing graphics (hand-drawn and in the Supergiant fashion)
o Fun and lively characters
o Very meaningful choices
o Extensive lore
o The story!
What some people may not like (I personally didn't mind these things):
= So much reading
= Rites
What I didn't like:
- Lack of choice in conversations with characters (You mostly listen characters, which is fine, I just wished for a little bit more interaction there.)
THE RITES: The gameplay takes place between three members of your group that you select. You control one and can switch between them no matter where they are in the play area. While not holding the orb, you have an aura around you that is bigger if the character is big, and smaller if the character is small. This aura can 'banish' opponents for a short time, usually around six to eleven seconds. When holding the orb, your aura disappears and you become vulnerable. During this time you can attempt to throw the orb into the other pyre or jump in with the character. If you choose to jump in, the character is not available in the next round. Throwing also has it's downsides. If you don't have time to fully charge the throw, then it won't be effective. Also, the opponents can catch it midair. Each of the characters also have varying speeds.
The reason some people may not enjoy the rites is because they can become repetitive. There are varying difficulty options, but for the most part it's pretty easy if you have decent reflex and an ability to plan. I personally loved this mechanic, as it really felt competitive. Instead of just having overpowered enemies, you have opponents with different abilities, but all of them can be countered with the right plan. It's a very fast-paced game and it keeps you on your toes.
THE STORY AND CHARACTERS: The story is very good, and features great character development. One thing this game does that many like it do not is that it allows for different understandings of each character. For example, when I met one main character a little before halfway through, I thought (s)he was an enemy or spy or something similar. Just the way (s)he spoke to the pc was agravating and I thought bad things were to come. And then once I started to understand that character, I changed my mind. It was a very neat experience that I don't see in other games very much.
I meant to play this game throughout multiple days to savor it, but I ended up playing it in one 15 hour go. I do plan to replay, as it is a very replayable game.
TL;DR: *10/10 Supergiant did it again.*

A lot can be said about Doom. It started a fascination with first-person shooters that still lingers to this day. It spurred a rise in violent video games that eventually necessitated a ratings system. It pushed the limitations of 3D graphics to breathtaking highs in 1993. It revolutionized LAN play and was the catalyst for internet TCP/IP play.
But by now, you probably all know that. Doom is such a big name that it was even made into a (rather mediocre) film in 2005. It's become part of pop culture and the media conciousness. To try and sum it up is pointless.
What you really want to know is whether or not grabbing the Steam version is worth it. In it's default state, I would say no. The copies on Steam are emulated through DOSBox, which kind of sucks. The games run fine and all, but they have low resolution, choppy sound and some obtuse key bindings.
Still, ID Software also pioneered a new file format when they released Doom; the WAD file. Since this version is basically the same one from the 1995 re-release, it has the WAD file that can be extracted to any numerous source ports available. There is even a method of making ZDoom (one of the most popular ports) work with the Steam overlay.
For that reason, if you don't already own Doom, then go ahead and grab it on Steam. $15 is a great price for 2 classic games and some expansion packs. It doesn't hurt that the fundamental design of Doom is timeless. Even if you have played it before, it remains addictive and ingenius all these years later.
If anything, I think I'll be playing this until I die. I may go years without touching a single WAD, but when the itch comes, I always stick around for a long while. Those source ports can also get you online multiplayer (along with a host of other "enhancements"), so you really cannot go wrong.
As for the game itself, I've always loved the simplicity of Doom's design. The level layouts feel like labyrinths and require some lateral thinking. The enemy design is brilliant; it conveys exactly what you need to know in seconds. Even the sound design helps with it's directional audio and individual sound bytes. This is one of the best examples of retro gaming, bar none.
While I may prefer the sequel for it's faster combat, it's hard to deny how well made each episode in Doom is. The first episode, to be specific, is one of the greatest collections of maps you're bound to ever find. I absolutely LOVE for honor, no other game has ever given me the experience this one has, its like no other. This is the first time I have taken the time to write a review for a game on steam I enjoy it so much. The gameplay is unique and immersive and the graphics, maps, models, and animations are almost flawless. Its a treat to just look at. The classes are unique and very fun, with simple combo's and more indepth styles and movesets once you have the basics figured out. Environmental kills are awesome with maps designed around various hazards. Gear is cool looking and some would say far to impactful, but is turned off in duel modes allowing for a completely skill based environment. The 4v4 modes feel epic and have awesome moments and comebacks.
The faction war is a fun distraction, while by no means being perfect, it really doesn't need to be to add a fun layer to the game and community.
The campaign was suprisingly fun and engaging. Not by anymeans an out of this world experience, but the settings, music and voice acting were well done. The story was interesting, and the gameplay was fun, especially when on realistic mode.
Complainst about pay to win and DLC splitting the player base is complete bunk, and makes me sometimes wonder if those people have even played the game. Gear stats for revenge mode are strong right now and will be brought back into line, but it is no where near what people claim it to be. Most of the frustration comes from having a fairly steep learning curve to the game, making it frustrating for newer players at times. As to the DLC, all maps and modes are going to be availible to everyone, as well as ranked qeues, and if it is also following the siegemodel in regards to characters, the DLC classes should be unlockable with in game currency. This means that once you buy the game, you have eventual access to almost all the same content a season pass holder would, with the only difference being the timing.
Connection wise, I have had very little issues, but I do know that is not the case for other individuals. With forwarded ports and high speed internet, I experience almost zero latency issues in duels and brawls. Most 4v4 modes are very smooth and lag free. But there are instancese where hosts keep rage quitting and it messes with the flow of the game, but this is few and far inbetween. On the whole, the network has performed very well for me.
In regards to the Peer to peer system, I was very critical of it until I actually played the game specifically dual modes. P2P gives you the lowest latency possible between two players period. In a fighting game like for honor, this is critical. Having a P2P system for duels and brawls means that we are only limited by our connection to eachother and will 100% of the time always be faster than both players having to comunicate with a server. In 4v4 modes this is harder to pull off as you now have to connect to 7 other players, most of the time in my experience, this has not been an issue and there seems to be minimal lag. However, there are times where a bad connection can result in some lag, or connection issues. But if you have an open NAT and a solid connection, latency should rarely be a problem for you.
There is a reason every competitive fighting game ever uses P2P, its not perfect, but for this style game, its the best availible option out there. Does it need work? Yes absolutely, but in no way shape or form will servers improve on what is being implemented currently.
