Date Completed: 1/7/17
# of Hours: 30+ Hours
Replayability: No
Game Type: Post Apocalytpic Survival
Score: 5 pieces scavenged trash out of 10
Spoilers Below: Always
Overall thoughts:
Sheltered masters the art of the skinner box video game methodology. I found myself staying up late going on expeditions in hopes of getting a little more metal so that I could upgrade my filter. Or trying to find that last tyre (tire? wtf.) for my RV so that I could finally do more expeditions with less water. That's not a compliment. It wasn't until 30 hours in I looked back and thought, "What have I accomplished?" or "What have I gained?" The answer was, nothing. They were conditioning me to press the button for my random reward.
Sheltered is like the generic's at the grocery store. They're cheaper, and they look sort of similar so you think, "I can get away with using non-labeled spaghetti sauce in a can". You go home, you consume it, and when you're in the bathroom re-contemplating your life, you come to the realization, "No, no. That was a bad idea. I should have bought the name brand stuff. Shame on me."
Sheltered is that generic knock off. It's the white label of This War of Mine, with much more micro-managing and none of the real engagement. There is no story like This War of Mine, there is no ending like This War of Mine, there is no challenge like This War of Mine. I survived 165 days before giving up because I was still on my first game with my first family, and none of them had died, and I knew it would go on into infinity. I had to create another family just to make sure I hadn't accidentally chosen easy mode. Around day 45 I felt my first bit of pressure when the water was running low, and the rains were scarce, and the nothing. Some of my family got whiney about shower, someone crapped on the floor. And then it rained. And then I went back to pressing the reward button.
To put this in perspective, the leaderboard has someone who has survived over 2 billion days.  Billion (WITH A B AMERICA!). Even the micromanaging aspect that sets it apart from This War of Mine allows you to put your occupants on robotic mode, micromanaging themselves as if the developers themselves were admitting no one would probably want to do it.
There are much better games out there, but if you're still considering it, I would say buy This War of Mine first. If you've finished that, the Sims. But... if you're done with both of those and you're looking to get a little more of that sweet sweet survival action, then MAYBE this game will tide you over. But then, only when it's on a discount.
Mechanics
Sheltered places you in a shelter that you and your family found, tasking you with micromanaging your occupants needs (or putting them in robot mode), going on expeditions to gather supplies, to upgrade your shelter. There is no end game.
Character Creation
Perhaps the best part of the game, you are able to create your own characters, name them, clothe them, and give them certain personality traits. I created a family, with me and Kristin (my wife), and our two imaginary kids. Essentially, I had to create my own story since the game didn't do it for me.
Micromanagement
Each occupant has certain needs. Hunger, Thirst, Tiredenss, Toilet, dirtiness, Stress, and Trauma meters exist for each occupant of the shelter. Each of these is reduced by fulfilling the requirement for that attribute. Hungry? Eat some food. Thirsty? Drink some water. Tired? Sleep.
Shelter Crafting
Crafting is the central point of the game, giving you a workbench that you can upgrade. Each upgrade of the workbench unlocks new patterns of items to build. Some of these patterns are upgraded versions of previous tiers (i.e. makeshift toilet to good toilet), while others are brand new. Through the workbench you are able to craft weapons, items for the shelter such as storage, lights, toilets, bullet proof vests, toy boxes, etc. In order to craft, you need to get materials, which are either gained from expeditions, or from recycling items you got on expeditions.
Expeditions
You are able to send up to two characters at a time on expeditions. Occupants sent on expeditions can be equipped with up to 4 items. A weapon, two supplementary items, and bag. The weapons require strength to use (but even if you don't meet the requirement, can still be equipped).  Supplementary items almost always include a gas mask (so you don't die), and some sort of other item that boosts your search capabilities. Sheltered then uses a slotting system (one square per item, all items take one square, but you can have multiple items in one square.)
Once items are equipped, you select waypoints on a map for your occupants to travel to. The farther and more waypoints you choose, the more water is needed to travel to those points. With no water, you are unable to travel.
Combat System
Occasionally on your expedition you may run into other individuals. When meeting with them, many times you are able to Trade with them, Bully them, Recruit them, or fight them. All are fairly straightforward and what you would expect.
Once you are engaged in combat, either by your selection, or some NPCs will force you into combat, you enter a turn-based fighting system very similar to the old Final Fantasy games. Almost always you can simply flee (and is generally what you do). However, if you choose to fight you are able to subdue a person (knock them unconscious), steal from them, disarm them, attack them, or use items from your inventory (like grenades or pipe bombs).
Trade System
You can either engaged in trade while on expeditions, or broadcast from your shelter to bring traders to your shelter. Trading is terrible. Whenever trading, most NPCs have 3-4 items at most, never in bulk, and almost never anything useful. It was mostly a waste of time.
Location searching
Occupants are able to search locations they come across. Unlike This War of Mine where you actually see the location and can navigate around it, Sheltered simply shows you what items are in the location, and you are able to take items from the location, swap items with the location, and then eventually leave, letting your merry band walk around.
End Game
There is no end game. You continue on indefinitely until all your occupants die, or you just stop caring.
If you don't have a decent graphics card or high RAM, dont bother.

TL;DR: If you love games with a rich story and artstyle, buy it right now. If you prefer games for the gameplay, maybe this is not for you, but it's still very worth it to give it a short.
When I first started playing Pyre, I was excited for it being a Supergiant Games title, but was a bit skeptical about it. The trailers had hyped me a bit, but even if I loved the artstyle and the music, I didn't believe the gameplay would be all that interesting.
After playing for a couple hours I was still confused, because the game had little of actual combat and lots of dialogue and rather linear interactions. Fortunately, the story and characters are very well done and interesting, so I kept pushing forward.
When you hit the ~6th hour of game, there's a turning point in the story. You discover lots of new things, new gameplay content and features, and that's when the game really starts to shine. You begin to understand what's happenning in the world, and you start treasuring and caring for your companions considerably more than before. At this point I fully accepted the fact that the game was a Visual Novel with a combat twist, and having this in my mind made me love Pyre even more. That's where the whole Pyre experience becomes very rich, the amazing soundtrack blending with the beautiful artstyle and story, everything just fits together brilliantly.
If you care for actual scoring, here's a humble opinion of mine
Artstyle: 10/10
Soundtrack: 10/10
Story: 8.5/10
Characters: 8.5/10
Gameplay: 7/10 (higher if you accept this is a Visual Novel, which is something very different from previous Supergiant titles.)

You try close betas and then open beta. And you are still thrilled about this concept.
You can see flaws and wrong decisions, but you know this is closed beta and theres still months before release. So you dont think about it.
In open beta you find out, there is nothing new added and much of the game still broken in same way.
You think, the lack of content is normal in beta, after all its to test not experience full game content. And that is correct thinking.
You think that the bugs, weirdness and no servers are still part of beta. They are about to fix them right? They dont have servers, because its beta not full product, it will be in the game later right?
. You had fun in betas, so full game must be even better. You wanna experience the full load not being restricted by beta boundaries.
And then a truck driving 200km/h strikes into your home and smashes you into next dimension.
You see that its exactly same as is beta.
Same stupid menu.
Same P2P connection solution.
Same low rewards for matches.
Same mods.
Same boring faction wars.
But you jump back to your dimension with your last breath, becouse you still believe in that good gameplay.
And if you close your eyes, the gameplay is good, really fun and good.
For the next 30 hours.
After the 30 hours you start to realize something. You like your main hero, he is fun, but now you wanna make him unique, to stand out.
But you cant, because after 30, 40, 50 hours, your hero will look the same as others. Becouse there no customization variants. Every hero has 3 "set" variants which looks kinda same. Want more sets? Try play 70 hours with the same hero, to get 4th set, which is just recolor of the default hero look. Want one more set? Maybe after 90 hours ...
After this time, you would expect to have maybe 10 sets and mix them to make unique look. Not here. No matter how many "mirror" matches you will have, you will look the same as the other guy with same hero.
But but ... the gameplay is still pretty good eh?
It was on the start before you played more than 30 hours. After this time, you will face the real problems of game mechanics.
People using certain heroes, using infinity combos which are harder to avoid and if you do, its matter of time, before they will initate this infinite combo.
But what about other heroes without these combos?
After the time, new breed of players will appear. These players will stay passive, not attacking you. Because they wait for you to attack and when you do, they parry you and punish you with unavoidable damage. And they will do this until end of match.
And we are not even speaking about people expoliting ways in certain heroes, that allows them to bend mechanics.
And if this is not what ruins your gameplay experience, dont forget about Peer2Peer multiplayer system, where errors, synchronization rollbacks and disconnects are more than you would expect in non indie game in 2017.
And there you are, you have +- 60 hours of gameplay.
You sit there thinking.
Connection is bad.
Life improving features nonexistent.
Gameplay is bad and boring.
And then you notice one more thing that you did not notice.
Ingame currency.
The slow gaining ingame currency, people can buy for real money and then buy a lot of gear to get advantage in more than half of mods.
And there goes ingame economics being bad.
We could continue talking and talking about these things, but theres not enaugh space here.
So lets make it simple for those who dont like to read.
- Gameplay is fun first 10 to 30 hours.
- Movement physics is great.
- Graphic looks good.
- Gameplay is toxic, boring and broken after +-30 hours (Explanation: People start to use exploits and unbalanced combos)
- Gameplay is still buggy and not polished.
- Main menus, aftermatch menus and etc.
- 4v4 mods are Pay2Win.
- Very low customization.
- Unbalanced matchmaking.
- Peer2Peer connection only. (Bringing a lot of issues with latencies and reaction times)
- Reputation system with no real rewards. (Every 20 lvl you get 1 reputation level. 1 rep lvl takes about 20 hours, theres 20 rep lvl in the game for each hero)
- Sometimes nonresponsive controls.
No
Only if Ubisoft wakes up and repairs all of this.
And so far, after two weeks after release, there have been no repair so far.

NOTE: This review is from April 2015. I don't see myself updating it and haven't played the game much since then so this review most likely does not reflect everything in its current state.
Survarium is an attempt at reviving the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series, which they are doing in an MMOFPS format. This attempt is a brave one and so far the game is decent for a beta.
When you first login, you go through a little tutorial that shows you the very basics of Survarium. After the tutorial you choose either the Scavangers or the Black Market faction. Once one of these factions is at level five, you can then start progressing into the other two factions: The Renaissance Army and The Fringe Settlers. You can switch between these factions at any time and in next update there will be no prerequisite to join the other two factions. Each faction has its own unique gear you can unlock and buy with the regular in-game currency, which is Rubles. Gear can also be attained via random drop at the end of a match.
Separate from faction levels, there are also character levels. Each level you will need 250XP more than the previous, to advance to the next level. Each time you level up, you get a skill point which can be put into the two available skill trees. There will be a total of five skill trees in the future. Currently, the maximum character level that can be attained is 100, however, when the other three skill trees become available, this number will increase to 500.
Currently there is one game mode called "PVP" which hosts 16 players in total, two teams of eight. This PVP game mode has three sub-modes in it which are:
There are plans to introduce “free game” mode which will feature a large-scale map. Co-op modes have also been confirmed. All game modes are session-based and will not feature hundreds of players on one map. I’m not sure how I feel about this but I have confidence that Vostok Games will do it right.
There are quite a few people that think this game is pay-to-win. I’m not going to say they are right or wrong but I will give my honest opinion on it.
The premium-account provides you with one extra profile slot, +50% experience boost towards character level, +50% reputation towards faction rank, and +50% Rubles income from matches.
Premium itself is actually fairly cheap. One-year premium is 5,000 gold, which is $50 USD. This is quite reasonable considering your average MMO subscription fee is $15 USD a month which would end up around $180 USD per annum. Mind you, you do not have to buy a year at a time. You can purchase premium in increments of 24 hours, three days, a week, a month, three months, six months or the year mentioned before. So far I purchased three-day premium once for 120 gold which translates into $1.20 USD.
Premium guns however, are quite expensive and don’t offer any advantage that is worth that price. Premium guns do not alter damage of the weapon but have boosts like +10% fire rate or +10% reload speed. I think this is a quite reasonable approach to combat the pay-to-win stereotypes.
I should also mention that without spending any real money, you can get these same +10% boosts on your weapons by upgrading them. They just won’t have the skins that the premium guns do.
Overall, this is a humble approach to a free-to-play MMOFPS. If you are expecting a polished game then you will be disappointed, but if you embrace the fact that this is still a beta, with a small development team which for the time being will mean a long development process, then you just might enjoy it.
Survarium is worth a try, it is free after all and it deserves more people in its community. Go ahead and install it. What’s the worst that will happen? You’ll actually like the game?

I love this game, had it and the first KOTOR on Original Xbox as a kid. Due to this game's development and publishing being rushed though, it was always left unfinished, with pieces of the story being left out of its official release. Since then though, The Sith Lords Restored Content Modification has restored all "cut content" that was meant to be put into the game by the devs, but didn't by the official release of it. Due to an unfinished game however, most people liked the first game more, still like the first game more. Despite its flaws at release, and especially now with the restored content, I have always, and will always love TSL sequel more than the original. The first game's story and the characters your player encounters is definitely top notch compared to the sequel, but this game has gameplay mechanics that push it over the top for me. The amount of Force Powers without bringing mods into the picture, is substantially much more by comparison. The difference between the first game, and half your party being Jedi naturally, compared to this game, where you can work towards strengthening your relationship with each party member, and then eventually are able to train them as Jedi/Dark Jedi... that's an amazing distinction, and provides a reward system for getting to know your party members, their personalities, their backstories, etc. In the first game, I would seldom talk to anyone on a regular basis other than Carth and Bastila, who always ended up as my main "crew." With this game, going to each character's "quarters" is both a story-heavy encounter every single time, but also always another nudge in the greater progress towards training a new force user. THAT is why TSL will always keep me coming back, even after 300+ hours of playtime, despite a full playthrough only taking 20-30 hours, depending on how well you know the story and any of its "surprises." That's how much I love this game, I have invested at least 10 separate playthroughs on PC alone. Give it a chance, you won't be disappointed. Trust me.

As a huge dinosaur fan, I was drawn to the Isle the moment it appeared on Steam. I got it as soon as possible. I loved it. Dinosaurs everywhere! The game had, at the time, many species to play as. Now it has several new species added, with more to come. It was fun to try out the different dinosaurs and try different playstyles.
This was, of course, before the progression system was added. I'm going to be completely honest: the progression system has its flaws right now. It takes forever to progress, and when you do, it is incredibly frustrating when you lose all your progress due to being killed in a cheap manner or because of a server crash. I won't deny that.
There's been a lot of negative feedback towards the progression system, but the problem with that is that the progression system is still in development. To respond to it in such a way now is like saying that a phone halfway through production is trash. If you hate the game because of how broken it is, remember that you got it in early access. Of course there will be bugs, and certain features may not be up to par. The developers made it early access so that we could provide feedback in a constructive way, instead of attacking the devs for not doing it right. If you hate on the Isle because of the bugs and flaws in the progression system, then you shouldn't have gotten it when it was offered as early access.
I like where the devs are going. Sure, right now it is buggy, but it's still in development, with more to come. If you have not bought the Isle yet, then wait. Check the updates. Watch videos. See how it is going. The devs usually update the game after a couple of days. Check it then. For example, they recently added a new dinosaur. Though this doesn't happen every time the game updates, it is still a sign that improvements are being made.
If, when the full game is released, these flaws are still increasingly apparent, then I will change my review. But I feel that most of that will change. I hold on to hope for the Isle. I see its potential. If you don't like it, then wait. Slowly but surely, the wrongs will be be made right.

I've not been too far in the game (chara lvl21 max so far), but i have the feeling this game should be considered at many points!
In term of atmosphere mostly. The Unreal Engine 3 is not really pushed to its best in Nether, but it adds some effects worth the effort. Talking truth, this game is so far the only that made me really think of a cursed world, fallen to monsters, creepy in every place. The work on Sound in Nether is nice, the empty streets had never been so horribly alive, thanks to the far aways moanings and the wind. With it, the particles system (newspaper flying around) and the grass movement gets it right.
So, I can assure you this game is one of the most immersive survival I ever played.
Now in term of gameplay, it's all good, classic i'd say. You can prone, crouch, run, sprint, jump etc. You have no cursor, so you need ironsight to aim. That adds difficulty and realism. Still, the gameplay is too shy.
I'd enjoy being able to throw a rock to make diversion, being able to use a "kick" to push ennemies or make them fall. A slide could be useful too (with an compatible level design). And finally revising the tchat system which is not beginner-friendly.
I like the fact this game has no vehicle system because of the mess in the streets.
The quest system is fine, but there again, too shy. You can only pick up pakcages from one town to another and that's it. There are no "wild" NPC in the games, nobody you can come across, giving you missions you didn't plan to do. It would make the game more dynamic. Yes there are escort Missions, but it needs more stuff to make this game content interesting.
There are also "events", like assault or town defense. These are entertaining.
And finally the loots are well balanced, not too much, not to few, they come right at times.
The skill tree is a nice idea even if you can't really tell what has changed directly. But the good point is that it's not too big, you can get it all quite fastly and the rest of your survival is up to your experience.
Well now Nether has a lot to work with until it gets a real game. Starting with the realisation. 80% of the environnement has no collision and you can walk through most objets, even walls sometime!
Then they gotta fix the overall character animations. They look like they don't belong to this game at all, nor human race... terrible animation work.
The interfaces when you trade an NPC are so bad. I know it's not the most important point, but it's not good looking, nor easy to use.
As a personnal request i wish there was various dynamic climates or weather events, like hell rain, burning days (mirage effect), or storm (push you while moving outdoor).
And in priority, as i'm a PVP hater, I'd enjoy a PVE server list, where you can't hurt other players, but passing by or giving help.
Nether makes me think of "Tom Clancy's The Division" in an indy way.

As of late, the 2D platforming genre has seen a bit of a resurgence, especially in indie games like Super Meat Boy, I Wanna Be The Guy and to a lesser extent in more high-profile titles New Super Mario Bros. and the like. Rayman Legends, the sequel to 2011's reboot of the Rayman series, Rayman Origins, is one such platformer, and quite possibly one of the best in its genre.
Rayman Legends, like its predecessor, is very simple in terms of its gameplay: Run, jump and punch your way through each of the levels, rescuing the small, fairy-like Teensies (who replace Origins' Electoons) as you go. It's actually quite a good thing the gameplay is this simple, because this game's difficulty is certainly not to be sniffed at. On some of the Challenge levels in particular it might take someone many different tries to get past a particular area of the game, and whilst at first this may seem aggravating there's no feeling quite like finally completing that ONE level. Another interesting addition is the Murfy mechanic - whilst playing, the player can use Murfy to guide their character through the level, by for instance moving platforms or distracting enemies, adding a little variety to the gameplay whilst still retaining the simplicity that makes it so enjoyable. There are also additional characters, but the differences are mostly cosmetic and don't change the gameplay, though in all honesty this is more to the game's benefit, since the gameplay is OK as it is, and doesn't really need any different character abilities to make it any better.
Also like Origins, Legends' story is barebones, quite possibly to the overall game's benefit. Not focusing much on the story means that the player can divert their attention to actually enjoying the gameplay and uniquer art style, which are the game's main points.
I have but two overarching criticisms of this version, however: First of all, the implementaion of the uPlay DRM system, even on the Steam version, which is unnecessary and cumbersome. Second: This game was clearly meant for the Wii U, a fact that shows as you play the game. I thought that maybe the Wii U's features would transfer more easily to the PC, but unfortunately Ubisoft didn't really take advantage of the keyboard ands mouse in the same way they took advantage of the Wii U's gamepad. Actions formerly performed by the player themselves as Murfy on the Touch Pad are now performed with a single touch of a button on the controller, which if you ask me is a bit of a missed opportunity.
To summarise, despite clearly being designed for the Wii U, Rayman Legends is the best anyone could ask from a platforming game. It's challenging, it has funny characters, enjoyable levels, it doesn't focus too much on the plot, and most importantly - It will keep you entertained for a VERY long time. Yes, it can get very, VERY difficult, but as you play it, you realise that that's the whole point: Trial and error, improving with every failed attempt, slowly but surely perfecting your strategy. And it's exactly that that makes Rayman Legends special.

Alpha Prime is a first person shooter set primarly within the titular facility, Alpha Prime. The game is something like a cross between Red Faction and Quake 4, but not nearly as good as either one.
Visuals - The graphics are definitely one of the game's strongpoints. It looks great, and I really don't have anything to say against it.
Story - The story is lame and entirely forgettable. Honestly, I hardly cared about what was even going on in the story while playing. It's the same guy-gets-sent-to-abandoned-facility-to-investigate-and-then-gets-trapped scenario we've seen countless times. Several characters are met, they try to work together to find a way off the asteroid, trust is questioned, relationships are strained, lame villain goes after artifact of mystical power, obvious traitor is revealed, etc. The characters are forgettable, and the writing is particularly awful, often leaving me staring slack-jawed at the screen wondering what the game was even trying to convey to me. It can certainly lead to some amusing cutscenes and dialogue, though. It's kinda one of those "so bad its good" things, except rather than "so bad its good", it's more "so bad it's passable and just enough to keep the game moving forward."
Sound - Mixed bag here. Let's go over the voice acting first: It's awful, but in a hilarious way. Some of the conversations heard in the game can be amusing just because of how poor the writing and acting is, and Livia's voice constantly sounds like it's coming over a communication device, even if she's in the same room as you are, which I found very strange. On the other hand, the music is actually quite good, especially in the later levels. The good tracks usually start playing when enemies are sighted and you start shooting, and they do a good job of getting you immersed into the action.
Gameplay - For the most part, it's typical FPS fare. Most levels are spent traversing rooms and corridors gunning down enemies, hitting a switch to open a door nearby, etc. The game is very linear, levels are a fairly straight path for the most part, with the exception of a few very small detours to hit a switch, or pick up and replace a broken circuit. There are 7 or 8 different weapons, and you'll find yourself with the full arsenal fairly quickly. Health does not regenerate, and you must find medkits or use med-stations on the walls to heal yourself (If you've played Quake 4, it's exactly like that) You have a hacking device which allows you to gain access to various machines that are within range, including cameras, gun turrets and even mines. Unfortunately, your chances to use it on anything besides cameras are few and far between, so its usefulness is fairly limited. This was an interesting idea that they could have done a lot more with. Some people have knocked the game for being very difficult, but those people simply don't know how to play. The enemy accuracy is EXTREMELY high, even at a good distance, they will likely hit you dead-on, and running into a room full of enemies guns-a-blazing is suicide. As I played, though, I discovered the usefulness of the lean function. By hiding behind cover and leaning out to shoot, enemy accuracy was pretty much cut in half. I took far less damage this way and it made the rest of the game fairly easy to complete. The game also has a bulletime function, which slows down the action and can help a bit, but I personally didn't use it too much. Thankfully, the controls won't be adding to your death total, because the game's controls are tight, aside from one of the late levels where you have to drive a vehicle across outdoor terrain. The controls felt slightly delayed, and the game wasn't lagging at all, everything was playing a top speed. I adjusted quickly, however, and this is the only level that has this. Another problem is that the collision detection between you and objects is a bit wonky. There are a few parts where you must jump over crates or onto other objects, and your character will be struggling to get over them as something seemingly pushes him back. Thankfully, moments like this are relatively few, so it's only an occasional annoyance. The game is also very short, clocking in at around 5 hours, though with the game's forgettable story and characters, I honestly see the short length as a positive rather than a negative.
Final - Alpha Prime is, overall, a fairly mixed bag. Great visuals, mostly functional controls, good music, but completely forgettable story, lame characters, very short length and pretty much no replay value whatsoever. If you look past the horrible story and characters, the game will provide some decent entertainment for a few hours. If the game was any higher than its asking price of $4.99, I wouldn't be able to recommend it because it's certainly not worth any more than that. I recommend either playing the demo to make sure you'll enjoy it before dropping the 5, or just wait for a discount and get it for a buck or two.

This is actually the best game I have ever played, It is so fun and the story is great so is the combat, I will break down the review into several parts.
Combat: The combat in this game is  fun and amazing, you get to hit people with the left mouse button but to make things more interesting is that there is a variety of weapons and durability for each weapon, you can go ranged by throwing weapons or shooting arrows from your bow, or you can roll  or use a shield to block impacts from ranged attacks and get up close and personal, it's a simple yet fun way to kill also blood is in the game.
Story: Similar to god of war, the story is that Zeus and the gods who follow him are destroying earth,but it's much deeper than that, you are trying to stop Zeus and the other gods from destroying the beloved earth, it hooks you into the game as there is plaques that teach you  ancient greek history.
Graphics:  Beautiful  ancient greek art style, (The one you'd commonly see on greek vases) it is amazing and yet immersive, the color use is amazing, usually the NPC's who are red , are either your enemies or someone who can die.
Mechanics: The game is deeper than Melee attacks and Ranged attacks, you can craft  health potions, Kill guards and pay the fee of commiting a crime or continue your massarce, you can find better armor, find tools to unlock doors (lockpicks, it auto picks) and Climb as it's a 2D platformer.
2D action adventure platformer, with very minimal RPG mechanics (perhaps paying the guards is the only RP I'm only 40 minutes in) and a fun Online mode where you can kill bots, and online players.
There is boss battles in this game as well and a map so you won't get lost, it's a fun game, being 40 minutes in, I can easily say it's a 8/10.

i ended up liking the game.
so here is my honest review.
now, as some may know, violette summers is based on a real life british spy named violette szabo. here a link to read about her:
it did make me wonder why they have changed the last name but i guess due her history that she was caught in her second mission and executed, would have been problematic from a historical point of view and maybe also due possible lawsuit issues.
now to the game it self. lets start with the pros and cons of the game.
cons:
- the AI has its dumb moments. (will mention it a bit later)
- repetitive remarks from the enemies.
- the shooting can be at times frustrating. especially the last mission. (will go in to detail later as well)
- at times enemies know where you are, even when hiding in the dark.
- HUBs dont really allow you to go around enemies. forceful confrontation is required.
- the protagonists character is not explained at all.

pros:

- great atmosphere.
- beautiful lightening.
- graphics are beautiful as well.
- the german enemies speak actual german (which should be expected since the company is from germany).
- the enemies have at times interesting and funny conversations.
- the english subtitles are very well translated. (i know german).
- it has its challenging moments.
- change costumes to walk among the enemy. (but has its cons as well)
- upgrading system.
- the game requires you to be careful.
- you can lure enemies in to the dark by whistling.
- peak through keyholes.
ok, now to the nit picky stuff.
as i said; the AI has its dumb moments. even when coming across a body, they will look around but then they stop and keep patrolling their fixed root like nothing happened. they dont call for backup or report it, nothing. also, most of the time they know exactly where you are when alarmed, even when hiding in the dark without making a peep or doing anything that would get their attention. and im not talking about enemies who clearly saw me making a mistake, even those who come later to the party where everyone is dead and they still see you in the dark. their weapons already aim in your direction even when a wall, crate is in their field of view. but shoot of course once there is no obstacle in their way.
in one mission when being inside the gestapo building, the enemies spotted me when i was looking through a keyhole to see if the area is clear for me to walk out. for some reason, the soldier who walks past the door was suddenly alarmed and pointed his gun at the door. also oddly he and the others, who were a floor below, never bothered to enter the room i was in. or the the once below bothering to come up. also when being on the catwalk, the enemy below was alarmed since i walked exactly above him. nothing really happened since i was above him and generally invincible since i was wearing a SS uniform. thats a mechanic that could have been looked in too.
which leads me to the change of costumes.
its a plus of course but it has its downside as well that you cant be too close to the enemies. you have a depleting bar when you get too close to an enemy. if you are too close, you get recognized as a spy. i sure would have no complaints if a good looking woman (and she sure looks good in a uniform) comes close to me. like to know how every enemy would know every single female SS officer. would make maybe sense with officers but not some random soldier. you have no chance of being stealthy either.
the shooting mechanic has its moments as well.
especially the last mission you are forced to shoot instead of being stealthy. her accuracy is not always good. but these of the enemies are very precise and can hit you from a distance with a 98% success rate. also it gave me the impression that an enemy can handle a few shots and the other can handle half a magazine. so the ending led to some very frustrating outbursts.
the reloading can be very frustrating as well. you must wait for the counter to display that it is full. if you start changing weapons or put the weapon away, it will not count as a reload. even when she clearly has finished it visually, you must wait a second for it to be displayed.
so much for the picky parts.
now to the parts why i ended up liking the game, even after mentioning a lot of the bad things of the game.
the stealth was very solid and you get immersed quickly. stabbing the enemy did not get old. she kills them in different ways like putting a bullet through their heads, stabbing them between the legs, slicing their throats, and stabbing them repeatably which are all visually very violent.
the game requires you to be careful and i just had to laugh when reading from others that the "checkpoints are too far away". i never thought they are too far away. they were placed very well. if you rush it, of course you will have issues. you have to be careful and observe the enemies what they are doing and then take them out one by one. avoid using the firearm since you will need it by the end of every mission to shoot your way out.
the missions are diverse. so not only "kill this guy and kill that guy". you have to find an fallen agent (and the ending of this mission is not what you expect) or plant a bomb.
also the germans speak actual german and was amusing at times listening to them. since i know german, after growing up in the german speaking part of switzerland, the repetitive remarks they have are these:
Hoffentlich kommt bald die Ablösung. - hopefull the replacement comes soon.
'nen Schanpps wär jetzt gut. - a schnapps would be good now.
So viel Spannung is es ja kaum auszuhalten. - so much tension is excruciating.
Hier passiert ja so wie so nichts. - nothing really happens here.
Und wer macht jetzt den Dreck wieder weg? - and who is cleaning up this mess?
Hab sie erwischt. - i got her.
Sieht nicht gar nicht mal so schlecht aus. Das Luder. - doesnt even look that bad. the minx.
thats pretty much it.
the locations are visually impressive to look at. some of them can be a bit dull but you are in a ghetto, sewers, prison complex, church, catacombs, a huge garden or a village.
also you see some graphic scenes as well like dead civilians lie around, hanging from trees, being burned. and children are among them too. so this alone creates a very intense atmosphere. plus the very well made dynamic lighting add more to these scenes.
even when violette at times looks like a plastic doll, so as some enemies, but since you will see her mainly from the back (which is a nice looking back) and the HUBs as such looks really impressive, i think i can close an eye on that little feature.
the gameplay is solid and works really well with M&K. it displays the M&K buttons, you can customize the layout to your liking but as mentioned before; for some reason you cant operate the menu with a mouse.
so over all, if you like a solid stealth game, have patience and can see away from the bad feature i have mentioned, you might find some enjoyment from this game which i think has been underrated.

Example:  Not being able to craft or find rope in the first hour of gameplay makes everything else you do pretty useless. It's random, so if you're unlucky, it's back to the family creation screen.
And that deer you snared? Can't slaughter it, because you can't store the meat. No-one mentioned you needed a fridge to even be able to tear into that juicy sack of meat.
Never mind that your family is starving and could likely devour the deer alive, ripping it apart with their bare hands if they had to. No, this is a fancy family. We have standards.
They will perish before dirtying their hands to dig in to some nice deer steak. And where would we store the meat after we've had our fill, huh? What? In a crate, temporarily, until we eat it within a reasonable timeframe? Don't be ridiculous, this is an apocalypse! Why create food safety issues when you can just starve? Why, we've already been defecating in a bucket that we wash out with our bare hands, but leaving meat out for a day? No way. That's taking it way too far. What if the dog's hair gets on it?
I mean, we poop in a bucket and smash people's brain in for a can of grub, but there's no fridge! What's the point of living if there's no fridge?
So let's not mention the deer to them. We'll watch our children die slowly. It's better this way.

We could use some rope to make it faster... oh wait, we can't. We couldn't find any.

(You could probably eat the bodies of your starved family. Can't touch the deer, though. I didn't wait for that option to come up.)
Anyway, I'll probably play it again, but I'm not much of a sucker for punishment when it's not ... deserved, and instead random.

Friday the 13th is the rare asymmetric game that "gets it."  Sometimes, losing is fun, and dying at the hands of a decent Jason Vorhees player is sometimes quite satisfying, especially if you managed to hold hiim off from slaughtering the others while they escape in a car or even just to the next cabin over.
Jason has monsterously dangerous powers, but even as overpowered as he is when compared to an individual counselor, all it takes is a bit of coordination and teamwork and he can be outlasted and outmatched in different ways.  The game absolutely rewards working together as counselors, or being wise enough to leave the stealthy ones alone and don't draw attention to them while they complete tasks and objectives.
Sure, server issues really hurt the launch, but that stuff is smoothing out nicely and I haven't had an issue in days.  Also, yes, there are bugs and glitches, but those are very minor in my experience and will certainly be patched out over time.  Nothing that really impacts gameplay on a regular basis.
A lot of people are complaining about Jason being overpowered with "shift/grab" but honestly a competent set of counselors will not lose to Jason.  Some people will die every round, but a clean sweep is almost unheard of if you've played any amount at all.  It's Friday the 13th after all, most of the time someone gets away and a lot of people die.
Other folks are complaining about the Savini Jason being DLC only offered prior to launch if you backed/kickstarted the game.  I commend Gun Media for sticking to their promise that Savini Jason would not be offered again, it was available for over a year and plenty of people paid for it.  It is honorable for a company to keep their word, and I think the folks who are complaining and slamming the game for it aren't being objective.
This game is vastly more fun than Dead By Daylight, which I do say I also enjoy.  I think though Gun really nailed the feel of playing the films here and making it fun.  Absolutely recommend.

I've been playing sheltered for quite awhile and have put in a good bit of game time. It's a fun, quirky survival game that really stands out due to its nature. Overall a very good game and I recommend it to anyone into the survival genre, it can be incredibly dark (Raiders killing even children, the family pet dying, etc.) or be kind of comical (With some of the other survivor's interactions or as they walk by the shelter.) I've found this game to be throughly enjoyable.
Let's get to it then!
Pros:
- Great overall idea and conveyance.
- Graphically pleasing for a 2D pixel game!
- The difficulty is based on generated luck! (Which is just awesome!)
- You have control over where almost everything is in the shelter and even some stuff on the surface!
- While not everything is fully customizable you can paint the walls a variety of colors and build quite a few floors to house your stuff.
- While not all pets seem super useful (Goldfish) many are. (Dog aids in combat, Horse makes exploration a bit easier, Cat handles mouse population which also provides food, and the snake also eats rats.)
- Pretty realistic in the sense of "It's not just a game" no one is safe and all of your little family can die leaving stress and trauma in their wake for the remaining members.
-A pretty large area to explore and gather resources, food, etc.
Cons:
-The area, while being fairly large, doesn't seem to be quite big enough to continue gameplay after you've discovered everything (Mostly this causes the game to get a little bit boring in the exploration aspect, yes you still run into other survivors but the spark of exploration at that point is really gone.)
- The game doesn't really have an end game. You get all of the achievements, fix up the van, discover all of the locations... and then you become self-sufficient and upgrade everything and at that point there's nothing left to do.
- Putting together the van takes too long. (I know it's based on luck, but...) I didn't even find the last tyre until I had explored the entire map and had become self-sufficient making the van pretty useless. I feel like van parts should be a little bit easier to find in order to be able to actually have a use for the van.
- The Mysterious Hatch doesn't really open. I've heard a rumor that you have to have a goldfish and count the bubbles for the code to open hatch... If this is true... that's really ridiculous. Why do I have to have a fish as a pet in order to open it. If there's another way I can't find it, and you can spend all day trying different numbers but I've even heard that doesn't work either. I haven't noticed this getting fixed in any later updates.
Overall I really like this game and found the mechanics and gameplay really fun, I just wish there was more to do or more to explore once you finished off the intial map. Otherwise I strongly recommend this game! It's really great!

Beneath a fateful exhibition of stars, an emblematic flame permeates the shroud of night.  Reflective ore imprisons the ambient glow of radiant runes, amidst ominous relics and perilous ruins.  A triumvirate of cloaked aspects materialize, brandishing an ancestral facade, analogous to that of their opponents'.  A lucent beam, thrust from the heavens, materializes into an orb of boundless energy.  Swiftly, the participants surge towards the orb with tenacious fervor and the circuitous dance of the wisps begins...
Forsaken, teetering upon the precipice of demise, you tentatively regain consciousness to find yourself under the scrutiny of a band of ivory masked demons, draped in opulent vestments, adorned with mysterious symbols.  One of the masked figures approaches you, removing his veil to reveal a personable mortal, concerned with preserving your waning existence.  This stranger introduces himself as Hedwyn, as his two cohorts contend the value of salvaging your life.  Devoted to intuition, the compassionate mortal convinces his allies to implicate you in their journey for absolution.
Pyre puts the player in the role of "The Reader," responsible for studying the Book of Rites, as a literate guide to freedom for the Nighthawks; one of nine original Triumvirates, created by the Eight Scribes for the Rites.  Banished to a vast purgatory known as the Downside, for cultural insurrection, you're tasked with directing your team through a series of trials designed to exonerate the supreme victors.  Ripped from the surroundings of the Commonwealth, the overall narrative begins to unfold, as the fate of the world above and below the constellations hangs in the balance.
Stratified lore evokes an insatiable yearning to uncover the mysteries of this dark fantasy, as the player traverses the world through a storybook interface.  Transitions between extensive textual elements and combat establish an intimate dynamic between characters and evoke emotional commitment from players.  Deepening relationships between characters span the moral landscape, cultivating a sense of belonging among misfits.  The game's choice system often forces one to choose between strategic preservation or consequential altruism.  An abundance of diverging story branches, revolving around navigation and character choices, provide ample incentive to play through the campaign multiple times.
Thoughtfully crafted backstories are delicately interwoven within the narrative, driving the core theme of enlightenment through trial and tribulation.  Each interaction between the expansive cast of characters feels fluid and natural, a testament to how comprehensively and cohesively Pyre was written.  Occasionally, the meticulous cultivation of the world results in drawn out text segments, which disrupt the overall pace of the action.
At the core of Pyre's unique experience are the rites: real-time, tactical sport, which pits two groups of three participants against one another, with the aim of extinguishing the opponent's pyre by casting yourself repeatedly into the flame -orb in hand.  The rites serve as the only path to redemption for exiles, desperate to reclaim their place within the Commonwealth.
Commanding narration amplifies the intensity prior to each match, as each team looms beneath a vigorous inferno they must preserve to achieve advancement.  Treacherous chasms, runic shrines and mobile impediments, promote mechanical and visual diversity within each methodically crafted arena.  Frenetic combat is navigated through astute positioning, as the player controls one teammate at a time in a rapid-fire exchange between offensive and defensive transitions.  Simple, yet intuitive core mechanics generate symptomatic moments of competitive euphoria.  Anticipatory maneuvering and clever timing open up holes in your opponents' defenses, in which you can make an attempt at depleting their pyre.  Proper team composition is paramount, and experimenting with each of the games' eight characters' varying aura sizes, abilities and mobility, produces a synergistic experience akin to most MOBAs.  Inventive gameplay, coupled with a practical leveling system, provides sufficient opportunities to implement creative strategies to stamp out your opponents in uniquely fun ways.
Versus mode pits player versus computer or player versus player, in custom matches which allow each participant to select their team composition, their desired soundtrack and stage.  I spent several hours competing against the computer in the early stages of the campaign, developing strategy and honing my proficiency with each character.  While I haven't spent time competing in local versus mode, I assume it has the potential to ruin relationships and cultivate bitter dispositions.
Supergiant Games is well known for the illustrious visual aesthetic of their earlier titles, Transistor and Bastion.  Pyre is no exception, and in many ways transcends the aforementioned titles with the breadth of its detail.  Surreal landscapes are brought to life with vibrant saturation.  Stark contrast between light and dark elements, utilize lush warm hues and soothing indigo; while ethereal lighting illuminates colossal idols, relinquished of their former glory.
Characters are illustrated with muted brushstrokes of flat tones, blending subtlety within each environment. Animations flow seamlessly in conjunction with spell effects exchanged across the battlefield in dazzling splendor.  The sheer volume of animations occurring in the foreground highlight the vigorous pacing of Pyre's gameplay.
Serving as a momentous backdrop for the overall atmosphere is a remarkable soundtrack composed by Darren Korb.  Robust acoustic guitar melodies, layered atop ubiquitous percussion, ebb and flow with spiraling captivation.  Haunting electronic notes transition into whimsical guitar riffs, subtle vocal harmonies and back again with compelling direction.  Korb's ability to merge such a diverse collection of sounds (harpsichord and electric guitar included), is uncanny, and a testament to his artistry.
Verdict 
Pyre combines inventive gameplay, emotive storytelling, alluring visuals and a moving soundtrack into one masterful adventure unlike any other in recent memory.  In an industry saturated with sequels and customary experiences, Pyre oozes originality and inspires imaginative risk.

I think this game gets kind of a bad wrap.
I think that the p2p connection is absolute garbage. But I don't think that this makes the game bad. This is more of a fault on Ubisoft rather than the developer.
The gameplay is much deeper than I expected it to be, it is sort of the "Rock, Paper, Scissors" type of combat that the reviewers tell us about, but the rock has a sheet of paper and the paper has a rock and the scissors have a sheet of paper and they all catch of fire when used in a correct combo. It really allows someone who knows what they are doing to kick some♥♥♥♥♥
Game modes are pretty diverse. However I don't see why dominion is the most popular. I do like the idea of it but ganging up and getting ganged up on makes the mode less than ideal. The real meat of the game lies in the 1v1s, 2v2s, and elimination mode. There is an unspoken sense of honor in these modes, I have seen bad mannered players but more than often people are very polite and will let two players fight it out. This sense of honor is completely absent in the dominion mode.
The campaign is average. Thats all I have to say about it. Don't bother.
The micro transactions are stupid. They are not required to win at the game. Half of their reason is for cosmetics.
I dislike the way that item progression works. You can eventually max out those bars that are labeled "stamina regen" and "revenge gain" which I don't have a problem with, but if they want to have a system like this then they should fix matchmaking so that gear levels have to be within five levels of your opponent. A lv 96 gear lv against a lv 32 gear lv is not a fair fight. Plus that would punish people who bought their way up to people that actually know how to play the game and have earned it.
The game is good, if you like weighty combat of dark souls then you should buy it.
If you like the complex and deep combos and counters of fighting games then you should buy it.
If you are neither, then don't bother.

I'll be giving this a solid 8/10.
I'm not into the whole beta access thing etc, bar a few MMOs,  so I dont know how much more work is getting put into this game before it's considered finsihed. But as it stands the game is an incredibly fun, fast paced yet still tactical game that any fps gamer or certainly any post-apoc genre fan should give a go.
The maps are interesting, expansive, good fun to explore and master with countless bottlenecks, sniping positions and storming points for players of all preferences to master; the weather changes and this has a vast effect on the maps themselves, forcing players to adapt. They include anomalies and radiation zones, poison clouds and all other manner of environmental forces that, when coupled with beartraps of thoughtful positioning make for a real challenge.
The Character customisation is a dream for the more rolaplying, kit orientated players (like myself). the choice is finite, albeit within four factions, two of which are open at the beginning of the game. select your gun, your clothing and kit, and off you go. it's quick, but in depth enough that you get the feel of a proper loadout. there are masses of guns and armour throughout the reputation stages, unlocked and then bought by grinding rep and currency. The end tier stuff looks amazing to me, which makes me want to continue playing.
The actual FPS capabilities of the game are very good. its well balanced and matched well to the maps, meaning everyone can play their own style, be it support, sniper or assault. its twitchy, visceral and VERY lethal, very realisitic. reminiscent of red orchestra, if not identical. you can attempt to heal yourself through kit, but honestly one shot is enough to have you scrambling back to cover and praying you dont bleed out. the gun sound effects are crisp and if you are carfeul you can tell which way battle or enemies lie which is a plus.
graphically, I found it a touch grainy regardless of a settings change; that said it doesnt look awful at all. it just means that at extreme distances it becomes hard to aim at enemies because thy begin to blur and pixxelate.
The 8/10 reflects that I would like to see more armour choices and perhaps physical customisation impemented, like bein able to choose items like knives or "trophies" to attach at points to your character. It also reflects that It has begun to become a bit stale after only a few hours of play, the fact being that ive ecplored a lot of the content that the game offers even after such a short time playing.

Why has nobody ever told me about these games?! I just bought the M&M bundle a couple days ago and started with this game. I'd only every played Dark Messiah, and that was not at all what I expected (see my review). I thought Heroes was going to be similar to Warlords: Battlecry or Warcraft. I couldn't have been more wrong.
The only thing this game has in common with Warcraft is the fantasy setting Warcraft is an RTS; M&M is a turn-based wargame with RPG elements. You start the game with one hero, who has a small army attached to her (like twenty troops or something). You run your hero around the map, picking stuff up and claiming buildings for your team. When you get into a battle, you get whisked away to a battle board where you play out a strategic turn-based battle.
The controls are so intuitive that there are times I can't figure something out. Them I DO figure it out and I'm like "oh. I didn't think it could be that simple."
I can't wait to play M&M 6, and I can't wait to play the two expansion packs for this game.
My advice: remove your head for a few hours and play this game. It's very easy to play, and there is a decent tutorial.

As a casual player I liked this game a lot: A God-of-War-like plot, classic platforming, a great variety of arms and enemies (though I hated all dog-like creatures, as I do in every game) and nearly everything of your heart's desire (if you're into platformers) apart from platforming challenges (as you can find them e.g. in Ori and the Blind Forest) make it really a great game. What I probably liked best was that every bossfight had its very own gimmick, so you don't just hit and roll and rinse and repeat all over hoping you can finally kill the boss and then do the same thing all over again with the next one, no, the devs have been really creative in designing customized bossfights (Yet Poseidon is a tough nut to crack and also the pre-final fight against Zeus packs a punch, but all the others are less difficult. Personally I liked best the fight for the Aegis of Athena, since in my eyes it's the most creative one and the reward one of the most useful in the entire game). Also the difficulty level is absolutely acceptable: It's neither too hard nor too easy, even on Olympian difficulty it absolutely remains playable and does not even become as difficult as e.g. Salt and Sanctuary ordinarily is. All in all a fantastic game.
But being a classicist, I was really impressed and astonished, downright fascinated of how meticulously precise the ancient greek art, culture and especially literature were respected in this game: Kudos to the devs for their dedication. (Warning: There are spoilers in the following, so unless you are keen on learning, how great their attainments actually are, do not continue reading.)
Throughout the world there are steles at some places, often before boss-fights or in front of doors and entrances, with excerpts of ancient literature written on them (translated into English of course), so it was quite fun for me to test myself, if I could identify the origin of the text correctly (like e.g. Hesiod's Theogony, Homer's Iliad, The Homeric Hymns, Apollonios' Argonautika, Euripides' Bacchae and so on), and sometimes I even knew the greek original by heart.
Moreover, the acting deities are sometimes addressed with their classical epithets, so for instance Thetis presents herself as "silver-footed" and Hera is called "cow-eyed" by Zeus in the final sequence, which indeed might be one of the greatest attainments of the devs: The scientific state of the art claims that "cow-eyed" is only used when a somewhat negative connotation should be conveyed, while in neutral situations Hera is more likely styled as "white-elbowed", and in the very situation in the game, where Zeus calls Hera his "cow-eyed queen", he vituperates her for treason.
Also the ancient architecture is respected with utmost dedication: Doric columns don't have plinths, Ionian and Corinthian columns have flattened canellures, the Corinthian capitals are precisely well modeled and no mere arbitrary accumulation of acanthus ornaments (like in GoW e.g.). What I really found impressive was that some buildings had pediments on top of them, which are copied from actual pediments of actual greek temples like the western pediment of the Aphaia-temple of Aigina or the eastern pediment of the Zeus-temple of Olympia, which - in fact - was the only place throughout the entire game, where I could find a (though neglegible) blooper: Some of the pedimental sculptures are in the "wrong" place respecting the state of the art of reconstruction, since the game uses the constellation proposed by Laeschke-Treu-Furtwängler, where Pelops stands on the same side as Sterope, which does not make any sense, because the topic of the pediments of Olympia is marriage, wherefore Pelops has to stand next to his wife Hippodameia and Oinomaos next to Sterope (which corresponds to the proposal of Hirschfeld-Kekulé). Also the ornaments used in the game like palmettes, frets, stylized flowers, etc. are without exception genuinely ancient.
Another great allusion to literature was that before fighting Ares you'd have to defeat Diomedes first in order to obtain his spear, which is the only weapon that could wound Ares, since it already has done so once: This occasion was in the fifth book of Homer's Iliad during the great aristeia of Diomedes (one of my personal favourites among the individual scenes of the Iliad).
Generally speaking, this is what I could find out in two playthroughs, but I suppose there might be even more details hidden in the game I have not yet found, so it will always be interesting to start a new game, since I do not yet know, what I might find out that time. The cultural details and allusions are exceptionally precise and I am more than impressed of the developers' dedication, since those are things you can't find in any old primer, but they really require a profound and thorough knowlegde of antiquity and at times even a consulting of scientific literature.
I absolutely do recommend this game, since it's fun playing and even greater fun inquiring all the details.

The storyline is sort of bland: Arnold, your silver fox, body builder, genius badass is mining a mysterious radioactive ore on some planet in some fictional universe with humans. He is the only one not being driven mad and so you have to shoot your way out of the space ship and blah blah standard Sci-Fi FPS.
Spoilers ahead???
The differences: Oxygen depletion happens when you're not in a sealed structure or breathing directly through an oxygen mask on a wall. When outside, you have to move quickly and get to the next oxygen mask to strategically plan your next move. You can also save at any time and will probably need to do that a lot because of how often you die. There are a standard set of guns, although the flamethrower is sort of sadly useless... There are some cool tech gadgets, where you can hack cameras and mines through the walls before entering a room. Some missions require you to carry [giant] batteries with you to restore power to doors and such. So overall although they did mix it up and add some spice to the gameplay, its still primarily an (almost) outdated FPS.
The storyline is lacking, but certainly has some [randomly] brash lines, and decent voice acting. The protagonist has solid voice acting actually, in fact, one of the better voices I've heard considering the lines he was reading were complete♥♥♥♥♥♥half of the time. Some of the other characters sound like they read one line per day with the same inflection and different words, particularly the foreign guy without much experience in English.
The most memorable and worthy lines of the game, that convinced me to keep playing during a hard and honestly boring part:
"Arnold, you'll have to hold them off just a little bit longer!!!", says the other character while he was hacking a computer-motherboard-mainframe-core-system to save both of their lives.
"Why? So you can finish surfing porn?" Arnold is a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and a badass even when a tech guru is saving his life and he is shotgunning 20 dudes at once.
The game is hard, like 2007 hard. I'm saying like you can't just play this game through casually on normal difficulty because people will actually hit you with most of their bullets and rockets (Although, even in the hands of the villain, the flamethrower sucks♥♥♥♥♥unless you're stuck in an elevator with them).
TL;DR:
I know I've just expressed a lot of conflicting like and dislike for this game, but that's how it feels to play it overall, you like it, and then you kind of wish you didn't spend an hour playing it, especially when you forget to save for a half hour and then get smoked by a big fat robot rocket.

It also has a veneer of Frictional's hallmark horror mechanics, basically hide/run from the monster, but this feels like its not a central aspect of the game, they could easily have made Soma as scary as the dark decent but clearly chose not to. Welcome to The Darkness 2.
The single player campaign is not too long depending on difficulty level and your level of expertise, but I found the story and atmosphere so refined that I thoroughly enjoyed my play through and recommended it. Also of note is the Vendettas campaign. There is a 4 player online co-op that intertwines with the single player story filling in some back story. Overall Vendettas is a fun diversion with friends but a little repetitive. You don't get to play as the main character Jackie, instead one of a set of four mercenaries that each have a personal weapon infused with Dark Essence.
Now for the gameplay. The Darkness II finally disproves the theory that developers have to leave the main protagonist as hollow as possible in first person shooters so that the gamers can fully immerse themselves. This is just lazy storytelling and don't let anyone tell you differently. The Darkness is a game of two parts. Light and dark. Players experience the tender heart of Jackie when he is around Jenny and Aunt Sarah. But then players go out and start shooting guys and flinging fan blades at them with one demon arm while decapitating them with the other demon arm. In The Darkness II you quad-wield and your survival depends on it. At first it can seem a bit much to keep track of, grabbing things and throwing things and slashing and shooting all at once. But once you learn to multitask you will feel like a God. It's intoxicating. The Darkness becomes an extension of your will and soon you are slaying rooms full of enemies with gleeful abandon. There is an upgrade system to tailor the combat to your preferences and the point system that pays for your new abilities will encourage you to perform gruesome executions. The game is bloody. But due to a smart move on the developer's behalf, the cell-shaded comic style graphics make all the gore less disgusting. This time around the enemies have their own supernatural weapons at their disposal, a noted improvement over the last game.
Inside all of us there's a violent beast that needs to be sated, lets it bleed over into our real lives. This game does just that. Incredibly violent, and intensely satisfying. My only wish is that it were longer. Great fun; A must have.

Beneath a fateful exhibition of stars, an emblematic flame permeates the shroud of night.  Reflective ore imprisons the ambient glow of radiant runes, amidst ominous relics and perilous ruins.  A triumvirate of cloaked aspects materialize, brandishing an ancestral facade, analogous to that of their opponents'.  A lucent beam, thrust from the heavens, materializes into an orb of boundless energy.  Swiftly, the participants surge towards the orb with tenacious fervor and the circuitous dance of the wisps begins...
Forsaken, teetering upon the precipice of demise, you tentatively regain consciousness to find yourself under the scrutiny of a band of ivory masked demons, draped in opulent vestments, adorned with mysterious symbols.  One of the masked figures approaches you, removing his veil to reveal a personable mortal, concerned with preserving your waning existence.  This stranger introduces himself as Hedwyn, as his two cohorts contend the value of salvaging your life.  Devoted to intuition, the compassionate mortal convinces his allies to implicate you in their journey for absolution.
Pyre puts the player in the role of "The Reader," responsible for studying the Book of Rites, as a literate guide to freedom for the Nighthawks; one of nine original Triumvirates, created by the Eight Scribes for the Rites.  Banished to a vast purgatory known as the Downside, for cultural insurrection, you're tasked with directing your team through a series of trials designed to exonerate the supreme victors.  Ripped from the surroundings of the Commonwealth, the overall narrative begins to unfold, as the fate of the world above and below the constellations hangs in the balance.
Stratified lore evokes an insatiable yearning to uncover the mysteries of this dark fantasy, as the player traverses the world through a storybook interface.  Transitions between extensive textual elements and combat establish an intimate dynamic between characters and evoke emotional commitment from players.  Deepening relationships between characters span the moral landscape, cultivating a sense of belonging among misfits.  The game's choice system often forces one to choose between strategic preservation or consequential altruism.  An abundance of diverging story branches, revolving around navigation and character choices, provide ample incentive to play through the campaign multiple times.
Thoughtfully crafted backstories are delicately interwoven within the narrative, driving the core theme of enlightenment through trial and tribulation.  Each interaction between the expansive cast of characters feels fluid and natural, a testament to how comprehensively and cohesively Pyre was written.  Occasionally, the meticulous cultivation of the world results in drawn out text segments, which disrupt the overall pace of the action.
At the core of Pyre's unique experience are the rites: real-time, tactical sport, which pits two groups of three participants against one another, with the aim of extinguishing the opponent's pyre by casting yourself repeatedly into the flame -orb in hand.  The rites serve as the only path to redemption for exiles, desperate to reclaim their place within the Commonwealth.
Commanding narration amplifies the intensity prior to each match, as each team looms beneath a vigorous inferno they must preserve to achieve advancement.  Treacherous chasms, runic shrines and mobile impediments, promote mechanical and visual diversity within each methodically crafted arena.  Frenetic combat is navigated through astute positioning, as the player controls one teammate at a time in a rapid-fire exchange between offensive and defensive transitions.  Simple, yet intuitive core mechanics generate symptomatic moments of competitive euphoria.  Anticipatory maneuvering and clever timing open up holes in your opponents' defenses, in which you can make an attempt at depleting their pyre.  Proper team composition is paramount, and experimenting with each of the games' eight characters' varying aura sizes, abilities and mobility, produces a synergistic experience akin to most MOBAs.  Inventive gameplay, coupled with a practical leveling system, provides sufficient opportunities to implement creative strategies to stamp out your opponents in uniquely fun ways.
Versus mode pits player versus computer or player versus player, in custom matches which allow each participant to select their team composition, their desired soundtrack and stage.  I spent several hours competing against the computer in the early stages of the campaign, developing strategy and honing my proficiency with each character.  While I haven't spent time competing in local versus mode, I assume it has the potential to ruin relationships and cultivate bitter dispositions.
Supergiant Games is well known for the illustrious visual aesthetic of their earlier titles, Transistor and Bastion.  Pyre is no exception, and in many ways transcends the aforementioned titles with the breadth of its detail.  Surreal landscapes are brought to life with vibrant saturation.  Stark contrast between light and dark elements, utilize lush warm hues and soothing indigo; while ethereal lighting illuminates colossal idols, relinquished of their former glory.
Characters are illustrated with muted brushstrokes of flat tones, blending subtlety within each environment. Animations flow seamlessly in conjunction with spell effects exchanged across the battlefield in dazzling splendor.  The sheer volume of animations occurring in the foreground highlight the vigorous pacing of Pyre's gameplay.
Serving as a momentous backdrop for the overall atmosphere is a remarkable soundtrack composed by Darren Korb.  Robust acoustic guitar melodies, layered atop ubiquitous percussion, ebb and flow with spiraling captivation.  Haunting electronic notes transition into whimsical guitar riffs, subtle vocal harmonies and back again with compelling direction.  Korb's ability to merge such a diverse collection of sounds (harpsichord and electric guitar included), is uncanny, and a testament to his artistry.
Verdict 
Pyre combines inventive gameplay, emotive storytelling, alluring visuals and a moving soundtrack into one masterful adventure unlike any other in recent memory.  In an industry saturated with sequels and customary experiences, Pyre oozes originality and inspires imaginative risk.

I'm not into the whole beta access thing etc, bar a few MMOs,  so I dont know how much more work is getting put into this game before it's considered finsihed. But as it stands the game is an incredibly fun, fast paced yet still tactical game that any fps gamer or certainly any post-apoc genre fan should give a go.
The maps are interesting, expansive, good fun to explore and master with countless bottlenecks, sniping positions and storming points for players of all preferences to master; the weather changes and this has a vast effect on the maps themselves, forcing players to adapt. They include anomalies and radiation zones, poison clouds and all other manner of environmental forces that, when coupled with beartraps of thoughtful positioning make for a real challenge.
The Character customisation is a dream for the more rolaplying, kit orientated players (like myself). the choice is finite, albeit within four factions, two of which are open at the beginning of the game. select your gun, your clothing and kit, and off you go. it's quick, but in depth enough that you get the feel of a proper loadout. there are masses of guns and armour throughout the reputation stages, unlocked and then bought by grinding rep and currency. The end tier stuff looks amazing to me, which makes me want to continue playing.
The actual FPS capabilities of the game are very good. its well balanced and matched well to the maps, meaning everyone can play their own style, be it support, sniper or assault. its twitchy, visceral and VERY lethal, very realisitic. reminiscent of red orchestra, if not identical. you can attempt to heal yourself through kit, but honestly one shot is enough to have you scrambling back to cover and praying you dont bleed out. the gun sound effects are crisp and if you are carfeul you can tell which way battle or enemies lie which is a plus.
graphically, I found it a touch grainy regardless of a settings change; that said it doesnt look awful at all. it just means that at extreme distances it becomes hard to aim at enemies because thy begin to blur and pixxelate.
The 8/10 reflects that I would like to see more armour choices and perhaps physical customisation impemented, like bein able to choose items like knives or "trophies" to attach at points to your character. It also reflects that It has begun to become a bit stale after only a few hours of play, the fact being that ive ecplored a lot of the content that the game offers even after such a short time playing.

Supergiant Games creates a lively, foreboding, and hopeful world in the Downside, where exiles of the civilized Commonwealth are sent "to carry out their rightful sentences". While it can be branded as a "sportsball" game, Pyre instead acts like a visual novel+party-based rpg. The Rites are as much as a battle system as any other game, but in addition to banishing your enemies you must get the Orb into the opposing team's Pyre (make sure to turn the difficulty up to Heightened! It's too easy otherwise). Each character has a unique skill set, some of which are harder to understand than others, and your skill at them can directly reflect onto the story. The story ACTUALLY changes based on your actions, conversations, and the outcome of the Rites. If you lose a Rite, you don't get to try again. The story continues and the characters reflect that. This creates an extra sense of tension during a Rite, especially a certain special few. Just be aware that there is a ton of reading in this game, way more of that then Rites gameplay.
It's no secret that Supergiant Games is my favorite studio, so take this review with a grain of fanboyism, but they have created another fantastic world and gameplay experience that everyone should at least try.
Also, the soundtrack is fantastic, but that is just a given at this point. Darren Korb is one of the best composers in games and Ashley Barrett returns for another fantastic performance. ("Dread Design" and "Will of the Scribes"!)
