This pickle recipe is great for pickling cucumbers as well as a variety of other vegetables. That's right—you can make pickles out of cucumbers, cauliflower, green and red peppers, onions, green tomatoes, summer squash, baby ears of corn—lots of different vegetables can be pickled!
Make a brine of 3/4 cup of pickling salt, 2 1/2 quarts of water, and 1/2 cup vinegar, heating to dissolve the salt and cooling before use. Alternate layers of vegetables—small (3-4 inches long) whole cucumbers or large pieces of other vegetables—with layers of fresh dill in a large crock or ceramic bowl. For an extra kick, add hot red peppers and peeled garlic cloves.
Pour brine over vegetables, and weight down using a cloth, plate, and a canning jar full of water.
For 2 weeks, white scum will appear on the top of your pickles. Remove it daily.
When the two weeks is up, pack vegetables in hot, sterile jars. Heat 1/2 cup pickling salt, 1 quart vinegar, and 4 quarts water to boiling, pour over vegetables, and seal. Process for 15 minutes in boiling water bath.

Apotheon is a really excellent game. Saw this years ago before it was released and knew it would be special. I am not remotely disappointed years later. There was way more depth to it than I thought there was at the start, and the art will likely never age due to being high resolution and scalable. I'm very glad I finally got it. Should have bought it sooner. It is a new classic.
Apotheon is a really cool Geek Mythology rich brawler-scroller where you get to Zelda-smash all the pots as you slash and stab your way across the realms of the gods; all against a gorgeous backdrop of Greek inspired art with a multitude of gorgeous colours. And it is precisely as fun as that sounds.
My only annoyances are:
- Linear Narrative in an open world. Nothing wrong with that, Just would have enjoyed picking and choosing my alliances like I did my progression. (Dionysus is my man, everybody else deserves what Nikandrios does to them -- especially you, Apollo!)
- Frame Rate Drops in random places. No idea why.
- A few crashes, but no lost progress. The game was aware of when it crashed too, which helped. That's just good coding. You don't get to praise a crash report very often, but that was pretty elegant how you fell on your face.
- I am consistently annoyed by the less responsive weapons, especially when you are getting bunched up. A cool fix for that would have been to make characters mildly repulsive, so that they push each other away rather than letting them stack on top of each other. Instead you'll furiously try to attack something on to of you with the sword and not hit them, which is annoying, when the spears especially take forever to recycle before you can stab again. A controller rather than keyboard&mouse may be a different experience.
Otherwise, the game is packed with great entertainment and the above don't really both me enough to really care, honestly. Some people may be more easily frustrated, especially depending on your mood when you approach the issues above, but if you're excited about this and give it an hour you won't really care.
Your unique weapons are not as unique as you think they are - you can always get them beck. I thought there were 4 voice actors - there were like 30, but they sound the same to me due to delivery. Again, doesn't bother me. I thoroughly enjoyed it.
The world is super well thought out and very ornate, so that levels don't get too stale as you see them again and again. (The forest is gorgeous, Ares' blood level is brutal, Hades is a dark and chilling place, and Athena's labyrinth is very clever. All while not being typically tropic of the water level, fire level, etc. They use the tropes in a clever way that follow the myths they embody.
Doesn't matter if Apotheon is on sale or not. Buy it. You'll enjoy it for at least a day.

Okay first off, for all those who want this game but read the system requirements and thought "Oh drat, I cannot play this on my system, I have a windows 8 and it says up to XP only". I have GREAT news for you-I have this game, on a cheap 350 dollar notebook from walmart. It has a windows 8 OS. This game-runs PERFECTLY on it. I did not even need to change or alter any compatibility settings or mess with the graphics or audio configuration. On default layout, no changes at all-it runs perfectly. Now, obviously, I cannot guarantee this will be true for absolutely everyone. I can however say given how cheap my own computer system is-I think this game would work for almost everyone running a windows 8 system. Probably also the same with windows 7 but I cannot say for certain on that one.
Now onto the game itself. Heroes of Might and Magic series is a well known and well loved series for a number of good reasons. First of all, there are different races, all with their unique units and hero specializations. This particular Heroes of Might and Magic is I feel the best of the series so far (Yes, better even that Might and Magic Heroes VI.) The graphics are fine if not great, but the game itself is what makes this game so much fun. With both single player, multiplayer, and even hot seat player capability you can play with friends far or near, or solo. It has campaigns for each race, all of which combine into one epic story on love, loss, and each faction.race fighting to survive and rule over all.
Combat is laid out on a open fiend or fighting to defend or gain control of a castle/keep with wall fortifications between you and the enemy. You have control over all of your units and can even through leveling you hero, gain control over the war machines in your unit such as the first aid tent, the ballista, and the catapult, allowing you to heal the units of your choice or aim the ballista at a particular target, or have the catapult try and take out only the door or remove the turret towers aimed at you as a example.
The units themselves can have special abilities. For example, the demon units can use a skill called gating, to summon up more of their own kind to join you for the battle (These gated units are temporary and vanish after each battle). The Undead units with the help of their hero can rise again after death, and if you defeat living targets, can even spend dark energy points to raise them again as undead units in your army (the type of unit they turn into depends on how powerful they were before). The list goes on.
Outside of the campaigns which are fun and throw new challenges at you to keep the game fresh and fun (and also tie into the storyline perfectly), such as having to avoid a enemy or outrun them to a safe zone to meet up with a particular hero or town. Other times you have one week to take over a town and set up camp before having to wipe out the enemy that stands in your way and so on.
The game play itself has a little learning curve, to understand what different objects on the map do for you, and figuring out how best to defeat units or how to control your own to the best advanatage-but the learning curve is built into the storyline so you are not derailed by some overtly lengthly tutorial. You simply learn as you progress and by the mid-part of the very first campaign, you'll be a expert hand at building up your keep, controlling your units, and understanding how to level your hero to your advanatage (Though more time playing with all the races will be needed to fully see what is the best way to level a particular hero).
Each hero has it's own unique talent as well. There is a elven hero who has a powerful ranged strike and boosts the damage of all it's groups hunter (archer) units. There is a demon hero whose spedciality is making each ballista shot explosive, doing extra damage each time the ballista's turn comes around. There is a Magic Hero who specializes with the smallest of units, the gremlins, who jhave a ranged blunderbuss shot attack that means a huge army of many small minions with a combined strength enough to take down far more powerful units of lesser numbers. The list again goes on. So it is in your interest to read up when you build your tavern, where you recruit new heroes, to see what each hero does and choose the one whose specialization you need most-someone who can race over the landscape and explore it our simply outrun the enemy, someone who brings extra firepower, or someone more specialized for a particular foe or to best defend your keep while you take your main hero out into the fray.
The game is, in fact-complete in every sense as is, but if you finish the campaigns and want more-good news again! There are two expansion campaign games for this game (look at the DLC for the game or buy the whole collection at once for $19.99 USD). Each one adds a new race and continues the storyline. First, the dwarven race and then the orcs-also calle dht eribes of the East.) I highly recommend both expansions as the races are fun, enjoyable, and and a completely fresh set of skills and tech and units to the game. The orcs are particularly amusing, as you can have cyclops through goblin in a kamikaze fashion into the face of enemy units. It only costs one mere goblin, the cheapest of units, to do a massive damage spray with the help of your powerful cyclops' throwing arm.
If you love having complete control over a army, a castle, and a hero-if you enjoy besieging castles and trampling the enemy under hoof and claw, if you have ever enjoy any turn based, fantasy game with a bit of storyline-then this game is for you. You will NOT be dissapointed by it.
For this game by itself without the DLC, it costs a mere $9.99 and offers many hours of gameplay and has endless replayability with the multiplayer mode (Which you can play solo as well against as few as one or up to 8 AI competitors).
So really, there is no reason to NOT buy this game unless you truly despise everything turn based.Even then, this game may well change your mind or at least make you willing to put up with the turn based combat for the sheer fun of everything else about the game.

+Puzzles are not abstract, they are smart and fit to the setting.
+Strong themes and philosophical debates on transhumanism, existentialism and the concept of identity.  What makes us human, our biological entity or consciounsness? That is the question that will haunt you at the end.
-Game mechanic is the only problem in Soma, it is limited and mediocre, there is no improvement after Amnesia. Alien Isolation is a perfect example of how crafting and inventory management improve gameplay experience, element of horror and storyline.
Frictional Games is definitely on the right track and Soma is their real masterpiece. I am looking forward to their next title.

There is a certain niche of gamers that play games as a pallete clenser for reading books. These are your Baldur's Gate enthusiasts, your Final Fantasy fans, and the folk that suffered through Dragon Age II for the lore. Pyre is a game for these people. That's certainly not to say that Pyre is bad. Rather, that the focus of the game is narrative, and that there are many for whom that would be turn-off.
Fans of Bastion and Transistor will recognize the storytelling and art quality that have come to be Supergiant's calling card. The gameplay is a deviation from usual one-person dungeon crawl, to the delight of some and the chagrin of others. Those who loved Fire Emblem and XCOM might be pleasantly surpirsed should they give it a shot. The characters are one-and-all interesting, and their fates are in your hands. A single lost match can irrevocably change how the story ends (beware ye save scummers, you'll find no purchase here).
Overall, Pyre is a good game that appeals to a specific kind of person, which may not be the same type of person that enjoyed Bastion and Transistor. Readers are encouraged to think about what they want out of a game before purchasing.

It does not have the tactical depth of Doorkickers nor the smoothness of X-COM, but it manages to fit snugly into the tactical games scene with both its special operations theme and generally thoughtful gameplay.

Nether is an aspirational and very seductive concept. A horror survival game set in an open city? It sounds too good to be true. Unfortunately it is. The game is, despite being marketed as a finished product for sale, late alpha to early beta *at best.* It's fun, but so unpolished I can't help but feel somewhat decieved.
The server select screen is met with intense lag that can take up to ten minutes to resolve. Joining a server more than half-full means being stuck as a spectator for another indefinite amount of time. The map has collision issues and lazy or sloppy design choices (Such as cars or stairs being half submerged in the street, or literally not even bothering to utilize invisible walls so players will fall off the edge of the map in certain areas.) The inventory management is one of the most unintuitive I've ever dealt with (second to the Day Z mod for Arma II) It is slow, clunky, uncooperative, and overall frustrating to use. Combat is a chaotic mess, as sometimes melee attacks won't even connect.
The game does have its plus sides, though. The game is fun, and the rare encounters with other players are often adrenaline pumping sessions that I don't get in normal PVP games. The game allows you to keep cosmetic items and money after death, which makes it significantly less discouraging, but still worth avoiding. It's a great concept, and it's a really great rough draft. It's not a final product. It's something that should be early access. Not a full game.
If it's on sale, it's worth dropping a few dollars on. If you're paying more than $5 though, strongly consider other options.

I'm changing my review recommendation from a yes to a no. To be certain I enjoy playing Friday the 13th. The game has a number bugs both big and small, unrefined mechanics. and missing content for the price tag. But the problems were never so overbearing that the game's good points couldn't shine through. Playing as Jason and damning the rowdy and noisy counselors to my own personal idea of hell was extremely vindicating. And escaping from Jason was oftentimes tense, but when you succeeded it was satisfying to walk away leaving  Vorhees to wallow in his failure to catch everybody.
However, the reason I no longer recommend this game is because Gun Media have damaged their professional integrity as a company. Gunmedias system for reporting players in Friday the 13th for breaking  punishable rules or just plain outright cheating states in its fine print that you 100% need evidence of the punishable action you are accusing a player of doing. (ie a video recording) And I agree with the system as whole, certainly it might make the reporting system a little slower because you need to handle reports on a case by case basis. But it's a great way to ensure there are no victims of an incorrect or unjust banhammer.
That is until it came into light that a member of Gun Media has been confirmed responsible for banning players without the needed evidence to do so. Trusting instead the word of mouths of friends and colleagues, despite the fact that it is a clear violation of the system itself. The reason I am so upset about this is because by one single case of foul play coming to light. We NOW need to call into question every single banning case prior. We can no longer be certain of the integrity of Cun Medias prior convictions nor the integrity of future action to come. Just how many peopel perior have been pushished for being reported without proper evidence? We might never truly know.
As a result my view on this game will remain negative until Gun Media publicly addresses having failed our trust in them as a business. Individuals responsible have been properly reprimanded, and compensation is offered for the players wronged by the misused system. Until then my position will remained firmly in the area of “Don’t buy this game.”

Rainbow Six Siege, what can be said about this game that a few thousand other people haven't said already?
The game isn't terribly complex, not when you've settled into the way of thinking this game will push you in. Shooting through walls, proper trap placement, different strats for different sites and objectives. It's very open ended in how you approach things. If you want to rush and try to shoot the first thing you see, you can do that....just don't do it without a backup plan.
This is heavily team oriented, and having a microphone is a very crucial part, since even after death, you can assist your team by watching cameras or drones, letting them know when someone is coming up on their flank. Choosing an operator is based on what the team needs for the most part, but not required in all situations. It is needed to win, sometimes, especially more the case in Ranked where everyone brings their best strats that require an even spread of gadgets and assets. Learn to work with your team, and don't be afraid to experiment with ideas.
Learn the maps as fast as you can. Make custom matches and fully explore what you can do in the game, with that knowledge, you'll know exactly what your enemy can do, in return. When new maps come out, /especially/ take that time to learn it, you will have the upper hand for a good while before everyone learns the rotations and routes of movement and fire.
Walls are destructible for the most part, but there's a simple rule to follow to help you know which you can spray. A thin material you could imagine bullets going through, you're good. Solid brick or concrete walls, your bullets aren't going anywhere. I can't express how useful it is to know when you can spray a wall that an enemy just ran behind to secure a kill, nor can I count the amount of times someone has purposefully neglected that walls could be shot through for a cheap and easy kill when they know exactly where an enemy is sitting and waiting for you.
The game can be highly addictive if you're constantly wanting to find new ways to kill and win, new strategies and tactics to abuse to make the enemy rage quit. The gameplay might start to seem stale, but like I said, so long as you're experimenting and thinking, taking new paths or different angles, you'll always have something to come back to.
As for the bad, I'm not going to sugar coat it. The game is a dumpster fire, a steaming hot, messy pile of flaming rubble. You'll run into more bugs than a trip into the Australian Outback. Ubisoft always has this habit of fixing one big thing, but creating several smaller things, time and time again. Some funny, some stupid, some outright annoying. The current state of the game, as weird as it is to say with all the things going on now, is in a better way than it was a year ago. Lighting is fixed, shields are fun now, gadgets do what they're supposed to do. It's good. That being said, there will always be more bugs to go around, and you'd do well to remember that.
As a last note, don't buy the Starter Edition, please. There is no way to upgrade it to a full version, and you'll be stuck paying the renown price of DLC Ops for the starters, which are 100% necessary to get, since they are the cheapest and most varied. Save that money, wait for a sale, then get the full game. And don't you dare come into multiplayer without playing the tutorials. I say that from a place of understanding, you wanna play the game, I get it, but play the tutorial so you can get an operator or 4 to use. You don't want to subject your team to having a recruit without a gadget when you could be an Op to further help the team. And to finish it off, do go on youtube and watch good people play, pay attention to what they do, and remember what you see, because knowing a few tricks will help you survive a match

Ignore the comments that bash combat controls or gameplay. If you're playing on PC master race, you have nothing to fear.
First, I'll talk about the pros and then the cons of this game.
+ The COMBAT is so innovative for a 2D platformer that can result in engaging battle situations. Many different weapons, each has its use. Multiple choices how to take down your oponent. You use your mouse for direction of the attack/direction of block/style of attack.
+ I especially like how this game tackled 2D space, making it multi-leveled, where forests, streets and rooms are built not into length, but into height. The battles often take place on multiple levels, where you can easily descend or jump up. It gives you freedom to fight how you like, compared to all the others 2D fighting games that are fought only in one line/one level.
+ You have many different oponents and each is vulnerable to different weapons. (Remember to use grenades, traps and flasks!) Same goes for boss battles.
+ The LEVEL DESIGN of this game is just fantastic! Every level and area was something new. Playing the hunter and prey game with Artemis, exploring scary♥♥♥♥♥dungeon of Hades' Underworld, solving the Athena's level was something to remember, must not forget on Ares' level - one huge♥♥♥♥♥death match with immortal warriors who were stuck there in never-ending battle.
+ Beautiful greek pottery art style. If you are a man/woman of culture, you'll definitely appreciate this jewel of a game.
+ Fantastic greek mythology setting.
+ It has an interesting ending that made me think after finishing the game.
- You have tons of weapons and sometimes it gets pretty hard to scroll through all of them in the middle of the action. Some hotkeys implementation could be needed. You can pause the game and choose it manually in the inventory, of course. It breaks the immersion, though.
- Lack of deep story. Of course, there is some story, but it's not enough. It has very little character development and the protagonist has no personality, which is such a shame! A good story, with plot twists and sidekicks and engaging antagonists and mainly, likeable protagonist with a personality, could have improved this game so much! (This is a message for devs :D )
- The greek mythos was mostly presented through tablets that you could read (quotes from real ancient greeks who wrote about the mythology). This could have been much better, if the mythos was implemented directly IN THE STORY, or shown in the environment. Message for the dev. team: Remember the main rule of story-writing: "Show, don't tell."
- It's short for such a good game! (I haven't finished the game on this account, so it's more than just my current "hrs on record")
Final conclusion: Do I recommend this game? Hell Yes!
It has fun innovative combat, the greatest level design I haven't seen in a game for a long time, and beautiful art style. This game definitely moved 2D platformers into a new, good direction and I would like to see more of it. Something like Apotheon 2, for example. :)

The Sith Lords doesn't play out remotely as you'd expect the sequel to the bombastic, twist famous, Knights of the Old Republic and it's all the better for it. Its cast of flawed, colourful characters are interesting from the get go and keep you entertained as you wind your way through the story of the Jedi 'Exile'.
By today's lofty standards the gameplay and graphics can seem a little dated, but it's more than worth sticking with it. Even if you are used to newer titles, it tells a Star Wars story unlike most of those that have gone before.
Go and try it out, after all "apathy is death".

While many things could have gone worse, Alpha Prime finds itself so deep in the uncanny mediocre valley that it just annoys me. At times the action is fair and challenging, only to then become frustrating and unfair moments later. Sometimes the story hints at a better direction, but then falls back into of the pit of Not-worth-caring-for.
All in all, the two euros I got it for wasn't a huge setback. But with so much potential for something cool and possibly refreshing at best, the most infuriating thing about Alpha Prime is that it never gets anywhere near you think it should. If you're starving for a bit of Sci-Fi action and find it cheap, go ahead if you're willing to risk it. There were moments when I enjoyed myself, but they were too weak, as well as scarce.
But despite any redeeming factors it might have, you're better off playing almost anything else.

How to know if you will like this game?
- Do you like atmospheric platformers?
- Do you like an interesting story told through decent (sometimes even great) voice acting?
- Do you like a large map divided into smaller sections you can clear in any order you like?
- Do you like an unique art style, both in sound and visual?
If even one of those apply to you, then this is a game you should buy. The controls take a little bit of getting used to, but it's not too difficult. Upgrading weapons is fun, finding the hidden chests is fun and the bosses are always fair and not too gimmicky. If you love Greek mythology you should definitely get this wondeful game. Highly recommended!

Velvet Assassin had potential to be a good stealth game. The design was sound and it has a decent story about slowly drifting into madness from all the monstrosities of war. Sadly, the total lack of a saving system turned it into ‘Reload Last Checkpoint: The Game’ instead.
Velvet Assassin is very loosely based on an actual World War II French–British female spy, which in this game is translated to a British agent who spends most of the game lying in a French hospital bed, reliving her previous missions. This formula serves as an excuse to freely jump in time and space with little connection between the levels.
The story works surprisingly well given how disjointed and short it is. The voice actress made a good job portraying Violette as she slowly descents into madness from all the cruelty she has seen and inflicted.
As a game, it is a budget version of titles like Metal Gear Solid or Thief: you sneak around on a linear level and silently dispatch enemy soldiers (in our case this means slitting their throat with a bayonet). The AI is quite inconsistent though: sometimes you stay hidden in broad daylight, sometimes they instantly find you in pitch darkness.
Although the game is roughly 2 hours long, thanks to the broken save system it takes more than 10-12 hours to finally reach the end. There are many checkpoints, but since getting discovered means almost certain death, actually reaching one can take dozens of tries and reloads.
If this fundamental flaw wouldn’t exist, Velvet Assassin could rank at least 20% higher in many reviews. But as it is, nobody will remember anything else about the game but the constant reloading and frustration.

Whether you are looking for a mindless relaxing game, a challenging puzzle, or a strategic race against the clock, this game has a mode for you! The music is great, the narrator sounds epic, and the graphics are gorgeous and shiny. I warn you now, you WILL become addicted to this game.
There are four regular modes and four unlockable secret modes.
Classic Mode: The matching game we all know and love. Match three or more in a row for points until there are no more available matches. Match four or more to create powerful special gems.
Zen Mode: Same as classic, but endless as your moves never run out. There are also additional options you can add for relaxation such as aural tones and breath modulation. I like to play this mode on mute while I listen to a podcast or the news.
Ligtning Mode: Race against the clock and get as many points as possible! You can extend your time by matching up the special time gems. Match quickly to get a speed bonus.
Quest Mode: Forty puzzles and eleven mini-games all using the various available modes but with a specific objective. Beat the clock, only use so many moves, etc.
The Secret Modes: Butterflies, Diamond Mine, Ice Storm, and Poker.
I'll let you discover those on your own. Personally my favorite of those is Poker, with Diamond Mine a close second. Now get this game already, and have fun! :)

There is a certain niche of gamers that play games as a pallete clenser for reading books. These are your Baldur's Gate enthusiasts, your Final Fantasy fans, and the folk that suffered through Dragon Age II for the lore. Pyre is a game for these people. That's certainly not to say that Pyre is bad. Rather, that the focus of the game is narrative, and that there are many for whom that would be turn-off.
Fans of Bastion and Transistor will recognize the storytelling and art quality that have come to be Supergiant's calling card. The gameplay is a deviation from usual one-person dungeon crawl, to the delight of some and the chagrin of others. Those who loved Fire Emblem and XCOM might be pleasantly surpirsed should they give it a shot. The characters are one-and-all interesting, and their fates are in your hands. A single lost match can irrevocably change how the story ends (beware ye save scummers, you'll find no purchase here).
Overall, Pyre is a good game that appeals to a specific kind of person, which may not be the same type of person that enjoyed Bastion and Transistor. Readers are encouraged to think about what they want out of a game before purchasing.

But the problems were never so overbearing that the game's good points couldn't shine through. Playing as Jason and damning the rowdy and noisy counselors to my own personal idea of hell was extremely vindicating. And escaping from Jason was oftentimes tense, but when you succeeded it was satisfying to walk away leaving  Vorhees to wallow in his failure to catch everybody.
However, the reason I no longer recommend this game is because Gun Media have damaged their professional integrity as a company. Gunmedias system for reporting players in Friday the 13th for breaking  punishable rules or just plain outright cheating states in its fine print that you 100% need evidence of the punishable action you are accusing a player of doing. (ie a video recording) And I agree with the system as whole, certainly it might make the reporting system a little slower because you need to handle reports on a case by case basis. But it's a great way to ensure there are no victims of an incorrect or unjust banhammer.
That is until it came into light that a member of Gun Media has been confirmed responsible for banning players without the needed evidence to do so. Trusting instead the word of mouths of friends and colleagues, despite the fact that it is a clear violation of the system itself. The reason I am so upset about this is because by one single case of foul play coming to light. We NOW need to call into question every single banning case prior. We can no longer be certain of the integrity of Cun Medias prior convictions nor the integrity of future action to come. Just how many peopel perior have been pushished for being reported without proper evidence? We might never truly know.
As a result my view on this game will remain negative until Gun Media publicly addresses having failed our trust in them as a business. Individuals responsible have been properly reprimanded, and compensation is offered for the players wronged by the misused system. Until then my position will remained firmly in the area of “Don’t buy this game.”

Hello guys,
I just went trough tons of reviews, and I couldn't help but notice that lot of them was full of hate, far too often mentioning the "Pay2Win" factor. Shortly, I read very few of objective ones. Since I played this game earlier in closed beta, I've seen gameplay trough all tiers of gear, as well as I played this game in different phases of development. Basically, these are the few points I want to highlight and explain to new members of community.
#1 - Pay to win
Like i wrote above, lot of people mention this factor as main problem of the game. Truth is, there is possibility of buying items with premium currency. Those items come with unique stats and look, but i never found them extremely overpowered since A) almost none of those guns and equipment is effective in higher tier matches and B) even on equal tier u can still get similar or better equipment by regular mechanics.
#2 - Slow development (upcoming free world mode)
This is second hot topic, from which Survarium gets lot of bad reputation. Lot of players who stick with game for a longer time, like I do, are angry with how slow progress on game development is. I must agree that it was a bit slow earlier, but on the other hand, since open beta VG done lot of changes and patches are coming more often and with more content. I must say that devs posted lot of plans from their "to do list" to the community earlier and since they weren't capable of completing these tasks, lot of people turned their backs on VG. Today I think, VG are more responsible and they do their job in the way they present it to community. From this i assume that the progress will be faster in future and fans of Survarium will get what they are looking for.
#3 - Matchmaking balance
This is I think the biggest problem of all. Lot of players experience matching with people with lot more skill and are frustrated when getting quickscoped in environment they barely know. Development is aware of this and even upcoming patch (0.28) will adjust matchmaking to be more fair to newcomers.
---
That's all for now, thank you for reading so far and please, don't be so hard on Vostok Games, i sense great potential in this game and community which supports devs with new ideas would be so much better then community of people picking on them.
Good luck, have fun - Prowler out.

This game is pretty great. If you liked Rayman:Origins, you'll like this one. If you don't have Origins, you don't really need to buy it, since this game contains almost every one of the origins levels as bonus levels. It's a great idea, and they're fun to revisit.
If you like fun, cheerful platformers with good music, good controls, and a good difficulty curve, you'll really like this game.
However, unless you really enjoy pain, I'd recommend finishing the main levels and quitting.
By the time I realized that was what I should have done, I was close enough to 100% that I just soldiered through, but it really left a sour taste in my mouth in places.
One of the best parts of Rayman:Origins for me was how the difficulty ramped up through the whole game, culminating in the Land of the Livid Dead. Those levels were monsters, but practice and a bit of luck would see you through, and
did I feel accomplished when I beat them. You needed every single trick you'd picked up in the game, and maybe a few more, but they weren't unfair, just brutal.
Rayman:Legends on the other hand, has a land of the livid dead that's not new, it's not interesting, it's just selected levels you've already beaten with hideous graphical filters over them. Pixelating them, adding pulsing static and other visual noise, oh, and removing the checkpoints. Two of them gave me hideous headaches.
Just for that alone, I'd have to say Origins is the stronger game.
Legends also adds a whole bunch of timed mini levels, some of which can take dozens of runs if you're trying to rescue all of the smurfs that have been captured. Some of them are a nice break, but having so many of them makes the magic run dry very quickly.
I'd also like to know why there are ~40 unlockable playable characters when there aren't appreciable differences between them. Not sure what the point there is.
Anyway, overall, this game is in places good, even great, but for completests, it's a bit of a kick below the belt in the places it should really shine. I recommend it, but with the caveats mentioned.

Context:
Well polished and rich game, reminds me of the rich, unique, original and well polished work that used to come out more often in the past, caring so much about the finer details that make a game a universe of its own.
Considering how the CoD and AC series were initially at a such high level of quality, especially the first releases but later declined with every sequel. It is therefore a surprise how Ubisoft with its overall declining quality, managed to produce such a great quality work with this one. Could this mean the same for its other series? Only time will tell, since as Ubisoft has shown here, it's never too late to get back on track.
Some snippets from the game itself:
+This game as many others have mentioned, is suitable for all ages and is great for gathering friends and family in playing such a fun game cooperatively or competitively.
+Every level is unique on its own, giving a different flow, challenges and experience to every level, this is one of the major factors that make the game so replayable.
+Small details regarding playable and non-playable characters in their movements and reactions to the envirnoment, which are so well made that not only do they truly give an impression of the personality of the character, but aids in making the gameplay experience so fluid.
+Manages to instill an actual sense of achievement, versus a ton of modern games that reward 'achievements' without the actual sense
Minor negatives:
-Requires Uplay which constantly and forever will have sync issues with achievements or saved games. (I never needed to backup saves for Rayman, but for AC:Unity and Sleeping Dogs, which overwrote my progress, I needed to backup my saves constantly mid-game)
-Only local Coop +Counter: However this encourages getting actual persons to play with you in the same room, which enriches the experience. Also, there is an online score ladder, with other player's ghosts to compete with in the weekly/daily online competitions.
Rating: 9/10

I bought this game like a year ago. I played it for a couple of hours and was turned off by what seemed a very loose control  scheme. After playing through and loving a previous title from the developer Alientrap (Capsized), I decided to give it a chance a week or so ago. Having completed the game at Champion difficulty, I can definitely recommend this game. The visuals are unique, you may love them or hate them but there's no denying there's a lot of personality in this one: characters and backgrounds are drawn like they were on ancient Greece vases (tasteful nudity and all, as in the nymphs and some of the warriors) . The style is consistent throughout the entire game, but there is enough variation in the different stages to make you believe you are in a forest, or a river of blood, or a temple... The music is fitting to the general theme and well orchestrated, I would say it feels as it had been composed for a bigger game. The voice acting is also really well done, although to be fair, I didn't pay much attention to it as I usually don't play games for the story.
But the real strong point of this game is precisely what initially put me off: its combat and control mechanics. You have a lot of options to go to battle: sword, mace, spear...ranged weapons like bow, javelins, other throwables, traps that you can set... Besides you can equip a shield (which has a bashing move) to block attacks and a roll to evade. The timing and reach of each weapon is different, and attacking drains your stamina. So as you can see, the depth is enormous. The thing is, as there is momentum and you can aim your attack with the mouse, it can -will- be overwhelming to control well the first few hours. Keep at it, and it pays off- you'll be slaughtering armies like a pro. And it will be fun.
Among the negative points,  I found a lot of crashes to desktop, sound failures and other technical issues which detracted a little from the experience, but all in all, at this price this is a solid "recommend".

This game to some people will be boring at first, as the sole objective is similar to garrys mod: Clown around using a game engine, doing anything you can really think of. This game will make you want to drive like a dumbass in real life just to see if when you crash it will look just like in Beamng.
Most car simulator/racing games today focus on the graphics and making the game LOOK good, while the gameplay is lacking in detail and realism, creating beautiful games, but not realistic games that actually PLAY good. Not this game. The cars and crash modeling in this game are so similar to real life its insane; just search up a beamng crash vs a real life crash test and the cars, the results are shockingly similar. This game has realistic physics that feel as if the car is an actual automobile with weight and power, you can feel the difference in the cars which is something most "racing sim" games lack. The damage on each car goes deep down to every single node and beam in the car models, ensuring no two crashes are alike in this game.

In most racing/sim games made nowadays, the cars can crash full speed into a wall and go off as if nothing happened, with a few bumps and scratches, smoke coming out of the hood, and MAYBE, just maybe if youre lucky, a missing bumper. Missing bumper after going 200+ mph into a wall? Should be a missing EVERYTHING after a crash at that speed. And those same games are the ones that claim to be the most "realistic" games out there, which is just a sad excuse for realism.
This is one of the few games that was made putting the GAMEPLAY and physics first, graphics second (and theyre still pretty damn good). It is a damn shame that this game isnt more popular than it is now. The base game alone is pretty interesting and gives you a good introduction to what it is all about, and you can easily get plenty of gameplay out of it, however the huge variety of mods make this game worth buying even more. Do you want to drive a raging monster truck inside a demolition derby arena and spawn four honda civics that try to chase you around the arena, crushing them under your wheels in ultra realistic damage modeling until their engines seize up? Do you want to drive down the highway in an old school muscle car, pedal to the medal, only to fall of the edge of a cliff and go tumbling down, breaking every part along the way? This game is the one for you. Hell, this game could even be used in a real life driving school simulator, with a wheel and pedals connected to it. Its that realistic.

The only problem i see with this game is that you need a fairly powerful computer to run it well as this is a very demanding game due to the next generation physics and detailed crashes. Soft body physics stress the cpu as it doesnt render the car as a "hardbody" car like most games do, it instead renders every single part as a seperate piece and kind of "glues" them all together.

There are infinite possibilities in this physics engine, and a huge mod database for this game as well if you get bored of the base game vehicles.  If you are like me and are sick and tired of all these crappy games coming out nowadays that claim to be realistic but offer no damage modeling and arcade like physics, do yourself a favor and purchase this game. It is what you are looking for. I can only sit back and wish that racing games nowadays could follow suit and start putting gameplay before the graphics like this game does.
Runs at below ten frames per second on a high end PC. Unplayable. Maybe this is for some reason an issue exclusive to me, but I can't recommend it in such conditions.

Due to my hearing that the servers were optimized I will now change this review to a positive.
I have removed most venom from the review because it is most likely not needed now.
From what I hear, they are making efforts to make things smoother for the players.
----------------------------------
MAIN REVIEW -
I believe that discerning people at Ubisoft should swallow their pride and take notice of what I list as good and what I list as bad. Advertise the good things better so people know! Fix the bad things!
Points in favour of this game:
1. Character customization - on half of all characters, half of all characters are either gender. This is unprecedented for this sort of game and allows people to generally pick a character they like and immerse themselves slightly better in it. I appreciate this design decision. More of my friends will likely play when they can customize their characters. Some people complain about historical accuracy but they are boring and not fun, to put it bluntly. Let people have fun, it isn't like they made the female characters 4 foot tall with noodle arms.
2. Singleplayer - A proper, from what I have seen polished singleplayer campaign in an otherwise multiplayer game. The voice acting looked nice.. etc.. Dynasty Warriors and other similar fighting games just meanwhile have a guy pop up on the screen and tell you stuff you are supposed to be interested in. (No offense to DW, I love the games but.. this is next level.)
3. Bots -  and player versus npc bot matches that reward progress. Appreciated! You don't have to deal with people, if you don't like to.
4. Pseudo Historical - As I watch many HEMA (historical european martial arts) channels on youtube, although the combat is not 100% realistic, it IS more realistic than many games out there and some research was done to make things more immersive and incorporate real world movements to some of the attacks. Half swording and other techniques have made it in and this is rare to see. Warden will grip the blade of her sword and then use the guard to bludgeon enemies. While some people might assume this is a flashy video game thing.. this was actually done quite often because blades are less effective against armour than the blunt end of the sword. Go figure.
5. The animations and environments - are spectacular in my opinion. If you switch guard, your animations will not clip and your movements will properly go through each detail in order to properly swap. If you are turning and rushing your character might show a bit of excitement as it scans both directions. Serious immersion.
6. Pay2win? - From what I saw there is no outright pay 2 win, just pay to progress faster. This should stay this way, I think people can appreciate that.
After being able to login briefly:
7. Community - The player versus npc part of the community seems friendly enough and I still quite enjoy the elimination mode. If you fail to win against your opponent your friend might come help, likewise you can help someone who is struggling after killing your opponent.
8. I might be imagining things but some parts of the customization seem more in-depth than the beta. There may also be new maps.
9. Coop - The singleplayer campaign is apparently coop. I have not tried it in coop yet but if it works, that is pretty stellar.
10. No massive paywalls to use your chosen hero - They give you enough funds to unlock a few characters starting out. Most games like this make you grind for what feels like decades to unlock your favourite characters and this is a welcomed change.
11. Hidden Rewards - You might not notice, but in uplay there is a reward section under the game that you can use the point things to unlock some additional emblems and etc. If you were in the betas you get some for free and the others seemed relatively easy to get considering I am only level 3 and have half of them. Be sure to check the section out if you missed it or are unfamiliar with uplay.
12. Hidden... soundtrack? - The soundtrack is quite nice in my opinion and although it does not mention it, I was able to find in the reward section the ability to download the soundtrack...
Why was this not featured or mentioned anywhere? Still a fairly nice addition. It was so easy to get that I find it odd they don't just remove the tiny reward currency cost (I spent no extra rl money on this) and just advertise the game as coming with the soundtrack. This just seems obvious to me.
Bad stuff:
1. Mandatory Connectivity - Server access is required for no reason. Even in singleplayer. Yet the servers are terribad. Fix it... There is no reason for this. We are in 2017, if you can't figure out we don't like this by now, what is your issue? Whats your damage, ubisoft? Whats yer damage? Cha.
2. The servers in competitive seem to not be the best as it is peer to peer based so perhaps the net code needs some revisions. This is a highly twitchy type of game and while many people can laugh it off, you will kill off your competitive players this way. Likewise some characters have too long to switch guard and this ends up making them useless late game from what I have been researching. This combined with the other thing will cause a heavy emphasis on certain characters and builds which will.. again.. kill off your competitive players. Don't let it happen. Fix it.
UPDATE: Apparently they fixed the guard switching problem and balanced some things.
Thank you for reading, I hope this was helpful in some small way and I do apologize for the text block.

Apotheon is a stunningly beautiful sidescroller based on Greek mythology. However, it has some key issues that bog down gameplay to the point of making things just... dull. Apotheon is a fantastic work of art. If you're interested in Greek art and pottery, you'll eat this game right up as I did... for a little while. The root of the issue with Apotheon is it's just not that good of a game . There's no advanced mechanics, no thrilling boss battles... although exploration does offer rewards and killing enemies does drop loot, there's just nothing exciting about either event. Visual upgrades do happen, but the combat mechanics themselves don't really advance a whole lot with new gear and new settings. I've never had to retry a single boss encounter (on normal difficulty), and I basically use the same exact tactics every single fight - button smash, aim at the bad guy, and guzzle the pleantiful potions that are strewn everywhere. Sure, you may have to change up weapons or aim at a specific part of the enemy, but still... there's just nothing thrilling or satisfying about the fights. The story is reminiscent of God of War, and is a rather standard Greek tale of the gods and goddesses being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. I can take the story or leave it, but it certainly follows the traditional epic storyline usually presented in Mediterranean mythology. In conclusion, Apotheon really offers a great backbone for a great game - and yet, does not capitalize on this. Apotheon simply gives you a few hours in which you're stunned by its beauty, and then leaves you sad and wanting more. If you're ok with not wanting to complete the game and are just wanting to see some lovely art, then sure - by all means, get it. I just cannot recommend it in context of a game.

Bastion and Transistor are my favourite games ever, and honestly Pyre is just very disappointing.
The biggest flaw of Pyre compared to Supergiant's last two endevours is that the story is straight up told to you. You're this lifeless character who has no other purpose but moving the story along. Characters will talk to you, but they're really just telling you information in a pretty boring way.
The gameplay is just as shallow as the story, trying to be strategic but ultimately failing. The game tries to introduce new characters, some that move fast and some that move full into this Pyreball sport but the lack of depth in the gameplay makes it so it's best to avoid slower characters in battle and instead just use quicker character and carrying the ball into the pyre almost immediately. It's not fun after a while as even on the highest difficulty the same strategy will win you every battle without a worry.
Pyre is a disappointing effort from Supergiant and I hope their next game goes back to intertwining gameplay with story.
EDIT: After getting further into the story, the game is a lot more enjoyable. You start to have to make decisions for your crew
. The gameplay still feels so distant from the story though, and that's really a shame. I would only recommend this game if you aren't looking for something like Bastion and Transistor. If you are look somewhere else as Pyre is not that.
EDIT 2: After finishing the game, I found that using optional difficulty settings the game has become quite difficult and has made strategy in the battles needed. Bigger units are given a use at this point of the game and that helps it feels a lot more diverse.
Final statements: Pyre is the worst game by Supergiant. Is it bad? No. Is it great? No. What Pyre is is a well fleshed out sports game (towards the end of the campaign) that features a decent story that is told in an uninteresting and disconnected way from the gameplay. If you're a fan of visual novels I suspect that this game is for you. If you're not, pick it up when it's on sale in a few months.

After playing through Bastion and Transistor about 4 times apiece, I was stunned and thrilled to see that Supergiant was making another game. I bought Pyre 12 hours before release with the soundtrack and literally sat at my desk waiting for the magical 12pm EST to roll around. After a 15 minute download I played the game for 6 hours straight, having to stop for work and proceeded to on and off play it hours at a time, completly enraptured in the story, characters, gameplay and music.
Easily the strongest aspect a Supregiant game, with such an impeccable history from the art team, there were expectations to meet. However, the game itself is on par if not more spectacular than Bastion and Transistor's incredible aesthetic appeal. With a glorious soundtrack by Darren Korb] and once again featuring the lovely Ashley Barrett's voice, each ballad, lilt, theme, and duet is outstanding. The beautiful hand-drawn characters that come to life with individual narratives each more interesting than the last and a vibrant Seuss-like world brought to life by the wonderful Jen Zee, you are immediately absorped into this incredible alternate reality that refuses to let go. Each individual character is totally unique in how they approach eachother, you, and the world around them and they all have their own interactions with other characters that give them a new level of depth, helping you to bond with them as they accompany you throughout your journey.
Imagine an Association Football or NBA game but it's 3v3 and each player is completly different from the other. The tight controls and and fast-paced strategy that the game forces you into will challenge you on a higher difficulty and verily entertain you on the lower. A few annoying hitboxes and one crazy character archetype in particular can be cause for a little frustration, but at the end of the day the game handles nicely and each "class" has a specific set of tools that balance ou ver nicely. The diverse cast and addicting nature of the actual game will cause you to come back for another Rite constantly.
This is probably my favorite Supergiant Games video game ever released and I would sell my soul and body to this studio to experience for the first time again. Easily the best game I've played in the last 5 years.

Sheltered is another one of those survival games that overthinks the minutiae and overlooks the obvious.
There are a few strange choices in this game's presentation, notably the sparse retro-pixel look, and some of the sound choices. There are only two levels of zoom, and switching between them plays a noise like a warning siren, which I initially interpreted as something going wrong somewhere on the map. The atmospheric sound and music are passable, though some of the incessant pet effects can be grating. It's sometimes difficult to issue commands to your people, because the game doesn't intuitively differentiate between clicking on someone to select them, clicking on an item to interact with, or clicking on a location to move there. Some interactive items, such as the radio, don't even require a character to be anywhere near them (or awake, for that matter.)
Like most survival-type games, you're going to have to learn the idiosyncrasies and die a few times before you learn how to establish a rhythm; what goods are worth keeping, how to mitigate risks, what upgrade paths are useful, vital, or just pointless wastes. Most of the time, you aren't going to realize the game requires you to have something until you discover you lack the materials to craft it, and you have to make a mental note to earmark such-and-such. Better luck next time.
My biggest gripe is that there so many figuratively invisible walls in the game, where forced mechanics impede logical solutions, leading to frustration.
For example, I didn't realize you couldn't harvest meat unless you had a refrigerator. Because searing, salting, or drying meat is apparently too hard. Why not simply allow harvested meat to slowly spoil instead of making it impossible to collect because the resource doesn't fit within the narrow confines of your design? My wasteland scavenge teams can bring back a treasure trove of essential salvage, but we're required to throw excess things away because we don't have any "crates" to store them? How about under the beds, or in the camper, or in any of the giant empty rooms I've built with all my excess concrete? If we can't afford gas masks to prevent radiation poisoning, why can't we just wear the hazmat suits? And how can my explorers carry an additional 6 bags of limestone, but not a simgle nail, just because the sacks stack in the inventory?
I feel like a lot of the difficulties presented to the player could have been solved with some simple, common sense options.
If you can't craft a "stove," take some wood and make a campfire aboveground, provided there's no weather to impede it.
If you're about to wet your pants, and you don't have a "toilet bucket," step behind the broken-down camper and squat.
Use a bucket of water to take a sponge bath instead of blowing all the drinking water on a shower (or slowly going mad from filth.)
People have done these things for hundreds of years; I don't understand why the developers decided they were impossible now.
And for the love of god, if your pet is about to starve, set it free to take its chances hunting vermin on the surface, rather than forcing it to slowly starve in your bunker.

A very simple and fun stealth game.
Enemy AI is basic, unaware of their missing comrades, and blind to the hazards of their surroundings. Mind you, if you're spotted, they are above-average shots and will swarm upon you. In these scenarios, you can either shoot back -- with gun-play that doesn't operate well, outside of sneaking head-shots -- or hide -- enemies stay in their zones, you can identify zones by the doors that you can enter but have no opening animation --.
There are three skills to level up, to help you along as you play. You gain experience by completing secret side-missions and by picking up collectibles. While you will not gain experience for most of your kills, sometimes a collectible can be found when searching the bodies of your fallen enemies.
The one unique feature of this stealth game is the "Morphine" item. Upon use, time will stop momentarily, giving you the opportunity to run away/past a tricky situation, or silently kill an enemy head-on. It can be a saving grace when backed into a corner, but you also might forget that the item is even there.
Game-play becomes very repetitive, quickly. To keep the game fresh, I can not play more than 1 or 2 missions in a session. Which is a shame, but with a bargain asking price of $5 or less, it's hard to regret this purchase.
Over-all, I'd give it a grade of C+.

Summary: If you're a fan of the genre, it's the same formulaic gameplay you expect from a turn-based fantasy game. It gets amazingly repetitive halfway into the game, there is a fair amount of challenge to push you along the way but the game has its' bugs and the difficulty spikes unrealistically at times. The lore and storyline is there to string a series of missions together, the characters for the most part unremarkable and limited development put forth.

I've been playing the HOMM series since it first came out on my father's i386, playing custom maps and amassing a ridiculous stack of creatures to steamroll through the enemy. The game was addicting because there was nothing like it for its' time and to have limitless power and to just build the most amazing kingdom you wanted held its' charm on me. This and Civilization were the PC games that I remembered burning hundreds of hours playing as a child and so I have a certain nostalgic leaning towards them.
For those that have never played the series, it's a hex turn-based strategy role-playing game. It is a strategy game from the perspective of the combat involved, the resource collection and kingdom management, and the numerical emphasis of armies. At the same time a role-playing game from the hero creation and customization, to the fantasy lore and storyline, and the implementation of spellcraft and quests. Resources and territories will be contested by players and those that can manage both kingdom and hero well will be favored to win.
Now to speed forward to the fifth installment, at its' core HOMM follows the same formula from previous games. But to me, take away the updated graphics and audio enhancements, and you're left with a game that is remarkably similar to the very first HOMM. This can be great for enthusiasts, but you would expect for a fifth entry the formula could be improved, a more compelling method of storytelling created, just a greater way of being both a strategy and role-playing game at the same time. The storyline is weak, the cutscenes really don't add depth or character development, at the end of the game I felt that I was just controlling 5 very bland heroes on a rather generic mission to save the world from another trite demonic nemesis. We could probably comment and say, "well the cutscenes were done with in-game graphics, which didn't detract from the presentation." But I would say, watching every character go through his in-game idle animation is really annoying and that was seriously the best they could do? Give me a past, something to make me feel emotion for this character, some anguish that they must overcome, some sense of an impending danger to evade, just an event that makes me feel for the protagonist(s). Sadly, there just isn't any.
Another point and the final one I'll make is about the buginess of the game. The game is not nearly as polished as one would assume, especially the base game which has two official expansions made. On probably 4 separate occassions I had not followed the 'script' that the mission 'suggested' (and I use the word suggested because the cutscenes rarely connect with the mission's objective) and it resulted in the game not properly triggering events to progress/finish the level. Just so many frustrating times where I would spend 1-2 hours on a level, completely destroy the enemy and just because I didn't do something in order, the triggers did not execute as it should have. It's BS, cheap, and ultimately buggy. The difficulty even on normal can be challenging, but a lot of times you'll realize that you've invested about an hour into a level and you're in an irreversible situation where you cannot win. Save often, turn on the auto-save, and don't rely on it. Save at key intervals to be efficient with your time. The game is frustrating and many times it's not from the player but just the way the game scenario was coded.
Now I'm going to say that I would not recommend this game, which I think it fails on so many criteria. It's not a game I would play again after finishing it, not a game I would tell friends about and insist on buying, and it just did not have anything compelling enough to keep me happy while playing. I am not saying the game is bad, but it certainly isn't that great especially in today's VG market.
(Overall 3/5)

Due to my hearing that the servers were optimized I will now change this review to a positive.
I have removed most venom from the review because it is most likely not needed now.
From what I hear, they are making efforts to make things smoother for the players.
----------------------------------
MAIN REVIEW -
I believe that discerning people at Ubisoft should swallow their pride and take notice of what I list as good and what I list as bad. Advertise the good things better so people know! Fix the bad things!
Points in favour of this game:
1. Character customization - on half of all characters, half of all characters are either gender. This is unprecedented for this sort of game and allows people to generally pick a character they like and immerse themselves slightly better in it. I appreciate this design decision. More of my friends will likely play when they can customize their characters. Some people complain about historical accuracy but they are boring and not fun, to put it bluntly. Let people have fun, it isn't like they made the female characters 4 foot tall with noodle arms.
2. Singleplayer - A proper, from what I have seen polished singleplayer campaign in an otherwise multiplayer game. The voice acting looked nice.. etc.. Dynasty Warriors and other similar fighting games just meanwhile have a guy pop up on the screen and tell you stuff you are supposed to be interested in. (No offense to DW, I love the games but.. this is next level.)
3. Bots -  and player versus npc bot matches that reward progress. Appreciated! You don't have to deal with people, if you don't like to.
4. Pseudo Historical - As I watch many HEMA (historical european martial arts) channels on youtube, although the combat is not 100% realistic, it IS more realistic than many games out there and some research was done to make things more immersive and incorporate real world movements to some of the attacks. Half swording and other techniques have made it in and this is rare to see. Warden will grip the blade of her sword and then use the guard to bludgeon enemies. While some people might assume this is a flashy video game thing.. this was actually done quite often because blades are less effective against armour than the blunt end of the sword. Go figure.
5. The animations and environments - are spectacular in my opinion. If you switch guard, your animations will not clip and your movements will properly go through each detail in order to properly swap. If you are turning and rushing your character might show a bit of excitement as it scans both directions. Serious immersion.
6. Pay2win? - From what I saw there is no outright pay 2 win, just pay to progress faster. This should stay this way, I think people can appreciate that.
After being able to login briefly:
7. Community - The player versus npc part of the community seems friendly enough and I still quite enjoy the elimination mode. If you fail to win against your opponent your friend might come help, likewise you can help someone who is struggling after killing your opponent.
8. I might be imagining things but some parts of the customization seem more in-depth than the beta. There may also be new maps.
9. Coop - The singleplayer campaign is apparently coop. I have not tried it in coop yet but if it works, that is pretty stellar.
10. No massive paywalls to use your chosen hero - They give you enough funds to unlock a few characters starting out. Most games like this make you grind for what feels like decades to unlock your favourite characters and this is a welcomed change.
11. Hidden Rewards - You might not notice, but in uplay there is a reward section under the game that you can use the point things to unlock some additional emblems and etc. If you were in the betas you get some for free and the others seemed relatively easy to get considering I am only level 3 and have half of them. Be sure to check the section out if you missed it or are unfamiliar with uplay.
12. Hidden... soundtrack? - The soundtrack is quite nice in my opinion and although it does not mention it, I was able to find in the reward section the ability to download the soundtrack...
Why was this not featured or mentioned anywhere? Still a fairly nice addition. It was so easy to get that I find it odd they don't just remove the tiny reward currency cost (I spent no extra rl money on this) and just advertise the game as coming with the soundtrack. This just seems obvious to me.
Bad stuff:
1. Mandatory Connectivity - Server access is required for no reason. Even in singleplayer. Yet the servers are terribad. Fix it... There is no reason for this. We are in 2017, if you can't figure out we don't like this by now, what is your issue? Whats your damage, ubisoft? Whats yer damage? Cha.
2. The servers in competitive seem to not be the best as it is peer to peer based so perhaps the net code needs some revisions. I don't even know anymore how this game ended up on my list. It must have come in with some humble bundle or any other multi-title. I've been confusing this with Alpha Protocol all that time, so I didn't bother to install it. When I recently got Alpha Protocol with another bundle, I wondered what this second entry was, so I clicked "install".
First of all, Alpha Prime is a classic story driven sci-fi PC shooter, so expect more or less linear gameplay with single room based exploration, some switch flipping, hilarious voice acting and a story you will probably laugh about in a coupe of years, when you look back at all the trash you've been watching, reading and playing before you got married. I have not been very far in the game, but far enough to know, what might expect me for the rest of the game.
The story:
You are a tough guy who knows a tough lady and you both go on a dangerous quest to save her boyfriend, so you venture to Godknowswhere on some distant planet. There is some sort of valuable mineral, that turns people into crazy idiots with guns and there are robots, not as crazy, but at least as well armed. That's pretty much all you need to know, if I lost you at this point, don't bother playing the game.
Gameplay and technology:
This game plays like most sci-fi shooters before the lack of buttons on console controllers found their entry to mainstream shooters. You can lean around the corner, a feature that was used by one half of all gamers and never even discovered by the other half. Bullets fly where you point your gun at. Instead of iron sights, you get a small zoom animation. Health does not regenerate. If you are on the planet surface outside the buildings, oxygen is rare, so you need to find refill stations. You can push around objetcs like crates, pick up items and throw them for damage. It's even encorporated in the few puzzles the game has to offer. You can shoot and destroy most glass surfaces. Imagine my surprise, when I tried to take cover in a room with a window, just to be gunned down by the guys outside. It lacks all the handholding of modern shooters. There is no "Press F to pick this up", maybe once on the first encounter, but after that you are on your own. The visuals are nothing to write home about. For a 2007 game, that didn't have a Crysis budget, the game looks solid and runs well enough. There are little to no glitches and the framerate is great on modern hardware.
I will definitly try to finish this game and I'm glad I didn't miss it, even if I'm a little late to the party.

Velvet Assassin interested me when I first saw its gameplay. Games where stealth is the primary focus are not made that often. However, after seeing the relatively average review scores on Metacritic and Steam, I decided to wait for the price to drop. After seeing it for about $1 on Steam I decided to buy it. Let’s just say it turned out to be worth much more than $1. While the game obviously doesn’t have the massive budget and polish of AAA stealth games like Metal Gear Solid, it’s still a great game. You traverse through a great variety of levels, often equipped with nothing but a knife and pistol with few bullets. You generally need to stay hidden since all the Nazis have automatic weapons and you are rather defenseless making this a true stealth game. Running and gunning is rarely an option when up against multiple opponents. The storyline is virtually non-existent and is there just for the sake of having one. Graphics and audio are above average. The game is about 10 hours long.
Bottom Line: If you’re looking for another stealth game to play, then Velvet Assassin is for you.

Summary: Velvet Assassin has the atmosphere of Return to Castle Wolfenstein with the gameplay of a stealth game like Thief or Dishonored.  If you can forgive some functional issues (enemy-proof doors, sparse checkpoints, poorly explained interface), you’re in for a well-written adventure on the macro scale and thoughtfully crafted, varied stealth gameplay on the micro scale.
Pros and cons:
+ You have a variety of tools at your disposal.  You can sneak up and backstab a guard, or pull the pin on his grenade if he has one.  You can use one of your very scarce bullets, or use an environmental hazard like electrified water or poison gas barrels.  You can take a shot of morphine and charge an enemy before he can react.  You can stay in the shadows, break a fuse box to darken new areas, or hide in tall plants when outside.  You can also peek through keyholes before you enter a room, and whistle to draw the enemy away from his normal patrol route.
+ The game looks good, and the art supports the gameplay.  Strong shadows make it clear whether you’re hidden in the dark or not.  The enemies don’t look like clones of each other, which helps you keep count of everyone when sizing up a room.
+ The story ties things together well.  A large part of the game is presented as the protagonist recounting her adventures.  So she says things like “I had to find a key” which sounds better than her talking to herself in the present.  A major plot point is foreshadowed bit by by bit through flash-forwards.  The enemy guards frequently have long conversations with each other which, along with the collectible treasures, enrich the experience and sound very authentic.
- About half of the doors seem to load a different section of the map.  Enemies can’t follow you through these doors.  So no matter how hot things get, if you can reach a ‘load’ door you’re totally safe.
- The game only saves at checkpoints, which are often annoyingly far apart.  Most enemy encounters have one of two outcomes: you execute your plan perfectly, or you die and start over.  There’s not much middle ground, so even with upgraded health, most of the medkits go unused.
- While the game isn’t totally linear, player movement is tightly controlled.  You can only crawl, jump, or climb at specific places where the game allows it.  Invisible walls insure you can never step off a ledge, or even wade through a foot-deep pond.  So basically, don’t expect ‘outside the box’ thinking to get you anywhere.
- Some of the interface and instructions are confusing.  For example, you don’t use ‘aiming mode’ to backstab somebody.  Even though you raise your knife and it looks like exactly what you’re supposed to do, you’ll clumsily poke the guard, and almost certainly get shot before he dies.  You *can* get more than one morphine needle, but you need to upgrade your morphine multiple times.  There are things like this that weren’t communicated well, which you’ll have to figure out through trial and error.

A tactical game that is surprisingly rewarding.
Pick a special force, it can be SAS, US Special Forces, SEAL, even russian specials, and use them to clear different objectives and places. Some places are more difficult than others but overall good planning will lead to successful execution. the unmanned reconnaissence vehicle makes alot of mission a bit too easy on the lower levels, but can really be the difference between success and failure on the toughest level.
The different special forces start with different advantages, but with experience your troopers will level up and you can forge them somewhat into having the skills you prefer. There seem to be a cap though so you won't be able to level everyone up to max on everything, instead you have to plan well here too so the troopers will fit your playstyle.
Equipment is also something that can be altered, you have the option of buying new guns, better body armor, buy lockpicks, door breach charges or shotguns for blasting door locks (can also be used against enemies), but there's also options to upgrade weapons with sights, grips, silencers etc.
Overall a game that for its price gives alot of interesting gaming experiences for anyone interested in tactical combat with small units. Anyone interested in learning about such combat would probably also benefit from picking this up.

I so desperately wanted to like this game, even more than that, I wanted to *love* it! The setting and story is fascinating, based on the real life French-English spy Violette Szabo, during WWII. She's a great character and her model is gorgeous, the soundscapes are great, the enemies actually speak German (it used to be rather uncommon a few years back that any character spoke their native tounge, unless it happened to be English), and the light effects are nice.
But the fact is, the game is punishingly difficult. Relying mostly on stealth tactics, the fist few episodes works fine to ease you into the games mechanics. You can even feel it is a bit too unbelievable that guards patrolling would spot you only to forget you were crawling into a vent or something a moment later, even for game logic. But then there's a difficulty spike that will have you ragequit the game after a number of failed attempts. It's not that you don't know what to do, it's how hard it is to actually do it in this game. Surely, some will find this challenging and truthful, I can appreciate the fact you don't survive bulletstorms for example, but damn...
