This is one of those rare gems of a game which is seductively simple while still being skillfully satisfying. When watching the trailer, I was baffled as to the mechanics of the game, but I was certain that I would enjoy figuring it out as I went. I am surprised after playing it that I didn't understand how it worked; it really is that simple!
In playing Hook, one takes on the role of "machine disassembler". You're trying to unwind, or rather un
, these schematic-looking devices and pull everything through to their sources without getting tangled in the other components. That's really all there is to it. Through tracing the paths and carefully selecting which one can be pulled out without bumping any of the others, you continue to choose which to remove next until all the pieces are gone. If you mess up and tangle the pieces, you must restart the level entirely, but choose your calls carefully and it's not an issue. From level 40 onwards you receive three lives before a mandatory restart instead of one. The levels do become very complex and visually-daunting, but take your time and make sure you know what pushing each button is going to do and everything will resolve. A treasure trove for the detail-oriented mind!
There's something deceptively-pleasing as you watch the piece successfully slide out, a casual reminder of your shining brilliance and mastery of puzzle games. But alas, with an intellect such as yours this game will not last long, and soon you will need to move forward into different lands of puzzles to deduct and conquer.
I picked it up and played through it in two days. It took me 77 minutes to complete this game's fifty levels. That wasn't long, but a couple of days later I showed it to my girlfriend, who proceeded to beat it in a single session, trying initially to beat the game without messing up, but (after that failed) resolving to beating my time. She finished in 67 minutes (which doesn't mean she is smarter than me! I'm just more methodical and patient! Yeah, patient...), a satisfied faux-mechanic as well. Then days later we showed it to her younger brother, an engineer wanna-be. He enjoyed it until about level 42, when he was going too fast and on a complex level. Once he had to restart it, he decided he wasn't patient enough to try again. He never completed it. Then a relative of my girlfriend came over with her boyfriend. I wasn't feeling overly social that night so while the girls played "makeup" I brought out Hook to show the other boyfriend. He played slowly for a good while, and didn't end up completing it because the night evolved otherwise, but enjoyed the game and resolved to purchase it on his own!
So there you have it.

Heroes of Might and Magic has always been a puzzling franchise to me and the fifth game in the series is no exception. Heroes of Might and Magic V is a turn based game that goes into a turn based (very turn based) combat system when you meet enemies in similar fashion to the Total War series.
Presentation
A turn based battle system would be an entirely acceptable thing except that the game has so many variables and numbers that trying to get into it is endlessly confusing. In addition to that we have the fact that the "armies" are represented by mere numbers and a single unit model. It does seem like the game could have supported far more models on screen but sadly the user interface hinders you from having more than 7 stacks of units on field, this makes the game's presentation of allowing you to command vast armies seem very dishonest to me. It's always fun to stack numbers up but a game has far more potential for visual presentation that the game truly takes advantage of.
What really strikes me with the game is it's fantasy. The basic game of Heroes of Might and Magic offers 6 different factions: Haven (Humans), Sylvian (Elves), Dungeon (Dark Elves), Necropolis (Undead), Inferno (Demons) and my favorite Academy (Wizards)! All of these factions feature classic mythological and fantasy creatures and gives them stats to reflect their strength. Every race is relatively well balanced as well I would say, at least for first appearance. Every single race has 7 available unit types and each of them can be upgraded once (or twice of you got one of the expansions). Haven's units starts off with the lowly peasants and end with bloody angels, in-between they have a sweet mix of medieval flavored units. How these armies are built up are pure genius and there seem to be little to no redundancy in the units neither.
I also need to praise the city screen with looks glorious and the upgrades to it is amazing eye-candy.
Gameplay
I cannot keep praising the game much longer though. I have a real problem with some of it's gameplay mechanics. First off is the unit growth system. In order to get together an army the player must build special buildings for each type. You even need to upgrade these buildings in order to upgrade your troops. Fair enough. However, there's a serious flaw that your units numbers don't grow without the buildings. So potentially another player could end up with far more units than another, and there's no way as far as I'm aware to even such a setback out, short off trying to win a battle early on. It seems to be then that unless you get a perfect start a game isn't truly worth playing to the end.
The heroes do have magic powers that could be used in an attempt to even the odds between the players but these spells mostly cannot be learned (at least not over 2nd circle of spells) without the respective skills in the magic field. This becomes problematic due to the fact that these skills are awarded to heroes at seemingly random. In addition to that the magic spells are also rewarded at random in different Mages' Guilds in different cities. Due to these facts it seems like the game is controlled solely by luck of the draw and little of good skills. In battle the randomness seems to take far less importance, instead the amount of randomness is mostly determined by creature characteristics.
The RPG elements in the game seems to amount solely to stacking stats. A hero with plenty of artifacts and a large army seems to be a force of nature and entirely unstoppable. There seem to be no apparent penalty for having large armies like having logistics problems or slow progress, instead large armies travel with the same ease as small armies, making taking on more powerful opponents very tricky and seemingly impossible.
Conclusion
There's a lot to admire in Heroes of Might and Magic V. You might have noticed that I like using uncertain words like "seem" a lot and that's because I have only played this game for approx. 15 hours yet and I'm still figuring out the quirks of the game. This pretty astonishing to me really as I've been annoyed at several core things in this bloody game and I still keep playing it for some reason. I guess it's extremely addicting and it shows giant amounts of potential. I still think that the greatest flaw as far as I'm concerned is it's presentation. There's never any real big army feel and as time goes on you, as a player only end up to feel more vulnerable. Don't think I haven't searched for any gameplay guides for this game, there isn't any! There's no good documentation either and pretty lousy "tutorials" and it shows that this game was made mainly for the fans of Might and Magic and few others.
The gameplay in itself is bad enough and due to the lack of being able to even out unbalances during the game's progress and the dishonest presentation doesn't help either - but in the other hand the game is also very addicting, has great potential and the fantasy aethetics are gripping. Sadly because it's so hard to play this game for anyone new to the series I have to refrain from recommending this game.
Do I win?

This is what sequels should be all about. Taking mechanics that worked from the first title and buffing them to a mirror finish, and then introducing new ideas to make it original.
For me, Origins was a really, really fun and solid game and a great return to form for the Rayman franchise. I've sunk many hours (three digits) into it and, despite not being the completionist type, have been pushed to try quite hard to do so by it's captivating art and great soundtrack, plus pile of content. With Legends, Ubisoft has managed to recreate this gem, but better. It's as simple as that.
The UbiArt engine is slick at all times and always stable, the game is even prettier then the first and, somehow, even more tuneful. I haven't anything to complain about yet, except perhaps that it's not occasionally as brutal as Origins in spots, but there's always plenty more in the game, and I haven't even mentioned the online challenges yet where the player competes against a global leaderboard.
If you like platformers, you'll probably love this game. It's fast, it's competitive and is sensibly integrated into online challenges, and doesn't suffer very much from being originally WiiU exclusive. It's my favorite game of 2013 (previously a title given to Revengeance), and a perfect 10 in my books.
I do recommend picking up Origins before this one if you're a newcomer to the franchise, though. You will simply be missing out otherwise and it has come down drastically in price.

Heroes of Might and Magic V is a turn based strategy game in a long series which started back in 1995 with Heroes of Might and Magic: A Strategic Quest and has been an extremely popular and successful strategy game for many years with the 6th game in the series coming out in October of 2011. As mentioned, HoMM V is a turn based strategy game where you control one hero for each army. The hero has 8 slots for 8 different units but they can have as many units as they would like under their command with that unique unit. The different units include classes such as archers, soldiers, cavalry, archangels and devils, ghosts, ghouls and many more. When your hero travels along the map they can pick up different relics and items that can increase attack, defense, luck, moral and other abilities and items that will help in a battle. They hero can only travel so far per day and after they are done they pass their turn on to the other opposing player whether that be AI or Human.
During their turn they can fight any enemies within their range which in turn starts a battle with a grid like system. These battles are also turn based and are based on the units speed not necessarily strict turn order. If an archer gets a lucky shot in they can get a boost and moral and actually go again either right after or sometime before their original turn order. Some units are faster than others; for example, griffins can go twice before the peasants even go once.

During the game the player can also take over cities, towns and keeps. The main city can be upgradable which allows you to build different units and upgrade others. Along with that the player can also higher other mercenary heroes that can have their own armies and travel around under the player’s control. Towns and keeps have certain units tied to them that each week replenish and can be bought by the heroes to add to their armies. In order to upgrade/build buildings and buy these units the player must capture strategic resources all along the map that include wood, ore, gems, mercury, sulfur, crystal and gold.

The story is a pretty simple one and spans across 6 different campaigns (the expansions add 2 more) which include Haven, Inferno, Necropolis, Dungeon, Sylvan and Academy. I only got through the first campaign as the game is very long but in this one Isabel the Queen is about to get married to King Nicolai when the demon invasion causes them to get separated and she is working towards getting back with the King while killing as many demons on the way as she can. She eventually finds him dying from some demonic spell that Agrael, a demon, attacks him with and is determined to get revenge against all demons and after which the dying king declares her ruler of the Holy Griffin Empire when he dies.

The graphics of the game are fairly basic and even for their time they weren’t anything special. In 2006 when we saw this game launch we saw other RTS and TBS games such as Empire at War, Company of Heroes and Warhammer 40k. So even if I was judging this by today’s standards it didn’t really even live up to the standards of 2006 when the game launched. Though there isn’t anything really wrong with the graphics, they just feel dated and not as impressive as other games of the time. There was one thing that kept bugging me about the game and that would be the camera. You couldn’t click on different items in the world without moving it around or if there was a fog of war it forced the unit to go all the way around or wouldn’t allow the unit to go forward at all.
The Sound was also equally bland and the music was very repetitive. The music didn’t so much get in the way or be annoying it just didn’t change very much. The voice acting wasn’t anything special but it wasn’t awful either. However the sound effects were unique for each unit so there is that. The biggest thing for me however was the setting the game was in. There are so many different areas and creatures in the game that it made for a very interesting adventure through the first campaign just getting to know this world.

Overall I can’t really compare this to any other game in the series as I haven’t played them however I have really enjoyed the gameplay of the game so much that it made me want to buy the 6th game in the series since I know the graphics have been vastly improved and look very impressive. I am giving the game a little boost in rating due to the limits of technology at the time however my 5 tiers are what the game rates to today’s standards.
•	Story  - 2 out of 5
•	Gameplay – 5 out of 5
•	Graphics – 2.5 out of 5
•	Sound  - 2 out of 5
•	Fun – 5 out of 5
Pros:
-	Great Turn based gameplay
-	Can be Hard and rewarding
-	A nice learning curve
-	Interesting world and lore
Cons:
-	Music/Sound are ok, nothing thrilling
-	Story is ok however the world is great
-	Irritating Camera

The Isle had a good start.  Indeed, the idea of an open world dinosaur roleplaying simulation was a great niche market, which quickly earned a bit of a cult following.  The ability to play in a sandbox mode, and practically let human nature dictate how the game played out, was one of the features of the game which was interesting to study.  Sure, people would Kill on Sight, or CareBear (Use T-Rexes to protect herbivores).  But for the most part, it was a social platform which allowed people to get together, roleplay and socialize.  In the few weeks I played The Isle, I met many wonderful gamers, more so than any other game I had played before, save for maybe TF2.
The developer, however, had other plans.  He has a vision, and his vision doesn't include allowing unrealistic behaviour to occur.  Probably some of the worst Public Relations representation was displayed by the developer during this games development, basically berating and making fun of those who got enjoyment from his product, through ways he didn't condone.  He also began to ban people who spoke negatively about his game on the forums.
Sure he has a vision.  His vision, I can understand.  However, the way he went about achieving that vision, and his brutal mocking and behaviour towards those critical of his vision was a huge factor in why most of those people I met who enjoyed this game, no longer play it.
If you want to play a very challenging, very paranoid simulation of dinosaur life, where you can't trust anyone, and must hide in the shadows and wait for your progression points to level up, so you can become slightly more powerful, so long as you are able to stay alive - than this game is for you.   If you are looking to socialize, and relax, this game likely isn't for you.

The developers themselves have not been winning the acclaim of the players. For some reason the developers decided to push out an unstable and untested update and now the modders have to update the maps. There's no telling how long that will take. For now, we're stuck with V2. This map has certainly recieved more aesthetic appeal but all the good bushes we could use as hiding spots have been removed and there's nowhere left to find cover. Considering there's very little space in that map, it can be a nerve-racking experiance for lower tiers. I'm sure some of you might even remember maps V3 and V4. Those where both fairly large and very beautiful maps, but for reasons unknown, those maps are currently messed up because of missing foliage, horrible terrain texters, etc. To be honest, the modders do a far better job at map-making than the developers in my opinion.
Lastly, theres the issue I have with the current progression times. It use to be that the developers gave control of progression times to the server owners. Some severs had longer times, others had very short times and all was dandy. But  the developers decided that the minimum progression times should be extended and the herrera and austro should have their hunger degrade ubsurdely fast. It takes 150 points for a player to go from herrera to utah plus with the increased hunger depletion. I don't know why they made it like this because now it's damn-near impossible to reach anything past tier two. Increased difficulty doesn't always mean increased fun, but no, the developers want this game to be more "hardcore" I guess. They don't realise that not everyone has time to play a game with that amount of time consumption. They don't realise that SERVERS ARE DYING because of this decision. I sure do hope they give control over to the server owners again because quite frankly, this is bull s**t.
Anyways, that's my review. I wish it the best and will keep playing it in the future (just much less now).

Though I was initally put aside by the mixed reviews, I thought "screw it" and bought it as it was on sale. I thought I would be disappointed by the quality, and would stop playing relatively early on. Nope. This game's athmosphere is exceptionally well made, and I feel that not enough games have really stepped into the "supernatural but not really" genre, involving Bigfoot and other creatures that people claim to have sighted. Thought I didn't have the opportunity to try "Ultra" as I would've been watching a PowerPoint, I was really happy with the quality.
Now, here comes the bad. The animations are alright. Firing a gun looks ok but doesn't have the same feeling as in other horror or fps games. The controls are somewhat tricky in the beginning, but thankfully you can change the scheme to whatver you'd like. AI is ok, though I feel it could be greatly improved. The ability to hide in hunting shelters is nice, but the fact that you're literally invisible to non-player-controlled things isn't that immersive.
Overall, I'd give it a 7/10. I think that while it is a lot of fun, there is still a lot that could be added, and I'm really looking forward to when it is complete.

The single player story is nor very interesting, nor long. The main character seems to fall for traps way too easily. But that is ten times over compensated with a rich and authentic world, take for example the descriptions for Relics(game's collectibles), which are both cool, interesting and sometimes funny. Not surprising, since the Artifacts universe (Darkness-Angelus-Witchblade-someelsewerethere)  is one of the most rich around.
The game is the first-person shooter gameplay-wise, but with a lot of twists. There are various darkness powers, not much, but every one is useful. Using them turns combat in a brutal  beatdown for your enemies. But the light is your enemy, so standing under a bright lamp you become blined/lose armor/cant use powers. That's something I didn't encounter in any other game so it's at least somewhat distinct.
The multiplayer has not much to offer either. There are four characters, each with his own backstory and abilities (ability trees are cut out of a main protagonist's), playing through a short cooperative campaigh (which completes the singleplayer story)
One of the games I cared enough to complete 100%. It has no super-hard achievements requiring fiftysomething hour grinding though. Everything there is to do can be done in a week of playing in the evenings. And that can be counted both as an upside and as a downside - the main story is short, completely leveling a multiplayer character can be done in two days, and thats it. You can play it through completely and move on. But god, do I hope for "the Darkness III"

Velvet Assassin is a stealth game, set in World War 2, in which you take the role of a british female agent and fight against Nazi Germany in 12 missions.
It's a nice game,probably not a top notch stealth title,but good nonetheless.I would rate it somewhere between 7.5-8/10.
This game DOES NOT deserve the mixed reviews it has now.It has mixed reviews for 2 major reasons :
1) this game might not launch on start for everyone, but this issue can be solved by doing some damn research.I fixed this issue in less than 5 minutes.Most people are just too lazy or stupid to do a simple research.
2)This game relies a lot on stealth,you can't shoot your way through a mission because you die fast.Even if you are sneaky, you will still die quite often.That means the game is quite hard and you need to use stealth.The difficulty of the game is increased by the checkpoint system it uses.So,if you're a ♥♥♥♥♥ who thinks Assassin's Creed or Dishonored are stealth games...this game is not really for you.
PROS and CONS:
Pros:
+ very good atmosphere: the enviroment is simply amazing, you get to see some well made surroundings(like a gestapo prison, or a ghetto from Poland).You will see dead civilians, you will hear different conversations between german soldiers(which might tickle your emotions a little) and so on..
+ good music: the music is tense,without being intrusive
+ good graphics: especially amazing lighting
+ stealth: the game has different ways in which you can kill the enemies, from killing them with the knife, guns, to shooting explosive barrels, barrels with toxic gas, triggering grenades on unsuspecting foes and so on.As I said before, you can't just shoot enemies and expect to finish the mission..you have to be sneaky, observe the patterns the enemies and be really careful,because mistakes are easily punished in this game.Also it uses other stealth elements like hiding bodies,disguises and broken glass to reveal your position when sneaking
+/- checkpoint system.I set this as "+/-"  because some people don't like it, as it makes the game more difficult.However I find it more enjoyable than a quicksave/quickload system, because it makes the game more intense and makes you play carefully. Also, the checkpoints are placed pretty conveniently
+ it's a pretty cheap game
Cons:
- the AI is stupid sometimes. However it didn't upset me much, because that's the case with most stealth games (remember splinter cell aka "lightbulb assassin")
- shooting sucks.It's fortunate however that you will stab people most of the time
- the game is linear for most of the time
+/- checkpoint system again( for me it's a + however)

This is Bejeweled 3. In case you haven't realized that, now you know. Go buy this game now.
Alright, fine...
Bejeweled 3 is the fourth game in the brilliant match-3 puzzler series by Popcap. Yes, this was before King and their copycat ways made them #1 on the mobile industry, and before we got an explosion of lazy, cash grab bejeweled clones on Facebook. Bleh. Alas, we still need to be thankful for the game that not only made others copy from how good it was, but also improved over its previous games in many ways.
The gameplay is simple, match 3 gems or more to clear them. Matching 4 or 5 will give you flame gems, hypercubes, and lightning gems, so you'll be able to clear more gems at once later on. While the mechanics are simple, Popcap managed to twist up the rules in fun and exciting ways in their eight different game modes. Classic has you going for high scores, Zen lets you relax and match gems..forever, really, Lightning makes you panic as you try to gain extra time while using the 60 seconds given to score tons of points, the amazing Quest mode that REALLY changes the way you play Bejeweled, and there are so many others.. Well, 4, actually, but they're so deep and compelling, it just leaves me begging for more.
Bejeweled 3 is no diamond in the rough either, its visuals are absolutely stunning. Whether it's an explosion from flame gems, a lightning strike for lightning gems, or the beautiful (active) backgrounds while you play the game modes, it's truly pure eyecandy. Speaking of candies, this game has awesome earcandy as well. The music is quite enjoyable and another thing I adore about this game..
I honestly can't say more. If you haven't bought this game, I HIGHLY recommend it. While you could play something like Candy Crush and wait a whole 20 or so minutes just to have another go at the levels that almost always end up weaseling money out of you, instead, play what the fools were trying to imitate, but failed to do so. Bejeweled 3. OUO

While I recommend this game, there are a few things I need to mention:
1) Yes, Bejeweled can be played elsewhere for cheaper/free. This does not inherently make this a bad game. Achievement support and a centralized location make it desirable to buy it, if you are so inclined. I wanted to add this game to my collection, so I bought it. (This game also goes on sale during major sales if it's too expensive for you.)
2) The developer (PopCap) has a history of publishing bad ports of its own games, and most of its games' steam forums have posts asking for help. There are probably some negative reviews of this game solely because of it. The tell-tale sign of an issue is their crash reporting system. What PopCap fails to mention is that there are only a select number of resolutions that the game supports. I normally run on 1280x720 for my setup, but have to switch to 1920x1080 to launch the game, before switching back to my normal display. (Try this before messing with regedit.)
For the actual review:
It's not a bad game; your classic match-3 game, with several different modes. The main 4 are Classic, Endless, Lightning, and Quest, plus 4 'secret' modes. Players have a rank system, which doesn't seem to do anything, and a badge system that marks your general progress, and counts towards achievements on Steam.
I would recommend this game, but more-so when it goes on sale.

I have beat this game multiple times on console (don't hurt me), and I can easily say that this is one of the best platformers ever...hands down! Whenever people hear "greatest platformer ever" people always point at the original Mario games, Super Mario Galaxy, etc. However, this easily joins among their ranks.
This game is a breath of fresh air in the platformer genre. Along with its counterpart Rayman Origins (which I have also beat), they are both really refreshing platformer games because of their unique style, in graphics, gameplay, and level design.
Firstly, the game is visually stunning. The game uses an engine called the "UbiArt" engine, which is used to easily animate any image. The animations in this game are flawless given the many different movements that Rayman can use. Plus, the game feels INCREDIBLY smooth, and there are no visual flaws whatsoever. If I was to ever to die in this game, I cannot fault the game for choppy frame rate... I always blame myself!
Speaking of which, the game has a difficulty balance that can accomodate both new players and old players. Some levels can be a breeze, but then others you can die A LOT, especially some of the later levels.
The level design is really good. Like most platformers, each world typically has a "theme". In my personal opinion, I believe that the "Fiesta de Los Muertos" world in Rayman Legends is the best, clearly because the level design is so great in every single level (if you play the first level at the world, you will see exactly what I mean). What a lot of platformers truly fail at achieving is creating MEMORABLE levels, and Rayman Legends has at least a few memorable levels that will be stuck in your head. Even the boss battles are really great!
The gameplay is also really addicting, with plenty of different moves to learn. This can range from a series of simplistic punches, all the way to cartwheels (a slightly more advanced move). While the objective is to complete a level, there is also a ranking for each level to grab a both a certain number of lums and "teensies". Lums, unlike the last game, are accumulated and can be used to unlock new variants of characters. Plus, lucky tickets unlock plenty of different things, including updated Rayman Origins levels!
...and the multiplayer...oh my....the multiplayer is GOLDEN!!!! This game easily has the most fun local multiplayer in a long while! The multiplayer is perfect for anybody, whether you want to play seriously or if you want to troll your friends. :)
Another memorable part of the game, even though it is not as prominent, would be the soundtrack. The soundtrack really compliments the game in different ways, and I had a couple of tunes stuck in my head. Overall, the game can last you quite awhile, maybe about 15-20 hours to complete everything (depending on how good you are). What can also add to the length would be the daily and weekly challenges, where you can REALLY hone your skills.
There are a few flaws, given the overall grand scheme of things, but hardly hold this game back from sheer greatness. I think that there should  have been more minigames along with "Kung Foot" because "Kung Foot" isn't necessarily my favorite part of the game. Also, I think that there are also too many "clone" characters (variants of Barbara in particular).
To whomever might read this review, I would not even hesitate getting this game. Play it and love it! You won't regret it!

Very fun platformer, for sure.  Difficulty starts low but it ramps up as it goes, and the game feels challenging yet rewarding.  This is at its core, a platformer, though.  Don't expect much from combat and don't expect much from the boss fights.  The platforming itself is spot on, and arguably the game's best strength is its music levels (watch some videos to see yourself).  The visuals are breathtaking and just in style with Rayman, and the soundwork is equally top tier.
HOWEVER
While this game looks, sounds, and plays like Rayman, thats as far as it goes.  If you are looking for a Rayman nostalgia trip, I wouldn't exactly say this is it.  Beyond what I mention above, this game holds little in common with its predessesors.  First off, Rayman Legends fails to live up to the tones of the previous games.  The trademark "grimdark hidden by a humorous and groovy world full of adventure and mystery" has been thrown out in favor of a completely light hearted and juvenile tone, but somehow isn't even big on the humor from previous games to make up for it.  Rayman Legends is as it implies; its all about adventure, mystery, and exploration, so it manages to keep those at least.  Its not about saving the world or laughing your♥♥♥♥♥off, its about running through various locations while you beat up random monsters that happen to find themselves in your way.  You won't feel much for the characters and they won't inspire you to feel much yourself.  Every character is a cookie cutter of the last; they offer no unique expressions or unique performance.  Rayman won't be offering his snarky comments and you won't get the comic relief you expect from Globox or the Teensies.  Villians from previous games do not make appereances.  None of the additional characters have anything to offer rather than a sentence of flavor text and are cookie cutter skins, and feel quite out of place given the Rayman universe.  Nobody even SAYS anything to characterize them or add any semblance of a plot.  The most plot you get is the order in which you play the levels and the progression between them.
Note this game is still quite good, but its sad given that this game is literally half of Rayman; Rayman was known for its superior universe / tone AND its gameplay.
Legends and Origins are supposed to be prequels to the 3D games, but since there is no dialogue or plot its highly arguable that this is a completely standalone title.  This dissappointed me quite a bit, since the game's sells itself as Rayman's "origins" and "legend."  Please keep that in mind when purchasing this product.
Also if you are eyeing Origins, don't bother since this game includes Origins.
Another thing that might really get on your nerves is that because of the game's target audience, there are a bunch of really dumb minigames that the game is constantly shoving in your face, such as the Monster Room or the Lucky Ticket game.  In fact, in order to even play the Origins half of the game you must play that minigame around 100 times.

I have always been fascinated by the Rayman series because of the good graphics, but I never liked the games very much and never related in any way to the main character. However, giving this newest part of the series a chance was a very rewarding decision. The developers did nearly everything right in my opinion:
gameplay - just great, you have perfect control over the character and a lot of different moves, in part depending on your environment
amount of content - the game is really exemplary in this respect: multiple playable characters, a huge amount of levels and additional daily and weekly mini challenges that remodel certain areas
difficulty - even though challenging at times, the game always seems to be fair and does not lead to a lot of frustration (and I played all the locked and hidden levels)
design - the graphics are beautiful, especially the vegetation and the sci-fi stuff. the level design is very good and keeps you entertained with varying design elements and a lot of funny and crazy ideas
sound - the sound effects and most of the music is great and original, sometimes very atmospheric, more often very funny. some of the tracks could have been better suited to underline the atmosphere of certain areas. the music-themed levels (in which your movements have to be in line with the music) are awesome in general, as is the music for the underwater levels
In sum, I can really recommend this game to everyone who likes to play platformers. Even If you only like some of the platformer classics, but stopped playing that type of game for a long time - you probably should give this game a try :)

I want to love this game so badly. I really, REALLY, want to love this game so badly. The combat is fun an interesting and the experience is one of the best I've had in a while. Launching a new game as a new class was fun and the diversity of the characters was really something that has kept me coming back.
The opening day was great, everybody was digging in their heels, and starting to really try out the full breadth of what the game has to offer. I had some of the greatest matches the first week of release, the stretching of legs and the testing of mettle.
The campaign is solid. It isn't revolutionary, and everything happens just a bit too conveniently for the villian to not be seen as a tad contrived. The Warden and Knight cast are ok, nothing special, but no one really awful, either. The Viking Cast is forgetable, save the warlord who was very well-developed. The Japanese seemed to be the best cast of the campaigns, as each character seems to recieve more development than the other factions. The campaign and tutorials give you benefits, too. It's great, and by the time all is said and done, you start with a cool 7000 steel. The villian is kinda lacking, honestly, and ends up being the sword equivalent of a bullet sponge,
The multiplayer is wonderful. The classes feel like a geniune puzzle, and your dedication to learning each one will be rewarding. Your first character will be new, fresh and exciting, and you may even forgive the connectivity mishaps that plague the game. You'll have a blast earning new items, gear, customization, etc...
Until you hit Reputation 3; Level 63, for those who would like to know. Sadly, this is where you can encounter end-game content. For perspective, there are at least 30 reputation ranks in this game. 600 levels! So, what's after end-game rep 3? Nothing. 108 gear rank is the absolute maximum. So, you max out your character and can slay God, what now?
Start a new character, right? Wrong, my good sir/madam, because after you cross the magical Reputation 1, you will find that the matchmaking doesn't care about who you're matched with. Trying to start a new character will see you put against max-rank enemy players, often with players of your skill/Gear rank on your team. It is actually impossible to 4v4 with a new character, game being as it is now.
But all of this is in spite of the horrid connection, and the overall imbalance which persists throughout the matchmaking. But that's not all, folks. In addition to all of this, Ubisoft (in their infinite wisdom), just hand your open IP to anyone you're connected to. In this P2P only game. So, that means that you are quite like to encounter a gru, meaning someone who is probably going to DOS you while fighting.
But there's still more! Better hope that the game agrees with you, because otherwise you may find yourself banned, even if you have never played the game. Wonderful!
Now on to steel. Honestly? It's fine unless you want cosmetics, that's all I've got to say. Cosmetics are stupid expensive.
So, while I detest numerical ratings, what would I give this game? Probably 5/10. If Ubisoft fixes this game, it will probably be an 8 or 9, and I will update this review accordingly.

Apotheon is a damn fun action game and a damn fun exploration game all mixed up with an extremely accurate depiction of Greek Mythology and one of the most damn gorgeous art styles you'll likely ever see in a video game, though it is not without it's short-comings in a few areas.
The gameplay of Apotheon is primarily split between two elements: Combat and Exploration. The areas of Mount Olympus are fairly large and have a lot to see and do in them, as well as a lot to murder in them. First off, the combat. The player wields a variety of ancient weaponry that you can stab, slash and throw; as well as wielding a few other fun toys such as ancient Greek molotovs and grenades for some reason (it's not as out of place as it might sound). Combat is a simple matter of rolling, attacking and blocking, but it's simplicity is it's strength. I will never forget the moment I set a man on fire and then harpooned him into orbit with one of my spears as he fell of a ledge. The combat is very much a sandbox and can be approached in whatever way the player chooses and as such is extremely enjoyable at times, though not without it's frustrations. The smaller more common enemies tend to dodge a lot making landing melee hits quite frustrating at times though it's not a huge problem. The other half of the gameplay is exploration, running around the various hubs collecting things, looting, questing, etcetera. This is great fun for the most part and everywhere has somethign to find, though it has more frustrations than the combat portion of the game. The games "quests" aren't tracked and you aren't given any indication of where you need to be for anything other than the main story, which means finding things can be a pain and is heavily reliant on your memory of the levels, though clearing out the various hubs is an extremely rewarding experience. Boss fights are the biggest Strength and weakness of Apotheon. Certain fights, such as the fights against Zeus and Poseidon are incredibly enjoyable and present something new to the player, though other fights, namely Ares, can play out just like any other combat encounter in the game and let the player down after the huge build up to them; though I must say the variety in the level designs for each God's domain is amazing, and the objectives required to reach them never leave the player bored, e.g. Kill a variety of Greek mythological figures, storm a castle with a group of undead minions, traverse the seas to defeat Poseidon. All in all, Apotheon is just a brilliantly enjoyable game.
Apotheon's story is nothing special, but the way it's presented is sure to please those with an interest in Greek mythology. You play as Nikandreos, champion to Hera, ascending the slopes of Mount Olympus to challenge the gods that have abandoned your people, taking their power via either their allegiance or their death. Ultimately, it's a fairly generic story, though the presentation of the various mythological figures is spot-on throughout making it fairly compelling if you are interested in that sort of thing. There's nothing inherently bad about the story, and it's certainly accurate, but it wasn't anything special.
The sound design is good overall. Nothing great, nothing bad. Weapons sound as you'd expect and are fairly enjoyable to use as such. Every single sound the player makes is fine, although environmental sounds are lacking. Enemies and NPCs seem to make almost no sound whatsoever outside of speech and combat, which whilst not entirely bad is a little strange. The voice-acting is passable. Whilst it's not awful, it's also not that great. The dialogue did not engage me at any point (not due to the writing, that's fine, it's due to the voiceover) but it also never bored me to sleep. Rising above the complete averageness of the sounds and voices though is the music, which whilst not always noticeable is fantastic and definitely adds to the mood of the game, especially during some of the more climactic moments such as the climb to fight Zeus.
In Conclusion, whilst being flawed in many ways and having it's fair share of frustrations, Apotheon offers what I consider to be an extremely compelling and entertaining semi-metroidvania experience that constantly presents the player with something new and interesting to do. If you can ignore the relatively minor flaws that this game has there is an absolutely superb experience to be had.

From the very first time I saw pyre's reveal trailer, I was excited for another supergiant game and it turns out to be another great experience, at least for me. Pyre is a very linear, story-driven game where your task is to conduct a rite to free your fellow exiles by playing some mystic basketball as a reader. It's not just a title apparently since most of your time is spend on reading, whether it's the character's dialogue or the book of rite itself, which contains background information of the world that you unlock by doing something (e.g fighting other triumvirates, visiting different lands, etc). If you don't like visual novel, or games with too much reading I don't recommend this game for you. If you also thought that most of the playtime is for playing the sports game I assure you it is not.
-GAMEPLAY : the gameplay for the rite (the mystical sports game) itself is pretty simple, control one character, take the ball, dodge the enemy's defense and attack, and plunge yourself into the enemy's flame (or throw the ball into it). If the enemy has the ball, you will have to guard your triumvirate's flame. The RPG element comes in the form of leveling-up and gaining mastery (special perks), however that's it, everytime your character leveled-up they won't get any raise in stat. raising your character status can be done by pursuing vocation, an activity you choose to do in your free time. You can also buy or find talisman, an equippable item to give your character certain effect, like increased movement speed or bigger auras, though for me it barely have any effect at all. What's somewhat annoying is that you can only move one character at a time for every rite, so if you take control of one character the others will only stand still. A strange design, but justified in the game's lore as one of the rite's purpose so it's okay I guess. Just like there ire idols in bastion and limiters in transistor, there are titan stars, which gives your enemy some advantages, increasing the difficulty of the game. However there is no new game+ mode, which means when you play a new game there is no titan star as an added challenge, or your previous progress which makes it kinda annoying since that means you have to complete everything in one playthrough.There is also a versus mode, where you can play against CPU or your friends in a local coop. Sadly there is no online play, so if you want to play this game with your friends, this is something to think about.
-MUSIC : For the music, I have nothing to say. From the very moment I heard "in the flame" from the trailer I trust that Darren Korb and Ashley Barret will return with another amazing soundtrack, and they do.
-GRAPHIC : Simply beautiful, and breathtaking. there's a different types of terrains which you can visit and each of them looks different and feels like something that came out of a fantasy world.
-STORY : Now the main meat of the game lies in the story and its diverse cast. Before that, I must admit that the story-telling is a step back from bastion and transistor, with too much reading a la Visual Novel (which I don't mind at all, but some people do). While at first you will meet with three characters who belong in the nightwing, it will only grow from there. As you meet with different character you started to learn more about them and eventually care about everyone as your fellow exiles and friends. The story while linear, sometimes give you choices. The choices may look like it doesn't matter for the story's purpose, but it may matter to your characters and it will affect them in their journey, and that is what pyre is all about, the journey, yours and theirs (the cast). Life is all about choice and their consequences, and pyre wants you to continue with your choices. this game will continue with all your choices, and there is no correct or true path. Even in the rite itself, whether or not you win doesn't matter much, since the story will continue. While playing this game, various thought will come into your head, mostly about wondering whether or not your previous choices is worth it, and even if it is worth winning or losing this match, and all you can do is continuing on with those choices set in stone, since the game is autosaving itself, a clever idea I personally think to force the player to accept their choices. The many choices also makes the game worth to replay if you're curious about the different results, and the game accomodates with giving you many save slot to start a game. Each playthrough will have a little difference from each other, which is why I believe pyre is something you should experience for yourself, after all it is about your journey.
TL;DR :
-an enjoyable experience, something you should try for yourself
-great story with diverse cast, that you care about, and many choices, resulting in many different playthrough
-high replayability value
-beautiful world with beautiful music to accomodate
-a different experience from bastion and transistor, especially in story-telling department
-a game designed for an offline single player experience
-lacking online play, local versus only
-the rite gameplay is enjoyable although a bit strange of a design choice, for only 1 character to move
-lack of new game+
-80% of your playtime spent on reading (especially if you read the book of rite for the world's lore), those who do not like VN stay away

Bastion is one of my top games of all time and I thorougly enjoyed Transistor so when I saw Supergiant put out a new game I bought it without looking at any trailers or anything. This game is even better than Bastion in my opinion. Its all rather subjective, especially since this game is much more story oriented and honestly not terribly gameplay oriented but that didn't get in the way for me. The art, music, and voicing are all amazing as to be expected from a Supergiant title. I highly recommend this game. It has a handful of flaws certainly, but I was too captivated by the story and characters for them to bother me.

While it felt like SOMA took a long time to reach some of the atmospheric tension of Amnesia, it definitely got there. To boot, the game has a fair variety of gameplay, and actually has a story that both makes sense and preserves the sense of dread instead of devolving into a hero-vs-badguy fight (unlike most horror games!)
The storytelling does not assume stupidity of the audience. A major plot point that I thought was going to be revealed at the end of the game hours after players have figured it out through genre savviness was instead calmly "acknowledged" in a conversation, under the presumption people have figured it out. The game brings up similar quandaries as Fallout 4 and The Talos Principle have recently, but presents them as much more demanding ethical dillemas. Are robots alive? If they are, are you okay with committing cold-blooded murder to do something that might benefit humanity more as a whole? I definitely finished feeling satisfied with my experience.
Words of warning though: The monster sequences involve fewer options for escape in SOMA. On occasion, I was backed to a corner and just threw down the controller as I waited for the monster to kill me. Thankfully, this is not a huge percentage of your time in the game. Secondly, the game is poorly optimized - I decided to overcompensate by only playing it after I had upgraded to the GTX 10xx series. Before doing so, I was repeatedly crashing at a checkpoint soon after you first meet Catherine; and I never got word of a patch.

Well , this is a strange one.
It´s a stealth game with some parts of the game that you need to shoot through.
Set in the war , you play as an british assassin (or secret agent or whatever ) Violette Summer (or Violet Szabo - which appears to be a real person , you can find more about her on wiki).

Over the course of the game you will see her in various outfits.
The game itself has 12 missions and lots of colectibles to be found  which grant exp  , this leads to an another thing that is an mini-rpg system : Every 1k exp gives you a star and you can spend the star in 3 categories : Morphine (increases the duration),Stealth (increases your speed when sneaking),Power (increases you HP pool) , up to 5 stars/per 1 thing.
Additionally you don´t just need to sneak up to someone and execute them (btw some of the executions are nice) you can also kite them to your liking with whistling OR you can lead them to into various traps.
Your main weapon is a knife , sometimes you find or start a mission with a silenced pistol or find an unsilenced pistol/flare gun/shotgun/rifle , but these are usually very limited so you need to use them wisely. The voice acting is also very polished , if you want , you can listen to some guards - sometimes they meet and talk about various thing in german language.
And one last word to the graphics - Quite gorgeous ,especialy the lightning and shadows.
Overall a good game , not very long , but still makes me wonder how cheap it is.

This game is.... good.  Not great, but definitely good.  I picked it up on sale and it was worth every penny.
The who major issues that desperately need addressing are the UI and the (seemingly intentionally) repetative, grinding motions required.
The UI needs a lot of small tweeks, with some menus referenceing your overall stock and other menus not.  The creation of an expedition requires navigating several blind-menus with big bold text about STR requirements for weapons, but nothing about the stats of the characters being equipped.  Don't remember what the last character had equipped?  Going to have to start over from the top!  And for the 5,000,000th time, I understand that if I click on something to ransack and it doesn't move to my inventory... it's because there isn't enough room.  No need for a popup that has to be clicked out of.
The entire radio/expedition relationship needs some serious, serious work.  I'll give somebody 15 food a day just to work the radio.  Yes, I want you to go to the location I specicially sent you too.  No, I don't want you to try and recruit anyone (haven't seen a single character in the wastes with stats worthy of note:  I have no idea why they even give you the option)  The mind boggles that I would send somebody out into the wastes to wander (without food or water, since apparently that's covered) but every time a character even considers taking an action (which is about every 10 seconds.... no, I'm not kidding) they need to call in to verify before they even consider doing what they set out to do.  Right-click on the radio, answer the radio, tell them to do search the building....
.... again.  And again.   And again.  Up to 3 radio answer per location.... and many of my trips are 16-32 locations.
If they could move past those 2 STAGGERINGLY painful roadblocks, I would have happily forked out $15.
The combat/choice/recruit also needs some work, as it's far too black/white in both choices and distribution of xp.  More of spit and polish, less of a roadblock.

You lie in the corner of the objective. The game is 1 vs 5 and your teammates are getting angry at you. You want to go outside, but you are too afraid to leave the warm glow of the objective. Your t-shirt is glued to your sweaty armpits. You watch the door to the objective. Someone is writing something (probably about you) in the chat, but you cannot read it because you have to keep an eye on the door you have been watching for the last 2 minutes. Suddenly the moment comes: someone is at the door! Hastily you pull the trigger, but you are already dead. Vote kick is initated.
TIme passes and you feel more comfortable with the game. Still you frequently die of spawn peeking and it makes you angry. Such cheaters! You make a vow to yourself: never to spawn peek. Sometimes you run into people your teammates call `smurfs'. Those games are hell. You cannot comprehend what makes a person go so low that they spend 15 euros just to kill lower level players. Disgusting, you think but you know there is yet another class of people, even lower than the smurs: teamkillers. What on earth could motivate these people? Their behavior makes you wonder: can a cancer take over a person and through the infected host spread over a gaming community?
You have put 500 hours into the game. The game mode is casual. 15... 14... 13... There is a barricaded window in front of you. 7... 6... 5... You pry the planks loose and the window opens. 3... 2... 1... You let loose a spray of bullets. Enemy operators die as you perform brain surgeries one after another. A terrified recruit is trying to take cover, but it is too late. A chuckle escapes your throat as your bullets punch into the back of the already limp recruit. The match is over. The enemies are complaining. Your tk'ed teammates are complaining. From the muscle memory of your fingers comes a stream of characters to the public chat: izi pizi ezezezezez. Everybody is reporting you, but you know that it does not matter, because this is your alternate account.

Heroes of Might and Magic V is yet another attempt to revitalize the franchise. A new developer with a new vision, only the developer has no vision. This installment is in many ways just a recreation of Heroes III with a few features and some new technology. Unfortunately simply recreating an old game isn't enough to warrant a new purchase and the new features introduced does not quite meet the standard you would expect from a big name franchise like this.
Although the basic gameplay is still great there simply isn't enough new in the game to really consider it a continuation of the franchise. New features, like spell-less heroes getting a free attack and an initiative list that lets you see in what order units are going to get their turn, are nice additions to the core formula but they don't really add anything new to the game overall when not combined with more extensive overhauls and improvements.
One of the more significant additions to the game is the new racial abilities that helps distinguish between the heroes, separating them into more sub groups than the usual Melee vs Magic that previous games in the series used. Unfortunately, as with all such systems, without proper balance it adds very little and this was not properly balanced which makes much of what the system tries to do an exercise in futility. Once you realize which abilities are strong and which are weak you will pretty much only have one or two hero builds that are worth following, regardless of what racial abilities are available to you.
The second and without a doubt the biggest change to the game is the move to full 3D. The game sure looks pretty but a number of bugs, jerky camera movements and items on the map being obscured by the wrong camera angle detracts much from what should have been a major graphical improvement.
The multi-player is heavily marred by bugs and crash. In particular the out of sync issues makes it near impossible to finish a game online.
Heroes of Might and Magic IV is not a very notable step in any direction, it seems like the developers was so scared of doing any wrong that they ended up doing almost nothing at all which leaves us with what is just a prettied up Heroes III with a few new issues that need fixing.
Like Heroes III it is still an enjoyable game however because of many lacks and faults in the game you can't help but feel it is a step backwards for the franchise.

This is my favorite game of all time. Not my favorite FPS of all time, My absolute favorite. This game was a technical marvel of its time. If you take the SNES verision of this game and put it next to the PC version, you will see that PC blows console out of the water(As usual).  Now that we have all of the tech and bashing out of the way lets get into the actual game! You are an unnamed space marine for the UAC. You are stationed on one of Mar's moons on a base that has been attacked by the horrors of hell. Enough story I want to shoot some demons! As soon as you press new game, choose which episode you want to play, and which difficulty you want to take on hell with, you are immediately dropped into E1M1, The Hanger, with pistol in hand with demon zombies to kill. There is no health regeneration in this game, no M4 carbine with unlimited ammo, no automatic checkpoints, and no hand holding what so ever. As soon as the level starts you are on your own to kill and explore. That is the beauty of this game there is no restriction on where you can go. If you see an area with bad guys outside? You can go there. You see a chain saw and you want it more than anything in the world? Look for a wall to open and go get it and find some meat! The gameplay is the best thing about this game. The primal satisfaction from seeing that enemy go down in a bloody gorey mess from the blast of your shot gun is like no other. The story is there, but it never really matters that much. John Carmack, the lead programmer for the game, has stated this hilarious phrase, "Story in a game is like a story in a porn movie. It's expected to be there, but it's not that important." The music in this game is absolutely phenomenal. At DOOM's gate, the music from E1M1, is ingrained into every person who has played this game. The music is down and dirty metal. It fits the game very well. All in all, I would absolutely recommend this game. For $5 dollars this game is a no brainer. Especially when it's on sale for a little more than a buck.
Now that the sales pitch and review of this game is done, I will have to say that the MS DOS port does not look good in today's standards. I do recommend that you pick up a source port so that you can have the game support your native resolution, mouse support, mods, etc. It's not hard to install or set up, it just consits of finding the source port, I recommend Zandronum, copy the WAD from the location you installed and paste it into your source port. That's it!
I may be a 16 year old kid, but I see what this game has done to the FPS genre. I love all of the mechanics of this game and will always be coming back to this game for years to come.

In the slew of bad reviews, I've decided to finally review the game, though I do think it's kind of silly to 'review' a game in early access, since it's not representative of the final game.
Alright, first off. I have had many, many good experiences playing this game. In fact, I met one of my now best friends while playing this game, and I'm very thankful for that. Essentially, if you like dinosaurs, and like running around AS a dinosaur, you're going to have a fun time.
Right now, the game is quite bare-bones, unbalanced, and to be honest, playing it has nearly brought me to tears with how dang frustrating it is sometimes. There is a lot of waiting around doing nothing right now, which makes it nice to have people to play with. Or necessary, really. But despite this, and no matter how many times I logout in a rage, I still come back.
There's something here that is addicting, maybe it's the dinosaurs themselves, or maybe it's the community, when you get in a game, and join a herd or pack. There's a feeling of comradeship in those moments, and it's amazing. For me, this makes up for every bad experience, and the frustration. I have high hopes for the future of this game, and I'll probably continue to play through all the problems and issues that arise!

Apotheon is one hell of a pleasant surprise. Don't let yourselrf be scared by the simple graphic style, it is a competently made game.
An interesting spin on the metroidvania type of games in which you will travel to multiple areas to explore. Altohugh due to the choice made regarding the style, environments tend to differentiate little one from another. Nonetheless different areas have different rules: hub areas are mostly populated by normal people (or gods?) require you not to mess too much or guards will attack you, other areas are instead populated by beasts and monsters all will provide environmental hazards and puzzles. Secrets and puzzles are rather simple, although they can require you to travel through multiple areas in order to get correct keys, unlocking some important abilities, although not really essential or game changing.
The combat is also based on few simple mechanics which tend to repeat themselves, although playing at higher difficulties will require you to use at best all the mechanics at your disposal.
For as much as it is simple, the combat mechanics are well executed and robust. The combat basics use a shield and a weapon, which can vary between swords, daggers, axes, pikes and many more, with the addition of buffering potions, summons and range weapons. Each of the melee weapons behave very differently regarding damage, strike direction and wind up time, which allows for strategy in combat even though there is almost no variety of move sets for all of these weapons.
The story is simple but solid: greek gods are abandoning humanity and you have been chosen (randomly) to face them and bring back to the world the gift of the gods that allowed life to prosper. Dialoges have not great animations (due to the style choice of paper cut animations), but are always voice acted and actually well voice acted (quite rare for an indie game). The story will drive you through the world of ancient greek gods with some interesting and almost educational expositions (optional).
In conclusion Apotheon is a very unique type of game regarding its style and story, combining well executed metroidvania gameplay with a solid but simply melee fighting system. An easy recommendation for lovers of the style and for those who are intrigued by the choice of style and subject.

While it felt like SOMA took a long time to reach some of the atmospheric tension of Amnesia, it definitely got there. To boot, the game has a fair variety of gameplay, and actually has a story that both makes sense and preserves the sense of dread instead of devolving into a hero-vs-badguy fight (unlike most horror games!)
The storytelling does not assume stupidity of the audience. A major plot point that I thought was going to be revealed at the end of the game hours after players have figured it out through genre savviness was instead calmly "acknowledged" in a conversation, under the presumption people have figured it out. The game brings up similar quandaries as Fallout 4 and The Talos Principle have recently, but presents them as much more demanding ethical dillemas. Are robots alive? If they are, are you okay with committing cold-blooded murder to do something that might benefit humanity more as a whole? I definitely finished feeling satisfied with my experience.
Words of warning though: The monster sequences involve fewer options for escape in SOMA. On occasion, I was backed to a corner and just threw down the controller as I waited for the monster to kill me. Thankfully, this is not a huge percentage of your time in the game. Secondly, the game is poorly optimized - I decided to overcompensate by only playing it after I had upgraded to the GTX 10xx series. Before doing so, I was repeatedly crashing at a checkpoint soon after you first meet Catherine; and I never got word of a patch.
If Red Faction and Half Life were cousins and had a long drunken sexcapade, this would be their horribly disfigured love child.

Alpha Prime is not a bad game, it's just boring. When I started playing it, I expected something Doom-3-esque, with elements of thriller and an atmosphere of a dead mining station, and first couple of levels looked exactly the same, but 30 minutes into the game it became dull. I really appreciate the fact that you can die fairly easily if you are not careful and an encounter with two enemies is already a problem, but it's done the way you wouldn't want it to be: enemies absorb bullets like sponges and can survive even after half of a machine-gun clip is shot in their head. The other problem is a permanent lack of ammo towards the end of the game. "Hardcore" you may say, "Bad game design" i may reply. This game also has some interesting features, like hacking system, and it's a shame that it hasn't been developed enough anв there's almost no use in it, except the parts where you must hack something to proceed further into the game. The last, but not the least problematic thing is the plot: it is silly, illogical, predictable and even naive, not to tell that voice acting is fairly below average (seriously, I couldn't keep a straight face while listening to that Italian guy).
I found myself enjoying playing some of it's parts and rather liked than disliked the game overall, but I'm almost sure that you won't. Every gamer has his own standards and mine are low enough to play this boring piece of crap and even don't mind some of it's major problems, but seriously, go play Doom 3 or Escape from Butcher's Bay, or FEAR instead, they are worth your time much more than this.

I purchased this game for $3 along with the sequel spinoff, Deadline Rebirth. I've owned it for about 48 hours now and I've completed two of the three game modes on normal difficulty, and while that does sound like the game doesn't have a lot to offer, that isn't necassarily true. It's rather addictive, allows you plenty of room to improve your room clearing tactics, and each locale offers its own ups and downs, such as Germany having forests and so many god damn snipers.
Pros: 3 unique game types, varying locations, plenty of character customization options, rewarding gameplay
Cons: Doesn't take long to beat the game types if you're good, the locations are recycled across each game type, and the customization options could be better
Honestly, the only complaint I have is that the character outfits could allow some more variations. For example, each vest has a set pattern and color, and if you had some level of control over that instead of having to sacrifice protection and speed just to have an aesthetically pleasing look, I'd say this game was damn near perfect. The vest my team uses is the Crye Precision JPC vest, which boosts speed and adds almost 50 armor, but it only comes in multicam. I had hoped I'd be able to make it black, or even a more pleasing camoflauge, but its only multicam, so now, all my guys have to be decked out in full on multicam, head to toe.
tl;dr: Good game for those who enjoy a bit of a challenge and like a game where tactic trumps running and gunning, but lacks in the wardrobe department.

From the very first time I saw pyre's reveal trailer, I was excited for another supergiant game and it turns out to be another great experience, at least for me. Pyre is a very linear, story-driven game where your task is to conduct a rite to free your fellow exiles by playing some mystic basketball as a reader. It's not just a title apparently since most of your time is spend on reading, whether it's the character's dialogue or the book of rite itself, which contains background information of the world that you unlock by doing something (e.g fighting other triumvirates, visiting different lands, etc). If you don't like visual novel, or games with too much reading I don't recommend this game for you. If you also thought that most of the playtime is for playing the sports game I assure you it is not.
-GAMEPLAY : the gameplay for the rite (the mystical sports game) itself is pretty simple, control one character, take the ball, dodge the enemy's defense and attack, and plunge yourself into the enemy's flame (or throw the ball into it). If the enemy has the ball, you will have to guard your triumvirate's flame. The RPG element comes in the form of leveling-up and gaining mastery (special perks), however that's it, everytime your character leveled-up they won't get any raise in stat. raising your character status can be done by pursuing vocation, an activity you choose to do in your free time. You can also buy or find talisman, an equippable item to give your character certain effect, like increased movement speed or bigger auras, though for me it barely have any effect at all. What's somewhat annoying is that you can only move one character at a time for every rite, so if you take control of one character the others will only stand still. A strange design, but justified in the game's lore as one of the rite's purpose so it's okay I guess. Just like there ire idols in bastion and limiters in transistor, there are titan stars, which gives your enemy some advantages, increasing the difficulty of the game. However there is no new game+ mode, which means when you play a new game there is no titan star as an added challenge, or your previous progress which makes it kinda annoying since that means you have to complete everything in one playthrough.There is also a versus mode, where you can play against CPU or your friends in a local coop. Sadly there is no online play, so if you want to play this game with your friends, this is something to think about.
-MUSIC : For the music, I have nothing to say. From the very moment I heard "in the flame" from the trailer I trust that Darren Korb and Ashley Barret will return with another amazing soundtrack, and they do.
-GRAPHIC : Simply beautiful, and breathtaking. there's a different types of terrains which you can visit and each of them looks different and feels like something that came out of a fantasy world.
-STORY : Now the main meat of the game lies in the story and its diverse cast. Before that, I must admit that the story-telling is a step back from bastion and transistor, with too much reading a la Visual Novel (which I don't mind at all, but some people do). While at first you will meet with three characters who belong in the nightwing, it will only grow from there. As you meet with different character you started to learn more about them and eventually care about everyone as your fellow exiles and friends. The story while linear, sometimes give you choices. The choices may look like it doesn't matter for the story's purpose, but it may matter to your characters and it will affect them in their journey, and that is what pyre is all about, the journey, yours and theirs (the cast). Life is all about choice and their consequences, and pyre wants you to continue with your choices. this game will continue with all your choices, and there is no correct or true path. Even in the rite itself, whether or not you win doesn't matter much, since the story will continue. While playing this game, various thought will come into your head, mostly about wondering whether or not your previous choices is worth it, and even if it is worth winning or losing this match, and all you can do is continuing on with those choices set in stone, since the game is autosaving itself, a clever idea I personally think to force the player to accept their choices. The many choices also makes the game worth to replay if you're curious about the different results, and the game accomodates with giving you many save slot to start a game. Each playthrough will have a little difference from each other, which is why I believe pyre is something you should experience for yourself, after all it is about your journey.
TL;DR :
-an enjoyable experience, something you should try for yourself
-great story with diverse cast, that you care about, and many choices, resulting in many different playthrough
-high replayability value
-beautiful world with beautiful music to accomodate
-a different experience from bastion and transistor, especially in story-telling department
-a game designed for an offline single player experience
-lacking online play, local versus only
-the rite gameplay is enjoyable although a bit strange of a design choice, for only 1 character to move
-lack of new game+
-80% of your playtime spent on reading (especially if you read the book of rite for the world's lore), those who do not like VN stay away

This might actually be my favorite game. Ever. My most recent favorites were Bioshock and Alien Isolation, and this is basically them combined. I had high expectations for this game and it absolutely shattered them.
Gameplay: Similar to other Frictional Games titles, you can grab and throw various objects, but there aren't nearly as many physics puzzles. Instead, they use computer based puzzles without giving any instruction to use them. Lots of games will show a quick tutorial on how to do the minigame/puzzle, but this game just thrusts you in and expects you to figure it out. The only other game I've seen do this is Alien Isolation, which also did it magnificiently. The sneaking gameplay is also great, as usual.
Graphics: It's no groundbreaker in terms of graphics, but they get the job done and look nice for what they are. I thought the setting was captured perfectly, I was completely immersed throughout the whole game. Playing this in VR would be ridiculous.
Ambiance: AMAZINGLY well done. Similar to Alien Isolation, the soundtrack is totally dynamic. The video and sound work together beautifully and create a ridiculously immersive and terrifying experience.
Level Design: The game is entirely linear, but it does a very good job of giving an illusion of open world by making each area large, without obvious boundaries. You're also without a map in most areas, so it's up to the player to explore the area and figure out where to go.
Story: Probably the most intruiging and engaging story I've ever seen in a video game. It really puts you in the shoes of the main character, many times I was thinking the same questions he was asking. This game is full of thought-provoking concepts and moral conflicts. Also, the voice acting is phenomenal. They actually sound like real people with real emotions, which is part of the point of the game. The length is just about right too, and the ending is very well done.
Frictional Games never fails to please, but this time they outdid themselves. I was expecting just another horror game, but this was a heartwrenching, terrifying, and creative take on the horror genre. If you like crying, smiling, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your pants, you'll enjoy this one. 10/10

Velvet Assassin is an excellent game, let me tell you why.
PROS:
You're an agent behind enemy lines and you have to take out important people or sabotage bases. The gameplay is great, the stealth system fairly simple; hide in shadows, don't walk in front of people, but it can get pretty intense, especially the later levels where there are less shadows to hide in and you need to perform more daring assassinations on patroling enemies.
The weapons you get are true to the era (no crossbows or whatever), fitting for an assassin: a knife and a pistol. You can't carry around clunky weapons on your back like you're some sort of Wolfenstien. However there are portions of the game where, after blowing something up, you need a less tacticle approach to escape and the shotgun is your friend. It makes sense, it doesn't seem realistic that you can be a ghost 100% of the time. Besides, if you don't go out with a bang, how are the Nazi's gonna know you were there? :)
Content, I've played the game for about 8 hours and I'm not even halfway done. There's also rewards you get for exploring, albiet within the confines of the level. Not every game has to be open world/sandbox. Also, it seems there's a new way to kill enemies almost every level. The levels are also pretty unique from each other, and a lot of effort was put into level design. It doesn't get dull.
Great voice acting. Excellent grahpics. Nice execution animations.
CONS:
You can't pick up enemy weapons, which may be helpful if you get discovered. But I guess an assassin doesn't want to be loud even if she's getting shot at.
The story is a little disjointed. There isn't too much of a connection between missions, but it doesn't hurt to use your imagination a little bit and pretend that the British sent you on a new mission somewhere else, leaving the old mission behind you, cause after all it's finished.
Very rarely the character movements and controls seem unnatural, like when you're trying to sneak around a corner and you have your face pressed right up to it. It's not enough to detract from the fun though. And I feel it's due to the Nvidia physix engine (AMD users can still play the game though!).
Checkpoints happen about four or five times during a mission. If you're trying to play a perfect game, be prepared to reload. But, it's challenging! Not a "kill an enemy, save" type of game.
Leveling up is done through finding hidden collectibles, and if you don't find them you can get underleveled. It doesn't make the game impossible, just harder than it already is.
Overall, this is an excellent game even for full price which is still pretty cheap. A great way to spend a few bucks and get a lot out of it. 8.9/10
