Sheltered was a fun experience that lasted me 16 hours, well worth the price in my opinion. (I got this game on the Fall Steam Sale for $5.09)
You start out in the world with no clue as to how you're supposed to go about things, the environment seems very harsh, and the encounters with other people and events are very exciting at first.
I'm going to list the things I enjoyed, as well as the things I didn't care for, as
best I can.

On my first playthrough I barely managed to survive for 60 days before my family died. We encountered ferocious wolves and bears, other hostile survivors, and so, SO much food poisoning. I was having so much fun trying to survive and I wanted so badly to do better the next time that I started a new game instantly after the first one.

Even just the little amount of knowledge I gained from the previous playthrough, the second time around was WAY easier. Simply taking precations to have enough water containers to collect plenty of water for excursions pretty much made everything else a walk in the park.
At the time of writing this, my family has been alive for 120 days, we have over 100 gallons of fuel, 400 gallons of water, 100 pieces of food (with 2 deer caught on the surface with no room in the fridges) A full medicine cabinet (Even though no one even gets sick anymore) and 3 motion sensor rifle traps (Not that they are ever used because all the raiders give up before even breaking the first door)
I don't need to leave the shelter anymore, as just broadcasting for traders brings everything I need straight to me. In return, I give them some meat so I can grab one of the deers up top and the process repeats.

I was really hoping this game would have some sort of end goal, and for the longest time I thought completing the van was the ultimate goal, (maybe to escape to some nicer, less apocalyptic area of the globe?)
However, upon completion of the van, I realized it was only a alternate method of travel. I actually feel like it would have made the game better if it HAD been an end goal, then players could try and see how quickly they could win, rather than see who can stay alive the longest, which according to the record boards someone has made it to over 199,999 days, which is about 450 years longer than the average human lives. (Man, people are surviving a lot better in the apocalypse than we are today!)

So at this point, my little virtual family is surviving just as comfortably as I am, with no need to worry about anything, as traders will always give them exactly what they need.
What's left for me to do? Try and beat the high score? No thank you. xD
There are a few secrets to this game, and a mystery hatch that very much caught my attention. Could this be the end game goal?

So... yeah. Just kind of done at this point.

Even though there's nothing left for me at this point, I greatly enjoyed the experience while it lasted, and just viewing the completion of the van as an end goal was enough for me. My family will live comfortably and listen to wonderful records on the jukebox for decades to come.
Waste of 75 cents.

Game had a pretty terrible launch, servers were so screwy that a rather large number of players couldn't play, those that could play were greeted with game breaking bugs.
Servers finally fixed and people can play now, but there were still pretty awful bugs to deal with, that a lot of people exploited...
However, slowly but surely, those bugs are being patched out, the infinite stamina bug being chopped up and left in the middle of the street made me happy, oh so happy. Hiding is viable now that the inhale when holding breath doesn't play, but letting go is still very scary to have happen. Driving in reverse is no longer the beat all end all, as Jason can stop it from behind with proper use of his abilities.
Counselor gameplay can get a bit boring sometimes, and you will feel that hopelessness at the start, going through houses to look for your objectves and/or items to help you stay alive. They are far from completely hopeless with a good team though, a sloppy team will get wiped out farely fast especially if the Jason knows his craft.
Playing Jason is the big highlight in the game, you feel empowered, people run at the sight of you... but being against a team of clever counselors can give you a run for your money.
Jason is OP, he is meant to be, else he wouldn't be Jason... Nowhere near unbeatable either.
Be warned that currently you cannot rebind your keys, hopefully that will come soon, as that is a big turn off for a lot of people.
Pick up the game and give it a shot yourself! There's still a number of bugs to iron out, but they are slowly getting murdered, just need to be patient. Just be glad you weren't around for launch day! haha

This game was my dream game that has come early, a Dinosaur survival similator. I loved this game once I saw it but right now in the state its in its just dissapointing. I may go into a rant but heres my review as of now and all the grudges I have with this.
Progression (and Sandbox...)
Sandbox was one of the main reasons I bought this game the ability to pick any Dinosaur we got so far it was fun and entertaining but all of that went down hill when Progression came along. Progression is hard and tidous, and frustrating in the current state its in and also the Devs removed sandbox untill Progression is finished(Or it will never come back.). You start off by picking which kind of dinosaur you want to be either a Carnivore or a Herbivore. However on the V3 map this makes playing as a Carnivore damn near impossible because of how big it is! You will barely find any prey if you spawn in the wrong spot, like in the edge of the map, where nobody goes. The next map that will replace V3 will be bigger and have more hiding spots for carnivores... WHAT IS THE F**CKING POINT OF HIDING SPOTS IF YOU CAN'T FIND ANY PREY, WITH THE PLAYER COUNT FOR EACH SERVER ONLY BEING 120 OR 80! Region 2 and Misty Vally was the perfect size for Carnivores. This makes carnivore players just find a lake wait for prey and kill and just sit and wait and hide in a bush untill you get enough points to get to the next teir, and its not easy either you get 1 point each minute and if you die once or if the server crashes your points are gone and reset back to 0. Lets say that your an Austro or a Herra about to progress to a Baryonox or a Utahraptor or even if your an Acro just 1 point away from getting a Giganotosaurus, then suddenly a KOS Shant or a Spino appears out of nowhere and kills you immeaditaly, your points reset back to 0 and back at teir 1 and you want to just toss your computer out the window! Playing as a Herbivore is soooo easy. Basically as a Herbivore you only have one place to go... and thats the Redwood Biome, as it has the most blue plants, which you gain 1 point for each blue plant you eat. Or if your luckey enough you will find a vally of blue plants. I managed to progress to Shant in no time. Oh and Herbivores now eat plants they see in red, no more Dryos or other small herbivores eating big trees. Progression right now is tidous and should not been released to the public yet. I'm not saying that i'm a progression hater, I think it has potential. The main thing that can help it is that...IT SHOULD NOT BE SO PUNISHING! And it should not take 10 or 15 hours or 5, to get to apex or medium size carnivore. One way it could not be that punishing is that you only lose points and get a second chance, or you go down a tier and not lose points. Heres an example: Your a Spinosaurus and you just got killed by a T-Rex, you only lose 30 or 40 points and get a second chance. Instead of ♥♥♥♥ing dying and going back to Velociraptor!
Gameplay
The gameplay is not the best but its descent. But there are times where you can get stuck in a Shant, Trike, Rex, Giga, etc, and just die imeadility just because you don't realize whats going on in time. And another annoying thing that how its sooooo easy to break your leg, just run off a little hill like 2 inchs from the ground and you break your leg. I pretty much loss count over how many times I broke my leg as a dino over the years of playing. If I had to guess, I'd say 154 times? Just imagine in real life if someone was on the street and jumps off a bump off the sidewalk about an inch or 2 off the ground and ends up in the hospitial. It least tail biting isn't a thing anymore now that Alt turn is here. And Night Vision, Pretty much dosen't work (For me I guess) I deleted my saved files about the 4th time and turned post-processing up and still...Grey vison that is basically useless at night, and day... And lastly lag. Lag has been a problem since V3 even for people who have powerful PC's they still get lag. Even I have a great PC, that should run on medium or high settings, but I have to put it on low so that it could run smoothly.
The V4 Map
The V4 map is not finished, but I highly doupt that it would be fun to play on. Why? Because First of all, its mostly a vally filled with cayons, hills, mountains, that its pretty much garanteed that your gonna break your leg at some point. Second of all, its so dam big, even bigger than V3 that its pretty much a rarity that your gonna find another player because their all at the water sources (Good luck playing as a carnivore). Which brings me to my 3rd point. They're litterally not that much water sources, I was pretty much dehydrated 3 times while trying to find water. Even when I managed to find water I haven't found a single player, I traveled an hour to get to the water source, I haven't found a single player! The server I was in was completly full but it feels like a wastland, then before you know It, I starved. I'm starting to miss the old days when Region 2 and 1, and misty vally was around. Region 2 and misty vally was the perfect sized maps.
The Community
The commuity is Toxic, ranging from KOSer's, (Kill On Sight) Carebears, and Dinosaur fans, and Indominus Rexes. KOS players will just kill anything on sight even if your the same speices, and have enough food, they do it just for fun. There will also be KOS herbs, Mostly Shants ( I'd like to refer them as The Shantu Empire.). Carebears are like friendlys from TF2 if anyone attacks them or their friends or even a Dryo, they will hunt you down and kill you no matter what. Indominus Rexes are players who grind their way all the way up to a Hyporendocrin Rex and do what the Indominus Rex does in Jurassic World, kill for sport, even if they have plenty of food, and make some friends with Utahraptors to spy and scout lakes and tell the Hypo to go there for food.. And Dinosaur fans just live and act like the dinosaur their playing as, forming packs and herds and fight for survival, being a Dinosaur fan myself I enjoy this part of the community not the others.
The Devs
These are pretty much the only devs I know that are complete jerks. Why? Because they don't care about the players or fans that play their game, they like to refer to them as "Lab rats, Test dummies, Peasants, you name it." If you ask a dev for help like if your game is lagging or it crashes or if nightvison doesn't work they will respond "Get a better computer." Or "Thats your problem not ours." Sometimes they would even attack a player who gives a negative opinion on the game. They would even reject good ideas that players came up with. If your a dev and want your game to succeed, be nice and respective to your playerbase, and use some ideas that they came up with that you could not.
Overall
Last time my rating was a 3/10 to 4/10 and now to a 2/10 Its getting worse?!. But every early access game deserves a chance, but not this one. The Isle has (Or had) so much potentional but right now in the state its in don't buy it, and just wait for future updates or even if the game releases that will hopefully change the games course if not this game will die out and all its players will move to Saurian. About a year ago during the sandbox and Region 2 days If the game stayed on that course and if the devs were nicer and Ironed out all of its major flaws this review would be so much different it would of been a 8 or a 7/10, but as of now its a 2/10. Before anything else is said, this game still needs a lot of work. I come online maybe once a month to check out progress, and I was pleasantly surprised by the change of feel this month, but the maps are still empty, there is a lot of walking before you even find anyone and the servers are too glitchy for this progression thing to work.
Edit: To reflect the strangely amazing gameplay I have experienced over the past two days.
An empty map isn't necessarily a bad thing. Plenty of space to roam, plenty of space to avoid predators. I ended up on a 100 space server, if you look for it, its the HD version of Isle 3. I met some great people on there.
We made a huge herd of herbivores, and I died a couple of times but I managed to get to anklyosaurus. It was great. The herd was so big that we could never stop at a lake for too long for fear of carnivores showing up, but we were big enough to defend ourselves. A couple of folks were lost along the way, but the herd survived.
It's annoying that the carnivores group up like a pack, but with the idea of death being incredibly annoying and tedious, it has changed the way everyone behaves. No one takes risks unless they have to.
If you're dying of thirst then you won't want to go down to the water, BUT YOU HAVE TO.
It adds depth to a game that for soooo long has been completely boring to me. It's suddenly stepped up.
Progression is interesting. Instead of everyone being trexes, people are forced to try and new dinosaurs. Some people forget they can progress and just keep playing and don't even mind. So many people have been running around as Gallimimus and they weren't bothered.
The new no1 enemy is a dryosaurus you don't know, which is bizarre but amusing.
Every day on the server is a fight to get to a pool that isn't already swarming with carnivores, and if it is, can you dive in quick enough for a drink before legging it again to the next lake.
I can imagine for carnivores it's much the same. Pool to pool hoping you come across some herd on the way.
We had a massive conflict between trexes of all sizes and our herd. The anky and stego were front line, knowing they could do some damage while the others ran away. You want to see how far you can push the enemy before you put yourself in a bad spot you can't get out of.
It was truly awesome. For that experience, I can deal with the tedious running from spawn points in between.
It takes a while to get back to where you are if you die. Some things need to be fixed. The retention of unused points perhaps, the ability to go back to dinosaurs in the tree that you already had, with the points you have. I got stuck and respawned as a theri, but I couldnt become and anklyosaur again once that was done. I will go from the beginning again just to be an anky because its the derpyest, most fun dinosaur i've played yet.
TL;DR, I actually enjoyed this game as a full game for the first time since I bought it. Progression did this. Play on the 100 man server on the map Isle 3 HD, if you can. There's good people there, and the more people the better.
Also Anklyosaurus is awesome, top notch work on that dinosaur.

Oh man I had so much fun with this game.  On every level, it was lovely, the gameplay was fun, the art style was beautiful, and the presentation of Greek Mythology was absolutely spot on.
Honestly, thinking back on it now, I'm just amazed at all the things you get to do in this game!
I understand a lot of people have trouble with the combat, so they come away thinking it's floaty and imprecise.  I absolutely loved the combat, so here's some advice for anyone about to start the game:  it's all about controlling the distance between you and the enemy!
A spear can only damage at its point, so if a baddie gets between you and the point of your spear, you won't be able to hit him until you put some distance between you.  Spears are good if you want to stay at a distance, but you have to make sure the enemy doesn't close in on you.  Swords are close range and deal damage along their entire edge, but are easily blocked by shields.  Axes and Maces are slow to attack, but do so at an arc - if you're really good you can time your attacks to swing over an enemy shield and hit them on the head.  Swords > Spears > Axes > Swords, it's really well-balanced, and you'll be switching weapons all the time to get an advantage!
On top of that, you get to explore this beautifully-drawn world of Greek pottery and meet some of the biggest names in Greek mythology as you ascend Mount Olympus.  I whole-heartedly recommend it!

With it's story depending highly on your experience of Starbreeze's console exclusive release of 2007, it is some wonder that this sequel to Darkness was made available for PC or, heck, even at all when you consider how the first game even ended. Yet with the stark differences in art-style and ultimately approach to the structure itself  in The Darkness 2, Digital Extremes also wisely fixed the cumbersome combat of the original Darkness with much better shooting mechanics and much better implementation of the titular demon itself during fights. Additionally, the co-op heavy Vendettas game mode is a nice surprise and a lot of fun both online and off. Performance is neither an issue here or there with this one, The Darkness II can be maxed out smoothly on modest DX10 video cards and budget Dual core CPUs although it doesn't quite have proper full-frame support, squashing the picture similar to Digital Extreme's previous work on Homefront. Otherwise, aside from the occassional cheap enemy chokepoint, you're more than likely to enjoy what you get out of The Darkness II, especially if it is less than £5.

This is twice now that Alientrap has tricked me with a promising game spoiled by bizarre, floaty combat. Capsized was a beautiful little odyssey on a hostile alien world, but the enormous cluster♥♥♥♥ that battles inevitably became in every level turned me away. The saving grace of Apotheon is that there's a lot more going on than awkward swordfights, enough to keep me invested and poking through the ruins of antiquity. It's a testament, in fact, to how interesting the world and its secrets are that I can continue to put up with this awful flailing to see it.
The Greek pantheon has turned their back on the mortal world (as they so often do in games), and you just happen to be the lucky stiff who gets to sort them out. With the aid of Hera you travel to Olympus to steal back the divine powers that keep Earth spinning and hospitable, but don't expect the gods to take this lightly. You'll need plenty of weapons, armor, potions, and gizmos to survive in their domains and overcome the unique challenges each god presents.
Apotheon carves out an interesting niche where games like Zelda II and (funny enough) Journey to Olympus existed so long ago. It's not a metroidvania, but rather a side-scrolling adventure with a whole world to explore as you gain the power and resources to explore it. Olympus serves as a hub for shops and services to spend the gold you find, and then depart into the realm of the next god on your hit list. Major story beats open up new sections of Olympus and new deities to challenge, and there's an appropriately epic tale to carry you along.
You may be surprised at the variety of environments you face when you seek out the power of a god. Each realm is cleverly designed to represent their patron and also provide an experience unique from the others. In the forest of Artemis you'll find wild animals to hunt and neutral hunters to compete with. Hades is a land of darkness and lost souls that constantly hound you. And Apollo's realm is a lavish palace that you'll take a very unexpected route through. Each of these areas includes tons of secret rooms and stashes to uncover, as well as unique secrets like special NPCs to meet or legendary vaults to raid.
Most realms will have you turning to combat at some point or another, and this is where the game stumbles almost as hard as its goofy combatants. Apotheon takes a stab at 2D tactical melee combat, complete with facing, blocking, locational damage, and stamina. There's even rolling if the comparisons to Dark Souls haven't already made themselves. However, this is all taking place in a realm of platforming where you and your opponents can run like Sonic and leap three times their own height. If combat were somehow slowed and grounded (or even just had player collision) it would work as intended but what you end up with is an insane gaggle of bounding, stabbing bodies flailing at each other until you get enough lucky hits off. Even one-on-one duels devolve into leaping and swiping and missing like spastic, jousting field mice.
As bad as the combat is, strangely enough the boss battles almost make up for it in how creative and challenging they are. Not every realm ends with a boss battle but the ones that do have themes just as creative and diverse as the realm itself. Your quest to overcome each god is incredibly faithful to historical legend, with hunts and epic voyages and deception pulled straight from epic poetry. There are labyrinths to escape, seas to sail, and pitched battles between dozens of soldiers, each adhering perfectly to the myths surrounding the deity they fall under. And it's worth mentioning that the ending is spectacular, both in spectacle and stakes.
The further I got into Apotheon the more I found myself drawn into its clever world, and not just for the brilliance of the realms. There's a wealth of items and secrets to discover, owing to the transitive nature of the gear you'll use. Your weapons all have durability and break once it runs out with no recourse, so you'll need to constantly be collecting new ones scattered liberally around the world. There are dozens of potions, bombs, and gadgets to help you as well, either found or crafted using easily-gathered materials. You can upgrade your armor and your weapon skills permanently for gold, so accumulating wealth is another driver in the quest for secrets. And then there are legendary items like burning blades and radiant shields to recover and make use of.
All this happens in a world that's surprisingly open to how you want to approach it. Hub areas have locked doors and guarded treasures to explore if you choose to challenge the guards. Unique keys and clues access side quests and hidden relics throughout the realms. There are breakable walls, secret switches, and special characters to find as well. By the end I felt like Apotheon had more fascinating secrets than most proper metroidvanias, and my curiosity still has not abated. There's so much to compliment about the game without even touching the incredible art style or sound design that the shoddy, floaty combat seems almost an afterthought. Not many games nail the feel of epic mythology like Apotheon, and fewer still build such a quality game on it.

Overall i think, that Darkness is the best singleplayer experience in its genre since Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, if not better.

I wish I could do a neutral review, because this was a complex experience. I'd definitely recommend this game for the story and overall atmosphere. The themes aren't as original as others would lead you to believe, but SOMA's story is very thought-provoking and memorable nonetheless. The other elements in the game are... not as strong.
The monster encounters were a major problem for me. Not that they were too scary, on the contrary. I beat Alien: Isolation right before starting SOMA, and that really brings the outdated and terrible monster mechanics to light. The Alien in Isolation is a real and unpredictable threat that you can't kill, but distraction and evasion make these encounters tense and horrifying (helped by the godlike sound design). Bottom line: you have a lot of options when facing it.
The monster mechanic in SOMA however feels extremely dated and is more annoying than anything. First there's the designs of all the creatures, which are not imposing or threatening at all (even though this is the intention). Some of the monsters scuttling towards me served more as unintentional comedy than anything else. You'll eventually get hit though, but you can retry from that point onwards. Good news right? Well not exactly, because in a wounded state your sight gets impaired, you limp and the screen gets filled with distracting effects. So sometimes an escape gets difficult because of this retry system. Luckily there are healing points in some places. Still, the monster encounters feel extremely limited and one-sided, because your only options are running, evading, or hiding in a corner hoping you don't get seen.
So if you want to get the most out of SOMA, I'd actually recommend the 'wuss mode' (ugh) mod, which disables enemy hits. I played through the vanilla version, but if I'd ever replay it, I'd do it with the mod enabled. It's obvious this team handles story and characterization better, I find it odd that they still cling to this outdated Amnesia monster mechanic. It's like they forced themselves to include it, because they felt the game needed tension. I agree with the
in that sense:  "Their strong suit may have been in horror at some point, but sometimes moving forward means leaving something behind. In the case of SOMA, they've traversed far into the future without leaving the past where it lies."
Had they ditched this, they could've invested more in the puzzles, which were for the most part pretty entertaining and never too hard or frustrating. I'd rather have more puzzles than a half baked revolving door of monsters.
So ultimately I decided to grade based on the vanilla version, where I found that the terrible monster sections dragged the entire experience down. If you're okay with these, or decide to try out that mod, I'd easily recommend it. The sci-fi tale and its ending will likely stick with you for a while. I definitely felt like reading up on it after I was done. Play this if you're a fan of Moon, Ex-machina, Blade Runner or the work of Philip K. D1ck.

First and foremost, many players need to realize that Nether is still in Alpha. There are far to many complaints about buggy issues. Yes, it does take awhile for the server list to load, and occasionally you do get stuck in certain parts of the map, but the developers are constantly fixing issues that arise, and adding new game content.
The constant threat of the nether, as well as hostile players, is what sets Nether apart from other Apocalyptic-Survival games. Many different elements are included in the game: a basic crafting system for many types of guns, and a trading faction that will exchange the worthless nether body parts for useful items including food, ammo, and even weapons. Upon death, you will find that your character's level reverts back to 0, adding to the realism of a survival game. This game has a poor community of players, i.e. most of the players you meet will attempt to kill you.
As I mentioned previously, this game suffers from occasional bugs, but as the Alpha gets further along the game will get smoother, and many more elements will be added to make this feel more like a whole game.

Let me start off by saying I have never played the Amnesia series, but after experiencing SOMA it's safe to say I am a lot more inclined to do so now.
Developed by Frictional Games, SOMA is a sci-fi psychological horror that puts you in the shoes of a Simon Jarrett. After a brain teaser of a prologue (pardon the pun) you find yourself in a research facility at the bottom of the ocean known as PATHOS-II. It isn't long before you soon realise that something terrible has happened here, it is then you embark on a journey to not only unravel how this event came to pass but to find a way to escape the inevitable despair that lurks in the shadows.
Whilst the game-play is by no means revolutionary I still thoroughly enjoyed playing it. For the majority of the game you will be exploring the vast, highly detailed facility and its connected stations. Uncovering and piecing together the remnants of this forsaken place through the use of audio logs and terminals scattered around, traversing the ocean bed floor in order to reach your next objective and so on. Although I did enjoy the scenery I do feel some of the exploration, specifically the long ocean walk segments did become a little repetitive towards the end but this didn’t hinder my overall enjoyment. The rest of the game is made up of monster encounters and puzzles that obstruct your path and must be completed in order to progress. Personally the monster encounters were possibly some of my favourite moments of SOMA, the designs of these AI controlled creatures were horrific alone but being trapped in a small area, in the dark, defenceless, had me on the edge of my seat the entire time. As for the puzzles there were some highs and lows. Interacting with a person’s consciousness and manipulating their reality via computer in order to obtain needed information, that I find to be interesting, but flipping a few switches in a specific order to summon transportation isn’t that engaging to be honest but they did add some variation to the game-play.
Where SOMA really shines is in its storytelling, from the opening scene to the end credits I was captivated. It’s been quite awhile since a games story has grabbed me the way SOMA has, if I’m being honest I’d go as far to say since the original BioShock which happens to be one of my favourite games of all time. The concepts that Frictional explores such as the relationship between the body and the mind, artificial intelligence and so forth is something I find fascinating and the way they are implemented into the story is simply genius.
Verdict
No game is perfect and SOMA isn’t I can assure you but what Frictional have crafted is something more than a game, it’s an experience. The mechanics are decent at best and there are some repetitive moments but it’s compelling and engaging story, exceptional writing, outstanding voice acting and memorable intense monster encounters all come together to create a superb horror experience that should be played by all horror fans alike.

I'm not one for the serious reviews, as you can quite clearly see in my previous ones. But anyway; I've been following the game for a while as a genuine fan of the series itself.
I can't really bash the game in all entire sections as it definitely has the pros towards it as a game, but I still personally feel the game itself struggles because of how popular the series is and the want for a genuine Friday the 13th game. The bad NES one doesn't count. The game has a good idea but it's fairly flawed in the idea.
Having spent about 75% of my time as a counselor I can definitely say that it's primarily luck based on whether or not you can escape, I've had cases where I've spawned in a cabin with the necessary tools to escape via car or boat in cabins relatively close, in other cases the opposite side of the map. While not necessarily a gripe it comes into place on one of my main issues with playing as a counselor; the idea that Jason can Morph almost instantly is incredibly harsh considering there's been cases I've spawned and within the space of half a minute I've been killed by Jason, as a result it gets quite boring watching an entire match where I couldn't participate due to the circumstances of the Morph system.
Another issue in regards to being a counselor is the idea of the composure mechanic, in the menu it states composure influences how easy it is to escape from Jason's grip, but with how Jason's grip mechanics work you have roughly a two second window (without the use of a pocket knife) to escape from his grip before he can execute you, but I've only escaped from his grip about...three times without assistance due to Jason wanting a specific kill or their general incompetance. Even with a character who has high composure like Adam or A.J; I've never been able to escape aside from those three (at minimum) times which almost makes the idea of the primary selling point (to me at least) moot. While there are perks what can allow you to escape more quickly it's based on the RNG whether or not you get said perk and even then, it may only provide a miniscule benefit such as 2%.
I've also had cases of major hitbox issues with Jason, there've been times I've hit Jason numerous times yet he's been unaffected despite playing as someone with relatively high strength (Adam in this case), I was completely dumbstruck at this as I was suffering from the cooldown where Jason was able to grab me and kill me, I could easily blame this on ping but both of our pings were relatively low. Another case of hitbox issues is when I was playing as Tommy Jarvis (my boy I might add) and shot Jason through a door he was breaking into with a wide enough hole to realistically stun him, yet there was no effect. Because of this I'd wasted my only means of defence and died as a result.
Playing as Jason while fun, gets a bit boring if you're a Jason with restricted stats in terms of movement. Part 7 Jason suffers from this heavily due to his lack of ability to run and Shift which is a major mobility ability being restricted. While Morph is unaffected that's based heavily on the perception of the location and having a general idea of where the counselor is going. If you fail to utilise Morph to get a counselor and your Shift is regenerating you're going to suffer heavily especially if they're someone with high speed like Chad and unless you have throwing knives or they run out of stamina you're out of luck for that time which if the police are ready to allow you to escape really dampens the fun of it.
While I could write about the Jason's I've unlocked (aside from the Savini skin which I wasn't really able to purchase due to curreny exchange rates and the BackerKit not having Paypal, but that's not really relevant) it's hard to talk about all of the Jason's without having really been able to play as him much. Part 2 definitely feels like one of the stronger Jason variations due to him having increased traps when spawning and having the ability to run with his Morph ability regenerating faster.
I'll give credit to the developers for definitely making Jason FEEL like Jason, with the reprisal for the motion capture by none other than Kane Hodder with the executions being well performed and having a nice variety between them.
Overall, while plagued with issues what I believe to be easily fixed the game's pretty functional, I definitely feel the game plays better with several friends than playing with random people while it can be fun with randoms as it adds to the tension but at the same time if there's ongoing hostility it takes the fun out. Proximity issues in regards to spawning in are somewhat forgivable but it's still quite irritating. Another aspect of proximity is the voice chat, without utilised external voice chats it gets really fun with immersion. I give the game a recommend if you're into F13 and want something fun for the friends.
I recommend the game, but be prepared for issues in terms of balancing.
EDIT: I've only just recently remembered. Melee is incredibly poor to work with as a counselor, because your swing is significantly slower than Jason's speed he can easily just walk away and grab then execute you, there's no fairness behind that and detracts from any resonable fighting chance a counselor has. Not only is it in poor taste it's absolutely pathetic in terms of trying to give a counselor some chance of fighting back when Jason just simply walks off then grabs you. It requires either a faster melee speed, or at least a better chance to escape from his grip (which I've mentioned above).
Score; 7/10
Pros;
Good immersion with voice chat.
Jason feels like Jason
Fun mechanics
The idea of working together to survive or risk it out yourself and attempt to survive is definitely interesting and adds a layer of fun
The ability to kill Jason through methods reminiscent of the movies.
Cons;
Poor hitbox detection.
Jason's a little too powerful with his grab being insanely broken regardless of character composure and the lack of a cooldown before he can execute you.
Certain Jason's are insanely underpowered in terms of Weakness and Strengths.
Limited counselor variety.
Melee is incredibly clunky as a counselor and for Jason by some extent.
I get the counselors aren't meant to have much of a fight againt Jason but even in combat stance the dodge mechanic seems to have little effect at times.
Edit: As of late, I've been plagued with issues on the game such as atrocious hitboxes, constant crashes and radio silence in regards to updates. Recently an update had been given to nerf one of the more popular perks for a counselor with no indication or information from the developers that it was going to be happening.
Apparently the perk itself had an issue with it giving a double benefit to the damage resistance which made it more difficult for the counselor to be killed by conventional means of damage such as falling and even being hit by a car. It was also probably one of the few methods to fight back against Part 3 Jason and Savini Jason who have massive buffs to their weapon damage. Because of how fast Jason hits in comparison to a counselor even with Swift Attacker there is almost no chance of being able to fight back unless you have someone with you.
Thick Skinned while in the common opinion, overpowered it still provided means to be able to fight back against a Jason who continously swung at you due to the stun locking effect.
The way the developers are also prioritising banning players instead of fixing general issues such as Jason's grab range and game breaking bugs such as the car flipping in certain areas is cause for concern, while banning is completely justified in regards to people helping Jason and exploiting out of the map. I still feel that people insulting and in general using crude language isn't necessary to provide a ban, you can't censor the human language and trying to force it is completely asinine.

Supergiant Games just scored a hat trick with Pyre, a fantasy basketball/football/Oregon Trail adventure, a strange combination which has led to the masterpiece that is Pyre.
Bastion, Transistor, and Pyre are all very different games in a sense of gameplay, aesthetics, style, and appeal, however, they are all similar in a sense of incredible soundtracks, memorable characters and fluid gameplay. I fell in love with every character I met, as they were all so well written with their own backstories, lore, interactions, and voice acting. The announcer during your "Rites" will constantly mock you and your adversaries, creating a strong sense of desparation, allowing you to better understand the reader and how the society that they lived in viewed their actions.
Pyre has a lot of reading to do, something new in Supergiant's title. Previously, the characters would speak their lines, with the exception of Red from Transistor, as she could not talk. However, the only characters with spoken lines are the announcers, and very rarely, the characters will read their lines. Usually, they will talk in a fictional language, however. A superb thing that the game has done, however, is highlighting key terms that you may not understand, such as character names, mythology, places, and terms, allowing you to hover over them to recieve a brief description of what they are, usually accompanied by a quote.
I am only about 7 hours into the game as of writing this review, however, there is much more game to be played, as it is the longest of Supergiant's games, allowing for much replayability.

This review is completely biased. I'm a Grecco-Roman historian, and seeing the classical artwork brought to life, coupled with a fantastic soundtrack, was a total win for me.
This game looks FANTASTIC. The use of classical artwork from black-figure pottery just fits, and is very true to form (no removal of Priapian appendanges, ahem). The fact that the background is actual a marble wall with the game painted on, is such a cool touch. Also, the different evnironments are unique and varierd - the forests of Artemis felt very different from the levels in Hades, and the tone was just right. The voice acting is pretty top notch too, better than some AAA games even. As should be the case, all classical figures are Britsh. This is correct and proper.
The mythology of ancient Greece is nicely incorporated into the story, and the plethora of classical Greek weaponry gives a lot of diversity for playthrough. The combat can get a little hectic and clumsy at times, but the overall polish of the game overroad that for me.
I only had a few stability issues, with a couple of CTD, but the autosave function is well implemented and meant that I didn't loose a lot of time.
Overall, very enjoyable sidescroller, with absolutely stunning imagery, well voiced and fleshed out story, and an awesome soundtrack, which I'm intending to buy.
if you'e any interest at all in Greek mythology, I would wholeheartedly recommend this game. But even without that, it's different, well paced, and stylish.

Playing with cars in a super-realistic physics engine with vehicle deformation and simulation that is close to real life is a bunch of fun. At the moment the game is mainly a giant sandbox where you can fool aroud and do pretty much anything with cars, just like you might have done with toy cars as a kid. Only this extremely realistic.
The way each tiny part of the car is simulated in game is just astonishingly detailed. The crashes are beautiful and super realistic in every single way. Even small details like radiator damage causing steam to raise from the bonnet, and evenually causes the engine to overheat, damaging piston rings and other parts which affect performance and reliability. Or rupturing your fuel tank, which may cause your car to run out of gas or become a rolling fireball. Even just 'boring' things like brake fade after they overheat has been given so much thought and detail.
Granted, there isn't much of a career mode yet. But there are scenarios that can really test your ability to control a given vehicle and campaigns which are, as I see it, a set of multiple scenarios. The scenarios are well thought out and fun to do. The campaigns still need some polish and the career mode is still missing (but will be added later on in development).
The vehicle selection itself is fun and varied. There's everything from a small 1960's Japanese sedan to a massive 1990's American SUV or 1980's Italian supercar. Or even a silly 3 wheeler. This game has a pretty large vehicle selection already and is only set to grow.
The modding community is amazing and incredible mods are released regularly on the game's official website. You can download lots of stuff. Sound mods, new areas to explore, new and interesting vehicles (like a monster truck, airplanes and even boats) and way more. Mods make the game even more fun than it already is.
The areas to explore are large, detailed and pretty. There are plenty of maps in the game you can play on and like the cars, this selection is only set to grow.
There is at the moment not much of an online aspect to the game. There is a hotseat multiplayer demolition derby mode though, which is lots of fun to play with friends.
The game is being fully supported by its developers and it doesn't seem to be a 'stuck in early access forever' title. The updates have recently become less frequent, but way more volumous in content. And even if it were stuck in early access state, the game is as is, totally worth the price for what you get. It's fun, addictive, with loads of different settings to mess around with (like pretty much the entire car or other things like day/night cycles, fog or even gravity levels (if you ever wanted to drive a supercar on jupiter, this is your chance)).
This game is a total reccomendation to anyone who is into cars, flat out realism or destruction. This game has you covered. I've had this game for a while now, and I'm still not bored of it. I'd rate this game a 9.5/10

While loving the first, The Darkness 2 felt like a disappointment.
You are two years later, and are still very much feeling the aftermath. You're a Don now, leading a crime organisation that seems to feel smaller than implied.
You go to a restaurant and get attacked by a bunch of janitors. Almost intently, they force you to survive by releasing the Darkness, which Jackie had locked up ever since last time.
What follows is a path of revenge. First to retalliate, then avenge your Aunt, then recover a plot-vital artifact... you're basically on a railroad of motivations, which feels artificial.
No surprise that the story really isn't engaging.
But the surrounding side characters are a redeeming factor. NPC's are often in pairs and have some funny banter. And spamming talk to hear them out leads into a long strain of comments about their own backstory. They may be somewhat shallow characters, but there's a sense of personality to them.
In particular, the Darkling seems to be filled with it. He slowly starts to play a big part in the story, and is generally a hoot to listen to. A major improvenemt over the first game.
Gameplay wise, what's changed isn't per se for the better.
You still have your whip, but it feels much shorter and riskier to use to whip out lights. It relies on your input to see what direction to swipe, which feels counter-intuitive.
You can grab a car door or anything shield-like to carry in front of you as protection while you shoot. A great idea at first, but impractical over time, as eating hearts removes the shield and you can't use the whip. Not to mention that the smallest light drops it.
Not much of a problem at first, until you start encountering the Brotherhood...
Corpses still carry hearts to consume, but living ones serve a different purpose now as well.
Instead of four awesome Darkness powers, your powers now largely revolve around stunning an enemy, then grasping him.
Upon which you can then decide what to do with them.
Mainly, they can serve as a quick health refill, an ammo refill (yep), a shield creator or a cooldown reducer.
You also have two active cooldown-based abilities.
One is swarm, which briefly blind/stuns your enemy, making them vulnerable.
The other briefly infuses your guns with the Darkness, giving you infinite ammo and raised damage. But it's not really a lifesaver.
All of this fancy stuff however has to be unlocked first, using points you earn in combat. The fancier the kill, the more points you get.
In general, the upgrades are okay. They're nothing spectacular. Although the Darkness armor does look mighty nice. It seems based upon the armor from the comics.
In the end, I felt like the Darkness was more of a crutch that slowed me down. I was constantly juggling with my Gunplay and my Darkness powers, annoyingly so.
The Brotherhood, which past halfway will be your mainstay enemies, often carry light-beams, which will just annoy the hell out of you. Whenever you are in light now, your screen goes black and white and drop any non-weapon you are holding (such as shields). It's quite disruptive.
Not to mention the Whip guys.... These guys will snatch whatever weapon you are holding.
Or the shielders who knock you around, while requiring either swarm or multiple whip slashing to be knocked away.
Or the Heavy guys that, for some reason, blink around the place whenever they are hurt.
These guys get my vote as most-annoying ever.
Thankfully you're done with the story in about eight hours.
Vendettas seems to largely be a redeeming feature.
You can pick one of four that each have one Darkness ability.
This is a good thing, as the focus seems to be much more on the gunplay. You still get the annoying light effect, but you feel much less disabled.
Quite frankly, I feel like I'm having a much better time in Vendettas.
The Darkness 2 is like a bad sequel to a good movie. You cringe, but you can still see what you liked about the original.
Get it while it's on sale, play the Single Player on Easy and try and make the best out of it...

Simple list format for those who just want to know if they should get it by reading reviews:
Pros
+The atmosphere that this game creates is top notch, 11/10, I can't say that I've played many games that create a space so well.
+The plot is very well done for a video game. Emphasis on sci fi elements, specifically philosophy related to consciousness and the self, artificial intelligence, and life after death.
+Lore is given to you in-game via computer terminals, photos, paper scraps, etc. This adds highly to the immersion.
+Very nice graphics, amazing use of DoF and Chromatic Aberration which are usually not implemented well.
+Horror elements are well done and can genuinely make you nervous without being jumpscares, though a few of those are present.
Cons
-Very linear, can almost be called a walking sim.
-Most puzzles are very easy, with a small handful that aren't very intuitive where you basically just click around until you get it. Not a huge negative by any means.
-Only a single ending despite a few actions you can take. This presents the illusion of choice but I was slightly disappointed that the few choices don't really matter all that much.
-The horror elements, while mostly well done, can get very tedious at times.
I'd give this game a go, but pick it up on a sale. I place the value of a game as time spent in hours = money paid for a game (eg. $10 for a 10 hour or more game is great), so in my opinion, it's far too short to be worth $30, but I would pay $20 or less for this experience.

For a long time I wanted to play Velvet Assassin, so I decide to give it a go. The short answer did I like the game is– yes, I did.
The game takes place in the WWII and you take the role of Violette Summers, British spy, tasked with hard and sometimes impossible jobs to do. The main character is based on Violette Szabo, real spy and saboteur in WWII. This is the only connetion between the game and Szabo. There isn't a story in here. You will be tasked to assassinated someone or blow up something. That's it. It would be nice to have some sort of story, but you fight againts the nazis and this is enough for me.
The game is console port and it's very good one. The graphics are decent. Bear in mind that the game came out in 2009. All human model stand the test of time, but I can't say the same thing about the envoirment, especially some buildings. Some textures are just awful. But graphics are not that impornat. The gameplay is what matters here. One word – solid.
Like I mention before, your main objectives are assassination and sabotage. On your way you will end prematurely a lot of nazi lifes. The game is linear. The fans of Hitman may not like this. Through the hole game the you will face 3-4 soldiers in a area, walking on their predetermined routes and you will have to find your window of opportunity to act. The sneaking and killing enemy is awesome. Lurking in shadows, hiding in wardrobes, toilets, bushes and waiting for your moment. Most times you will be moving slowly and silently. But be careful not walk on piecies of glass on the ground, they will announce your presence. In the down left corner is Violette silhouette. It shows your life and when there is an blue aura around it and around Violettes model, you are hidden completely, unless some enemy is pretty close to you.
Your main weapon is knife. Also you have pistol with silencer, but be careful when using it, it will attract soldiers. Like in real life and in this game, it doesn't mean that the silencer stop the sound completely. Sometimes it's too bright or you don't have window of opportunity. When this is the case, just whistle to attract a soldier. If you find pistol without silencer, shotgun, sniper rifle or assault file StG44 you'll have to know one thing – drop the sneaking and start shooting. You also have flare gun. It's usefull for setting enemies on fire. You can't get the weapons from dead enemies. You can find them in lockers.
Sometimes you may want more direct methods of extermination. Engaging a firefigth is possible, but not recommended. You can use the environment –  shooting barrel with gasoline or anohter with toxic gas, electrocuting and even pull the pin on a granade hanging on soldier belt and that way you will kill multiple enemies.
But here lies a little problem for me. When the granade explode, nearby soldiers doesn't react. This is the same with the barrel and even the doors. Every single door is making a sound when you open it and unless someone is really close, he won't here it. This just take me out of the game, when I was immersed. But this little annoyences are not everywhere, except the doors and thigs like the barrels and granades are not always required.
There is one interesting mechanic, which often will help you a lot. This is morphine. You will find syringes with him and when yo use it everything freezes and you may to kill the enemy or run past him.
Sometimes is required to dress in nazi uniform, but then sneaking is immposible. You will have to walk slowly and patiently and to stay out of sight, because enemies will recognize you. The AI is okay. Soldiers are not too curious and the don't do anything unexpected.
And in this game there are upgrades. They are in 3 categories – morphine, stealth and strength. And how do you acquire points for them? By finding hidden items. Here is the biggest problem I have with the game. If you don't look for them you can't upgrade. It will be more practicle to be awarded with more points for stealth kills. This seems more reasonable to me.
For a game to be fun it need also a good level design. Here you can find it. The level maybe linear, but environmentally they are really good. You will see village, church, harbor, bunkers fill with toxic gas, museum and others. The lighting and sound design are great. The guns sound great, footsteps are loud when they have to be, pounding music contribute for really good and tense atmosphere. The voice acting is also great. Most of the time you will here Violette narrating in the beginning of every mission and germans talking to each other.
There a lot of little touches in the gameplay and in the atmosphere that I quite like. For examaple: you can push a box so you won't be lighted or you can smash electric panel for the same reason, soldiers are singing and so on. Nothing, gameplay-wise, is necessary for you to do, but it's nice to know you some variety.
The game is using PhysX and you may have a problem with it. It may be missing a folder that is required for the game to run and you have check Steam forum how to solve this. It's nothing too difficult.
When you remove the annoying things and you don't mind linear level design, I think you can find pretty good stealth game. And if you want to make the Velvet Assassin more hardcore experience, there is a mod that removes all highlights on characters, loot, all UI messages and subtitles, decreases the grain filters on assassination animations. It also changes Violette's costume to the pilot suit during Morphine mode. I recommend it.

Pyre is an enjoyable emotional ride, but takes a bit to get there. Starting off with the bad, the first 2-3ish hours of gameplay are boring. In that time, you're essentially introduced to all of the characters, and the gameplay takes a while to get used to. The gameplay gets a lot more fun when more character choices are unlocked, and the difficultly picks up (by the time you're a few hours in). But after that point, the world opens up to the player, and they are able to fully enjoy the game. The world is beautifully crafted and extremely stylized. All of the characters have impactful stories and the choices you make affect the outcome of the world around you. Doom is one of those genre-defining sacred cows of gaming that are too often treated as unassailable classics by virtue of being one of the first in the room. While it deserves its place in history for setting the standard for the FPS genre, I think it's worth pointing out that Henry Ford's Model T probably wasn't a very good car.
Which isn't to say Doom is bad. It's okay. Competent. Functional. It's an entertaining enough experience that it warranted a recommendation after all was said and done. Which I'm sure most people would consider obvious, but given that I think that Quake is an overrated brown turd of a tedious slog, I'm saying Doom is a decent game based on actual merit and not because it served as my father figure in childhood.
Both Doom and Quake are stupid, stupid games from any sort of intellectual standpoint, unsurprising since id Software's development team of the era always came off as smirking fratboys who probably had to provide proof that they had the Slayer logo stenciled onto their trapper keeper in highschool to get hired. But the chief difference between the two besides technical advancement is that Doom was not visual diarrhea. While it was hardly a visual design masterpiece, if nothing else I could actually tell the levels apart and was given some basic context for what was going on, as opposed to Quake's completely arbitrary procession of indistinguishable green-brown castles and vaguely-defined plot with lazy pretentions to cosmic horror.
In retrospect, that's honestly the only meaningful difference between the two games. Color and coherent setting. id Software games of the era almost came off as contemptuous of the idea of thinking about things, so everything else is so much window dressing for the killing sprees. But what a difference those small things make when you have literally nothing else worth talking about.
In conclusion, Doom isn't awful but is complete empty calories. Star Wars: Dark Forces is still far and away the superior title if you're looking for old-school pre-3D FPSes.

Sheltered is a rpg style management game that is randomly generated and offers a ton of replaybility. You start out with a family of 2 adults and 2 kids who are customizable to an extent. You can change the visuals but its a pixelated kind of game so it really doesnt matter much and you can customize each individuals roles. You can have a family that focuses their stats on attacks or passively surviving the wastes by recycling and growing your own food.
This game will punish you for poor planning and poor decision making. But even then, random events do and will happen during gameplay. Sometimes you'll be granted a cache of military firepower other times your character will just die outright.
The first couple of games will be very frustrating because their isn't much to it in the tutorial. You just learn as you go and struggle to try and survive with what meager supplies you start off with. But after trial and error you can definitely micro-manage your way to a steady shelter that can produce its own food, water, and ammunition.

I am through and through a Supergiant fan. I love Bastion and Transistor. They're as successful at being games as they are at being beautiful works of art. I wish I could say the same for Pyre. I wish I could like this game. I have tried... but after 8 hours, I can say the gameplay is shallow, repetitive and just not very much fun. The nature of the gameplay thus leads to a story that is just as tiresome, as the game is structured in such a way that it's quite impossible for anything truly novel or engaging to transpire (the very rigid mechanics of the Rites must be preserved, therefore you can always count on certain characters being around, going to places and choosing between a talisman, a Vocation, or a junk item you can sell, and so on). Once you've played through the first 4 hours, you've seen pretty much all you're going to see of the Downside. Even the artwork and music doesn't evoke the same inspired immersion that we saw in previous Supergiant games. The world isn't crafted and realized so much as it is stamped together with modular parts that feel overly formulaic. The soundtrack in particular feels drab and often times invisible in the world. I can't name one track in Pyre in all my playtime that has caught my attention.
I appreciate that Pyre is different, and unusual, and artsy. Those things are great. But in the developers insistence to make something unique, they unfortunately seem to have forgotten to make a game. I hope that Supergiant keeps making weird games, and I hope that I'll be able to keep supporting their ability to do so. That said, I can't recommend Pyre, not even to fans of Bastion and Transistor.

I love Dead By Daylight (the game most often compared to this one), but this game differs in a ton of ways.  Overall, I believe it is a much better game.  I still love DBD, and will probably play it some, but this game is 100% worth the price (which I initially balked at), and I think I will get enjoyment out of it longer term.
Best things I love:
Each character has different stats that really allow people with different playstyles to enjoy it. You can play a character with high stealth if you like to stay in the shadows and hopefully sneakily escape.  You can play a super fast character who just jukes all day, or a brute who can knock out and stun jason easily.  You can play a middle of the road char who is good at most things, or any real combo inbetween.
There are perks (similar to the DBD bloodmap/perks) that can counter balance some of the weaknesses of chars, or just give bonuses like starting with a map or item.
Jason is super fun to play.  He definitely feels kind of overpowered right now, but so did the killer in DBD when it first released...people are still figuring out best practices to win as a counselor.  He doesn't feel super clunky and you get a bunch of Jasons to choose from who also have different stats (like counselor).  I prefer a Jason who can jog.  Others rather one who can break down doors easier, or one who can swim fast, etc.
Overall, I would 100% recommend this game to any of my friends.  The online is great; the private matches with friends are great; and the voice integration is well done and not obnoxious.  Try it out.  It's worth it.

I bought this game during a Steam winter sale.
Apotheon is a very enjoyable 2D action platformer about greek mythology where you play as the champion Nikandreos.
I think that the story was enjoyable and that the gameplay was fun with the just amount of difficulty needed (you have the possibility to choose between several difficulties). The music was simply put epic - it was really well made and fit perfectly into the theme. Another plus about the music is that it changed with very good timing depending on the situation and area.
Apotheon have a decent amount of achievements that aren't too hard to obtain and they're quite fun - no need for boring endless grinding to achieve them.
I do only have one major and one minor issue with this game.
Beginning with the minor issue is that the game crashed twice shortly after I started it. However, this is only minor since it only happend in one save and the game was smart (and nice) enough to autosave just before crashing since the crashes came upon entering new areas. Other than that I didn't stumble upon any lag issues or bugs.
My major issue with this game is a part of the combat system. The combat itself is fun but the drawback is how you attack with your character. You have to move your mouse up or down at the same time as performing an attack to do anything else than a thrust. It is very similar to how you perform special attack-moves in TES-games. However, in the TES-series these are special moves and they're easy to pull of without fail and performing another attack than what you wanted to do. Apotheon doesn't do that and these attacks are supposed to be "normal" attacks.
To add onto the negativity of the combat system is that these swinging/swiping attacks have a high tendency to attack the ceiling and floor and thereby having a huge tendency to fail at hitting your opponent.
In the end I think this is a great game that people should try out

This game is destined to be a survival-horror game. Involving dinosaurs, as in the future there will be humans as well as weird humanoid things such as cannibals. At its early days, it used to be a dinosaur sandbox simulator with many dinosaurs coming in. It was basically a survive-as-a-dinosaur type of game during that time. It was pretty barebones, but that's how the game basically started out. I will warn that it is laggy to some, however.
The dinosaur models are beautiful and well-detailed, for sure some of the best dinosaur models I've seen, with many great animations given to them. Then there's many skins for the dinosaurs. There used to be a lot of old ones, but they got removed because they weren't compatible with the new overlay system they have, however they're replacing them with new skins which, imo, will be worth the replacement. The environmental maps are also highly beautiful as well. Unfortunately, many of the old maps are going away, but the Isle V3 map looks beyond amazing as it's not even done, it should become even more amazing later on. Overall this game takes the visual part to the extreme in a good way, even in lower settings.
At this time, they recently put in the gamemode Progression, which is what the game is meant to be. Granted, it is very, and I mean VERY underdeveloped. It's far from perfect and I'm not happy with it right now at this moment, but then again it's underdeveloped, so obviously it will vastly change over time. As of now, it's basically that you have to start out as a small dinosaur. You have to survive for a certain amount of time with that said small dinosaur, and if you survive long enough you can progress and become bigger dinosaurs. At least this gives the game something to do, and not quite as barebones as just simply walking around, eating and drinking like it was in its earliest stages. Right now, the developers have removed sandbox temporarily to focus on progression, and when progression is done, sandbox will come back.
Unfortunately though, Progression is a big reason for most of the negative reviews. But really, in all honesty, they're mostly from people that are like "I DONT WANT TO START OUT AS SMALL DINO!!!1111 I WANNA BE WHATEVER DINO I WANT!!!!1111" and are salty because they can't have their birdbath simulator, as many of them probably just played only Tyrannosaurus, carebearing and mass murdering everything on sight 24/7. It should be blatantly obvious that they did not read the store page. If you ACTUALLY BOTHER READING THE STORE PAGE, you will plainly see that the game is meant to be a hardcore, survival horror game. Many of those people are just noobs that don't want to try, but too bad. It looks like now eventually you have to work hard and earn to get your wanted dinosaurs (even though progression being a prototype is very easy to some right now, but it will get harder and harder in time hopefully). And again, sandbox isn't gone forever, IT WILL COME BACK WHEN PROGRESSION IS DONE. Yet people are still blind and still complain about sandbox being gone, it amuses me really. You just have to be patient for progression to be done, folks. What's also not surprising is that many of these people came from an awful game known as Primal Carnage: Extinction, which is a game with absolutely horrible gameplay and doesn't head the direction of where it should be.
The developers are the other aspect that is the foundation of the ridiculous swarm of bad reviews. Well, they DO act idiotic on occasion, but at least they're actually focusing on working on the game in the way that it is intended to be. And they're making the game the way that the lead dev, Dondi, had dreamed it to be. It is often said that they don't listen to feedback, well obviously they aren't gonna listen to whiners that repetitively complain about sandbox being temporarily gone to this day! And I think that a lot of stupid actions from the community had driven the devs to be snappy at them too.
So really, I think that the biggest problem about The Isle is the community, not the devs. This game's community is frankly, very stupid (not as bad as PC:E's community, though). At its core this game is an amazing idea. It has all the weighty impact and crazy combos of a fighting game packed into a medieval melee, and anyone who says they don't have wet dreams about Vikings, Knights and Samurai fighting it out is lying. It's so satisfying to swing a huge axe into the neck of a foe, and the sound design makes the meaty clunk all the more satisfying. Sadly there's not much more to say about the positives of this game, not because I couldn't go into detail about all the good bits (I really, really could) but because the game is so dreadful, so utterly despicable in every other way that it is impossible for me to recommend this game to anyone in its current state. So let me begin my review by stating the singular biggest problem with the entirety of the game:
That's right. Basically everything that drags this game with such potential down into the gutter can be traced back to Ubisoft and their anti-consumer business practices. I'll be coming back to this point throughout the review for obvious reasons but Ubisoft is at the heart of perhaps the most salient problem with the game currently...
(or lack thereof)
To play For Honor you MUST create a Uplay account and connect to Uplay. If you aren't aware of what Uplay is, oh sweet naive child, let me fill you in. Uplay is Ubisoft's own game platform (like Steam if Steam were awful) and a constant connection to Uplay is required to play For Honor at all. This includes the single-player story mode. That's right, if you lose connection to Uplay, you'll be kicked out of the single-player campaign and lose all your unsaved progress in the process. Of course, this applies to multiplayer games too. This can't be too bad, right? Well let me put it this way: Uplay has had an outage of several hours across two days this past week, one of which was during prime-time hours on Saturday. I'm writing this review precisely because the servers went down on me again. I last played this game on the Saturday before now (where I was forced to stop playing after one round because of the aformentioned server outage.) They even had the audacity to 'address' the issue on Saturday only to have the exact same problem occur two days later.
So let's say you've sat down to play some For Honor, Uplay is online and functioning and everything seems to be going well. You queue up for a multiplayer game, let's say a round of the game's 4v4 'dominion' mode. You sit in the queue for a good minute or two, and then it proclaims it has found you a game. ...and then it tells you that the game you were attempting to join is full. Huh? Okay then, guess it's just a hiccup in the system. Oh wait, it's removed me from the matchmaking queue. But why? You'll have this problem several times over the course of a couple hours' gameplay. It's tedious and helps contribute to the feeling that you're spending more time in the menus than actually playing the game.
When you've finishing wrangling the matchmaking queue, you'll eventually be dropped into a game of For Honor. This is where the real problems begin. You see, even though you're required to have a constant connection to Uplay, ALL of the game's matches are hosted via a peer-to-peer system. There are NO dedicated servers and Ubisoft has never made any mention of adding them in the future. PC gaming veterans will be able to predict the contents of the following bullet-points but if you've never had the joy of dealing with a peer-to-peer multiplayer infrastructure, read on.
As a last little sidenote: Uplay is a hunk of garbage in ways other than the forced connection, for example repeatedly telling you a friend is playing For Honor whilst you're in a match with them (sometimes two or three times in a 20-minute timeframe) or failing to join groups after you accept invites, causing you to have to request another. You can also just be randomly dropped from your group after a match finishes with no discernable pattern as to why. I'm quite sure I could program a better gaming platform and I'm just one jobless loser, not a multimillion dollar games company.
(or lack thereof)
Ubisoft have no clue what they're doing on this front, and they've shown this clearly in the game's first patch. Since release certain characters have run rampant whilst others have been left in the cold. The most startling example of this is that the game's fastest characters are, on the whole, the best characters. This is because your ability to switch attack stances is fundamentally tied to your guard stance switching, and thus characters that can switch blocking directions quickly can also attack from multiple directions quickest. At its worst, this offers players a SINGLE frame to react to an oncoming attack and block it succesfully. Expect Peacekeepers and Orochis to take a dump on you if you're playing a slower character by spamming insanely damaging light attacks that you cannot humanly react to.
The game's first balance patch, 1.03, buffs Peacekeeper, who is potentially the best character in the game right now and nerfs down Kensei (a middle-tier character) whilst not touching Lawbringer/Shugoki at all (slow characters that are underperforming and potentially the worst in the game.) Also not touched is Warlord, a 'jack of all trades'-type character who fails to be a 'master of none', instead having some of the best offence AND defence in the entire game.
I know it's beating a dead horse at this point but if it weren't for peer-to-peer connection faster characters would be a lot more manageable at higher levels of play, since p2p favours characters who leave only small openings for opponents to react to.
(in a full price, '$60' game)
This game has great customisability. There are tons of visual appearance options to choose from including an array of colour schemes, symbols, armours, etc. to deck your characters out in. All of these cost Steel (the game's currency), and some of the prices are waaay too high. I mean you could get about 3000 Steel each week doing all your daily quests but then do you really want to spend that much time to get that sweet 15,000 Steel outfit? It comes with radical flame wings! If you just want it now you could always buy Steel straight out of the in-game microtransaction store. And I'm not even going to mention their greedy premium subscription system in a full-priced game.
Overall this is a game that had such amazing promise but was cut down before it had a chance to grow thanks to greedy publishers and general mismanagement. I wish I could get a refund. Don't buy this or any of Ubisoft's products unless they greatly (GREATLY) improve.

I was super excited for this game when I found it, but after playing and earning all of the achievements, I'm not quite sure what to think of it.  I'm reminded a lot by the PS3 games God of War, which maybe what I'm trying to compare this too, which is not fair.  Apotheon is a stylistic side scroller for one.  The graphics are excellent - nothing realistic mind you, rather what you'd see on ancient vases which provides an excellent ascetic.  The story is nothing special, simular stories have been told in a variety of settings.

The controls on this game are what bring me down.  Playing on a keyboard maybe the issue, instead of a controller.  Be prepared for tons of dodging.  I wish after earning of few of the gods powers you could take more of a stance, however that is not the case.  As the game progress you'll find yourself spamming the dodge keys more and more, until frankly it feels like that is all you ever do.  I ended up starting to run past enemies to get to doors or other key points to help speed the game along.
There is no multiplayer or DLC available for this game.  I played through the game twice, which the second time was quite a chore, but required to earn an achievement.
If you like the genre like I do, then I'd recommend purchasing it.  If however you could care less about ancient culture, then I'd suggest looking for a different game.

When I first started playing For Honor I was having a really fun time. I won some battles lost some, it was fun. Now that I've played some more I'm starting to see all of the flaws in this game. First off, the connection issues. I haven't really run into these a lot but lately I'll play one round and then for honor will freeze and I'll have to close it and boot up the game again and that's if I can get a match against someone. Next there's the matchmaking. Not only does it use peer to peer but when it says the player level is strict (basically so you'll go up against someone with the same skill as you) is complete BS. My "main" is the raider because he's my highest level, 18, and when I do get into a match most likely the guy I'm going against is gonna be persitge 1 or past that. Normally I wouldn't care if someone was a higher level, but the only problem is that's when the partial pay to win aspect comes in. The higher the level you are the better gear you can get, but you can pay money to get your level up quicker and get more gear. I don't have too much of a problem with this, but when someone's gear rating is 10x better than yours, you're gonna have a bad time. It just upsets me because I use to have fun with this game now I can't go two games without raging and that's even if I win. I can't recommend anyone to spend $60 on this game unless there are some major fixes. Thanks for reading my review and I hope it helped you out!

Picked this up during the most recent sale.
Simple list format for those who just want to know if they should get it by reading reviews:
Pros
+The atmosphere that this game creates is top notch, 11/10, I can't say that I've played many games that create a space so well.
+The plot is very well done for a video game. Emphasis on sci fi elements, specifically philosophy related to consciousness and the self, artificial intelligence, and life after death.
+Lore is given to you in-game via computer terminals, photos, paper scraps, etc. This adds highly to the immersion.
+Very nice graphics, amazing use of DoF and Chromatic Aberration which are usually not implemented well.
+Horror elements are well done and can genuinely make you nervous without being jumpscares, though a few of those are present.
Cons
-Very linear, can almost be called a walking sim.
-Most puzzles are very easy, with a small handful that aren't very intuitive where you basically just click around until you get it. Not a huge negative by any means.
-Only a single ending despite a few actions you can take. This presents the illusion of choice but I was slightly disappointed that the few choices don't really matter all that much.
-The horror elements, while mostly well done, can get very tedious at times.
I'd give this game a go, but pick it up on a sale. I place the value of a game as time spent in hours = money paid for a game (eg. $10 for a 10 hour or more game is great), so in my opinion, it's far too short to be worth $30, but I would pay $20 or less for this experience.
