Game was a nostalgic blast for me. Solid shooter that clearly takes its influence from the Half-life 2 style era while looking like a prettier and more optimistic Doom 3. However it honestly has better gunplay than both. ADS, peeking, solid hit detection, good feeling to the guns, and challenging shoot outs with an optional bullet time element and some occasional triggerable eviromental bits through the game's "hacking" feature. The game is also a lot of fun with how it lets you toy with the world around you with some gimmicky but fun physics that range from lifting lids off of crates for ammo to simply playing basketball in a gym room. Oh and no regenerating health, you find your supplies across dispencers and pick-ups like it should be done giving the game more depth and challenge. Its mostly raw solid gunplay and shooter action following familiar mechanics that works out pretty well. The game also has some of the best music I've probably heard in a long time from an FPS game, and the best part is it's free on their website.
The game attempts a story, but the less said about it might be for the best as it really isn't that great and far from the highlight of the game. By the end the plot seems a bit confused of itself and ends on a note that will likely just leave you scratching your head. Meanwhile another thing worth noting on the downside is that several of the game's special mechanics get a little underplayed on the last two levels with the bullet time recourse running low, and hackable objects basically removed from battles. The game is also critcized for near perfect AI aim, which is true but honestly I think it actually added to the fun. Peaking around corners and trying to hit headshots before they shot back at me was just a part of adapting to the gunplay and felt natural. The AI also moves around, doges, calls out orders, and fliches to damage also giving them more life and opening them up to weak points making their aimbot skills more tolerable.
At the end of the day I really enjoyed this game and it kind of made me sad we don't get games like this anymore. It had a weird plastic sci-fi feeling with amazing industrial techno rock music that felt right and sort of felt nostalgic of the 90's/early 2000's while giving me gameplay from a better era of corridor shooters. I'd recomend this game to people who grew up around an earlier era of FPS, or just want a bit of an escape from the current market for a good cheap action packed FPS. I suppose you could look at it as a cheesy fun comfort game in that regard. Oh and again, its cheap... $5.... considering people are buying retro 2D torture platformers for double or more, I'd say this is a steal of a deal by comparison.

SOMA is one of those games that's so good you must tell everyone about it.
You're Simon, some dude that got himself in a car accident and had a severe brain trauma. He decides to try an experimental treatment to have his brain scanned and wakes up in a complete different location after the scan. You, playing as Simon, must explore this new place and find out what it's all about, how you got there, et cetera.  I can guarantee you, the story is MINDBREAKING and I will refrain from speaking about it any longer to prevent spoilers.
It's amazing how thrilling and immersive this game is. You'll be carefully exploring the station, hearing all kinds of noises around the corner, peeking to check if there's something there, looking over your shoulder to see if you're being creeped on... while you wonder what the hell is going on.
Technically, it's not THAT impressive, considering that SOMA has been released last year. The graphics are excellent, the textures are great, but it doesn't feel like a "current-gen" game. There's a lot of stuff laying around on the floor, on top of the tables, inside of drawers, stuff you can grab and examine although nothing is of some use except the items required to proceed with the story. Not that's a problem in any way, because the game shines either way.
The sounds and effects are top notch. You must play SOMA with headphones on, because you will get scaried like HELL. You will accidentally kick stuff laying around on the floor and it will make noises, making you feel that's something lurking around as you explore. The voice acting is excellent as well, specially Simon's and Catherine's.
About the gameplay: don't get your hopes very high. You will basically walk around, browse terminals, do a little item gathering and solve very straightforward puzzles once in a while. Something worth mentioning is that sometimes you'll have to decide for yourself what you will do, putting you between a rock and a hard place because some decisions out there will challenge your morals. There's no combat in SOMA, you will have to sneak past the enemies and hide from them, in case you get spotted. The focus of this game is it's story and the immersion.
And man... THIS is where SOMA gets scary as ♥♥♥♥. It manages to make you desperately run like crazy to evade the enemies because IT IS SCARY LIKE♥♥♥♥♥♥WHEN THESE ♥♥♥♥ERS COME AFTER YOU! The game does a hell of a job to make everything extremely terrifying, be it exploring the dark corridors and rooms of the station or be it running from the enemies giving chase.
I can tell you all that have been reading so far that SOMA deserves to be played, with lights out and headphones on. You will be amazed by the immersion, by how exciting it is to explore and how the story will develops. And what a story it is, my friends.
If you're out there looking for a narrative thriller game, SOMA is your game. Get it now, don't even wait for a sale.

Build up your family's shelter after a nuclear apocalypse. Focus is on building up your base and sending out expeditions to explore the world and gather materials.
You spend most of the game looking at your base, interrupted whenever expeditions report in if they encounter anything worthwhile. Your characters skill up and there's a tech tree of stuff you can work through to build stuff.
My biggest complaint is that the game gets very slow after you get mid-level tech. There are a few specific mat types that are just a pain to farm up and it adds a ton of time grinding out expeditions to find them. I'd rather enjoy a 10 hour game that felt a little too short than a 30 hour game that starts dragging halfway through, especially at this price point.
Second biggest complaint is that if your base gets attacked you are 100% dependent upon traps, your nicely trained survivors and their weapons inexplicably will not fight the intruders. Fortunately attacks are few and far between so this is only a minor annoyance.
Overall a fun game that could have been better if it played a little quicker. Recommended if you want a nice simple base building survival game and you don't mind a little bit of a grind.

A beautifully rendered platformer, with an exquisite soundtrack, and exciting worlds, challenging single-player, baffling co-op... typical Rayman awesomeness. It refines the way Rayman Origins handled, resulting in a much more satisfying game to play than the occasionally slippery original. Honestly, there's little to criticize - Rayman, as a series, has an infectious optimism and joy, and Rayman Legends has it in spades; the music, characters, collectables - everything contributes to an atmosphere of happiness and fun. The only problem is that it's a game developed for the Wii U. And, nothing against the Wii U, the unique control system that influenced a lot gimmicky levels in this installment does not translate well to PC. Neither does Ubisoft's proprietary Uplay system, which is insultingly tacked on and is required to be open to play.
Rayman Legends is, thankfully, a game awesome enough to overcome being a Wii U ex-pat and a Uplay software. Any other project would likely be irrepairably tarnished for it.

This art game, although a bit strange is worth checking out.  "how do you Do it?" brings to light a concept that many adults haven't thought about for years.  It really is a perfect simulation of what it's like to be an adolescent who is confused but still aware of the concept of sex.   Many may recall some of the thoughts that went through our heads during this time in our development.
This may be reading a bit too far into the game, but I believe it's a well thought out indictment of how we introduce our children to the concept of sex in our society.  Most of us were probably told very little about it by our parents and were left to futily attempt to uncover the mystery of sex on our own or told about it from our older "knowledgable" friends.  Perhaps this game is trying to make the point that if we spoke candidly about sex to our kids, they might not develop the common misconceptions about it and maybe people would make less mistakes in that realm of things.
Either way, I recommend how do you Do it? because it is a truly unique and well executed concept.

I mostly try to write helpful, at least semi-in-depth reviews, but here, I just don't know where to start.
It works ok save for the occasional glitch (save often and in MANY slots), it looks 2005 apropriate, and the soundscape is once again amazing, as is customary for SW titles.
The main strength of this game is the writing. There are well-written games out there, and this one just trumps them all, in my opinion. It's a game with so much dialogue my roommate commented "dude, you've been playing this game for 4 hours straight and all you've done is frickin' talk!!!", but that's just how it is, and believe me, you wouldn't want to wade through tree upon tree of badly written dialogue (the fact that the voice acting is also stellar for the most part helps). The companions are interesting and far less generic than in KoTOR 1, the atmosphere is bleak, grim and dark as is the story. The quests are intriguing and challenging, character development is excellent. Most dialogue choices have an effect on your world (you can spot them with some practice and common sense), so choose wisely. That's really all I can say without giving away any story spoilers.
Other than that... this is a slow game (albeit with decent action) and it's like a good book. You're sad when it's over and the journey was amazing. However, unlike a good book, you can re-play it four times and have a completely different experience each time. That's because there is less of a division between light and dark side, and in general, you'll find it hard to stick to one path - that's good, because it makes you reflect on morality, free will, apathy and so on. I'm not exaggerating when I say this is a game that might end up changing who you are, or at least showing you who you are (provided you really immerse yourself and role-play).
One of my best friends said these words about KoTOR II and I feel they're fitting to end this review: "I wouldn't want to die knowing I hadn't finished KoTOR II in my lifetime."

Okay now the serious review:
The basics
To start off, this game is one of a kind. You will not find another (modern day) game that has this realistic of vehicle physics. The game has countless things you can try, and no two accidents will ever be the same. You can simulate everything from hitting a wall at 25 MPH to being rear ended by a APC at 300 MPH. The crash physics of this game is so realistic that we actually use it to sometimes recreate accidents that have happened in real life. Accidents aren't the only thing you can do in this game. You can have vehicle pursuits, plane crashes, off roading, hill climbing, racing, truck driving, or just general dicking around. There is always something new to do in this game, it ends at how creative you are. My favorite thing to do is have AI cars driving around, and me in a police car chasing another AI. Every turn is a risk, and intersection is a risk. Will there be a car there? Who knows.

Pros:
The game runs pretty well
Good FPS
Don't need a NASA computer
Very Fun
Always something new
Great modding community (No steam workshop yet)
Very realistic crash physics and vehicle handling
Cons:
Does sometimes crash at very high speed accidents (Talking like 350MPH accidents)
Makes you lose track of time
No multiplayer and probably won't be ever.
Updates for the game come out every few months, which can get old if you experience a problem.
Overall this game is very fun and is a great time killer. You will never have two of the same accidents, chases, or race. The graphics are pretty amazing for the game and it runs well for how complex the physics engine is. If you're looking for a game that does not get old, something you can alwasy try something new in or just something to kill time with, this is your game.

Just another great game ruined by Ubisoft.
The game itself is very fun. There are some gameplay issues that absolutely need to be sorted out (defense is too strong at higher levels of play, lv108 revenge builds rip through new players, reviving an ally to full health in 3 seconds, etc.) but overall the core of the game is great fun and I enjoy it a lot. The problem is that there are so many technical problems you can't expect to just turn on the game after a day of work and have fun for a few hours. There will be some sort of issue. You have to suffer through so much BS to enjoy the game that's beneath.
There is lag in games. I've seen people rubberbanding but it's extremely rare. However, the issue of delayed inputs is much more prevalent and very frustrating in a game that demands quick reactions. There are frequent connection issues that will kick you out of games. There are a lot of questionable design decisions. For example, why am I removed from queue with a message informing me that the matchmaking system tried to place me into a full match? And then I need to dismiss the message and requeue? Why can't your system quietly acknowledge that joining failed and replace me into queue without user input? Why would you suddenly add the "Quit to desktop" option on the postgame screen with your most recent patch (and putting it as the last option in the list where "Quit to map" used to be)? Why is the faction war aspect of the game (a huge selling point that was hyped up) completely useless until the last day? (e.g., if faction A holds 99% of the territory every single day of a round but on the last day faction B suddenly holds 51% then faction B wins it all). Why is it that the guy who no-lifes 16 hours a day every single day receives the same amount of "reward" for participating in the faction war as some guy who played a single match? Why does getting to the enemy stronghold do literally nothing?
I could go on and on but I'll stop there. The main point of my review is that this is a great game that could be made absolutely fantastic with a few gameplay tweaks. However, there are relentless connection issues and some seriously horrid design choices that ruin the experience. I have hated Ubisoft for a long time and avoided any game that they produce but this one looked so good I just had to give them another chance. Clearly that was a mistake. I will continue playing For Honor and hope that they sort out the issues but this was their last chance for me and I know now to avoid any Ubisoft game. Period.

This game currently has countless issues that make it almost unplayable in its current state. I understand that it is early access, but this game is not currently worth the money that it is, and it certainlly should not be at a 0.9 state.
First problem is the loading screens. Everything takes 15+seconds to load regardless of the hardware I play the game on. Not to mention the optimization is garbage. Everytime you save a custom vehicle (which I will elaborate on further), the vehicle re-renders. The re-rendering can take anywhere between 10 and 30 seconds and with all the parts that the game has, creating a custom vehicle is a time comitment.
Which brings me to custom vehicles in the first place. It takes almsot twenty minutes to create one because of the loading and re-rendering, and even after that when you save it doesn't always work! I have tried to save 3 custom vehicles, each of them taking a good amoutn of time to create, and I can't load any of them.
Then there is the interface to begin with. The mix of long and glitchy loading screens and then the userface being slow, unresponsive and laid out like garbage, is very hard to deal with. On many of the 'campaigns', there is a large box that takes up most of the screen which I assume was meant for text, but it is just blank or has 2% of it used by the points you got. And there is a left column that has nothing in it, and then at the bottom left there is the next or retry buttons. The big menu that you see in some of the game shots as well may as well be trash. It is slow, unresponsive and extremely complicated and not thoughtout in terms of layout or readability.
The missions are fun, and for the most part work well, but you can't select specific missions within a group. You just have to play all of them together. There is a pretty fun cannon mission where you get to shoot a car with a cannon, however, you have to play through 4 somewhat ok missions before you can get to that one!
The game also only comes with 2 missions, and the rest are lack-luster user creations that you have to download from a pretty sketchy website. I haven't had much luck with finding good missions there.
Finally there is the controls and drivability of the vehicle. The tires, I'm pretty sure, are made of butter. If you driver more than 60mph, even the slightest movement left or right will cause you to go into an uncontrolable spin. Driving quickly in this game just sucks, cause you always know you're about 20 seconds away from having you car trashed. But this is also mostly a problem with how you control the cars. You can only go FULL THROTLE or NO THROTLE. There is no inbetween. You can also only go FULL RIGHT or FULL LEFT, which makes doing small constant turns impossible. There is a 'big loop' set up on the grid map, and just getting around the turn is damn near impossible due to the constant clicking you have to do to turn in a slight manner.
Overall I would say this game is currently worth around 5 dollars, at most. The destruction is nice, but the camera doesn't always let you see what happens to your car once a mission decides it is finnished, and the free roam will decide to spawn you in weird places if you change vehicles part way through.
Very disappointed compared to the videos and other reviews I've seen.

Apotheon is a 2D game about Greek mythology. Apotheon means “exalted to the state of godhood.” The Ancient Greek gods that we know from Greek mythology and their powers are on display in this game. The storytelling feels quite accurate and would make anyone with knowledge of Greek mythology feel welcome to play this game from the beginning.
The protagonist is Nikandreos. Nikandreos means “victory of a man.” Combine Apotheon with Nikandreos and you can imagine what direction the story of this game will be taking. As Nikandreos you will traverse the map ascending to Mount Olympus and be asked to topple Zeus, the father of the gods. The art direction is quite impressive for a 2D game, which includes patterns, shapes, and figures known to be found on Greek pottery. There are diverse weapons and armor that appropriately reflect Ancient Greece. The weapons and armor tend to wear out from use, so you must find or buy new weapons and armor. This is when marketplaces such as Agora and Acropolis come into play. Agora and Acropolis are marketplaces that include weapon merchants, armor merchants, and black market merchants are selling their items. Black market merchants sell the rare weapons, weapons you will find that have unique properties.
There is a world map and a local map, both of which will make it very difficult to get lost. The objectives are always well laid out and do not have to be complete in any order. There are Olympian guards in the various towns who will fight you if you try to pick any locks. There is a lot of freedom to move around from town to town. You can try to fight specific gods or goddesses, but you can spend time exploring areas for lockboxes that contain valuable weapons, armor, lockpicks, and potions. You can also complete side quests for other gods and goddesses to gain other powers.
I had read from some players that the combat mechanics were clunky. It took me some time to get used to the controls for combat, but the learning curve is not too steep. I used the keyboard/mouse control and I managed to play to the end of the story. The biggest problem that I had with the keyboard/mouse scheme was when I faced three or more enemies at once. This is when your rolling ability is put to the test. Rolling and jumping are the key to winning battles against any enemies, including Olympian guards and gods or goddesses. There is the feeling of using proper tactics against different types of enemies. Simply mashing your buttons will not consistently help you win battles. Every battle, great or small will require tactics to minimize health damage and for victory.
It feels disappointing when you lose weapons and shields due to wear and tear, but there will always be new weapons and shields available to replace the old ones without having to pay too much in coins. There are also enough nectar potions and repair kits to help with your health and armor. There are a few difficulty levels such as Warrior, Champion, and Olympian. Olympian is unlocked only after beating the game once. Olympian will not allow Nikandreos to regenerate health after the health is extremely low.
As entertaining as this Greek themed game is, it feels like it could have used a little more polish. There were times when I received an error message when trying to reload a save game. It was not much of a big deal, but a more polished Apotheon would have prevented the error message from happening. There was also an apparent bug at the Refuge of Athena, a place where Athena challenges Nikandreos to find keys in a labyrinth. Saving the game where the platforms are always moving then reloading the game caused me to fall to my death every time. I realized that I had to save the game at the beginning where the platform is not moving at all. I believe that a more polished game would have led to a more accurate and less awkward combat system.
There is a multiplayer feature for Apotheon, but there is not option to play with the mouse/keyboard scheme. It requires two controllers, which I found strange. There is co-op play, which was included in a recent patch. However, I think that the crux of this game is single player.
I found Apotheon to be a decent game with excellent art direction, interesting story, and satisfying gameplay. I firmly believe that with a little more polish this game would have been a classic one. I still recommend this game to anyone, including those with lots of knowledge of Greek mythology and those with casual knowledge of Greek mythology.
My Score: 7/10

The Darkness 2 is a game that tries to break from the conventional game molds and provide you with something completely unique. The result is a masterpiece, placing it as the best game of 2012 for me.
You control Jackie Estacado, a mafia lord who has the power of Darkness itself. The atmosphere of the game and graphics really makes the world vibrant, while the characters are all amazing. From the dialogue to the story, it goes beyond just being solid and keeps you in the whole thing through. A must experience.
Gameplay wise is shines just as well. You can control the darkness, represented by 2 serpent heads, through your mouse and keyboard. Between grabbing enemies, blowing them away, beating them down, throwing them, or performing the gruesome finishers you always feel like it's a fun experience. You start off feeling like a god and progress to the more difficult enemies. It works out really well.
The biggest downside to the game is that it's very short. You can beat the main campaign in a few hours, but you'll end up going through it a couple of times for the fun achievements and maxing out all of the ability trees that carry over to New Game+. You can play in side missions with other characters that lets you experience a parallel story (ie, While Jackie was doing so and so, these guys were doing this to help). They also have dark powers that are all unique. This can be played in single player on lower difficulties or in co-op on higher. The story is the same for all of them, but it's still a great additional mode.
While this game has multiplayer, in my opinion it shines best as a single player experience. The weapons are fun, the enemies are great, the storyline is a masterpiece and the game looks and feels amazing. It's something I feel everyone owes it to themselves to get. The only gripe I could have is that there's no announced sequel or dlc. 10/10 - Get it. It goes on sale for such a low price that it should be a sin not to pick up a copy.

Is this game worth the full asking price?  No, probably not.
There's simply too many other, better games out there to be had for the same price.
Is this game fun? Sure it has it's moments. At times it feels more like a strategy game than a straightforward shooter.
At no time in this game can you do anything even resembling what is shown in the videos above, as far as running around jumping at enemies throwing grenades and shooting rampantly. You will always be low on HP, and low on ammo. The enemies always shoot first and they never but rarely ever miss. Most of them take 8-10 shots to the face to kill, and they come in groups.
The weapons are frustratingly bad.
Others here have mentioned how incredibly terrible the shotgun is, and I agree, for a game anyhow.
Most FPS players are used to an overpowered unrealistic shotgun. In the MW and COD games you are using a rifled barreled fully choked military grade weapon. In this game, the shotgun is basically a sawed off shotgun from a seedy pawn shop. Surprisingly is shoots very similar to a real sawed off shotgun, but that doesn't mean it should ever have been put into the game this way. You'll need to be no farther than about 15 feet from your target if you hope to even hit it. About 6 feet if you hope to kill anything. It's just frustrating. Especially since the game keeps giving you ammo for the damn thing, over and over and no ammo for the assault rifle, which itself is pretty underpowered.  I found myself going for my pistol, over the shotgun, because the pistol is so overpowered compared even to the AR that it's kind of silly. Too bad you rarely get any ammo for it.
The best gun in the game by far in my opinion in the sniper rifle. Though throughout the entire game, you'll only get about 40 rounds for the thing, and all but the lowest enemies require 2 or 3 shots to the face to kill with it. Why is it my favorite? I don't know, I guess it's the only one of the weapons that almost felt like it was done right.
The grenades are a joke. You can toss one 4 feet from a guy, and he won't even go into the damage animation.
You literally have to hope the grenade lands at his feet, preferably ON his feet if you want him to die.
I suppose I should mention there is a Flamethrower, a Rocket Launcher, and a Hammer for a melee weapon.
No real reason to mention them though.
On several occasions I hit an guy in the face with a rocket, and he didn't even care. I'm sure it did some damage, but it's comical to see such a huge explosion, and out of the fire and smoke the guy is still shooting at you.
The Flamethrower has the range of a hairspray can lit with a lighter. It's sometimes funny to watch the flame thrower enemies shooting flame at you from 8 feet away and you not taking damage. It's not so funny when you're the one using it though. Also it's comically underpowered. A complete botch of a weapon and no surprise, there's plenty of ammo to be found for it. The game also hides the damn things in secret rooms, as if it's some super weapon you'd actually want to use.
The Hammer is your melee weapon.
It's so pathetic that it even exists that it's hard for me to find words as to describe why it's even in the game.
Enemies shoot you with unmissable headshots from hundreds of yards away, and the game gives you a frigging hammer.
Do I even need to mention it's uselessly underpowered?
The levels are passable. They are strictly linear affairs, which isn't uncommon. The amount of unused and useless rooms was probably meant to give the game some feeling of depth, but to me it just felt unfinished.
The platforming parts of the game are stupid. This game should not have them. The jumping is beyond bad. Your legs are made of glass, because if you fall or jump from more than about 6 feet you will die. I'm no badass weapon weilding space marine like this guy but I've somehow managed to survive jumping off the side of a pickup truck. That would be death for the hero of this game.
The physics in the game are annoying. Throughout the game, most things you grab will fall through the floor, or go into a frenetic jiggle spazm until it flies across the room, only to then sink into the floor when it comes to a rest.
It was kind of cool to have to take the lid off of boxes to see what was inside though. Unfortunately of the hundreds of boxes in this game, only about 10 have anything in them. Which lead me to beleive the location for the game is a facility to mine and store Empty Boxes.
There's an F5 quicksave feature that eventually becomes so necessary that you become glad it doesn't take but a second or two for it to save. I found myself killing one enemy, hitting save, killing another, hitting save, etc.
So why am I giving this game a thumbs up?
Truthfully, it's a bad game, but I had fun in spite of myself.
Plus there's 90% off Steam coupons to be had which means you can experience the pain of this game yourself for only 50 cents. It's hard to pass up anything for that price.
If nothing else, you can have the experience of what an FPS game is like when you do nearly everything wrong in making it.

Maybe SOMA is closer to being a walking simulator than a game, as the term is understood in the conventional sense anyway. It doesn't matter how it's labeled frankly. The smart, ambitious storytelling and themes more than compensate for the simplified gamplay mehcanics. Not doing an intro to the story because it's in the game description when you first loaded the store page.
It's a perfect blend of Sci-fi and horror, but it's not as oppressive and scary on a visceral level as Amnesia was. On an intellectual level, however, SOMA is more terrifying than Ameneisa and most others in its genre. Specifically, the questions it asks (or spring in your mind as you progress) and its thematic elements.
But SOMA isn't smart or scary just because it asks philosphical questions about consciouness and what it means to be human. Heck, SOMA isn't even the first game to ask those questions. It's because the game forces you to reflect upon those said questions from a dark, uncomfortable perspective you may never thought of using.
This is why I think the simplified gamplay mechanics add to game rather than serve as a detriment. It allows your mind to do all the beautiful work of reflection and introspection while the game is tormenting you in depths of ocean hell. And then you employ your stealth or run the **** away and hide here tactics when you do encounter the occasional monster, much like Amensia. Speaking of Amensia (again), if you played thourgh to the end of that game and felt relieved (or umimpressed), SOMA's ending, not to spoil it, will leave a more powerful impact on you, as in your soul and mind.
Sound design, storytelling, and detalied environments are top notch, exceptional quality. It's worth full price and your hard earned cash doing whatever.

This is going to be just about as long as some of the other long-timers' reviews has been. So, sit down, buckle up, and geta  coffee.
Executive summary:
In this review I hope to explore some of the major pros and cons comparatively through the year life span i've been playing Survarium. From closed Russian-only server beta, to, now, Steam release. I hope to explore, in some depth, how mechanics have evolved over time, how Vostok has added additional content over time, how they've chosen to balance the game over time, and how they've slowly begun to monetize the "F2P" model. I sincerely hope this helps other players, old and new, in their perception of Sarvarium going forward, to, hopefully, a fully released, polished, and complete game.
Some background.
I found this game after seeing some sparse reddit posts on the STALKER sub about a "spiritual successor." Well before we saw that obvious scam with that other one, I saw Sarvarium. It had the look and feel of STALKER, it had a working beta game play, and, well, looked legit. So, I signed up for the lotto, and, after a few weeks, received my beta key. When I started the game, the top level was Equip 12, or whatever. Overall, it was people running around with old Soviet machine guns mowing people down. With some sparse attempts, by players, at a slower, more calculated game play with rifles. (This hasn't changed one bit, mind you.) I advanced through the player levels rather quickly until I hit lv30, when I slowed down. Back then, there were few Russians at lv100, and they were top rankers who grind all day.
Throughout they've added more guns, and more equipment levels. It was until a few months ago they revamped the character leveling (skill) tree. In my opinion, this was a big welcome as the old system was, to be honest, rudimentary. Although much to a large dedicated player base of International and Russian and Ukrainian player's bemuse. Many were calling for a total revamp how match making worked at the fundamental level. Instead of adding more tiers of equipment levels, we wanted them condensed; refined, even. Instead of of the game system making the distinction, much of the community was split on whether or not to include things like rank, player level, and equipment level. In my opinion, the game should *never* put someone with top tier equips into a match with the lowest tier guns/armours. Ever. Period. Yet, it does. Even when there are seemingly enough people on at a certain level where it could match someone up with same/similar-leveled characters and equips.
Speaking of equipment, and balance in general: I like that, the higher one progresses in ranks, the more access one has to with armour/pockets for items, more artifact slots, and more mag pouches. However, I feel there has not been enough focus on the consequences of overloading the avatar. I have been outpaced, as a 23kg/45+kg with +5% movement speed boots and pants, with high stamina regen +%% and lower energy costs modifcations on pants and boots, and in the character level - by a player with full Zubr equips, PKP, huge backpacks, and, enough stuff on them to be close to, or over burdened. Now I don't know these player's character screens; if they're lv100, have "perfect" mods on everything for speed/movement, that's one thing, but generally, this shouldn't happen. I'm not complaining in as much as pleading a argument for refinement of game play: Less time spent trying to make money off the player base, and adding new content, and more time really refining a solid gameplay support structure to build new content off of.
Survarium devs need money to further develop the game; I get it, it makes sense. But I don't like it's sacrificing it's potential on becoming another vanilla PvP arcade shooter with a STALKER-isk atmosphere. This game idea has a lot of potential to revolutionize how we, as lovers of PvP shooters with RPG elements think and approach the genre.
On the topic of communication from Vostok with the fans, it has often been said that we lack a good outlet to voice our opinions, and air grievances about direction. If what they say is true that they value community input, communication lines need to stay open and fair-minded. Instead we have community managers that, for the most part, say: "It's in the works." or "Vostok are considering what you (the community) have been saying." or "It's your problem, not ours." Or, or... or... so many other *deflections.* Community managers should be (mostly neutral) liaisons between community members and the devs, not spoke-persons for the devs. They should communicate directly with concentrated efforts about what the Devs are thinking and considering, explicitly, and vise-versa. Instead of just spouting more, "it's going according to (Vostok's) plan. Nothing to see here." "There is a language barrier, Vostok being from Ukraine, and Russian-speakers, and the rest of the community." Isn't a valid excuse. This is 2015, we have means of translation. So, translate for us!
In conclusion:
This game needs further refinement of it's core game play mechanics. It doesn't need new content *right now,* it needs balance. This is what Survarium suffers from the most; it isn't new content, it isn't monetization of "pay to advance faster," it's focus on balance and refinement. I recommend this game, although reluctantly; it has lots of solid potential, and, in my opinion, it's at a crossroads in development. It will be interesting to see where it goes.

The Isle: An early access game currently in Alpha.
The developers have done a great job in making a playable game. It's quite frequently hard to remember that the game is still in alpha, as some people confuse it for a complete game already.
Current State: The developers are currently testing a new progression system, and a new map. Many people have been annoyed that sandbox mode was removed, which forces everyone to participate in the alpha testing of the progression system.
Part of this progression system locks more powerful dinosaurs behind multiple weaker dinosaurs. Each one of those dinosaurs must survive for 30 minutes or more depending on the tier of the dinosaur. This prevents the constant spawning of predators for revenge killing, ensures players think twice about taking suicidal risks, and provides a food chain (and challenge) to carnivores. It's a work in process that addresses many problems of the game (Why spawn in anything other than a Rex in Sandbox?). Unfortunately, this phase of development has not been popular, and many people have chosen to change their reviews to negative because of their displeasure.
Are the Devs Jerks? Not really. But if you are reading this, please be aware that the steam forums became exceedingly toxic for period of time. The devs and moderators tried for a long time to clean up the steam forums and make it a constructive environment... They failed, and decided to put in place a more draconian system. And for the first time in months... the forums are cleaning up and becoming a civil location. You can still disagree with the developers, and dislike the phase of the game to be clear... but you need to have a constructive attitude and not just complain.
Some things the Devs have commented on:
1) The game WILL have sandbox servers again either later in development, or at release.
2) The game WILL have modding capabilities, so you can choose not to have humans in your game if you want.
3) As optimization improves, laggy conditions will also improve.
The Isle:
The isle is a hard core survival game where you can play as any number of dinosaurs, humans, mercenaries, survivors, and natives. At currently, only the herbivores and carnivores are developed enough for public gameplay. As a dinosaur, the game varies widely from cat and mouse to chase and combat. 90% of the time (especially in early game), you end up hiding skittering through the thick jungle foliage, listenning for footfalls or calls, seeking food. While the wilderness is vast, everyone must come to water holes eventually... and that's when the challenge occurs, where you must trot into heavily camped watering holes crawling with predators... raptors... rexes... and while you may get your prescious gulps, the chances of being found by bigger or faster predators is great.
Combat itself is high speed, with predators and prey circling each other, predators looking for an openning to swoop in and take bites out of it's prey, while herbivores try to minimize their weakspots either by joining herds or attempting to run. Either side could win... Unless there's a Rex, they almost always win.
Eventually, technologically equipped survivors and mercenaries will join the game, and also natives and cannibals. And if the developers put as much effort into the future races/classes as they have in the current content, this game will shape up to be really fantastic!
Pros:
1) Very atmospheric gameplay.
2) While people say the game may be boring at times, when you find yourself running for your life, or perhaps hunting your food, it can be very thrilling!
3) The developers have done a great job attempting to build and balance a challenging game.
4) The game has a lot of potential.

Playing Apotheon (Alientrap, 2015)  is like diving in the registers of a Greek vase, and fighting giants and chimeras. Apart from a light narrative, and low play time, it’s the nods to ancient Greek themes, mythology and their emulations of them that I found rather enjoyable.
The platform game developed and published by Alientrap in 2015 is a 2-D action roleplaying game that has you play as the protagonist Nikandreos. The game features esthetics that emulates the black figure and red-figure painting style found on Attic Vases, as well as takes their mythological storytelling dimensions. The main narrative is propelled by Hera, making you her champion, wishing to rebel against Zeus’ desire to see the world of man reduced to oblivion; to accomplish this: she instructs Nikandreos to seize the divine powers from the Twelve Olympians, and then defeat Zeus himself.
While the story line is rather simplistic, the art style, immersive atmosphere of the game, and copious mythological references give it its redeeming grace. Each level is tailored from the nuanced color scheme, to its supplemental steles that enrich the lore of the divinity with citations from Homeric, Hesiodic, Greek tragic sources, and other eclectic Greek works; that serves to give a greater comprehension of the themed level. A level of appreciation and respect for the ancient sources were applied to the game without warping the narrative of ancient authors, instead it works in the gaps between them; at the end of the Hesiodic Iron Age.
The first thing that you will undoubtedly notice is the fantastic art style; it basically looks like a playable ancient Greek vase. The classic side scrolling open world renders all the game as a flat field and registers of buildings and the impression of the painting’s figures that are coming to life to tell their mythical narrative. The character are little more than black silhouettes with “incised” details It’s a game that is always a pleasure to look at. Most of the game has a wonderful orange tone, but some areas use a different color palette. If you are even moderately familiar with Ancient Greek art, you will find its representations are very similar to those of the original pieces, such as the Olympian Zeus, Artemesium Zeus or the Discobolus of Myron- to name a few, as their attention to detail seeps in the majestic representations that permeate the entire game's style.
The game’s soundtrack composed and produced by Marios Aristopoulos features lyre and a chorus out of combat and a more animated chorus singing around beating drums during. These Classical instruments have variants for the realms of gods from the chirping of nature with a calm lyre in Artemis’s forest , to the enlivened drinking party of Dionysus  marked by an ever increasing rhythm of the aulos flutes ; to the brass instruments and drums in the Sisyphean eternal state of war in Ares’s realm, with an underlying guitar rhythm . Or the dismal din and sharp notes of piano with lingering chorus in Hades’ realm of the dead . The lyre, aulos, and chorus immerse the player in the Ancient Greek theatrics of the game even further.
Even the battles against the Gods are proper to their theme: Nikandreos and the Goddess of the hunt takes turns being the hunter and the hunted; Aphrodite must be shot by Eros three times; Dionysus has inebriating drinking games at a party of Satyrs and Maenads; Demeter tasks Nikandreos to undergo a katabasis in Hades’s Realm to reach her daughter Persephone at Hades’ side. Not all gods agree with their lord, Zeus, and will be more than happy to help you out, but you’ll also face some of them in direct combat. Some wishes to be remembered in sympathetic pathos with the plight of man and gift you their powers
The hauntingly poignant pathos of the narrative’s dialog and conflict follows in the clichéd footsteps of Greek Classical Tragedy, where the conflict between heroes and gods, ends in the demise of the hero’s by an act of Hubris, or by being saved by divine intervention. The pathos of the Gods, in Apotheon, gives them a complex emotional character. For example Athena makes the allegory of Olympus being troy, and Nikandeos the Trojan horse, perhaps the most poignant is when Aphrodite's dialog:
“But it is my nature! Would you mortals worship me if I was anything less than what I am? What share of privileges will I have when there is no one left on earth to love? Please accept my sacred cestus into which is woven my powers of beauty and desire. A token of remembrance from a goddess with no worshipers left.”(Alientrap, 2015)
However in the modern twist from the game, the Gods become the tragic figures, that needs to be saved by an act of hubris…well those with compassion for mortals, and those that oppose Zeus. This drama works because it’s relatable. At the final level, while climbing Olympus to confront Zeus, he narrates the “Five Ages of Man”  as described by Hesiod, and locates Nikandreos within the Iron Age, and adds the Dark age twist continuing the tradidion of Hesiod.
In sum the game Apotheon takes elements of above common knowledge from Greek vase painting, sculptural art, mythical narrative, tragedies, and sources- even chorus and music to present them to the player in an unencumbered and seamless episodic narrative-albeit rather simple. But that is the beauty of it-exposition thought artistic emulation. I hope, this review made you wish to try the game for yourselves. Thus is game is a pleasurable way to introduce Greek Classics, and Myth to video gamers, or immerse yourslevs in a fun and light game , and prompt you to dig for obscure parts of lore across the game.
-Cedric

If you like ancient Greece and/or action platformers, you should definitely give this game a try. It is worth it.

This is the first time I've ever taken it upon myself to write a review so I guess that really says something about this game. When I saw the first trailer I was pretty hyped and couldn't wait to get my hands on it. After it released I decided to try it out at a friends house on his PS4 and it was everything I had hoped it to be, fast paced combat where good memory and even better reaction time play a key role in achieving victory. It's high skill ceiling makes the game very competitive and lets you feel like you have a chance at success regardless of which class you choose and who you're going up against. Anyways, after being thoroughly impressed with the console version at mi amigo's house I decided I might as well fork over $99 for the deluxe edition for my PC, after all I knew I liked the game. That was a mistake. On paper it would seem to be a straight upgrade, my computer is no lightweight so beautiful graphics at 80 fps was what I had to look forward to and thats what I got. For about five minutes... turns out the game uses peer to peer hosting instead of dedicated servers which prevents a single host from having an unfair advantage in theory, what this actually means is that anybody who doesn't have great internet speed is going to get shafted constantly. I have the best internet I can get in my area, which being Central Texas isn't saying much, but I have been disconnected from more games than I have finished to completion and I am not exaggerating. I'm honestly surprised when I manage to get to the end game screen. This is just an exercise in frustration and I don't know what's worse; waiting five minutes to get into a game only for it to dc you immediately or getting three quarters of the way through a great match only for it to dc you right before the end causing all your kills and xp to be flushed down the proverbial toilet. You would think that Ubisoft being a multi-billion dollar company would be willing to spend some extra cash for some actual servers on a supposedly AAA title but then again...Ubisoft.
TLDR: It's a great, satisfying game but good luck actually playing it for longer than 45 seconds if your internet isn't top tier.

I have to say, I didn't really know what I was getting into with For Honor when I purchased it. I only got to play a small sliver of the open beta, and I was really hoping that a lot of the kinks that were apparent would be fixed. Unfortunately, things took a turn for the worse.
Even with a good internet connection, you find yourself constantly plagued with various errors, or matchmaking incongruities that should not exist in this type of a game; common sense would dictate that while I am searching for a match to join, the matchmaker shouldn't try and connect me to an already full lobby, and then gives me an error stating the lobby was full only to kick me back to the mainscreen.
As the time that For Honor has been released increases, many of the veteran players find themself prestige 3 with multiple champions, and a near maxed gear score. This makes sense from a certain standpoint that players that "main" a certain champion, and pour forth time and energy into leveling them should be better equipped than someone just starting off. However, this leads me to an aspect of the game that is rather difficult to explain fairly. Often times, the algorithm that is used to matchmake is fairly balanced, but as of late, as I continue to level up other champions I have wanted to play for a while and having no gear on them, I find myself at an extreme disadvantage when put into a lobby where at least 2 of the enemy players are prestige 3 and max gear score. The enemy players get Revenge extremely quickly, and they all but two-shot me as I have no gear since I am leveling. I can understand that this game is geared towards a more "hardcore" audience than other MOBA games, but if Ubisoft hopes to prolong this game, they need to lower the barrier to entry, or risk not having a lot of new players enter the ranks of the Vikings/Knights/Samurai.
TLDR: In it's current state, I cannot recommend this game, but I definitely feel that I have got my monies worth from it.

Maybe SOMA is closer to being a walking simulator than a game, as the term is understood in the conventional sense anyway. It doesn't matter how it's labeled frankly. The smart, ambitious storytelling and themes more than compensate for the simplified gamplay mehcanics. Not doing an intro to the story because it's in the game description when you first loaded the store page.
It's a perfect blend of Sci-fi and horror, but it's not as oppressive and scary on a visceral level as Amnesia was. On an intellectual level, however, SOMA is more terrifying than Ameneisa and most others in its genre. Specifically, the questions it asks (or spring in your mind as you progress) and its thematic elements.
But SOMA isn't smart or scary just because it asks philosphical questions about consciouness and what it means to be human. Heck, SOMA isn't even the first game to ask those questions. It's because the game forces you to reflect upon those said questions from a dark, uncomfortable perspective you may never thought of using.
This is why I think the simplified gamplay mechanics add to game rather than serve as a detriment. It allows your mind to do all the beautiful work of reflection and introspection while the game is tormenting you in depths of ocean hell. And then you employ your stealth or run the **** away and hide here tactics when you do encounter the occasional monster, much like Amensia. Speaking of Amensia (again), if you played thourgh to the end of that game and felt relieved (or umimpressed), SOMA's ending, not to spoil it, will leave a more powerful impact on you, as in your soul and mind.
Sound design, storytelling, and detalied environments are top notch, exceptional quality. It's worth full price and your hard earned cash doing whatever.

If one thing is for certain, it's that this game is not for everyone. If you don't like lots of text in your games, if you don't care about the lore or the story so much and if your focus is absolutely the gameplay, you're probably not going to like Pyre. Certainly don't go into it expecting the kinds of games that Bastion and Transistor were. And finally, although it's advertised as an RPG (and it is true to some extent), it is definitely not what you typically think of when you hear that term.
If, however, you are willing to take things slow and explore what Pyre offers you, then you're in for an amazing experience. This is Supergiant's greatest achievement yet, in terms of the depth and sheer size of the world they created and your ability to participate in it. Of all the ~25 characters you meet in your journey, there is honestly not one I found shallow or that I didn't like. They are all unique personalities, with their shortcomings, their virtues and their quirks. They all have a story that makes them feel so much more alive, interesting and important. As the game progresses and thanks to the key position you assume in your party, you will begin to care more and more for, not only for your own party members, but for your opponents as well.
The art and soundtrack are, as you would expect, absolutely top-notch. All the visuals, from the locations you visit, the map, the characters and the gameplay segments themselves are stunning. Each and every one of them could easily be a painting hung on your wall. All this just reinforces the feeling of being in a very vibrant, dynamic world.
But what most struck me about Pyre is how well the "combat", if you will, fits the narrative and the world the game is set in. You will see many people describing the Rites as a weird sort of wizard basketball and, although technically they are right, they are also quite wrong; the Rites don't feel like a cheap game, they feel like important rituals, with huge rewards at stake as well. Everything from the outfits the characters wear to even the rules of the game itself, are explained and rationalized in terms of the lore. The outcomes of the Rites also have significant impact both on the story itself as well as on how you will need to approach your strategy in the future. And, as for the gameplay of the Rites themselves, it is much more tactical and deep than it first appears. If you're finding that you're plowing through every Rite without much struggle from your opposition, do yourself a favor and turn up the difficulty. You will soon need a better approach than running and diving with a fast character in the opponents' pyre.
Overall, Pyre is a very beautiful story that you can impact as you choose, intermittent with very solid and challenging gameplay. A single playthrough takes 12-15 hours, depending on how much time you spend with the lore, and there is a good amount of replayability as well looking to get different endings or different dialogues with characters - plus there is also a local versus mode. I think, at its starting price, it's an amazing deal.

Before I begin, let me say this- If you have no patience for text-heavy games, or sports games, leave now.
With that out of the way, Pyre is the third game from Supergiant games. I adored their first two, Bastion and Transistor, and I adore Pyre as well. Pyre is a game about you, an exile to the purgatory known as the Downside, leading a band of exiles to freedom. I cannot say more, or risk spoilers.
Gameplay- The game has two main "modes". The first is a Visual Novel style interface where you interact with caracters, view your roster, make decisions on where to go, etc. The second is the Rites, a sort of fantasy-celestial ball game. You play as three exiles, each with their own abilites and strengths, but control only one at a time. Your goal is to either carry or throw the celestial orb into the opponent's pyre. You have multiple abilities both for movement (such as sprinting or jumping), and for offence, which will temporarily banish your allies. Overall, I found the system quite deep, with the perks and talismans for different character classes all making tangible differences to how that character played. If you find it too easy, there are three difficulty modes, and modifiers you can set which will cause negative effects (such as your pyre starting with less health), but giving you more experience.
The other half is hardly much of a game, except as you make decisions about what skills to train, or what routes to go, which may help or harm your next rite.
Story- There is a LOT of text in this game. Thank goodness it is extremely well written and compelling. The lore in the story is largely contained within a book, whose pages are slowly revealed to you, so it never feels overwhelming to read it. The dialogue, meanwhile, fleshes out the characters and their relationships extremely well. I felt a real connection to each of the members of my party, and several times was almost moved to tears.
Art and Music- The dynamic duo of Jen Zee on art and Darron Korb on music work their magic again. Pyre is absolutely stunning. Supergiant seem to have a thing for vibrant, colorful wastelands/apocalypses, and the Downside is breathtaking, if inhospitible. The characters are expressive and well designed. Meanwhile, Darron Korb, assisted by the vocals of Ashley Barret, creates memorable and beautiful tracks for each of the opponents you face, and for the spaces in between the rites.
Little Touches- This game is full of little things that didn't need to be there, but give so much texture to the world. Like the little items you collect as you explore, or the items which tell you where each party member is at that moment, or the fact that there is one character you can name one of about 20 names, which will then be reflected not only in text, but also in many voiceover sections as well. This attention to detail is what sets Supergiant apart from other developers.
I highly recommend Pyre. If not now, then next steam sale. And pick up the soundtrack while you're at it. It is well worth your time. It is truely unique.

Really unexpected gameplay and a touching story with character interaction that makes you long for NG+.
Soccer matches for combat are definitely not for everyone. However for those just in it for the story, they pose little challenge. In fact, losing a match doesn’t result in a game over, but is actually valid path to continue the story on from. For those determined to win without a restart, the more high stakes matches can feel intense, and scoring a goal with only your slow moving, bulky tank character left on the field is always exciting. I would recommend switching up your team regularly, especially with later game characters as their move sets are more unique than your beginning party.
Pyre is very dialogue heavy, which is definitely not for everyone. Fortunately, the biggest lore dumps are all contained within an ingame book that can be read at your leisure if that’s what you’re into. Interacting with your party in completely optional conversations can provide buffs or debuffs during the next combat section, depending on how well the conversation goes. As “hope” is an important character stat, the affect your conversations will have on it is clear. As all of your party are criminals, trying to coax them into revealing their past crime gives you something to look forward to.
There was clearly a lot of care put into the world. Hovering over the items in your wagon to get unique flavor text on your party members’ current locations was always endearing. Logan Cunningham (who recognized him?! Yo, that range!) as the narrator has voice lines for the two dozen possible names you can give a specific character, which definitely surprised me. If you tell your lovely moustached dog that his moustache is lame, he’ll
Because of little details like those, the story heavy sections never felt like a chore to play.
I highly recommend this one, especially for those who enjoyed Supergiant’s first two releases. Pyre has a lot of heart and a lot of possibilities that you can’t discover all of in a single playthrough. (I’m really adamant about this needing NG+ though. Please.) I know it’s easy to wish it was more like *previous game of your preference* but if you keep at it, you’ll definitely find yourself engaged in the lovingly crafted world they created.

Well, I say "Recommended", but really it's because there's no in-between.
I sank about 28 hours into this game, and it was perhaps only worth it for the first few.
Sheltered is a survival, resource-management game that tries very hard to be unique in its own way. The game starts off as challenging, with only the bare essentials you need to survive, and perhaps not even that. The game throws you to the wolves, and you flounder for the first half an hour or so before you realize you need to build a toilet, a shower, a bed or even find out where the workbench is to do all that.
After you've got the basics down, you start learning to forage for items, or at least to send people out to forage for stuff. You don't actually control them while they're out there, only where they go. Then it becomes a hectic flurry of actions you need to take, between managing your people's needs, sending them out on foraging missions, expanding your base and repairing stuff that constantly break down. It never ends.
Sooner or later, you get the ability to recruit more people into your base, and you'd think this would help lighten the load - but it doesn't. It's just another person to feed, bathe, rest and micromanage. And you're going to want to recruit more people as soon as possible, because it increases the number of people you can do things with. The ability to make your survivors automatically care for their own needs matters very little, because that's just one thing you don't need to do, and there's always more.
Sheltered quickly dissolves into a hectic micromanagement simulator where you're hopping between people again and again to figure out who goes where and does what. It's very challenging the first few hours into the game, and in there lies its replayability value, but once you're past that, it simply becomes a chore hopping around from task to person to task.
If you like survival-type games, you can choose to pick up Sheltered for a short while. For all its flaws, it's not really a bad game, just that it becomes more of a chore than a relaxing past-time quickly enough. But I'd advise waiting for it to go on sale before you purchase it, because it's simply not worth the price it currently is (I got it off HumbleBundle).

The sequel to Knights of the Old Republic is a departure in many ways. Gone are the Bioware's colourful characters and the campy dialogue that would continue to be a feature in future Bioware titles. Instead we are thrown into a Star Wars galaxy that is more gray and a generally a more gritty place. The companions that tag along on your epic trip across a wartorn galaxy are a lot more conflicted and deeply marked by the devastation of war. Mentoring yopu on your journey i Kreia, one of the best and most interesting Star Wars characters outside the movies.
With Kreia Obsidian invites you to question the basic philosophy of the Star Wars universe and the binary nature of 'The Force'. Unlike KOTOR 1, this game doesn't want to be a mere mirror image of the Star Wars movies and Obsidian's take on the universe stands out as unique. It is a shame that Ea's acquisition of the Star Wars franchise effectively prevents epic stories such as this one to be realized within the current generation of video games.
Don't let the slow start at the beginning of the game discourage you from continuing with the story, the more frustrating parts of the game (Nar Shaddaa, anyone?) are easily outdone by the majority of the quests. A restored content modification for the game improves the experience tremendously.
Obsidian also deserves special mention for updating the game a decade later, thereby avoiding many of the compatibility problems  that plague older Star Wars titles.

Deeply, Deeply, Deeply flawed. It wants to be a stealth action game drenched in gritty realism, but the level of bad game design decisions and massive number of bugs keep me from recommending this game to anybody.
* Don't expect to be able to avoid or sneak past encounters. Several guards and soliders carry critical items you'll need to proceed. Which guards, you may ask? The game won't tell you until they're dead.
*AI alternates between being too dumb to breathe and psychic supersoldiers. Sometimes enemies will spot you even though you're clearly in complete darkness. Sometimes they won't. Sometimes enemy soldiers won't be able to shoot you on full auto from three feet away. Sometimes you'll blink and fall over dead. Sometimes you'll kill an enemy and it will be completely silent. Sometimes it will alert the enemies the next room over.
* The shooting mechanics are bad, supposedly to discourage mindless combat. But then the game forces mindless combat on you, most of the time without warning you.
* The environments look good, but they'll repeat themselves so many times it legitimately feels like you're just playing the same level again and again.
* Checkpoints happen once every 20-30 minutes. In gameplay sections with lots of enemies where most of your time is spent waiting doing nothing, this can get very frustrating very fast.
Whatever this game's strengths, they're far overshadowed by really poor design and technical mishaps that really takes me out of the experience. Can't recommend it.

A highly entertaining, old-school point-and-click graphic adventure game, as well as a love letter for the time-traveling movie trilogy which inspired it. All in all, this game is a disappointment.
The linear level design pretty much puts you on rails, which would not be too bad a thing if it was compensated by some interesting stealth action.

There are scripted shootout sections, where you will be seen no matter what.

There is a fairly difficult mission where the primary objective is to retrieve weapons. You have to play using your knife only. You take great pains to dispatch ~ 20 enemies with it, each fully armed, but cannot pick up their waepons. You then arrive at a shed with the weapons your objective wants you to pick up. There is no story to speak of, and the ending is an insult to the player's intelligence.
If you're a die hard stealth game fan, give it a shot. Just don't expect much. It's not even comparable to stealth titles like Thief, Metal Gear Solid or Splinter Cell.

I loved Rayman Origins, completing it 100%, and consider it one of my favourite games. With that in mind, Rayman Legends is better. In every way, Legends has improved upon the formula from the previous one, itself a worthy and excellent successor to the classic Rayman games of old. With the power of the beautiful UbiArt engine, this is a uniquely pretty game. I sometimes find myself stopping to watch the backgrounds of the levels, before continuing on a mad, frenetic and incredibly fun romp through the fantastic landscapes. The music is also excellent, with the musical levels being particular standouts. These levels are strictly platforming, with the only cues for your jumping and punching being the music and occasional markers on the ground. They are tough, but even if you die, there are frequent respawn points to keep you in the action. This fits the game on the whole- it's grueling, but the respawns are fast and the lives are infinite. It's possible to rush through the levels while only collecting what crosses your path, but there are secrets all around which require some exploration to find.
This leads to my complaints about this game. Yes, I love it, but it's not perfect. Firstly, the Teensies and other collectables. They are hidden, yes, but usually not very well. There are some that I've found and thought were harder or more clever than the norm, but on the whole it's not hard to collect everything. It just requires some thoroughness. Second, Origins had a speedrun feature, where beating a level gave you the option to replay it with no checkpoints, and a medal if you finished within time. This added some good replayability, and while you can still run through levels in Legends, there's no speedrun feature. There are special short invasion levels which time you and post your time to a global leaderboard, which is cool, but ultimately I would have liked for the speedrunning to be available on normal levels too. Thirdly, I've had two levels actually glitch out on me. The second music level has a segment where you jump off a large cliff and fall, and my game does not allow me to do this properly- I die mid drop because the screen scrolls too fast for me to survive. I managed to get around this by pausing and unpausing repeatedly during the fall, but this is a fairly major problem. As well, the third music level has a section where you run through a skull, and come out the other side shrunken. The first time I played this level, when I ran into the skull, I died. Every time. The next time I loaded the level, it worked fine, but I was left thinking it would be uncompleteable. Perhaps the first bug is due to me playing on a laptop, but nothing else in the game has done that, so i have no idea. Finallly, my last problem is UPlay. 'Nuff said. I personally have had no real problems with it, but it's still annoying and unneccessary, and many people do have major problems. So keep that in mind when considering this game.
In conclusion, Rayman Legends is fantastic and I love it and it's one of my favourite games, but it has got problems, and I recognise that. Still highly recommending it, 10/10.

I'm generally very picky when it comes to Metroidvania-style games, but this game hit the nail on the head. Fans of either Castlevania or greek mythology need to give this game a try.
Pro's:
*A compelling world to explore. The artstyle and ancient greek lore work very well. There are also quite a lot of secrets to find. The Greek gods are the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s you expect them to be and it makes for a satisfying story.
* Good selection of weapons, which facilitate exciting and fast-paced combat.
* Combat AI of enemies seems well-made, ducking and blocking to avoid your attacks.
* Well-made boss battles.
Con's:
* The art style is somewhat low in contrast, making things hard to distinguish sometimes, especially in the map screen
* Weapon durability system. I'm generally not a fan of weapons breaking, and since you can't repair equipment you will need to find replacements. These are, fortunately, abundant, even for the magic weapons. The abundancy of said magic weapons makes them feel less special, though.
* the rewards for treasure hunting drop off when you have eventually found all types of weapons. There's not a new weapon around every corner, like would be the case in Castlevania.

Rayman Legends takes what was established in Rayman Origins and improves it. The vector graphics are back and look prettier than ever, there is the addition of a sidekick as well to help you get through some levels.
There is a lot to do in this game, each level has 10 teensies to find (The little blue guys), as well as the challenge to find enough lums (The yellow flying guys) to earn the Gold trophy. There are also unlockable characters as well, collectable creatures, unlockable bonus levels from Rayman Origins (each has teensies and trophies to collect) and Time Trial levels as well. If you're a bit of a completionist like I am with these sorts of things, you'll have lots to keep you occupied. There is also the new music levels, which are very much like the chest chasing missions in Origins, completely timing based where you jump or attack in time with the music. These are excellently thought out and the timing is spot-on. These are a bit more forgiving than Origins' chest chasing missions though, having checkpoints rather than making you restart after each death.
There are downsides though, this game is a console port and at times it shows, making some actions hard to perform using keyboard if you don't have nimble fingers. It is perfectly playable with the keyboard though and supports full key remapping (Which I suggest you do, I set mine to the Origins controls and it saved me a lot of trouble), but it may be easier to play using a controller. I can't say which is better, since I've only played using keyboard, although you can play one handed using keyboard, leaving your other hand free to do other stuff like eat a sandwich or write a book. It also doesn't really have much replayability, apart from the music levels which are awesome just to play occasionally, unless you are a big Rayman fan. Plus it only works through UPlay, which is not a bad piece of software but it does make things frustrating when you just want to get right into the game.
Overall, this game is worth picking up, even at full price and the annoying DRM. Graphics are pretty and there is a lot to do. I'm really looking forward to the next game in the series,

Alpha Prime is basically an extended tech demo, clocking in at 5 hours of playtime. And oh boy, does it show.
Let me get out the good parts first. As far as tech demos go, it looks pretty, with loads of cool effects on many interiors (outside doesn't look that good), and runs very nicely on my crappy laptop at 1280x800 resolution, except when there's too many particles (my NVidia G105M HATES them), you probably will run this perfectly. Also, ALL cutscenes are in-game, which is definitely a plus for both disk space and cutscene quality (seriously, ♥♥♥♥ those pre-rendered cutscenes).
...and that's all the good points.
As for the bad points, well... everything else.
The story is not just completely forgettable, it's also accompanied by hilariously bad writing and voice acting. I'll sum it up nicely for you: Miner has to find artifact on Mars-like planet because of ♥♥♥♥♥ ex-girlfriend, shoot many things because CORPORATIONS ARE EVIL (also evil robots for no good reason), ♥♥♥♥♥♥ boss fight for the artifact, dead because your ♥♥♥♥♥ was a ♥♥♥♥♥ all along. Seriously. I did not give a single ♥♥♥♥ about the story, except for the hilarious parts, my favorite being Paolo, the Italian with incredibly bad engrish, getting shot in the leg and saying "No! Paolo go nowhere! Paolo is a cripple! Disability pension!". Too bad the game kills him WAY too early, clearly he should've been the protagonist instead.
Oh yes, the gameplay. Enemies have perfect accuracy and INSTANT reactions, which makes even Easy a goddamn nightmare. Enjoy sniper shotgunners and exploiting their line-of-sight by leaning or crouching behind things so you become completely invisible to them.
Literally none of the weapons are either balanced or enjoyable, and ALL of them have ♥♥♥♥♥♥ damage. The first weapon is a useless hammer, you can attack as fast as you can press the mouse button but you gotta be WAY too close, not to mention every single enemy has a ranged weapon anyway, so good luck not dying. The pistol shoots too damn slow and feels underpowered. The shotgun is one of the worst i've seen in any game, you have to be almost as close as the goddamn hammer to do any decent damage (or any damage! Enjoy missing every shot while emptying all 8 shells!). The gatling rifle is the best one, which isn't saying much because it does ♥♥♥♥♥♥ damage and low ammo per clip. The sniper rifle would've been the best gun, had they not ♥♥♥♥ed up the zoom mode so badly that everytime you try to aim it's a goddamn chore and you'll miss many shots because of it. Both the rocket launcher and grenades are hilariously bad because you need sniper-like accuracy for it to do any decent damage, because the splash radius is just TINY. And finally the Flamethrower... the worst weapon in the game, yes, even worse than the hammer, you have to be almost as close to anything despite the flame going at least twice the distance for it to do any damage, and what it DOES damage is absolutely pathetic, a mosquito would deal more damage than this.
What else? The movement is hilariously broken, especially the jumping. They let you do a floaty jump but if you fall more than 5 meters you're pretty much dead. As for landing the jump itself, it seems to slide off things until it finds the flattest surface possible, it's really weird and it causes weirder deaths because of it. Because stairs are treated like ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ramps, I jumped downstairs and INSTANTLY DIED. And don't try to stand still either, because you'll slowly slide down that♥♥♥♥♥♥like's it's covered in butter. Also beware for anything with physics, it might just kill you, the most hilarious one is getting yourself killed by your own basketball. ON THE GROUND. JUST BECAUSE IT MOVED TOWARDS YOU. And finally, all the models barely look better than the ones on Doom 3, which is clearly what they were trying to mimic (some of them look just as ♥♥♥♥♥♥, too).
Bottom line, just... don't bother. Only reason I even got this was because of a bundle. Spare yourself the torture.
EDIT: Steam keeps putting this game on sale (I already regret making this funny), and I'd like to point out a few other things about the game, so here we go.
This game has a lot of stuff that's so underused and generically/badly thought out, you can seriously tell this was a tech demo from the start and didn't actually evolve past that, they just made it longer.
You get a hacking device early on in the game that lets you open locked doors and help you out in combat by making certain objects blow up... except sooner than you'd think, you'll never use it again unless you absolutely need to open a door. Zero combat use after a certain point.
Yes, you can hack one of those silly remote-controlled box lifters at least twice during the game. Oh boy, just what I was missing from my favorite FPS game, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ box puzzles! Good thing I'll never see them again.
Did I mention slow-motion? If you've paid any remote attention to the story, you know that stuff's Hubbardium, which is, you know... the very same reason that made everyone on the planet INSANE? And screw you if you think you deserve a good explanation for that (even in the end, it still doesn't make enough sense), so start pumping that♥♥♥♥♥♥into your veins and enjoy the orange effect.
And finally, yes indeed, you do get to drive a vehicle in one of the final parts of the game, with decent physics to boot (as far as martian-like physics go anyway). But once more, it was badly thought out to the point that you'll only get a brief section of it and never see it again. Come on, split that stuff out evenly.
