A fun little zombie romp.  This is the type of game you play when you just want to relax and zone out for a couple of hours.  Nothing challenging, just a colourful, mindless, zombie-bash-a-thon.
It clocks in at around 3 hours from start to finish so it doesn't outstay its welcome.  At first I was appalled at the graphics and horrendous job of optimisation, but it didn't take long for the cartoonish style to grow on me.  The zombies themselves are quiet varied, and the game throws plenty of easy bosses at you along the way.  Unfortunately the majority of combat is just bash the attack button and then throw out your special attack once its ready  (there are multiple special attacks, but when you get the best one right off the bat, that being the jump and stomp move, there really is no need to mix it up). There is only one type of powerup, beyond health items, which lets you speed up noticeably for a decent period and hit harder. There are stores where you can trade the coins you harvest from the zombies but you'll rarely bother as the zombies have healing items coming out their ears.  In terms of weapons there isn't a huge variety.  You'll end up hitting zombies with a baseball bat for 80% of the time, or your fists if it breaks on you.  And the rest is ranged water pistols, holy water (turns zombies against each other), and popcorn (to distract zombies).
The basic story is your girlfriend is stranded in the middle of the zombie apocalypse and its your job to rescue her.  This is the very height of it so don't be expecting a convoluted plot.  This minimal presentation however has you visiting an impressive array of environments, all of them appearing and disappearing one after another in quick succession so it doesn't grow stale.   They range from flooded church basements to ravaged towns, to mines, to army camps, to a haunted house.  There isn't much to do but run across them and kill or outpace zombies as you go, clocking up one objective after another.  It's very linear, and the most the game has you doing in terms of "puzzles" is pick up the key/explosive to open door/clear barrier.  There are a range of other collectibles but as none of them appeared to do anything they quickly fell by the wayside for me, and it just became of soothing journey of zombie whack-a-mole.  There is the very odd bit of imprecise platforming but thankfully this is kept to an absolute minimum.
People have complained about bugs/crashes in other reviews but the developers seem to have fixed the majority by now.  I didn't have a single issue the whole time.
Not everyone will find this fun and it isn't worth full price but get it on sale if you want a lazy evening to turn your brain off.
Also be warned, this game does not have developers who speak native English, so be prepared for some ridiculous dialogue.  Thankfully there isn't much, and it mainly consists of your character's hints whenever you come up to a door/barrier.

After the mediocrity that was Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, the highly anticipated follow up to Amnesia: The Dark Descent, a large portion of the Frictional Games fan-base began to question whether or not the company had lost its ability to scare audiences. This is despite the fact that Frictional Games had nothing to do with the development of A Machine for Pigs, but they went ahead and put their stamp on it as the publisher. Questions were raised, such as had they used up all of their horror creativity with previous Penumbra and Amnesia installments? Could they make a comeback from a massive let down? Only time would tell, and that time has now arrived in the form of a psychological sci-fi horror game called SOMA.
In 2015, main protagonist Simon Jarrett was involved in a car crash in Toronto, Canada. He sustained severe brain injuries that left the organ bleeding at all times, so he agrees to an experimental brain scan that's supposed to set him on the path to recovery; but instead after the scan is complete, he wakes up nearly 90 years in the future. The year is now 2104, and Simon soon discovers that he's in a deep sea research facility known as Pathos II. Early on, he also learns that a massive comet collided with Earth and set in motion the events of the apocalypse. Simon soon befriends a woman named Catherine, who sets him on a mission to launch a thing known as the ARK into space; the ARK houses the brain scans of multiple individuals, who can live on eternally as avatars within a virtual paradise on the ARK, so long as the device continues existing.
Out of the 9-10 possible hours of gameplay, there are only a small handful of events that involve "monsters" and those events can be separated into two categories; chase sequences and stealth scenarios. Every enemy that you encounter will either be blind with subhuman hearing, or supply you with no option but to run for your life. If you do happen to upset a foe who is meant to be snuck past, he will chase you down and hit you. If you're hit once, you simply black out and wake up where you left off, but your vision is left obscured; if the monster hits you again, it's game over and you're back to your last save point. These enemies are faster than you are, and as such you cannot simply run in a straight line and expect to get away; rather you need to find some corner to flee into and hide.
The mechanics for SOMA are very simple. If you've gotten hit by a monster, you'll need to find a glowing alien pod like thing, which will clear up your distorted vision and limp that you gain after sustaining an injury. When walking, crouching is of course quieter than standing, and is the preferred method of not getting your face bashed in by some moss and barnacle covered entity. Running and staying in the light is great for bypassing massive fish monsters who want to eat your skin. And not looking in the direction of a crying, sobbing alien woman will keep you alive to see another day. I'm really not sure why so many people and curators are deeming this title as "survival horror", because it simply isn't. If hiding and evading enemies is what classifies it as such, then Outlast, Amnesia, and Penumbra would all be considered survival horror as well. The only "survival" aspect is, well, healing yourself.
As sad as I am to say this, I wasn't scared at all during my time with SOMA. There's just something about the enemies that isn't particularly frightening in the least, but I really couldn't place my finger on why. I'm normally a sucker for chase sequences, I lose my cool, scream like a little girl, pause the game multiple times, and overall try not to have a breakdown. Towards the end of the game it felt like there were a lot of these chase scenes, to which I never even so much as sat on the edge of my seat. It very much suffers from the Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs syndrome when it comes to its horror aspect. However, what this game doesn't have in terms of scare factors, it makes up for with an amazing story and atmosphere; something that A Machine for Pigs could never accomplish.
A very strong bond is born between Catherine and Simon, even though Catherine can only communicate to you by means of your Omnitool when it's plugged in. The two become fairly close, and she's the only person that you communicate throughout the entire game. Since she's not always plugged in and available, there's an overwhelming sense of isolation and loneliness that increases tenfold by knowing that you could in fact be the last person on Earth. The deep, cumbersome sea doesn't help to alleviate this anxiety, either; it only makes matters worse once you descend further into the abyss. During the times that you're able to venture out of the Pathos II facilities and into the ocean, you can actually almost feel the crushing pressure thanks to not only the visuals, but also the overwhelming audio. I strongly recommend playing this game with a headset on to get the full immersive experience.
It's important to explore in SOMA, so that you take in as much of the storyline as possible. There are computer terminals with audio and text logs to check out, along with dead bodies that Simon can telepathically tap in to so that he can hear what happened during their last moments of life. You'll become acquainted with many of the last members of the Pathos II through their deaths, often learning about them before you end up stumbling upon their bodies. You'll want to keep going not only to find out what happens to Simon and Catherine, but what has become of the other crew members. The narrative is very deep, thought provoking, and engaging through the entire game, and it'll leave you craving more by the end.
To tie everything off, the title has some incredible visuals that are extremely well optimized. I found that I was able to maintain an FPS rate of between 70-115 consistently no matter what area I was in; including the outside, underwater sections that are the most visually stunning. You will explore lavishly detailed areas from overgrown, seaweed ridden facilities to rust covered, barnacle laden corridors, a very realistic ocean floor, to deeper depths of the ocean that are still unknown to this day. There are also plenty of gore-soaked rooms to appease most horror fanatics. Quite honestly, SOMA looks a lot like Bioshock, but plays like a heavily interactive walking simulator that uses monster evasion for puzzles.
Even though Frictional Games still haven't made a comeback with a game as strong in horror presence as that of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, it's good to be able to say that SOMA is a solid entry into their catalog of terror. While SOMA may not send you into a frenzied panic whenever a monster is present, it can sure send a good ol' tingle up the spine and goosebumps down the arms when the reality of the story begins to sink in. After all, what could be more horrific than potentially being the last entity on Earth, who is somewhere deep down in the depths of the unexplored ocean? The ending is also spectacular, and something to look forward to progressing towards. Overall, SOMA is an amazing atmospheric, narrative experience that shouldn't be passed up; just don't go in expecting to be terrified.

I've seen a lot of really bad reviews and complaints about Nether, and some of them are true, this game is very difficult and the learning curve is very steep. This makes it's very hard for new players go get going.
My own experience with the game is a bit up and down. I really enjoy the way the game works with a lot of grinding, looting and sneaking around, with levels(account and character), global inventory and accountwide cash, so you don't have to start from scratch every time you die. It makes it slightly easier the second time after dying to have a bit of food and ammo in your inventory, even a handgun or some gunparts for crafting can make a difference. PvP is a bit of an issue, it's kill or be killed for the most part, so new players without greater gear will have a tough time, if they don't watch out. PvE is great with crates to transport, escort missions for groups and bossfights with loot. Even the fights to secure Safezones can be devastating for an experienced group.
As i mentioned first in the preview I really agree on some of the complaints. #1 is probably the server list delay/lag, it takes so long, even with really good computer stats, and being new, you might think it's crashing, but really it's not. #2 is buggy pathing; swimming in particular. Sometimes you lose half your health merely touching the water, sometimes you can stand underwater for several minutes without dying, and even getting stuck in the water is quite common.
TLDR; All in all I like the game after playing it for a few days, even though the first 2-3 hours were really rough. The Nethers(monsters) are really challenging and the crafting works great. Some bad pathing problems is common and the lag on server list retrieval is really annoying. I would recommend this to any gamer who likes challenges in a fun and complex game, where death is final.

Pyre might not be the best game by Supergiant to date, but it is very inspired and enjoyable that I can absolutely recommend it.
The gameplay is split between travelling across the vast expanse of the Downside and conducting sacred rites in order to eventually earn the freedom of your party members. The former is very heavy on reading between character dialogue and lore, so be warned, if it's not your thing. The cast is very diverse (in a good way) and full of intriguing and likeable characters in your crew and in rival triumvirates as well. Most of the choices you make in this part result in getting stat bonuses, money, experience, though once in a while you do get pleasant surprises and quite unique interactions.
The rites are kinda like magical basketball. There is a number of characters, and you can only pick 3 for any given match. Each bring something new to the table, their own set of skills, tactics, and synergies. Also, each arena plays a bit differently. At some point the rites do get a bit stale, but then the game introduces titan stars (think idols from Bastion and limiters from Transistor) and feats of glory which add some challenge for bigger rewards. Though, no matter the difficulty, the AI struggles to handle some scenarios and can be exploited because of that.
Now, though the choices in the travelling part are usually quite trivial, the same can't be said about those in trials. Once in a while you'll be taking part in liberation rites, that allow the winner to send one of their characters back home from their otherwise permanent exile. Not only you'll have to face conundrums like "I really like this guy and he deserves to go home, but he is too valuable for my team", but sometimes you'll be tempted to throw matches in order to redeem your rival, at the expense of your own mates. Sometimes you'll get to know your rivals better after the liberation rite you won and regret that you didn't let them win instead. And it's quite sad, because the chance to face them twice in the liberation rites is low, if not zero. I feel It's relevant to mention here, no matter your choices, the ending leaves no questions about the characters unanswered, no matter what you'll get a satisfying and conclusive finale.
Now, the game looks fantastic, as do other games by SGG. The characters boast great visual design, it is perfectly implemented, the world and arenas look superb. The music seemed to me a bit weaker than in Bastion in Transistor (though it's entirely subjective and the game still has memorable tracks), but there are a couple of great ideas that work really well in the game and easily redeem this shortcoming. Remember how you could hum in Transistor, which added more dynamic to music, even if it was a simple gimmick? Well, here they really doubled down of this idea of making music more dynamic. Not only each team has their own themes, they are all layered, and during the match you'll hear a different variation during the dialogue, while controlling the ball, and near the enemy pyre with the ball. There is a theme for liberation rites, and it has its own spin (both in terms of music and vocals) depending on your opponent. Hесk, you get your own personal ending/credits song depending on the outcome of the story. Just how cool is that?!
So yeah, you see it what I'm getting at. It's a great game. Totally worth the asking price, as far as I'm concerned.

Velvet Assassin is a pretty basic “old-school” stealth game, however, the mechanics are solid and the unique setting and well thought out presentation turn it into an overall good game for people that like the genre. If you didn’t like the likes of Thief or the older Splinter Cell titles or need massive freedom in approaching your strategy like in Dishonored, Velvet Assassin will certainly not change your mind.
The title is very linear and the majority of time you spend crouching in shadowy corners, figuring out enemy patrol patterns and move slowly in for the kill, hoping you didn’t miss any observant Nazi in viewing or hearing distance. The enemy AI is not that good, they follow their patterns and investigate suspicious activities. Your hero Violette is not Solid Snake and there not many gadgets or weapons to be used, mainly it’s you, your knife and the shadows. The difficulty level is high and most of the time there is only one right way to get through a scenario. This means a lot of Trial & Error (and repetition due to a checkpoint system), but it makes success rewarding and the controls are precise enough to almost never make it frustrating. The almost comes from some forced action sequences that can get overwhelming too easily especially toward the end of the game.
Velvet Assassin takes itself serious, there is no humor to be found, the world is dark and depressing, but at the same time beautifully presented. This is very fitting for the World War 2 setting that is relatively fresh for this kind of game. The narrative structure interesting, full of dark themes and delivered by solid voice actors, overall I would call the game emotionally engaging and that is one of the things that definitely make it worth playing, even though the gameplay doesn’t offer that much variety. The campaign is relatively short and things wrap up before they can get boring.
I recommend Velvet Assassin to all stealth fans or gamers that are interested in a darker more personal World War 2 setting, definitely worth playing and the short campaign won’t take that much time to finish.
Pros:
- emotionally engaging
- solid stealth mechanics
- good story in a beautiful setting
Cons:
- linear (not much freedom) and short
- frustrating forced shoot-outs

Back when TellTale made actual Point & Click Adventures, rather than Interactive Movies, you had titles like Sam & Max, Puzzle Agent, Back to the Future, and many more.
Back to the Future: The Game displays a perfect balance of what made TellTale great in the first place, and what makes Point & Clicks a great genre in general. Here you have an excellent plot, writing, characters...everything you'd expect from your everyday TellTale game, but paired with some great puzzles that don't seem too hard, but can provide a fair challenge from time to time. In addition, it perfectly adds on to the existing franchise so that it basically serves as a Back to the Future: Part IV.
There's no story altering decisions here, aside from a few minor options that may just change a couple of dialogues. Then again, the vast majority of modern TellTale titles offer an illusion of choice, rather than actually letting the player make some meaningful decisions. With a linear, well crafted game like this one you at least know what you're getting in to, with no misconceptions of what the game actually is.
There's some technical issues to it, mainly with audio skipping a few sounds sometimes and the overally recording quality not being that great. I've also encountered a game breaking bug in Episode 5 where it's possible for you to progress without a needed item, making it impossible for you to go back and get it. Still, it's worth enduring all of that for the sake of everything else the game does right.
Here's to hoping TellTale go back to their roots, or at least figure out how to work an actual Point & Click into their modern titles. Until then, their back catalogue is filled with great games like this one.

This is a completionist game. Military turn based strategy. if you need more story than strategy, probably wont have much fun. You can manage a small squad through a skirmish / map, and control several variables inside of that. Trying different squad combinations (all shotgun crew, or 2 snipes and 2 heavy guners, etc), skill tree / talents, and with those you can get really invested into your team, IF you want to. if you just want to beat the game, it wont take long. If you want to get highest score in each campain, you'll have fun.
typical turn:
setup - chose your team and their equipment, such as drones, medpacks, etc. chose your starting point for each soldier. you can chose all 4 to burst into one door, or 2 teams of 2, however you like.  (if applicable in the game type. some, you start spread out on the map and try to escape).
turn planning - you pick one of your troops. you have a movement distance, so you chose where you want him to go. you chose how: sprinting, walking, etc. you chose WHERE HE LOOKS during that movement. you can get really specific with this, as in, take to steps, look left down that hall, take 2 more steps, look straight, last 2 steps, look right. i havent played another game that allows this, and it's smooth transitions between focal points. try to put your guy's head on a swivel, and he'll probably see nothing, but have him cover a direction, walk with a squadmate that covers the other direction. you chose where you want to toss a grenade, or who you want to use the medpack on an injured comrade. once you got your turn planned, you execute it
execution - you click the go button, and watch your plan unfold, did you have your guy looking the wrong way? did you have 1 soldier toss a flashbang while another walked right past him into the blast radius? did you sneak past the sniper without taking a shot in the face? could you have got that 1 bad guy hiding in the corner without losing a solider if you had come in a different entrance?
If you enjoy trying to get the best possible outcome with different setups of teams, using different styles of play, you'll have fun. If you need to know why the shotgunner carries a shotgun, or if you need backstory on the captian of the barge you're clearing out, you probably wont. It's a Turn-Based military strategy game from a commanders view, and not much more.

Please note: I have never played Darkness 1 nor read the comic books that the series is based on, so this review is going to be written from that perspective.
Darkness 2 is a sequel to Darkness 1 that was only released for Playstation 3 and Xbox 360 and the franchise is in turn based on the comic book of the same title produced by Top Cow Productions.
It tells the story of a mob boss Jackie Estacado and his tormented life living with a dark god / demon known as "The Darkness" which basically grants him immortality but slowly draining his humanity.
The main problem with Darkness 2 is that being a sequel, the player effectively loses alot of backstory about how Jackie came into being. Sure, there is an optional skippable prelude story narration that briefly summarizes his story, but it still feels rather empty because some of the later story elements (Such as Jenny) would have been more emotional and powerful if you have played the first game.
Gameplay itself is fun, and although primarily a FPS, you are given 2 tentacles that lets you eviscerate enemies in the most gruesome manner possible. Because the tentacles are so powerful, i find myself using tentacles most of the time and neglecting to use guns.
It also makes use of a light and dark mechanic where your character will be more powerful when in darkness, and the tentacles will not be available when there is light.
So the general gameplay goes like this:
1) Use guns to shoot out any light source
2) Use tentacles to eviscerate and kill
3) Repeat.
Graphics has a unique graphic novel look similar to a toned down Borderlands look and while not too bad, has a very jagged and rough look and bad frame rates even when put on the highest settings on a decent above recommendation computer. I suppose its a result of being a direct console port.
While the story is entertaining, it is rather short at about 7 hours. There also isn't much actual gameplay, and close to 70% of the time, you are either looking at cutscenes or scripted events.
Just a little observation i've noticed.
I also find it strange that every enemy would be so gung-ho to charge at you even after seeing what you've done.
Example: If you were to see your friend getting ripped apart at the spinal cord by a guy with 2 evil looking dark tentacles, would you still try to attack him? I know i certainly wouldn't lol!! I know games aren't meant to be realistic, but still....
There is also a multiplayer mode available. Unlike other similar games which offers this, somehow Darkness 2 multiplayer mode feels absolutely tacked on and unnecessary and is quite possibly the worst multiplayer mode ever made. There is absolutely no story, no thought gone into it and absolutely no entertainment to be gotten from it.
I've tried the multiplayer campaign with 4 friends and none of us knew what the heck we had to do except to just shoot everything that is not us. I would've rate the multiplayer mode 2/10 if it were a standalone product. Absolutely disgraceful addition and they should've just dropped it to make a better single player experience.
In closing, it is a pity that Darkness 1 was never released on the PC, as im sure the whole game series would've felt much better when played back to back.
Overall Rating: 7.0 / 10

Apotheon is one of the best side-scrolling games I have ever played. The gameplay is solid, including both combat and puzzles; the artwork is beautiful; and the story is a fantastic take on the mysterious Dark Age of ancient Greece. As a Classicist myself I found this game pleasantly familiar and the depictions of various Gods and Heroes are incredibly true to the mythology, something very rare in games based in the ancient periods. Furthermore, players can learn more about the mythology they are immersing themselves in by reading little passages from ancient texts located around the areas.
I cannot recommend this game enough. I really enjoyed my time playing it, and truly felt by the end that I had achieved Apotheosis.
And who doesn't want to be a capricious ancient Greek God?

Despite the short length of the single player campain - which took me about 7 hours to complete - The Darkness II was fantastic.  When you first start the game, you are given the option to watch a prologue which does a great job covering all the important events that transpired during the first Darkness game, so you don't have to worry about missing out on storyline if you have not played it. The storyline was very well written, the voice acting was top notch, the graphics were solid, and the game had a surprisingly great soundtrack. The protagonist, Jackie, is very fluid to control and the AI are very well developed. You gain experience as you progress through the game which can then be allocated to 4 different skill trees, making it easy to adapt the game to your play style. Just a heads up, The Darkness II makes use of it's mature rating. There is enough swearing, violence and sexual themes to instantly desensitize the player for life (you have to eat people's hearts to regain your health). That being said, all these themes were used properly and really draw you in to the atomosphere of the game - they were not used excessively to the point where it got annoying.. *ahem* Dead Island, *ahem* Hitman: Absolution.
Bottom line: If you are looking for a fun First Person Shooter and enjoy a dark, gritty, well-written storyline The Darkness II will not disappoint

Doom was another first person shooter that played an important role in the gaming community. Released just a year after Wolfenstein 3D, this game has similar traits except with a sense of movement on the camera, more 3-D depth on the levels, and added shadows. The plot is about a last surviving space marine who must escape from a marine base on the planet Mars that is being over run by demons and mutated marines. There are various weapons and items to collect in order to aid you on your survival. There's even an option to heighten the difficulty of the game for those who want more of a challenge. Two years after this game was released in 1993, an estimated 20 million copies have been sold, and various "Doom" clones and that is when the first person shooter genre officially became a thing in the gaming industry. Doom would become a very well known title that even non-gamers would immidiately know what it is without playing it. The success lead to a few sequals and updated versions of the game such as the "Ultimate" edition which is basically the same game only with an additional episode to it. So if you liked the Wolfenstein game, this is a must play game.

This is an odd one, it is actually on of the best and most promising games I have played in a while and I am really enjoying it. However there are HUGE issies that need to be addressed, They don't even have dedicated servers which is a no no in 2017 I MEAN COME ON, In pretty much every online game YOU NEED DEDICATED SERVERS never mind In one where half a second is the difference between either you or your opponent dying. The feats are completley unbalenced, they basically give players who are already doing quite well insane abilities that you can do very little about. Another thing is well... honour, it is literally the name of the game but people just love to screw you over, there is no incentive to play honourably when you can win so easy not doing so. Instead of just going all keyboard warrior on this I actually have a solution to this problem, we have feats which are a good idea but need to be unlocked in a completley different way to make them more fair, and we need to introduce an incentive to not play like Hitler, how about if you don't play annoyingly you get honour points (or something to similar effect) that you spend to use an active ability or to start the effects of a passive one. You would also lose honour points for being annoying (Like constantly running away from fights etc.). If you go into a negative amount of these honour points then you should get debuffs like no revenge mode. Also you could take people who regularly have low honour in games and pit them against others like them through matchmaking (or have them preferred or somthing). There should not just be good or bad things but also neutral things, things that arn't going to win you every battle in every situation but definitely isnt fighting properly (like arial attacks or throws off a cliff) in my opinion those kind of things don't annoy me too much because if some noob is able to throw you off a cliff constantly just practice countering guard breaks (which are pretty difficult to counter currently but they are fixing that for the next update), try not to go near ledges if you can and be careful when you are near one. Now we are onto balance, honestly, it's not too bad in my opinion as far as classes go (again the valkerie is getting buffed next update) they all have moves and combos that can be annoying but they do need skill to pull off and some classes are just good counters to others. For example I hear people say that orochi is powerful but when you ask them to play as them next game and they do they can be pretty poor as one. As gear goes, I again don't think that can affect a game that much, sure maybe like every dozen games or so they are able to get a kill they wouldn't have been able to get otherwise but good gear does not make up for bad skill (I personally have beaten heroes with 3 reputation and over 100 gear score with a 0 reputation 12 gear score quite easily, it just cannot make up for doing badly in a match). Also even when you have great gear it still has tradeoffs that can really cripple someone (eg. someone might have insane attack but no damn defence, so all you gotta do is block their attacks and just squeeze in the odd quick attack or two to take them out). However don't feel like this is a crap game, quite the opposite actually I gave it a thumbs up. There are really interseting mechanics at work here and is simple at first but when you add in: guard breaks, throws, combos, unblockable attacks and so on that it becomes a really intense and techinal combat game with the satisfaction of mowing down thousands of grunts in dominion. IT REALLY IS A GOOD GAME, or at least if you don't agree, one that has huge potential to become one, IF UBISOFT DON'T BALLS IT UP, SERIOUSLY IT'S LIKE YOUR TRYING TO. It's still frustrating at times and that's not including the connection issues from peer to peer connections and so on. Honeslty though, even though I reccomend it, wait, even just for a bit as it seems like Ubisoft don't want to put much effort into this game (legacy is spelt legavy in the valkerie's preorder green skin.). Wait for some patches to come out and then have another look, again this game has an insane boat-load of potential, just sitting there, that once properly harnessed can turn this into an absolute beauty of a game and will definitely make Ubisoft some serious cash. But for now wait, and once these kind of things are implemented DEFINITELY CHECK OUT THIS GAME, even with all this I still quite enjoy this game even though it is far from perfect and that's why it get's a thumbs up from me. Also if you look at the negative reviews they all basically say it's a great game that's ruined by peer to peer connection, seriously just having dedicated servers gets rid of like 90% if the bad reviews. Anyway that's my opinion, don't get too butthurt if it doesn't agree with yours that well, infact actually reply to this and I will probably enjoy discussing it with you.

So, in the '40s there was this little scuffle called World War II.
And during this time, a woman named Violette Szabo joined the British Army.
She married a French soldier, worked a number of military positions, found out she was a bit pregnant and took some time off to give birth to her child, then went right back into duty.
A few months after her little girl was born, her husband was killed in action.
And that just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥her off.
Seeking some Nazi-revenge, she accepted a field position, and went into Spec Ops.
The only thing she ever screwed up in training was a parachute landing. Once. Pulled it off just fine after she recovered from the sprained ankle.
Her only weakness was that damn ankle.
She had a talent for dead-aim with a gun, sabotage, and undetected assassination.
Basically she was a stone-cold Nazi-stopping machine, and one HELL of a spy.
While heading to a mission, she got stopped by an unexpected road checkpoint, at which point an apparent firefight broke out. Her comrade got away, but she sprained the ankle again, and was captured after running out of bullets.
She was taken prisoner, and almost escaped from the camp, before being moved. Eventually her true identity was discovered, leading to her interrogation, and tragic execution.
This game is inspired by her.
And I must assert INSPIRED BY, since it is not a telling of the Story of Violette Szabo, but a character based on her.
A strong, intelligent, skilled woman working as an active spy, infiltrating Nazi territory and getting some hardcore Nazi-vengeance.
If you like badass female protagonists, just go ahead and get this game.
It should be noted that there are some questionable choices, like the highly sexualised, skimpy gown she wears in "Morphine Mode" and some pre-rendered pinup-style loading-screen images.
And look, I'll forgive the pinup renders in general - it fits with the World War II theme... though it must be said that sexualising a hospitalised woman is incredibly problematic... but the Morphine Mode change felt mostly unnecessary.
Get past that, though, and you're sneaking about in a solid WWII Stealth game, taking down Nazis from the shadows.
You do not get the ammo to shoot your way through, so you will rely on stealth executions. You have a very small health allowance, too, adding to the "no really, stealth is the way to go" factor.
This is NOT a "shoot 'em all" WWII Nazi-killing game.
Go play Wolfenstein or something, if that's what you're after.
One of its shortcomings is the AI. Completely incapable, apparently, of thinking "hey, maybe that spy we were just chasing is on the other side of the door we just saw her run through!"
They have a very short memory, and attention-span.
Certainly, the AI is the weakest part of the game, and breaks the immersion, but as the detection mechanics are pretty unforgiving, you'll probably be grateful that all it takes for them to forget about you is to hide behind a door, and watch through the keyhole as they go back to their post.
One particularly interesting element was its presentation of the Nazi soldiers. Often dehumanised, faceless, evil goons, here you get to see what a spy would have encountered - casual chatter: Feeling sorry for the drunk guy (you just killed) for his apparent alcoholism after the things he'd seen during the war. General complaining about when the replacement next shift will arrive. Arguments over who stole someone's chocolate.
It's an unusual thing to see Nazi soldiers humanised, and it really does add a lot to the atmosphere - they're normal human beings; when unaware of observation, they will behave as such. It's a simple thing, but it really adds to the feeling of being a spy; seeing things you wouldn't normally see, like your enemy being so normal - so casual.
Perfect? No.
Good? Totally.
Recommended? Yes.

In theory this game is right up my street - resource management and a post-apocalyptic setting. But I didn't really get into it or find it very challenging. The trailers made me think there'd be a lot more psychology and personality involved, but I didn't experience this in gameplay.
The people in your shelter are pretty much interchangeable collections of statistics, with no personality or relationships. When not specifically assigned something to do, or satisfying an urgent need, they just stand around. The only time my residents experienced significant trauma is when I forgot to pause the game just after an attack on my shelter - they'd stopped looking after their own basic needs as a result of the attack, and when I returned some had died, presumably of starvation. Still, it didn't take more than five or ten minutes of matching statistics to actions to return the shelter to normal.
This is a fairly solid game, though the UI could use some work - being able to check characters' strength levels and weapons' strength requirements during equipping would be extra handy. I motored through it happily enough. With a bit more care and attention to the personalities of your residents, it could be much better though - what if staying cooped up underground got your residents so stressed that you need to rotate them on trips out of the bunker rather than always sending your strongest people? Imagine if people actually read books for fun, drank coffee because they were trying to stay awake to satisfy your orders, or turned on the lights because they were afraid of the dark? What if you could tell them to live off meat from the freezer before turning to tinned rations? What if some were vegetarian? If somebody snored so badly that nobody would share a bunk bed with them? There are lots of simple things that could be introduced which would cause the player to start caring about these characters and be more invested in keeping them alive.

(Originally written 1/16/2011):
Telltale, known for their brilliant graphical adventures in various franchises such as Homestar Runner, the popular but very weird cartoon website; Sam and Max, the dog-and-bunny detective comic and TV series; and (best of all in my opinion, though my subject this time may be a close second) Monkey Island, the classic pirate-themed graphical adventure series, now turn their attention to the classic movie series, Back to the Future.
Purporting to be a sequel to the third movie, this five-part journey chronicles Marty McFly’s adventures in time six months after his friend, brilliant scientist Doctor Emmett Brown, disappeared to an unknown period. In the first part, it turns out that Doc’s caught up in some big trouble back in 1931, being falsely accused of burning down a mob-protected speakeasy and thereafter being gunned down for it. It’s up to Marty to make contact with Doc’s teenaged 1931 self and enlist his help without revealing himself or his mission, or a deadly temporal paradox may occur…
Or at least that’s what the game would have you believe. No such thing is in danger of happening; in the grand traditions of adventure games past and present, no death is possible, only a delay in  getting to your objective. But that shouldn’t stop the player from being thrilled at the climax, which I won’t spoil here, or from being kept on pins and needles waiting for the next episode, due in February.
Controls are pretty simple; just click on an item to examine it or take it if it’s not nailed down, or on a person to initiate dialog. There’s a quite generous four-tier hint system for many of the puzzles you may find along your journey, so you never have to feel stuck.
Several lines from the series are re-enacted here, performed with admirable talent by A.J. Locascio as Marty McFly. Returning to his timeless role as Doc Brown is Christopher Lloyd himself, bringing forward a particularly memorable line in a flashback to the first movie (you’ll know it when you hear it).
The entire series (consisting of five episodes on a rather slow release schedule) is $24.99 on the digital distribution platform Steam. There will most likely be a retail package containing the series, released after the final episode is. But don’t wait to buy; this is a great series, and though you’ll have to wait (as I am) for the next installment, you won’t regret your purchase. I give this five out of five stars!

Great concept, okay execution, some gameplay issues.
The bad:
Inventory management is a nightmare. You literally have to scroll through every single item in your inventory to access the items stored at the bottom. Takes forever to do what should be just a couple clicks. Search bar maybe? Scroll bar? Nope.
The UI has some serious issues. Selecting a character is more challenging than it should be and automatising tasks is seriously limited making micromanagement a clickfest nightmare. This is not, nor should it be, the main focus of the game.
Gets repetitive quick. There are only like 4 or 5 different ways an encounter can go but making you go through the motions over and over is mindnumbing.
♥♥♥♥♥♥ missions. Some missions just stop halfway through. No follow up. This is after expending considerable time and resources and then it just abruptly ends mid conversation. Sometimes it feels like they added missions as an afterthrought but never took the effort necessary to fill it out.
The good:
The atmosphere of this game is amazing. It's desperate and brutal. You can harvest the corpses of your dead family for food. They really captured the feeling of desperation. The way your character rocks back and forth as he squats on a toilet to relieve himself... I mean, well done. The detail. Amazing.
It's hard in a good way. They really hit that balance between doable and ♥♥♥♥ing impossible. Especially for the first few hours of gameplay. Beyond that, it gets a little boring.
All it together, it's a great little game worth a few hours of enjoyment. It doesn't have much longevity but I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys the genre. Good work!

This game is fantastic.
I'm not much of a platform gamer, but I grew up loving the crazy twisted world of the earthworm jim games, and many good games in the early eras of gaming were fairly platform-ish... but basically it's not been a focus for me.
That said, this game really brought me back and drove home what a great experience the medium can provide.
It's made by a team composed largely of the people behind the legendary game "Beyond Good and Evil" - if that's not enough to make you moist, you havent played that game, or you have no soul.
It's dripping with character, and the art is wonderful and consistent, portraying a bizzare, slightly twisted but incredibly bright and joyful world, even in the darkest places. The music is phenomenal, with a wide variety of excellent tracks, including some that are reditions of songs you may be familiar with.
What really got me was the well defined worlds and the sheer variety of gameplay mechanics. It seemed at times like every level was introducing a new mechanic, that may or may not be used in further levels - the path of the game is largely non-linear, with difficulty from level to level having little to do with its place in "order".
It's most definately not a difficult game, it's a very easy to approach platformer, and you'll quickly learn the ins and outs of what they expect from you. Checkpoints are generally numerous, though the game does spice things up as you progress, there's even levels that have no checkpoints whatsoever and are just a long string of potential deaths - this initially was a source of frustration, but after completing my first level like this I couldnt deny that the sense of satisfaction gained by beating the whole thing flawlessly was well worth it, and I'm glad they had it.
It's quite hard to really convey what's really best about this game, and that's the experience of playing it.
It's just... fun!
If there's a demo out, I'd reccomend giving it a go and seeing what you think. I cant imagine you not finding it worth your time and money though.
For long term enjoyment, they have 2 daily and 2 weekly challenges, that are varied in type and setting. While I dont particularily like all of the challenges, they're mostly very enjoyable - the distance based ones, where you're falling down an infinate pit, running up an infinately falling tower, or running across a seemingly infinate level are my favourites, and you'll find yourself rated based on where you stand vs everyone else playing the challenges. You can see the ghost players of other people who have played the challenge who are close to your score, see the markers where they bite it, and generally it just feels solid...
Oh yeah, and this game seems to include all the levels from the previous game, Rayman Origins, within the game, so you get 2 games for 1!
As for negatives... hmmm... well there's one level left that I havent finished that's hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥ though I dont think that counts...
Oh I've got one - there's a "creature" system, where you collect creatures occasionally when you beat a level, and they all go into a special room and once a day give out lums (the currency - which are these delightful little smiling bug things)  - and the system seems... pointless... you only get the monsters by beating levels, so you've basically beaten the game when you get them all, and the amount of lums they give is negligible compared to even just doing a normal level or challenge.
Also the large number of alternate skins for barabara, the female character, are... a bit weird if not downright creepy or offensive at times. Barabara is the character I played as most due to the incredible character design, she's just brimming with a joyful michevious character that really fits the game, and she swings a mean axe... and rayman's kind of silly. But every world you enter has 2 alternate skins for barbara - the first one's pretty tame, but from then on it gets... odd.... There's barabara's that are sexualized (pronounced curves and cleavage) in appearance, and weirder still, when you die in this game you expand and then pop like a baloon - barbara's regular death is fairly normal... but there's 2 skins for her where you get a weirdass panty shot when she dies... it's... weird, man.
But whatever, lets just blame it on them being french canadian. The game is absolutely phenomenal and any negatives I've encoutered, which are few, are greatly balanced out by the awesome.
So yeah, try demo, get game, enjoy.

Twelve years on, and with a popular mod restoring dummied-out content, KOTOR 2 is a franchise classic. Perhaps one of the best Star Wars stories ever written, its critique of the saga still stands, even if it seems a little caustic at times. Star Wars needs an emotional or spiritual core to be anything more than a vanilla science fantasy template, and its best iterations such as The Empire Strikes Back and, indeed, KOTOR 2 are proof of it.
The relative darkness of this game's story is often held up at its strongest point. However, this tone of dread is only effective because it enables the emotional stakes of the tale to be greater than ever before. As you'll soon come to know in playing it, the Galactic Republic that rules the universe stands at the crossroads, and you are intimately connected with its deepest wounds. Decline is an inevitable historical and personal force, and this game will test you on how you deal in those moments closest to death, and how you will cross the threshold at its climax. An emotional journey throughout, I would heartily recommend The Sith Lords to anyone willing to deal with themes of vulnerability, intimacy and betrayal against the backdrop of galactic downfall.

There are noticeable improvements in some areas, and lots of minor gripes I had with Origins have been addressed in Legends. There are some  new creative level design ideas and elements that really helped set this game apart.
This game is every bit as charming and fun as its predecessor. Both Rayman Origins and Legends make up some of the most creative, fun, and charming 2D platforming you'll ever get to experience. The Darkness released early February 2012 and was a game that didn’t receive much advertising or player generated hype. The Darkness 2 follows the story Jackie Estacado a mob boss who inherits a peculiar ability which is wielding the Darkness. The game uses cell shading similar to borderlands which compliments the game world well. The gameplay is quite original and lets you “quad-wield” which basically means you can wield a gun in each hand while also controlling your two darkness demon arms. The controls feel a bit fiddly when using a mouse and keyboard, if you own a controller I would recommend using that instead. This game has some of the most gruesome kills I have ever seen in a game. Using your demonic arms you can rip your enemies in half, slice of their head or even pull out an enemy’s spine from his butt the list goes on. The single player campaign took me about 6 hours on my first play through and left me wanting more, not because the game was bad but because it was so darn good. There is also a co-op campaign which was fun to play with friends but got boring very quickly. In summary, I really enjoyed this game and its unique gameplay but found it was bit to short.

I do not have to review this game to tell you it is a must own for all Mil-Sim fanatics! I bought Arma 2 eight or nine years ago by accident, at a Best Buy, and I will never forget being introduced to the Arma world through Zargabad Life (Most Arma 3 players don't even know about that). Zargabad Life was before DayZ mod, and before all of the little kids that came with it.  Zargabad Life and even the other gamemode servers had close-knit communities driving them. I loved the community the most then, and I still love it as it has evolved to what it is now. Despite Zargabad Life being a buggy mission file, it showed the game's massive potential. There was no other game out at the time like this one, especially with a modded multiplayer experience like this one.
I must have more than a couple thousand undocumented hours in Arma 2 and it's DLC. I own the complete Arma 2 collection on physical disc, and migrated over to Steam when Gamespy shutdown. I am sad to see the desmise of Arma 2 finally. However, Arma 3 is doing it's due dilligence in creating an even greater experience. So much has been added since Arma 2, and so much has changed!
This game feels like more than a game! I bought Arma 3 the first day I saw it in Alpha, and to watch it mature to what it is now was phenomenal! When they launched the Alpha it was great and all, but this completed game is so much better! All of the gamemodes are fun, the maps are beautiful, the game engine is a bit polished off, and best of all they finally managed to make this game 64-bit! Arma 2 was a very CPU intensive game back in the day, and even as PC builds got better, users would find playing that game difficult. Arma 3 has had to jump over similar resource hurdles back when it was in early Alpha, but now that they patched it to be a 64-bit game, I do not notice hardly any performance hits on my 7700k/1070. I used to play on a Cross-fired ATI 7950 rig with an AMD 8350 processor. While both games played well, I found Intel/Nvidia to be the better choice for this game. The game as I said still is quite a resource intensive game, even with its upgrades. Afterall it is a simulator, and a lot of animations, and calculations as well for bullets/explosions are constantly running in real-time.
With everything I have said, I hope not to dissuade anyone from purchasing this game. It really is a gem after you get over its rough edges. If you want an end all military simulator, this is it! Fly a heli, drive a tank, or run and gun as ground infantry. Hell, this game even has submarines, and boats! In this game you can literally have battles you could only dream of before while playing linear games like Battlefield. Which brings up another point! The replayability of this game is endless! The editor has gotten easier to use since Arma 2, and the amount of content you can play with is massiive, espeicallly if you have all the DLC. This game is like a big military sandbox. The steam workshop is where this game shines! You can mod this game to your heart's desire, and never get bored. I had a mission where I was in an AI controlled humvee shooting out the back at Velociraptors, and I thought that was one of the coolest things I have done in Arma to date. All of the cotent used to do that was from other users. Arma is what you make it!
10/10 Totally would buy again!

The Rake is a pretty underrated game in my opinion. You play as Gordon Davis, a man that wants to hunt the Rake. You start in an RV, which serves as your base camp. The open world is pretty big for the kind of game it is. Don't expect to be as big as GTA San Andreas, but try to imagine it taking about 4-5 minutes sprinting to reach the edge of the map.
Pros -
-Decent graphics, or at least pretty good for the Unity engine.
-A big map to explore, including abandoned buildings, a waterfall cave, a swamp, etc.
-A small selection of weapons, but it doesn't feel like there SHOULD be more, so its ok. The weapons include a rifle, a sniper rifle, and bear traps.
Cons -
-The developer has abandoned the game and is not updating it anymore. This means no more content for people who want more out of the game.
-Grammactical errors. This is a personal thing, I'm just a grammer-nazi.
-Difficult to set up multiplayer. You need to use other sites such as Himachi to play with friends.
In all, I'd say Rake is a worthy item in my library (Don't ask how I have so much time on record, I left the game running on accident for about 4-5 hours).

Welp i have ALOT to say about this version of ultimate doom, i bout it last year and was quickly disappointed because it would not work on my pc although i found a work around to that problem with took a bit but i still did it so for anyone that has had trouble with making this version work i will help. (Works on Windows 8.1 and Windows 10(?) as far as i know.)
!DISCLAIMER! i am not to blame if you mess up your game all i am posting is what i did to fix it
1.Install Doom & Doom II.
2.Right click on doom and choose "Properties" go into the "Local File" tab and go to "Browse Local Files".
3.Go into the folder called "Base".
4.Right click doom(.exe) and go into "Properties" and go into the "Compatibility" tab.
5.Change the Compatibility Mode to Windows 95 (dunno why but it works).
6.Then go to "Ultimate(.CONF)" and open it with Notepad.
7.Change "Fullscreen=True" to "Fullscreen=False".
8.Change "Fulldouble=True" to "Fulldouble=False".
9.Change "Waitonerror=True" to "Waitonerror=False".
10.Save the file and go to "Ultimatem(.CONF)".
11.Do the same as you did with "Ultimate(.CONF)".
12.Download ZDoom and run Ultimate Doom.
13.Have fun playing one of the godfathers of the fps genre!

SOMA far exceeded my expectations, and is one of the best games I've played in years. While it does contain horror elements, I would classify SOMA more as a science fiction story game (in a creepy setting) than a horror game. There are no jump scares here, or really much that I would classify as frightening. More of a creepy vibe.
The writing in SOMA is fantastic. Gameplay is relatively linear but you don't mind because the story keeps you engaged throughout. Just when you think you know what's going on, you learn more about the truth of the situation and new questions unfold. By the end you've confronted some very philosophical themes about human nature and AI. I can't say more without giving away spoilers, but I will say that several days later my kids and I are still talking about the story.
Get this game especially if you enjoy thought-provoking sci-fi games. The end is very satisfying!

When I purchased this game on the steam summer sale, my expectations were not high, I was in the mood for a good horror game & knowing the acclaim Frictional's previous games had received, I knew this would be a safe choice compared to most other horror games on the market, also it seemed far more interesting & better than generic "jumpscare" horror such as FNAF. I had read that some did not think this game was scary, and it gave me some concerns I would be disappointed, I purchased it anyway. Within the first couple of hours of the game, I realized that I was worried for nothing, this game was TERRIFYING, it is not scary in the same way people would consider FNAF scary, it heavily relies on the general atmosphere of PATHOS-II(The game's main setting) & themes to not only scare you, but to also make you think. Soma was both a terrifying and wonderful gaming experience. It was the most I had enjoyed horror in many years. SOMA is not only an amazing achievement in the horror genre, but also an achievement in gaming as well. Frictional Games should be appluaded for creating this masterpiece! I honestly thought this game was superior to Naughty Dog's The Last of Us, it was that good. There is not much else to be said other than SOMA is one of the greatest games ever made, SOMA was the most I enjoyed gaming in a VERY long time, I strongly suggest you buy this game if you are even slightly interested, you won't be disappointed.

I was happy to grab this up for cheap, I think less than 50 cents. When I loaded it up(after having to grab some physx legacy drivers) I was pumped because it looked good. It's not an ugly game. I started to play. Felt alright the first level. I was thinking that the story was pretty compelling because of quality character models, voice acting, and all that. But the second level reallllllly showed me why this game is so cheap. It's truly broken. I mean, the controls are kinda clunky, but they were tolerable. The problems though that exist are so awful that I don't think I can play this game ever again. The main thing that made me realize I probably don't have the patience to play this game is an enemy shooting through a concrete wall. No, I am not wrong about it. Clearly they can shoot through walls. Also, they can't walk through about 30 percent of the doors in the game(if not 100 percent IDK there is some "special" doors that simply don't open like others but give you a quarter second load time even though you can peek through them... trust me, it's stupid.) Their whole stealth kill mechanic is craaappy. I don't feel like explaining the details of it so just take my word, it's pretty awful. Now, I don't think this game was meant to be bad, but I feel like someone made the devs rush this out the door, or they were just wasted time on other things. Cause the game looks great. There is lots of well done animations to it and it has actually really good textures, models, sounds, and overall content in that nature. It just feels like the gameplay mechanics were just unfinished.
What it comes down to though is the price. I mean, I was reallly compelled by the female character. Her model is really awesome, and her voice actor is pretty good. If you have the patience to sneak everyone with a stealth kill using their buggy mechanics to progress through what I am assuming is a pretty decent story... then get it. I mean, if you liked playing MGS games on extreme difficulty, then you might be OK with this, not because it's totally intended to be played that way, but because you kind of have to due to the incomplete mechanics.
This is a seriously hard recommend for me, even on sale, even at it's price, but I have to because there is some love put into this game. Art direction and all the artists in general were really great(not so much over all level design tho). It's the programmers who failed, or the publishers or whoever made this game go unfinished.

, is a linear five-part point-and-click adventure game developed and published by TellTale games and takes place some time after the events of the third film in the franchise.
The player, controlling Marty McFly, progresses through the game in the style of a typical point-and-click game, with the highlights of the game being, among other things, an immersive plot and universe, and generally well-written characters. The game includes Christopher Lloyd reprising his role as Doc Brown, and A.J. Locascio doing an excellent job at playing Marty in the absence of Michael J. Fox, who appears as a cameo in the last episode. The game in general is an excellent addition to the franchise as a whole, and greatly adds on to the existing material and story of the franchise's previous film entries.
If I had to say anything negative about it, I'd start by citing the stark linearity of the game's progression, which is somewhat eased by the quality of the plot and its enjoyable nature regardless. I'd also cite the game's soundtrack, which, while fantastically written to mimic that of the original film(s), becomes overtly repetitious and at times annoying during longer scenes of player action. Though neither of those things would warrant dislike for the title.
In all, Back to the Future: The Game, is a great point-and-click adventure that will enjoy new and old fans of the franchise. Packed with slick references to the original films, a decisive and enjoyable plot, and fantastic voice acting by Lloyd and Locascio, I strongly recommend that you pick up this title.

If there are two things from my childhood that I can truly profess my love for, it would probably be the Back to the Future movies and the genre of point-and-click adventure games, like the Monkey Island series. Maybe my parents. But, on the other hand, they never taught me the importance of ensuring the fidelity of the time stream, nor the capacity of root beer to serve as ghost repellent in a pinch, so I guess I'd put them at number three. In what appears to be Telltale Games latest effort to lure in the coveted "me and possibly only me" demographic, they managed to somehow release a game that combined both of my childhood loves with Back to the Future: The Game. Like a lot of Telltale Game's games, Back to the Future: The Game is an episodic adventure, with each episode telling a mostly self contained adventure about how Marty and Doc messed up something in the past that they now need to fix. Regardless of how bad Marty and Doc are with time travel (really, really bad), the game itself is surprisingly good, and comes with a full recommendation for anyone who has ever shouted out "1.21 JIGOWATTS" in science class, before being sent to the principal's office for making out of date references.
The story takes place sixth months after the events of the third movie, and initially follows the standard Back to the Future plot of saving people in different time periods from whichever Tannen happens to be prowling the area. This time around, Doc Brown manages to get himself stuck in the 1930s, and Marty must go to his rescue. Doc had been investigating what he refers to as a historical mystery, and finds himself first accused of arson and imprisoned (bad) and then eventually murdered at the hands of an angry mob (extremely bad) Obviously the lesson here is "don't go visiting Hill Valley in the 1920's" especially when Doc's reason for doing so is figuring out an unsolved mystery. While interfering with a mystery from 60 years ago seems like it might have some ramifications throughout history and should go against the whole "not ruining the fidelity of the time steam" spiel they're always going on about, I'm assuming Doc Brown stopped caring about the time space continuum about the time he impregnated a woman from before the McKinley administration. As Marty McFly, you must save Doc Brown from the trouble he's gotten himself into, and presumably talk him out from going back in time to seduce some cavewoman hookers.
Now, call me a Back to the Future fanatic and make fun of me all you want for my desire to name my first kid Marty and my second kid Flux Capacitor, but I actually like the story of Back to the Future: The Game for the most part. It is genuinely amusing, and each episode manages to actually build off of the plot from the films, instead of just blowing the dust off of them, rolling them out, and going "eh, they won't notice." Telltale Games has actually done a nice job making this game feel like an extension of the movies and fans of the films will get that warm fuzzy feeling that comes from visiting an old friend or pretend movie characters from favorite films, depending on how lonely your childhood was. Creativity is hard, so too often, games meant to serve as an extension for an already existing piece of fiction pretty much just sit back and do a museum tour of everything that already happened. Here, the plot serves mostly as a tour guide for past exploits, loudly pointing and going "REMEMBER THAT? WASN'T THAT FUNNY?" and referencing the original work so frequently that you can only assume that the writers just wrote down the word "NOSTALGIA" in big capital letters before heading off for lunch. This is why it was so shocking to me when the story and script in Back to the Future: The Game was actually pretty good. It captures the feel of the series without aping it, and manages to build off of previously established characters without losing what made them unique. The writing is good, the characters are endearing, and there is enough humor to keep you smiling the entire time through.
Of course, there are puzzles here as well. Back to the Future: The Game is a point and click adventure sort of game with a decent variety of puzzles to get you through to the end. Gameplay is typically divided up into a series of small to medium size areas with one or two problems to solve and a handful of different things to pick up and use. Maybe you'll need to fine where Doc is in time exactly, or discover how to get alcohol, or how to get a notebook away from Biff. Goals are always clearly defined, and while the solution may not immediately be obvious, the game also does a good job making sure the solutions aren't too random or rely only on guesswork. Things might be a bit too easy overall, and it woud've been nice if there were a couple more difficult puzzles here. Most of the time, just by walking around or talking to people it becomes fairly obvious what you need to do to proceed. There are a couple good puzzles here, and overall the puzzles are solid enough to compliment to story and writing for a nice, cohesive package.
If I had any complaints, other than the relative lack of difficulty of the puzzles, it was just that this episode feels a bit short. It feels like you're just getting started and then the game kicks you out to the big TO BE CONTINUED text and a promsie that the next episode will be just as good. Luckily, this comes as a five episode package deal, but just because the first episode was good it doesn't necessarily mean the following ones will have the same magic. Still, overall this is definitely a promising start to the series with enough puzzles and entertaining writing to make you look forward to the next installment. This is just a good adventure game, one that should appeal to even people that aren't fans of the series, and comes with a definite recommendation for fans of the genre. It might be a bit basic compared to some other similar titles, but it is still very entertaining. Hill Valley is certainly worth checking out, even if Doc Brown seems to be trying his hardest to constantly mess everything up.

In the veins of Hitman (and I mean close enough that 47 would feel uncomfortable) lies this hidden little game. To my knowledge the company that made this shortly closed after the game's release, which is a shame because they could've patched this to be a great game or have worked on a sequel which wouldn't contain the same problems this faces.
Let's start with the obvious, shall we? The stealth mechanics in this game are a massive pain in the backside offering large amounts of frustration and jankyness. Guards that have the inexplicable ability to see around corners, their seemingly amazing eyesight from several hundred metres armed with sub-machine guns that act more like sniper rifles and the fact your silenced pistol will be completely useless the majority of the time add to a VERY perplexingly bad disguise system (Worse than the Hitman: Absolution one) makes this incredibly annoying.
The level design is often vague and poorly chosen too. Very few times will you fairly have a chance to avoid the Nazis patrolling around and instead have to pick several of them off one by one until the majority have been thrown off a cliff with a knife lodged somewhere in their neck. This leads to ENDLESS amounts of restarts because somehow you were spotted around a corner lodged in a bush and naturally, you can't survive more than a handfull of bullets. Even when things do go your way, checkpoints are few and far between and often after SEVERAL incredibly difficult scenarios in which you'll be beggining for a break.
The amount of content itself is nice though, you have a decent amount of levels often taking more than 20 minutes to complete in a good run, accompanied by collectibles (if that's your thing). The morphine feature is incredibly useful too. It stops time (removing your clothes too?) and allows you to have a clear escape from the people about to turn you into a bullet-ridden english woman.
All in all, I honestly wouldn't recommend this to anyone who's not INTENSELY desperate for a stealth game when the Hitman Franchise, Splinter Cell (minus Conviction and Double Agent) and Alien Isolation exist. Go elsewhere for your sneaky stabby fix.

Ok, so I was expecting a regular FPS.

Story: (Trying not to make spoilers)
The game is based on a comic series called, yep, you guessed it, The Darkness.
You play as Jackie Estacado, a mafia boss that possess the forces of darkness.
Jackie tries to keep his darkness at bay, but after a rival mafia tries to kill you, you have no option but to start a war and unleash the darkness within you upon your enemies.
But, when you unleash the darkness, you also cut a deal with it, and there's a price to pay at the end...
Graphics:
The game graphics reminded me Borderlands but more realistic, and i like it :) kinda gives you the feel of a comics (which it is based on a comic series)
Gameplay:
The game is FPS and RPG of some sort, where you gain XP from kills and level your skills, but apart from the guns and black magic you also have 2 tenticals that devours, kill, cutting off heads and ripping the limbs of people (Tons of blood and gore)
When you are not cutting and killing, you also play as your little lackey, which is more stealthy than just killing everybody.
Also, there are some levels that are purely for the story, they are short but very fun and delivers the awesome story to you, I loved those parts!
Conclusion:
This game kinda surprised me, I loved the story, the cut-scenes are great, the gameplay is fun, the graphics are very nice and feel you get is very good.
and even though it's short (took me about 6 hours to finish the game on Hard, but you can play it and make different decisions), it's really good!
Play it!

ARMA is truly what you make of it. Want to roleplay as a night-time specop raiding team? Or join a Navy SEAL underwater battle? Or maybe you like flying CAS for a tank battalion. Don't like anything like that? Play cops and robbers with the ARMA Life servers. ARMA gives you all the tools you need to craft a one-of-a-kind experience. The modding community is very active, and making missions is easier than ever with a 3D editor and Zeus in-game control of both enemy and friendly AI.
That being said, ARMA does have some limitations. Don't expect to get anywhere with AMD CPUs, or anything with a clock speed of < 4Ghz. AI often glitch out, or have super-human vision and accuracy. Multiplayer is always a bit laggy, and quite fragmented. Many servers have mod requirements you have to keep up with, which can clog your hard drive. Thankfully the Steam Workshop is now built into the game launcher, but it still is a pain to configure.
In terms of gameplay ARMA is a hit or miss. It has the breadth of an ocean, but the waves are very choppy. Any vehicle you can think of is drivable, and if it isn't in the base game it is definitly in a free mod. With the addition of helicopter flight models and aircraft damage modeling the vehicles are getting to the complexity that infantry have. However, there are bound to be issues. Vehicles often glitch out or explode at the slightest bump. The AI refuse to follow orders at times, or act like complete geniuses with laser vision. The netcode leaves a lot to be desired. You will scratch your head in close quarter battles wondering how you emptied a whole clip into someone, only to have them turn around and kill you in a shot.
All in all, ARMA is a very unique game, with a community many AAA games are lacking these days. I am willing to look past its weaknesses but can see why some cannot. I recommend this game for anyone who likes to roleplay and create. I do not recommend this game for people who just want to jump in casually.

I figured I'd write a review in case you have some spare coins and are looking for a cheap game.
I've played through this twice so I know this game and some of it's problems.
In short: This game feels like a mod for Doom 3.
First off, the game is really linear and doesn't sport much exploration. There are a few exceptions; secrets and alternative routes. Good level design helps very much in this regard as each area feels pretty well thought out and assets doesn't feel overly repeated.
I thought level design was pretty good. What messes things up is the scripted stuff. I.E take the wrong route, the jump-scare-enemy bugs out and crashes your game... twice.. or until you enter the room through the expected entrance. If you spot enemies and shoot them from afar, an elevator might not come down because the enemies the were scripted to use it and bring it down, thus, you'll have to reload to an earlier savegame.
Unfortunately, stuff like this screws the game up badly. Use quick-saves often.
This game is pretty weak on the story, which is delivered by some of the absolute worst voice actors I've heard. There are no exceptions. In fact, it's so bad it gets good. Ironic as it is, I laughed through the cut-scenes. Not much of it makes sense. Theese things, though unintentionally, serves as a comical break between game-play. It just feels funny.. for some reason. Brilliance in it's own, accidental way.
Difficulty wise, the game is schizophrenic. You'll have a complete breeze throughout the first third of the game. Braindead A.I. This gets compensated as the soldiers appear. It's not easy any more. The difficulty suddenly sky-rockets through the roof. It's braindead A.I but with pinpoint accuracy. Regardless, it's a challenge.
This game also features a hack system. You can hack surveillance cams, turretguns and locked doors to reach secret areas.
Hacking is really only required once, and that is to open a door. Everything else is solvable without it.
Vehicle sections in this game is bad. You'll want to get them over with as soon as possible. Thankfully you won't have to do it much.
Alpha Prime is not a game with a limited two-weapon system, you can actually carry the entire arsenal. However, you are most likely to use the assault rifle.. It's way too overpowered compared to the other weapons.
You'll only use the sniper rifle when the distance requires a scope, otherwise the assault rifle is about as accurate, holds more rounds and fires more rapidly.
In close quarters, you'd normally favour a shotgun, but a two shot burst with the assault rifle is just as good and ammunition is plentiful.
The use of explosives is rarely ever called for, and in those situations, they are so unreliable you might be better off with the assault rifle even in these situations.
Lastly, the embarrassing axe that leaves bullet-hole decals on walls. It fires as fast as you can click your mouse button. It's completely broken. Luckily, you'll never ever find use for it. It's exists just for the sake of it.
In terms of graphics, this game can't compete with the mainstream contemporaries of it's time (which would be Bioshock or ... Crysis). Rather, this game looks like a bright Doom 3, which means it looked dated even at release. But as this game is old and has a low pricetag, that shouldn't matter now.
Sound assets works. Nothing really special to mention here. None of the weapon-sounds makes them feel punchy enough, but the overall ambience is doing it's job rather well.
So, overall, this game looks and feels like a non-scary Doom 3 mod. It's kind of a B-graded game that certainly has it's problems. But if you are ready to overlook that and just take it for what it is, (a game that's actually cheaper than a subway sandwich) you might have good time with it. I know I had.
I like it for what it is.
Cheers!

I really really really wanted to enjoy this game and for the first five or so hours I really did.
I never play games of this 'top down' style but this game stood out to me so much and it was fun while it lasted, but it didn't last very long.
Pros-
The game has a really good set of missions.
There is a great character variety with full customisation over about 4/5 squads (based off real teams such as SAS and SEALS) including individualised stats for each character.
There is an in game market to purchase gear/weapons/attachments/UAVs etc which is purchased through in game currency.
The gameplay mechanics are easy to grasp and each mission can be carried out differently dependant on your weapon and stats selection.
The game has a kind of personal feel to it, there's no real story line but each character (maybe due to the customisation) feels real, if one goes down it impacts you massively in the field.
Cons (here we go) -
The game is too short, I completed the set missions in almost no time at all.
There's no massive replay ability factor in the game, there's plenty of items to buy from the marketplace but once the game is done you don't need them.
No map variety, there's maybe 3 or 4 different game modes but they all use the same maps.
Honestly if it's in the sale then I'd say give it a shot but maybe look at something else for the full price. Don't get me wrong I did enjoy this, it just didn't last long enough.
