I've played this game quite a bit on multiple accounts (probably more than a healthy amount)
My first time playing, I started the game up, made my characters (not knowing what traits or stat presets affected), started playing the actual game, and listened to my dog whine constantly, until he died from starvation because I didnt know how to feed the damn thing
It hit my family hard. I didnt know what to do with people. I couldnt figure out how to order them to go take a dump somewhere when they needed to. They all got more and more unhealthy. A random person came into my shelter, asking to join. I, of course, wanted to be nice, and let the person in. I finally figured out how to send some people out to scavenge. I sent them far away, and they took all of my water with them, because Im an idiot who didnt know what hes doing.
One of the children got food poisioning, and puked all over the place. Rats were squeaking every couple of seconds. Dust storms blew overhead. There was a dead dog by the enterance. Despite these awful conditions, 2 more people came by, wanting to join. I, of course, let them in.
My scavengers came back, both with radiation poisioning. I had procured some anti-rads, and healed them quickly.
Except there were far too many people in my shelter, so they all eventually died from lack of oxygen before I knew what was happening.
It's very difficult to figure out the start of the game, especially without a decent tutorial. I had to follow a few guides to really get to understand the basics of the game, but, once I actually knew what I was doing, it was rather enjoyable. I started up again, got going, and was having fun...
That is, until my base got raided and invisible people killed all of my survivors...
There are a few bugs with this game, and nothing of note has been added since I started playing this game around the start of the summer. It definately could be a bit better, but still can be fun nonetheless. The beginning is hard, trying to balance water and gas and your survivors health, but gets significantly easier as time goes on. The endgame is rediculously easy, with no real threat to your survivors. You can pretty much stick to yourself as time goes on, radioing for merchants to come along, and buy what little you need from them.
If this game is on sale, I would definately recommend it. Not worth 15$, unless there are some major updates to the game.

As of when I wrote this review, I have played through the first two episodes of the game. Both of them had interesting stories which are somewhat connected (as in, they make sense in a bigger picture) but are still playable on their own.
The game mechanics are simple: It's a point and click game with an inventory where you still have the freedom to control the character. You can interact with people and things either through talking or using an item from your inventory on them.
The aesthetics are interesting and and the art team did a good job with implementing their own specific style but still staying true to the movies. The levels are fun to play and the puzzles feel intuitive.
This game is more for casual playing as the puzzles are not overly hard though sometimes you might get stuck if you have been at it for too long. The interactions that the player can make and the limitations with them make sense to me and the dev team also did a good job there.
Kudos to Telltale Games, I will definitely play the rest of the Episodes and am looking forward to checking out their other arsenal.

Ok i haven't played the game too long but i can definitely tell you this game is NOT p2w like others are describing.
So if your a little skeptical of my claim keep reading. I'd like to adress and clear up the issue of p2w first as it seems to be of most intrest to people.
Reason why its not p2w:
-The game has factions, and to get armor you need to level up those factions. Ok so how does this make it not p2w you ask? lets go over the details.
+ First when you start out as level 1 and que for matchmaking, the game reads the level of your gear and puts you into the skill group to play with same level item people. So lets say your level 1 and rank 1 in your faction fresh after installing the game. If you spend lets say....30 dollars on a level 12 advanced faction weapon. Back to the Future: The Game is an episodic adventure game with five episodes, developed and published by Telltale Games, the same people behind other such great adventure games as The Wolf Among Us and Game of Thrones. The game is based on the film series of the same name
Although the game does not follow the same exact storyline as the first film, it follows the same universe as Back to the Future follows only seeing it in a different point of view
As mentioned previously, the game is split up into five episodes. The game works as a normal television series. Each length of an episode is roughly one hour long
The gameplay is very simple, you move around, selecting stuff and talking to people and using button prompts when told to. Choices don't really matter as to other Telltale Games
The game's graphics are okay for the most part however there are some ugly texture work here and there. The sound and music options also vary in quality. Sometimes the sound quality is really good and sometimes the sound quality is bad. I have encountered numerous amounts of glitches which seems as if Telltale Games never got round to fixing them, too many to mention in this review
Telltale's Back to the Future: The Game pays a good homage to the Back to the Future film series and is definitely better than Jurassic Park: The Game which is another Universal Pictures license

A great follow up to the original. Great story and characters just like the original, the story at points feels like it is better. It feel more layered, more intricate, the writing feels deeper like there is more going on. It expands on the events and characters from the original very well while also adding more great characters to the universe that are just as good. This time around the game has a very depressing feeling to it mainly because of the concept is you being ‘the last jedi alive’ and roaming around a galaxy that is struggling to recover from the wars that took place. The thing that holds this game back is it’s unfinished state which is why I can’t say it’s better than the original. You can tell when playing because there are areas of the game that feel empty like cantinas with nobody to talk to inside for example and doors that were supposed lead to other areas but unfortunately the developers just didn’t have enough time to finish those areas so the doors remain locked which is a shame. The game has less detail in the world and the environments than the original, it doesn’t feel dense like the original did. It also has a rushed ending so you leave the game with this unfulfilled feeling. I played without the cut content mod because I didn’t know it existed until I was halfway through my playthrough which is a shame because all I hear is great things about it like how it adds more dialogue and events to the game. I do want to play this game again for a third time with the cut content mod in the near future. This game is more of what you loved about the original so it’s a must play if you enjoyed the first.

10/10 I've played every supergiant game but none has stuck me like this one has.
In terms of playtime, it took me 3 hours to beat transistor, and 8 hours to beat this, take that as you will.
The game deals remarkably well with the themes of freedom, toil, and sacrifice. Alot of the lessons the game directly or indirectly impart translate well to modern events, making it a facinating story to think on.
The gameplay itself is smooth, the rites get harder as you prevail, and easier as you fail, I lost only one of the entire game. The dialogue after the loss did make it worth it however.
The music is incredible, blending together and working well to set tension and emotion during different events of the story, best they've done so far.
The story is fun and extensive, some people argue that the game is dialogue heavy, but the large majority of it is optional, although I do reccomend talking to the characters as much as you can to get what I got out of the game.
The graphics are amazing, I've never seen graphics that fit so well with the story and mood of the game. The hand painted art style shines through in this game better than in any previous game.
All in all, the best game supergiant has made by leaps and bounds, I look forward to their next.

As a true Rayman fan, who owns every single one of the Rayman games; I couldn't miss this one in my list.
Rayman Legends stays (just like Origins) in the old settings of '2D' gaming and is a nice reminder of the old days. The levels are well designed and just as lovely to play. The music varies from Orchestral to Rock, and the 'music' levels will surely get a smile on your face.
Besides the main games, you can also win in-game prizes, such as levels in the worlds of Origins, 'creatures' that give you free lums and much more.
Though the game is originally designed for kids, it is seriously difficult to play. Some levels are never saved inbetween and you seriously have to get it all through in one go... making even me, a rather often playing gamer, really frustrated.
Besides all that the harder levels, are seriously HARD.
I, myself, play on the keyboard, and the 'W' for help and 'S' to hit, arent always as ideal as thought by the designers. Fortunately you can change that in the settings.
It might sound all really intense, but I would really recommend the game. It's well worth it's money in both time to play and the in-game content (without paying for a DLC).

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews - Game 23
Bejeweled 3
Purchase Date: 3/6/2014
Match 3 puzzle games have been around a long time, and Bejeweled is one of the older series of these games.  If you ever played that awful Candy Crush Saga, then you can think of Bejeweled as it's much less obnoxious uncle.
Bejeweled 3 is a match 3 game first, and not a mobile game, so thankfully it doesn't have a lot of the annoying mechanics that you find in the typical mobile game.  It's not begging you to add friends or buy gems or enticing you to click on a picture of Kate Upton's boobs to download the latest version of Fire Age.  Bejewled 3 gives you a screen full of gems, and it wants you to match 3 of them, and that's as complicated as it gets.
In fairness, I should add that this version of Bejewled does come with 8 different game modes.  4 of these you get immediately, and as you progress in each game mode you will unlock an additional game mode.  So it does vary up the gameplay somewhat.  Some of the game modes are timed, while others are more strategic.  It also has a Zen mode where you can just mindlessly match gems as long as you want.
So the important question you need to ask yourself is, do you like matching gems?  Because if you like matching gems, then this game is for you.  If you don't like matching gems, then you should stop reading this review and get back to playing Fire Age.

My experience with this game have been a rollercoaster, the first hour i spent was trying to get into a server & actually play the game. Although the game feels like it's still in Alpha, I actually really enjoyed the game once I got started. The downside is, that it is one rough start, you'll find yourself scared, lonely, hunted by the nether or the ruthless players who kills on sight. Heck you'll even spend a couple of minutes to try and find your friend who you bought the game with.
But now, you've found eachother & you're thinking what now?
You go out scavenging for supplies, sneaking past nethers who seem very scary at first, and you feel like you're powerless.
But now you and your friend decide to try and take it down, you get a feel for the combat and realize they aren't so bad.
Now you've leveled up, you have no idea what the different skills do, what's good? what's bad? you decide because you're a viking, you'll skill up in melee combat. But right as you skill up and start moving again, your friend gets shot by another play, you panic, you run around in circles and what not. You now know how dangerous it is to be in the open. You think you see the other play, you only have a kitchen knife and the dude who just shot your friend is picking up the stuff you just scavenged together. You decide to go for revenge, you hack & slash at the player and you bring him down, he explodes with items all over the ground. You now feel satisfied, you've taken down another player with a damned knife. Now that you've picked up the players rifle & gear, will you start hunting other players just like he did? or will you try and protect players from nether & make new friends. That's all up to you.
The game has it's keeping players in it's grasp, in my opinion it's the satisfaction of killing someone geared & taking down the hordes of nethers. Sure, the game has it's glitches & issues, it truly is tough getting into the game, through the glitches etc, but once you've died the first 10 times maybe more maybe less, you get the feeling of the game, you want revenge on the nether that killed you the first time, you want to find that player and hunt him down for killing your friend. And you do it.
The leveling system is also a good thing in this game, the character levels you lose upon death, like most survival games. But you still keep your account level, which i find awesome, so you don't feel like you wasted too much time leveling up, you still have small perks from your account level that keep you going.
To wrap it up, you want to look at this game as it's still in alpha, expect alot of glitches, unmercyfull players & nethers. And expect to die quite a bit. But you wan't to stick to the game cause it is just downright awesome when you get into the gameplay.

Nether provides a very atmospheric experience even in it's unfinished form.
The name of the game is kill or be killed, whether that is from the various creatures scattered about the world or from the other players you share the environment with.
Nether players will quickly become your main concern when you are not within one of the safe zones located around the world. Nether players for the most part will shoot first and ask questions later so having your wits about you is key to survival.
The game world is a decent size and allows for up to 64 players connected to any given server at a time. The servers are plentiful and located by region so you can pick a server that is closest to you.
There are many areas of the map greyed out at the moment presumably to be added in a a later date.
You level up your character by carrying out courier missions, scavenging for  items, crafting and killing monsters. Perks are gained to add to your character as your level increases, and passive perks are gained as your account level increases. The former are lost on death and need to be reacquired so dying is not without consequence.
Equipment can be quite hard to come by but for those who wish to fast track to cosmetic glory you can pay real world cash to buy the items you want in game. But for those who enjoy getting things through game play there is nothing you can get by paying you can't get through play. These cosmetic items are found in golden loot containers and opened with keys you can buy with in game currency, and provided you are wearing them or have them in your global inventory they will not be lost on death.
there are some minor bugs still to be ironed out, including floating terrain features and some glitchy parts of the map that you can get stuck on or even fall through. Water also appears to be very glitchy as well but i feel sure these issues will be addressed in upcoming patches.

The only big issue for me is the other players killing me. I know that it is, of course, part of the game and the permadeath makes you lose your character and such. But every single time I've come across someone in the wilds, they have attacked me. That isn't so bad as dying. When you die you lose everything. All your inventory stuff, all your xp, all your levels, skills and abilities. Sure there is a global inventory back at the safe haven but that's a little far. Honestly, if you lost your inventory stuff but got to keep your levels, I'd be a lot happier. Just for the fact that it becomes incredibly tedious having to start from the very beginning again everytime you die. for me, it takes away the feeling of progression.
However, altogether, it is a very enjoyable game and I do recommend it.

The main problem is this game never really had a chance. Where the original KOTOR was developed by BioWare (later to develop Mass Effect and Dragon Age), LucasArts tapped the fledgling Obsidian Entertainment (Fallout: New Vegas, Pillars of Eternity) to develop a sequel on an accelerated time table. Ultimately Obsidian had to cut a significant amount of material from KOTOR II to meet the schedule and released the game half-finished and buggy. It's remained that way through til the time of this writing.
Yes, it's true, lot of the removed content wasn't actually (or just really poorly) removed and modders have made something closer to a finished product. The problem is that it doesn't amount to much. The game is *still* buggy and half-finished, and ultimately little more than an asset flip.

If you have enjoyed games such as the original Fallout, This War of Mine, the Sims or Fallout Shelter, I wholeheartedly recommend that you stick to these games and skip Sheltered.
Gameplay: waiting and inventory management
During most of the game, you will have several teams out exploring, because there is little to do in the shelter. About twice a minute, one of your teams will radio in because they need you to make a decision. Most encounters are either "we have found a site, should we search it?" (Yes) and "We have searched a site, which of the stuff should we keep in our limited inventory?", with some random "We have found a person/wild beast, should we fight/flee/trade/join forces?" thrown in. Radio events require you to right-click on the radio and then left click and will time out if you wait for to long. Once every few hours, you might actually reach a quest giver handing out such inspiring quests as "Please bring 15 pistol ammo". Most of the time not spent waiting or telling your teams that yes, you would actually like them to search the places on their route is spent managing inventories. "Hm, two scraps of plastics aren't worth a slot by themselves, but if I keep them, I can stack more plastics I might find on the slot." Combat is resolved using a very basic turn based system where you basically pick either fight or flight.
Difficulty: beach resort holiday
So you have a family with two minors struggling to survive  in a bare rock shelter in a post-apocalyptic wasteland. How hard can that be? Actually not so very hard at all, it turns out. In the ten hours I played, I did not have a single character die. People in random encounters are generally poorly armed, should you choose to fight them, and wild animals can be run away from until you find something to poke them with. Once, my water supply almost ran dry because it did not rain for some time, but that was the only dramatic moment there was. I guess you could inflict some rules on yourself, such as "my survivors are vegetarians -- no meat" or "my survivors will invite in any stranger who asks them for help" just as you can in nethack, but it seems rather pointless to me. In theory, your shelter might get raided, but I never got any raiders, despite little Timmy sitting alone in the shelter trying to attract traders by radio.
Immersion: as realistic as an ad for nuclear war
I have some suspension of disbelief when playing post-apocalyptic games. There are some simple pills to cure radiation sickness? Any gun-inflicted sublethal damage will be gone once healed? Okay, I am fine with these, it is a game, after all. So your shelter has two radiation suits, which you will use when you exit the shelter to fix above-ground stuff. There is no decontamination and you can also sleep in it, no problem. If you exit the shelter to go exploring, a gas mask will keep you save, no matter how long the tour, but will be gone when you return. A lot of effort goes to filter the oxygen and water in your shelter, but the most prized source of food is meat from wildlife. Attacking and killing a helpless stranger will cause marginally less trauma than killing a wolf in self-defense will. Even after a nuclear war, your survivors will still be like Sims and absolutely refuse to relieve themselves outside, instead spending freshly filtered water using the toilet. The generator needs fuel, but if you burn wood in the incinerator instead it will magically generate power, too. Still not sustainable enough for you? Little Timmy can just fix some solar cells out of a heap of old electronics. Yes, it's magic. According to the game, books, teddy bears and records will be among the most prized possessions (short of firearms) in a post nuclear wasteland.
Conclusion: This War of Mine copied badly
The basic concept of the game is just a reframing of the excellent This War of Mine: you have some survivors in a base, sometimes they go out to get stuff from places. The difference is that TWoM is deeply engaging (Will you donate some meds to kids? Will you steal food from an elderly couple?) where Sheltered is flat: Will you invite a survivor with these stats, or wait for a better one? Also, in TWoM, the difficulty is nontrivial -- you might get shot trying to loot a place -- and the gameplay actually works fine. Sheltered has picked the weak areas from various okay games, the need meters of the Sims, the inventory management from TWoM, the character depth of nethack, the realism of Worms, the graphics of Baldurs Gate, the combat system of a text adventure and the humor of Tetris. Just skip it.

Much of the hate this game gets has to do with things outside of the game itself or the recent progression system.
In my review, I will not be addressing things outside of the game.
Personally, I don't have many problems with the new progression system. Yes, it needs some work, but such a new system is expected to have issues. (I don't think it should take five hours to become an adult Tyrannosaur every time you die). People definitely need to have to work for better dinosaurs, and this (mostly) fixes rex hordes and funnels out noobs.
Here are my pros and cons:
Pros:
-Teamwork is pretty much mandatory to play properly.
-You actually need some skill to play the game.
-Dinosaurs, duh.
-Every thing is fairly balanced.
-The new map looks BEAUTIFUL.
-The devs plan on adding a wide variety of creatures to play as.
-It's all-in-all, pretty fun.
Cons:
-The amount of time it takes to unlock better dinosaurs. (It just needs about a 20% decrease in time, or maybe it could be longer and your progression woulod save?)
-You have to stand completely still and vulnerable for close to a minute to progress and safely log out.
-The maps are so huge, it can take forever, potentially until you starve, to find a body as a carnivore.
-If you're a medium sized herbivore in the vicinity of a large carnivore, you're f*cked.
-Smaller creatures have next to no chance of escaping larger ones.
-Every creature that is not your own species is almost guaranteed to attack you,
-The game gets kind of boring after a while, with you constantly doing next to nothing for hours.
Overall:
I personally recommend the game and enjoy it, but if you're too impatient to play for five hours or can't deal with issues, I suggest you wait a while until the game is out of early access.

I first encountered Apotheon through an article on IGN, and was immediately surprised that a developer had been both bold and creative enough to craft a game with such a distinct look. I soon purchased it and began playing in the company of my partner who, like me, is fairly interested in the history of art. To begin with then we were both positively biased towards it simply because of the art direction, and for most of our playthrough that was enough to keep us somewhat engaged. However, after making it through the majority of the game, our opinions had both turned towards frustration, and we decided to abandon the playthrough.
Needless to say, the presentational aspects of this game are top quality. It possesses a fantastically idiosyncratic visual aesthetic within the annals of gaming, and the animation imparts a sense of movement to the player-avatar and enemies that sits well within this aesthetic. Indeed, the game has a great sense of design unity between its gameplay, aesthetic and story elements that many games fail to achieve. What's more, the encroachment of cut-scenes and other non-interactive elements is pleasantly minimal.
Having said that, there are a few essential areas of design that are so disappointing that I cannot wholeheartedly recommend Apotheon. Firstly, if you are going to play it, do not use a keyboard and mouse configuration, as it renders the otherwise interestingly designed combat mechanics infuriating to use at times. Unfortunately, I was stuck using such a configuration for the majority of the playthrough as I had no access to a console controller, but I grinned and bore it as I recognised that the developers recommend the use of a gamepad. As others have also pointed out, both combat and traversal can sometimes seem floaty, and occasionally movement will glitch in irritating ways, but these are far from the designers’ biggest failings.
No, far less forgivable is the overall quality of game and level design. As a massive fan of Super Metroid, I expect certain standards to be met by Metroidvania titles. These include decent variety across level designs, a good degree of depth to exploration, and a reasonably high frequency of being surprised by what I encounter and uncover. Whereas other indie gems of recent years such as Cave Story, Guacamelee! and Axiom Verge triumphed in these regards, Apotheon severely lacks: level layouts are hugely uninspired and often seemed arbitrary; the breadth of discoverable items, treasure and upgrades is disappointingly limited; and there were next to no moments when I felt delighted, excited or impressed by a hidden/hard-to-find game element. By the time I reached the maelstrom of tedious traversal and bland level structuring that is the Poseidon portion of the game (no water-temple/IGN allusion intended), enough was enough.
In other regards the game wasn’t quite so disappointing. The narrative is suitably light and no more superficial than what I’ve experienced to be the general standard of game writing. However, unlike the visuals, the story-based elements did seem to lack ‘soul’, but I'm not the sort to be bothered by such things as long as the gameplay is well designed. In regards to audio, I recall not being induced to fits of unintended laughter or rage by the dialogue or voice acting - which is always a pleasant surprise given examples elsewhere in the industry - and I remember being suitably impressed by the semiotic aptness of the music.
Ultimately though, Apotheon lacks any great sense of charm or character outside of its aesthetic elements, and it doesn’t possess the level of game design polish or nuance its art direction seemingly suggests. The game is a triumph of visual style over gameplay substance, albeit in a way that differentiates it from AAA titles that could be described in the same way. Historically, it will likely become noteworthy for its experimentation with a unique visual design at a time when popular games were mostly polarized between pseudo-realistic hi-fidelity graphics and nostalgia-tugging pixel art. In the here-and-now though, if you're looking for something to scratch that 2D action-adventure game itch, I'd suggest you look elsewhere.

I'll list out the positives and negatives:
+ Spectacular presentation, both in video and audio department. This is one damn pretty game.
+ It's highly literate in Greek mythology. This isn't some cheap cash-in with a skin deep mythology paint on it.
+ The length is just right. I finished it at around 10 hours.
+  There are tons of weapons you can choose from and master, each with a different use, speed and reach.
+ The controversial battle system is actually pretty awesome once you stick with it and master it. I'd recommend using a controller and having both thumbs on the analog sticks for most of the game.
- The controls are too convoluted. Changing from a sword to bow or a potion is too messy because there are so many stuff in your inventory and when you're in the middle of a big fight, there's a high chance you'll select/use something you didn't want to.
- There's no point in fighting the enemies unless the game requires you to. You don't gain any XP or anything and since your weapons break more often than I personally prefer, I would usually try to avoid fights in the hub areas.
- the returning disc weapon is buggy. Sometimes when I changed to it, two of them would hover around my character and I couldn't attack or change weapons. I had to quit the game and restart from my saves.
All in all, this is a high quality game and a very intricately designed piece of art and experience in itself. You can definitely come out of this game with loads of more general information on Greek mythology. That ending definitely made me think and that's something I can't say about most games.
Despite the VERY minor glitches, If you can stick with the fighting mechanics and like action/adventure/RPG style gameplay with amazing presentation and art direction, you definitely can't go wrong with Apotheon.

Sniper Elite V2 can be a great game, but with many flaws.  First of all the AI is extremely poor, I found most soldiers could be baited and tunneled with ease, not to mention lured into the "pill box" for a line-up of kills.  Enemy snipers are also easy to spot and kill, you can just sprint, or get around cover and peak out fast and return.  They will surely fire their one shot, if it manages to hit you is another story.  Just hold your breath as you peak out, and aim above their head -> DEAD.
I played the game on my first play through on the hardest setting, which to be honest was extremely easy.  I ended up not even using the scope after a while and just holding CTRL and picking off guys with head shots.
The game has a lot to offer and ways to take out enemies.
- Standard Kills
- Baiting with explosives
- Shooting their grenades
- Blowing up explosives near them for double and triple kills
The story is subpar if anything, I never felt emotionally involved in the main character, nor any other sub characters.
One of the best experiences was getting waves of units sent at me for immediate slaughter.
The biggest issue in this game is the horrid camera.  I cannot explain how bad this system is, but it was way too touchy.  Sometimes you would be running and turn around not realizing you just did a 360, not 180.  I also rarely found myself using anything other than grenades, and maybe a few trip wires...  I think I only used two, one in the tutorial, and one for fun.
There is also CO-OP and Online Mode, I found these to okay if you can get the right group.
Overall I would say 6/10.
I also received this free during the promotion, and honestly would not buy this game.

10/10 I've played every supergiant game but none has stuck me like this one has.
In terms of playtime, it took me 3 hours to beat transistor, and 8 hours to beat this, take that as you will.
The game deals remarkably well with the themes of freedom, toil, and sacrifice. Alot of the lessons the game directly or indirectly impart translate well to modern events, making it a facinating story to think on.
The gameplay itself is smooth, the rites get harder as you prevail, and easier as you fail, I lost only one of the entire game. The dialogue after the loss did make it worth it however.
The music is incredible, blending together and working well to set tension and emotion during different events of the story, best they've done so far.
The story is fun and extensive, some people argue that the game is dialogue heavy, but the large majority of it is optional, although I do reccomend talking to the characters as much as you can to get what I got out of the game.
The graphics are amazing, I've never seen graphics that fit so well with the story and mood of the game. The hand painted art style shines through in this game better than in any previous game.
All in all, the best game supergiant has made by leaps and bounds, I look forward to their next.

This game is fun at first, but it gets very repetitive by the time you're halfway through.
It would be more accurate to call this a stealth game than a sniper game, though chances are most of the time you'll get discovered and it'll be a straight up shoot-out anyway. The game flies in the face of game logic that bringing a sniper rifle to a firefight means insta-death for you, with it expecting you to use the rifle in close-quarters combat, as the regular machine guns are the useless weapons this time round.
What you're left with is basically a shoot-em-up, going from point A to B, and repeat, plowing through firefights as you go. You might be expecting some sort of sniper simulator, but even in this game you're a super soldier single-handedly winning the war by wading into battlegrounds, walking up to enemies and shooting them no problem. On harder difficulties it instead turns to frustration as you have to restart the entire part several times because of a hidden sniper taking you out when the coast was supposedly clear.
With no variation, it gets boring fast, if not infuriating.

Game has great art and has some nice music but has some serious problems which render it a frustrating and un-fun experience.
The gameplay mechanics are inconstant and lack depth. Simple things like not being able to do a charge attack upwards shows how little polish the game has. The running attack mechanic is poorly designed and flings you forward causing you to lose the ability to accurately land after a run attack. You can't "hang" off ledges, which means you will spend a lot of time accidentally running off cliffs when you simply meant to get close to the edge.
Collecting random garbage is NOT fun. The game ranks you based on how many fairies and mini guys you grab but at no point do you feel rewarded for collecting these things. The fairies are ONLY used to unlock characters which don't have any different abilities or anything unique about them. The mini guys that you find unlock levels but having to find 10 of them per level makes the task feel like a chore instead of a game. Overall you spend the majority of your time collecting items that serve little purpose.
Enemies? What enemies? The enemies in this game are WAY too easy. It is almost impossible to die from them as they don't attack back, rarely move, and have such a short range of attack. The game would be more fun if you didn't have an attack button and actually had to land on the enemies heads, at least this would give them a shred of difficulty.
The saving in this game is absolute trash. Did you just spend 10 minutes collecting all the random garbage in an area. Well you better not die because if you do you will have to collect all of it again. In almost every other modern platformer I have played the things you collect are saved but you are returned to an earlier checkpoint. Making you go back and have to recollect every item is terrible design. Not to mention replaying the music over and over which is annoying to say the least.
90% of the levels are a complete bore and lack creativity.  Each world introduces some new level mechanic but none of these mechanics are really "fun". Flying = boring. Sneaking = boring. Hitting Y to move some element in the level = oh god so boring. Compare this game to any other platformer and you will see more creativity in one level than you would in this entire game.
Overall the game can be summed with two words "not fun". It doesn't hold a candle to  Braid, Super Mario, Little Big Planet and many other modern platformers.  It is a step back in patforming and I am surprised that people have given it such high praise.
It's 99 Cents and is sure to take up about an hour of your time, so decide if thats worth your money and give it a try.

Sniper Elite V2 is a great game revolving around sniping. It is very satisfying to see your bullets through the bullet cam hit targets and experience the gruesome impact dealt by your bullet on them via x-ray.
You play as an American elite sniper who is apparently able to take down a huge amount of soldiers from both the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany. You can either play it stealthly (Only shooting when there is a noise distraction and sneaking by) or go in balls deep guns blazing.
I played on both cadet (easy) and marksman (normal) mode. In cadet mode, you are basically superhuman, your shots land exactly on where you aim and enemies are much lesser and weaker.  In marksman mode, enemies are much tougher and you will most likely die when an enemy come too close. There is also bullet drop over distance and wind, this means that you have to either predict where your bullet would land or use the "iron lung" ability to have a marker indicating where your bullet would hit. It is good to see a unique varying difficulty in this game.
The single-player campaign consist of eleven missions. Each mission took me about an average of 15-20 mins to complete so there is rougly around 4 hour worth of content in the single player game. There are also collectables to collect in this game such as gold bars and wine bottles which are hidden throughout all the mission for those who want to do so.
For those who wants to play with other people, there is co-op and multiplayer mode. The multiplayer aspect is basically snipers vs snipers which can be pretty dull when everyone is just camping or hiding.
The graphics are alright but not very good. The environmental texture looks really low-resolution despite playing on max settings. Most of the enemies are basically clones as the enemies just recycle looks from a few character models. The enemies also repeat the same lines in their native tongue when they spot you or dead bodies, which can be pretty annoying after listening to them for awhile.
If you are looking for a world war 2 sniping experience with loads of action, this game is for you! If you are looking specifically for a world war 2 experience with deep narrative, this game is not for you as there is barely any dialogue interaction between characters and I feel that this game focus more on action than the story.
If I were to give this game a rating, I would give it a 7/10 as it is a solid sniping game with a serviceable storyline.

This game is a departure from Supergiant Games' more action-oriented previous titles.  But don't let that stop you from giving it a try.  Although its "wizard basketball" action sequences serve as a break from text and not vice versa, both portions of the game are enjoyable and well crafted enough to make it a worthy heir to the Supergiant legacy.
Pyre has many positive aspects.  The game is beautiful to behold.  The music is enchanting.  Most of all though, the characters are complicated, flawed, and worthy of love (even the supporting cast is richly detailed).  I found something to appreciate about each of the exiles in my crew and their opponents.
Its action segments, the "wizard basketball" alluded to earlier, are frenetic and challenging.  I can understand some of the negative perspectives on these segments, as I never really felt the need to employ all three exiles.  Usually I would have one exile carry my team and only rely on the others if I messed up.  And I can see this both as a flaw in the game and as a flaw in my skill as a player.
That said, the game is beautiful from start to finish.  I loved it, and I imagine you will too.

I'm not a huge fan of fighting games but I will say this is one of the most enjoyable ones I've ever played.  At its base core this game is a fighting game if you hate fighting games don't bother with this game.  The game suffers like many games do today from being released to early.  There were many unforseen bugs that could have been worked out from longer testing and a lot of most people's complaints about this game stem from these bugs.  There is a lot of exaggeration into the P2P connectivity for this game and how bad it is.  I at the time of writing this review have almost 46 hours and have only been booted from 2 games and have never experienced lag in the game.  Sure, I've experienced matchmaking errors but I've experienced that in almost every other game that has matchmaking.  When it comes to matchmaking in the modes with gear levels however there can be a lot of variation and one of the biggest problems in the game right now.  If you "main" a character and get Reputation level 3 and get purple gear you could be fighting against people that have played 3 different characters to Rep lvl 1 and in doing so your gear level could way higher than there's giving you a sizable advantage over other players.
TL;DR
The gameplay of this game is superb, the complaints about P2P over dedicated servers are greatly exaggerated, matchmaking in gearscore modes could use some work, overall 8/10 would recommend.

90MF is (still) a text-based MMO Football-Manager-Sim.
You choose your team name, dress colours, emblem (easy to import) and the time of the day/night at which you wanna play. (For example Late evening Football association = LEFA = 8pm-10pm UTC) Then you should be online at this time if possible. If you miss a match you still have 24 hours  to play it, if the opponent is there tho and requests to play, the match starts without you. Then you miss the chance to make substitutions and/or tactical adjustments.
If your team is the better one, chances are still good that you will win the game. (If you dont have 3 injuries that is...) If both opponents miss the game for 24 hours it will be autoresolved. You also have the option to play all sheduled matches from the next 10 days - only if one of the opposite sides is online too.
Most of the time i spend on searching for new players. You can always bid on players from any team. Players cannot be transferred twice a season tho. (A season/year takes one month). If you release the contract of a player or you are the first bidder on a player from the transfer list, then a 24 hour negotiation phase triggers, in which anybody can bid on that player. The highest bidder wins and pays the amount of the second highest bidder. If nobody bids on a released player he becomes a free player. After 7 days free players can be instantly transfered into your squad, for free. This is useful if you want to quickly form a Youth-team (U21 or U18) for example.
It is advisable to form Youth teams asap (or at least one U21-team) because they are the source of good future players that dont cost you money and they can be sold later with profit too, of course.
You practically get money every day. Stadium tickets, TV-payments etc. At the end of the season you get extra cash depending on your results in the League.
There are "timezones", just as mine which have almost 200 clubs which means there are 10 divisions of 20 clubs and there are "timezones" which have fewer, like 40 clubs ergo just 2 divisions of 20 clubs each. Being last in that second division would bring the same amount of money as being last in the 10th Division of the other (my) timezone. So there is no real advantage in joining an FA with lesser teams/divisions. Just take the FA where you have time to play.
There are also several Cup events, similar to the Champions League, EL, etc. Atm its all knockout but group stages will be introduced this or next month i think.
Staff has also been introduced recently, meaning it is advisable to sign a Senior Coach, a Youth Coach and a Physio who takes care of injuries etc.
This game got me hooked instantly. Everything is well organized and self explaining. There is an ingame guide also aswell as a steam guide to help you out if necessary.
Playing against real players is a whole different story compared to other football-sims. And if the other dude isnt online - the better for me. Sure, i lost games where i had 30-40 goal attempts and the opponent just 5 - but thats football, it happens. YES it happens and it can be frustrating.
I really like digging deep to search for players, finding talents or cheaper older players that can help me instantly. But you never know if you really get them (except they have been free agents for 7 days as mentioned). It can be pretty exciting.
Atm i am really enjoying this game and i feel it will last for a while.
Trying new tactics is fun but still a bit limited which brings me to the final chapter.
The remaining dev-team is small, really. They are working people like you and me. Still they want to introduce a 2D match engine and other features like more depth in tactical possibilities. Also tactical orders for every single player and other stuff. There are many stats already you can check out but there are more to come.

The mixed reception of this game is deserved especially since, at this late date, people are expecting a lot more in terms of freedom of movement and fluidity when it comes to controls. The game is technically a "stealth" game but it reminds me a lot more of the survival horror genre (particularly Silent Hill 3 in terms of controls, mood, its lighting/color scheme and female protagonist--the lady protagonist even shares Heather's psychically controlled pocket flashlight). Calculating open combat engagements is a must unless you plan on reloading quite a bit. The game rewards exploration with collectables, health, ammo, and morphine (Violette's "kill bad guys instantly" juice) hence its strong affinity with the survival horror genre. This is a game about patience, perseverance, and doing it the right way--the way the designers intended--the first time, so it might not jive with the average gamer. As far as the story goes, the lady protagonist is arguably not as fascinating as the real life French-English lady spy she is based on but she is more interesting and "strong" than the average female video game character--albeit she suffers the usual treatment of female characters in video games (she is often seen running about in her nightie) and moonlights as a helpless morphine addict incapacitated in a hospital. Ah well, at least she is complex. I just wish she was savvier in a fight and didn't die instantaneously. But In all honesty, I'm glad she is not a martial arts expert or gun toting "bro-girl," I'm also relieved she isn't a victim (though she is certainly vulnerable). She lends some much needed class to female protagonists and her touted desirability is admirably "kosher" in the sense that she is an independent and "full-bodied" woman--although the German uniform thing, I think, is a little iffy (I think of Charlotte Rampling in the Night Porter). I hope she comes back for a sequel. However, I also kind of feel that this historical fiction based on actual historical figures is better handled by Ubisoft. May Violette one day receive a big budget treatment so she can join the likes of Sam Fisher, Solid Snake, the guy from Thief and all the Brotherhood Assassins as a worthy protagonist.

Nether is fantastic... but not for everybody.
TL, DR = If you like a challenge, thrive on competition, and don't mind a scare, this game could one day result in perfection.  If you arn't willing to figure things out for yourself, think hackers are everywhere, or can't stand a cancerous-demon thing chasing your toon, look elsewhere.
Most common lies debunked: As of the 6/14 summer sale loot is regular (plentiful once you know how to look), 'golden chests' only seem to drop cosmetic stuff (and the occasional rifle frame), and you can buy keys to open golden boxes with money made from completing missions.  Further, even with 'coins' (purchased with real $) you can't buy anything BUT cosmetic, save for a few unique items (flashlight, hanglider, etc.) and need loot just like everyone else in order to build a gun.  Also no noticable hacking - some players glitch around a bit from lag, but they are the least of your worries, since the Nether will mug them long before those players can bother you.
The Good: Stealth is useful early and late, melee is efficient but cannot handle groups, run-and-gun is powerful but has some major drawbacks (cost of ammo and other players can find you easily), leveling up is painless, levels can be powerful but are not required to have an impact, and the freakin' demons (the Nether) are beatable, but still dangerous even after recognizing ai patterns.  Most exciting?  You are never perfectly safe (safezones fail but have built-in missions to bring them back up, and will recover on their own eventually), and the challenge and accomplishment from simply surviving long enough to make discoveries feels very rewarding.
The bad: Total types of weapons are limited for a game this crafting focused, the UI is limited and sometimes non-intuitive, dying can be more than a little frustrating, there are also some simple exploits left to be worked out, and some parts of the map are practically barren, resulting in a long walk on the beach rather than a daring courrior drop in a post-apoc world.  Camping PC's are not the issue most claim, BUT groups of PC's ANYWHERE, especially near the safe-zones in the boonies, make many missions near impossible without the help of your own group.  Also, when a safe-zone falls, if no-one fixed it within the first hour, you get no further warning that the 'walls are down,' and may wander into a warzone filled with gankers and demons during the 10/30/60min reset period.  Most promenent mistake?  Despite the teaser trailor filling your head with the hope for plentiful story, there simply is none.  Living in Chicago helps since the streat names mean something (even if they are rubix-cubed up) but there is simply zero story - interest in playing Nether is from challenge and personal accomplishments alone.
The ugly: The nether are freaky... for the first 12 hours or so.  After that it's less like running from demons and more like picking out game on a safari - you know the attack patterns, and seeing the same skin over and over makes them almost mundane.  That is not to say they arn't dangerous; simply running into a group of them means you need to pull out a gun, which in turn means players will come-runnin.  However, the more dangerous the Nether, or the more there are in one spot, the more easily they are avoided.   Also, losing so much on death is terrifying incentive... yet after the 6th time dying and losing guns, it became kind-of zen like.  You learn to not fear losing stuff and just get back in the game, since leveling happens so fast and global inventories exist to store loot you bring to a safe-zone.  It's certainly more complicated then just popping up in a typical FPS, but dying no longer persuades me to not try crazy things, and the survival feel is heavily dampened.
Total: once the glitches are fixed, the nether get more than one skin a peice, the map is completely populated, some dialogue is added to missions, and another sub-way is added (the red-line crosses the river underground!), I can see myself easily putting more that 100 hours into surviving the sandbox that is Nether.

Story-whise the game is confronting the player with multiple timelines when changing the past throughout the game (in a linear way admittadly). Apotheon is a fun, 2-D action game, with a few bugbears in the works, but nothing that stops it from being a wonderful experience.
The game is (if you couldn't tell) based on greek myth. The short version of the plot is that zeus is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at mortals and wants to wipe the planet of them, hera (his wife and sister, yes, greek myth is ♥♥♥♥ed up like that) doesn't like the♥♥♥♥♥♥he is pulling and decides to make you her champion. From there you go around God of War style and murder most of the greek gods, some of them help you, but most want your head on a pike.
The gameplay is rather simple, yet effective and varied enough to keep it from getting boring. You have two sections of weapons, melee and ranged, during the course of the game you'll pick up many different weapons and can scroll through them all with a flick of the mouse wheel mid combat to get just the right tool for the job. Anything from knives to hammers that cause the ground to explode are on offer, hell, even some arrows that turn enemies into allies later on to. You also get a shield with which to stop the enemies from turning you into crumbled red feta cheese. Everything has durability and will eventually break, meaning you constantly need to swap out weapons and your shield (which you can only carry one of) in order to survive in combat, this forces you to change your play style on the fly, which can be a bit difficult, but once you get it down your fine. Normally you can pick up weapons from more or less everywhere, same with shields, but they are just sparse enough to make you keep swapping them out.
Actual fighting is a little messy, since its all on a 2-D plane and normally its you VS three or four dudes at a time, all of which can attack as quickly as you. When you use the shield you create a barrier in the direction your arrow is facing, and anything that hits it is blocked, but this costs durability. Some shields offer bigger barriers than others, meaning it is possible to crack someone over the head with a hammer even if they are defending. The AI in this game is pretty good, as they will block if they have the time and will dodge attacks unless your quick and aim well. Its not so hard that its impossible, just that it requires good amount of concentration.
Visually, the game is very unique, its designed to look like the side of those greek vases, and it is pulled off really nicely. The soundtrack is also a rather lovely bit of work, you don't notice it much, but when you do its nicely themed and well composed.
The game also drops alot of greek mythology lore on you from start to finish, both in the form of actual levels and tablets that are scattered about. Its interesting to see how they use some of the tales, oh, and before you ask, yes, you do fight a chimera.
Its not the kind of game you'd use to teach people about greek mythology, but it is a game that you can play if your looking for a 2-D, budget God of War, or if your looking for a truly unique and overall satisfying experience in the form of a greek Metroidvania game.

The Darkness 2 is what I like to classify as a power-fantasy game. You will often find yourself wading into enemies, shooting and tearing your enemies to pieces all around you. Health and cover are not a huge issue as you can tear the hearts out of fallen/staggered foes for a health boost on the fly.
The game also boasts what they call "quad-wielding"; allowing you to use your demon tendrils as an extra 2 hands. This lets you actively grab items and enemies, hold shields or use the tendrils as a close range whip; all while keeping your actual hands free to fire your guns. The combat is fast and furious and feels very satisfying.
An interesting mechanic is the fact that your Darkness powers don't work in the light, and your enemies in the mid-late parts of the game know this. Enemies will come at you with shoulder mounted spotlights and employ flashbangs to try and slow you down. It keeps it interesting as the enemy with the light instantly becomes your priority regardless of the armored shotgunners 10 feet away from you.
The story is engaging and fun, but is not too long. You play the head of a mafia family with powers known as "The Darkness" as your organization engages in all out war with an ancient dark cult intent on stealing your powers and killing anyone in their way. Definitely not a plot you come across often! Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who thinks this sounds interesting as I had lots of fun with it!

Let me be fairly honest: I was not a big fan of the first Darkness game. While the ideas inside it were interesting, the sluggish gameplay, frustrating controls, and a severe shortage of actual times one may actually feel like they are a vessel for all of the chaos in the universe. I took the game as an interesting idea that fell flat.
This game, in contrast, did pretty much everything right.  A new, comic-book inspired look that harkens back to the story's roots, a large amount of gore, and a few entertaning side characters keeps the tone from becoming too serious, and the gameplay itself is not afraid to let you have a sort of power trip, being able to rip through large squads of men with a sort of balletic ease. The controls make enough sense for this to be a viable option. The Darkness in many ways is treated like an extra set of arms, which opens up a surprising amount of flexibility in combat, allowing players to keep focus on multiple enemies in a fairly natural manner.
One minor recommendation: play this one with a controller, if you can. While I'm sure the mouse and keyboard controls are serviceable, the mapping that was on my X-Box controller was so intuitive I don't ever remember being confused by the controls.

As a fan of the original Darkness game, i was left wondering if the sequel would deliver on the same level. While the game is fun, it doesnt have the same emotional kick as the original. Though, it does try, and succeed to a point.
The gameplay is solid, and standard FPS controls apply. Fighting entirely with the Darkness is exceedingly difficult to do, so you'll spend most of your time wielding guns. Unlike in the original, you can't simply impale an enemy with a darkness attack.
Using the Darkness is however, extremely fun. I found myself trying to spear as many enemies onto a wall as possible with whatever object that came to hand. The execution styles i never used much, i tended to just perform health executions, and there are about three execution animations for each type.
The game is bloody, and the graphics are enjoyable, though they're clearly meant to take on a more comic like feel, which it doesnt always succeed in. The game is surprisingly short in comparision to the original, and i finished it in just under five hours of play. I've logged more hours just trying to find collectables, and nailling enemies to walls. (Don't judge me!) it's a fun game overall, with a good amount of story depth, basic controls, and occasionally amusing dialogue. It's held back by how limited the Darkness powers are, in comparison to the comics, as well as how short the game is.
Definitely good for a play, though maybe wait for it to be on sale.

There are two games here. One of them is PyreBall, which is a sort of fantasy spin on 3 vs. 3 basketball: which is quick, hectic, and tactical. The other part is CYOA roleplaying: talking with characters, planning your journey, and travelling. What brings all these aspects together is a pure, child-like sense of amazement, and the sheer joy of wandering around and discovery, rather than going towards a certain destination. This weird, beautiful, and amazing world will remind you of when you read Narnia, Earthsea, or watched Spirited Away for the first time. This is the best game by SuperGiant so far, and a labor of love.

The Ultimate Doom takes the exceptional and timeless first person shooting classic Doom and adds a single new episode to the already three episode game. The problem with the Steam version is that it comes with an old version of DOSBox which crashes on startup. That's probably why this game is on sale so often for as cheap as it is. Sure you can download a new version of DOSBox or even go find a great source port like GZDoom to run the game, but the fact is one of the two of them should come with this Steam version. It should work out of the box, otherwise, I can go tell you "go find a PC from the 90s and you'll be fine playing this." Why should there be that extra step involved? When you buy a hot dog, does the vendor tell you go across the street to cook it? What's odd is that Doom 2 works with its DOSBox, but the Master Levels and Final Doom crash on startup.
If you really want to play the game straight out of the box, the Doom 3: BFG Edition comes with a playable version of Doom 1, Doom 2, the Master Levels for Doom 2 and more. That's what you want to pick up. You can still use source ports, mods and .wad files for that. What if you need the Ultimate Doom? There are Doom bundles on Steam that you should look into as a cheaper alternative to purchasing just this game.
Doom lives on forever. Its a game that's over twenty years old has been kept alive by the fans and its still going strong today with mods. I've played Doom over twenty years on multiple source ports with multiple .wad level packs made by the community. The source ports are engines to run the old game on modern technology. There are dozens of them, all free. I mentioned GZDoom before, and that's the finest way to play Brutal Doom that everyone has been talking about for the past year or more.
For those unaware, who have made it past my explanation, Doom is the father of all first person shooters and its predecessor Wolfenstien 3D is the grandfather or great grandfather at this point. Before first person shooters had their own genre, they were called Doom clones.
There is no story here beyond the back story that's unavailable unless you have the instruction manual from two decades ago. Demons have invaded and its up to only you. There are a few cut scenes after each episode as a reward and a calm moment to take a breather from all the chaos.
Doom puts you down into a science fiction, demonic, almost psychotic setting on Phobos for the first episode. Then Diemos for the second,  and Hail itself for the third. Where the game becomes Ultimate Doom is that fourth challenging, tough and yet fun fourth campaign.
Although Ultimate Doom came after Doom 2, the elements of Ultimate Doom are only from the original game. There are no new weapons, enemies or anything else other than a new orange sky for the fourth episode. Its more of the same fantastic game.
So what makes Doom so fantastic? Its simplicity. You are alone, kill everything that moves. Doom is known for being unable to move your mouse up or down. If an enemy is above or below you, your character will still shoot them, but you just have no way to look down on them.
Doom's combat is fast paced. Your character already moves fast, he can strafe and turn at a swift speed, but then he can also run to dash over small gaps. There is no jump button, why would you need one when you can dodge everything and the game is full of staircases and lifts to take you where you need to go.
Beyond fast paced action, you'll need to flip switches, open doors and hump walls looking for secret entrances. If you ever get lost, there's an easy to use map. There's a lot of exploration in the game and for every eight levels per episode there's a hidden secret level. You'll find soul spheres, backpacks that let you double your maximum amount of ammunition. Armor will take some damage and you'll need med kits and stim packs to restore your health.
Death will restart the level with a mere pistol, but you can save as often as you'd like. Every trap that has you falling into toxic waste, lava or something that hurts you will always have a platform to lower so you can escape. Its always a fair game like that.
At the end of each level, you're given a time, a par time, and percentages for kills, secrets and items. Having percentages and times is a good take on a score to keep you immersed in the game. There are five levels of difficulty. The nightmare requires a lot more strategy because enemies respawn a brief time after you've slaughtered them.
In terms of weapons, you start with a pistol, there's a shotgun that you can use as a sniper rifle. A chaingun that uses pistol ammunition, a plasma rifle that does more damage. Then there's a rocket launcher that does splash damage and you can watch enemies explode into mush. To top it all off, you'll find the BFG 9000 that uses plasma rifle's cell ammunition, but it can wipe out a lot of enemies. Its one of the more fastening weapons. It takes a moment to fire, it has a giant slow particle that when it smashes against something it melts a large radius of enemies.
The environments diverse array of colors and areas feel different from one another. Metallic bases, rocky mountains, red glowing lava caverns, rivers of toxic waste, bodies behind bars, walls of faces and marble structures. Areas are bright, some are dark, others have flickering lights. This is a horror action game rather than a scary atmospheric romp. Just know your shotgun will keep you safe and even when you're out of bullets you can run faster than a sports car. Who needs to run though when you have your fists and can find a chainsaw?
The enemies are a nice diverse array of creatures that ramp up as the game progresses. There is a set of two zombie soldiers, one with a pistol, the other with a shotgun. These two are more of a challenge to grant you a bit of ammunition. They still manage to be dangerous on higher difficulties, because they have hitscan weapons, meaning that if they can see you.
Larger foes like imps throw fireballs that let you dodge them before they hit you. Cacodemons hover and posture to belch lightning balls at you. Pinkie demons and spectres take a lot of damage and get in your face, but they're still quick enough to dodge your crosshair when they're a distance away. Lost souls dash forward and bash into you. Barons are grand versions of imps that throw plasma balls and take a lot of punishment. Beyond those enemies are two bosses that cap off the second and third episodes. A giant beast with a rocket launcher as an arm and a spider mastermind with a chaingun hitscan weapon that will keep hitting you with no cover.
The Ultimate Doom is a fantastic game, its just that it should be playable when you buy it. However, Doomers are known for digging through folders and getting programs to work. There are a lot of ways to get this to work and chances are if you're reading this you've already played Doom before, so go play Doom, but play it elsewhere than this specific version.

On a serious note:
This is the mother of shooters (next to Wolfenstein 3d being...the grandmother then?)
Who does not know Doom?
Doom pretty much made the fundament of what shooters are today. We cannot deny doom did nothing, they pretty much started with shooters back then, of course they had to test things. Why not demons? Ok, let's use demons and see how people react. And oh boy...what an impact it had, has and will still have. Let's be honest: Am I the only one who thinks E1M1's soundtrack (1. level) is pretty much the best? I am no big fan of metal, but omg, that one just makes me wanna go off an shoot demons! ...wait, that is the actual setting of the game...
What can I really say about the gameplay...well...the original controls were the arrow pads while Ctrl (I think) being the shooting button.  you have weak enemies, having a pistol or a shotgun, tankers, dealing mediocre damage but being able to take a lot of damage, and ememies, who are just strong, having the ability to fly and deal a lot of damage or just take a lot of damage and dealing a lot. Every enemy has a specific weakness, each one's different. Ofc, a BFG 9000 (i'll talk about the weapons soon) is definetly effective against everyone, but wasting that ammo for some Imps? Not useful. Ammo management is also important, so dont just foolishly spend your minigunammo. Use the shotgun or rocketlauncher, depending on the situation.
So we can say, the game requires you to think (*cough* COD *cough*)
The weapon choice is alright. In total, we have 8 weapons. The fists (pretty much your last choice you should use. DO NOT), the chainsaw (TIMBER), the shotgun (in Doom 2 we also have the double barreled shotgun), the pistol (semi-useful against weak enemies), the chaingun (your "rifle" in this game, sharing the pistol ammo), the rocketlauncher (dont need to add anything), the plasmarifle (strong, fast shooting rifle) and the BFG 9000, sharing the plasmarifle ammo (its name really is Big ♥♥♥♥ing Gun 9000). you will know how to use them when playing. BFG of course is the weapon against everything using 60 plasmarifle ammo. while the chaingun is actually useful against everything, it will show its weakness against tanks or high-HP enemies (you will have to use a lot of ammo). Again, the ammomanagement but also the weaponvariety back then! Think of it!
The last point I want to talk about are the maps:
We have 4 chapters with 9 levels each (if I am not mistaken). each of them isnt just like a narrow path you have to follow, you sometimes have to do some backtracking to collect that one keycard you need for the final door. Or you have to solve a little puzzle to reach the end of the level/the next segment of the game. Enemies are placed in a good way, not bothering you but still surprising you at least a bit. And, many people sadly don't know this anymore: Secrets! For those picky people not living with the fact letting bits o' loot in a level, you can look for secrets! Some are quite easy to solve (walking against a wall, pressing the interaction key, normally space; or shooting against a wall) while others require you to think (eg you have to walk back to a specific point of the map and then running afap to the elevator, leading you to the secret). Something for everybody: not too narrow and challenging!
Oh, the game has 5 difficulties. the first and second are not worth to try. go for the third or fourth, depending on how tough you think you are. DO NOT TRY NIGHTMARE. DO. NOT. DO. IT.
But if you do, record it and show the world you are one of the best players around. Only a few managed to speedrun nightmare (as far as I know). It's really hard. For more informations what NIGHTMARE covers, look it up.
One last tip:
Use a "newer" software for Doom. DosBos is ~quite~ alright, but I highly recommend programs like zandronum. It automatically sees similar doom programs (mods) and plays them with but a single doubleclick with the doom engine.

10/10; well worth the price of a lunch for two.

This game is a great puzzler, starting out very simple and gradually getting slightly trickier. I completed it fairly quickly, as there are only 50 levels at the time of writing this review.
The gameplay itself is very straightforward once you get the hang of what you are even supposed to be doing. Every hook in a level is connected to a wire, each wire connected to one, or several buttons. You basically have to figure out which wires to move and which buttons to press, to reel in the hooks without them catching on each other.
The game doesn't hold your hand at all, never telling you what you should be doing or how. It just throws you in to figure it out for yourself. As you get to the harder levels, the game introduces a 3-strike system, rather than making you restart the whole level for 1 mistake. This is represented by three dots that appear to the left of your screen.
Overall it is a solid game from the creator of 'Klocki' and the main reason I bought it on Steam, was that I enjoyed it on Android a while ago. The only downsides I can think of are; it's quite short. So if you are good at logic puzzles, then this game will only last you for around an hour, tops.
The games difficulty doesn't increase very consistently. You can be on a really hard run of puzzles and then the next one is suddenly super-easy.
However, even with these few minor gripes, I would still very highly recommend this game.

Date reviewed: 30/07/2016
Genre: Indie minimalist puzzle/casual game
My overall score: 9/10 Strong recommendation
Overall summary: HOOK is a very interesting indie puzzle game. Built on a simple premise of manipulating switches in a network to uncouple hooks (without any conflict between hooks), its a game that appears simple initially but will get complex quickly. While I believe there is no replayability, and there is a bug from getting you the only achievement, I was left satisfied by the experience.
Things I liked about this game:
+ Easy to learn concept, but not too simplified - as I mentioned, you will have to use your logic to uncouple/retract hooks without any contact between them. While I personally found the first 30 or so levels to be fairly straightforward, the last 15-20 levels will seriously test your logic/puzzle skills.
+ Very minimalist, quick into the game - I was happy that the game didn't include any tutorial and let me figure it out for myself. It makes you feel clever and is very rewarding when you solve the puzzles (kinda like the feeling of completing Sudokus)
+ Aesthetic & music design - I liked the game design, and I thought this was complimented by the simple, but relaxing, music. The music is never annoying, and seems to encourage you everytime you solve a hook correctly.
Things I disliked about this game:
- No replayability - after 50 total levels and 2.5 hours of playtime, I would probably never play it again. While this is ok for $0.99 price (or your regional equivalent), I can see for some people this might be a problem.
- Achievement bug - There is only 1 achievement in this game which is supposed to reward you upon completing all levels. While this might seem a little nitpicky, I was not happy that after 2.5 hours I didn't get this achievement because of a bug.

This is an "old school" Telltale game, designed before the release of the Walking Dead.  As such, the gameplay is really different.  In the newer Telltale games, you're basically playing a story generator with minimal puzzles to solve.  In Back to the Future, you spend much of your time trying to solve puzzles like an older adventure/point-and-click game.
I would recommend this game, but there are probably people who are fans of the newer Telltale games that wouldn't like it.  If you played (and liked) the Sam and Max games, you'll like this one.

The art style is what got me curious about the game and eventually to try it out. The story is pretty much what you'd expect from a tale involving an ancient Greek mythology setting: Nothing special, but keeps you working towards a clear goal and has a satisfying conclusion. The progression is fairly linear, though in some sections you can choose the order you want to complete the objectives and there are some optional ones as well.
The gameplay consists mainly of you fighting your way towards the current objective using a variety of different melee and ranged weapons. Combat takes a while to get used to as you're generally better off dodging or blocking first and delay attacking until there's an opportunity to do so. Some twists are thrown into the combat formula mix later, like the possibility of placing or using environmental traps or flinging large boulders at enemies. Movement and combat controls feel fluent for a controller, but I can't say how it would play out using a mouse and keyboard.
Some sections contain minor puzzle elements and require something a bit different than just travelling from point A to B. I wouldn't exactly call this a "metroidvania" -game though despite being tagged as such. To me that term implies that there is and exploration element and backtracking involved i.e. that there are (optional) power ups that allow you to access parts of the game that you can't when you first encounter them. Now there are some secret areas and things to discover here and there, but they're not gated behind the powers you unlock while progressing through the main story.
I had to give up on my completionist habit quickly as there's just an overabundance of breakable things and chests to loot and they rarely contain anything useful. That leads to the biggest issue I had with the game: The loot, crafting and the light RPG elements felt a bit tacked on. You can purchase better armor and attack training for various weapon types, but I didn't notice the effects of the upgrades in my ability to survive in combat. The crafting options are quite limited and I was mostly crafting health potions and bombs to blow up cracked walls.
All the weapons and shields, even the special ones, also have a duration and they wear down when used in combat. That made the special weapons feel more like consumable resources rather than actual difference making equipment upgrades and I think that also took away some of the strategy in combats. There are some weapon specific combat mechanics, such as you can destroy enemy shields with hammer weapons, have longer range with spears etc. but I just didn't bother since everything just breaks eventually. I frequently found myself just using whatever I had in my hand at the time until it broke down and a new weapon popped up from the inventory.
As final, shorter side notes: Music and sound effects did their job, but nothing apart from the (occasionally over-)dramatic voice acting stood out for me. The game also crashed on me once and unfortunately it happened when I tried to save, so the save file got corrupted. Luckily the game auto saves so I could pick up from the latest of those without losing too much progress.
I was expecting an exploration-focused, Zelda II-esque game where you wander around, talk to people in towns, accept side quests, buy stuff etc. but unfortunately it didn't turn out to be exactly like that. Although I was slightly disappointed with some aspects of the game and the gameplay not having much variety, it might be worth checking out even if just for the neat visual style.
