TL;DR - Great weapon variety, level design variety, and beautiful art. A bit clunky combat where you never feel totally in control, and occasional glitchiness.
The game's got beautiful art and an impressive array of level design, with combat-heavy areas, puzzle-solving areas, exploration-based areas, some minor side quests, it's great. The story is pretty hands-off, but it works. Feels more like you are exploring and choosing where you want to go next, it's nice. There are tons of different weapons to use. I sort of wish the weapon drops were less plentiful, as I felt like I never had a shortage of weapons. In games where there is weapon degradation/breakage, you want to save the best weapons for after the crappy ones have broken, or for important parts. The crappy ones just keep coming though, so you never switch to the good ones when they run out, cause they don't. Bit of OCD annoyance there.
The one notable negative to the game is that the combat feels awkward. I think they designed it to seem realistic? There's no true combo system, making it an exchanging-blows affair in the end. However, you can zip around super fast, switch weapons super fast, but regardless of those unrealistic factors, the weapons never feel like you can wield them effectively in comparison. Slow clunky stabs/slashes, and the idea that you have to be a certain distance from an enemy (ie, if you're too close, it won't hit) with weapons like a spear ends up making combat awkward, especially against multiple opponents on the higher difficulty modes where you flinch when being hit. You get used to it after a while, but it's sort of aggravating. Moreover, there's a dodge roll, but no invulnerability frames on it. What's the point?
It's kind of glitchy sometimes. Enemies that throw you wind up the throw with you in hand, and if you're near a wall when grabbed you'll for a moment phase through the wall. This instant-kills you. Extremely annoying, happened to me 3-4 times in the playthrough. There should never be instant death on going out of bounds. That's lazy.
Aside from those two issues, the game itself is fun to explore and experience. Collecting and trying out different weapons feels good, the soundtrack is suitable, with a couple of somewhat memorable fanfares amidst a mostly atmospheric set of audio tracks. The level design variation is probably the best aspect, regardless of which God's area you enter, there's always a different setting and gameplay style to experience. Great stuff. In the end, if you can get over the combat, which does get a bit more enjoyable at the end due to upgrades, it's totally recommendable.

What would look like yet another quality video game from Supergiant Games ends up selling itself short in the one department that matters for this medium; the video game portion of it.
Pyre is a fantasy quest similar to The Oregon Trail where, to an extent, your choices end up mattering enough to have the game decide the fates of you and your party, and I'll at least say it's a very unique experience. The gameplay portions compromise of something similar to basketball, or Final Fantasy X's Blitzball mini game to an extent, where you control a party of 3 interchangable members and fight against other "teams" to take the "ball" and shoot it into the opposing "goal." Obviously each of these has their own fantasy terms, but I'm simplifying it to give the reader an understanding of what they're getting into.
And really that's as simple as it gets. One of Pyre's major weaknesses is how barebones the gameplay aspects of it are. While different tech exists and each character (to an extent) plays differently enough to vary themselves from one another, there isn't much depth aside fom each race just functioning differently from one another. And the game never takes advantage of this as much as I'd like it to similar how Bastion's weapon upgrades provided a far more unique experience depending on what you relied more on as the game went on, nor does it get to a fun game-breaking compromise like Transistor did with how many different elements and powers you could mix and match to make each encounter feel unique. Pyre has none of that, where the most upgrades you'll acquire in this trip will amount to making your character slightly faster, making their aura slightly bigger, slightly reducing stamina consumption, and so forth.
To those that have already experienced Pyre and question why I'm harping on so much about this, the gameplay, might also understand where I'm at least coming from. Where in Bastion and Transistor, the video game itself co-existed with the game's narrative and story-telling, now the gameplay takes a much un-needed backseat to the story itself. While Bastion had minor interruptions or break points when you return to the hub every time you explore a world, or Transistor gives itself a break after every couple of battles to let you examine a codex or read up on a passed away citizen, Pyre does the complete opposite, letting you take a break from mashing through text with a 3 minute match of basketball. And while "mashing through text" is harsh, as I will admit that the rest of the game itself is amazing, from its visuals to its soundtrack to the amount of time and effort was put in crafting this world, its story, its characters, and so forth, it doesn't nor will it ever feel right to see what should be the most important aspect, the gameplay, being used to give players a break, rather than the other way around.
And as such, this becomes an incredibly hard game to recommend to others. $20 is a hefty price for a product that is essentially an interactive book, and while I would like many people to experience this adventure, it's hard to justify the support of a product that can essentially give the same exact experience if you were you just watch a playthrough of it instead. And that's really harsh to say about the game, because I spent an obscene amount of time playing the other games prior. I just don't see myself coming back to Pyre after this initial playthrough, regardless of the minor story changes that could await me on multiple playthroughs.
I'd say either get this game on a sale (obviously) or give it a download when it inevitably comes to Playstation Plus's "Free" Game program as Transistor did.

The Darkness is a pretty standard shooter with a little superpowers thrown in for good measure. The single-player is fairly well balanced if a little on the easy side even on the harder difficulties. The story is surprisingly decent and grey and gritty enough that you won't feel like vomiting too often.
The premise is simple enough. There is this thing, a being of pure evil, called The Darkness. It can't interact directly with our world so it needs to attach itself to a human being giving that individual incredible powers as well as slowly corrupting that person. You play as Jackie who's family is tied to the Darkness is some way that was probably explained in the detail in the first game, you have the Darkness inside you but somehow managed to contain it, until a weird old guy who knows a little bit of magic himself shows up and tries to kill you and everybody you know. You quickly abandon logic, unleash the Darkness and go on a killing spree.
The game plays out as a standard shooter most of the time with a few added elements, as the wielder of the Darkness you have two big snake like creatures growing out your body that can be used to hit things, grab things and eat things. You are also handicapped by being vulnerable to light. While a shooter with superpowers isn't exactly a new thing it plays fairly well, the combat is fluid as are the transitions between shooting at people and slashing them with your pet snakes.
The storyline is, much to my surprise, fairly well written and while not given you much choice it does ask a number of questions about morality and reality. The ending in particular will be a surprise to most players. In addition there is a decent amount of lore and back story available to those that seek it.
It all has one major flaw however, it's length. Even playing the game to 100% completion, which requires at least two playthroughs of the main campaign as well as playing through a number of multi-player mini-campaigns will only take you a little over 10-12 hours and that is quite simply unacceptable for a game that was originally marketed with a full 50$ price tag.
The graphic style is generally a bit cartoonish which contrasts heavily with the stark and grim story and gameplay.
All in all The Darkness 2 is a decent enough play, and some good fun with a couple of friends. It is however not a game you should ever contemplate buying at full price simply because of it's extremely short lifespan.

This review is 100% spoilers free and discusses why some people did not like the game.
First of all I would like to address that Transistor is my favorite game on Steam and Bastion is not far from there. I spent +60 hours in each one of them and absolutely love them. Supergiant Games however are famous for creating a totally new and differenet experience in each of their games, going from action RPG to mostly strategy and finally to some weird visual novel party based fantasy sport. I expected that Pyre would be different than the other two but some fans did not, they expected Supergiant to do their famous gimmick in which they blend the story telling in the middle of the gameplay. I personally believe that Supergiant should not be stricted to a system just because they perfected it and were famous for it, they might try something totally different
. I can understand why they want Supergiant to stick with their old system but that does not justify the negative reviews on the game just because of its genre is visual novel and did not use the same gimmick as the previous two games.
+ Amazing story which you can dive into as deep as you are interested.
+ Memorable unique characters, you might love some of them you might hate the others but in the end they're all interesting which creates the connection between you and them.
+ Do I even need to talk about the soundtrack? Darren Korb kills it again here.
+ Art style is absolutely gorgeous and developes an awesome atmosphere that pulls you into the game, in my opinion one of the best arts in video games by far.
+ The core gameplay (The Rites) is a lot of fun with great character differences and variety of play styles. You might find it too easy at the beginning, well, wait and see how the game can give you a good challenge if you're willing to accept it.
+ The RPG elements in the game are important and highly customizable, whether it's the items or chatacter upgrades.
+ On a technical level my mind is blown by how the story goes by with the decision making and your wins and losses. It's like every and each player will get its very own different story than the other. I played Telltale games and The Witcher but this one stands out among them as the highest number of possible results you can get. Like even in some major choice matters I found that my options were totally different than my friend's because of how we approched the game and our relationship with the Characters.
- I personally do not think this is a con but some people might be bored with the too much reading in the game and that is why I stated that Pyre is close to be a visual novel. So if you hate reading a lot of dialogues this might not be the perfect game for you.
- The core gameplay (The Rites) could've taken more parts in the story since each match lasts only like 4 minutes, that is not something annoying or negative in the game I just think it could've been a little bit better.
- My only take on Supergiant games is that they should've mentioned how Pyre is close to be a visual novel so that their fans who played Bastion and Transistor can understand the major changes happened here, in other words the game description is missing some elements.
I find Pyre to be one of the best games I ever played so far especially in terms of story and choice matters. The characters are strong part of the game and influence your choices a lot. The soundtrack and art style are on a different level. And last but not least the core gameplay is well thought and really entertaining and much deeper than what you think which most visual novels don't usually devolop.
Thanks for reading.

This is not a typical mobile or browser or facebook games like Top Eleven or OSM or Hattrick. The potential of this game is enormous, but it's true that the game at current stage is still far from what it can become.
About gameplay, you create a team, buy/sell players, playing matches in many different FA or Cup etc. a season lasts one month.
Most of the game design decisions are very thoughtful e.g. FA based on timezone so you can play games online, transfer took 24 hours to make sure people from all timezone can bid etc.
Having played quite many titles in Steam, I have not seen better Dev/Designer who is passionate and talented like Nick. I truly recommend this title.

Velvet Assassin is a fantastic game, with the elements and features that make third person spy/stealth games great. I found this game genuinely chilling and has numerous dark themes throughout. The devs really nailed it when it comes to the enemies in this game - I quickly learned how hostile and realistically powerful they are. This combined with their ferocious barks in German made me genuinely dread running into one around a corner, or being exposed in broad daylight in near proximity. Playing through each of the somewhat diverse levels (all of which are very dark and gritty - don't expect sunshine, mountains and waterfalls), requires logical thinking. I say this in terms of traversing between light and shadow, and studying each guards movement patterns before moving forth, being prime examples. I like this element as I felt even more engaged in the role of Violette, and in the precarious situations with her.
Despite the challenging and what I found to be personally enjoyable gameplay, I found the storyline was Velvet Assassin's greatest downfall. Throughout the game I found myself puzzled as to where Violette's fight for the Resistance would lead, and did not understand the relation between missions during early parts of the game. It was during the latter portion that I developed a better understanding for her purpose and started seeing a connection between the missions. This is the part of the review which will explain how my player-engagement and excitement quickly turned sour. It was only just as I was becoming heavily invested in the story, that I was completely disappointed.
Velvet Assassin, has one of the most disappointing endings to a video game I have EVER seen.
I of course will not reveal why, as I am not going to spoil the ending. But it was incredibly disappointing.
I would still recommend this game for people to play, for all the other gameplay positives I have highlighted in this review, however I am still shocked by this game's conclusion.

BTTFTG is firstly a puzzle game, secondly a narrative. I personally thought the narrative was more intriguing than the puzzles because they were getting kinda frustrating (knowing exactly what you need to do but not knowing the specific way of triggering it). Despite the frustration, however, the story kept me going because I wanted to see where it was going.
While I found it enjoyable, and I would recommend it, you have to realise that this predates the Telltale Games where you actually get to make decisions that change the story. There are no branching decisions, simply following the narrative. It is not the best Telltale Game ever, but it's an enjoyable one.
What really stands out for me was how messed up the time travel started getting, but because each episode is about two hours, you can follow it easily because each episode only adds one layer to the mess which is what lets it reach the chaotic climax.
That being said, I wouldn't spend full price on it. But does anyone really buy games on Steam except during sales??

Now a little rundown of my play through because it is a weird story to tell XD
(Warning, story has death and sadness :steammocking: enjoy)
Started the game with my family, me Christo, my husband Mr.Unknown, my sons Naruto and Sasuke XD (Nerd much hay XD).
Diary Entry - day 8
After a week in the shelter things seem to have gotten quite cozy, but all of a sudden Sasuke got sick … and I couldn’t help … the antibiotics didn’t work … nor did the anti-rads … so we watched him slowly die in front of us …
Diary Entry - day 11
After a few days of scavenging, we finally have enough resources to build a grave for Sasuke ... we needed to get rid of him … seeing your own child’s carcass is just too much to handle, especially for his brother …
Diary Entry - day 15
After my husband and Naruto came back from a scavenging trip things seemed off, none of us noticed it, and before we could help it Mr.Unknown passed away from radiation poisoning … it’s been days since we’ve had a meal … and lacking the resources to build a grave but having the resources to build a fridge only means one thing … we … we have to eat him … to keep on living … for Naruto and me to see another day …
Diary Entry – day 20
I and Naruto came back after scavenging the wasteland a bit, unfortunately, he got wounded and just wouldn’t stop bleeding, we had no bandages left … and no able bodies to go search for more materials and slowly we had to wait for his time to run out…
Diary Entry – day 21
We have space in the fridge … no food left … but I refuse to do to Naruto what I did to my late husband … I will not eat my child … I could not eat my child …
Diary Entry – day 22
We have buried Naruto, my new shelter buddies seem friendly, but I don’t trust them yet
Diary Entry – day 40
Since my last entry things have about been the same, I found myself surrounded by strangers, not caring about their or my own safety … how long is this nightmare going to last…
Diary Entry – day 219
I have finally done it all, travelled further than what my legs should have carried me, scavenged more than a cities worth of scrap, fixed the Caravan, upgraded all the shelters assets, and today I finally caught my 100’th animal … and after achieving all my goals I retire, I will go out into the wasteland, leaving behind the shelter I have built, loved, and lost. And now wait for the sweet embrace of death, to see my family once more.

I love platformer games.  They're such a nostalgia blast, taking me back to the old days where I was parked on the living room floor, 5 ft. from the TV trying master that epic double jump without falling in the hole for the 10th time in a row.  Rayman Origins came along and proved that that old school platforming action could still be viable, fun and challenging.  Now, Rayman Legends has managed to come along and actually improve on the foundation that Origins laid!
Rayman Legends packs a ton of fun in one single package.  You have unlocks to collect, in the form of lums, characters, monsters and even old Origins levels.  You have challenging platformer action.  You have varied platformer action!  You have a great sense of humor.  You have a great art style to make it all shine.  It's really great.
Sometimes, games of these types reach a point where the game becomes too difficult.  It makes the experience nothing but frustrating and then the fun falls off fast.  Even Origins suffered from this from time to time.  In Legends, they've managed to find a perfect balance in the difficulty.  Most maps are challenging, without becoming anger inducing.  You might have to take two or three tries and a particular jump, but the pattern will click.  These types of games can also suffer from repetition, but Legends break that up as well.  You'll find the puzzle style changing from level to level, even within the same groups, keeping the game feeling fresh and entertaining.
Beyond all the platformer action, I'm really impressed with the style and art direction going on in the game.  The end levels in each section doing something really great in how the tie in the games music with the game play.  This really stood out when I was playing a boss level to a Rayman-esque rendition of Ram Jam's "Black Betty".  As I came to obstacles, it because clear my jumps were timed to the drum beat of the song.  As you progressed, hearing that familiar back beat, you noticed the entire level was timed to it.  I couldn't help by smile and play the level over a couple times, just to marvel at the fun of it all.  They do this on every level and it's an attention to detail that you don't see to often!
So, should you snag Rayman Legends?  Yes.  Yes you should.  Don't even debate it.  Really, this game is worth it at any price.  Definitely bring your game pad though, I can't imagine pulling this game off with a keyboard and mouse.

Sniper Elite V2 was given away free for a day by Steam a while back, and it went into my backlog because I usually prefer shooters over stealth games. Fortunately, Sniper V2 blends the two genres together successfully and most of the stealth sections are where you’re trying to get to a good enough position to headshot your targets. The game’s difficulty is more customizable than most shooters, so whether you want to casually murder some people from long range, or sneak around silently lining up the perfect muffled shot, it’s up to you.
The game takes place during the latter days of World War 2, with you playing the part of an American sniper behind enemy lines in Nazi Germany picking off high value targets as well as trying to get your hands on certain German scientists. The race is on between the US and Soviet Union to grab up all the best Nazi scientists before the other side gets their paws on them. In this case, you’re looking for the scientists who worked on the Nazi V2 rocket program (long range missiles).
The gameplay for Sniper Elite V2 is third person shooter except when using the sniper rifle scope, which is first person.  The game is broken up into distinct missions, each being about half an hour long, and you start with all your equipment right from the start of each mission. You have your trusty sniper rifle, a Thompson machine gun, and a silenced pistol, as well as a couple of explosive items such as land mines and trip mines. You can switch out your machine gun with weapons from fallen enemies, but it’s generally a bad idea because the guns you find on the ground have like 5 bullets left in them. Besides, you shouldn’t be using the machine gun much anyways if you’re sneaking around as much as you ought to be.
Despite how important being sneaky is, the stealth system in Sniper Elite V2 is not heavily developed. You just crouch down and you’ll be walking silently. There is a colored arrow indicator when enemies are close to spotting you (kind of like Far Cry 3) except it usually happens so fast that as soon as you see it, you’re probably going to be caught.  When you get spotted, an alarm goes up and all the nearby enemies will start gunning for you at your last known location. The game uses a regenerating health system so as long as you don’t take damage for a few seconds, you survive. Of course you shouldn’t really be getting shot much anyways since the highlight of the game is long range sniping.
When looking through the scope you have the ability to hold your breath and focus in (steady your aim) on targets as long as you have enough stamina. If you manage a long range shot to an enemy’s vital organs (brain, liver, heart, etc.) the game will do a slow motion kill cam where you see the enemy in x-ray with the bullet piercing through and busting stuff up. It’s pretty cool in the beginning, especially if you just made a really long range shot. The game’s ballistics options let you decide if you want realistic sniper shooting with bullet travel time, bullet drop over distance, and wind trajectory, if you enjoy missing a lot.
Pros:
+A fun game if you like sniper action. You vs a bunch of soldiers firing at each over long distances. Boom Headsot! If there are bombs dropping the background, you can use the sound of the explosions to cover the sound of your rifle shots. The bad guys won’t even know they’re being picked off one at a time as long as they don’t see bodies. Once the alarm is raised though, just kill everyone.
+The stealth sections are fun for the most part when you sneak around with your silenced pistol. The game uses checkpoint saving, so you may end up replaying some sections over and over trying not to get spotted. There’s a Steam achievement for getting through a particular area without being caught and I must have played that section a dozen times before I made it through.
+Some multiplayer options are available and there seem to still be people playing the game online. In one multiplayer mode, you can co-op with a friend as your spotter who tags enemies for you to snipe.
Cons:
-You really do spend a lot of time crouched down trying to be sneaky, which greatly slows your movement speed. So many times I just want to run from point A to B, but I know if I don’t sneak I’ll probably be heard and need to restart the checkpoint. It can be frustrating for someone used to moving fast because unlike some other stealth games, you have no way of knowing whether or not there’s an enemy nearby unless you can directly see him (you don’t have an enemy radar).
-There’s not too much variety in gameplay/weapons. You get maybe 3 different types of sniper rifle found through the story, but really they’re pretty much the same. I think the better ones just have larger clips or an additional level of zoom.
Overall the game is fun if you just want to get some sniper action and kill a bunch of Nazis. And as a bonus, you may already have this game for free.

I think Apotheon might have gotten overlooked by many when it came out. It's a little sad, since the game is great. The multiplayer isn't maybe the greatest, but the campaign is in my opinion the sole reason to get the game. It's a great sidescrolling action-RPG experience which are actually quite rare these days. Completing the campaign takes somewhere around 10 hours, but there are a few optional bits around the place and there is room for replayability for achievement hunters.
If you're at all familiar with Greek mythology, visiting mount olympos and battling the different gods will probably feel awesome, especially with the absolutely GORGEOUS art style the game has. I mean just look at it, it's as if real pottery came to life. The combat is also potent and can be really fun especially when fighting harder enemies in single combat. It reminds me a little of games like Chivalry: Medieval Warfare for example, but with added rolling and jumping in a sidescrolling environment.
All in all, the game's visuals are justification enough for the purchase, and even though the multiplayer is a little dumbed down and the campaign can feel like it's over too soon, I would definetely recommend it. Especially during a sale.

Imagine Call of Duty where you mainly use a sniper rifle and a really bad machine gun all done in 3rd person camera. I can't recommend this game based solely on that but if that's what you like, then this may be for you. Essentially, the game has too many problems for me to have enjoyed it much: scripted events (what's that, you spent the last 10 minutes carefully picking off each soldier silently? Well, we'll just throw in a load of soldiers out of no where for fun...), switches quickly between stealth and guns blazing, awful AI that runs around like headless chickens, psychic AI that knows where you always are, NPCs that popup on trigger events, more linear than it wants to believe it is, secondary explosives that are really useful ... in the tutorial and very few other places (anyone else planted a mine on a guard in the rest of the game? No, me neither), bad hit detection, terrible level design and the NPC character models are quite jerky, making them difficult to hit on the move.
It's not a bad game, just not what I wanted from it although some of the game design seems a little lazy. It almost feels like they wanted to make some big open levels then ran out of time. I'd like to have seen this game in first person view, bigger, more open levels with a lot less scripting.
Fulfill your dream of being a lone wolf sniper, just don't expect the game to loosen the leash much.

I was in a milsim group called the 336th. I had the rank of PFC. (Private First Class). We had arrived in Takistan due to recent reports of Russian movement detected in the area. The mission objective was a Russian occupied town and the platoon was ordered to eliminate the threat. My squad was ordered to scout and secure an unknown fort to the north of the town while the Armor would drive into the town through the MSR once we confirmed to command that we secured the positon. As nightfall descended my squad loaded into a helicopter, it was dead quiet. My squad usually contained only 6 others including myself, that night it had 10. During the last AO another squad had been almost entirely wiped out due to their helicopter being shot down from AA. The remaining survivors merged with our squad for this mission.  We landed 2 klicks from our objective after our nerve wrenching ride. As we all rushed out of the helicopter we setup a 360 position around the helicopter while it dusted off. Once gone and we didn't take contact, our squad leader told us to move out as we formed a column behind the point man; giving a 10 m distance between each soldier. We moved along hillsides while avoid cresting on top of the hills, so we didn't attract unwanted attention. I was a autorifleman equipped with an M249 with 3 belts, one in the LMG; totaling 600 rounds. I also was carrying a light amount of medical equipment, extra barrel, side arm with 2 mags, a nvg set, a RCO for the gun, a short range radio for communication within the squad, and body armor with backpack. My squad mates always called me fat because of all the gear I had to carry which always gave me a smile on my face, so when I started to lag behind after moving 700m at a combat pace the Squad Lead decided to call for a stamina break. We formed another 360 perimeter grabbing any cover we could find along the hill. To pass the time some of the people in the squad started making banter over the fact that I was already exhausted, quickly followed by the SL barking at them. We reassumed the column once everyone was rested and continued to move out to our objective. After moving another 1200m west we spotted the fort. If you could call it that, it was a circle of sandbags and dirt trenches all in a circle surrounding a bigger wood and sandbag structure in the middle. We did recon on the location to find no hostiles occuping the construct, so the SL sent teams of three soldiers at a time towards the building while I provided cover fire incase they took contact while crossing the expanse of 100m between us and the fort. Once each soldier team was safetly across the SL radio'd in to me to move my a** over quickly. I sat up after being prone as quickly as I could and sprinted across the desert to my allies. As I approached only 1 squad mate was providing cover for me, so I assumed everyone else was on the otherside while they waited for me. I was entirely out of breath and crouched next to the east wall of the main structure to readjust my gear when the sound of a launcher echoed off the hill. It was a good thing I had earplugs in otherwise I wouldn't have been able to hear after the RPG hit the west side of the structure which was less than 10m from me. Thats when it hit me, mostly everyone other than myself and another soldier were on that side of the fort. I sat up as quickly as I could and rounded the corner of the north side of the structure with all the speed I could muster. I was met with a gruesome sight, I immediately saw blood and gore everywhere as three of my squad mates lay scattered across the ground in a mangled heap along the trench like on the west. I continued to find a similar fate had befallen 3 others counting up to 6 KIA. I managed to spot 2 alive out of the carnage which included my SL, although I didn't have time to help them immediately. The other soldier that was still alive with me began taking fire from a Russian force approaching from the west. I grabbed a firing position as quickly as I could and dispatched 3 enemy rifleman that were caught out in the open field. The other soldier told me to start dragging the wounded inside the wooden structure while he covered me, since I was the closest to them. I grabbed the first one and preceeded to make our way inside, which I layed his gorged body onto the wooden floor. I rushed out the door while taking care not to get shot when I saw at least 14 more Russians sprawled out along a sparse tree line. My remaining ally yelled at me to hurry the f*** up as I grabbed our SL who was bleeding from multiple velocity wounds caused by shrapnel everywhere along his body. I looked up at my last friend as he looked in my direction as a bullet entered his head sending a spray of brains across the wall. I cursed to myself while I dragged my SL toward the entrance of the structure. As I was about to enter I took a hail of bullets, one managing to hit me in the left arm. A 7.62x54R round went straight through and left me in a s*** ton of pain shooting up my arm. I barely dragged my SL next to the other body only to find that he had died from blood loss. Leaving only me, after that thought I peeked up from cover and sent 50 rounds into another 2 Russians that were approaching and suppressing the 3 squads that were converging  on my position. I began performing the best medical I could do to try and stop the bleeding on my SL by applying 4 tourniquets on all his limbs. I gathered all the medical supplies I could find off my dead comrade and started applying them to the SL, once I thought the bleeding had stopped I gave him morphine. I then sent another volley of 50 rounds towards the Russians that had now circled the position. I noticed warmth all the way down the left side of my body so I could only assume I had been losing a lot of blood. So I bandaged my own arm and gave myself a shot of morphine. The Russians didn't have night vision so it aided in my survival. Barely a minute had passed after bandaging myself and providing suppressive fire when the grenade landed in the "bunker", I dove as far away as I could from the nade when it exploded close to my SL's head turning it into mush. I crawled back up to find shrapnel in my left leg. Barely pulling myself up I fired another volley into the enemy force. I slid down and began treating my leg, applying a tourniquet and a bandage. The stalemate lasted 10 minutes, as the enemy attempted to reach the inside where I was making my last stand. I took a round to my helmet which didn't penetrate and a round to the right shoulder. On my last mag with only about 130 rounds left I crawled over to my SL's corpse in attempt to use the long range radio he was using to communicate to command. I spoke into the radio saying my squads callsign to Command, I did this two times when Command replied back asking for my identity. I preceeded to say my name, rank, and serial number to have to wait for a moment. They replied back after confirming who I was saying they had attempted reaching our squad to receive no reply so they assumed we perished, and they were suprised that I was still alive. I told them the sitrep and they told me that they were sending the Armor to my location now, so hold out as long as I can. I gathered the mags from the bodies inside the structure, since M4A1 mags fit in the M249. I fought for another 23 minutes while I limped from each side of the structure dispatching random patches of Russians, which they never seemed to end. Then  two Bradleys came to a stop outside the entrance and the Russians pulled out. A medical team grabbed me and loaded me into a Bradley while they operated on me. We barely made past the town when a MI-28 strafed the lead Bradley, it came around and did the same to ours. Everyone died from the Bradley explosion except me, I made it out. I limbed all the way back, finally coming into a town next to the FOB. An insurgent came out of an alley way and sent one round into my head. PTSD sim

The best bit about this game which differs from FML is that new guys can compete very fast and its proven time and time again in regards to finances and results.
The second best bit is the auction style transfer system which does much more to eliminate and possible cheating which burdened FML.
The ME is good but could be better , but i believe it is at the foremost of their upgrade plans along with a 2d engine and staff/stadiums.
Community is great and one suprising factor is the developent team play in game and often contibute to discussion.
Overall , a very sound investment.

The Good:
- Great lighting and environment design add immersion and remain consistent throughout
- Unique protagonist and narrative offer a refreshing perspective of the WWII setting
- Sound design is good; both music and voice-acting are executed well and add immersion
The Bad:
- Very "trial and error"-based; requires A LOT of patience
- The story is unimpressive and many levels feel fragmented or unrelated to each other
- Controls feel clunky and restricting (in both moving around and in combat)
In Velvet Assassin, the player takes on the role of British agent Violette Summers, infiltrating enemy lines to combat Nazi forces during WWII. Velvet Assassin offers an interesting and unique, albeit frustrating, stealth experience. While the game does some things well, it does many things poorly.
To begin with, Velvet Assassin's story is not very impressive. I found this to be the most disappointing part of the game, especially considering the high potential set in place by the game's unique protagonist and premise. Taking place during WWII, Velvet Assassin sets itself apart from other WWII games through the way in which the story is told.
After suffering a near-fatal gunshot wound during an assignment, agent Violette Summers remains bed-ridden in a state of comatose, recalling her missions through dream sequences. At the beginning of each level, Summers provides a little briefing on her mission, helping along the story via narration.
However, while helping to take down Nazi forces is satisfying in its own right, the goals of each level are pretty much unrelated; one level will revolve around sabotaging a German ammo depot, while the next level involves assassinating a key target. While these objectives seem like fairly standard spy operations, Velvet Assassin does a poor job of tying the levels into an overarching story, making the goals of each of the levels feel insignificant.
The game's story also finishes off in a sort of strange and unsatisfying dead end, which led me to question whether the developers had a different ending planned originally that was scrapped.
While Velvet Assassin certainly has its flaws, it does do some things well.
First of all, the sound of the game is great; the voice acting of both the protagonist as well as the frequenlty overheard conversations of patrolling enemies are believable and interesting. The music also does a great job of adding to the immersion and intensity of sneaking around in the shadows.
The environment and scenery of the game is also another high point. It is clear that a great level of detail was placed into crafting each of the levels, and the striking silhouettes created by the game's bold colors and deep shadows are dramatic and impressive.
The stealth in the game is suspenseful and carries with it a rewarding feeling when exectuted properly. The lighting really comes into play here; as long as Violette remains in the shadows, she is almost invisible to enemies, allowing her to close in for the kill. Velvet Assassin's lighting and ambience in each of the levels is excellent, helping to create interesting and believable environments. The game also provides ample opportunity for the player to manipulate the environment to create more shadows (e.g. disabling a fuse box to shut off the lights) so as to remain hidden.
Some reviewers criticize the AI in this game for being "blind," but in reality, I think the portrayal of stealth in Velvet Assassin is actually among the most realistic I've seen in a game.
However, the realistic and intense stealth does not necessarily translate well into fun gameplay. Ironically, Velvet Assassin's heavy emphasis on stealth is also what cripples the game in many other departments. First, the overall combat in the game is quite lackluster; aiming weapons, particularly in firefights, feels clunky and unnatural. While the game is obviously focused on stealth, there are several instances when sneaking around enemies is not an option and the player is forced into awkward combat situations.
Additionally, because crawling around and methodically eliminating enemies one-by-one is so time-consuming and tense, it makes it all the more frustrating when you are caught while trying to take out the last enemy and are forced to repeat the painstaking process all over again.
However, in spite of all of its flaws, Velvet Assassin is not a terrible game. It's a game that, unfortunately, could have been realized far better, but is certainly enjoyable at times, thanks to beautiful visual design, unique narrative and suspenseful stealth.

Velvet Assassin is a stealth action game with brutal difficulty where you play Violette Summer - a Brittish spy who infiltrates German bases during world war 2 and stab nazis in the backs, necks, throats, chests and groins. The story is told in past tense by Violette, who's stuck in a hospital while recalling the missions leading up to her getting there.
Controls are simple to learn but since checkpoints are few and far between, your best asset is patience - most battles will end in seconds if the enemy spots you and many of them are difficult to approach unseen. To help Violette, you can use abilities such as whistling to draw enemies towards you or use a silenced pistol to kill enemies without helmets from a distance or shoot things that explode to kill them, sometimes you even get to go all out with a shotgun - but mostly you will be stabbing nazis with your trusty knife. There are plenty of kill animations, some of which are pretty creative.
What is especially interesting about this game is that it adds psychological horror elements such as eerie, almost surreal, locales and certain rambling nazis that appear to have gone insane. There is also a limited use needle that Violette can use to inject herself with morphine, allowing you to perform stunts that would normally be impossible, and the boost is accompanied by an other-wordly effect where Violette's clothes changes into her hospital gown.
It doesn't go all out with the supernatural like Wolfenstein, but the hints are a nice touch that keeps the game fresh and interesting. The game also allows for multiple solutions to a given problem and collectibles, that grant experience points that you can spend on character upgrades, which makes going back to previously beaten levels worth-while.
If you like sneak-em-ups, punishing difficulty, good replayability and a slice of weirdness, then this game is for you.

This is a game of rare quality.
Unless you've lived under a rock these past few years, you know Ubisoft rebooted the Rayman franchise in 2011 with the critically acclaimed Rayman Origins. This game saw the limbless hero of many games in my childhood return to his platformer roots. The game was visually stunning and challenging with a superb soundtrack to boot.
And now we have Rayman Legends. This game is quite literally the logical next step for the reboot of this franchise. It still has the cartoony visuals, but this time it looks like you're watching a moving painting instead of a colourful cartoon. The level design is top notch and can be very challenging at times (which led to frustration in my case. Not that that is necessarily a bad thing as it made overcoming these obtacles that much sweeter) and oh my God is the soundtrack even better than the last one. Everything just breathes atmosphere and polish and the attential to graphical detail and the interaction between what happens on the screen and the music/sound design is nothing short of a victory in game design. Well done.
So, for a fair price you get a whole plethora of levels set in different worlds, loads of collectibles, online rankings (with daily and weekly challenges) and a host of levels from Rayman Origins with updated visuals.
In short: best platform game in recent memory. Worth every penny.

I've been following this game for many months now, and I've enjoyed this game almost every single time I've played it.
The progression system has been planned for a few months now, and anybody that has actually bothered to keep up with the community would know this. It was never a "keep in the dark" sort of deal, many people knew it was coming and what it would be composed of. People now complaining about the progression system not being what they purchased and a "punishment" are very ignorant and clearly haven't put a single minute into seeing what the developers are up to.
I'd also like to add that progression is a heavy W.I.P so a lot of the issues people have currently would most likely be addressed. You are still able to play sandbox, because there are servers that host sandbox gamemode and do get quite a lot of traffic.
That out of the way I'd like to address a few pros and cons with this game.
I'll start with a few of the things I dislike.
Austroraptors being able to solo animals such as the acrocanthosaurus (which is an animal that you have to spend hours grinding to get) is extremely absurd. However, I'm fully aware that this is going to be addressed. Things like trample damage and collision will most likely lower, if not get rid of anklebiting forever. I'd also like to add since austroraptor is a tier 1 animal most people are more likely to take risks with it since they can just be respawned. However, in the future the first animal is no longer going to be an austroraptor and you will have to spend time to actually get it which will also most likely lower anklebiters due to people not wanting to risk their progress.
Spawns are another issue I have a problem with. For example, I spent a few hours grinding to a sub adult rex. As soon as I progressed I was so happy, but as soon as I spawned I spawned less than 50 feet of a hungry acrocanthosaurus and ultimately died. Another example is when I was climbing a mountain as a gallimimus and got stuck in a small crevice. I nearly got out until an austroraptor spawned in the crevice. I managed to kill it but I could not rest in the crevice and was killed from the bleed.
However, I'm aware the developers are also going to fix this issue, maybe in the V3 map.
Another thing I dislike about the game is how merciless the game is. You can be grinding for hours only to lose all your progress in a matter of seconds. However, this game is marketed as a harsh survival game, so expecting anything other would be ignorant of me. And, like I stated before, progression is a WIP so a lot of the things that can cause you to lose your progress (Spawns, austroraptors, etc...) will be fixed so it would be more easier and less frustrating to play.
Another issue I'd like to address is the toxic community. Yes, people can be rude, a server I've been in (not going to give names) is full of remorseless KOSers. However, practically every single online game in existance has a portion of its community that is toxic. It's inevitable. Whilst there may be a toxic community, the entire community is not. I've met many, many kind people on the Discord, and in the game itself and the majority of these people ended up being my friends.
And another issue I'd like to address BRIEFLY is the developers attittude towards their customers. Most of the times the developers lash out against their customers is where they are very obnoxious and act stupid. The statement they don't follow critscism is very ignorant. If they really did not care about what their customers say then they would not make an effort to fix issues people have been having with the game. But, I'm going over this briefly because this is a game review, not a developer review.
Most of the issues I have with the game are predominately temporary.
Now I'm moving onto things I like about this game.
While there are people who are rude towards you in the community, there are many people who can give you a helping hand. For example if I play as a utahraptor and meet another utahraptor we would form a small pack. And every single utahraptor we ran into would be part of our pack until we formed a massive utahraptor. The way you can just meet someone and immediatly coordinate with them straight off the bat is a quality of this game I really like. You can easily set up ambushes, and other ways to kill prey with a person you just met a few seconds ago. I've met a lot of friends just by the group system. I cannot describe how exhillerating it is to make a successful kill with your friends.
Another thing I like is the detail in the game. The game looks tremendously beautiful, and on the lowest settings it still looks very beautiful. Sure, it's a bit unoptimized but that's another issue being addressed. The V3 map so far is one of the most gorgeous things I've seen in a video game.
The attention to detail on models is something I enjoy very well, too. The attention to detail on animations is also amazing. The smallest details such as your throat sac moving when you drink water are beginning to appear with newer dinosaurs.
I also like how the game is not only limited to dinosaurs and eventually will have more things to choose from. For example, cannibals, tribals, mercenaries, etc... And I like the fact that there will be strains and other improvements for your dinosaur. Monsters other than dinosaurs that you have to watch out for is something I enjoy.
I like the fact that the enviornment and players are both a threat. It is something that keeps you on your toes.
This is a game that I can truly call a survival game. It is harsh, but it is also fun.
I could go on and on about this game, but I cannot recommend this game enough.
Try it for an hour, if you don't like it simply ask for a refund.
Hope those who decide to purchase it have a great time.

So far I got 3/6 worlds finished, not counting the Origin Worlds that you can unlock and not counting any challenges or hidden areas. This game continues where Origins left - gameplay and "story" alike. It also adds some things to the formula, like your pixie helper you can raise bridges, cut ropes and eat cake. Also you can be turned into a duck or infiltrate a James-Bondian underwater lair. So far, so Rayman.
If you played Origins, you already know the new Rayman is a splendid combination of Mario, Sonic and Rayman games in terms of Jump'n'Run, Speedrunning and Wackyness. Legends doubles the fun with perfectly speedrunnable maps, many secrets to find and even Rythm levels. The game is smooth, beautiful and has even more gorgeous soundtracks the the previous title. To the less important additions count a strange monster collecting game and ticket rubbing.
Rayman Origins is, in my opinion, the best Jump'n'Run in history. Rayman Legends comes close, but despite the greatness of the levels, the less punishing checkpoint system and the TLC overall, I feel slightly disconnected from the overall story. You can skip worlds and levels and do them in your own order (with boss and rythm levels being an exception) and the feeling of advancement is overshadowed by the "Do whatever you please" attitude. It is probably more fitting for a Rayman game, but Legends cannot quite grasp the tone like Origins did it, where the the transition between the worlds was smooth and logical.
P.S.: James Bondian Laser Security System can be run through without you needed to stop which felt so forking awesome!

Unlike the single-player, single-character, first-person POV experience you might have expected, Pyre takes a sharp turn away and instead plays like an action visual-novel. Dispite what many early-access critics are saying, Pyre is unforunately not Supergiant's best work. While Supergiant has raised a bar with their first two titles, Pyre just approaches it. It's good, but not as good. Except the soundtrack. This soundtrack is definately the best of all three games, and probably the best OST of all time.
While the characters can be quite static and predictable, their writing is so well done to the point where you feel a legitimate connection. Minor spoiler:
. The dialouge and narration is word-porn. Love reading them through.
Unlike what you might have epxected from the first few trailers, navigating through the Downside (the main setting of the game) is incredibly linear, even after the first "phase" of the game. It's as though Supergiant made a compromise between art and functionality, and while the scenery is certainly pretty, it falls short and even feels empty due to the lack of any exploration.
The real action from the game, The Rites, is done well, although the controls are a bit funny. I recommend that you go into the settings and changes the controls to the "WASD" presets, but that's up to you. As you progress, you get more thrills and excitement from The Rites than you'd expect. Even though it's a single-player experience, you still feel like a badass when you pull off a sick successful counter-move. That's how I know the action is done right.
I haven't 100% completed the game, but from what I've played so far, it's already been worth the pre-purchace. Again, do NOT expect another Bastion or Transistor, but still know that there's a very little chance you'll regret getting this game.

It is essentially 3 on 3 football, except instead of an endzone, you have a pyre.  You control one character at a time to grab the orb and race it to the enemey's pyre.  While holding the orb, you are vulnerable to enemy auras, which banish you temporarily.  There are some special maneuvers you start out with and as your characters level up, you can unlock more.  If you don't possess the orb, you can throw your aura out and banish the enemy.

The outstanding art and theme really outshine most of the problems with this fun and immersive game about man and god duking it out in ancient Greece. This is a game in the style of Metroid where dungeons/levels can be tackled in any order.
The game aims to resemble a rotating vase of Greek origin and succeeds magnificiently.  It looks like you are playing a game on a piece of ancient greek pottery.  The unique art style and story wasn't thrown together in a couple hours; the developers really did their research when it came to Greek mythology and captured all the flaws and craziness of Greek dieties.  There are flavor text signposts all around the world and great voice acting.  The final climb up to Zeus is awesome and has memorable voice acting.  Levels and boss battles are unique; my favorite was the fight against Artemis when you alternate between deer and hunter.
Unforunately there are a couple flaws which may turn off some people.  The game is physics based so fighting and jumping is "floaty". Control is not precise like a Metroid game.  Also, the inventory management is a mess and there are way too many weapons and items.  I understand the developers wanted to give the players choices but there are too many weapons to cycle through during combat and selecting items is a similar pain.  There should have been fewer weapons and items or you should have been able to set certain items to quick keys/buttons.  I recommend a controller for maximum enjoyment but still expect to be frustrated by the inventory system.
I understand the game will not be for everyone but give it a chance (at least until a boss fight) as I think the developers did a great job capturing the world of ancient Greek gods in video game form.

I've been playing FM for 15 years and also played FML, so was naturally attracted to this game. But even though I tried to keep an open mind because of the early access, this game is too short on quality at the moment and I can't recommend it, even as a work in progress. Main impressions are:
1/ Lack of activity from players: I didn't expect this to be the worst feature of the game, but it was for me. Basically there is hardly anyone to play with, and you end up playing most of your games randomly against the AI. Most days you'd log on, there is no-one online so you can't play, you log off, try the next day. Then some days later, all fixtures pile up and you click through games agains AI opponents.
I guess this one is a bit of chicken and egg, because the game is so undeveloped there aren't many active players, which makes the in-game activity worse. But I wish the devs found a better match-timing algorithm to make this a bit better at least.
2/ Player attributes: almost all of these seem way too random, e.g. a center back with 15 finishing, 3 pace, 5 tackling and 15 endurance. With a totally random name and nationality. More care is needed with attributes and players, instead of just passing stuff through a random number generator.
3/ Match Engine: as others have said, this is very rough and feels pretty random, too. I finished second-bottom of my qualifying league the first season, next season with the same tactic I was consistently in the top 4 of the Afternoon league. Because of this randomness, and because commentary is very simplistic you can't tell what changes to make to your tactic and just end up stabbing around in the dark.
4/ UI is clunky and doesn't work well on the Mac.
One positive is that the people in the game seem really nice, both players and debs, I really hope this game becomes a success with further development, and I'd like to reconsider it in the future. But at the moment it seems a bit stuck in a rut; you should feel free to try it for a month or two, but otherwise I'd at least wait until full release.

- For Honor's execution of medieval warfare is excellent, and the combat system is unique and enjoyable.
- The combat system does take a while to adjust to, but once you've got the hang of the basics it's really easy to improve on.
- Although it seems like the game would get repetitive, it really doesn't. Since you're going up against different players and heroes with different playstyles, it's challenging and fun.
- The campaign was quite alright, not the best in the storytelling aspect, but an enjoyable experience, even though it was quite short.
- The graphics are georgeous ! For Honor is also optimised quite well, I've seen that it plays smoothy on older rigs, and still look really nice !
- Every hero is unique and really fun to play ! It's always good fun trying to learn the playstyle and moveset of a new character.
-Playing with friends is bliss. It's a huge amount of fun. Whether you're going against each other in custom games or teaming up with them to do Brawls or 4v4 gamemodes, it's hard to feel boredom.
- Ahh, Peer to Peer matchmaking...
With Ubisoft being a AAA game company you'd expect them to learn from the horrible matchmaking system that Rainbow Six: Seige has (also Peer to Peer), and maybe set up some dedicated servers for different regions. Nope, definitely not. I haven't noticed many issues with matchmaking latency problems, it seems to be smooth going during matches. HOWEVER, host migration, as per usual, is a huge pain in the backside. I was in a 3v1 battle at one stage, and was actually pulling off a potential win. However, I must've got the host of the game frustrated and he left the game. The host migrated, and the two opponents I killed came back to life, and in the end they managed to eliminate me. This was really frustrating. Host migrations happen quite often, the multiplayer is not perfect because of that.
- Always-Online.
This doesn't bother me in the slightest, since I always have a connection to the internet. However, it does affect quite a lot of people and thought I'd include it here. You CANNOT play anything in For Honor if you have no internet connection, not even the singleplayer segments of the game. Like I mentioned, doesn't bother me but it was better to include it.
-Gear Level Statistics.
Oh boy where the hell do I start here... In Dominion and Elimination gamemodes (4v4), there is a thing called Gear Stats. Gear Stats are completely broken, and have no balance whatsoever. I have a fully maxed out Peacekeeper with a Gear Stat of 108. 108 is the highest Gear Rating you can reach. Now, if I get hit around 4 times, or manage to block attacks 4 times, my Revenge is up immediately. While in my Revenge state, I can 2-hit anyone with heavy attacks, and my Revenge lasts a good 10 seconds. I basically have it back up within 3-5 seconds of using it all up. All I have to do is stand on an enemy objective and hold off against waves of players without even trying, I feel so awful for doing it, but it's part of the game. Ubi need to sort something out about this, since it's completely unbalanced and probably shouldn't have even been a thing in the first place. I reckon they should keep default statistics (like in Duels and Brawls) and just have cosmetic gear drops. This would eliminate the Pay to Win side of the game for sure. It's so incredibly Pay to Win at the moment, it's not really even that funny. It's a crude joke.
Overall, would I recommend For Honor ? I would. It has a decent amount of flaws, but those flaws can be easily forgotten when you get into a battle, and feel the satisfaction of digging your steel into the opponents gut.
It's a superb game, with the exception of poor matchmaking choices, always-online, and unbalanced 4v4 player statistics.
If you have a friend that's interested in getting it, get it ! You two will have plenty of fun together, and you'll definitely get your moneys worth.
If you're thinking of getting it, and you play alone, your choice may be a bit more difficult. I find 1v1 Duels and playing other gamemodes with strangers good, I've met a good few friends through For Honor, so if you have the money and are confident you'll like the playstyle, fire away !
I'll give it a 7/10, only because of Ubisoft not pulling it together and giving us a trash matchmaking service, and the monstrocity that goes by the name of "Gear Stats".

It's not bad, but it's not the best Strategy Game I've played.
Graphics and animations are acceptable, nothing too fancy. Gameplay and mechanics are easy to pick up with a "straight to the point" tutorial that teaches you what you need to know for first time players, and the experience and customization systems are fairly decent.
How does the game play?
It's a "Pre-Planning" style strategy game that's broken up into "Phases", Similar UFO or Frozen Synopsy. Simply put, you start each Phase by giving your soldiers orders, either to move from one location to another, deploy a grenade or equipment, etc. Once you have a pre-planned set of actions and routes set, you hit the "Breach" or "Exicute" button to watch it play it. It's a fairly basic system and it works fairly well, but the only problem I find with it is that the game's intro boasts about how this is supposedly a "Realistic Tactics Simulator" but if your soldiers are suddenly engaged by a new threat, rather than react accordingly or like in UFO halt their last action and pause for you to give them a new order to finish their phase, they just continue to follow the path set out for them. so if you give a soldier or soldiers to breach and clear a room and there's a wall of enemies on the other side waiting, your soldiers are going to continue walking into the hailstorm of bullets and taking hits instead of doing the more "realistic" thing and withdrawing back to cover.
Aside from that though, it's a decent game. Would I recommend it? Sure, I can definely say that if you like turn based tactic games, give it a try. Personally I think another game like "Door Kickers" is a bit more "realistic" in terms of CQC Tactics, but this game is decent enough on its own.
Overall Personal rating: Fair/Average. Nothing Too special about it, but can't find much bad about it either.

Back to the Future is one my favorite movie trilogies and was super stoked when I received the digital download copy from Line Sommer Hoel for my birthday. Lots of thanks and love to you.
Back in the Hill Valley of 1986, six months after the third movie, Doc has been missing for quite some time and the bank decides to foreclose his home and belongings. While Marty McFly rummages through Doc’s stuff, the DeLorean appears in front of the house with Einstein, Doc’s pet sheepdog, in it. A tape recorder inside the car explains that the time machine’s automatic retrieval system travels back to a certain time to call for Marty’s help, should the Doc ever end up in any kind of distress. Marty then sets out to find out to what time his friend travelled to and how to save him.
Back to the Future: The Game is one of those productions where the people behind it went all out; they knew what the fans loved about the original and tried their best to allow fans to relive the adventure and excitement. And given the studio, you know the game will have a strong narrative. It is an episodic point & click adventure from the time before Telltale Games, the developer and publisher, made episodic graphic adventures. What’s more: Back to the Future: The Game serves as an official fourth instalment to the series and the developers even received help from the original cast in its production. For example, Bob Gale, co-writer and co-producer of the original Back to the Future film trilogy, helped in creating the script, Christopher Lloyd reprises his role as Doctor “Doc” Emmett Brown Ph.D., Michael J. Fox makes two cameo appearances – once as future Marty McFly and once as his great-grandfather William McFly – and finally, since an update from October 2015, Tom Wilson once again plays the role as Biff Tannen, who was previously voiced by Kid Beyond in this game.
I played BttF:TG on the trusty 32-bit Windows Vista toaster with an Intel Core 2 CPU, 3070MB RAM, and a GeForce 9500 GT graphics card. As with other point & click adventures, there aren’t a lot of gameplay mechanics to talk about in this one, however, Marty McFly can be controlled either with the classical mouse, the keyboard, or a gamepad. So, pick your method and explore Hill Valley to your heart’s content.
Each episode will take players around two hours to get through, resulting in around 10 hours of gameplay. Generally, the puzzle can be quite hard for novices and are definitely more aimed at people familiar with point & click style puzzle solving. Genre veterans, on the other hand, might occasionally feel that a number of riddles are too easy, especially given that there is a hint system. On a personal matter, one aspect I always find sad about the Telltale games is that they got rid of inventory puzzles that require players to combine items with one another. One more little subtraction is for how few puzzles there were in the latter part of the adventure. Despite that, none of this deterred me from enjoying this experience.
Back to the Future: The Game proves to be an eminently enjoyable game that, unlike many other adaptations, sequels, or reboots, provides decent content instead of leaching off of fans’ nostalgia. As it was co-written by Bob Gale, an Academy Award nominated, Hollywood screenwriter, the plot of the game is well thought out and, for the most part, manages to walk the fine line between good movie and good video game. That is until the climax. While the overwhelming majority of the BttF:TG is loads of fun, the story’s high point exchanges puzzles for filmlike segments that are great visually, but not fun to play. Instead, it leaves players slightly disappointed, because the road leading towards it did so very well.
What surprised me about the game is that the writing had a much heavier focus on the effects of time travel on individuals. Even though Marty and Doc only travel back and forth between 1931 and 1986, changes in the past drastically altered how the personalities of the Hill Valley residents in the “present” developed. In defiance of this being logical, it did become rather unsettling at some point and I applaud the writers and actors for conveying that feeling of unease. The other intriguing aspect was that the story focused far more on Doc Brown’s history, wherein the movies centered mostly around Marty and his family.
Before you consider buying this one, remember that it takes place after the movie trilogy, so watching all three films beforehand comes highly recommended, despite that not being necessary to understand the plot. Visual novel enthusiasts might find the puzzles a bit too hard, while point & click fans will feel that they have … hills and valleys … and are typically easier than the ol’ Lucas Arts brain twisters. With all that in mind, Back to the Future fans will have a great time. The story is good, the voice acting great, the visuals stunning, and fans of the series are most definitely going to play through this more than once, I know have.

The mechanics are introduced naturally, no tutorial or instructions needed. In fact, I'm fairly certain that the only word in the game is the title. There are numbers for the levels, of course, but you get the point. It's minimalist done right, beautiful in its simplicity, and a downright steal at this price. I love this game.

I revisit this game several time every year. It's a great rpg and excellent Star Wars game. It's far more morally grey than a lot of the universe, and explores one of the best periods in SW, the Legacy Era. Combat is D&D/D20 based, level and character building is easy to get, and you experience one of the best support characters ever written. Get the restored content mod, it makes it a fair bit better.

This game has potential, but it fails in trying to be too complex. I get survival games are supposed to be tough and stacked against you, but the RNG shouldn't be the biggest killer in a survival game.
Take my latest (and possibly last) play session. My people are all starving, meanwhile there is an elk and a rabbit snared in my traps, but I can't harvest them because I have no meat storage. What's the lowest tier meat storage? The freezer, which I can't build because in 15 days I have never encountered a hinge. In fact, the only reason why I have snares, is because I just so happened to have a trader come by who had rope. There is no need for my people to be starving, the meat is there, I just can't get it, because of a damned hinge.
Devs either need to allow for basic component building or being able to tear apart that broken down laptop for its hinge by hand and not need a recycler.
As I said the potential is there, but the RNG and poor execution stack it unnecessarily against you.

Possibly the most uniquely stylish Metroidvania ever. And even once you get used to that (it's visually brilliant all the way through, just look at those images up at the top of the page there), it's a very solid game - some fairly complex combat with an impressive variety of weapons and potions, all while working your way through the diverse lairs of the gods, with plenty of secrets to uncover.
The story makes excellent use of its mythological roots, and many areas even include markers with relevant excerpts. It's really an impressive game all around - the only things I can even think to point out that weren't excellent were that it can be slightly awkward to switch what you have equipped midcombat (switching from melee to ranged to potions is fine, but switching from one ranged to another requires actually opening your inventory, which is slightly inconvenient with a WASD/mouse control setup) and that I managed to glitch outside of a certain giant spinning level by saving in a weird spot (the autosave was kind enough to rescue me).
In short, if you've ever read Greek mythology and thought "those gods are a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, someone needs to take them down a peg", or if you just want a nice Metroidvania with some seriously snazzy aesthetics, get Apotheon and you'll have a godly time.

I'm all for Rayman, I'm a fan of the original Rayman on the Atari Jaguar/PSX, it was colorful, and I was a huge fan of the very difficult and challenging nature of the platformer.  I have not played any other Rayman games except the original, so I'm not sure of those leading up to this game.  The art style in this game is very vivid and colorful, just like the original, which I really like.  The music is also okay, though I was not a huge fan, that is just personal preference.
The main "lobby" for selecting worlds and levels feels cluttered, like they just threw it together.  The movement is pretty good, my only gripe is that you can only charge your punch standing flat on the ground.  My main problems begin with level design.  They really like to use these chains/ropes which you can grab onto and slide down, but unfortunately if you even get CLOSE to anything that you can grab onto, it will auto grab whether you want to grab onto it or not, and you have to hold down and jump in order to let go.  After grabbing onto, say, a rope that you can slide on, you gain a lot of momentum almost instantly, which means if you are trying to get to something to the left, you have to let go of the rope and walk back, which, if there is an obstacle you have to jump over, you might accidentally grab onto the rope again and have to repeat this same process over and over.  It's little things like that, those which happened often enough to be annoying but weren't huge playability issues, which stacked up just enough to make the game feel awkward and tedious.
The level design isn't very interesting, every level blended together, felt pretty much the same, and left me bored very quickly.  Everything is very simple and quite easy, for the most part you can just hold down the run button and blast through all of the enemies without a second thought or ounce of difficulty.  They introduce a basic enemy right off the bat which is almost no threat at all whatsoever, I don't know how anyone could ever get hit by them.  Later on they give those enemies wooden shields, but you can just kick and one shot them just like the others, what is the point of them having shields if they are literally the same enemy and the shield does absolutely NOTHING?
Basically, I just feel like I am just playing Super Rayman Bros. Wii U.  They don't really do anything interesting to pull you in and get you addicted and wanting to play more, it felt more like a chore going through each level like a zombie hoping that the next level would be exciting (never happened).  I will say, though, that this game would probably be best to play co-op with friends and not single player.  It seems to be designed with the exact same co-op as Super Mario Bros. Wii U (and the four five or six or how many other generic mario bros. platformers Nintendo made for the Wii, not including Galaxy of course, those games were a breath of fresh air).  Easy to say that I would not recommend a game that left me wanting to quit after getting halfway through the second world.  It's not interesting, it really doesn't introduce anything new or exciting, it's just, well, a generic, unmemorable platformer.

This game is very unique and that's what I love about it. It is based off of a comic series where you play as a mob boss named Jackie who has inherited an ancient power known as "The Darkness," which is basically two tentacle-like creatures coming out of your back. The combat can be "quad weilding," using the two Darkness tentacles and two firearms simultaneously. The tentacles can be used to pick up, tear apart, throw,and slash eniemies into oblivion. The game is very short (6-8 hours) but it is a great story. You don't need to play the first game to understand what is happening in this. The end leaves you at sort of a cliffhanger, and from what I've read, there may be a Darkness III in production. The graphics look very nice, even on my low-end PC and it runs very well too. There are a few minor texture errors, but nothing too big that affects the gameplay. There is a multiplayer feature too, but from my experience, it is dead most of the time.With all of that said, I'd give the game an 8/10 and well worth $5.

The Darkness was the first game Yahtzee ever made fun of, and it got a bad reputation as a result, which it mostly deserved. The sequel is based on the same unfortunate premise and gameplay mechanics as the original, but it's put together very well, and it really makes the best of what it has, which is two demon arms and a gremlin. It's an improved take on the gameplay from the first game, which you should know by now if you enjoy.
David Hoffman is really fantastic as the friendly raving occultist Johnny Powell, and his readings of the flavor text about the artifacts are one of the two major highlights of this game for me. The other is Vendettas, the online mode they've bundled with this game to satisfy the legal requirement that all FPS games have at least a thin multiplayer component. Vendettas puts the player in charge of one of four heroes, but the heroes actually have different powers, making the selection more than trivial. This mode plays a lot like what I'd want a FPS version of Hunter: Redeemer to play like. White Wolf, I'm looking at you.

Unfortunately not many people play it so you might have trouble finding a server that you like, most are team deathmatches. People there are also quite nice, you won't be called out even if you suck.
My biggest complaint is the unrealistic bullet trajectory. Bullet from a Springfiled rifle doesn't drop one meter when you're shooting a target 160 meters away, but that was done to simulate longdistance shots since it would be too easy to snipe someone from across the map and too impractical to make huge maps in which you could actually make a proper long shots.

I'm giving this game a positive review despite everything here being negative:
8 hours in and I'm not sure how much more of the game I have left - and to be honest I just can't bring myself to finish this. After playing for about 20 minutes each session I just have to stop. I feel that the mechanics are not varied enough and I'm suffering from an epic Metroidvania travel fatigue. The levels are very large, and each God has their own area which requires a lot of back tracking. The distance between the objectives are lightly spattered by very similar human enemies with different weapons or animals trying to lunge at you. Once you have an optimal set of items, it's hard to move away from them.
There are some standout moments, such as an interesting battle involving alternating between being hunter and prey, but other than that I'm not a fan. Having said that, why I'd recommend this game is that the art style is nice, the mechanics while I personally feel aren't varied enough, are pretty solid. And I think I'm a minority on the reasons why I find the game boring.
Get it on a sale, give it a go. It's decent enough.
Oh and everyone saying it's 2D God of War.. it's a stretch. Thematically definitely a borrowing heavily from Greek Mythology, but style and execution not quite there.
