Half visual novel, half tactical magic sportsball simulator, all fantastic.
The actual ritual contests (the gameplay so to speak) are deeply tacitcal, while still attaining a frenetic tension in the later levels. I feel I could best compare it to speed chess, where the funamental structure of the game is methodical, but actions and judgement calls come in such rapid succession that a pitched battle feels more dynamic than some fighting games.
In-between matches, you work through scripted sequences filled with lore and dialogue that really makes the world and its characters come to life.
All in all, the contrast works, giving you a chance to soak up the world between matches, then losing yourself in the frantic energy of trying to snuff the enemy's pyre.
All in all, I'd reccomend this game to anyone without reservation.

This is the day and age of bigger and prettier is better.  Longer quests, longer stories, better graphics, better voice acting, etc, etc. Yet we often forget about where it all began.  We forget about the free demo of doom with it's whole 9 levels that came on a floppy disk (8 levels if you don't know what you are doing).  We forget about how much we could get consumed within those 9 levels alone, just hunting for that wall that moves, or that pathway to the health booster we can see but can't quite reach.
Brightness settings?  Doom has 2 brightness settings.  Bright, and pitch black.  You pray for bright.   Even in poor graphics of the early 90's, the ambiance that is created in the levels of Doom is what makes it a classic.  To open a door, and find a room that is pitch black, with only the flicker of the light near the exit, and the haunting sounds of cloaked pinky demons inside, while low on shotgun ammo, and only at 40% health and 0 armor.  That, my friend, is to know what it's like to fear a room in a video game.
To turn a corner, thinking you are safe, only to have that imp that's been hunting you finally pop out in front of you and make you jump in your stomach.  Only Doom can bring that reaction to this day.
Clostrophobic levels that are more dark than light, secret doors that are often easier to overlook than you would think, and in the end, a non-stop action thrill ride.  That's the father of modern gaming.
So go ahead if you dare.  Go all out pre-2k.  Put on some Hells Bells by AC/DC, load up E1M3 on Nightmare mode.  Remember what it's like to try and survive hell, long before anyone else thought of it.  Back when Carmack and McGee were just some geeks with an old IBM PC.
And as you are playing this, just remember this was the "realistic murder simulator" that lead to the Columbine massacre....Think about that one.
Rating 10/10: Would jump at pink blobs in the darkness again.

WARNING: THIS REVIEW IS BAISED AND CONTAINS PERSONAL OPINIONS. YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED.
First off, I want to argue about the concerns many players are having which are Permadeaths, Lack of Content, and "Glitches/bugs".
1. Permadeaths
Many people like this mode, others hate it. Losing all your skill points and levels is a real b**** when it happens. I agree that instead of making all servers permadeath, make some servers permadeaths and others without it. However, complaining about it in a review will do nothing. Address your concerns on the main fourms of the game developer's website. Pretty sure Runescape has permadeath but they keep their levels so meh.
2. Lack of Content
I was pretty mad when someone mentioned this "lack of content" and comparing it to DayZ/WarZ. I've never played WarZ, but I've definently played DayZ. This was everyone's goal in DayZ: Find the airfield and kill other players. What about Nether? Tribes competeing for territory, safe zones being compromised by Nether monsters allowing players to either repair Anti-Nether devices or kill each other, supply drops in random parts of the map, THE MOTHA-F******* BAD♥♥♥♥♥REAPER, scavenging for supplies and food, BEING A COURIER TO DELIVER PACKAGES FROM SAFE ZONE TO SAFE ZONE AND LEVELING UP DOING IT WHILE AVOIDING OTHER PLAYERS? I really don't understand what people mean by lack of content. All of this, combined with permadeath, makes for a truly realistic survival horror game.
3. Glitches & Bugs
Every single game has bugs and glitches. No game is perfect. I've put in a few hours into the game and none of the glitches I've experienced have bothered me in the slightest. My main issue is my fps. I can play all games that exist today on meduim settings but I can barely run Nether on meduim. A bit optimization would be nice but that won't happen for a while.
As far as survival horror games go, take your Resident Evil/Dead Space/Slenderman copies and delete them. On high settings, this game is truly beautiful and atmospheric. You can be traveling from roof top to roof top or walk around on the sidewalks, but you never know what might be around the corner. I entered a gas station expecting it to be empty. Then my heart jumped when I saw 3 players lunge at me with axes. My heart jumped again when a GOLEM AND A FLYING MONSTER THINGY-WHATEVER WERE AFTER ME ON TRAIN TRACKS THEN HEARING GUNS FIRE NEAR MY LOCATION AND PANICKING NOT KNOWING WHAT TO DO OFMG JWUAIFHNDSUI
If you want a realistic survival horror game, like, REALISM MODE, please purchase this game. You won't regret it. Even at it's current state, you should still get it ESPECIALLY during steam sale. This game only has room to improve from now on.

The game starts off with the counselors in the middle of the woods gathered around a campfire and a guy walks up and is suddenly attacked by Jason. The counselors get frightened and scatter in various directions. And you start off as random counselor with nothing but your sony walkman "Joking". You literally have nothing and must gather supplies found in various dressers, desks, bookshelves etc..
You have a stamina gauge and you have to use it effectively otherwise if you encounter Jason you will be an easy kill.
Whenever Jason is close by the music becomes more intense (Like in the movies) And you better either find a nice hiding space i.e a wardrobe, under the bed, in a shed, Yes! Jason will chop off your head.
I enjoy the gameplay. You really are in survival mode while evading the masked psychopath and keeping your composure while figuring out how you're going to make it out alive.
You can play in team mode or you can use the other campers as bait giving you enough time to flee still in tact.
Their are various weapons to use to slow down Jason while you escape but you can only use one item so find something you're good with and keep it handy.
Pros:
The game is fun by yourself and even better with friends.
Lots of potential to be a great multiplayer survival horror.
The animation and gory deaths scenes are accurate to the movies.
Cons:
Jason has the power to see through walls and objects so it makes the game sorta unfair
Jason can teleport so again.. not really fair
The game has occasional glitches and bugs that need to patched.
If you're easily scared or not this is a great game that has room for improvement.

Gameplay is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. When everything works and the game is how it is meant to be, you really feel like you are your character.
However, if it doesn't then you're pretty much screwed. Every other review is raging about P2P connection, and their complaints are valid. Network issues are numerous and annoying. It's a stupid system, and it creates unfair play due to lag switching and hosts leaving. But the real thing that ruins this game is the balancing. In other words, it's complete crap. The "vanguard" characters can 3 or 4 shot lower health characters while also taking 10 or so hits to take down. "Oh, but the lower health characters are faster and can guard break", you say. Nope. Guard break is a joke once you actually start playing anyone who's had the game for an hour, and the tanks can just parry or block and then one shot you.
But hell, just for the fun of it we'll say the stats are balanced. So you get into a 1v1 and you're doing great. You haven't been damaged yet and you've gotten your opponent down to one hit.
Then, one of three things happens.
1) They run. No explanation needed. They run and grab boosts or revive teammates. And you can't do crap about it because they have leg armor that makes their sprint speed three times as fast as yours, or they pick up a speed buff.
2) You get pushed off a ledge by one of the numerous, almost undodgeable, attacks that the tankier classes have which push you 10 miles until you fall off a cliff. "That's part of the game, you need to watch your positioning" you say. Ha. When I am fighting 20 feet from a ledge and I can still get carried off of it, something is wrong.
3) Revenge mode. Don't get me started on this disgusting system. It's meant to help people that are being ganked or aren't quite as strong as their opponent. But in the end, people just build their character's gear to get revenge in three or four hits. And when they get it, it's basically like fighting Bastion from Overwatch, but this time he has unlimited health and tracking bullets.
Anyways, I got lost a little bit in my rant there. But I think I captured the spirit of For Honor (Also known as No Honor to a large portion of the Community). The game is a great idea, and sometimes it really shines. But it sure as hell isn't worth the 60 dollars I paid for it. I'd say wait for the price to drop or for them to fix some of the issues, god knows their are plenty to choose from. Either way, it's your own choice, but I hope I helped inform you a little bit.

If this is not your favorite star wars game...then you need to immediately look up the Philosophy of Kreia video. Best two hours of any star wars nerd's youtube experience.
Cons:
This game gets flak for not being as accessible as its predecessor, Kotor, and you would be right to agree. The story is more philosophical and muddled, as opposed to the relatively simple point A to B framework of Kotor 1. The mechancis are more dense, with influence and the spread of your Dark/Light alignment to other characters. The ending is ambiguous, and the feeling of a rushed sequel that pressured the developers is quite apparent.
Did you notice how none of those were solid cons?
Pros:
With TSLRC the game is more complete, and therefore can be appreciated for its beautiful qualities.
the story is a flawless examination of star wars, with everything centering around what Star Wars actually means. It asks deeper questions than any other medium could: Who are the Jedi, the Sith, and do they represent good and evil as clearly as we thought?
The game centers around Kreia, this will change the way you attend to your gameplay for sure. her strange role and heavy emphasis is odd for a first time player, but if you tackle her character not as a random NPC that the devs want you to interact with the most because she gets the most dialogue, but instead as the host of "certain point of view" that assesses the world of Star Wars with more honesty and intelligence than any other character in the canon or legends, your story experience will mean much more to you.
Your relationship with each character is dynamic and meaningful, your actions have true consequence, and the arc is not necessarily as obvious as in the first one. The story is hidden within the character's motivations. The first game is like indiana jones, strong characters with clear motivations. the second game is more like a character tale a la Into the Wild; Characters have adventures but are discovering who they are, are influenced by others, and their core can shift and change, therefore their motivations do too.
The plot is in the characters, not the events of the galaxy.
Gameplay:
some say the turn based combat is not accesible. They would be right, but not necessarily correct in saying it is a con. the combat is not a sucky version of gameplay, but a different genre of it, and therefore not meant to be as accessible as popular combat mechanics (shoot, cover, counter, context buttons). It runs off of an archaic D20 system, and is a revolutionary way to portray an old system of gameplay. If you watch Harmon Quest, DnDiesel, or even the Community episode centered around DnD, your appreciation of the sheer technical prowess will increase dramatically. in short: everything is a dice roll. your attacks are actually a roll form 1-20, and depending on your stats you can get numbers added to your success. everything else follows the same rule, and it offers the game a new way to look at strategies and combat if you understand the system. This leads me to the biggest gameplay change between the two titles, and the strongest way the roleplaying of Kotor2 is superior: your skills matter. Your character has more dialogue and action opportunities because of your skills. Therefore it is more meaningful to pick a non-guardian class, because the investment into the softer parts of gameplay will make a rewarding difference.

I loved it for the dark tone and the sheer size of the story, as well as the advanced gameplay mechanics, but KOTOR 1 still was my favorite, the story seemed better, clearer, and more enjoyable. years later, after learning the Star Wars DnD system, I watched a little video called the philosophy of kreia, which I mentioned  earlier. If you love star wars, and you have completed the game before but maybe want to try it out again...then watch it. It will rekindle your love for the impeccable writing, and it will help you to see the story as it was meant to be, not as an action adventure tale, but as a deep philosophical journey into the nature of star wars.

This is a review for the entire season of Back to the Future:  The Game, not just for the first of the series.  I would only recommend this series as a complete season (As there's cliffhangers at the end of every episode, so that's the best way to review the games.)
I'm recommending the game for the following reasons.  It's Back to the Future (And a sequel) if you haven't seen Back to the Future, you should because it's amazing.  If you don't like Back to the Future for some reason, then you probably won't like this game.
It's also a Telltale point and click game, and I don't believe they can really make a bad game as long as they tell a good story, and this is a good story.
It's a good game, if anyone other than Telltale made this game, it would just get a glowing review.  But Telltale has a history in this space so there's both good and bad.
The first big thing to note is voice actors.   Christopher Lloyd is back!  That's huge and the voice is spot on.   Every scene with him you feel like this is really Emmett Brown and that works wonders!   The down side, Michael J. Fox isn't back as Marty.  That's not as big a negative, but Marty always sounds like he's someone doing a Michael J. Fox impersonation.  He's not awful, but often times he doesn't sound just right.   Granted there's a lot of dialogue, and only about ten percent of it is bad, but still noticeable in my opinion.   Not a huge negative though.
To me the real negative is the locations in the game, or lack of them.  While there's a lot of variety of the locations, the player really only deals with two time periods.  Over 15 hours of game play, you're going to see a lot of the same areas even though they're going through minor changes.  This isn't a huge deal breaker, but by the fourth or fifth story I went "Really?"  I wanted to see something different, and mind you there's nothing amazing here.  There's a few interesting versions of the locations but I want to see the future! I mean 2015 in Back to the Future's timeline is fun, let's go to the better version of "now".
The story is a mixed bag, while it’s usually pretty good, there’s a few points where I went “Really?”  at least four episodes of the series is really good, but the reuse of locations wears on the player.  It isn’t a huge turnoff either, but the series goes on a long time on a specific topic, when they could have had two mini arcs.
The puzzles are the one thing I will say is a “huge negative”.  There’s three problems with the puzzles.  First they’re too easy.   Often times it’s as simple as listen to some text, and then go grab an item that’s in plain view.
The second is that the game is extremely linear.  Often times you have to do X Y and Z in order.  If you want to try to do Z too bad, you can’t because something has to happen before it happens.  The game gives you a flat goal that’s clear on what it expects you to do next, but it’s a story progression most of the time.
Finally the game has a hint system, and unlike the Sam and Max games.  So that’s both good and bad, but unlike sam and max, there’s not a huge need for the hint system and no penalty to using it.
With all those negatives, is it a bad game?  Well it depends what you want.  If you want a deep Point and Click game, this isn’t it.   If you want a story based game though, this is perfect.  There’s no Pixel Hunting, there’s no very hard puzzles, and there’s a hint system that makes it exceedingly easy.   Still it’s a rather fun game, and I enjoyed the experience, so it’s an easy recommendation.

I find myself playing this game from time to time whenever I am in the mood for something that makes me think. What does it make me think about? Well, lots of things. Both good and bad. The game really is not very well made, but that's not what it is trying to be. It has some nice touches here and there that come off as very cool. There are moments when things come off just right and you think to yourself, "If only it was like that always."
There are things in this game that are just down right stupid. For example, I killed three guards outside of a building and just left them there in the open. I go inside the building and change into a disguise, then proceed back outside just to find all the bodies are gone and there are new guards standing there talking.
I am able to deal with almost anything if the story is compelling. Come to mention it, the story for this game only goes as deep as you want it to. You play as a killer, who knows that's her job and is on a deathbed remembering all the horrible things she did. I enjoyed the fact that it was all over the place, even if it was bad writing. It wasn't trying to shove some point down my throat and ended up almost being a surreal experience more so than a coherent one.
Now, do keep in mind this is a very ugly game, with poor AI and too many annoying events that will take place. Still, I enjoy playing it in short bursts whenever I want to get and old-school vibe. I know this is for 2009, still when I play it I remember why I loved Hitman and Tenchu when they first came out. This is not anywhere near as good, but it is like a fever dream from those days. Something I tend to find myself trapped in, then before I know it I want to get back to where it's peaceful. This is that nightmare you might enjoy for a moment, until it's just too terrible to deal with.
So, sitback, get ready to rage and think of it like a Mars Bar.

The truth is that its not that different than the Android game, which is certainly not a bad thing. You're still getting the beautiful, Disney-esque environments and character models and absorbing, challenging platforming. The difference is that the full scale version offers a great deal more variety and is all the stronger for it. If you yearn for a pure platformer, there's nothing better.

In a way i almost feel as if i am obligated to write such a review. Let me start off this review by saying that the two kotor games symbolically represent the two very very different sides of life that you are going to encounter throughout your life. I was a child when the first game came out and ironically i had acquired it by accident, I had asked my mother to get me Jedi knight academy for the original xbox because i really wanted to play a star wars game where i was in control of my jedi. She had went to the store and asked the clerk about the best new star wars game that was available and he pointed her out to Kotor. At first i was heartbroken trying to figure out how to play this game where i would miss a sword strike 5 times in a row when it clearly looked like it hit on my screen. Regardless i didn't get a chance to play new games very often so i stuck with it and played until completion which took me 60 or so hours when i was 8 or so years old. Kotor 1 was the perfect "dream of being a jedi who saves the universe" simulator if you will. Everything was very black or white/good or bad that my young mind  could understand. Its kind of like how i viewed the world we live in as a kid, Its either you're a good or bad person and there is no in between.
Kotor 2 however blurs the line between what is considered "bad" and whats considered "good". When i was a kid a few years older then before i couldn't rationalize this concept. I would think to myself "why is kreia lecturing me after i just healed a wounded man with medpacks that i wouldn't need?" As i grow older upon every subsuquent return to this game i learn something different about myself. I've seen it first hand in my own life, sometimes doing something good for another person could lead to unforseen consequences. Sometimes people will use you if you have a mindset where you try to make everyone happy around you, if you practice "the jedi" way in real life you'll attract those who can feed off your intentions and find a way to use you. Same with being mean and promoting ill will towards another, Karma can sneak  up and hit you when you least expect it. It is the proverbial grey line that we must all walk that would promote the most beneficial way to live. Kreia really nails this home every chance she gets. Anyone who lives in absolutes is a fool as its unrealistic to live a life that way. The tone of the game is very dark, From the art styles to HUD layout everything just seems bleak. As i see it the bleakness of the games color style replicates the bleakness we all feel in life when we start to really learn about human tendencies. Even on a "green" planet like dantoine you cant help but feel that depressing vibe in every place you visit. Although i dont personally like the vibe of KOTOR 2 i cant help but appreciate the artistic style they went for because it really does work. When i stopped playing this game as a star wars game, i started to play it as a real life simulator in terms of the actions i choose and it really works well in that aspect. The music is just as memorable as the original game but also in a much darker ominous way. Gameplay For Kotor 2 really feels perfected compared to the first game in terms of progression and most importantly the clipping is way better in KOTOR 2 and that really helps the fluididity of gameplay.  Kreia might just be one of the best written characters in any video game ever, but all the other party members you get minus HK and atton are pretty forgetable to me compared to KOTOR 1. All in all You have to have intelligence and some kind of understanding of human psychology to fully appreciate this title. But either way it is a game you can enjoy for a litany of different reasons as i have over the years. I'll five the KOTOR 2 a solid 9/10 Highly recommended for anybody who loves story driven single player experiences.

Pyre is not just a game -- It is a an audiovisual experience.
Gameplay
This review is based from the first 6 hours of gameplay. Pyre is a unique sport game with RPG elements, one that really defies classification. At the very basic, the player controls a team of three in matches known as "rites", against an opposing team. The goal is to bring the orb, spawned in the middle of the court at the beginning of each round, to the opponent's flaming target -- and douse the flame. Everytime the flame is doused, it loses a certain amount of HP, depending on your units, skills, and equipment. Pyre demands not only that the player is skilled enough to maneuver the court, but to also choose the appropriate team member for each rite, as each of the crew member has a distinctive skill and play style.
Graphics and Sound Design
Like their previous two releases, Bastion and Transistor, Supergiant Games did not fail to impress with an excellent art direction and a wonderful soundtrack. Really, I cannot emphasize less about the beauty of the artwork. The world and characters meticulously detailed in vibrant colors and are very creative, if not fantastic. The music matches every occasion very well, with some of the best soundtracks voiced.
Story and Writing
The writing is definitely a very strong point for Pyre. Every character is unique and sympathetic in their own ways, and as the player progresses through the game, they would learn bits and pieces about each character, forming a special connection. And without giving too much spoiler -- the player decides the fate of each character. There are also numerous snippets of story within the codex known as the Book of Rites, which provide insight about the game's mythos and world. In addition, there is no true "Game Over" in Pyre, and each rite have their own consequence, whether the player wins or loses.
Performance
Generally very smooth, but there are one or two framerate hiccups, usually during rites, and I've encountered a freeze a few hours into the game.
Recap
Gameplay 8.5/10
Graphics 9.5/10
Music 9.5/10
Story 9/10 so far
Performance 9/10
Highly RECOMMENDED.

The Tune Squad is back in action, in Supergiant's thrilling sequel to its 1996 classic "Space Jam".  However, instead of a voyage through space, the gang is transported into a timeless purgatorial fantasy realm from which Bugs and his zany crew must liberate themselves through the power of 3-v-3 streetball.
==========
With Michael Jordan retired (for real this time!), the cartoons' saga forces them down a new path alone.  The overworld is a network of important choices, rather than the exploratory realms of other Supergiant romps.  While many of the game's choices are binary, you can immediately see the impact of what you've done (and the potential losses borne by the choice you didn't make).  What the game lacks in exploration, it makes up for in these grand purposeful decisions which have a salient impact on both the narrative and how the game will be played.
The storytelling is superb; it stands as a cut above its predecessors in a lot of ways.  While Bastion, Transistor, and 90's cult classic Space Jam emphasized art as a means of conveying their messages; Pyre has stronger dialogue, character-building, continuity, and purpose.  Perhaps others will find its story less compelling than those other examples, but the game's narration uses more layers to impart that message and gives the player more agency over that message.  The frequent branching options presented in the game's story help provide that agency, in a powerful way.
The game's music is truly incredible, with a diverse set of tracks, all provided by the legendary Quad City DJs.  The game contextually pulls tracks in just when they're needed, reinforcing the themes and mood in a subtle and natural way.  Ethereal harps and acoustic instruments, combined with a fusion of heavy guitar riffs and modern sounds, transport the player to an anachronistic and foreign world dominated by mystery and magic.
In sum: You have a game that truly includes the player in the narrative, while using its art and unparalleled soundtrack to instill a sense of place and tone.  Recurring characters--allied and enemy alike--make for a comfortable space where this narrative can take place.
==========
The gameplay is much more akin to Jam than Bastion or Transistor.  Three Tunes (selected at the start of the match) must use the power of the Pro Ball, which contains the collective b-ball skills of Earth's greatest ballers, to triumph over enemy teams of three.  You can only command one baller at a time.  When you've got the ball, you must rely on your mobility to move rapidly down the court.  When the ball is in the Monstars' possession, you use your deadly auras and special techniques as "crowd control" to force your foes to respawn and create an opening for your own team.
The gameplay is quick and has an emphasis on rapid decision-making.  Switching gears from defense to offense and back again is a primary concern.  After laying down a Slam Dunk, the character who jammed is temporarily removed from play leaving just two Tunes left on the court.  There were plenty of times when I'd use Speedy Gonzales to slam a quick jam, only to find that I had no fast Tunes left for the next jump ball.  Instead, I'd have to rely on the slower Porky or Gossamer to jam slams.
Each Tune can be advanced and outfitted with ACME gear that improves how they ball, the attacks they can use, how quickly they respawn when outballed, and whether or not they jam.  Some Tunes can fly (Tweety, I'm looking at you!) while others have powerful ground attacks--none more powerful than Foghorn Leghorn's.  Balancing your Tunes and deciding when to use whom is critical to your success in the game.  There's a suprisingly depth of strategy here, especially on the game's higher difficulty settings.
============
In the end, I recommend this game to any b-ball fans, Tune Squad alums, Supergiant enthusiasts, or anyone who likes a good narrative.  Happy Jamming!

Pyre is a game that does a lot of things very well. At its heart, the core gameplay loop is an unholy fusion of magic-infused NBA Jam 3v3, and a dash of Oregon Trail on the side. You pick a place to go, on the way there you get a choice of things, and once you do one of the things you reach the destination. Then you get a last chance to prepare before you face your opponents in a very solid and enjoyable match of class based basket ball. Win or lose your story continues, just the choices you get to make and events in the world around you change. Not even strictly for the worse.
Sadly, the thing about Supergiant games is that to offer you more in-depth coverage would be to drop hot, spicy spoilers upon you, which I shall avoid. But suffice to say, at some point there is a twist that exposes the endgame, and adds more intensity to your choices, and weight to every win or loss.
The music is lovely, though there was no real gut punch that caused me to start crying as there was in Transistor or Bastion. That said, it was more unanimously enjoyable, and I've found myself humming most if not all of the soundtrack on my day to day at some point without thinking about it.
Characters are well written and likable for the most part, even most of your opponents. There will very likely be at least one person that resonates with you, whether they be charming or relatable, or simply adorable. Every member you add to your team also has their own uses, nobody really feels like a sub-par version of another character, as even those with largely similar move sets very vastly as you level them up and choose skills.
However, the game is not perfect. If you're quick on the uptake and got fast hands, you should be able to choose whether you win or lose every match on the normal difficulty. It starts easy, and by the time the difficulty starts pumping up, you've got enough levels and trinkets to sort of brute force your way through most challenges, though the potential for some tricky, flashy plays is certainly there. There are, after a certain point, the return of difficulty modifiers that may be turned on or off before each match, which should be familliar in execution if you've played a supergiant game before. I've always liked that way of adjusting difficulty more than just shifting a slider, but it can be intimidating to mess with too much, and it's easy to promise yourself the highest chance of sucess by leaving them all off, especilly since the xp rewards for toggling them on feel a tad stingy. As a result, I ended up beating my first full story playthrough in about 10 or so hours, I want to say.
This feels a little rougher because, unlike the last two games, there is no new game plus. The idea is that the player is given at least 5 save slots, and there is so many chances for the story to branch that starting a whole new game could turn out completely differently. Which is certainly fine, to an extent. However, the game treats the new save like a fresh, brand-new save. No option to skip tutorials or cutscenes that there is no possible way around that you could have changed in any meaningful way beyond mashing through the dialogue.
Besides that, there is the versus mode, which can be done against people or AI. It's competent and fun, though there is no online play. But it feels like there's something missing. The game would have been greatly helped by the addition of some sort of world map mode outside of the story. Just have your whole team, and let you lose yourself in going from place to place, enjoying the gameplay loop of "Pick opponent, do event, prepare, face opponent, repeat." The only way to do that is starting an entirely new game, and unfortunately that does still give certain spoiler-riffic time constraints and pressures that would be kinda nice to just... not have to deal with.
If those things are game breakers for you, then I offer my apologies and hope you find a better game. However, for all my complaints, the game was fun, charming, and I'm already well into another playthrough of the main story, because it's just that good. I would suggest giving it a try, even if you're not into sports games, as there's plenty to love no matter what you enjoy.

First of all let me say, I wouldn't pay the full price for this game.. But if you're a fan of turn-based tactical strategy games & it is on sale, this game is a must buy. I'd probably describe this game as a stripped down version of X-COM. Instead of killing aliens around the globe, you are put in "raid" type scenarios against terrorists. Unlike X-COM though, there is no real story, you just complete missions & earn a number of stars depending on your performance. As you gain stars you unlock more levels, gear, etc. You earn silver each time you complete a mission, which you can use to to buy the new gear. You can make more than one squad & you can chose what Branch they are, such as SAS, SEALs & Rangers, etc. You're men level up allowing you to allocate points to certain attributes & they gain perks relative to what they specialise in. At the end of the day, this game is a fun strategy game with a heap of levels & difficulties to play on. The graphics, sounds and controls are basic, but good & overall the game is a great time killer. So I would definitely recommend this game if its ON SALE. I would not recommend it at the full price of $15 which in my opinion is a joke.

I find myself writing this review to try and be fair to the developers whilst at the same time hopefully helping some potential buyers from purchasing this game under false impressions.  I don't know exactly how one is supposed to review an Early Access game.  Everyone seems to be doing it differently.  I believe this game should be reviewed in its current state, but it clearly also matters where the game is going to end up as well, and it also is extremely important in my opinion for EA how well the developers are supporting and progressing their game.

First and foremost I would say: read the information on the store page, especially the Early Access information.  I have no idea how on earth anyone could possibly buy an Early Access game without reading this information first, but it seems many people do.  This game is in the middle of being developed.  Anyone expecting a completed game is going to be left disappointed.   That being said, I find the current state of the game highly enjoyable, as do many others, but it is certainly not for everyone.

I believe it is causing a problem that is potentially misleading people, both with positive and negative reviews and comments, that pretty much everyone seems to be constantly comparing this game to Football Manager and the no-longer-existent Football Manager Live.  It is absolutely ridiculous and wholly unfair to the developers of this game for it to be compared to either of these games.  One of them is a single player game and the other one doesn't exist.  It just doesn't makes any sense to me.

If what you want is a single player football management game, then you should not be reading this review - you should be playing Football Manager.  You should only stay here continuing to read my review if the online multiplayer aspect is important to you.

What this game should be getting compared to are all of other online football management games that do actually exist.   Games like Hattrick, Top Eleven, Virtual Manager, Trophy Manager and the 100's of other games like these.  The thing that initially drew me to 90 Minute Fever was  precisely because of the online aspect and their promise of no pay to win elements as I absolutely hate any games that have these.  From all of these other online football management games the best experience I could personally find was playing Hattrick, which is in theory free to play but in reality you pretty much must have a membership package in order to play properly which can cost upwards of 20 Euros per month.  90 Minute Fever costs a fraction of this amount to play and in my opinion offers a vastly superior play experience to all of these other online football management games, even in its current state.  It's an added bonus for me that it also comes with the promise that it is only going to get better and better and better.   It is obvious that this game has been designed to have no pay to win elements, which is critically important for me - I wouldn't care how good this game were - if it was pay to win - I would not have any interest at all.

This game is extremely challenging.  It is PvP on a balanced, well designed and fair playing field.  It is clearly designed with the long term in mind.  That you need to build towards goals over time.  Anyone who is unable to handle losing is going to struggle with this game.  Anyone with a 'win now' mentality is also going to struggle.  For me this is great, I want a long term and engaging challenge.  But this type of game is not for everyone.   I would say as a general rule, if you have ever quit and loaded up a saved game in any single player football management game because you lost a match you feel you shouldn't have lost - then this game is not for you - it's as simple as that.  There are no second chances.  Every single result has to be earned.  It is ruthless, it is challenging, it is emotional and it can be extremely frustrating at times.  But all of these things are what make the play experience so rewarding.  I want my success to have meaning, and the only way it will have this is if it is a real challenge to achieve it.

As many other users have said in their reviews, I also feel this game has huge potential.   More importantly, I believe this game is going to live up to its potential because from what I've seen from the developers I am very impressed.  They are engaging with users, working seemingly all hours of each and every day, are very responsive, are highly active on the forums and have already released a major update to the game despite having been on Early Access for less than 1 month.  They are clearly very passionate and committed to developing this game.  How the developers engage with their community, how they support their product, and how much progress they are making to further develop their game, are in my opinion, the most important things by far for an Early Access game, and the developers behind this game I believe are right up there with the best you're ever likely to find working on an EA game.

I'll have to start off by saying this game isn't for everyone. There's not much gameplay to it other than a few puzzles here and there and waiting around while a monster/robot walks by. While a lot of people may see that as a problem, I didn't mind it at all.
The atmosphere makes up for it (to me) and I really did enjoy the story. Honestly, the monsters were just an annoying obstacle to get through so I can continue to enjoy the story; that's why I didn't really enjoy Amnesia all that much. The "scare factor" for the monsters wore off rather quickly and I didn't really care all that much about the castle itself. In SOMA, I really wanted to get to the next section to uncover more of the plot and learn about what happened. I actually felt pretty immersed and Simon felt believable, mostly anyways. I actually felt some pretty hard emotions when the ending hit, although I could do without the end credits scene. I like it when a game makes me feel like a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥and lets me just sit there :^)
So finally,
Pros:
- Immersive story (if you allow yourself to be immersed, because that's how these things work)
- Great atmosphere
- Game wasn't too long, but wasn't too short
- Ran well on a mid-tier system (a few framerate issues, but there's an optimization guide that worked well)
Cons:
- $30 is a little pricey, I'd say $15-$20 is a reasonable price
- The monster sequences towards the end got annoying. It was hide for a minute, make some noise to distract the monster, go back into hiding, etc.
- Not much gameplay other than simple puzzle solving
- Little replay value
I'll say it again, it's not for everyone. I see people calling it a "walking simulator" and in some cases that's true, but it's not necessarily a bad thing. Some games are open world sandboxes where you can run around and do whatever you want, this game isn't that. I'd probably compare this to a VN without the waifus and way more interactive. Between the monster sections, you're going through and experiencing the story. I don't see why people think it's a bad thing when the story isn't terribly written.
TL;DR, if you're the kind of person that wouldn't mind paying for nothing else but a good story, this game is for you. Otherwise, look into getting Alien: Isolation or just save your money.

Bejeweled 3 is probably one of the best Match 3 games available on Steam, or if not, then it's definitely the most complex one. It features various game styles, thus satisfying different gamer personalities.
If you like to be under pressure, then there's the Lightning Mode, in which you have a timer that you can be increased by quickly match some special time gems. Diamond mine provides a similar tension: there's a timer too, but in this mode you dig in the stone and sand by matching 3 - 5 gems in order to uncover treasures. However the most stressful game mode is probably Ice Storm - in which you have to fight the climbing columns of ice that quickly threaten to cover the entire board; to prevent this you need to have quick reflexes and a very good perception of the available matches. In order to beat this game mode, I had to switch to mouse and keyboard controls (mouseovering the tile selects it and WASD moves it in the corresponding direction).
On the contrary, for those that like a more relaxed approach, there's the Zen mode - the classic Match 3 in which you can enable/disable different relaxing background effects and positive affirmations. Another relaxed mode, but more suitable for those that have an analytical mind or love to strategically solve a puzzle, is the Butterfly mode, in which some of the gems are transformed into butterflies that automatically move one tile up whenever another match is made; having one of them reach the top of the board ends the game. This implies that you have to plan ahead your moves and optimize the matches so that they contain as many butterflies as possible.
I found Poker mode to be the least attractive of all these modes - you are required to build certain poker hands by having consecutive matches of the same colors. It's a game of chance, since your poker hands highly depend on the randomness of the current tiles.
Lastly, there's the Quest mode that contains 40 variations of all these described above: finding a certain number of treasures or freeing a certain number of butterflies, or ticking bombs that need to be matched before the timer wears off etc.
The game adapts itself to the game mode you're playing. For example, in Diamond Mine or Ice Storm mode the game will provide you with suitable gems to create matches or 4 or 5 which result in special gems that help clearing up the board faster. In Poker mode you’re more likely to have gems of the same color grouped together, thus facilitating the process of obtaining good poker hands.
All-in-all, this is a good Match 3 game, if you enjoy the style. But it's quite addictive, so it will probably keep you entertained for hours. Even more so, going for 100% achievements requires a lot of time of grinding.

The game starts off with the counselors in the middle of the woods gathered around a campfire and a guy walks up and is suddenly attacked by Jason. The counselors get frightened and scatter in various directions. And you start off as random counselor with nothing but your sony walkman "Joking". You literally have nothing and must gather supplies found in various dressers, desks, bookshelves etc..
You have a stamina gauge and you have to use it effectively otherwise if you encounter Jason you will be an easy kill.
Whenever Jason is close by the music becomes more intense (Like in the movies) And you better either find a nice hiding space i.e a wardrobe, under the bed, in a shed, Yes! Jason will chop off your head.
I enjoy the gameplay. You really are in survival mode while evading the masked psychopath and keeping your composure while figuring out how you're going to make it out alive.
You can play in team mode or you can use the other campers as bait giving you enough time to flee still in tact.
Their are various weapons to use to slow down Jason while you escape but you can only use one item so find something you're good with and keep it handy.
Pros:
The game is fun by yourself and even better with friends.
Lots of potential to be a great multiplayer survival horror.
The animation and gory deaths scenes are accurate to the movies.
Cons:
Jason has the power to see through walls and objects so it makes the game sorta unfair
Jason can teleport so again.. not really fair
The game has occasional glitches and bugs that need to patched.
If you're easily scared or not this is a great game that has room for improvement.

Short: Overall, I enjoyed SOMA. I'm not running to go buy it a line of credit at Amsterdam's red light district, but it felt a good deal for the price. Everything below's a just-finished summary of criticisms rather than a balanced review, so take it at face value.
Long:  Soma's a nice addition to a pretty sparse genre; it's not the genre-busting masterpiece you might've been waiting, a saviour to a neglected breed that Dead Space left pretty hard in the cold after 2.

Interactions were clever, the responsiveness to player actions felt natural, the interactivity was rewarding, (Even if it did taper off nearer to the end, especially in black-box form.) and it was nice to read logs in the scant few moments some Gribbly didn't want to angrily choke me. The atmosphere in the beginning is excellent, the tension completley thrown askew into confusion and deep unease by the first meeting with a robot, and (accidentally) discovering you can read brains, and robots, somehow. Blessed be the Omnissiah. Gameplay wise; Throwing things to make distractions, console interaction, computer logs, all feel very much like it's sitting next to Alien Isolation's desk and taking more than a few notes, but it's not really something to hold against it, the real-time nature adds well to the tension in the same vein, and in return, Working Joes always gave me that Tuurngait vibe back from the Penumbra days.
The issue kicks in when you present a rather clever idea, the irritable, often insane robots, absolutely hell bent convinced they're human, and throw it out the window so early in favour of Squidward Tentacles and his Motley Gribbly Crew who've been floating about since the Tuurngait; there's a lot of buildup and nervous hiding from an obscene VIRUS-like robotic monstrosity who doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about your pithy metal walls and only lets you down by not being Donald Sutherland, who then proceeds to completley disappear, followed by his equally disturbing mini-sub ilk not another chapter later. For how much the game kinda sells itself on them, it's really disappointing, summed up with their exile around

Overall, it's a vague decline rather than a sheer cliff drop, and apart from a vague sense of disappointment from an underutilised gem of an idea,

The ocean itself felt more like a plot device, or at worst, an annoyance. It never felt threatening in the slightest, which detracted a lot from the whole 'inescapability' of being trapped underwater or at risk of constant decompression. It just feels there occasionally, when the game reminds you you're not in space or on Deimos as much as it feels the same at times.
Lastly, there's an ineffable, almost infuriating trend for sci-fi horror games to turn into Meat Circus funland at the halfway point that has mystified me to this day. To me, the whole point is a future gone wrong, where the high-tech familiar becomes hostile and unsafe, not walking through a Kebab shop dumpster for ten minutes, wondering where my hilariously unsafe workplaces and insufferably obstructive technology went. Sure, the Many pulled it off well, but it's not a contractual obligation. The most unnerving places in SOMA were precisely the ones that looked the most 'human', as broken and worn down as they were. Either way, it's just a nudge over £20, and that's not counting sales, I still definitely recommend giving it a runthrough yourself and make your own mind up, because it does render some of its ideas very brilliantly, if very briefly.
Here's hoping Routine stays the course, whenever it's coming out.

While the game is similiar to DayZ, and those who say it is, are both correct, and wrong, it has the same PVP-E aspect, loot-loss on death, and including the gameplay(some ways more than others), it is also different, in DayZ it's just the same old zombies.  There wasn't any type of variety other than the clothing they wore..but they were still just regular zombies.  Nether has a different variety, which sets it apart from DayZ.  I agree that it isn't "ENTIRELY" set apart, but it branches out further.  There is the ability to have somewhere to be safe, I.E: Safezones, which at times go down, so they do offer the ability of a huge concentrated area OF the creatures given the name of "Nether".  The game is indeed very aggitating, but just like anything else, you learn to deal with it.  Players camp and cheat, it's pretty much unavoidable, every time some sort of Anti-Hack/Cheat shield gets better, somebody runs out hacks to go and well.. maneuver through it.  Think of the cheating like this concept: You can't KILL 100% of germs, it's impossible, they just multiply back in numbers, so you can't forever be rid of something.  It will always come back. | With that concept, it applies to the same with cheaters/hackers/exploiters.  You can't FOREVER be rid of them, they, just like germs, multiply, yet they have a spot to go and do that, and not be penalized for it, which enables those WHO DESIRE TO PLAY LEGITLY (boldened for emphasis) to go and play without that constant fear of hackers.  While I do admit they occasionally appear on SECURED servers(not to be considered 100% HACKPROOF) they don't happen AS often as they used to.  It gives the concept of what happens when you die in DayZ, you lose everything.  (Well, minus very small details) yet it's a simple Open World, PVP-E survival. Meaning just like in DayZ, you have to survive the ENVIRONMENT(Which means what the world THROWS your way) PLUS the players.  Yes, people camp, but there are those who go and kill those who SZ camp.  While the game is still RAW, it's being refined. So if you're going to whine about the PVP aspect and whatnot, it isn't for you, but don't sit there and complain about how much you hate the game, just write a review, but don't make it toxic, or thrown with a lot of swearing, it just makes your arguement/review, less likely to be given any heed.  I do understand the game is frustrating.  What isn't nowadays? It's at that point, you take a break, come back, and try again.  You might ACTUALLY find something you like about the game, instead of being constantly hateful towards it.  We as people get angry, but it is just a game, not life itself. (I do know I set myself up for that "YES IT IS!" deal. Yet I speak truth.  Consider what you consider life to be.  I'll leave it at that)  Just enjoy(or don't) a game.  It's meant for fun.  Besides, dying in the game, gives you another chance to go about a different route or playstyle.  It's a CLEAN SLATE moment.  Even the best players end up dying in video games.  It's a very addictive game, once you know what you're doing.  Two tips that have kept me alive would be worth noting: One; Watch who you trust. Two; Safety in numbers.

Рецепта - Таратор
Необходими съставки:
краставица - 1 брой
кисело мляко - 400 грама
копър - 1/2 връзка
чесън - 3 скилидки
орехи - 20 грама
олио - 2 супени лъжици
вода - 300 мл
В дни, в които термометрите показват близо 40 градуса, всеки търси начин да избяга от жегата. Разбира се най-доброто решение на проблема е да се цопнеш в морето, но за жалост не всеки има възможност да го направи. Една студена напитка, или супа връща желанието за живот в подобни моменти. Испанците си имат гаспачо, а ние си имаме таратор. Противно на разпространеното мнение, тараторът не е уникално българско „изобретение“, а по-скоро балканско, но това не пречи да е любимата студена супа на всеки българин. Таратор в купичка, таратор в чаша, а даже и таратор в бутилка, има ли лято има и таратор! Избягай от жегата – изяж един таратор! ;) А ето я и най-пълната рецепта за класически таратор!
Първата стъпка от рецептата за таратор е подготовката на краставиците. Измивате краставицата и я обелвате. Ако сте успели да се сдобиете с пресни краставици, произведени от някоя баба на село няма нужда да ги белите. Нарязвате я на много малки парченца / кубчета. Много домакини настъргват краставицата, за да спестят време. Така краставицата омеква повече и тараторът става като каша. Но в случай, че сте наистина жадни и не можете  да чакате дълго, можете да ползвате и този метод.
Изсипвате краставицата в голяма купа и прибавяте към нея ситно нарязания копър (може да ползвате и сух копър), смлените орехи и чесъна, който сте счукали, или нарязали на много дребно. За разлика от французите обаче много българи не обичат чесън, затова можете да не добавяте чесъна към таратора, а да го оставите в отделна чинийка, така всички ще са доволни: любителите на чесън ще си добавят в последствие, а противниците няма да се мръщят.
След като сте прибавили чесъна, орехите и копъра поселете, добавете и олиото/зехтина и разбъркайте добре. След това разбийте една кофичка мляко с една кофичка студена вода, добавете към сместа с краставиците и пак разбъркайте. Тараторът е вече готов.
Съвет: Ако ви се стори, че тараторът не е достатъчно студен, може да добавите и няколко кубчета лед.
Рецептата за таратор е изпълнена!

Knights of the Old Republic 2 (KOTOR2) followed up one of the most successful Star Wars games at the time (and rightfully so), and managed to be just as good of a game, although without the shocking twist. KOTOR2 is definitely playable without having played the first KOTOR, as it follows a different cast of characters set a few years later, but if you plan on playing KOTOR at any point definitely play that game first as the story will get spoiled very quickly in this one.
KOTOR2 is basically a cRPG-lite; you have 3 classes to choose from, using a kind of DND system with automated dice rolls determining anything from hit chance, to damage, to saving throws, and makes it accessable. The party has decent AI so you don't have to micromanage every battle, and there aren't many abilities that abuse positioning to where pausing and shifting every second is a necessity (e.g. no attacks of opportunity, which would result in a free attack against any enemy unit moving within a certain radius). The RPG elements themselves are very good, with an interesting and malleable character that can either be Jesus reincarnated or somebody who steal a box of cookies from a Girl scout and then sue for damages, with very little in between. The supporting cast is okay, about par for the course, but what really shines is the main theme of the game: What is the force? A staple of the entire series, you get to explore what the force really means to the universe of Star Wars and its symbiotic relationship with its denizens.
The gameplay mechanics are pretty good but not spectacular. There are options to crank up the power and smash people with a lightsaber, or blast them down with the Force, or be a deadly sniper and pop people with blasters of all kinds, and thats about it. There isn't a huge variety of force powers, feats, or weapon classes (although there are a lot of options within the blaster and melee categories), which means that most builds will most likely funnel into the same spot. You can still choose to be an egg head that can repair droids and plant mines to bait enemies, which can be a fun way to set up particularly pesky enemies.
Overall, Knights of the Old Republic 2 is a good follow up to the award winning Knights of the Old Republic, with most notably having great RPG elements and a deep question being asked throughout the game. Great entry into the world of RPGs, and possibly even the rat's nest that can be cRPGs, and this version handles very well on Steam, unlike it's predecessor.

Short short: Good for killing time, but a lot that could be improved. And not really the "educational" experience that was particularly advertised.
Long story:
The game has little control. No audio options, not even the basic "Mute Music" Option that even web games have. The minute you click outside the window (which DOESNT scale to match the screen - it's a set size and that's it) it pauses and gotta click back into it, which is kind of expected as the game is time restricted. As for the actual doll controls, they're alright - you can only rotate the dolls in a single direction, so if you mess up, you have to rotate them the whole way round. X/Y controls are mirrored around a central axis, but then again no more controls are really required. A harder mode could possibly be added, where each hand has individual control.
As for gameplay, frankly it's boring. You move two dolls into each other and try to line up their crotches before smashing them together - Think the Team America sex scene, but with none of the comedy appeal.
And that's it - you smash dolls together till your mum gets home, followed by a "You maybe had sex however many times". If you get caught, your mum is clearly embarrassed, but otherwise there are no consequences.
The graphics are very retro, but in a warm, less mechanical variation than some other retro games. Warm colours, and basic sprites. Sorta like some of the early 90s educational games I played before my parents started giving me money to buy my own games.
Music is... interesting, potentially out of place, as it doesn’t really add much, and even distracts at times. Sound effects are really basic, but they work, again fitting in with the retro feel. And as I said before, there are no audio controls.
As for the intent of the game? No clue.
It doesn’t match up with the "experience" the devs promise (purely going from the promotional video and the description here). I can understand how children will try and recreate sexual acts with dolls or soft toys, but from my own memory, there was a lot more "passion" involved, starting off with some kissing, followed by gentle cuddles, and then some crotch bumping or rubbing, rather than the pelvis-shattering hip motions illustrated here - maybe this was meant to be a reflection on sexual activities in modern society, and how we lack a lot of intimacy within out sexual relations. Or lazy dev work, but I'll leave you to decide that.
What I can determine though, is that the controls are limited, the Audio is quite nice but could do with some controls, the gameplay and story leave a lot to be desired, and there is no sense of realism, which I wouldn’t really mind had the devs not promised something based on real experience.
However, this is a free game. I admire the devs for working on this and creating something for the community. What bugs me is the fact that it delivers something other than what the devs seemed to intend on delivering.
In summary? It's good to kill time, but if you were looking for anything deep and meaningful, vaguely exciting (sexually), or a way of introducing sex to the kids, don't even download the game, because you'll be sorely disappointed and maybe even angry.
Then again, ANYTHING would help ease the pain of the GTA 5 delay, so knock yourself (and maybe the dolls) out.

Ohhh jeez, where do I start with Pyre..
I expected this to be rather easy. I enjoyed previous Super Giant Games a lot (Transistor slightly more), so pre-purchased this without a shadow of a doubt along with Soundtrack. Frankly I was not completely sold on the whole sports-gameplay idea, but trusted SGG's judgement.
So what's the catch? The catch is I didn't fall in love with this one instantly as with the Transistor or Bastion.
Not before the first 3 hours of playthrough that is..
Let's start with the good stuff, the things I enjoyed from the get-go:
Darren Korb strikes again. Not a single time the music felt out of place, distracting or monotonous, on the contrary it only improved the experience by immersing me deeper into the atmosphere and story. The SGG staple - the songs - are here yet again and as touching as ever.
Vivid and beautiful as in previous titles. Just check the screenshots or reviews! And it all is animated just as masterfully.
The settings feels unique and interesting with whole lot of lore to it (way more than in previous titles). There is a whole range of different characters that fit the picture nicely. Rarely do they feel too cliche, come to thing of it, some of them are, but the devs went extra mile to ensure they are not just a one dimensional cardboard cut-outs. Some got to me, turning seemingly trivial choices into a struggle.
This is not a game related, but SGG-related rather. Massive kudos to you guys for quick forum replies and more importantly swift and relentless bug-squashing. Seriously though, as a software development person, I can confirm that handling customer issues is most difficult task, exhausting even which eats so much time. The <24h patches on an error some random player happen to stumble on felt really good.
So what are the cons (actually just one):
Not the mechanics themselves (matches are ok and kinda unique), but the gameplay volumes. For me it felt little less than a game, but more of a tale (a book) that sometimes gets interrupted by some interactive, gameplay pieces.
Imagine Bastion where Hub (+cutscene) sequences and combat sequences where swapped around. This creates an interesting predicament: until you get invested in the story (which at start you know nothing of) you simply sit there waiting for the rites to start; but should you click through the dialogues, chances are you won't care much for the story. Though game does it's best to get you involved, after all it is its strongest suit.
So yeah, that's my main gripe with Pyre (then again I never was a "visual novel" genre fan).

It's great, fun and touching at (many) times.
Nah, I still like Transistor more :) But hey Pyre is times longer (20H on one playthrough) and has a happier ending (at least I got that).
PS: suggest raising game's difficulty to the maximum. After all, freedom is a privilege one has to earn.

Pyre masterfully blends a compelling story with engaging gameplay.
The immersive world is enhanced by the colorful cast of diverse characters. The first few hours of the game involve recruiting these characters while learning the ropes of the "rites," a sportlike ritual that forms the majority of the gameplay. Each character has a unique set of abilities during the rites that allow for you to develop your own style of play. The gameplay evolves over the course of the 10-15 hour game, remaining challenging without becoming too difficult. Despite the simple concept, the rites never become repetitive, due in part to the large variety of enemies and settings.
Because there is no "game over," your actions during the rites have a genuine impact on the story. It truly feels like you have agency in the game's plot. Regardless of whether you win or lose, the game continues, presenting unique circumstances that culminate in the final arch. The finale capitalizes on the strength of the characters and writing, and relies on your actions throughout the game.
I fully recommend Pyre, it feels like a combination of basketball, the Banner Saga, and a Telltale game, and is one of the best games I've played all year.

I was 4 years old when Doom came out. Wow. Has it been that long? 4 years old, and I would never had thought games could be any better than Doom. It still almost seems that way. It was Wolfenstein 3D, and Doom, that got me hooked on FPS games. Later when the other FPS games that followed after Doom came out like, Quake, Decent 1 & 2, all would solidify my cravings to be the one to pull the trigger. Doom is a household name! The somewhat endless stories of people suffering from sleep depervation because Doom was so addictive is just awesome to hear, because I know personally what they mean. I remember I would sometimes through a fit, because my parents would make me go to bed. But, I know if my parents would've let me played as long as I desired, then I would definitely have stayed up for days playing Doom. That's not good for the health. Nope, nope. Hey, one time my friends and I stood up for three days straight just to beat Duke Nukem 3D. Lol, good times. Awe, man! When, I turn 40 years old, I will expect you future kids to know Doom. You kids now have the privilege to either choose to play this old Doom game, or some new, hyped up, Next-Gen, game coming out next week. When I was you're age, Doom was the Next-Gen game for us, and boy does it still rock! Not to make you kids feel underprivileged because you were born late, no, I'm just suggesting you to buy Doom, and see why it became a huge turning point in the history of gaming. You're gonna wish that you love it as much as we who grew up with it do, and that's an encouraging thought. There are so many great FPS games out there, but Doom will always have its rightful spot in my collection.

This game is a close as I've ever seen to Football Manager Live - the online version of the popular game series which was around a few years back....and quite a players in this game were veterans of that. There's an active and helpful community, and the dev's are pretty communicative about the direction of the game (for example with forum post updates, end of season reviews/quizzes).
The game itself will initially see you in charge of a new bunch of randomly assigned players, and entered into a qualifying league. You get to choose an FA for your 2nd season; these are broken down into timezones when you're most likely to be online to play.  It really is a case of learning and working your way up the rankings and the leagues, it's not an instant gratification game like FIFA (as I'm sure you'll be aware if you played FML). There are also many 'Reborn Legends' in the game - that's any famous players who have retired from the game and been added in from some quota or requested to be added by Patreon's (people who opt to help the devs by paying a monthly sub - that is not compulsory but if you love the game it's a way to help it to continue to improve).
There are NO pay to win elements in the game at all, and the dev team are strongly committed to ensuring it remains that way.
Strongly recommend you get this game in the current sale for less than £4, especially if you're a fan of the previous FML, Football Manager or have ever loved playing as lower league sides and developing into a force to be reckoned with!

SOMA is a great game that somehow slipped under the radar.  Gameplay and graphics reminded me of BioShock, only creepier with no weapons. Encounters with aggressive creatures are minimal (maybe 10 total), but when you happen across them, the only means of survival is stealth and avoidance. Very different than what I am used to. About 20% of the way through you meet a travelling companion. She offers roughly the same amount of dialogue and interaction as Elizabeth from Bioshock Infinite (if you are familiar).
Pros
- Excellent story that will keep surprising you and make you think.
- A game with no weapons was a refreshing change of pace.
- A travelling companion
- Amazing Voice Acting.
- Two Endings (though not the result of game-wide choices)
Cons:
- Game is linear. This is the price we often pay for good stories.
- Choices have immediate consequences, but never extend beyond the current area/chapter.
- Saving is a pain. No "Save" Menu option. Only "Exit and Save".
- Most audio recordings found in the game are hard to understand. Turn subtitles on.

Nether is a Survival Horror game that gets a lot of flak for doing exactly what it says on the tin.
Asking you to survive.
People will complain that they die too frequently, both from players and nether, Loot drops are terrible, and that you have to pay to access some of the loot chests.
But none of these are really drawbacks (or true!) and only really come into play if you intend to attempt to play Nether like you'd play Call of Duty.
If you bought Nether and intended to run all over the map and just shoot and kill everyone, then you bought the game for the wrong reason.
If you're dieing too frequently, then change your routing. Go through buildings, stick to foliage, and generally look around before diving into the next area. Unlike other games like Infestation, there are much, much less wide-open fields for other players to see you from miles away from, so stick to places where you'll be difficult to spot. If you're falling to Nether, simply avoid all of them but the Crawlers and the Lost. You're not supposed to be a Nether-killing machine. What kind've survival game is it if nothing's a threat to you? So if you're treating them like they're not a threat, they WILL kill you.
But this is by no means game-breaking. Even if you choose to avoid players and Nether, you will still level up. A new system gives you experience for surviving extended periods of time, and with the Packages you can take rom safezone to safezone, it's quite easy to hit level 10 and not have killed much of anything, if you're playing properly.
Now people are complaining about loot, but really it's gotten considerably better than what it was. Guns still aren't particularly hard to find, they're just a rarer drop or you have to craft them, which really isn't a bad thing, and could probably go for being a bit more rare, given that there are still people running around willy-nilly with guns because they know they can easily replace them. But aside from that, the inclusion of the loot chests and other random drops makes it so that it's a lot easier to gather supplies where-as before you could run for hours to find a bag of chips.
If you're having difficulty finding loot, I'd suggest two things: 1. Check buildings, especially ones with bright signs. THe signs mean 'Regular drops here!' and 2. Just keep your eyes open. Honestly, if you've managed to go from a safezone like Museum Outpost to Ridge and haven't found anything? You're sticking too close to the roads and not really exploring.
The addition of the 'Use a key to open the golden chest' thing has really gotten under some players skins, but I don't really understand that one either. Golden chests tend to be pretty uncommon, and even if they weren't you can trade your in-game money to get the keys anyway. There's no need to pay unless you want to.
In the end, Nether's a good survival game. Unlike other survival games, where you'll spend hours trekking across an empty and bland forest to get to the next town, the entirety of Nether is a big city, with plenty of things to look at and hundreds of buildings to explore.
But also remember this is a survival game: You're guaranteed to die. What's important is what you get done in the interim. Look around for supplies, loot those containers, go out of your way because you just saw that glowwy container, then sprint all the way to the safezone to store it.
