I got this game in the humble monthly bundle but had it on my wishlist every now and then. I never convinced myself to actually buy this game and now that I got it ... I am glad.
What starts out as an interesting, charming concept with best intentions, will rapidly fade to a boring beyond belief, grindy UI obstacle course. To keep this whole review as short as possible, let me just list the flaws that actually make this game "unenjoyable" for me:
- The tutorial: Its short, but not in the good way. I was left with so many questions that I had to go with trial and error for the first three families just to see what does what. So, I had to lose on purpose before I could start my actual playthrough, which killed alot of immersion for me.
- Balance and basic logic: The beginning of the game was, well ... partly challenging. I did not have plenty of everything, but that would change very soon. Why? Because of the trading system. Its not broken beyond repair, but it is still flawed and will kill immersion to "balance" the game. Everybody will accept everything. Thats why I survived in the beginning. I kept selling teddybears and vinyls to strangers. While the value of the item may vary, you will still be able to make a good profit under any circumstances. I sold teddybears to random strangers in the wasteland and got their rations, electronics and all the stuff I wanted for it. Read that again. Lone survivors in the wasteland gave me their rations for a teddybear. The reason why its so valuable is because it reduces the stresslevel for children. So, the trading system does need a huge overhaul. People that need their food and/or have no children should not accept teddybears as a trade item at all. The same goes for vinyls. The random strangers do need priorities. Some should not accept basic materials, others should only accept medical supplies and so on. Otherwise, you will most likely play like me, the teddy trader or you will have to force yourself to make your own fictional game rules in order to save your immersion. By the way, after I sold enough teddies, I as able to construct the recycler and thus, had as many water containers as I desired. Which lead to the next trading problem: Water. Once you control the water, you control everything.
- Your family: As mentioned, I had some trial runs before I created the family that I wanted to use for my playthrough and one thing that I noticed is that ... nobody gives a moist♥♥♥♥♥about each other. "Trauma" does not work correctly or is not well balanced. So one of the kids died of radiation poisoning, but I had no nails and of course, you can't construct a grave without nails. So the corpse lay there for quite some time. The trauma levels raised, but I did not really feel any impact. Like, people being depressive, not leaving the beds, sitting in the corner and cry. They don't really care. Once one of the kids "got lost" in the wasteland. The mother came home, took a shower, ate and thats it. Once, wife and husband went out and were ambushed by 3 bears. I just wanted to see how far I can push them, so I killed two of them but then, the husband died. Wifey killed the last bear with her brass knuckles and I took a look at the result screen. She did not gain any trauma, regardless of her beloved man that was ripped into pieces by a wild animal. But ... he gained trauma. In order to be an immersive simulation, there is still a long way to go when it comes to emotional stuff. And as you can guess, the combat system needs alot of work aswell!
- The AI: While trading teddybears, many people loved me, of course. They all wanted my fluffy stuff. So, many people knocked on my door and asked me to take 'em in. I refused every time. Why is that? Let me explain that! More people means less work to keep the shelter intact, right? Riiight? Wrong. Its the other way round. Every AI person you take in is another person that needs commands for every basic aspect of his simple life. Automation is no help there. If you put them on automation, they will do the basic stuff themselves. Like eat or drink, shower and sleep. But, they will manage to♥♥♥♥♥up. If you sent them scavenging and they come back, you can bet your smexy booty that they will be comeplety dirty but even if the shower is empty, they will eat first. That will lead to food poisoning and that will lead to a shelter filled to the roofs with endless waves of vomit. So you have to command them to shower first. You have to command them to clean the bucket after they filled it. You have to command them to feed the horse; to repair; to train; to care for the planter; to clean the shelter and so on and so forth. Meanwhile, you have to answer every radio message yourself. "Yes, I have send you to the apothecary and yes, please search the place. That is why I sent you in the first place, so why bother me? Oh and if you meet a stranger, sell him 2 teddies for anti bioticas. Paul has food poisoning again ..."
That micromanage would not be a problem if you could avoid it to some extent. For example, if you could add "looping or permanent tasks". Like fixing stuff. A permanent command that orders Paul to fix stuff every few minutes. Not until he starves to death. No, like a job. Like a tiny job. Until you order him to stop. The same goes for training, planting, feeding the horse. In the end, I had 4 people, 3 on auto pilot (after I forced them to take a shower of course) and one that I used to do all the necessary stuff in the shelter. So 3 people were standing around until they had to eat or poop or sleep. One kept feeding the horse, fixed stuff and punched the bag. But, there is another reason why I did not take in more people. And that is ....
- The UI: "Paul has radiation poisoning". Why is that? Well, I might have sent him into the wastes without a hazmat suit. Why? There is no reason. I did not want to do that at all. Paul was active when I tried to click Ryan. But the system did not realize I tried to click Ryan. It set a waypoint for Pual instead who gladly went outside without any kind of protection. Misclicking will happen ALOT. Like AAAALOT. No, you don't get it. It will happen AAAAAALOT! Constantly. Two people standing on the same spot, click one, move him away, click the other one. Sht, he vomitted the moment I wanted to click him. Now I have sent the other guy back again. ROOOAR! Many times, my 2nd command in the indiviual command list was blocked by a waypoint that I accidentally set. And thats only one of the major issues the UI struggles with. You will have alot more where that came from. For example, if you realize, you didn't set up the first steps of a scavenging party correctly or you simply want to change something, you cannot go back. You have to abandong the whole thing and set it up again. I am just grateful that I can see my mouse cursor.
So, to quickly sum up: The game is not horrible or something. But to be a good game that can actually be enjoyed, it still has a long, long way to go. In this state (the one I described here), I can not recommend this game at all. It starts out with a forced, useless tutorial and turns into pure boredom. And thats where it stays, trapped like that kid that fell into the well.

I came to this game having loved Bastion and Transistor and rank them in my personal top 20 games ever for the way in which they blend gameplay with story delivery and an exceptional soundtrack.  Therefore, I had very high expectation for Pyre but had noticed in early previews that the gameplay was quite different from those previous games I loved.
As other reviews have stated, Pyre is not similar to Bastion or Transistor in gameplay or story delivery, but I do think it is equally novel.  Pyre plays as something of a mashup of interactive novel and 3v3 sports game with lite RPG leveling and equipment progression.  A somewhat unique mechanic for the game is that winning is not neccesary to progress, and in fact the game presents you with strong cases for some of your opponents deserving their freedom more than you.  This led to some very difficult decisions, and honestly affected me more than the ethical choices that are commonly seen in games (i.e. left click to EVIL).
In the end, while I didn't enjoy the 3v3 combat aspect of the gameplay as much as the action of Bastion or Transistor, I still found the game compelling and my connections with the characters pushed me ever onward towards the end.  Overall, I enjoyed the experience and appreciate how SuperGiant is innovating instead of pushing out standard genre games, but I can see why some people might be turned off by either the interactive novel storytelling or the 3v3 sport/combat.  I highly reccomend not giving in to the natural desire to win every match, and do NOT restart a match that is going against you.  Makes the triumph and defeats much more impactful.
I'll close in listing off a few pros and cons.
Pros:
-AMAZING soundtrack.  Teams and areas have catchy melodies that weave together with the music of the rites.  High point for any SuperGiant game.
-Interesting characters that you get attached to.  I was truly torn on freeing my favorites as I was sad to see them go.
-Beautiful art, with strong character designs and lush, colorful landscapes.
-Customized story and ending.  Every choice you make alters the tree of outcomes, and which characters you choose to free and the decisions you make along the way mean that most playthroughs are very unique.
Cons:
-I personally disliked that only one character moved at a time for the 3v3 sections.  The AI has a habit of knocking out any of your characters that you arent controlling at the moment, and they can't defend themselves.  I would have preferred this style be one variant of the rites, but in others have AI controlling whatever teammates you werent controlling.  I think this would have made for much more dynamic 3v3 gameplay.

The Isle is going to be a great, realistic dinosaur simulator if it gets enough support. Playing the game for some months made me notice some things, which I liked:
- Different types of vocals - It's a big advantage of the game, which allows you to communicate almost without chat.
- Nesting - Maybe it's still in progress, but it makes the game interesting. You can avoid tiring progression and become a baby dinosaur. Growing takes time, though. Perhaps nesting in as herbivores isn't really good idea (Progressing takes about 30 minutes, while growing can take much longer). It's also big fun to be a parent of a small, cute baby that requires you to hunt to feed it and protect it from strangers. Perhaps hunger needs a bit changes.
- Big amount of dinosaurs to choose - There are about 20 totally different dinosaurs in game - herbivores and carnivores. Each one has it's own animations, stats and vocals. Developers work hard to keep adding new stuff, to interest players.
- Huge, detailed maps - For me, map cause big lag, but as they say - Notebook isn't good for the game. You can easily get lost in the map, especially when you are a new player. It took me some months to study map and remember where to find food and water. You can travel through different types of forests, walk around the mountains and see those amazing views.
But also, there are some things I didn't like. I'm not a hater, I just suggest a little changes.
- Collisions - It's really hard (especially when running away from a hungry predator) not to get stuck on tree or rock. Fortunately, developers have added a turn-around system, that allows you to escape, but still, it really annoys and literally brings death. When two big dinosaurs fight, they usually get stuck and bite each other. It makes the fight less dynamic, while dinosaurs should move around, trying to avoid being wounded.
And a word about Progression System. IT IS an advantage on game. It reduces the amount of KOSing to minimum. When a player gets killed, it won't become a huge predator just to kill you in revenge. Perhaps the waiting is tiring and you can get really irritated when you die. That's why the nesting is there, along with sandbox being added in future.

Sniper Elite V2 is a sequel to a game that I'd guess not a lot of people played. The basics are: It's a third-person shooter that switches to first-person scope view when you're sniping things, which is often, because the maps are structured so you have nice long sight lines, and it's not fun to have angry nazis up close. Also, it emphasizes sniping as an element of stealth, which is pretty cool. The sniping wasn't exclusive in Sniper Elite 1, because it supplied you with some really great back-up guns, including (my favorite), an MG42.
Sniper Elite 2 improves significantly on the sniping action with a great slow-motion bullet cam that shows x-ray views of your bullets tearing your enemies apart. The third-person shooting isn't as great with the removal of most of the decent third-person weapons, but the game doesn't really suffer that much for it. It is true, though, that the large set-pieces in big open areas are significantly more fun than endless bombed-out streets with only one path. The large open set-piece battles are about equal in number in Sniper Elite V2 to the original Sniper Elite, but if anything, they should have drastically changed that ratio to make it mostly, if not completely, open area set-piece battles. Third-person shooting down a corridor is just not interesting anymore.
This game really does deliver, but maybe not as much as I'd like. Buy it if you want a decent action game about sniping, and if it's also cheap. ARMA 3 probably has more realistic sniping, but then again, it's ARMA 3.
Remember: Between this game and Sniper: Ghost Warrior, pick this game. Do not play Sniper: Ghost Warrior.

Summary: Not currently worth the subscription fee. Plays reasonably well and never crashed on me, but the massive amount of missing features (compared to Football Manager) and general lack of things to do in the game prevent me from recommending it at this time.
The good:
-Helpful community
-Runs fairly well (though the UI is slow at the moment)
-Those familiar with Football Manager will pick it up quickly
The bad:
-Match results are basically random. Playing with an attacking mentality seems to cause my team to concede more, but that's about the only consistency I've found. Possession, for example, seems to be totally random and not at all effected by match mentality or passing style, or even home versus away.
-Tactics are limited to choosing your formation and setting a few match parameters (match mentality, passing style, closing down). Seriously, that's it. There are no individual playstyles for any position. If you want one of your central midfielders to act more defensively or offensively, the best you can do is put a player in that position with attributes that match how you want them to play. But even then, the game gives no indication of how (or if) player attributes are used for different positions.
-The match itself is currently only viewable in commentary form. Not even a 2D topdown view is available yet, although you would think so if you watched the preview videos.
-Player development has not yet been implemented. About the only things that can happen to your players right now are injuries, disiplinary actions, and reputation changes. The latter seems to be based on match performance versus matches played, and seems to only effect the player's value.
-When you create a team, the game places you into a league with other newly created teams. The only options you have are to play in that league or to play friendlies. The problem is that in order to play against a team in your league, the other player has to actually be online and up for a game. That makes sense from a tactical perspective, but when half the teams in your league either never play a match or quit the game after just one or two matches, it really takes away from the realism.

I have so far gotten to what I assume is the halfway point of the game, if not the second third, and I can already say that this game is worth the price (even though I only got it for $3 over on Humble Bundle)
The story is basic, but enough to keep you engaged. This game takes place during the times dypicted in Ancient Greek Mythology (if you haven't learned much about it, you can get a basic idea from the Disney movie, Hercules, since you don't need to know much to be familiar with the lore this game covers). You play as Nikandreos, a warrior who is sent by Zeus' wife, Hera, to climb Mount Olympus and destroy the gods that abandoned mankind. Like I said, there isn't much to the story, but it does give you the motivation to pursue the task at hand.
The presentation is very well done. The artstyle perfectly replicates the artwork of ancient greek, both in environments and characters. Just a quick heads up, however, that the artstyle matches a bit TOO well; like ancient greek artwork, character models and environmental statues and paintings will feature nudity, such as genitalia (both the male and female variety) and breasts, so if you don't like seeing that sort of thing, it's best to tread lightly. Rest assured, however, that it does not go any further than that. I also like some of the more subtle details, such as the glossy shine that follows your mouse, implying that the game is played out on a clay pot or jar similar to most ancient artwork of the time.
Gameplay is just about what you expect from a Metroidvania: Expansive levels with numerous secret passageways and goodies to find, special abilities that you can unlock as you defeat more gods of Olympus, and the ability to take on the objectives you are given in any order. What makes the game a bit more unique, however, is the weapon and crafting system. To any Anti-Minecraft people out there, don't worry, crafting is neither required or even complex; there's only a handful of items you can craft, such as your basic potions and bombs, as well as consumable weapons like traps. The weapon system is also unique; unlike most other Metroidvania games, you're not just stuck to one weapon, with there being numerous weapons to find ranging from knives, arrows, spears, swords, and sheilds, with each type having their own varied range of weapons; some weapons do high damage when used a certain way, others have elemental abilities like burning damage, and some even provide explorative uses, such as lighting your way through dark areas. It's a bit like Dark souls in that regard, as you also have to keep in mind that some weapons are heavier than others, meaning they have slow attack rates but high damage capability. It's also worth noting that all weapons have stamina, meaning they break after significant use. Thankfully, though, you can purchase any weapons or sheilds you find in the field via the black market, so getting your favorite weapon back isn't too much of an issue if you have the gold to purchase it.
Overall, I can easily call this one of my favorite Metroidvanias so far. It may not be as good as Ori or Dust, but it does what it intends to do very well.

I recieved this game for a 2 months subscription due to a promotion by WorkTheSpace and the developers of the game.  This is also for a beta build that is missing features such as staff and an advanced match engine.
So let me preface this review by saying what this game is not.
Firstly, while it is heavily based on Football Manager, it is not a "ripoff" of Football Manager, the closest comparison however would be to an MMO version of Football Manager.
So firstly, what are the positives?
One thing is community, in 21 hours of the game, I have only seen 1 negative comment in the chat which ironically was due to the community helpers asking for people to share their opinion for the game. Everyone that I have spoken to so far has been very nice and very helpful in certain aspects of understanding the game.
The next positive is the fact that everyone starts on a level playing field. When I first launched up the game, I saw that I had an absolutely stunning 21 year old left back who was the best that has been found so far, but I was suprised to see that when I played my first league match, he also had some very good players.
This game is not like Fifa 16 Ultimate Team where you have to buy coins or FIFA points to buy half decent players and there are zero microtransactions in this game (as of 18th July 2016)
One extra part of the game I like is the "negotiations" tab. When someone accepts a bid for their player from another team, instead of that player going instantly to that team, a 24 hour blind bidding process starts where other teams try to sign that player. This system not only prevents cheating but it lets casual players ignore the mostly tedious manual scouting process that Football Manager offers.
The last positive is that you can actually sign legends in the game in the form of a "youth intake" in the Youth Players tab, so far none of them are available, since they "unlock" from the 24th July onwards if I remember correctly, but it sounds like a very good system and the developers also have the player's wikipedia pages linked to them if you want to learn about their history.
However there are a few negatives to this game aswell.
Firstly, the match engine so far is not nearly advanced enough to be considered adequate, there are some stats that are far more important than others, for example strikers with good finishing are typically much better goalscorers than ones with better dribbling or better physical stats.
One other feature that is suprisingly not in the game yet is the lack of a rating system for your players, in Football manager you have a star system that represents how good your player is compared to the rest of your team, however here the star system is used to represent reputation which seems somewhat meaningless considering a simple post in the chat can increase a players reputation due to the people viewing his player page.
The last negative is the fact that you need to subscribe to play. The price is very tempting I must admit, and it does enable users to pay a small amount and if they dont like the game they can just not renew their subscription, but for long time players you have to pay a lot of money just to play the game for a year.
This game has bucketloads of potential and I just hope that the developers will keep updating the game. I advise that if you wish to buy the game, get 3 months first and see how much the developers update the game.
TL:DR
+ Not P2W
+ Very good community
+ Actually fun for casual and serious players alike
+ You can buy legends
- Some features are lacking
- Match Engine needs an overhaul
- No direct rating system

An action platformer that goes all-in on the Greek mythology theme. Uses an art style that reminds me of ancient Greece's black-figure pottery.
The game has main areas with doorways that lead to realms of gods you have to defeat and eventually you can reach the big boss, Zeus. That's a pretty simplified but accurate description of the game but they use several things to give it more depth: side quests/crafting/simple upgrade system/large variety of weapons/simple puzzles.
Controls feel a little different from regular platformers because there is momentum in your movement and the arc of your attack changes based on your position, angle, and weapon choice.
If you enjoy the idea of Greek mythology, the theme will pull you in. If you're very familiar with Greek mythology, this game is based on and refers to the mythology but isn't something that really goes deep into it. It's a challenge the gods story and that doesn't really lend to very deep storytelling. There are references and (hopefully accurate) quotes from ancient Greek literature scattered about that give it a little more credibility.
Worth a look if you like action platformers and a try if you're into Greek mythology.

This may sound strange, but I've never played the original DOOM (or really any DOOM title) until now. But I figured I wanted to play the title that cemented the FPS genre as we know it today, and also have a**loads of fun.
However, I'm not one who gives titles free passes just because they're "historic" or "influential". You can tell me about how important Super Mario Bros. was for saving the video game industry from crashing in 1985, but I'll simply reply, "It's still just a platformer with no real substance. It's fun, I'll give you that, but there's not much to it." And that's the same argument I'll make with DOOM. There is no cohesive narrative. You just run from level to level, shooting demons in the face until their faces explode from the amount of lead you pump into them. Again, it's really, really fun... it just lacks enough substance to be considered substantial compared to the more narrative FPS games of today.
Now, don't think for a second that I hate DOOM. Because I don't. Much like Super Mario Bros., DOOM is fast-pasted, aesthetically pleasing, and incredibly addicting and fun. I enjoyed the weekend I spent wasting my time getting to the Spider-Demon.
However, there are some problems that popped up while I was played. In my very brief Half-Life review, I commented on how Gordon Freeman hovered and slid a bit. DOOM must have started that trend, because controlling Doomguy is a pain in the a**, especially when running across a ledge and being shot at, where I'd normally fall back down into the pit of lava or poison I had just come from. The level design can also be a bit cryptic. I didn't mind the first three Episodes, they were pretty straightforward. But Episode Four took all the conventions of its predecessors and threw them out the window. I like consistency in my games, is what I'm saying. I like to know that the game is following its own established rules.
Other than that, there's isn't much standing in my way for recommending this game. It's an old 1990's PC FPS classic, and I certainly think anyone who loves Call of Duty, Battlefield, or Halo should go back and check out the game that started it all.

Like a simpler version of Doorkickers that uses turns instead of real-time. Unfortunately the amount of time a turn is, or what will happen during said turn, is never explained. As far as I can tell the turns end once all your characters are done moving.
Its very much a weird mix of XCOM in the way your characters (or "operators" if you prefer) gain perks as they level up, and a weird mix of Doorkickers in regards to position and movement. The movement is controlled by the same button that moves the camera around, so prepare to accidentally swoosh the camera across the map instead of moving your unit a lot.
The orders you can give your units are extremely simple. Move, move at this speed, look this direction, or use a perk/inventory item. That's all. There is no synching up actions to "go-codes" as in Doorkickers. I guess you could synch up actions by just doing them in the same turn but depending on the stats of your units things might not happen at the same time.
Speaking of stats, you can slap all sorts of tacticool♥♥♥♥♥♥all over your units and their weapons. Each thing will affect the weapon or "operator" in someway, but it usually just ends up being "+3 to Accuracy."
Probably my biggest gripe with this game is how hard it tries to be high-speed low-drag hooah operators operatin' operationally. From the intro cutscene to the voice lines to the unit photos it tries so hard to be gruff and tacticool that it just ends up coming off as comical, almost a parody. But I could only listen to what sounded like a teenager saying "AREA SANITIZED" so many times before it stopped being funny.
This might be fun for an hour or so, I picked it up for 99% off. I couldn't see myself getting this for more than a few dollars.
A fun spin on the original, definitely worth your time. I recommend this game to anyone looking for robust point-and-clicks.

Frictional Games... you've done it again.
Came into this spoiler free and was a little concerned when playing the first few minutes of the game. I was a little biased, thinking that they were trying to reskin Amnesia in space but I was wrong. VERY wrong.
Everything in this game is unsettling in the best possible way. Fictional Games have once again proven that they are the best in the industry when it comes to tension and atmosphere. A welcome surprise is the emphasis on beautifully engineered sound design. There are locations in this game that simply must be experienced because of it. You will never see or hear anything like it in any other game. It is that good.
Seriously, if Frictional Games doesn't get some kind of award for their sound design, the industry is beyond saving.
The story could be considered even better than the audio and video in the game. It starts off pretty ambiguous and makes more sense around the same time as its moral compass starts to veer south. Without giving anything away, its themes on existentialism may stick with you long after you've finished the game. It's one of the few games where I just zoned out for a few hours and thought about not just the fate of the characters, but the fate of the world the characters lived in.
This is the kind of game that appeals to both psychological horror fans and sci-fi buffs. Make no mistake, this is not a game about hiding from scary monsters. If you're looking for that kind of experience, Slender or Amnesia might work better for you. There's no hiding from the horrors that exist in SOMA.
Where did my hour go?

It's been a while since I played this game, but I saw it again in my library and do have some very fond memories playing it. The game focuses on stealth much more that brute force, not meaning that a fair deal of the situations you might find yourself in can't be solved with the latter method. Having shot, run around, and in any other way killed a bunch of soldiers while they are openly firing at you will cost more than you would ultimately like.
The best feeing I remember having while playing this game, is that it gave me a feeling of grittiness and a constant vigilance. It felt like the character is a spy with limited supplies and not some über-fighter, dual-wielding a rocket laucher and a sniper rifle. The missions were very enjoyable and their themes varied, as were the little introductions before each one. Getting to know your target helped with the immersion before each mission.
Apart from those things though, there were some aspects of the game that did stand out as not so good. At some missions where targets are heavily guarded, a sense of repetition does become aparrent, though this is not too often. My biggest problem was the enemy's visibility, and that most of the time I could use it to my advantage. There were a few cases where my character was obvious, though none of the soldiers seemed to care. Apart from that, a few tweaks with the movement system would have been nice, though I could personally overlook this problem due to my overall fondness of the theme of the game.
I would give Velvet Assassin a solid 6.5/10. Though problems undoubtebly exist, the theme and feeling this game provides is enough to overcome its flaws. A little more work, maybe in form of a patch would make this a far better experience.

I tried this game thinking it would be interesting.  I liked the two sniper games I played recently, and although this is a different type of game, I thought it would be good, too.  I understand that stealth-based games tend to be difficult, but I think this one is excessively hard.  Even on the easier difficulty level, after ~30 minutes of playing and making multiple attempts, I was still unable to pass the first pair of guards.  Killing the first was easy, but I couldn't get past the second after that.  I expect the beginning of a game like this basically to be instructions on how the game works and what you'll need to do throughout the game.  The start should be relatively easy.  Here, it's not.  There's little instruction besides wait for the two guards to separate (which is semi-obvious), and you're pretty much on your own to figure out how to pass the second guard after taking out the first, something I wasn't able to do.  Had this happened later in the game, I'd accept it as a tricky part of a stage, but having this happen right in the beginning of the game is extremely frustrating.  Maybe I'll come back to this some day, but for now I've uninstalled it.  It's hard to get into a game when I can't even pass the beginning section without massive difficulty.  More dedicated players or people who like stealth games might enjoy this.  But given what I see as excessive difficulty right in the beginning of the game, I can't really recommend this.
Update:  Thanks to a comment on this review, I finally passed the intro mission and got to the next one.  However, I still don't really like that the intro wasn't a self-walkthrough, and I'm still finding the game overall to be slow-moving and rather difficult, even very early on.  That's probably the point here, but I'm not really enjoying it.  Every time I die at a harder part, I have to redo the easier parts before it, and this happens over and over again, making things feel repetitive.  Also, in some sniper games I played recently, I felt like I had a fighting chance if I got spotted, but here I feel like I'm just dead meat.  Maybe this isn't my type of game.  Perhaps in small doses, it will be OK, but I think I'll just end up frustrated if I try to play this for a long time at once.  As I said originally, if you like this type of game in general, you'll probably like this specific game, but I don't think it's for me, and for more casual gamers like me, I wouldn't recommend it because of the rather high difficulty level it seems to have.

I've played this game when it was first released for the original Xbox over a deacde ago, and while the base game is fine as is, I would
recommend installing The Sith Lords Restored Content Mod. That mod restores several plot points and quests that were cut in the original version and makes for an all-around much better experience.
Much like the first one, KOTOR II is a story-rich game that revolves around player choices and allows you to complete various quests and the storyline itself in several different ways. Except, this time, you're able to influence your companions to shift their alignment. Most of your companions are interesting, complex characters, and offer unique viewpoints on the universe they've found themselves in. Unfortunately, this game is incredibly glitchy, with bugs ranging from getting stuck to game-breaking bugs that prevent you from completing the story. , but aside from that, I have very few negative things to say about this game. If you haven't played this game yet, I would recommend giving it a try.

This game is quite simply the best. Rayman is at it again as he traverses 80 creative and often hilarious levels to save the world from nightmares. You'll be swimming, flying, transforming and more through 8 incredibly stylish and unique worlds. With each level you will surely be trying something new, with a huge variety of gameplay mechanics involved.
Level designs are incredibly fun and fast paced, including musical levels where your actions are synchronized with the music. While we're on this topic, the score is awesome. There is everything from tropical ukulele driven tunes to stealthy James Bond-esque ballads. Did I mention this game is really pretty? Especially the remastered throwback levels where the detail is immense.
Don't even get me started on replay value. Not only are there 120 levels to master, but in each there are plenty of collectables and secret areas. Online challenges also ensure the introduction of fresh new content EVERY DAY. Finally, the ending includes the most creative credits sequence I have ever seen. Never have credits been so much fun.
There are only two minor gripes I have with the game. There is no online multiplayer co-op, and there is Uplay integration, meaning you must create a Ubisoft account in order to start the game. Otherwise this game is absolutely brilliant.

Ohhh jeez, where do I start with Pyre..
I expected this to be rather easy. I enjoyed previous Super Giant Games a lot (Transistor slightly more), so pre-purchased this without a shadow of a doubt along with Soundtrack. Frankly I was not completely sold on the whole sports-gameplay idea, but trusted SGG's judgement.
So what's the catch? The catch is I didn't fall in love with this one instantly as with the Transistor or Bastion.
Not before the first 3 hours of playthrough that is..
Let's start with the good stuff, the things I enjoyed from the get-go:
Darren Korb strikes again. Not a single time the music felt out of place, distracting or monotonous, on the contrary it only improved the experience by immersing me deeper into the atmosphere and story. The SGG staple - the songs - are here yet again and as touching as ever.
Vivid and beautiful as in previous titles. Just check the screenshots or reviews! And it all is animated just as masterfully.
The settings feels unique and interesting with whole lot of lore to it (way more than in previous titles). There is a whole range of different characters that fit the picture nicely. Rarely do they feel too cliche, come to thing of it, some of them are, but the devs went extra mile to ensure they are not just a one dimensional cardboard cut-outs. Some got to me, turning seemingly trivial choices into a struggle.
This is not a game related, but SGG-related rather. Massive kudos to you guys for quick forum replies and more importantly swift and relentless bug-squashing. Seriously though, as a software development person, I can confirm that handling customer issues is most difficult task, exhausting even which eats so much time. The <24h patches on an error some random player happen to stumble on felt really good.
So what are the cons (actually just one):
Not the mechanics themselves (matches are ok and kinda unique), but the gameplay volumes. For me it felt little less than a game, but more of a tale (a book) that sometimes gets interrupted by some interactive, gameplay pieces.
Imagine Bastion where Hub (+cutscene) sequences and combat sequences where swapped around. This creates an interesting predicament: until you get invested in the story (which at start you know nothing of) you simply sit there waiting for the rites to start; but should you click through the dialogues, chances are you won't care much for the story. Though game does it's best to get you involved, after all it is its strongest suit.
So yeah, that's my main gripe with Pyre (then again I never was a "visual novel" genre fan).

It's great, fun and touching at (many) times.
Nah, I still like Transistor more :) But hey Pyre is times longer (20H on one playthrough) and has a happier ending (at least I got that).
PS: suggest raising game's difficulty to the maximum. After all, freedom is a privilege one has to earn.

If I knew what I know now back before I bought this game, I wouldn't have wasted my money. I can't recommend the game to anyone, aside from the whole 'misery loves company' thing. You'd definitely have a better time spending your money elsewhere. However, you can make up your own mind. Also, keep in mind this is early access, so things are bound to change, though they've stated they will be making it more difficult from here, not necessarily better.
PROS:
- You get to play as a dinosaur, and that in itself is a big draw. There are multiple choices, both carnivore and herbivore.
- The maps are large and beautiful, with more improvements to come.
- It can be a relaxing background game while doing other things.
CONS:
- The community is extremely hostile, both in game and on the forums.
- This is not a game where you can find your own place. As the devs have stated multiple times, you play it the way they want you to play it, or not at all.
- The progression system, while challenging, is a mess. You can work your way up the tiers for an entire day, and finally attain your prize at tier 4, only to be killed by a laggy tier 1, who will erase all progress you've made.
- The progression system is tediously slow, requiring you to have others to socialize with, or other games to play in the background as you wait. Out of 30 minutes required to progress, you may spend 3 minutes playing, and the rest sitting and waiting.
- The laggy servers pretty much guarantee your fate, with rubberbanding being a constant issue. The issue being on their end, not player sided.
- There are multiple exploits in game that are not being addressed or punished.
- There are no instructions or tutorials, no explanaitons for anything, and very few guides availabe on the internet. You have to learn through trial and error, or by the helpfulness of other players.
As I've mentioned before, this is still early access, with actual release planned for just under a year from now, so it will change between now and release. As an early access game, you're going to be risking a lot in the way of gameplay enjoyment, and it's up to you to see if the risk is worth it. If you really can't decide, read some reviews, and watch some gameplay videos and make up your own mind.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: Rayman Origins was a very fun and generally very well designed game, if slightly flawed in certain areas. Rayman Legends is a very fun and generally very well designed game, if slightly flawed in certain areas. It's the same "old-school" platforming experience delivered in Rayman Origins, but this time it's delivered just a bit better. Gone are some of the absolutely infuriating and sometimes unfair memorization-heavy levels (for the most part; I'll get to that later). Out of the core five worlds, there were really only three levels that I wasn't too terribly fond of. For a game that has about 40 levels in the core worlds, that's quite good. In fact, my only "minor-major" complaint about the core worlds is the implementation of Murphy. It shows that he was meant for the Wii U version, but it's not that much of a deal breaker; just that it maybe could've been handled in a slightly better manner (let's say controlling Murphy with the right analog stick).
Note that I signified the fact that the ratio of good to bad levels was quite good in the core worlds. There is also a portion of the game called "Back to Origins," which is essentially a best-of collection of levels from Rayman Origins. Again, most of these levels are pretty good, but it just seems lazy to me to only bring back some of the levels, rather than bring back all of them. They've essentially given us all of the good stuff, leaving us no reason to go out and buy Origins. Much to my annoyance, they also brought back the boss fights from Origins, which are the aforementioned unfair memorization-heavy levels. They were the worst part of Origins in my opinion, but they are not the worst part in this game.
That "honor" goes to the Livid Dead Party world, which in my opinion contains some of the worst levels in the game. The Land of the Livid Dead level from Origins was easily my favorite level in the entire game, so you can imagine my disappointment when I found that all that was new and Livid Dead related was another music stage. It wasn't bad, but it was still very disappointing. Then... the remixes strike. These are 8-Bit reprises of the music stages that you unlock at the end of each world, with the two primary differences being a lack of checkpoints and an (in my opinion) incredibly stupid and infuriating visual filter(s). The first stage wasn't so bad; it just kinda hurt my head since it was a fisheye lens. The second stage... made me not want to 100% the game, even though I had gotten 682 Teensies up to that level. I don't get motion sickness, but that stage nearly made me throw up about three times due to the godawful visual filter done exclusively for "LAWLZ RETRO GUIZ." The rest of the stages were more of the same, albeit not nearly as bad as the second remix stage.
Again, despite my negativity, I will wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who anyone who just wants a pure fun platforming experience. Just stick with 100%ing the core worlds; the rest of the game ain't worth it. For an incredibly well crafted and fun set of core levels, a mediocre way of padding out the gameplay, and an immensely disappointing Livid Dead world, I will give this game an 8.5/10 for gameplay.
Story: Skipping this, as the story can literally be told in less than a paragraph.
Graphics: Man, I wish Ubisoft would release the level creator/editing tool to the public so that we can do things with it. Then again, maybe it's for the best that they don't; it'd only be a matter of time until the Internet poops all over such a glorious utility. What I'm trying to say is that this game is gorgeous and that we (as consumers) should totally be able to get our hands on the editor to make more amazing stuff happen. The character design is quite good as well, if some of the characters start to look like the others after a while. Despite this, there's a great deal of characters that you can switch between, so that you're not stuck staring at the same character the entire game. For proving yet again that style trumps number of polygons, this game gets a 5/5 for graphics.
Music: You can tell that the composers had a great deal of fun with the music in this game. That fun of composing transcribes into additional fun in playing the game. It's not something that most people would want to listen to outside of the game (at least I'd think so), but it's still very fitting and lends itself quite nicely to the ambiance of the stages. The songs chosen for the music stages puts this soundtrack over the top, allowing it to receive a 5/5 for the music portion.
Overall score of 8.5/0/5/5; cumulative score of 9.3/10. If I didn't decide to be a completionist for this game, I would've rated it higher; however, the Livid Dead Party is still a pretty large blemish on an otherwise excellent game. Again, the best experience is achieved by just sticking to the core five worlds in my opinion.

Pyre masterfully blends a compelling story with engaging gameplay.
The immersive world is enhanced by the colorful cast of diverse characters. The first few hours of the game involve recruiting these characters while learning the ropes of the "rites," a sportlike ritual that forms the majority of the gameplay. Each character has a unique set of abilities during the rites that allow for you to develop your own style of play. The gameplay evolves over the course of the 10-15 hour game, remaining challenging without becoming too difficult. Despite the simple concept, the rites never become repetitive, due in part to the large variety of enemies and settings.
Because there is no "game over," your actions during the rites have a genuine impact on the story. It truly feels like you have agency in the game's plot. Regardless of whether you win or lose, the game continues, presenting unique circumstances that culminate in the final arch. The finale capitalizes on the strength of the characters and writing, and relies on your actions throughout the game.
I fully recommend Pyre, it feels like a combination of basketball, the Banner Saga, and a Telltale game, and is one of the best games I've played all year.

Apotheon is an action adventure that even casual fans of Greek mythology can appreciate. I’ve always had a relatively cursory interest in Greek mythology. The plays and stories are important for literature because they are the stories we continue to tell. I could easily get lost in the family trees and names, but I love the stories that I can remember, and that’s more than enough to appreciate Apotheon’s setting.
The black-figure pottery art style is delightful and timeless. It translates the action and feel of the game incredibly well. It effortlessly brings to life all the classic mythos and godly figures of Greece. The music pairs together nicely, but the visuals steal the show. While other games can plunge further down into the uncanny valley, Apotheon can relax comfortably in its mountainside estate.
The main plot is that Zeus is having a bad week and tells all of his many children/inbreeds to stop blessing mortals with their gifts which include just about everything they need to survive. Hera enlists our protagonist Nikandreos to fight the Gods of Olympus. The story is predictable in its major points, but I suppose that’s just how classic tales go. The game really shines in its attention to mythos, or so I have heard from those more versed than I. The pacing of the game works in the narrative’s favor as I never found myself listless: I was either enjoying the ride I was on or I was hopping on for another to hunt down secrets and side quests.
The gameplay all around is really enjoyable. The game has a good sense of adventure, and Apotheon is willing to commit to the feel of the various areas and scenarios, which makes them all the more satisfying. Having to find a buried treasure sans waypoint, fighting a master huntress as both predator and prey, traversing a spinning labyrinth to lead a small squad against the goddess of wisdom are just some of the many great moments of the game. While it may average around a dozen hours for some, those dozen hours feel expertly designed. Almost every new area I went to felt like an enjoyable spinoff of what was already a fun game, and that’s what makes Apotheon so engrossing: the boss fights and various areas are constructed so well that they can stand on their own but easily fit into the rest of the game.
With all the praise out of the way, it’s time to strain out some of the weaker points. While the situations that the game throws you feel fantastic, the game itself does not really grow. You get some new abilities, but otherwise your armor increases and weapons feel the same. There is not much to tweak around with apart from special weapons, there are not skill points and the like. This game keeps the mechanics simple and then surrounds the player in exciting scenarios. Along with this, the main narrative takes a backseat against the different deities the game showcases, which can be a downer for some. The game is not stuck-to-the-rails linear to where you just move forward through set pieces, but rather the player is free to explore the game. These are rather small details that I would not call negatives, but notable qualities.
While players should not go in expecting the visceral, veiny phallus of vengeance that is God of War, Apotheon is a delightful action adventure.

Very enjoyable experience with some minor issues. It definitely has one of the finest art-style I've seen and gameplay wise it's also great, but there are some things that would be welcome in sequel if that ever happens. It's definitely not one of those Art >> Gameplay situations. Premise is really simple and quite similar to God of War games - Ancient Greek mythology + overthrowing gods
You have a wide range of weapons at your disposal and combat involves attacking and blocking/dodging. Nothing complicated, it just works. Would be great if there would be light/medium/charged attack system (instead weapons themselves replace this system) or better directional attack system. Weapons lose durability over time so when your favourite fiery sword reaches 0, it's gone.
There are numerous destroyable objects, that can contain ether health/armor replenishers, ingredients for crafting potions/bombs or weapons. However if you destroy these objects with your weapon, durability is lost which is a bit annoying. You can still break everything with your fists so gameplay-wise disabling durability loss when not attacking enemies would be much better than just cycling between primary weapon and fists.
You can't repair items, but plenty are lying around and you can easily buy them (rare weapons are actually more easily acquirable, since every time you find a rare weapon/shield, it's added to stock). Buying things from black market merchant also involves the biggest bug in the game - If you unlock enough rare weapons, you can't see bottom items when trying to buy from black market merchant (at least on 1366x768)
Feeling of the game itself is entirely positive. It looks perfect for the setting you are in and it's not repetitive. Locations differ and feel unique from each other. And it's not just looks, gameplay/platforming differs in each location. Some acquired powers/gifts from the gods however feel a bit uninspiring. Who cares about +X % when using potion trait?
Multiple secrets that gives you a bit of a boost in your journey. Some feel a bit disappointing, but who does not like hunting for secret locations?
Super minor, but a really smart element in the game - when you collect new armor, you can change to previous look if you don't like the new one without sacrificing stats.
Achievements are gathered as you play along + side objectives, so there are no "Kill 12 wolves in 1 second" medals
In conclusion - an instant recommendation, feels like AAA platformer with some polish would make this an AAA+

The Ultimate Doom is a re-release of the original Doom and features an entirely new episode on top of the three that were previously available. In addition it know supports modern controls of “wasd” and mouse support, though you are still unable to look vertically like in the original. It is the spiritual successor to Wolfenstein 3D and is credited for popularizing the FPS genre. This time around you'll be facing the forces of hell instead of Nazis and their dogs. The tone for this game is much more morbid and disturbing than it's predecessor's endless blue and gray hallways. You'll often times find your fellow space marines dead or still alive and twitching if they are unlucky. Rooms can now be pitch black and you will have to slowly inch yourself forward, toward your objective in fear of being caught by surprise in what may be lurking in the darkness. Without the awesome metal soundtrack blasting in the background, Doom would be pretty unsettling at times.
Unlike Wolf 3D this now has floor and ceiling textures, which make for far more immersive environments. But there is no mistaking that these are indeed graphics from 1993 and what may have seemed impressive back then like vertical environments , flickering lights and gore, are typical these days and will no longer impress anyone. Where Doom stands the test of time is in it's gameplay and level design. It's rapid movement and maze like environments to explore are likely to be strange to those that have not experienced an old school FPS, but they do insure ensure fluid, exciting gameplay and replay value as you seek the hidden goodies like extra levels that you didn't find your first time through. There is no iron-sites or reloading here, instead we have an auto-aim feature that will see to it that you hit an enemy if you are facing it, though it does freak out at times when fighting on a vertical plane.
Starting off you will be able to choose any of the four episodes to start off with though I highly recommend starting from the first as to allow the game to introduce weapons, enemies and game mechanics. There is no story to keep track of but if you are to start on the later episodes without a firm understanding of the weapons and how to fight demons, you will surely fail. Then you will chose from five difficulty modes that change the type and amount of enemies you will encounter throughout the level. And as soon as you pick one it's straight to the game. No story and no explanation, just you and a pistol. You will soon come across the body of a deceased marine that is facing the door and you will be able to hear a monstrous gurgle beyond the door. Meeting an enemy for the first time is always an epic encounter and you will not have any time to gawk at it. You just have to try to gun it down and hope that strange creatures goes down before you do. It is scenarios like these, that make me highly advise starting on anything other than episode 1 your first time around.
Unlike Wolf 3D most enemies are not hit-scan and usually have projectiles that you can avoid if you react fast enough. It makes it feel like a really deadly match of dodge-ball as you zoom across the levels, avoiding multiple projectiles and gunning down all in your path without a single scratch. If you do get hit your characters face shown in the bottom of the screen will get bloodier and bloodier, until the point that he is near death and in tears. This is one of the small details that frightened me as a child, seeing your badass space marine bloody and in tears is something still not seen in many games and reminds you that our hero is indeed human, even if it has no gameplay effect and he still moves faster than Sonic the Hedgehog. If you are injured you will have to find a medkit to restore your health and if you are lucky you may also find some armor to absorb some damage. There are also power-ups hidden across the level like a Berserk orb that causes your fists to cause much more damage for the entire level. Some are necessary to progress though like the Hazmat suit that allows you to walk on lava and other hazards.
Thinking outside the box will sometimes be necessary  in your search of the three keycards you will need to escape the level. Like in E4M6 there is a teleporter that will teleport you to different locations depending on which side you step on it, it may seem like a simple puzzle but you have to run across lava to access that tiny teleporter. If you quick-save in certain locations like that, it is possible that you will doom yourself to death if you already used the hazmat suit and don't have enough health to run across that much lava. In that case hopefully you had another save or you will be put on the start of that level with just a pistol. Most of these instances are found in Episode 4 as they tried their hand at some light “platforming”  but with Doom's inability to look up and down, crumby auto-aiming if you are not on the same plane as enemy and lightning fast movement, tiny platforms that you must traverse are quite an annoyance.  It is also the first Episode in which you ever have to use the run key and it overall felt like the weakest link out of all Episodes.
Weapons are usually hidden throughout the levels giving you yet another reason to explore areas carefully. These can range from chainguns, rocket launchers and the legendary BFG-9000. You will have to find ammo for them as well and as you can tell by now scavenging for supplies is very important. Ammo backpacks are very will hidden but if you find one they will allow you to carry more ammo at once. The zombie grunts will drop either pistol or shotgun ammo but neither of these will do you much good against the more powerful demons. Demons are very aggressive and this can be used to your advantage. If a demon accidentally hits another demon they will fight to the death and you can use this distraction to either sneak away or to easily take down the victor of that skirmish. They are quite varied and have different methods of attacking, so dealing with each one is requires different method and learning how to identify your largest threat is a must. Confidence can also lead to your downfall, you may think you have taken care of every enemy in the level and spot a powerful gun in the open, only to be ambushed by demons that were hiding. Be it creepy noises, distant groans or evil looking background, this game does a great job at making sure you rarely feel safe.
I did have a problem with the Steam version of this game having distorted colors and flickering. I was  able to fix it by following this
With that said, this game should last you around 6 hours but it does have decent replay value and plenty of secrets to find. After each level it tells you the percent of enemies killed, percent of secrets and the time it took you to complete, which may lead you to want to do better. Most levels before Episode 4 have a unique song that plays throughout that further helps differentiate the levels from one another. The environments are mostly brown and gray, so they start to look the same after a while but thanks to excellent level design, no two levels feel the same. If you ever get lost, there is an in game map for each level, though it can be confusing when levels have some verticality to them. While Doom's graphics are now laughable and can be run on most consoles or even your local ATM, it's now extinct form of gameplay is still as fun as ever.  I wouldn't recommend Doom to those that need a plot to drive them forward or to those that hate exploring. Those that don't mind the lack of narrative and want fast, unrelenting gameplay, are more likely than not going to have a heck of a time with this title. While it is starting to show it's age, good old grandpa Doom still has plenty of fight left in him.

Rayman Legends is a must have if you; enjoy sidscrolling platformers, played Rayman Origins and liked it or you are a fan of the Rayman franchise.
First of all, the art style is outstanding! I was amazed after playing Origins as it just looks beautiful. Everything is very unique and have very smooth animations with each boss being 3D but looking like they are still 2D.
Secondly, the sounds and music are amazing with comedic sound effects for hitting enemies and great music that suites each atmosphere very well.
The level design is very well done with many challenging and gorgeous looking levels you won't get bored, with levels filled with secrets normally hard to get to, intense boss battles, fast paced music based levels and difficult time trials. There is also a extra area containing levels from Rayman Origins with the new art style and new lum system.
The game also supports controllers and allows up to 4 players locally, unfortunately like Origins there is no online co-op support, although it does have a daily and weekly challenge which has online leaderboards and gives you prizes depending on how high you were in the leaderboards.
The length of the game is hard to say but as you can see I have played quite a bit of it and still have not got everything with there being 700 teensies to collect and the addicting challenges you will pump hours into this game, if you do have people to play locally with then there is a game mode called 'Kung Foot' which is a football game where you have a very small area to play with 2 teams. The ball is very bouncy and can be hit all over the place making it very chaotic and fun. Although there is a lot to do once you do it all and collect everything you most likely won't play it an awful lot after although you may replay after a year or so or if you have a friend to play it with again.
Some improvements from Origins stand out other than the extended gameplay and improved art style which is that they removed the annoying thing where enemies turned into bubbles on death, although the player bubble death is there which isn't a bad thing. The lums have also been improved making it so the first lum in a row of lums is purple/pink and if collected will give 2 lums and will pass onto the next lum unless a yellow one is collected making collecting the lums in order more important and can be challenging when they moving around. The amount of collectables has also been increased.
Lastly, the characters in the game are similar to the ones in Origins just with a few more reskins but also the addition of the princess-barbarians which wield an axe as a weapon the first one being Barbara which each need to be rescued. Although there are many characters the reskins are very minor for the princesses mainly.
Overall I highly recommend buying this game it is certainly worth it full price, one problem people may have is that it is run through uPlay which means you need to make a uPlay account as well and can sometimes be a problem for people. I was very pleased with pre-ordering this game for £25 which also got me Rayman Origins free with it.

This is the best platformer I have ever played. Take everything great about Rayman Origins and make it even better. All the great stage design, boss fights, and challenging difficulty is back. There is so much content in this installment of the Rayman series. Online challenges, remastered Rayman Origins stages, Local Co-Op mode with a fun minigame, Time Trials, creatures to collect, characters to unlock and a ton of awesomely designed stages in the main section of the game. There is also a nice statistics screen to keep track of all your progress.
There are online challenges that change on a daily and weekly basis. Every player in the world competes in them and gets ranked by how well they perform in the challenge. You can also race against the better ranked player's ghosts. It basically shows exactly what they did during the challenge, while you are playing. You can also increase your trophy level by placing high in lots of challenges and clearing portions of the game.
The music themed stages in this game are probably my favorite platforming levels in any game ever. Playing a whole level in sync with the music feels very satisfying. There are also a ton of other stages that are amazingly designed. The boss fights are very satisifying to play. The Time Trials portions of stages feel perfectly designed for running through them as fast as you can. There is quite a bit of depth in making your character move as fast as possible in all situations. These Time Trials make you realize how fast you can actually go.
I have spent around 40 hours to 100% the game and do some of the online challenges. You can probably spend around 30 hours just to 100% the game and around 20 hours trying to complete the levels. Some of the levels are very hard and the online challenges have sections that are even harder. They bring back portions of the Land of the Livid Dead from Rayman Origins for some of the online challenges. You can also play a lot of the Rayman Origins levels in this game, but they have been remastered to make the levels a bit better designed.
This game has everything you could want in a platformer. It is highly recommended and I don't think you can find a better designed platformer game than this one. Go buy it now!

Y'know, if you asked me 3 months ago, I would have passionately recommended The Isle to everyone I knew. In fact, back then I did.
But now I honestly can’t do that. I can barely even play it anymore.
I'll parrot most other negative reviews:
We've heard all that before.
My main complaint is no one plays their dinosaur as a living animal. There's little to no roleplay. Players just go for the big pointy monsters and kill everything that moves.
As a budding paleontologist with a day job and a lack of real-life hours to pour into progression, I miss sandbox the most for those reasons.
Some of my fondest memories in The Isle were finding friends within my species and just travelling around the map, sightseeing, enjoying each other's company, and providing mutual protection from predators. I even recall some pretty chill predators. I'm not talking carebears, I'm talking raptors and even carnos who knew they couldn't take on the herd but walked with us because they knew we were heading towards water and other groups. Preds don't
to kill everything they encounter.
You may have noticed from what I said above that I'm strictly an herbivore player. Yeah yeah I know some of y'all will stop reading just because I said that. But with the forceful addition of progression there is damn near zero motivation for anyone like me to even play the game anymore, let alone try to be an herbivore. I can't find any herds, I can't survive long enough to progress, and when someone brings this up all anyone does is scream at them to git gud.
This is a video game.
Video games are entertainment.
Maybe it's just me, but I feel no immersion, investment, or fun in hiding under a bush for real-life hours hoping to wiggle up the herb progress tree at anything faster than a glacial pace.
Look.
I never wanted to be the best Isle player in the world.
Sadly, the game has reached a point in development where the words "hardcore survival" are now dead serious in their description of the gameplay, and it is no longer for me.
If you are in the market for killing time on the computer with an animated nature-themed screensaver and a dinosaur in the middle, this is the game for you.

Rayman Legends is a fun, addictive game, that improves upon the originals with slightly improved graphics using the beautiful UbiArt Engine. The level design as well music are fantastic, A few shortcoming held it back from completle greatness, but I still thorougly enjoyed it.
Foremost, the interesting level design really shines with the varied levels that you have to overcome. The goals is always the same if not slight different. Rescue a certain number of teensies by finding the secret rooms as well as scouring the level for invisible walls and areas . The journey is accomplishing this and there is nothing better then finding them all  and getting 100% on the level. Other levels of interest are the boss levels as well as the timed ones that keep the variety up. Continuing on, the music levels that you find at the end of each area in the game are fabulous and are always something to look forward to as well as challenging in their own right. Lastly, the simple fair gameplay and tight controls. Everything required for a great platformer. Xbox controller is what I used and what I would recommend althought I'm sure keyboard works fine.
For the negatives I wouldn't really say they are complete negatives, but something that people like me will have to learn to live with. There is a lot of online/leaderboard type integration. There are dailies and weeklies. They are indeed fun and definetly challenging. By doing them you are rewarded with lums which are used for unlocking differnt characters in the game that you can play as.The majority can be unlocked just by beating the game but there are a few that require you to do them for awhile. Although I have no idea if these characters are worth the effort or if there mere recolors they are considered superior in terms of cost and I would assume they are pretty good. The positives of this is there is added gametime to the game as well as a stretch goal if you really enjoy it. The negative is not everything is unlocked right after beating the game which means you were probably wont go back unless you really are dedicated. Definetly the most frustrating thing would have to be the Back to Origins levels. While all the good levels in the original Rayman Origins are included they are not unlocked right away. You will unlock all of them sometime after you've beaten the game which means you cant play them in their original order until then. This is extremely frustating as after you beat the final boss and done the extra world the last thing you want to do is go back and 100% those levels that you have done before if you played the original. It would of been a lot better if they were unlocked in order after beating each area of the main game. At the very least I am happy they are included in game as extra content and I applaud the devolopers for not making someone purchase Rayman Legends if they want to experience it.
Kind of ranted on about the negatives, but I figure people know or have heard about how great is and should hear a different side. Definetly worth the puchase!
