When two characters fight in a movie, the viewer needs to have stake in the outcome in order to be engaged.  Regardless of whatever choreography or explosions might be on screen, unless the audience both cares about the characters and fears that they might fail, the conflict will not be interesting to watch.
Games don't neccessarily have this problem, as overcoming obstacles as a player is satisfying regardless of context.  Pyre isn't a game to rely on this, however, which might be a turn off to some.  In fact, Pyre goes to great lengths to make sure that narrative context is at the forefront of every encounter, in a way that no other game has managed in the past.
Part of conflict in film and literature is the supension of disbelief, because there's a very good chance the protaganists will come out on top regardless of what they're stacked up against.  Many good works offset this with their characters and doing a good job of convincing the audience that failure is possible, but truly great stories embrace failures.  It gets a little bit tiring when the world is going to end for the fourth time and the heroes save it, but when what's at stake is a setback rather than death things become far more believable, especially if failures have already occured in the story so far.
Generally, games will handle failure with a game over screen and make the player restart.  Some will up the ante by imposing larger punishments for failure, further increasing the investment players have in their successes and mistakes.  Pyre on the other hand, is structured to allow the game to continue through any outcome.  Even if you end up restarting anyways, the existence of an unfavorable outcome removes the need to suspend any disbelief.  Add on to that the fact that the outcome relies on the performance of the player, and you've got a personal investment that feels unlike any other game.  I can confidently say that for these reasons, I found many of the battles in Pyre more intense than the closest ranked matches of the competitive games I've played.
Of course, none of this matters if you aren't interested in what's happening to begin with.  Luckily Supergiant has a good track record with storytelling and Pyre is no exception, even with its ambitious non-linear structure.  Though to be clear, calling the story of Pyre non-linear might be a disservice, as that would imply that it follows a format of branching off of player decisions, which isn't entirely the case.  Instead, the narrative of Pyre is more accurately expressed as instead the story of each of its characters woven together, each with their own goals and motivations.  Each character has a part to play in the "bigger picture", but at its core Pyre focuses on the path of each of its characters and how they affect eachother.  The way that each character expresses their own ideas and motivations is intoxicating and incredibly easy to get sucked in to.  And even if you only connect with one of the characters off the bat, well writted dialogue and relationships will quickly get you to fall in love with the rest of the cast by extension.
Another large part of the narrative is the role of the player as both a driving force in the plot and as a character who interacts with and influences the cast.  You don't just play as the leader overseeing the group, you play as a part of it, and the characters treat you as their equal.  When the nightwings are competing in the rights, they aren't just relying on you as their leader to lead them to victory, they're relying on you as their friend to help them achieve their dreams.
Supergiant Games is known for integrating art, music, and narrative in the creative process from the get-go, and it shows in their products.  Bastion and Transistor boasted concise and well developed themes that were expressed through every aspect Supergiant had at their disposal.  By contrast, Pyre seems less focused, when you can often go between whimsical to heartwrenching, sea shanties to hard rock, or from relaxing exploration to fast paced gameplay.  Despite this wider scope Supergiant has taken on with Pyre, everything still manages to feel like it belongs as part of the world, and much of that has to do with tying themes and tones to members of the extensive cast of characters, and to specific events and locations.  This variety adds a lot to the world of Pyre, and serves to further the distinct nature of its characters.
All of this so far isn't to mention the truly unique experience that is the rites.  Pyre brings combat mechanics and respawn timers to a "sports game" premise, where traditionally you wouldn't be able to knock your opponents out of the field.  The combination yields something that might be considered an entirely new genre of game.
Many others have stated that the gameplay can feel repetitive later on, and in some ways I'd tend to agree, but not in a way that's uncharacteristic for Supergiant.  In Bastion and Transistor, balancing different approaches is done in a way that lets everything be strong once you figure out how to use it.  You can usually find a strategy or loudout that you can rely on for most of the game, and variety comes from level design and enemy variety.  Occasionally you'll be put into situations that will reward you for switching up your tactics, but very rarely will your strategy simply not work.
In Pyre, every arena is an oval with two goals and some obstacles, and each side is made up of three characters all trying to do the same thing.  There's the potential for finding variation with the classes, but many of them just feel like different ways of doing the same thing, just a little bit better or worse.  There's also the potential for building strategies around items, abilities, and combinations later into the game, but the campaign is for the most part paced such that it ends as soon as you've reached that point, which is probably the appeal of versus mode.  This is also held back by mechanics put in place that both reward and force the player to vary up their character usage to a certain degree.
It's very possible I ran into repetitive rites because I found a character whose class and dialogue I really liked, and used them as much as possible.  As much as it seemed like a good idea to keep using the character I was attached to, I wonder how much I would have enjoyed learning to effectively use each member of the cast instead.  Part of this might also be that the game encourages and sometimes forces you to vary your team of three, but does little to dissuade you from using one star player for the majority of the campaign.
Despite these complaints I still had a lot of fun with the rites.  They're unlike anything I've played before and the core mechanics are very satisfying and well developed.  Even the AI is surprisingly well done despite its quirks when dealing with certain classes (at least on standard difficulty).
Pyre is unlike anything I've ever experienced and that alone is enough for a reccomendation from me.  But even without all the unique ideas I covered in this review, Pyre is a well done game, and I don't think I really mentioned that enough.  I suppose that's just expected of Supergiant at this point, and they're somehow still outdoing themselves.

In my mind, Supergiant are held to an almost unrealistic standard. Bastion and Transistor are two games that not only stand out as favourites due to the superb quality of both games, but also show a clear ambition by the developers to stride towards something new in video games. The integration of gameplay and storytelling is yet to be fully realised in this medium but I feel both games make considerable leaps in realising that goal.
In a way, Pyre is a step back from this mindset, and it would seem the focus has shifted towards a more traditional structure of storytelling found in classic RPG’s a visual novels. Attempting to lump Pyre into a single genre is difficult, not only because it clearly takes elements from sports games and the aforementioned visual novels, but because it fuses those elements so seamlessly it almost makes it’s own genre; a genre I doubt we’ll see other developers looking to capitalise on. In this regard Pyre is worthy of attention alone, and the attention you give it isn’t wasted when you realise what it does is more than a mere experiment but is a full fledged experience similar to the time I had with Supergiants other installments.
At it’s core, Pyre is a character driven journey where you occasionally take a break to play some basketball. I’m not underplaying or wholly criticising the gameplay by saying this, rather I truly believe the heart of the game is in the characters and the themes the game explores. Much like many big fantasy franchises in film, literature and video games alike, the characters are put at the forefront and through them the story unravels. Pyre excels in telling the story purely because the characters are so well defined, relatable, diverse and unique. First introducing the hero, bruiser and jovial sidekick, the game delves deeper into different lands, races and backgrounds, with not only forms the basis for the story and lore of the world, but creates a truly memorable cast of different personalities.
Through the characters a story revolved heavily around freedom takes place. Whilst the theme at the forefront is obvious, less apparent motifs crop up as a result of the internal struggles between the party members, ranging from the ethics of betrayal and disloyalty to simple love connections that form resulting from the harsh conditions each character is put in. Player choice is given in deciding what stories you reveal, since it was made apparent quite early I wouldn’t be able to fully explore each one. Your choice and actions not only affect your, as the player’s, own perception and understanding of the party members, but also how they act in game and plot points as you progress. For example, one member, Pamitha, betrays her sister, which you only learn on the playing field. As a result, she begs you to let her win for she feels to much shame to again put her sibling down. What result agreeing with her would have I don’t know, since I chose the option to beat her, but the choice is there and the game makes it apparent choices are permanent and losses merely occur and don’t create fail states.
Leading into gameplay, the handball/basketball combat the game showed prior to release had many people on edge, rightfully so. A story driven fantasy sports game is ridiculous in concept, but it actually turns out to be quite fun. I most liken it to handball, where you throw a ball between teammates in the hope of throwing said ball into the opposition goal. Unlike the real sport, you can “banish” the other team, removing them from the game temporarily through attacks. The depth lies in the variety between the races, where some are more defensive and offensive than others and have different abilities to reflect that. The trinket system is mostly good too, where a lot will give special effects like double jump and infinite stamina.
Do I think it is as deep as it could be? No. You’re restricted to moving only one character at a time, and due to the limitations of being human, playing against the hard AI means they can maneuver their team much more efficiently than you which sometimes leads to moments where you feel you’re being cheated. Conversely, the first 2 hours of the game are insanely easy to the point where I don’t think it’s possible to fail. In addition to trinkets, some tie into the run of the mill stat system, where 4 different factors affect how your team perform. The problem lies in the fact it’s all very generic, where one measures speed, the other attack size etc. Stat modifiers are generally so small it’s hard to notice a difference and makes leveling those modifiers feel pointless.
Like the previously stated spoiler example however, the gameplay can serve to enhance the story and characters, where sometimes a team will not show up or be replaced, adding to that faction's lore and motives.
In my opinion, I’d rank this at the bottom of Supergiants catalogue. I don’t think this is because the games bad or that Supergiant didn’t try by any means, but it is only because the other games are so good. The restrictions of the genres they take elements from are essentially the game's weaknesses, and yet still the game is an absolute marvel and worthy of anyone's time.

Aside from this I completely enjoyed the 20+ hours i spent in this game, and if you are even remotely a Back to the Future fan, you will probably enjoy it too.  Telltale did a great job on it, and now I'm hoping they will continue with another installment - don't leave us hanging!

Boring. You wander around, trying to get the drop on a monster that is invisible, while also setting up cameras at predesignated points so that you can do surveillance during the night. Or at least try to surveil; the cameras are basically useless because you can only set up 3 of them, and only at precoded points in the map, and none in spots that are any good. What this means in practice is that when night falls, there's a 5 minute dead zone where you need to hide in your trailer in order to not die, and there isn't anything you can do in there besides flip through those three cameras and wait for something to happen. If you're really bored, you also can go back outside and try to hunt the invisible thing in the dark.
The game is mind-bogglingly ugly. What is easy to overlook/missing in the store screenshots is that there is almost no grass anywhere, and so long stretches of flat polygons remain an unbroken parade of the same unbump-mapped, un-mip-mapped, flat-as-the-♥♥♥♥in-polygon-it's-obscuring-underneath texture. Take any memory you have of a game from ten years ago and throw it out the window, because at least level designers then knew enough to obscure the simplicity of the assets they were working with by adding some geometry to their planes.
You might be thinking that there is some sort of story, or progression in the game. Maybe there's lore related to the rake and its appearances that you can find throughout the wilderness, environmental storytelling. Maybe Gordon Davis has a story; past cryptid encounters that you can read about, or maybe even just some one-liners that he'll drop when something happens. Nope. You start the game much as you end it: alone in someone else's body, out in some low-res woods, wandering around until it's time to retreat to your RV for a few minutes. What you do in there is your own business, but let's just say that the options given aren't as diverting as what any sane human would choose to do.

- The gear system. Every time you complete level 20 on a class you earn 1 Reputation. With that Reputation you gain the ability to raise another 36 gear levels. So you start with level 1 gear that can be upgraded to 6. Then at R1 you get gear to be upgraded from 7 to 12. Anyway, you see how the system works. At R3 you can hit the max gear rank of 108.

All in all a great game, for the game play. Addictive puzzler.
When I first loaded up Bejeweled 3 I was thinking to myself "Here we go again, another puzzle game". Incredibly, such game had me hooked for 1.5 hours straight and still manages to intice me to play some some more.
Gameplay is reminiscent of other puzzle games with a few twists in store. The aim of bejeweled is to match 3 of the same shapes together horizontally or vertically. You do this by swapping two shapes through clicking on one shape and then the other one. Each match removes the row of shapes, earns points and allows other shapes above to drop down. You can improve your score by doing combos (which is matching one shape, causing other shapes to match as well). Should you match a group of 4 or more shapes, the shapes will become charged up. When charged up shapes are matched with the same shapes, they explode, destroying shapes in a area around it and earing extra points.  When you are struggling to find a match, you can click on the 'Hint' button which indicates a shape you can move to form a match. There are various game modes such as a casual (no timer or set objectives), challenges (must meet objectives to pass), endless mode etc.Extra game modes can be unlocked by meeting a set score in previous game modes. With plenty of game modes to play, unlock as well as achievements to gain, there is plenty of replayability available.
Music instills a feeling of serenity. Calm music is played, which is great for calming yourself when solving puzzles. Sound effects for matches and explosions are good as well. The announcer who basically shouts comments based on how well you play (number of combos), reminds me of the announcer from Mortal Combat (which is a plus).
Graphics are colourful. The 2D graphics are vibrant and eye catching.
As with many puzzle games there is no story, which isn't necessary anyway.
If you want to play a puzzle game that will have you hooked, you will not be dissapointed with Bejeweled 3.

PROS:
- Gameplay is easy to understand
- Story is enriched and enjoyable
CONS:
- Dumb way of explaining the story
- Stealth feels unrealistic and choppy
- Tries too hard to limit your resources
- Unforgiving checkpoints
OVERVIEW:
Velvet Assassin is not an easy game to play. Not at all and only because the developers tried to emphazise the idea of limitation to your surroundings. It doesn't make the game more of a challenge it just makes the situation much more fustrating and headache-inducing. Of course, with that, it means you can't run and gun, so if you're that kind of player, this title is not for you. This game requires heavy thinking and planning. If you just run in and try to come up with a plan along the way it will not work and you will see yourself dieing and trying again. Speaking of dieing, this game has unforgiving checkpoints. You can die almost completing the level and end up halfway back into the level. Storytelling is only told through flashbacks which really just makes the whole game feel pointless to play through if the story is only unlocked that way. As for the stealth mechanics, this game just fails to impress. Stealth controls are easy to understand and are easy to use but the response from the game just feels way too dumb and unrealistic. Say you shoot an oil puddle to set an enemy on fire. Well the screaming causes another enemy from across the map to come over, but due to the poor AI, the enemy arrives and automatically knows where you are, just making you waste more of your ammo that cannot be recovered. This game is for people who can take an extremely rough challenege, but I can't find it in myself to recommened this game to anyone.

This game is simply AMAZING. Absolutely fantastic. This is EXACTLY how you make a sequel to a good game!
Firstly, the artwork of the game is just like Rayman Origins, only there's a lot more detail going on here to make the colors and art style mesh a bit more together. That being said, the artwork is beautiful and despite the main characters' very colorful, silly appearance, the settings and areas match them so well that it's hard to say that they feel out of place. The music is just as good, and also brings a more thematic feel to the game, seeing as how Legends takes a bit more of a civilization styled world as opposed to the open wilderness areas that Origins featured. The soundtrack fits each world nicely, nailing a variety of genres and styles almost perfectly. My only complaints with the music would be the oddly off-putting Invasion level songs, which don't seem as urgent as they're supposed to feel.
As a modern platformer game, the amount of levels in the game is extremely important, and Legends most certainly didn't disappoint. There's TONS of levels in the game spanning over five unique worlds, and for those who dearly miss the content from Rayman: Origins, there's 60 levels from Origins included in the game to satisfy both crowds. Legends' levels also add a bit more challenge to the levels which partly secures my previous complaint on the easiness of Origins' levels. Though some levels still did feel a bit too easy, I feel the challenge is still decent in the game for what it was going for; a game to please both casual and hardcore players.
The amount of unlockables in the game is a great deal more than Origins, but it is a bit lacking. Once you've unlocked all of the normal levels, and the Origins levels, the only other things to get include costumes for the four main characters, though they aren't that special as many of the costumes follow a set theme with each of the characters, such as a Knight costume for Rayman and Globox, a Caveman costume for the Teensies, Rayman and Globox, a Dark Rayman and Dark Globox costume, etc. As far as the methods to unlock them go, it all depends on how much you've played the game as most of the costumes are locked behind a set amount of Lums collected to unlock them, going all the way up to 1 million lums for the final Rayman costume. Collecting all 700 Teensies also rewards you with a costume, which I think is pretty underwhelming. Though the Warrior Princess characters are just different costumes for Barbara, I do like the different amounts of variety in clothing, hair styles and colors they use with each of them. It's a nice touch and they at least added more than 2 extra costumes for Rayman this time.
The game plays very fluently, the controls are very well thought out and easy to use, so most of the gameplay is reliant on the player's skill. I've never felt like any death in the game was on part of bad level design or poor control design as they're damn good. I would recommend that people play the game with a gamepad though as playing with the keyboard can get a bit awkward.
Speaking of level design and levels, the way they presented the levels in each of the worlds was fantastic. Although each world spanned across at least 10 different paintings that counted as levels, I felt as though I was transitioning from one part of the world's story to the next. Additionally I will say that each world seems to have it's own story, rather than seeming like each world is connected somehow. It makes it seem like each world is separate from the others moreso than just in setting and appearance and gives the game some actual life and a sense of freedom and adventure despite being in a large tent with a bunch of old, crusty paintings.
My absolute favorite part of this game that got me hyped were the ingenious music levels, where every action int he level is set to the beat and rhythm of a song, remixed in a very special way for each world's music level. Though there's only a handful of music levels in the game, I feel like this isn't a bad thing as each music level plays out fantastically. The look of sheer joy on my face when I realized that the song playing in the level Castle Rock was a Rayman style remix of "Black Betty" is something I can never forget. And although the music levels are seen as the biggest selling point of Rayman Legends, Ubisoft went the extra mile to ensure that they put effort in all of the levels, and used the music levels as a lure for players, which makes the game that much richer in the experience.
In terms of story, I'm willing to forgive Rayman Legends for its very basic storyline. Rayman games never exactly had a great story to them, and the fact that there's no set canon of the Rayman games just adds to the charm, which this game is chock full of. The basic goal of the game seems to intertwine itself with the individual stories that come along with each of the worlds.
The Challenges and Kung Foot modes of the game add a bit more of a competitive side to Rayman Legends. Competing in different challenges every day and week for a chance to be seen at the top of the leaderboards is very nice, but I feel the PC version's Challenge mode is sort of sullied with the rise of many cheaters, especially in timed Challenges. I don't consider timed Challenges of any sort to be very serious on the PC version as people just cheat to get sub 10-second times as opposed to the people who actually have skill and talent in the game. Lum collection and Distance endurance challenges are just fine though as it's very hard to seem like one's cheating at these challenges as they can be done at one's own pace.
I don't have any experience with Kung Foot though as I haven't had the chance to play this game with multiple people.
In conclusion, this game is absolutely fantastic. Rayman Legends is a damn good example of how to make an excellent sequel to a good game. Legends builds upon the foundation and base of the original Rayman Origins and addresses many other issues that Origins had and aims very high to correct them. I would certainly say that Rayman Legends is much better than Origins, despite Origins also being an excellent game in its own right.
Oh, as an additional warning, you have to make a separate U-Play account in order to play the game from Steam, which I honestly find annoying and a little pointless.
Overall I'd give this game a 10/10

Before I start my review, I do want to say that I used to really enjoy this game. And yes, I know it's early access, but right now I'm not enjoying playing the game. I may change my review if/when the things I'm complaining about are improved. The dinosaurs have nice models, and it's fun to play as them, but the recent update honestly ruined it for me. First of all, most populated servers have a horrible delay, which makes it impossible to defend yourself and just makes everything in the game generally very clunky. Second of all, progression. Waiting an hour for a dinosaur that can die just as easily as the one before just isn't fun. In the state it's in right now, everyone is aggressive. I've met about two friendly dinosaurs in total. I know that it's part of the challenge, but I can't seem to enjoy it. I've played a lot of progression servers to try and get myself to like it, but I can't. It's not even that it's too difficult. It's simply that it takes too long to progress to anything worthwhile, and since everyone is desperate for food, you either have to kill them or you die. Another bad thing about progression is that if you die, you lose everything, which is ridiculous. Waiting an hour for a utahraptor or something else just for it to get taken away after five minutes is absolute crap. And because of this system, there is very little variety of what you get to play as, unless you're in the mood to play for three hours without dying. As of now, I would not recommend the game. But to conclude, I just can't enjoy this game like I used to, and for now, I don't think it's worth buying. But again, it will improve, and there's a lot of content to come.

The only strong suit of this early Telltale title was its ability to construct an interesting overarching plot that works outside of the canon of the films. Unfortunately, if DeLoreans like that existed today, I'd want for nothing more then to go back in time and take back the six hours I spent playing it. Hell, I'd take it back even further to try and stop Humble Bundle for giving it away in the Telltale bundle.
While Telltale has really finessed how intuitive their puzzles and point-and-click elements occur, some of the actions were far too repetitive and bizarre. Plot elements mixed with gameplay were too drawn out, and connections between the in-game actions were not intuitive and required an overreliance on the game's hand-holding hint system. Overall, the core mechanics and repetitive gameplay oversold how zany they wanted it to be, and they got too carried away at the participant's expense. The dialogue was exceptionally corny, and that kind of poor writing was just something you can't pin the time period on. However, I'm only saying this to justify everything in between the plot points - I respect them for making the most out of the pseudo-science behind the DeLorean and weaving that into a cohesive story with a satisfying ending. It just didn't seem so satisfying after the 6-8 hour slog to get there. You might enjoy it if you've seen the films.

Also, the guys behind this game must have either really loved or hated Dreamwork's How to Train Your Dragon movie, hahaha.

Let me say first and foremost before going into Pyre that if you're going into this game thinking it will be exactly like Bastion or Transistor, throw that thought out the window. If you're going to get this game, go into it with an open mind and treat it as something different than those 2 games, because it's rather different than both of them.
That being said, I felt like I got so much more from this game than I thought I initially would. SGG once again has brought back their amazing storytelling, beautiful artwork and memorable soundtrack for this game. Where I think this game contrasts most to SGG's previous games are the choices. There are a lot of moments where you can tailor the story to your liking, whether they be significant choices or small choices such as the background of your character. Not only are some of these choices done through text-based dialogue, but some choices can be made through the gameplay itself during the Rites. Your choices will affect the people and world in this game, making the more minor characters feel like they have a bigger a role. This makes every character more memorable, but I'd wish there were more interactions with people like your party members. While I see this as a con, I can also see this as a pro, as this reinforces the replay value since your choices will affect the dialogue and outcomes for each playthrough.
The gameplay consists of 3v3 matches called "Rites" where the goal is to get a celestial orb into the opposing team's pyre until you or your opponent's pyre is extinguished. To me, the gameplay is interesting and engaging, even though at times I felt like switching between characters was not as seemless as I would've wanted it to be. I understand why this would probably be the weakest point of the game for someone, but playing the game on a higher difficulty with smarter AI adds on to the game's strategic value and makes those moments of victory very satisfying. SGG also did well at making each party member have their own pros and cons, which allows you to go over multiple strategies when examining your opposing team before starting a Rite. Additionally, your party members can level up and gain masteries that will benefit you in Rites.
This wouldn't be a Supergiant game if the soundtrack wasn't slick as hell. Every song will always compliment a character and/or setting. Some songs even change depending on who you face in Rites, adding a little spice to the song everytime, rather than listening to the same song over and over. The soundtrack is definitely one of the game's strongest points.
Overall, if you're into a story-rich, real-time strategy/action game with decision making aspects, this game should be right up your alley. It's truly a great experience and a beautiful game to add to your Steam library.

Pyre is many things. Foremost among them, it is unique, charming, and radiating quality in every sense that you can experience it. And though Supergiant made Bastion and Transistor, the core of this game is quite different from either of them.
It should be obvious with Supergiant's track record that it is beautiful in sight and sound, at times arrestingly so.
So here's what's less obvious. The gameplay is hard to compare to anything else, because it isn't much like anything else. I cannot do it justice by simplyfing the matter into, "it's a visual novel with some sportball." It's actually a lot more than that.
The matches themselves are awkward for the first five or so minutes as the game teaches you the mechanics, but it's quite easy to pick up. The comparison to any given sport is obvious, but each match is equally about actual battle;
. It is remarkably simple, yet grows much deeper when unique units, tactics, and upgrades are factored in.
It never grows too complicated, there are relatively few actual mechanics involved, but a lot of possibility is given to you (and your opponent) in their combinations.
The game has a rather nice difficulty curve, at least as far as I've experienced with Mouse + Keyboard. Much like in Bastion and Transistor, there are ways to accrue greater rewards by inflicting penalties upon yourself, however I'll warn you that mastering this game is not going to be as easy. Luckily, there are also difficulty settings, should you find yourself overwhelmed or underwhelmed, and no penalties or achievements for availing yourself to them.
One thing I'll admit is that the game's progression structure changes after the first act, leaving you with choices, but also leaving you to revisit levels and opponents. It's the classic Vanillaware problem: when the asset quality is this high, you have to make sure you adequately reuse them.
But even then, every time you go to re-engage an opponent, you'll learn something new about them, about one of your crew, about the world, or about the overarching plot.
If you were a fan of the small tidbits of Bastion's old gods or Transistor's citizens, Pyre has by far the most fleshed out cast, worldbuilding, lore and backstory. Each character has their own past, their own motives and goals and resolutions. You are left with the choice of which ones to see through to the end-- and that choice is not to be made lightly. Between the lore's presentation, discovery and even diction; the way characters interact and develop; and your many available plot choices, it's got the strongest writing of Supergiant's three games. Though you wouldn't expect it from the visual novel-esque storytelling, it's also probably the least railroaded.
And though the subject matter is at times dark: your party faced with the bleakness of exile into an unforgiving wasteland, it is not afraid to be charming. In fact, so much effort has been spent polishing all the neat little things (to name a few: the many trinkets in the blackwagon, the work put into all the ways you and another character are addressed, the way the music layering and the minstrel is handled) it was easy for me to find myself charmed.
I definitely believe that Pyre is more than worth a chance, and earns its price point. If you're on the fence because the gameplay doesn't look like it's up your alley, consider buying it and giving it a two-hour chance before Steam stops accepting refund requests.

Generally I only write reviews after I 100% a game, but this one is beyond casual that I feel it is my duty and obligation to warn others:
--- 80% narration / 20% Gamplay ---
I don't recommend this game for anyone looking for pure gameplay. Simple as that.
Let's put it this way... if you're REALLY into story telling / narration, and the kind of person that gets absorbed into high quality presentation then this game is for you.
But DO NOT buy it for the gameplay, as it is almost non-existent.
It's amusing how the game tries to teach you to play as a team, but all you gotta do is basically grab the orb and run into the other team's goal, that's it. Every turn you use a different team member to do it with barely any real resistance.
When I'll get back to it, I plan to skip all dialogues and just get it done with.
Developers need to understand something simple: unless you're an RPG, then story must ALWAYS come second to the actual meat of the game = the GAMEPLAY!
They had it right with Bastion, they got it with Transistor, but here all we get is text and more text, then 3 minutes free combat, then back to more text.
♥♥♥♥ it, I would've just got myself some VN if I really wanted to read, or better yet - an actual book.
Not what I expected from Super Giant to say the least.

Can Supergiant make a bad game?  I'm not sure, but let's assume the answer is no because they've done it again.  Art, sound, story is all exactly what you would expect from a Supergiant game: cohesive, unique and absolutely beautiful.  There are gameplay elements that, much like Transistor, will probably rub people the wrong way.  If this is a barrier, it's a pretty low one and I'll admit I didn't really get the sportsballing until a few hours in when I realized it was less 3-man pseudobasketball and more 1-man primary, 2-man bench/support where you sub out someone from the bench each time your primary scores.  There's even more complexity to this system in the form of individual stats and unique abilities, a small skill tree for each character, assignable stat-boost items and the ability to score without temporarily sacrificing your current primary for the round by tossing the "ball" into the "basket" instead of slamdunking the character.  There is also a lot of worldbuilding via text in the form of character discussions or unlockable chapters in a sacred book, which is a nice addition.  I don't think it's Supergiant's best game, but it's definitely still a great one and absolutely worth buying.  In fact, Supergiant is pretty much the only game dev I would ever preorder from at this point.  What a rarity to find a company that has such a consistent voice and unique vision for their games and pulls it off not once, not twice, but THREE TIMES IN A ROW!

So you start with level 1 gear that can be upgraded to 6. Then at R1 you get gear to be upgraded from 7 to 12. Anyway, you see how the system works. At R3 you can hit the max gear rank of 108.

Recently I've been looking for less graphics-intensive games to play on my mac laptop.  I wanted something fun with cool artwork that would look pretty on my retina display and this game knocks it out of the park. The ancient Greek style artwork is really cool and well done, while the gameplay is exciting and addicting. I really did not expect to like games such as this (2D, platforming, sidescroller) because I mainly game on my desktop and play all of the huge, popular RPG's and action adventure games. But I'm really glad I gave this a shot so that I can game on my laptop when not at home. Apotheon is great and I look forward to playing more games like it.
**Update post completion of game
In my initial review I focused mainly on the pretty graphics and artwork and the fact that I could play this on my macbook, which in my opinion is not intended for gaming. Now that I have finished the game, I thought it warranted a second review of the gameplay and story.
As stated before, this game exceeded expectations. The gameplay, while simple, is subtly complex in ways that I did not realize until I was further into story. My favorite thing about this game is that it has many of the classic action-rpg elements, albeit a slightly simplified version. There are a variety of weapons to find/use, including "special" weapons for which you must complete side quests that are not obligatory in the main story. I particularly enjoyed the fact that the game encourages the use of all weapons and items in order to overcome different enemies. Sometimes I found using a spear the best option as it gave me range when fighting multiple enemies, while other times I used swords or hammers for speed or damage. Sometimes, I would lay traps while luring enemies to their doom. Furthermore, all weapon damage can be upgraded using gold at weapon trainers in markets. Armor upgrades come with increased defense, as well as cosmetic changes. When I found the Strategos helm, a large Spartan type helmet, I was elated. You are also able to craft various items and use them to different effects. These range from a simple health potion or firebomb to summoning animals and the undead to fight alongside you. Finally, the movement in this game takes a little getting used to, but once comfortable is very fun. I found out late in the game that in the air you can press the dodge/roll button to do a front or backflip that came in very useful for avoiding projectiles and accessing hard-to-reach places.
As for the story I was pleasantly surprised. As far as plot, it is nothing new or unique but is still very well done. Whenever I beat bosses (typically greek gods) I felt a sense of badass-ness, and the final boss fight was as epic as I expected it to be from a mythic Greek hero story. I found the voice acting surprisingly good, which always elevates the story and game for me. Add in the beautiful art style and I was pretty impressed.
For a 2D sidescroller that I picked up for 15 bucks, this game was more complex and fun than I thought it would be. It provided me with 20+ hours of gaming, and a very fun experience. I highly recommend it whether you just want something to play on your non-gaming laptop or high-performance gaming rig.

its an amazing classic game. but if you want to open the game on windows 8 and make it work do the following:
Run it in compatibility mode for Windows 95
Then you have to edit both the Ultimate.conf and Ultimatem.conf files to change this:
fullscreen=false
Then look down a little further and change this:
waitonerror=false
BOTH files have these settings and BOTH files must be changed AND be the same.
If those dont work do this too:
fulldouble=false
in both ultimate.conf and ultimatem.conf.
Now when the game starts, to use fullscreen just hit Alt+Enter.

A classic game from a simpler time before day 1 DLC, always online requirements, big budgets and forgettable storylines, DOOM still stands up as a boatload of fun.   The premise is simple.  You are a space marine trapped on an installation on the Martian moon Phobos.  Something has happened to turn all of your fellow marines into zombies, and daemons have been unleased.  Everything wants to kill you in some horrible way.  Pick up some weapons from wherever you can find them and kill everything in site before it kills you.
The gameplay still stands up after all this time, however compared to a modern game, the controls feel quite clunky.  Due to limitations in the game engine, you cannot for example, look up.  In the steam version you do get the option to re-map the forward / back / strafe left and right from the "traditional" arrow key controls to the more familiar WASD keys.  So you will use the mouse to look left and right, and fire your weapon.  The space bar is the catch all key to open doors; operate switches and levers etc...
I had DOSBox already installed on my PC for some other classic games, so I don't know if you need to have this already in order to run it, or if Steam will take care of this for you.  The game was originally coded to run on the MS-DOS operating system, and the fact that it runs at all on a modern Windows OS is pretty neat.  DOSBox is a free DOS emulator which you can install to run DOS applications (such as games) on your Windows PC.  A simple Google search can turn it up.
One thing I have found is that the graphics in the game will occasionally glitch out and stop displaying properly.  Saving, quitting out and restarting seem to fix the issue.  The fact that it is running at all is a bit of a triumph, so this is really a minor issue.
Perhaps the best thing about DOOM, and something that still shines through in this version is the sound and music.  The music is simple, but at the same time it's one of the best soundtracks for a game ever.  It manages to crank up the tension so well that the game is still able to make you jump out of your seat when a daemon shrieks at you from a darkened corridor and launches a fireball in your face.   The sound effects are some of the best ever put into a game.  The visceral feeling of the sound of cocking and unloading the shotgun has never been matched   in any other game since, IMHO.
My only other minor complaint with this version is the apparent lack of multi-player support.  The game itself is great on its own, but most of my best memories of playing DOOM where sitting around the flat in uni with my flatmates and our PC's connected via NULL Modem links playing death matches until the wee hours of the morning.  I believe DOOM 2 had support for IPX/SPX connections.  I've not seen anything to that effect in this version, so perhaps it's no longer an option.  Which is a bit of a shame.
Bottom line, should you buy this game if you've never played DOOM before?  In short, yes you should.  Just don't expect it to be anything like a modern FPS shooter.  This game was an evolution from Castle Wolfenstien, and was incredible for its day, and it's still a blast to play, however you need to expect that the graphics are going to look dated and that the controls are nowhere near as smooth and intuitive as in a modern game.

This potentially brilliant title crumbles by midgame under a burden of poor interface design and its dedication to micromanagment within the shelter.
Like some other bad reviews for this title, I wanted to like it so much. With recent titles such as Kingdom, I expected a level of contemporary elegance in how the game plays and unfolds. Instead, this feels like an unfinished title from 1987.
Much of the footage within the documentary is not from this game. It is either from the game jam or tests from early development.
What stands out most at this point, after about 24 hours of play (grinding to get the final achievements associated with this title), is the interface issues when switching from one survivor to another in the shelter. It is frustratingly easy to misdirect a survivor when simply trying to select another. Add to that the constant intrusions of "Incoming Radio Transmission" which is where the bulk of the scavanging game is played, and the game feels like a herky jerky mess of mircomanagement of bad AI via a poorly designed interface.
The game theme, aesthetic, and concept all hold promise. But the execution sinks this title for me.

So, I like this game. A lot. For the first while, it plays like a much better version of 60 Seconds, especially since you can craft and check up on people during expiditions, which means people won't just not come back from expiditions. If you check in on them, you'll know what was going on and why you lost that family member or this new recruit. And the resource management is so well done. Water is your best friend in this game, btw. Seriously. The moment you get in that shelter, build extra water butts. But... I now can see why so many people are frustrated with day 100+. So, day 100 was the day of my first raid, but I'd already set up traps so everyone survived. The thing is, if you're not expecting them, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. Straight-up. You cannot tell someone to take a hatchet and a hazmat suit and go to town. And the maps are really, really small. Like, tiny. If you've been building water butts at every opportunity, you'll have a steady water supply by day 80, and you'll likely be doing a lot of long expiditions, so you'll get to the end of the map by then. Day 100+ starts up the idea of factions, but...there really isn't much point to them, as you can usually avoid them, even on such a tiny map.
And there are a few glitches, like random radiation poisoning. I had a family (and hadn't lost a member from day 1-118) who were getting raided. A family member had FOOD poisoning. During the raid, she dropped dead of RADIATION poisoning. I know she didn't have radiation poisoning, because she'd been vomiting all over the place and we 5 bottles of anti rads....
In addition, automation is a little..♥♥♥♥♥♥ Family members won't take care of wounds, and will sometimes wait til their needs are super in the red, making it difficult to organize expeditions.
Also, some things about characters and recruitment are bizarre. So far, only the attributes Strength and Perception have day-to-day uses, in expeditions. Intelligence is only useful for operating 2-3 machines you can't craft until you get to the level 4 workbench. Everything else seems useless.
When missions come around, there are sometimes no nonviolent paths to take. Let me explain.
There was one mission where a man asked you to find a man and KILL HIM for a photograph. When you go there, the man says its a photograph of his children and insinuates that the other man is going to use that picture for some awful thing...and you have to either kill him or run away. Instead of asking him what the hell is going on.
All that said, I would recommend it for the first 100 days, and the first few times you play (where youre constantly dying) if you're a fan of variable repetition and simple, turn-based combat.

tl:dr;
It's not a bad game, not really. It's not a great game either. Recommend if on sale, sorely lacks content for endgame and many functions that you would expect from resource management  and survival combo game are not present.
Long version:
Sheltered is a cross between Fallout Shelter and This War of Mine. It lacks in every aspect when compared to the above titles.
Audio: 7/10
Amazingly good. Ambient sound and sound effects constantly remind me of Fallout1/2.
They are great in building the atmosphere of the game and definitely fit the setting.
However the music (either battle or jukebox) is like 12 sec long loop that gets pretty annoying fast.
Graphics: 6/10
Ok, nevermind pixelized "oldschool" setting. The problem with graphics is that every shelter has the same background, locations have no variety to them (each farm has dead cows) and there are very few character clothes to choose from.
Asset variation is simply POOR, and considering everything else there is no excuse for it.
Also the UI. UI will overlap parts of the shelter, making sometimes invisible to see. Apart from that it's crowded and non-functional. It really would use a bar with all the most important actions visible clearly.
Also no help accesible from inside the game nor the full list of the people and their stats in a survival/management game is f*king insulting.
Gameplay: 5/10
So it is not a bad game. For around dozen or so hours. It really gives you something to do in the beginning, there really is some pressure and tension and fun initially.
Problems starts when you finally get a grip of the situation and get some more people and build up your shelter.
Here are the issues:
- some facilities are unbalanced in terms of mats required versus what they give. For example it is better to build lvl 3 store boxes and lvl 3 pantries above them, as top level storage facilities take more space but give the same amount of storage.
- upgrades end too soon
- some materials are too difficult to come by, like ropes and hinges that are needed for most stuff
- space in a shelter is very limited (obviously) but still some facilities take way too much space for what they offer.
- everything breaks so fast it's just stupid! really need to fix a bed every five days?! really?!
- you can't rename nor change appearance of your toons. Why? why not give nickname or new harcut or new pants?
- no automation for characters beyond basic eat/drink/sleep/sh*it actions
- no crafting of weapons! you can have tons of nails, duck tape, pipes, metal and wood, but you cannot craft a baseball bat or a spiked mace!
- very limited character inventory. worse, you do not have character management screen, you cannot give them some items permanently.
- water requirements for travelling
- random loot! you are likely to find a single bulb, a single nail, a single duck tape, a single pipe, a single wood plank in a location than simply 6 nails! and you need dozens of them to craft upgrade, so there is always a problem with the flow!
- random encounters! only single people, no caravans, trading usually has very little to offer (one nail, one pipe, one water bottle etc)
- unable to store excess items in external nearby locations
- cannot change your weapons or use medkits while on expedition
- very limited and repetitive diary entries. like wth devs write more than 3 entries for a new recruit please?
Ok, so basically the worst part of the game is that you cannot equip your sheltered people, arm them and have them fend of raiders in battle. Either you build some crappy traps (selection VERY limited) or they rob you blind. You just cannot fight back.
Another major issue is lack of roles in the shelter. See, there is basic needs automation. But there is no roles automation.
I would love to mark a single person as botanist/cleaner and have them only plant and water seeds and clean the shelter.
I would love to mark a person as maintenance, so all they do would be fixing stuff and cleaning the shelter.
I would love to have a doctor, who would check the wounds, if there would be any wound system in place and feed the pet from time to time.
I would love to have a guard, who would be walking armed and fight back against the raiders, spending his time to train stats.
A scientist making research in the lab and reading books?
And finally. There is no entertainment facility in order. I wouldn't mind a poker table or an arcade machine for my toons to spend some time and relax.
Conclusion:
This game is bare bones as it is now. It was released 5 months ago and I am not sure if there will be any serious updates to it (homepage seems empty). If you find it with price tag below 10$ grab it. Support devs.
We need games like that, but we need them finished with some late-game goal to aim at. Right now it is dollar per hour and little more of value.

Pyre is many things. Foremost among them, it is unique, charming, and radiating quality in every sense that you can experience it. And though Supergiant made Bastion and Transistor, the core of this game is quite different from either of them.
It should be obvious with Supergiant's track record that it is beautiful in sight and sound, at times arrestingly so.
So here's what's less obvious. The gameplay is hard to compare to anything else, because it isn't much like anything else. I cannot do it justice by simplyfing the matter into, "it's a visual novel with some sportball." It's actually a lot more than that.
The matches themselves are awkward for the first five or so minutes as the game teaches you the mechanics, but it's quite easy to pick up. The comparison to any given sport is obvious, but each match is equally about actual battle;
. It is remarkably simple, yet grows much deeper when unique units, tactics, and upgrades are factored in.
It never grows too complicated, there are relatively few actual mechanics involved, but a lot of possibility is given to you (and your opponent) in their combinations.
The game has a rather nice difficulty curve, at least as far as I've experienced with Mouse + Keyboard. Much like in Bastion and Transistor, there are ways to accrue greater rewards by inflicting penalties upon yourself, however I'll warn you that mastering this game is not going to be as easy. Luckily, there are also difficulty settings, should you find yourself overwhelmed or underwhelmed, and no penalties or achievements for availing yourself to them.
One thing I'll admit is that the game's progression structure changes after the first act, leaving you with choices, but also leaving you to revisit levels and opponents. It's the classic Vanillaware problem: when the asset quality is this high, you have to make sure you adequately reuse them.
But even then, every time you go to re-engage an opponent, you'll learn something new about them, about one of your crew, about the world, or about the overarching plot.
If you were a fan of the small tidbits of Bastion's old gods or Transistor's citizens, Pyre has by far the most fleshed out cast, worldbuilding, lore and backstory. Each character has their own past, their own motives and goals and resolutions. You are left with the choice of which ones to see through to the end-- and that choice is not to be made lightly. Between the lore's presentation, discovery and even diction; the way characters interact and develop; and your many available plot choices, it's got the strongest writing of Supergiant's three games. Though you wouldn't expect it from the visual novel-esque storytelling, it's also probably the least railroaded.
And though the subject matter is at times dark: your party faced with the bleakness of exile into an unforgiving wasteland, it is not afraid to be charming. In fact, so much effort has been spent polishing all the neat little things (to name a few: the many trinkets in the blackwagon, the work put into all the ways you and another character are addressed, the way the music layering and the minstrel is handled) it was easy for me to find myself charmed.
I definitely believe that Pyre is more than worth a chance, and earns its price point. If you're on the fence because the gameplay doesn't look like it's up your alley, consider buying it and giving it a two-hour chance before Steam stops accepting refund requests.

The other things you can expect are normal for a Rayman game - tight controls, great humor, heaps upon HEAPS of levels to run through, a bajillion collectible items, AND remixes of select levels from Origins (only this time without any King Lums).

Generally I only write reviews after I 100% a game, but this one is beyond casual that I feel it is my duty and obligation to warn others:
--- 80% narration / 20% Gamplay ---
I don't recommend this game for anyone looking for pure gameplay. Simple as that.
Let's put it this way... if you're REALLY into story telling / narration, and the kind of person that gets absorbed into high quality presentation then this game is for you.
But DO NOT buy it for the gameplay, as it is almost non-existent.
It's amusing how the game tries to teach you to play as a team, but all you gotta do is basically grab the orb and run into the other team's goal, that's it. Every turn you use a different team member to do it with barely any real resistance.
When I'll get back to it, I plan to skip all dialogues and just get it done with.
Developers need to understand something simple: unless you're an RPG, then story must ALWAYS come second to the actual meat of the game = the GAMEPLAY!
They had it right with Bastion, they got it with Transistor, but here all we get is text and more text, then 3 minutes free combat, then back to more text.
♥♥♥♥ it, I would've just got myself some VN if I really wanted to read, or better yet - an actual book.

Can Supergiant make a bad game?  I'm not sure, but let's assume the answer is no because they've done it again.  Art, sound, story is all exactly what you would expect from a Supergiant game: cohesive, unique and absolutely beautiful.  There are gameplay elements that, much like Transistor, will probably rub people the wrong way.  If this is a barrier, it's a pretty low one and I'll admit I didn't really get the sportsballing until a few hours in when I realized it was less 3-man pseudobasketball and more 1-man primary, 2-man bench/support where you sub out someone from the bench each time your primary scores.  There's even more complexity to this system in the form of individual stats and unique abilities, a small skill tree for each character, assignable stat-boost items and the ability to score without temporarily sacrificing your current primary for the round by tossing the "ball" into the "basket" instead of slamdunking the character.  There is also a lot of worldbuilding via text in the form of character discussions or unlockable chapters in a sacred book, which is a nice addition.  I don't think it's Supergiant's best game, but it's definitely still a great one and absolutely worth buying.  In fact, Supergiant is pretty much the only game dev I would ever preorder from at this point.  What a rarity to find a company that has such a consistent voice and unique vision for their games and pulls it off not once, not twice, but THREE TIMES IN A ROW!

TL;DR: I don't enjoy the games main mechanic, a sort of magic basketball type ritual in which you have to throw an orb repeated into your enemy's Pyre. It makes it difficult to enjoy anything else about the game
After playing for two hours, I gotta say I'm pretty disappointed. I loved Bastion and Transistor but Pyre doesn't really leave me with the same impression. The music doesn't seem to fit too well to the sadder nature of the setting (the Downside and exile), the main mechanic is not something I like (I think advertising this as a party RPG is a little farfetched).
It doesn't really feel like you can implement any sort of strategy during the Rites ("Combat"). All I did was use the dog dude, get the orb and run as fast as I could to the pyre and that seemed to work every time. Defending your pyre is pretty easy, mostly just setting people with big auras by it or shooting all the other dudes.
I also have a particular distaste for the narration/commentary voice during the Rites. It's very grating and generally unpleasant, which suprised me considering the richness and bass of the past two narrators.
The art style also leaves something to be desired as it is way too guady. At times I actually feel like it's really hard to look at and the details of the landscapes get lost on me.
I'm not sure if I'll keep playing. The story is didn't pull me in very much, and, while the characters are interesting, having to play through the Rites is just kind of killing it for me.

The game's great. The core mechanic of the rites is not as interesting as Transistor's combat, but Pyre makes up for it with narrative and lore. I enjoyed my time with it greatly, but someone looking just for a mechanical challenge will be disappointed.
Outside the rites, the game progresses almost like a beautifully illustrated visual novella, where gameplay decisions, failures and successes end up mattering more than in "decisions matter" games like Mass Effect or anything by TellTale. The lore is extremely well written, so much that it's interesting to just read dead text about the world. Unfortunately, most of it is revealed through dead text, but it's still an enjoyable enough aspect of the game that it's worth mentioning.
Unfortunately, the AI in rites is neither particularly bright nor fair, so that aspect can become repetitive. For the latter half I was just rushing through the gameplay to progress the story. Mechanically, the rites are interesting, but only when facing human opponents.
I love this game. It was a simple concept, limited scope, and well-executed. Controller integration was perfect.

I was hoping that a realistic sniper game would be about long preparations with sudden bursts of violence. The tutorial that teaches the player to lay traps made me hopeful, but then the real maps were just as linear as the tutorial maps. There is no scouting of the location, no finding alternative exits, etc. There is only one road and after you take your sniping shot, the game will tell you when to run and which way to run. This game resembles typical shooters way more than I'd like it.
I'm not an expert on AI, but it takes me out of the game when the enemy is coming towards me in a single line one by one and they don't react when I shoot them one by one. It also breaks the illusion when the level designers intentionally set up a bossfight-esque event when dozens of enemies are aware of me and shooting at me and I have to snipe them all before I can go on. These kind of things shouldn't be orchestrated, but naturally emerge from the gameplay.
All in all I was very disappoined by this game as a sniper game, especially because this title is such well recognized as a good sniper franchise.

It's a fun game with a simple and concise premise, but it probably isn't worth $40.
You've got a decent selection of Jasons to pick and and equally good selection of counselors, all with unique stats. Jason can equip different brutal kills that the player can use on players in-game.
Players rank up through a leveling system similar to Dead By Daylight (but it doesn't encourage playing the game incorrectly like in DBD). You also earn points which can be spent on different killing abilities for Jason, as well as different costumes and randomized perks for counselors.
There are curently 3 different maps (Packanack, Crystal Lake, and Higgins).
Currently, there is no region-locked matchmaking, which means you'll be matching with a lot of Russians and Asian people, who may or may not speak your language. I'm mentioning this because communication in this game is key, and having a language barrier makes this game significantly harder.
Matchmaking can also be hit-or-miss, and it's not unusual for a few players to have ping over 100 ms. This obviously leads to problems in-game.
Each map has randomly spawning items hidden around the camp, whether it be weapons, walkie-talkies, health spray, or what have you. Your objective is to escape the camp, kill Jason, or survive the duration of the match.
Jason is very, very strong and counselors are extremely weak. I realize that this makes the game pretty unfair (despite it being 7v1), but it gives a feeling similar to what the movies portrayed: Jason is an unstoppable undead nutjob who will do everything in his power to kill you and your friends.
That being said, I really hope that they add more maps and more Jason variants. This game is in a league of its own in presentation and gameplay (I know there's DBD, but it's a bit more convoluted than F13, which is much more a game of cat & mouse). All in all, I enjoy the game quite a bit but I'd really recommend buying it through♥♥♥♥♥or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or something where you're not paying the full $40 entry price. It's really not a $40 game.

SOMA is a sci-fi survival horror game made by the same studio that gave us Amnesia: The Dark Descent. As a result the two games share quite a lot in common with one another. They are both survival horror games where the player is completely defenseless, and the only way to avoid death is to hide in the shadows from the enemy. They also share completely immersive worlds where each environment in the game can tell you a story based solely off of the objects that populate that specific environment.
However, SOMA, unlike its predecessor puts more of a focus on its story rather than the horror aspects of the game. Normally this would be something that would detract from a horror game, but in this case the story itself is incredibly compelling and wholly unique. SOMA's story is a unique one that focuses on the concept of transhumanism, which is a concept that has been touched on in other games, but not nearly as well as it has here.
Even if you don't care much for horror games, SOMA is a game worth playing through for its story alone.

Following off the glorious footsteps of the fantastic Rayman Origins, Rayman Legends successfully follows in the footsteps of its predecessor and delivers another high-quality entry into the Rayman franchise.
The rebooted Rayman series are 2-D platformers that do away with the traditional lives and continue system in most platformers in favor of a fair balance of high yet-fair difficulty balanced out with a good checkpoint system, making the game more about overcoming obstacles rather than trying to beat a game in a single sitting. The spot-on controls make it so when you die, you feel it was your fault rather than the game messing up or the game being cheap.
Since this game was originally planned as a Wii U exclusive, there are several stages that are clearly intended to be played on a touchscreen, which involve using longtime series character Murphy the fly to do tasks such as moving blocks, rotating wheels & cutting ropes. These features work perfectly fine on controller, but these particular levels are not nearly as engaging as the rest of the game.
This game also supports four player co-op and has a fun multiplayer mini-game. Sadly, the multiplayer is only local. There is also a daily challenge mode that gives players the opportunity to complete with other players in several time trial courses complete with player ghosts to help feel the competitive spirit of the addicting game mode.
This game has a great deal of content that can be enjoyed both in single player and multiplayer and is a title that deserves to be in your library.

As a massive fan of the 2015 version I was eagerly awaiting this, and I was not disapointed. Nearly every facet of game has been improved from the previous version, though still rough around the edges, is a fun experience.
Pros:
- New match engine: This iteration is less arcady and better simulates a realistic match.
- New dynamic progression system: Players now gradually increase until their peak years, then decline after peaking. Players can now change calibre also. Developing juniors is much more organic now and is an important addition.
- Clubs now actively sign players from one another and free agents have been added. This creates a more immersive transfer market and makes exploiting a lot harder.
- Scouting: Having to scout directly for players and staff again makes additions harder, meanign tougher decisions need to be made when allocating funds and staff actions.
- Training is now much more improved also, allowing for more personalisation.
- Brilliant Suport from developer: After playing this game I noticed a bug. Within 12 hours of sending an email I had been responded to and the game had been updated with a fix!
Cons:
- Ui takes a while to get use to, but once used its fine.
- Is somewhat buggy, but as stated earlier, the developer is super responsive to being notified.
This isn't Football Manager or Out of the Park Baseball with massive backing and staff with decades of experience. This is a small project and we should offer as much support as possible so they can continue to improve this series which has so much potential. Also, I noticed other reviews have bemoaned a high number of injuries, if you hire a good doctor and physio injuries become a lot less frequent.
Relaxing, Intuitive, Elegant, Masterful!

Ok, this is my second review of this game so I hope it helps those looking to buy this game. This might be a long one but bear with me.
The first review I did was very negative as there were too many injuries. By the 6th game a third of my team was injured and they were mainly anyone I put in at hooker. I was Workington Town which is a semi-pro team therefore they have very little money. I had 1.5 star facilities and 1 star doctor and physio. The attrition levels of all my players were low and most were rested when I put them in at hooker yet they still got injured playing in the number 9 position or during training. Since I put the negative review one of the developer’s, Roger, messaged to say they were working on a fix for the unrealistic injuries and especially to all being in at hooker. I don’t know whether it has been fixed but the way I got around it was to basally cheat. I used ‘cheat engine’ just to give me enough money to buy a 5 star doctor, physio and upgrade my medical facility to 2 stars. No money was spent on players etc so I could play and enjoy the game as it is meant to be. Because of the better doctor, physio and medical facilities I have really really enjoyed this game. It seems if you choose a club lower than professional level who have no money everyone gets injured and you can’t enjoy it because it’s not realistic and you spend most of the time frustrated because you can’t field a team. However, if you get the physio, doctor and medical facilities upgraded it’s an amazing game! I still get injuries but its more realistic and you can manage the gaps it causes in your team.
Some of the things I really like is that you are an employee of the club. It’s your career and can apply to be the manager of other clubs to continue your career. You can advertise for staff positions so coaches etc apply to you. The negotiation system is amazing with different stages to signing a player. It’s a lot more in-depth than the 2015 game. I find that the biggest improvement has been during the matches. Firstly, the 3D graphics is a lot better than the 2D in 2015 and secondly, I no longer stack my bench with only forwards. On the 2015 counterpart you only really had to worry about your pack. If you had average backs and halves but a great pack you’d win because they build the platform to score from. Also, the backs never really got tired so you’d just have forwards on the bench. However, now the backs suffer from fatigue just like the forwards so you must really plan your bench and substitutions which puts you more in the manager role. It’s not all around the forwards anymore which, in my view, is great. There are other great parts of this game and improvements on the 2015 version but i cant write them all as i'd end up being able to publish a book.
The game is still in the early stages so there are a few bugs that need ironing out such as the injuries when you have a low-level team without money or facilities. Also, another bug that popped up was this, I won League 1 in the English league and got promoted to the Championship (where I’m now getting destroyed which is also realistic). It said I had met the board expectations as it should do. But, it then sent an email to my team saying ‘Executive board’s seasonal Super League expectation not achieved’ and penalised me accordingly. How have I been penalised for the Super League when I’m not even in it yet and have been promoted to the Championship? It’s only a little glitch so nothing to bang on about and doesn’t affect much. The only other issue is that 99 is the highest attrubites rating for a player but when im searching no-contracted players in the Championship or Super League im finding loads of players who ive never heard of with attributes in the 80's or even 98. This is the level of players like Jonathan Thurston, Sam Burgess and Cooper Cronk etc in real life but its seems like a lot of players in the Championship are rated just as amazing. I hope im wrong and have missed something with it though as i dont want to buy Joe Blogs who is rated at 98 to compete with the likes of JT with the same attributes. Even with this though the game is great. It doesnt take anything away from the game and is only a small issue for now.
One question from me for the developers, I’m not in the super league yet but does it have the marquee signing like the real life super league?
Finally, I had to cheat but if Roger and the other developers have managed to fix the injuries as they said they were doing then other people won’t have to cheat like I did just to enjoy the game. Since my fix though I love this game. To Roger and the other developers very well done!! Great game and I definitely recommend it.

The first thing I noticed is how dated this game is. It is a 6 years old game already so I didn't expect it to be state of the art but it looks and plays like something from the 90's. Then again, it is based on a franchise that started on the 80's so it's oddly appropriate. Plus this game does not just repeat the story of the movies but adds an entirely new adventure which makes it rather intriguing.
The game runs without a problem in my below average windows 10 pc and I didn't encounter any glitches or crashes.
The animation isn't that impressive and neither is the voice acting. I'd say it's the less refined telltale game I've played so far but it's still somewhat ok even though the animated characters sort of slip to the uncanny valley at times. The controls and especially walking around could use an improvement though now it's too late for suggestions to the developers I guess. I still wish navigating the map would be less awkward.
The story however is pretty interesting and fits the movies. The over the top personality of the characters, the god-awful clothes, the DeLorean, all bring back nostalgic memories from the movies.
The movies themselves weren't technically masterpieces themselves either. It was the concept and the characters that I liked back then and the movies that didn't seem to take themselves too seriously and weren't even apologetic for focusing less on science and more on fiction. On that regard this game could be considered a spiritual successor to the films. It's not polished, not well thought of and reeks of cult which makes it fit to the franchise.
It is a risk creating content for or trying to add to an old franchise when people have already immortalized it and worship it. I'd say this game compliments more the back to the future movies than star wars episodes 1-3 compliment episodes 4-6 and considering it is not written by the same person I find the effort pretty good.
So If you've never watched the Back To The Future movies I'm not sure if you will enjoy or even understand this game but for an old fan it's like looking at childhood pictures. Or, more accurately, like learning what happened to old classmates after graduation. With all its flaws I still recommend this game mainly because it picks up the story from where the movies left it and takes the DeLorean out for a few more spins. I did not get the "this should never have been made" or the "they destroyed the franchise" feeling while playing the game. No, it is not great. It does feel part of the franchise though. Part of the classics. I don't know if they made the gameplay dated for even when the game came out intentionally or not but it somehow felt appropriate. And as a stand alone point and click game I would probably just pass it by but this game is what it is and the story redeems it a lot in my eyes which is why I end up recommending it.
There's a lot of exposition and character building if you get into dialogues which is sort of the point of these type of games. The objectives are clear for the most part but I actually got stuck a few times which made hints come in handy. Most of the time hints are useless because it really is better to just figure out how to progress on your own but it's still nice that they're there.
What you usually see in telltale games is little reminders that a character will remember something and it will matter later on in the story. A cheap illusion of choice making you believe that every player gets a unique highly personalized experience. Here the story is as linear as it gets and very few responces actually matter and give you a slightly personalized experience. I don't feel strongly about it either way seeing how in every one of their games you get the same ending regardless of how you play. Here you just go around, solve puzzles and party like it's 1931! It's more or less a conventional point and click game and a conventional video game based on a popular movie franchise. But since it adds a bunch of new content to the old space travelling mythos many know and love I say go for it. I am wary of people unfamiliar to the movies so if you're reading this and you've never watched the films, don't intend to watch them but still want to buy this game I'm not sure what advice to give other than this: Watch the movies and then based on how much you liked them you decide whether you want to play the game or not. To me this game earns the right to be considered a sequel to the films and this is how it should primarily be viewed as. It is ok as a standalone experience but it really can't be enjoyed properly and judged fairly out of context.
