This review gets kind of spoiler-y, so if you're just looking for a recommendation, only read the first paragraph!
Overall, this game is stellar for what it is. It's a quirky, but fun, little gem and is astoundingly fun. Of course it's flawed in a couple areas, but is an overwhelmingly positive experience that I highly recommend. The game is modestly and reasonably priced, and is a steal for the in-depth gameplay and gorgeous, polished graphics and animation, and outstanding music and ambiance you receive.
The gameplay is fairly simple. It runs on point-and-click mechanics and you really don't need the keyboard at all. It's intuitive and works well with the style of the game, but beware if you were hoping for more keyboard controls. There's also no tutorial, so don't get your hopes up for your first family surviving more than a few weeks. It's chock full of micromanaging, which is mildly comparable to something along the lines of Papers, Please. To give you a taste, you have to manage repairing most of your systems, your ongoing party(s, you can have as many as you can stomach- and have people for), individual stats, food and water levels, fuel for your generator- and that's just off the top of my head. It's a lot to take in and can be pretty overwhelming at the start.
There's a hint of character creation at the beginning- you can customize your family! There's a huge array of physical traits your characters can have (minus fat characters, unfortunately), and you have the joy of creating 4 people to start- two kids and two adults. They can be male or female, and there's a small selection of preset stats and traits to give your little people. It's standard fare as far as character creation goes, but effective. Throughout the game you can get more and more people to live in your shelter with a variety of randomly generated stats to help you with completing tasks and living. After they're loyal enough to your cause you can even send them out on adventuring parties. As a side note, you get a cool pet that you gotta feed or else it dies but can give your family some cool perks, and they're all very cute.
Throughout the game you'll be faced with an overlying issue- trauma and stress. You get trauma by killing things, more or less, or when a person or a pet dies. Stress is accumulated.... somehow... and while obtaining it is, in my experience, kind of rare, it, along with trauma, goes down over time as your family chills out around your little bunker. A minor complaint of mine is that these aren't bigger issues, and I could see it making this game, which is already kind of easy when you know your way around it, a little more challenging.
The battle system is simple if not unremarkable and serves its function well. You can avoid battles by fleeing and you can attack and kill, subdue, steal from, or disarm your opponents. Battles seem either too easy or too hard at times and there's really no middle ground. It could use some developing, in my opinion, in the balancing department.
While I don't want to bog this review down with a long-winded rant about the things I dislike about the game (which is slim pickin's, honestly,) they still need to be addressed. This game has a few major flaws- the raiding system, the replayability value, and the difficulty. We'll tackle these in order.
Throughout the game you'll get raided by, well, raiders at random times. This wasn't an issue for me early-game, so I'm assuming they only occur after a certain date. With raiders, all you can do is attack with traps around your shelter, some of which are more or less effective depending on their rarity, and all having to be armed when the raiders get there, not before. What ends up happening is this crazy mad-dash to get to your traps and then get to safety before the raiders bust through your two bunker doors. This is easier said than done, especially considering you can't pause the game to queue commands. I'm a fan of the lack of a pause feature purely because it really weighs on you that you have to be quick on your feet to make it through this game. It's really not a huge handicap and I don't think it's necessarily an issue that needs to be fixed. Anyway, raiders are a pain and you can't fight them except with traps. You cannot equip your survivors with weapons to fight and all they can do is cower. I have had, once, a raider engage a fight with one of my people, but all they had was their fists against the raiders knife and was easily killed. There's a handful of traps and all are pretty creative, but seem ineffective and the raids are really lackluster and you end up just getting out of the raiders way and let them steal your stuff.
The replayability value is pretty... not there. While it's fun to struggle in the beginning, eventually you just get overpowered and annihilate the wasteland. There's not a ton late-game to spice things up and you end up aiming for a cute, efficient shelter and maxed-out systems until you get bored.
Finally, the difficulty. This game is challenging until you figure out what to do. After that, it becomes pretty formulaic and you end up dashing through it. There's a lot of waiting around, thankfully spared by a nifty fast-forward button, but it slogs on from time to time.
Overall a really positive experience, highly recommended, but if you're not willing to suffer through a little monotony for $7, wait for it to go on sale.

Video Review (for those who don't like reading):
Back to the Future: The Game is a puzzle-adventure game taking inspiration from point-and-click titles. You click on various items to interact with them or investigate them, and use the items and your surroundings to solve puzzles that advance the story. Does it work? Well, yes and no. When it comes to video games, there’s an age-old question: Gameplay or Story: which is more important? Well, if you’ve ever been on the fence about this question, then Back to the Future: The Game will solve it for you in the first half an hour.
First, the story is astounding. It manages to fully capture all the magic and feel of the original movies while still being its own thing. After playing through the whole game, I, and I’d say most other people who played it, felt the story alone made it worthy to bear the title of Back to the Future Part IV. Considering that it was a collaboration from the people at Telltale Games, the people behind Tales from the Borderlands, and the guys who made the original three movies, and the story writer for this game happens to be the very same person who wrote the original three movies, I’m not all that surprised, though I am impressed that they managed to capture the same magic of the original movies more than twenty-five years after they released. The voice work is fantastic all-around, unsurprising since they got some of the original actors to play their parts, and every new character feels like they always belonged in the Back to the Future universe. For the most part, the dialog is well-written, the graphics are surprisingly fitting and work well, and the music is…directly stolen from the movies. Of course, the soundtrack of the movies is fantastic, so that’s not necessarily a bad thing. In addition, the puzzles are clever without being completely unfair. My favorite part of the game was during the last episode, where you have to jog somebody’s memory through giving their brain certain stimulations to represent what happened in the past. A mop head on a cactus makes a grandpa, a sign on an outhouse makes a saloon, and so on. I only ever had to look up the solution to one puzzle in the very first episode, and that ended up only being because my controller didn’t recognize a required object as an item.
And that’s where we get into what’s wrong with the game. After all, when you get a bunch of movie producers to make a video game, you can expect the story and dialog to be good, but the game itself? Not so much. Where should I start? Well, the camera is among the worst I‘ve ever seen, being annoyingly hard to control, and since most of the time you never need to manipulate it, you end up forgetting you can entirely, which makes parts of the game later on when you do need to manipulate it very confusing. It also picks these strange moments to suddenly switch perspectives, which throw you off whenever you’re trying to go somewhere across town. There are invisible walls everywhere, giving you a sort of fake-3D experience, but then often you can move around freely, and you just can’t tell the difference. Despite Hill Valley feeling so big, I feel just so constricted because of this. Plus, Marty is so slow! Even when he’s running, which, if you’re smart, he’ll always be, it still feels like it takes forever to get anywhere. All three of these aspects combined makes traversing the world around you a chore. That’s not mention the terrible controls. Here’s the thing: you’ll spend half of your time clicking, and the other half walking. Initially, it seems that a controller is the best option for both of these, as one of the control sticks can be used to skip from one clickable item onscreen to another with ease, and the other can be used to walk freely, whereas you have to drag the mouse a couple of inches away from Marty in whatever direction you want to go if you want to use the mouse. However, as I mentioned earlier, sometimes your controller will skip right over items, because it doesn’t recognize them, and very often, those items are required to solve a puzzle in the game. So you end up constantly switching between two means of controlling, using the controller to move and the mouse to click, and, trust me, it gets REALLY annoying. Also, if you hold down either the mouse or the button for more than a half a second during dialog, it sometimes acts like you clicked twice, and skips important pieces of dialog. Also, just a tip: in the first episode, a reporter will ask Marty for his name. Just tell her it’s Harry Callahan, because no matter what, everyone is going to refer to him as that.
Is playing the game a chore? Not necessarily. The music and characters keep the atmosphere up, the puzzles are fairly good, and the story makes you want to keep going. It’s more of a whether or not the story is worth drudging through the terrible camera and controls. I’ll tell you this; if Chuggaconroy ever made a let’s play of this game, I’d recommend watching it well over playing the game yourself. However, when you look at the other Steam reviews for the game, you’ll see that the vast majority are positive, and most of the negative ones simply say that the game is “meh,” and the story and gameplay cancel each other out. Many of the positive reviews say that the story is what makes the game worth playing. And here’s the thing: I think they’re right. The game is going to be really annoying to play through due to the controls, but the feeling you’ll get when you solve a puzzle is never to be underestimated, and every resulting cutscene is a reward in and of itself. I certainly wouldn’t recommend watching a walkthrough over playing it, but if you have a character of interesting personality doing a let’s play, you might want to stick to that. Still, the story, music, dialog, characters, and perfect capturing of the feel of the movies makes this game more than worth the while. On the gameinformer scale of 1-10, with 7 being average, 10 being perfection, and 1 being the Ouya controller, I’d give this game a 4 for gameplay and 9 for story, which rounds off to 6.5, and I‘ll bring it up to a 7 just so I can recommend it officially.

At the time of writing this review, I have played the game approximately 10 hours.  I bought the game during the Steam Summer Sale for $7.49, and for that price I am quite pleased with my purchase.
This game is an enjoyable resource management game.  You must help a family of four survive in what appears to be a nuclear fallout zone for as long as possible.  At the time of this writing the furthest I have gotten is 50 days.
The first game I played, I had no idea what I was doing and wasted a lot of my beginning resources on things that were not absolutely necessary for the first few weeks of survival.  Once I realized how scarce food is at the beginning, I restarted my game.
My second game I began sending my family out on solo missions thinking it would be a better idea to get more ground covered.  Well, it is and it isn't.  My boy Ryan was brutally murdered when he was attacked by some loner who"wanted his blood".
My third game I got far enough to set animal traps and begin harvesting meat.  Unfortunately, I didn't realize what food poisoning was and poisoned my entire family.  Simultaneously, one of the recruits that I had gained the trust of went on a mission and was stabbed.  I was unaware that he was bleeding and he died in his sleep.  Instead of burying him, the mother of my family cut up his body and put him in the fridge.  Come to think of it, that may be why I got food poisoning.  Poor Matthew.
The fourth game is the one I am currently still playing. At 50 days in, I have kicked two survivors from my home because I didn't realize that there was a capacity limit and they were suffocating me.  One went quietly and the other contaminated my water supply in retaliation.  I currently have 6 survivors in my shelter with an upgrated O2 unit that is able to support us all.  Edward and Richard, my two recruits, bravely go on constant runs for supplies while my core family sits at home and repairs things, slowly makes some progress creating new rooms and better furnishings, living the good life and awaiting the day that someone comes knocking on our door with less than decent intentions.
I have read the negative reviews, and it seems that a lot of the disappointment in this game comes from both the repetetiveness of the constant need to gather supplies, and the unfortunate RNG of having people come to your base intending to kill your family and ravage your shelter of supplies.  That hasn't happened to me yet, but I am waiting for it, and I know with absolute certainty that it will tick me off to no end when it happens.
However, this game has already provided me with 10 hours of entertainment, and I think that's pretty good for a $7.50 game.  I may even have paid $15 for it, given that I am not finished yet and I am more than likely going to start a new save after this one inevitably goes horribly wrong.
In short - If you like resource management games, don't mind a bit of grinding, and can deal with sometimes having some bad luck, don't shy away from this one.  It is fun.

Rayman Legends is just so much better than Origins. I remember talking, erm.. not so positive,.. about Origins. aside from the wonderful, colorful graphics. Well, let me say that Legends is a bigger and better game in every way; customization, unlockables (oh man, they keep on coming), secrets; there seems to be much more variety this time around and I couldn't recommend this game more.
There are 6 worlds to be completed, with the last one being more of a bonus world. Each world has about 8 to 10 levels, and each level could you take at least 5 minutes to complete. So it's a big game. Add even more secret and unlockable levels to that number and you know why it's called Legends.
Each of the first 5 worlds end with a musical level where you just run, punch and avoid enemies based on the music. It's brilliant and it works very well. In general there's much more variety gameplay wise as well, with the aforementioned musical levels but there are also stealth levels, and levels where you have to rely on a (CPU controlled) co-op partner.
The animations and graphics are top notch. Rarely have I been as impressed with 2D visuals as I've been with the last few Rayman games. No words can describe how this game looks and plays, you really have to witness it for yourself. This is art !
By the way, the boss fights aren't as frustrating as the ones in Origins. There was only one boss that, in my opinion, was more of a trial-and-error boss fight, the rest of them could easily be beaten the first time around, if you pay enough attention.
Rayman Legends surprised me in a big way and I'm saddened to hear that it didn't sell all that well. It has tons of content, so much even that most games look empty in comparison.
Buy it. Cherish it. Love it. Play it. But, more importantly, enjoy it. How can this game not put a smile on anyone's face ?

is an action/adventure title following the the fictional epic of Nikandreos (a spin off of Nikandros, meaning victory of man), in which Zeus has turned his back on humanity and destroyed it.  Nikandreos then goes on a journey through Olympus to avenge his people.
is a beautiful game with a gorgeous pottery-esque asthetic.  Being two-dimensional and having long, horizonal areas make the game feel like it was developed on an ancient vase documenting the tale as you write it.  Damage you take will chip the background, making contact with an enemy provides a satisfying sound of the tympanum, and the game never seems to break character.  All of that combined with a splendid soundtrack, made areas like Posidon suprisingly memorable and provided the atmosphere to make Hades and the Artemis Swamps genuinely unnerving.
also has a very steady learning curve, and I never felt like I was being pushed too hard or taken too easy.  That being said, I never ran low on health supplies, but found it an interesting challenge to keep myself well stocked.  All the way up to the end, the player is still being introduced to new weapons, techniques, and button presses.  There isn't a true tutorial, which I like.  The game knows the player isn't dumb, and though fairly linear, there's a lot to do off the beaten path.
For all it's worth, there were a couple of times where the control scheme felt difficult to work with.  It almost felt like a great indie game that was morphed into some sort of flash game from 2006.
has a combat system completely based around the orientation of your mouse.  So Nikandreos will do some contortionist movements to shoot an arrow directly upwards, but it also means that enemies will only be hit if you
, which was particularly challenging for me.  Not that it's a bad thing, but there's a lot of mouse movements that one needs to execute in simply landing successive hits.  That, and weapons seem to have some sort of random attack pattern.  Nikandreos seemed to swing, stab, and thrust with whatever execution he wanted; be it overhand, below the belt, behind the back, etc.  I couldn't control that, so when using something longer like a Doru or Sarissa, you might just end up hitting the cieling and smashing your weapon on their head, instead of thrusting it into their unprotected thigh.
There's only a few other minor gripes I've got.  For example, Nikandreos has some sort of acceleration that leads to him sprinting full speed until he gets to stairs, and then loses all of his momentum.  The development team was a little frugal with their voice acting talents, and many characters sound similar.  Nikandreos also doesn't seem to develop in an emotional sense, but rather the Mega Man sense, where unlocking more weapons and acquiring health upgrades simply enable the player to do more.  Though the game acknowledges Nikandreos getting stronger and bases the story around it, I can't help but feel detached to the main character like when reading stories like
and
.

Though I have a few gripes with the movement and combat, the game feels very much representative of the God of War series - if written by Greek playwrights.

A:TTD isn’t what I expected nor was it what I was hoping for. Friends seemed to rave on about it endlessly.  Admittedly I came late to the party. Still, it was a solid premise wrapped up in a walking simulator. I put in ½ an hour before I honest to god fell asleep. When I woke up, I honestly asked for a refund.  If a game a) doesn’t deliver what it promises and b) is no fun then why keep it? Yes, I picked it up at 85% off and that’s still no excuse.
I guess the game is 7 years old and people’s expectations back then were about 500x lower. If you enjoy walking around a series of dimly lit rooms and getting a headache from motion blur because you can’t find oil to keep your lamp lit then you might very well enjoy this style of game, I myself however at no point felt my level of survivability was under threat
– the game tutorial was poor and the scare factor was non-existent.
I may as well go back to RE4 or even Five Nights at Freddy’s or at the higher end Outlast or Alien Isolation at least seem to have some merit and at least they’re well-lit and have thematic reasons to actually allow you to see what you’re doing without giving you a terrible motion blur headache. It’s hard to even pretend to be scared when you can’t even concentrate because the game mechanics are giving you a literal headache.
I could honestly have more fun beating my head repeatedly against a brick wall until I passed out from the blood loss, and that would even look gorier than this so-called ‘game’, I’m sure if you look around there are better walking simulators out there and in this day and age if A:TDD is still the same retail price as Outlast, which is a newer release, then clearly your money is better spent on Outlast which has gotten even cheaper since Outlast 2 came out.
You might call the game tense, atmospheric horror at its primal best. I call it bland, uninspired and overhyped and from what I’ve read the sequel was just more of the same.  At this rate I may as well go back and play the original Resident Evil, that was a true classic.  Still if you can pick this up for 85% off and you dislike it for the same reasons I did, you can always get a refund.  Like I did.

There is one man left on the planet. A russian scientist, who, before the world ending cataclysm, set up a cloning project that would soon doom the world. When the ashes cleared it was discovered that the cloning facility had been pumping copies of the scientist into the world. His clones rose up and repopulated, but only in the absoulte worst possible places. They grew strong. Too strong. They began to splinter. They created factions that innevitably went to war over the giant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that had arisen in the landscape during the cataclysm. Eventually the scientist began to grow mad, seeing himself anywhere he went. He lost all sanity. One fateful night he retreated to the top of some incredibly generic rusty russian industrial platform and put a gun in his mouth. He knew that this was no way to live. He had to kill himself. As his fingers' finely tuned muscles began to compress the trigger, a light bulb illuminated the depths of his mind. "NO! his brain cried out". He had to kill... HIMSELF. He pulled the gun out of his mouth and grinned. He would be the first person in the history of the human race to commit the act of homi-suicide and set out to murder... himself, with the help of a few of his clones. You are this scientist, Russian Woody Harrelson, and it's your goal to eliminate yourself. Over and over. And over. And over. And over. And over. And over again.
Anyway, for a real review of this game... I've made it out of noob hell. If you can suffer through levels 1-10, you'll like what comes after. If you can't make it that far, you can expect:
The least inspired shooter to come along in awhile. there are 0 new mechanics added in to the game and nothing makes it stand out, gameplay wise.
A hundred thousand of the same player model.
2 guns, though slightly satisfying, are all you'll get for too damn long.
Unbalanced levels. If you spawn on the wrong side and your team has a single weak link, expect to get shot almost as soon as you spawn.
Every other match you'll find at least one guy running around shooting teammates with that blank, homicidal look in his face, Eyes, unblinking as he just blows holes in the back of his colleagues heads, his face, expressionless.
Every time you lay a trap down you can expect to get more team kills than enemy kills even though all friendlies can see a giant god damned trap icon directly over the thing. Or you'll get those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that walk up to it and just ♥♥♥♥ing disarm it because ♥♥♥♥ you.
Every 3 matches you'll run across a person 10 levels higher than every one in the group and a few premium nubs. All you get is a single grenade or trap and your mothers hand knitted sweater made of fluff and love. Have fun fighting walking tanks, son. Everyone says premium isn't pay to win but every time I see a premo walk into a match they always seem to come out mvp.Sure, they're killable, but the scoreboards don't lie. They should have allowed premiums to only use premium gear after level 10.
At first It felt like you could get by with out premium but they start shoving it all up in your face. Eventually you feel like you're falling behind in gear and money so it starts to look tantalizing, then you get into higher levels and you're the only dude without an AK... and then you accidentally leave auto-buy on for the most expensive ammo and you go in debt, leaving you with nothing but starter gear... then the pop ups start with the buy premium button exactly under the confirm button for exiting a match. Don't click too fast.
Good notes:
Even though level design is unbalanced on most maps, the levels themselves are beautifully crafted and incredibly immersive. The level of "God took a dump on the earth one day and russians decided to colonize it" apocalypse and S.T.A.L.K.E.R level of detail is just beautiful. I've never played another shooter that made me feel this way. I absolutely get a kick out of crouching and running through overgrown grass and shrubbery, shooting my mosin through slats in run down cabins (yes, ♥♥♥♥ windows, you can shoot through cracks in the wall). The devs pay beautiful amounts of attention to making it seem believable and making you feel like you're really there. I absolutely love these maps and cannot wait for Free-roam.
The guns themselves, at least the ones I use (Mosin, Uzi, and Winchester) feel like guns. In call of duty your weapon feels like a feather. There's no repurcusions for firing. You go about with reckless abandon, spraying rounds left and right only to reload in milliseconds. In Survarium every shot is important. Your guns, at least for the beginning levels, are old and heavy and you definitely feel it. It sounds bad but... it feels so right. SMG's have iron sights that, once you start firing, you might as well just not iron sight because dat recoil and flare though... Rifles have a satisfying gun shot noise followed by a plume of smoke that clouds your vision, sometimes obscuring targets, which is neat. You may shoot and miss, but you dont notice them slip off to your left because the gun smoke was in your face Nothing is more satisfying than getting a kill at any range with a mosin. There are shotguns and assault rifles but the only shotgun I've used is the starting shotgun which is utter butt. Don't pull the trigger unless you're close enough to hit them with thing, and in which case don't pull the trigger, just hit them with your double barreled baseball bat.
Tl:dr: Suffer through the crap hole of the first ten levels and something fun starts to show up behind the grime and muck of that old familiar russian apocalypse.

After about 75 hours with For Honor, I feel that I have had enough time with it to make my call. The aspects that shine are well refined and refreshing, so much so that For Honor exudes originality and promise. The unique combat system really tries to make it all about a players skill, resulting in fresh and consistent mechanics.

However, its issues are glaring and in some cases it struggles earnestly to be something more. Matchmaking can be abysmal, there are no dedicated servers, and load times can be horrendous because of the P2P system. Quite frankly, for a multiplayer based game in 2017, the systems being used are poor at best. Revenge definitely needs a revisit, 4v4 modes can feel very unbalanced with high level gear, and the elimination game mode struggles to find its identity. The campaign is completely forgettable and lackluster; I can excuse this to a degree, but there were times where I was playing thinking, "Why is this even here?" Unfortunately, the online issues can lead this game to an early decline for those who choose to stick with it and its community. Some of these decisions really do hinder this from being something more.
All of this said, fighting games are usually not my forte, but my time with For Honor has been one of learning, becoming a better player, and ultimately striving to win. In this area, it succeeds and gives me much of the same satisfaction that the Souls series has with its PvP. It is a fun skill-based brawler with its sole focus on player-versus-player multiplayer.
I am sure that For Honor will definitely inspire more games to model themselves after it, and it is a game that will probably continue to see play here and there, but ultimately not one that will keep me for a long time like other great games. I recommend it to those looking for a good brawler, but only if you can deal with these issues upon purchase or want to wait to see if Ubisoft plans on fixing them. For Honor is a 3/5 for me personally. Is it a must buy for everyone? No, it is not, but I still recommend taking a look at it if you are into this genre.

Let me just start with this: I know that the plot is incredibly farfetched from Ancient Greek Mythology in the sense that the gods could not just be killed by a mortal.  As a student of Ancient Greek litterature and mythology, this is a bit "out there" in that respect.  That being said, in every other respect I can think of, the game was spot on.  More than spot on, in fact.  The little tablets with ancient translations were incredible.  The names of the weapons were all in correct Greek spelling.  I was truly impressed with the detail that was put into the game.  Both the mythological and historical accuracy were amazing.
Moving on the graphics: I was a huge fan.  In creating a platformer, I know that there are a lot of options for styles of the visuals.  The choice of Ancient Greek art style was genius.  It puts the gamer right in Ancient Greece.  This art is the same as that on greek pottery.  Once again, an awesome detail that really made the game that much better.
Don't worry, I am certainly not going to overlook the gameplay.  It was a blast.  I was impressed with the combat in the sense that you have to judge your enemies next attck and there are so many possibilities to destroy your adversary.  The designers managed to make each stage tailored for that god, leading to underwater bouts, chases on horseback, and tricky mazes.  These all integrated combat with unique foes.
In addition, your practically endless arsenal of creative Greek weapons and shields makes sure that each fight is interesting.  Once again, many of these weapons are found in ancient Greek culture, but many new weapons were created based on stories myths.  Discovering these weapons is really cool as you find more specialty items.
This game is a must-have for everyone (especially for any of you classics students like me!)

Pyre is, in my opinion, the best game Supergiant has developed to date. Unlike their previous work, Pyre has a huge cast of unique and likable characters brimming with personality and individual motives. The story itself feels epic is incredibly engaging.
Although, as you can see from other reviews, there is quite a bit of people that don't share my enthusiasm. It should be noted that Pyre is Supergiant's riskiest and most ambitious project to date. The gameplay is vastly different from Transistor and Bastion. Most of the game you're just reading and making decisions, and between these decisions you play Rites. I personally found a lot of enjoyment out of the rites. I think they're fun and often I'm at the edge of my seat with my heart beating through my chest in worry that I might lose. If you lose, the game continues, and depending on which rites you win or lose, it effects how the story progresses and how it ends.
I understand if buying it is a risk, but if you're looking for an engaging story, brilliant characters, and a truly unique RPG experience, I suggest you give it a try. I do find the items to be quite useless, but I don't care; if I'm this invested in a game, it deserves my recommendation.

There's something to be had for shooter fans from all different walks. Whether you're playing for the sake of chasing the carrot on the stick (which is really an exaggeration, more on that later), competitive gameplay, or coming along to sight see/explore (it's awfully pretty at times) and experience the inevitable PVE content that has been promised and with the currently designed levels could be easily implemented - It's all here (or soon to be)!
Gunplay is tight and efficient, reminiscent of fast paced shooters such as Call of Duty. You get a small handful of weapons to play with based on what you're interested in, a couple of loadouts, and off you go. The biggest customization in this game comes from equipping different sets of gear and decals/materials to them - and there's plenty. You're given ample resources to spend on purchasing new equipment, and almost as fast as your character levels up, so does your faction rankings and bank account. For every new tier of gear you unlock, starting off with only a few matches to do so, it only takes an hour or two at most to reach the next tier - and you have more than enough money if you were careful with it (and performed well) to buy out the entire set of upgraded stuff.
The world is very well designed, and you'll notice right away just how lush and alive the landscape feels. It's got an otherworldly vibe, but is oddly familiar at the same time. Past the impressive visuals and atmosphere that the game creates, the levels are designed in such a way that clever tactics and exploration are encouraged. Anomalies at various locations add a nice twist, with my personal favorite being the moving electric anomaly on the Vostok Array map, and if you lose track of what you're doing you'd quite quickly mistake yourself to be playing STALKER again. If you've got the gear to resist anomalies, new pathways are opened up for you. If you've got the time and patience to explore the outer reaches of the maps, or explore every nook and cranny, you'll have plenty of alternative routes to take and skirt around the conflict in search of a better vantage point. On top of all that, there's artifacts which can be found in anomalies to give your team temporary bonuses per map - and can be activated for further effects. The artifact gathering aspect is promised to be fleshed out later, so let's see how that goes in the mean time.
As far as free to play is concerned, I'd hardly know. You make so much money while playing that by the time you reach your next tier within your faction, you'll be able to buy everything - and faction advancement is quick and easy. In about 6 hours of playing I managed to make it all the way to the second highest faction rank, and was having fun the entire way through. Might slow down a bit later, but not by much from what I've experienced thus far.
Game balance as it stands could use some work, with SMG's being very powerful in comparison with other weapons (I'd argue they could use their effective range toned down, along with less accuracy to boot) it's a bit of an SMG spraydown in some matches, but most maps have enough sections with large distances between you and your foe that rifles come to shine in their own right. Shotguns are a very destructive although rather hit and miss type ordeal until you're able to get something that holds more than two shots, and even then you'd better hug some corners because short range is the definite, absolute name of their game. The sawed off side arm which can replace your standard pistol is an absolute blast however, and makes clean up or close quarter battles a breeze when you blow them away with a double tap and lighting fast reload.
All in all, I like this game. It's solid for what it is, and seeing as there are plenty of changes and new content yet to come - it's something that if it continues to impress me as such I might consider investing some money into. Vostok is doing a pretty good job with what is the spiritual successor to STALKER as far as I'm concerned.

In a generation dominated by Competitive Shooters and MOBA's, SOMA is a breath of fresh air that reinvigorates the enormous power of Video Games as a story telling medium.  SOMA has by far one of the most intense and compelling story lines I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing in a video game. Rich with Philosophical context, Enthralling Atmospehere and Nebulous World lore that is gently introduced and progressively fleshed out makes the experience almost cinematic. The philosophical thematic of SOMA dives in deep into 'What it truly means to be human?' and 'What does it mean to be alive?' and many more existential questions regarding the existence of humankind. All this is executed so well that the way each question is explored is absolutely fantastic.
The gameplay of SOMA is tagged with 'Horror', While that is true, There is a marked difference between the gameplay of a typical horror game and SOMA.That is the fact that the horror in SOMA feels genuine, It doesn't rely on cheap jump scares to create a superficial sense of fear to make you scream. The horror SOMA is more of an innate feeling of helplessness against the most deadly of scenarios. For someone who dislikes jump scares this is one aspect that I found genuinely laudable. Apart from it's atmopsheric thrills, The gameplay of SOMA generally relies on puzzle solving, Exploration and a small amount of stealth. All these elements encompass together to create one of the most thrilling and fullfilling gameplay sessions ever.
Overall, This is by far one of the best story driven games I have played till date.

Sniper Elite V2 is a 3rd Person Shooter with the 2nd World War as the setting.
___________________________________________________
++Story++
You are a (correct me if I am wrong) nameless sharpshooter who was sent to Berlin to kill important germans. On your way, you find out that the nazis have a last ace, the V2 Missiles, brutal weapons of mass destruction that are aimed at London, and you make it to your mission to destroy the V2s and defeat the Nazis.
++Gameplay++
The game has the typical shooter corridor as the leveldesign: Take way A, B, or C, but in the end, all ways lead to the same destination. But what is different? You can sneak completely unseen past the enemies, or kill them all with your sniper rifle. Loud noises can drown the noise of your rifle, so you can shoot without warning the enemy. If you just shoot the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything, you will alert the enemy and get quickly killed, which is positive because snipers are not supposed to take a lot of damage. You have some tools like mines and grenades to prevent soldiers from following you or flanking you. If you take out an enemy with the sniper rifle, you will most likely trigger a bullet cam that shows precisely how your bullet penetrates the body of your target, which can look disgusting at times because you see in X-Ray how the bones and organs get damaged (looks very amazing when you shoot your enemy's eye).
++Grafics++
The grafics are the usual standart for shooters back in 2012. Not amazingly good, but not bad either. The faces have
animations, the bullet cam looks great.
++Music++
The music gets annoying fast and is brutally loud, so turn it a little bit down before you start playing. Better play with some own music.
++Features++
Your sniper bullets are actually influenced by gravity and wind if you do not play on easy, which is amazing and makes the shooting harder, and requires you to think a little bit when you shoot.
___________________________________________________

In its current state, it's hard to really recommend it, if only because what they have planned will likely change the gameplay experience.  However, I have become thoroughly addicted to playing this game, so I have to recommend it based on how many hours I've logged already.
When a friend asks me, "So, what do you do?" I don't have a good answer.  I... um...  I run around as a dinosaur and look for either dinosaurs to either a) roam with or b) TEAR DOWN AND EAT THEIR CORPSE.  You know.  Depends on my mood.
The fact that I never know what's going to happen whenever I log into a server is fun.  I might find a friendly carno.  I might find a friendly herb.  I might come across a kumbaya carno-herb circle and be the jerk who mows them down just to be a jerk.  I might, as a raptor, find a daddy T-rex.  I might, as a T-rex, have other carnos start following me like I know where to find food.
There was one time where I, as a Rex, found myself a little baby raptor.  We palled around, tracked down an herbivore to eat, and in the middle of battle... he jumped in the way.  I nommed my babby.  I was legitimately kinda sad, because he was cute and affectionate.  I finished off the herb and sat down, pondering what I would do next.  A few moments later I hear some happy raptor chirps and look over to see a raptor—same skin as my babby—bouncing toward me.  We reunited!  Joyous, and now full from the kill, we ventured off.  We played in some ruins, we jumped off some rocks into a lake, he broke his leg and I sat by him until he healed...  Over the course of three or so hours, we died and found each other again about five times.  The whole time, never using chat, so when the server crashed, I realized I had no idea who he was.  It was kind of a heartbreaking moment!  My babby's lost to me forever!
Anyway, the point is, if you like dinosaurs and a little bit of roleplay mixed in with LOTS OF DYING because yeah you're gonna die, get over it and start anew...  *ahem*  I highly recommend trying The Isle out.  Experiences may vary because you literally never know what's going to happen every time you log into a server.  Like finding a server that had Quetzas turned on and omg I really want them implemented for realsies because they're amazing and aaahhh!
But know going into it that the gameplay will change drastically as they add more of their planned features.  The hardcore stuff they have planned doesn't sound like it's up my alley at all.  However, I am having a blast now, and so I recommend this game.

Ask yourself this."Do I enjoy the Back to the Future trilogy of movies". If the answer is in any form "Yes", wether you were around when they were first released or it's something you have discovered at a later date then you owe it to yourself to play this brilliant gem of a point 'n click adventure.
It's the closest we're ever going to get to a 4th movie. With a plot taking place after the third movie (orginal writer Bob Gale consulting on the story)  and original cast members Christopher Lloyd (Doc), Claudia Wells (Jennifer) returning to voice their characters while a brilliant A.J. Locascio preforms a Marty that's virtualy indistinguishable from Michael. J. Fox (who does return to perform a small part in the final episode). Previously I stated that Thomas. F. Wilson returns as Biff Tannen, however this is only true for the 30th anniversary edition released for consoles.
+ Epic continuation of a movie classic
+ Great variation in puzzle difficulty
+ Amazing voice cast
+ That music!
- A little unwieldy with 5 separate installs/playtimes for the 5 episodes. Thankfully Telltale abandonded this model in later products.
Veridict: If point 'n click adventures are your thing treat yourself to this at the next suitable sale. The short playtime of the episodes and the limited replayability makes it a little hard to justify paying full price for a 5 year old game, even if it's good.

This game came out in 2011. Can't believe it's been that long already! It would be silly of me to make assumptions, but what the hey ... it's fun :) I'm willing to bet that Back to the Future: The Game is what set the precedence for the success of The Walking Dead and then later The Wolf Among Us. It's as clear as seeing the connection between Call of Juarez: The Cartel being a precedence for Dead Island.
I haven't played the CSI series from TellTale Games, but I remember a friend speaking highly of it to me one day whilst we were travelling to Uni. My gut feeling tells me that would have contained the ground work of the TellTale Tool (game engine), enhanced over the years.
Back to the Future: The Game is more akin to a true point and click adventure. There are triggers embedded within dialogue that progress the story as opposed to The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us, in which selecting dialogue has no effect other than customising the story to the player's liking. I mean, there were some portions like that, but it was quite impassive. And your choices in one episode will not be carried to any other episodes.
The gameplay is quite challenging in figuring out what to do next. Sometimes there are tiny interactive hotspots on the screen that you never think about clicking on (like a small switch), other times you have to figure out which item in your inventory that you must use on an interactive hotspot.
Luckily there is a pretty cool system that gives you hints bit by bit and only when you want them. I found myself using an average of 3 hints for each episode (mainly out of impatience). If this were the early 90's, this would be the type of game that you'd get stuck on for a day and try to figure it out by asking friends at school, lol.
The story in Back to the Future: The Game was actually kind of painful. Each episode was about fixing Marty's broken 1986 reality after accidently altering an event amongst characters back in 1931. The annoying feeling is the same thing you feel when watching Back to the Future 2 and Biff Tannen owns everything. But there are also hilarious moments in the game. It's very up and down. Some parts in some episodes you'd rate 90/100 and other parts you'd give as low as 40/100. If I had to give an aggregate score, I'd probably rate the entire game 68/100.
For the die hard fans, there are lots of cameos and parodies made via dialogue and recognisable 3d model objects. This may sound lame ... but this game is very Back to the Futureish and wouldn't be so if there wern't all these cameo's like a guy yelling, "Hey! He just took that guy's wallet! I think he took his wallet."
In conclusion (and please don't hate me peeps), but this game really ain't worth $5USD on special. I remember around the same year this game called L.A Noir was released. In my opinion that game whilst being open-world ... was very much an advance point and click adventure as well. Shortly after, L.A Noir hit about $3.75USD. But the point is, it was pretty damn advance compared to Back to the Future: The Game, engine-wise ... which did seem unfinished somewhat ... I mean invisible walls ... really? Even each episode (1-5) was released as a separate game download causing you each time to configure things like screen resolution.

REVIEWS DONE QUICK BY MAX TURBO
- Why should you get this?: It's now a classic in the "weaponless horror" subgenre of horror games. Highly atmospheric and decently scary. The graphics still hold up surprisingly well as they were focused on the artistic experience rather than photorealism. The story is an intriguing mystery with Lovecraftian influences all over it.
- Why shouldn't you get this?: You're easily scared or dislike tense, slow games. You're going to be doing a lot of sneaking around and hiding in cupboards. You also have no ability to fight back against the monsters, so if you don't like feeling helpless, this isn't for you.
- Did Max like this?: Yes, even though I didn't find it as outright terrifying as many other people did. I think the atmosphere that Amnesia created was phenomenal, and it's fun (or as fun as Cthulhu-esque madness can be) to see where the story takes you.
- Similar games to check out: Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, SOMA

Let me just start with this: I know that the plot is incredibly farfetched from Ancient Greek Mythology in the sense that the gods could not just be killed by a mortal.  As a student of Ancient Greek litterature and mythology, this is a bit "out there" in that respect.  That being said, in every other respect I can think of, the game was spot on.  More than spot on, in fact.  The little tablets with ancient translations were incredible.  The names of the weapons were all in correct Greek spelling.  I was truly impressed with the detail that was put into the game.  Both the mythological and historical accuracy were amazing.
Moving on the graphics: I was a huge fan.  In creating a platformer, I know that there are a lot of options for styles of the visuals.  The choice of Ancient Greek art style was genius.  It puts the gamer right in Ancient Greece.  This art is the same as that on greek pottery.  Once again, an awesome detail that really made the game that much better.
Don't worry, I am certainly not going to overlook the gameplay.  It was a blast.  I was impressed with the combat in the sense that you have to judge your enemies next attck and there are so many possibilities to destroy your adversary.  The designers managed to make each stage tailored for that god, leading to underwater bouts, chases on horseback, and tricky mazes.  These all integrated combat with unique foes.
In addition, your practically endless arsenal of creative Greek weapons and shields makes sure that each fight is interesting.  Once again, many of these weapons are found in ancient Greek culture, but many new weapons were created based on stories myths.  Discovering these weapons is really cool as you find more specialty items.
This game is a must-have for everyone (especially for any of you classics students like me!)

NOTE: this review is written by a person who doesn't have any sentiments for Rayman having never played original Rayman titles on PS/PS2.
i did, however, play previous Rayman game, Origins, and it was great. truly, a 5-star platforming experience. when i found out that there is a sequel on the way, i was all over it.
i was playing on the launch day already, in fact, the two of us were. it's a great title to have fun while playing with family or friends and i highly recommend.
(pros marked with '+', cons with '-')
+ GRAPHICS.
gorgeous, simply gorgeous. it was hella hard to beat the look of Rayman Origins, but Legends managed to do it. what's amazing too, it's that it has considerably low requirements for what it is, i play it on Intel HD Graphics completely fine.
+ CONTROLS.
works wonderfully, as you would expect from a game that has pretty difficult time attack levels.
+ LEVEL DESIGN.
platforming is amazing, it's tons more fun to do local co-op in this one. fighting is easy, but then again enemies aren't supposed to challenged you, they're rather obstacles in this game, similarly to barricades.
my only gripe with level design is time attack/rush levels in co-op - the player who is slightly faster will always activate some events that lead to another player dying, at least we couldn't find a way around it. maybe it just requires being in complete sync, hehe.
+ SOUND/MUSIC.
music by itself is amazing. it's quite different from Rayman Origins, which had also had a stellar soundtrack, but while the first one was cutesy pitched-up singing, in Legends we platform to cinematic/orchestral top-notch quality music.
special mention: musical levels are best thing to happen to platforming in a good while. Castle Rock is the best level in any platformer i ever played.
+ CONTENT.
there's quite a lot to do.
collect 700 teensies - and it is pretty fun to do it. main levels have 8 (6 scattered across the level, 2 found in special puzzle rooms) in them, with time attack/rush/boss levels each having 3.
collecting lums net you lottery tickets, which are a fun side activity - they unlock collectable creatures and also remastered levels from the previous Rayman game, Origins. yes, they are gated between the grind, as in you have to collect enough lums in each available level to get a ticket to get a chance to unlock a level, but without trying to get a maximum rating we easily unlocked more than 16 remastered levels by simply beating the levels.
5 colourful words, each having two additional character unlocks, a boss level and a musical level. 6 world, as a bonus one, contains remixed musical levels. strangely enough, those are quite nauseating to play because of the fish-eye effect.
there are lots of other unlockable characters as well.
+ DIFFICULTY CURVE.
Origins had one very annoying feature, or rather, lack of one. proper checkpoint system. often you had to redo way too long sections of the level, especially, if you missed a Teenie, and that was one of the reasons we couldn't finish all levels from it. i feel like Rayman Legends, while easier overall, is a good balanced game, and much, much less rage-inducing that it's predecessor.
- STEAM INTEGRATION.
yes, that is a con for me.
i'd have loved getting achievements from this game. i'd love trading cards and background art for my profile from this game. i think workshop could have been pretty wonderful too, you know how many amazing talented people are there in the mod community.
i must mention the uPlay thing. i hate being forced to use their DRM on top of Steam. it's unnecessary. and i'm never going to spend money on a platform, that is trying to force itself on me. i bypassed uPlay requirement in my own version, so i'm missing out on the leaderboards, but so be it. i don't consider this to be a fair requirement to begin with.
- MINOR PORT SYNDROM.
well, it was originally conceived for Wii U, only later brought to other platforms.
this is not a major problem, trust me. the thing is. Murphy levels, which are based on QTEs and moving certain level props as you progress through them were originally controlled with special controller Wii U has. instead, in the port we control Murphy with a button push ('Y' on XBOX controller). sometimes he's focusing on the wrong platform depending on which player is ahead, and that can cause problems for players to progress at a slightly different pace.
that's not too bad, but it could be better, simple as that.
to sum up, it still is an amazing experience, despite the uPlay DRM inconviniences. i highly recommend it, this is a great, family-friendly, couch co-op experience that will net you many hours of enjoyment.

THERE WILL BE MILD SPOILERS
First off, I loved Bastion and Transistor to bits, so I was really looking forward to another Supergiant game. I've played through each of them multiple times, and was looking forward to more of the deep combat complexity that showed up in the prior games. With Pyre I played it to completion, and it was ok, but I don't recommend it.
The storyline is functional, but it doesn't feel like the writers did anything to make it more interesting than just having a goal and slogging through 10 hours of gameplay to get to the end. I was fond of the characters, one and all, and I was a bit sad when the first one left. After that it was both clear that the rest of the game was to give them up one after another, and that is what they wanted, so there was no conflict or interest in the action.
Combat-wise, there was really no reason to care about one character over another. You have the fast ones, the medium ones and the slow ones, and there's not a ton of reason to care for one over another. Their abilities make them unique-ish, but the same strategies work across everyone of a similar speed. As such, there's no need to get attached to your "best fighter" because there is no such thing. The speed of combat and the softness of the controls combined with a bit of stickyness on the edges of barriers made it more important to stick with simpler strategies. I did appreciate that fighters not in a match got a boost to future xp gains, as it did make it much easier to keep people balanced. However, on the default difficulty I was able to max out all characters level without ever needing the "Titan Stars" (Pyre's version of the challenge/xp boost mechanic seen in both Bastion and Transistor.
The combat was the thing that kept this feeling like a slog for all 10 hours. You get minimal variation in your 8 fighters, and you're fighting 8 classes of enemies exactly modeled on your own fighters, so there's never until the last fight or two anything of interest to change things up. You go back to the same areas repeatedly to fight the same teams again to advance the plot some more, but you're always fighting the same folks that you trounced before, just with higher stat numbers and a new passive ability that changes things very little.
The abilities and equipment also rarely felt consequential. The bonuses are often quite small and rarely change the basic nature of the situation. "Oh! Now my shotgun blast is wider! How amazing!" Compared to Transistor's deep ability system with remarkable changes depending on your layout, the variations and upgrades are flat and uninteresting.
Replayability really depends on how much you want to play another 10 hours of it to get another round of "Here's where they are now" as a text dump at the end of the game. Who escapes to the surface can be endlessly variable, with presumably a huge number of potential results. There is NO WAY I'm playing through another 10 hours of flat combat and long unskippable voiceovers to find out that things went slightly different if I saved a different set.
I played it to the end. I don't recommend anyone else do so. If you want to feel how it goes, buy it and play the first combat. Then uninstall it and get your money back. You'll get 90% of the fun I got out of it, and you'll save 10 hours and $20.

First, due to the overwhelming amount of reviews stating so it is important to state this warning to all people seeking to play this game.
I would still heavily recommend this game as i found it quite enjoyable but for those that are looking for what some might consider "Supgergiantgames" style of gameplay this is not it.
What Pyre is however is a visual novel/sportsball game with a somewhat odd execution on all of it. The game can be simply broken down into three sections
- Sportsball
This is the core of the game and I would say is its best aspect, simply put if you enjoy your first ritual (sportsball game) then you will probably enjoy all of the others to varying different degrees. How this mode works is that each player picks three different characters each one with their own skills, pros and cons. You can only move one at a time but can freely switch between any of them and your goal is to pick up and move a celestial orb into the enemies pyre (goal). The entire time your characters exude each individually a radial aura which if the enemy touches it causes them to be eliminated for a few seconds allowing you to get closer to their pyre. Picking up the celestial orb causes you to lose your aura which is where most of the difficulty stems from. There are other abilities such as being able to cast your aura forth as a wave but this changes on a per character basis.
Overall this core mechanic which you will be playing a lot of is rather fun if not a bit too easy, until you get access to optional difficulty options which give the enemy a heavy upper hand you probably will not be challenged to much even on the hardest difficulty setting. However again it should not be understated, even towards the end of the game (near 7 hours in) i did not grow tired of the sportsball and i will most definately be playing it more with friends as it simply is a good time.
- Story content
As one might expect from Supergiant games you have a really rather interesting setting with a rather straightforward story. Where bastion was a ruined world you were trying to reconstruct and Transistor was the resurection of a ruined city, Pyre is about your band of exiles called the "nightwings" who through your guidance as the "reader" will absolve them of their crimes and allow them to return to civilization. As with previous Supergiant games there is more too this than the simple footnotes but this is the gist of the story. Sadly where this falls flat is in several areas, for instance with Bastion the worldbuilding was given through narration which did not hinder the speed of the game. However, with this game you are presented with a tome which slowly gets filled as you traverse the world and sadly unless you are willing to read it you won't know the lore of the world. Even then, knowing the lore of the world is rather pointless as almost none of the ancient structures you pass by have any importance in the actual story. They simply exist in my opinion for being striking visuals and nothing more. Secondly after about the 4th or perhaps the 5th hour of the game i was still heavily invested in the overall plan to get my exiles absolved but the game constantly insisted upon one event being extremely important yet with it constantly pressing the matter it made me care all the less for it.
Overall the story is straight forward and altough it does lack some meat on its bones I would say that it at the very least it ends satisfyingly if not in a slightly expected way.
- Narrative content
Between your rites and the characters giving their story expositions you will have random little events, giving you a chance to explore your nightwings motivations, aspirations and previous struggles in life. These were what mainly drew me into the game as the characters themselves are all rather interesting in their owns ways each one having a clear reason as to why they would want to return to the commonwealth and why they set about their journeys. However here again the execution is somewhat mixed. You have a huge oppertunity to lose out on a lot of the individual characters dialogue options and interactions as the events themselves happen at set times and there is only so much time for each character to tell you their lifes story. Along with this there are sometimes pressing matters that in universe never get approached until a few days later, which strikes me as odd and took me somewhat out of the experience when you are talking about such extremely important matters as getting out of exile or talking of a lost love. Along with this, sometimes the dialogue can be a little basic and could have done with more refinement.
However, I don't want to sell this any short without getting into spoilers a lot of the interactions you will have in this game will be at the very least entertaining or interesting as some characters are in shades of grey and you learn that perhaps there is more to them than you previously though and to a certain point you might not want them unexiled simply because you wish to hear more about their story.
Overall supergiant games made a really rather nifty little package with charming characters, a focused story and a great and enjoyable core gameplay loop cut short only because of how tedius it might become near the end game and because of their lack of execution of making the lore of the world actually important.

Video Review Here:
The video covers more in detail the various issues I have with the game.
There is too much to say on how this game is done wrong. If you ignore the launch issues, progression loss, and various bugs, you still have a very unbalanced game. I know that Asymmetric gaming is meant to be that way but this takes it to a whole new level. Jason is beyond powerful and the only way to defeat him and survive is pure luck. You, as a counselor, rely on if items spawn in convenient locations. Otherwise a decent Jason will put an end to all survivors in a matter of moments.
Counselors are capable of using Stealth, Combat, and Speed to counter Jason. However, Jason has tools to stop all of that as well. Stealth is ignored through the fear mechanic as no matter how much composure you have, your character will become fearful at some point giving off your location to Jason. Combat is pointless since Jason can just grab you which will execute you instantly leading to your death. Speed is fancy and all but completely useless when Jason can teleport directly next to you and proceed to grab you into instant death.
So far the only times I’ve ever escaped was a series of lucky events such as Cops being called early and Jason was only ever to kill a few counselors due to a very low time limit, or Jason lacked the knowledge on how to use basic Jason abilities and I was able to sneak out.
As Jason the game is immensely fun if not at times a little boring for how easy it can be to play Jason. Playing Jason is not your choice either. You’re given a 1 out of 8 chance to randomly be selected as the game loads to play as Jason. I’ve gone up to 40 games in a row without being able to play as Jason making that grind for Jason very frustrating as teammates can ultimately lead to your demise.
The game has a ton of promise and the mechanics feel that they could work properly with a few tweaks to what Jason is capable of doing. The game would be very solid if they would tone him down and make sure Counselors can actually do something that matters rather than Relying on Repair and Composure stat to get through the game. Half of the game’s mechanics are useless simply because Jason is so powerful. Also yes I get it, he should be powerful, but there is a difference between powerful and broken. He is currently broken. The game is currently in a state that can get dull without friends. A huge price tag of $40 is not justified on this game.

TL;DR: When playing this game, 80% of your time (if not more, depending on how fast you read and understand text) will be spend reading TEXT. Yeap, simply reading text, no voices, no moving characters, no fighting, no gameplay. Juuust reading text for 80% of your time.
I expect that many people getting this game are not aware what a visual novel is, since it has absolutely 0 connection with SuperGiant Games (SGG). A visual novel is not a game - it is a novel. The only aspect of visual novels is telling a good story through **text** and nice visuals and artstyle. There is almost no interaction by the player besides choosing what to "say", which most of the time has no impact (this is true for Pyre; your choices have no impact).
This means that for 80% of your time spend in Pyre, you will be reading text, without hearing any VOICE to narrate this. This is a big difference from the previous 2 titles, where almost your every move was narrated by a VOICE. I disliked that heavily.
Furthermore, the small amout of time (10-20% at most) you spend during actual gameplay (performing these Rites) is completely without impact for the story: Whether you win or lose makes no difference whatsoever; you only have to win the final battle of each "Cycle" (meaning, you only have to win 1 every 5 battles to have any impact on the story). In addition, this impact on the story you have is simply a progression bar going from 50% to 60%. Holy **** come on, this is pathetic.
In conclusion, this title was such a humongous letdown from SGG. Of course the story, art and music are amazing, as expected. But they are focused waaaaay too much on these. When you play the game you actually want to play a game, not read text! It would be much better if the game revolved around the Rites, instead of being a visual novel. Even though many people found the Rites trivial, if SGG focused there it could become something good!
The advantages of the game (e.g. how well each character is individual etc.) are well stated by other positive reviews, so I don't see the need to write them here. Lastly, a benefit is that this game is only 20 euros. This can be considered cheap, but ONLY if you actually enjoy reading text when playing a video game. Books are better at this, last time I checked.
EDIT: SPOILER AHEAD------------

Pyre is, in my opinion, the best game Supergiant has developed to date. Unlike their previous work, Pyre has a huge cast of unique and likable characters brimming with personality and individual motives. The story itself feels epic is incredibly engaging.
Although, as you can see from other reviews, there is quite a bit of people that don't share my enthusiasm. It should be noted that Pyre is Supergiant's riskiest and most ambitious project to date. The gameplay is vastly different from Transistor and Bastion. Most of the game you're just reading and making decisions, and between these decisions you play Rites. I personally found a lot of enjoyment out of the rites. I think they're fun and often I'm at the edge of my seat with my heart beating through my chest in worry that I might lose. If you lose, the game continues, and depending on which rites you win or lose, it effects how the story progresses and how it ends.
I understand if buying it is a risk, but if you're looking for an engaging story, brilliant characters, and a truly unique RPG experience, I suggest you give it a try. I do find the items to be quite useless, but I don't care; if I'm this invested in a game, it deserves my recommendation.

Have you ever thought of yourself as a cold blooded killer focused on your mission to eradicate the Nazi scourge infecting 1940’s France? Then this is the game for you
This game is a great third person action/stealth game with a fairly good combat system. The game is full of tense moments and tight confined spaces. You can approach almost every situation by either gunning down everything that breathes (you will die quickly) or you can sneak around in the shadows and strike decisively and killing indiscriminately before fading away leaving the remaining Nazi’s to wonder who you will butcher next. Also with the addition of Morphine mode you become indestructible and storm through everyone that stands in your way.
The story, based rather loosely on real life events, is sparse but enjoyable, not everything has to be massively in depth but here is enough going on to keep you interested and playing. It’s pretty standard for a world war two spy setting, your job is to defeat bag guys and gain intel. It does take place in retrospective, you see what’s going to happen but it’s the getting there that’s interesting. The characters themselves though are rather two dimensional to be honest, it’s hard to pin down why but I didn’t feel particularly connected to Violette, even when the story develops.
Pick this game up and enjoy the ride, especially if it’s on sale. The game has not aged amazingly and there were several glitches, none of which game breaking. However I had a good time with it right up to the end before the final mission changed everything. So as with a lot of games from this era I would recommend playing it but don’t feel the need to finish it.
Have fun ^_^

is the kind of experience in which its only downfall is that, when playing for the second time, it won't hit you as it did at the very first. But even so, you will never forget that mix of opposing feelings, the wondering of having accomplished or not what you strove for all along the game.
The ambientation is one of the best ever. It is really immersive, rich and daunting, keeping you tense and aware of your surroundings, with well elaborated puzzles that don't get in the way, but that actually fells like part of the world, accompanied by believable characters, and with such great voice acting that you simply dive deep in the feelings of living in such an unsettling world, of going through such unsettling situations.
The gameplay surely doesn't bring anything new, especially for those who played other
titles. If you're not familiar to them, it would basically feel like a walking simulator if it were not for the fact that you are not alone and that you are vulnerable. You can't fight back the creatures that live in the bottom this ocean. You have to hide, keep yourself in dark corners where you can't be seen, and don't, no matter what, look at them.
But it is the story that SOMA tells us that makes it unique. Unfolding with its puzzles, characters and the vulnerability you're in, it is going to make you question things up to even the definition of what is being human, and is surely going to linger in the back of your thoughts after several days you played it, mostly due to its great, bittersweet ending.
In my particular opinion SOMA is what horror games should be and I just can't wait to see what else Frictional Games is going to came up with.

TL;DR:  Very well written game that makes you think and challenges your perceptions. Mechanics and visuals are a little clunky and dated, but the story and writing are still totally worth it. Get the restored content mod.
Oh boy, here we go. KotOR II is probably my favorite game of all time. Boom. There it is. Mechanically and visually speaking, this game has not aged very well. The character models aren't great, the animations are pretty ugly, the environments are samey and a little boring, and the combat is at best pretty alright and at worst totally annoying. Coming into this game from a more modern RPG will take some getting used to.  Now, if you've played the first KotOR, know that the mechanics here are just straight-up an improvement on that game in every way. More options, more party members, more interesting weapons, more feats, force powers, prestige classes, etc.  So that's all the negatives, and a brief comparison to what came before, now let's get into why this game is my favorite.  I'm going to try to avoid specific plot-related spoilers, but I do recommend going into this game knowing as little about it as possible.
KotOR II makes you think.  It gets into your head and makes you ponder your pre-conceived notions of the Star Wars universe and our own universe as well.  I have never seen any other Star Wars-branded media go so deeply into what the Force is, how it works, what it feels like, and why it may not be entirely benevolent. And even though "WAR" is in the title of the darn thing, I've never had a Star Wars movie really make me think about real-world war as much as this game has. As much as I love Star Wars, its movies and games and novels and whatnot tend to be a little shallow.  That's fine, nothing wrong with that, it started as a fun fantastical sci-fi blockbuster, who says it has to be a deep discussion on war and its effects on the people involved?  Nobody probably.  Nevertheless, here we have this game.  Anyway, as you make your way through this game, going from planet to planet on your mission, you encounter NPCs and party members along the way.  These people have all been affected by the titular Wars of the game: the Mandalorian War and the Jedi Civil War, galaxy-spanning conflicts that touched every world from the core to the rim, and changed these people.
You'll encounter soldiers from all sides, veterans, mercenaries, widows, orphans, profiteers, relief workers, tyrants, and monsters.  Through interacting with these people, and hearing their side of the bloody story, you'll get a living, breathing picture of what such a large-scale war would look like.  And all of this I'm saying now I only picked up on in my most recent playthrough.  Every time I go through this game, I get something different.  And that's not because there are a huge ton of choices to make (there are a decent amount, and they change a bit of what happens, not the best I've seen, but better than some), but because the writing is so damn DENSE and has so much to say.  Your party members in this title may not be as immediately likable as other titles, like KotOR I or the Mass Effect series, but they are deep, realistic, and have experiences outside the player character.  They are probably some of the best written characters in a game like this that I've ever played. They have a lot to say about philosophy, and each one will give you different insight into how the world (theirs AND ours) works.
This game won't be for everyone, and I'm perfectly aware of that.  If you're looking for a game that will make you think, and don't mind listening to a TON of wonderfully written dialogue, pick this one up.
Oh, and definitely, DEFINITELY play with the Restored Content Mod. It should be in the workshop, it fixes a lot of bugs and restores a lot of good content that got cut in this game's rough release.

A Telltale game that's more of an adventure game than an interactive story, somewhere between their Sam & Max stuff and what they're churning out now. Marty controls with WASD and the emphasis is on puzzle solving rather than "choice & consequence". The lion's share of the game takes place in the Prohibition era with jaunts Back to the Future (generally to see what sorts of dystopia's you've created) and into the wild west ala the third movie.
It does a pretty decent job of capturing the feel of the movies and does a much better job of presenting the player with challenges than the current Telltale products do. The puzzles vary in difficulty from ones that you can breeze right through to some that will actually hold you up for quite a bit, but there's a hint system you can use if you get frustrated. There's also content you can miss, so be sure to search areas thoroughly.
Overall I found it to be a pretty solid puzzle game and would recommend it to fans of the genre, the franchise, and/or the developer. It ends of somewhat interesting cliff-hanger too, so I hope it gets a sequel someday.
Edit: Forgot to mention, it takes up five seperate entries in your Steam library. Pretty annoying.
