This was the second time I played Amnesia: The Dark Descent and I must say it was almost as much fun as it was when I first did, not knowing anything about the amazing story. I now had the luxury to pay attention to the smallest details, submerge into it and finish the additional story - Justine and of course to explore every little corner and unlock the achievements (most people played the game when there were none, as these were added later). So now it's the second time I'm amazed by how good and well put together this game is.
We play as Daniel, a man who awakens in a huge castle in Brennenburg, Prussia (Germany) with no memory whatsoever. No wonder: as we find out from a note (which he wrote to himself), he intentionally drank a powerful potion that caused the amnesia he suffers from. The note also tells him that he must kill Alexander, the baron residing in the castle.
As we progress in the game, we gradually learn - along with Daniel - of his past and the reasons why he decided to forget everything about himself. And as if the menacing castle (which trembles from time to time) and the horrible monsters that roam its hallways weren't enough, there's a sinister entity stalking our hero which must be connected to the blood red goo that seem to appear all over the castle...
The lore built around the game is exemplary. Most of the mentioned characters we won't be able to meet in the game, yet the written texts do a great job introducing them successfuly to us. I've been a huge fan of this type of storytelling ever since System Shock 2. I also loved some small elements, such as how the game tried to correlate a key artifact with the globus cruciger held by medieval european kings.
The first thing we notice in the inventory screen is that Daniel has a sanity meter (a bit like in Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth), below his health. Unfortunately he is extremely easy to scare, so his sanity will evaporate from basically everything: looking at monsters, disturbing images, bones or hearing loud noises, even staying in the dark for too long. Yes, darkness, while it could be our ally it's also our enemy: if we hide from monsters for too long in the dark, we can get spooked. When this occurs we'll experience distorting visual effects, the screen blurs, Daniel starts to gnash his teeth and see imaginary things. This can apply to monsters as well at some locations and these imaginary monsters can actually hurt us. At extremely low sanity we can also slow down or even fall unconscious (which is strangely not as horrible as it may sound). Either way, low sanity is not a good thing and we should stay in the light when there are no monsters around. Our sanity can be replenished by solving puzzles or leaving main areas.
The second thing is that we are completely unarmed. I usually find this a cheap method of making a game scarier by depriving the player of weapons, but in Amnesia it seems somewhat justified and I actually enjoyed it: being defenseless fits well to the tone of the game.
Puzzles represent a dominant part of the game. While there aren't many items we can collect (tinderboxes we can light candles with, oil we can use for our lamp and healing items) most of the puzzles make great use of the physics (much like in Tresspasser or Half-Life 2) the game's engine utilizes (also present in Frictional Games' previous games, the Penumbra series). The quest items are also not numerous but some of them can be used several times (prepare for the most bizzare uses ever) and the game will always tell us whether the item has any function in that exact location or not, so we can't screw up permanently (by filling up a bucket with oil instead of water for example). The physics also requires us to interact the doors, levers, valves and drawers manually, so instead of clicking on them, we have to pull or rotate them by moving our mouse. It's a really nice touch, but it can also be a pain during chase sequences when we have to do something within a given amount of time.
The other things we are going to collect are notes, letters and diaries, written either by Daniel, Alexander or any of the supporting characters of the game. They are necessary to understand the story, not to mention they usually contain the solution to some of the game's more complex puzzles and the key to experience the game's 4 different endings.
A problem I could mention here is that some locations must be visited in order for the full experience (we can miss some notes when the portion of the castle becomes unreachable later).
Strangely death is handled very liberally in the game. Usually when a monster kills us, we don't even have to reload, we'll just wake up in a random location in the area with all our stuff and progress preserved. In addition to that monsters are quite easy to avoid (especially once we learn their behaviours and patterns), most of them disappear completely if we lay low for a while (crouched). That being said, Amnesia requires little stealth, rather a quick and resolute jump behind an object, whenever we hear a monster approaching (they let out a pretty loud howl). Their arrival is scripted, so most of the time whenever we pick up an important quest related item, we can expect a monster to appear close by.
The game also contains and additional adventure (can be reached from the 'Settings Launcher') called Justine. It is related to the main story (both by some characters and the major theme - the Amnesia potion) and a bit more action-oriented. Interestingly, death here is final and once we fail we have to start over, since there's no save feature.
This one is quite short, but contains multiple endings as well and the story is almost as good as the one in the orginal, which I'm not going to spoil, but let's just say after having played Amnesia, we'll immediately know who Justine is and who's giving her instructions :)
The graphics is a bit dated, but still effective and by no means would I call it ugly. It has a certain distinctive look and can produce nice graphical effects, but these extra effects can cause minor slowdowns here and there. Make sure to turn off 'Imagetrail' in the options menu as it ruins the graphics, plus makes the game look choppy.
The dark, menacing, derelict castle makes a perfect location for a horror game and although it loses its charm on some occasion as we descend deep underground, it still features amazingly atmospheric and eerie environments. Some of the interiors are massive and I found myself looking into the seemingly bottomless abyss below several times. I loved the series of paintings and drawings adorning the walls, even though some of them were pretty disturbing (well, it's a horror game :)). There aren't many types of monsters in the game (one of them is invisible furthermore) but they are genuinely scary and I couldn't wish for better ones.
The sounds were equally good, but I did miss one thing: environmental audio. I loved the sounds of the monsters, the occasional tremblings in the castle but they could have been so much more with the proper use of surround sound.
Amnesia: The Dark Descent really is a huge step in the history of horror games. I could compare it to Alien: Isolation where I had to take breaks because of its depressive and dreadful nature. It really is a classic now and shouldn't be missing from any horror fan's library. And if it's there and you haven't played it yet, what are you waiting for?
PROS
+ excellent story told through notes
+ amazing horror atmosphere, creepy monsters
+ great physics-based puzzles and brain-teasers
+ detailed lore surrounding the main story
+ disturbing insanity effects
CONS
- lack of advanced surround sound
- Daniel is way too faint-hearted
RATING
9/10

is an action adventure platformer based on ancient Greek mythology.  The gods have turned their backs on humanity, and you play as Nikandreos, a mortal warrior who takes up arms against the gods in order to save mankind.  Choose your weapon and get your war-face on, because it's about to get bloody divine up in here!
++ Artwork
++ Level Design
++ Challenging Combat
+ Voice Acting
+ Music
- Combat Controls
- Inventory System
-- For starters, the artwork is amazing and really gives this game that ancient Greek mythological atmosphere!  It seriously amazed me the whole way through the game, because all of the different characters and monsters and maps kept bringing something new to the table.
Speaking of which, the level design was incredible.  Each level and location had it's own style and theme, not to mention it's own challenges and puzzles and combat strategies.  Not once did I feel bored or think to myself, "Oh, this again...."  because
keeps mixing it up and throwing something new at you every time you turn around.
As for combat, I found it to be quite a challenge, especially in the beginning when it took some getting used to.  Enemies are really good at dodging and blocking your attacks and putting themselves in great positions to attack you.  You'll need to master blocking and rolling, but also how to press an attack.  There are so many different weapons and fighting with each one can be a completely different experience.  For example, keep your distance and be sure to hit the enemy with the point end of the spear, not the shaft.  Use maces and clubs to break shields faster.  Hit enemies in the legs to take them to the ground, and use the momentum of a jumping attack to do more damage.  All these things matter!  Simply diving into the fray and mashing buttons won't be very effective.  In fact, it's more than likely going to get you killed!
After all of that, it's the voice acting and music that breathes life into
, making the game that much more immersive and exciting.
-- Admittedly, the first hour or so of the game was a bit of a struggle for me, thanks to the controls, which were somewhat difficult to master.  This made combat even more challenging too, at least early on in the game.  There was a point near the beginning when I questioned whether or not this purchase was a good one.  If you ever feel the same way, take a deep breath, and keep trying, because it won't take too long before you're a force to be reckoned with!
Sort of related to combat controls is the downside of the inventory system.  As I mentioned earlier, there are a ton of weapons to choose from in the game, which means there's a lot to cycle through when you're changing weapons.  And it's an even bigger pain in the middle of battle.  Honestly, I'm not sure how it could have been done any better, but you do learn to plan ahead (where you can), selecting your main melee weapon, ranged weapon, potion, etc, before charging into battle rather than after it starts.  Still, it's a constant struggle regardless.
--  There's not much debate to be made here.  I'm extremely pleased with the game and even the early struggle with the controls can't come close to changing that.  If you are thinking about trying the game out, DO IT.
is a real gem, and I highly recommend it!

Apotheon is an imperfect delight. The major selling point to this 2D action game is its unique and gorgeous art style, at all times evoking an epic tale, painted in loving strokes on ancient masonry. It's like nothing I've seen before, and it elevates this game well above the clumsy inventory or irritating weapon degradation that could have dragged it down.
The boss fights are many and varied, which means some are poorly designed♥♥♥♥♥♥ while the creative mechanics of others shine, making for tense memorable battles where one can prevail through skill and wit.
While the deicidal plot is predictable (and awfully similar to God of War i'm told), all the little details add up to a very authentic feeling of whimsical brutality that characterizes greek mythology. Much like a video game's protagonist, Greek heroes would leave a path of carnage littered with slain foes and fools too weak, slow, or dull to follow the hero's path. Apotheon is full of moments that look and feel worthy of a hero's tale.

There are many cartoony indie side-scrollers available on Steam, most costing under $15, so $40 for Rayman Legends may seem steep. However, this game is much bigger and more detailed than most of the indie titles. The game appears to be bigger than its predecessor, Rayman Origins, as well. There are 60 main stages, "Back To Origins" levels re-playing some Origins levels, rotating daily and weekly challenges, and more little stuff. All of that adds up to a lot of gameplay, especially considering you'll want to go re-play stages multiple times to get the fastest time, or collect all the things.
Speaking of which, this game is a collector's paradise. Every corner of the game is littered with collectable items, which the game constantly tallies and rewards you with new levels and characters. There are a lot more characters in Legends than there were in Origins, and they all have their own amusing animations.
This game is highly polished on every level. From the character animations, to the visual style, to the music, this game is a joy to behold, unless you're only interested in the brown-grey wash gritty shooters. In a way the game is visually old-school, in that every level has a theme(swamp, fire, etc.), but it's always interesting to see new scenery, and it's all beautifully drawn. I can't tell for certain, but I'm pretty sure the soundrack is recorded with a live orchestra. The resulting sound appropriately zany, but rich and authentic at the same time. Again, this is on a level beyond what an indie side-scroller can offer.
The gameplay is fairly old-school as well, in good ways and bad. While the simple, classic controls never seem to get old, the game can also be very demanding, requiring split-second precision. If you want to get a perfect run through a stage you pretty much have to retry and retry, and basically memorize every button press, or every attack in a boss fight. While it can be frustrating, there are relatively few moments where you're bottlenecked; you don't have to grind unless you're a perfectionist.
I was happy to get the game for $20 during the holiday sale, and I think the game is absolutely worth it at that price. Is it worth $40, though? I'm inclined to say yes, simply because of the amount of content and the level of polish throughout. This is a full-size game, and it comes at a full-size price. If you can get it at a discount it starts to be a great deal.

Pyre boasts a fantastically realized setting and an engaging, emotional storyline featuring rich, multi-dimensional characters, and a many, many branching narrative (I can't say with certainty how much the player's choices impact the end result because I haven't played it through more than once, but I will say that after getting to the end, it certainly *feels* like the player's actions have a huge impact, which is enough for me). If you enjoy a good story, augmented by the amazingly expressive music we're accustomed to from SGG games, and don't mind a lot of reading, you will not be disappointed in Pyre.
Be aware, however, that the bulk of the game is spent on storytelling. This seems to be offputting to some; the trailer is somewhat misleading in this regard, as it spends about 80% of the duration showcasing the "combat" sequences (known as Rites within the game), whereas while playing, the Rites account for perhaps 5%-10% of the total experience.
Regarding the Rites, one of my favorite aspects of this game is that there is no 'Try, fail, reload, try, fail, reload' loop here. Whether you succeed or fail, the game continues, and the story adapts to accomodate the consequences of the outcome. This creates a very nice sense of tension when going into a pivotal encounter, as you're behoved to live with the outcome, be it good or bad.
Personally, I love a good story, particularly emotional ones. If a story makes me *feel* something strongly, whether it's happiness, grief, anger, fear, or any other emotion, I generally enjoy it, and in that regard, this game succeeds fantastically. If you don't enjoy reading, or value action over storytelling, this game may, sadly, not be for you. For everyone else, pick this one up, it's a winner.

First off, I'm disappointed that so many big reviews got this wrong and call it a sport game or basketball or even dodgeball game because this is nothing like a modern sport game.  It's more like a magical style capture the flag game with a isometric perspective.  During the "Rites" an orb appears in the middle, one person on your team can move at a time which is the same for the enemy team, you try to either take out the enemies with your abilities or take the orb to their base to reduce their flame until it goes out.  You can walk it in, fly it in, jump it in, and throw it in from a very short distance.
The rest of the game is a choose your own adventure decision based story that revolves around choices that affect how you power up and what character's stories you focus on.  That part is OK.  If you really like the characters and the story, you'll like that part.  The decisions might make you stop to think for a minute.  But the main story is straightforward and linear.
The gameplay part, the rites, I feel really mixed about.  They started out interesting, but quickly certain strategies become obvious and powering up certain characters can give them very abusive tools.  Luckily there are challenge options by way of Titan stars that open up that make the CPU go from a wet noodle to obnoxiously unfair - but the rewards are fairly meager and it's debatably if it's even worth activating the titan stars as opposed to just moving through the story.
The animation and music are top notch.  I like the "Voice" during the rites, but feel like it was a missed opportunity to not have voice acting for the other characters, the mumble-talk wasn't for me and made the characters seem cartoonish and distant (Tizo is an exception to that).
It's not as good as Bastion or Transistor as far as gameplay but the story is just as intriguing.
For me, this is a solid 8/10 game.  There were several disappointments, but the story, animation, and music make it a worthwhile experience.

I honestly don't understand why so many people are saying this is a bad game. And yeah, it's true that the log in system is absolute crap, and I did have to come up with a crazy username and password to get it to work. There also is a glitch at the server selection screen, where it'll freeze for a good 2-5 minutes (though I think it's been said that it only does this because of the abundance of people playing). Still, that is no good reason to give it a bad review.
I wouldn't pay the full $15 for it, but I'm satisfied with the $3 I spent. The graphics are pretty, the enemies are creepy, and it has a pretty great map. The combat, although not the best, is still pretty good. There is a decent selection of masks that you can choose from, something that I like a lot (mostly because I found a gnome mask within the first ten minutes of playing). It's a bit realistic as well, with the safe zones being, well, unsafe and getting raided by the Nether every now and then. There is also the factor of starving to death, which makes it so you have to keep searching for food.
Let's not forget the skill tree concept that is used. Each time you level your character, you're given a skill point to spend in one of six branches: guns, stamina, survival, strength, stealth, and melee. This is great, because maybe you're someone who enjoys brute force; you have an option of levelling that up. Or maybe you enjoy hiding in the shadows. Same deal, you can make your character good at that.
People are complaining that they got killed by another player. No duh! It's almost as if it's a PvP game! I mean, it does suck sometimes, like when get to level twenty or higher, with all of this good gear, only to get sniped in the head. But still, it's a PvP survival game, that's what happens. Shoot or be shot, yeah?
But yeah, all in all, the only reason I would say this game is bad is because of the server selection freeze, and also because there are items/poses/characters you have to pay real money for (which is dumb, considering most people already payed $15 for it). I definitetly would recommend to people who enjoy PvP and apocalyptic survival games, though only if it's on sale for $10 or less.

is the kind of experience in which its only downfall is that, when playing for the second time, it won't hit you as it did at the very first. But even so, you will never forget that mix of opposing feelings, the wondering of having accomplished or not what you strove for all along the game.
The ambientation is one of the best ever. It is really immersive, rich and daunting, keeping you tense and aware of your surroundings, with well elaborated puzzles that don't get in the way, but that actually fells like part of the world, accompanied by believable characters, and with such great voice acting that you simply dive deep in the feelings of living in such an unsettling world, of going through such unsettling situations.
The gameplay surely doesn't bring anything new, especially for those who played other
titles. If you're not familiar to them, it would basically feel like a walking simulator if it were not for the fact that you are not alone and that you are vulnerable. You can't fight back the creatures that live in the bottom this ocean. You have to hide, keep yourself in dark corners where you can't be seen, and don't, no matter what, look at them.
But it is the story that SOMA tells us that makes it unique. Unfolding with its puzzles, characters and the vulnerability you're in, it is going to make you question things up to even the definition of what is being human, and is surely going to linger in the back of your thoughts after several days you played it, mostly due to its great, bittersweet ending.
In my particular opinion SOMA is what horror games should be and I just can't wait to see what else Frictional Games is going to came up with.

*sigh* what to say.. this COULD of been one of the best Star Wars games I have ever played.. severely let done by corporate greed however.. this sequal to KOTOR was rushed out in time for xmas and it shows.. badly!! KOTOR was epic.. truly epic!! This sequal could of been so so soooo much more!! But unfinished story arks due to Lucas Arts pressuring the devs to get the game out quickly meant plots were unfinished (droid factory for one) and the ending.. the ending.. I won't spoil it for you but it just screams rushed and unfinished.. so many questions unanswered.. thankfully there is a community mod to try and "finish" the game off to how it should have been, if Lucas Arts hadn't demanded this game be rished out too quickly..
Is it a bad game? Definately not! It was very enjoyable!! And I do highly reccomend playing this AFTER you play the prequal KOTOR as the story does lead on from the first game (you control a different character some time after the events of the first game but still.. trust me.. you will thank me for playing the first game before this one). The shoddy ending and blatent "rushed" feel to this as you get firther and further into the game aside.. a highly enjoyable game! Take ont he role of a force sensitive individual and go your own way.. will you be a jedi.. or a Sith? Each party member reacts to your descisions and affects the story. Hook is a calm and short puzzle game that was developed by Maciej Targoni ,    Wojciech Wasiak and published by Rainbow Train. With it's simplistic art style, and easy to grip mechanics, Hook really is such a insightful puzzle game that most other puzzle games seem to miss.
Hook is one of them insightful and peaceful puzzle games that is relaxing to play and doesn't frustrate you throughout. This is what a puzzle game is meant to be like, the game itself challenges you in the way of cause and effect which brings you a different level of challenge as you play through the levels. Through the levels you play, you will need to prepare for the unexpected movement that may occur that you hadn't thought about or planned on that one thing moving. There are 50 levels in total, taking about an hour to and an hour and a half complete them all, I myself felt satisfied within completing each of the puzzles as I progressed through the game. The game does get more complex as you progress, as to be expected in almost every game, but it's difficulty curve is rather slow and steady.
The music in this game is very much why the game just seems to relaxing and enjoyable to play. Throughout playing the levels, you will endure the relaxing music to keep you calm and collective throughout the game.
The graphics for the game are simplistic, but not much else can really be said about that. It helps keep the player engaged and I feel like it also comes to play with the calm and relaxing part of the game as well.
+ A relaxing and insightful puzzle game
+ Addicting gameplay
+ Great price for the game
+ Simplistic Graphics
+ Calm and relaxing Music
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements
- Only 1 - 1.5 hours of gameplay (but was is expected for such a low priced game)
Hook is such a relaxing and peaceful puzzle game that most other puzzle games don't really have. The game's' graphics are simplistic which I think helps with the game being calm, as well as the music. It's addicting and is great for the price you are paying. Highly recommended for puzzle and non-puzzle gamers.

If it's ever $15 or less, get it, enjoy it and look forward to a potential sequel.

Hook is a minimalistic puzzle game that couldn't have used this style paired with the puzzle genre better. With a $1 price, it doesn't feel like it is over charging, so if you're looking for a cheap game, you can stop searching.
Hook does a great job in conveying how to play the game without having to have a set of 'tutorial' levels (or videos) or giving you text to read. As soon as you have the handle on a new control (such as turns), it puts in another control. I feel lke they introduced more controls the most effective way by having them feed off the previous one. The difficultly level progresses in a way that goes with your skill and sure, it may drive you crazy trying to get one piece out of a tangle of lines, but it does seem rewarding when you figure it out.
The only thing I have a problem with is the trading cards (and I have the game running right now trying to activate card drops). I know that Steam set a time limit as a way to combat refunding, but when Geometry Dash gave me a card in 16 minutes of gameplay while I got one in 2 hours and 40 minutes in Hook well... thats a problem. It takes aound 1-2 hours to complete, and I believe that should be the timeline the cards drop.
Either way, I recommend this game and suggest completing it, as the first 10 levels does not compare to the next 40. On a last note: I'd like to say that there are a lot of games that are overprice (or the game isn't worth the price based on multiple reasons) and Hook does not deserve being put in with those games.

Back to the Future: The Game is now over 5 years old. It was released in conjunction with the 25th anniversary of the first film. Now that the 30th anniversary is behind us, and 2015 came and left, can this game survive on its own merits?
As a "Back to the Future" game it hits all the right notes. References to the films aren't clustered too close together and surprise you when you least expect them. It feels more like "Back to the Future" than any other game that shared that title before. The characters are familiar and their portrayal in this game feels very authentic. In many ways this game feels like a genuine piece of the film's legacy that had been lost to the ages.
As a point and click adventure game it is a bit too simple. The puzzles seemed too easy at times and there were very few times when I needed to consult the in game hint box. Every puzzle has an obvious solution and the game's objective reminders guarantees that the player doesn't get too far off the path.
Simple though it is the game is fun and I would gladly reccommend it to any fan of the series.

I just want to make a quick review to express my enjoyement for this game. It's only been out for 14 days as of this review and I've already spent 56 hours playing. I'm just going to set out what I have to say as random points, hope it helps you out:
The price is high, yes, but the content is going to expand and become more and more worth the price. On top of that, the developpers actually listen to what the players are saying and are adapting the game as they can (check out the for honor subreddit).
People seem to complain about the gear but I find that it makes it fun. It's not pay to win since you actually have to level up to get high level gear, and collecting gear is a cool part to any competitive multiplayer game (I mean take a look at rocket league!) and I hope they keep adding more gear to the game in the future.
The game rewards skill, and I love that. The P2P connectivity that most of the community complains about (although it does have it's problems) allows for a surprisingly precise gameplay and is (most of the time) lag free. This helps with honing one's skill in the game. The truth is that in for honor, you have to GIT GUD! As much as in a dark souls, if not more when you consider that you're playing against humans who have a lot of different options at their disposition.
As for the story mode... It's not an AMAZING story, nor is the voice acting exceptional, but it's fun! Yeah sure, today we have high expectations with most games having prestigious writers working behind the scene in order to give the best possible experience, but for a multiplayer oriented game I think they did a good job in making something original and fun to play through.
There you have it, my short review. I know I probably sound biast when talking about the game but I thoroughly enjoy it and I wouldn't want to put myself in another position when talking about my personal experience. I feel that for honor does deserve better reviews than it's currently getting and I hope our community can keep expanding.

Being now around 5 hours into this game, I think I've played enough to share my opinion. I think this game is a disappointment if you directly compare it to SGG's other titles and you expected a direct sequel with similar mechanics to the first two. Yeah, you'd be right to say it doesn't accomplish the same things as Bastion and Transistor, but that shouldn't be the point. They didn't make this game advertising it as a sequel, and frankly, everyone writing negative reviews about this only has their own assumptions to blame for their disappointment. Now, on to the game.
At first, I was a bit hesitant to like this game playing through the first few rites, but something kept me playing. I slowly got more wrapped up in the story, and though it is told more clunkily (through text on screen as opposed to the narration of SGG's previous titles), it works in the context of the world. It took me the better part of today to place where I had seen a game with similar pacing (and why I liked it despite people harping on it for separating story and gameplay), but I finally realized that the way the game is laid out is very similar to Fire Emblem. The games are not the same by any stretch, but the same structure of story through dialogue in between strategic battles is definitely a commonality, and like Fire Emblem, this separation makes sense in the world's context. In this world, there will always be downtime between Rites, since there is travel and astral-body-alignment to account for. There will be dead time that the characters would naturally converse in.
Being where I am in the story now (no spoilers) has hooked me even more into playing. As I neared what I previously thought was the end, I realized this game still had way more to show me, and also that I need to seriously hone my skills if I want to reach my goal. That said, when this point is reached, the incentive to sit down and play for extended sessions decreases due to the nature of the game (you'll understand when you get there), so beware that trying to plow through this game would be extremely tedious. You definitely would be better off playing it in shorter chunks.
Pros:
Cons:
Ultimately, if you like other story-centric games like Undertale or OneShot, or tactical RPGs like Fire Emblem, I think you'd enjoy this game. If reading dialogue to consume a story isn't for you, or you want more seamless integration between story elements and gameplay, then I'd recommend sticking to SGG's other two titles. I personally don't mind, and while I would love to see that wonderful blend of elements again, I've enjoyed Pyre's story and mechanics enough to warrant its purchase.

An almost Souls-like experience, Apotheon follows Nikandreos, lead by Hera as he slaughters everyone on Olympus one by one, and sometimes house by house, eventually usurping Zues himself. Refuge or god, none are safe from Nikandreos' primal rage as he fights to avenge a quite literally god-forsaken humanity.  A suprisingly varied experience as brilliant in aesthetic as it is in satisfaction from start to finish. I do reccomend playing on the harder difficulty on your first playthrough to get the most out of this game. The lower difficulty leaves you with far too many resources and breathing room. You are killing gods after all, prove yourself worthy to walk upon the Olympian summit.
One thing to note about this game is that a lot of your learning is done in a heavily autodidactic fashion. Such little tidbits will follow. Semi spoiler alert relating to the specifics of combat.
1: Sweeping an enemies feet out will throw them into the air.
2: Hitting them in the head with your swing will do more damage.
3: When blocking, you need to aim your shield at the point of which the attack will impact with you. This is particularly needed in the final fight.
4: If you get into a fight with guards around the 'non-combat' areas, either run as far as you can and hide. (The top left of the screen shows you portraits of who you are in combat with, and will fade away if they lose you.) But if you choose to fight, make sure you don't let them blow their horns. They will summon more dudes to fight and can do this endlessly.
5: Middle mouse while blocking to do a shield smack, knocking people back and putting their guard down.
6: Stackable weapons durabilities are individual to that weapon. For example, if you have a spear in your hand it's durability isn't shared with the other 4 hidden on your person.
7: When breaking open stuff, if you have the time switch to your fist not to waste durability on weapons.
That's all that comes to mind right now just after finishing the game. I would love to see a similar style game but for Norse mythology instead of Greek. It would be brilliant. Absolutely reccomend this game for fans of souls games type combat.

Pyre boasts a fantastically realized setting and an engaging, emotional storyline featuring rich, multi-dimensional characters, and a many, many branching narrative (I can't say with certainty how much the player's choices impact the end result because I haven't played it through more than once, but I will say that after getting to the end, it certainly *feels* like the player's actions have a huge impact, which is enough for me). If you enjoy a good story, augmented by the amazingly expressive music we're accustomed to from SGG games, and don't mind a lot of reading, you will not be disappointed in Pyre.
Be aware, however, that the bulk of the game is spent on storytelling. This seems to be offputting to some; the trailer is somewhat misleading in this regard, as it spends about 80% of the duration showcasing the "combat" sequences (known as Rites within the game), whereas while playing, the Rites account for perhaps 5%-10% of the total experience.
Regarding the Rites, one of my favorite aspects of this game is that there is no 'Try, fail, reload, try, fail, reload' loop here. Whether you succeed or fail, the game continues, and the story adapts to accomodate the consequences of the outcome. This creates a very nice sense of tension when going into a pivotal encounter, as you're behoved to live with the outcome, be it good or bad.
Personally, I love a good story, particularly emotional ones. If a story makes me *feel* something strongly, whether it's happiness, grief, anger, fear, or any other emotion, I generally enjoy it, and in that regard, this game succeeds fantastically. Another tough call for me to make, as I also generally liked this game along with it's predecessor. Though, I won't pretend that it's weaknesses are not glaringly obvious. I'd say that this barely gets a 'Thumbs Up' from me. Although, I am going to let you know what you are likely getting into...
For one, the game is old. Sure, it's fairly fun... but it's age shows. And I'm not talking about it's graphics. I don't normally care if graphics are dated. Like for its time, this game is still pretty to look at, at times. No, my 'Holy Trinity' on what makes or breaks games tend to be Gameplay, Story Presentation & Stability. In this regard, KOTOR II: The Sith Lords is very "win some, lose some" here. If one ignores the bugs and crashes to desktop, then the gameplay might be considered better than it's predecessor.
If you like Jedi/Sith, then great news! You are playing as one from the get-go! I am kind of okay with this, even though it takes centuries to get a damn lightsaber. But fine, let us 'earn' that iconic weapon later to represent that as a milestone of character growth in the story. It's a respectable idea, just as long as the story can keep me interested in the time it takes for any cool Jedi/Sith stuff to happen (as did original KOTOR, and I went into that game expecting I'd just stay a bum scoundrel the whole game). Sadly, it's lacking strength in the plot department (more on that below). As for the gameplay itself, it delivers and with a few improvements from the original game. And quite honestly, the only thing I like better about this game compared to the first. As for story and characters, well...
Even with 'from solid-to-good' voice-work, key characters tend to have that stale "tacked-on" feeling with their given places in the narrative. The story and overall world wouldn't feel quite so linear to me if the characters could take my mind off of it (with more mystique and less transparency). The first KOTOR video game usually gave bits and portions to me in a reasonable story pace, making me eager to see what would happen next. As they sometimes say: "Less is More". It is unfortunate that this was something that KOTOR II had always missed, in my opinion. The first few hours of gameplay are practically front-loaded with most of the plot before taking a boring exodus for a while. Then after a couple of more hours of being bored, plot comes back to spice things up for a few minutes. Then... back to boring again. A lot of this wouldn't be an issue if the writing didn't show hands at the table so early (and so often). Oh, and did I mention there was this weird issue with dialog sometimes skipping itself? If only this happened consistently. Like for the boring parts, but it seems to be random.
On party members themselves, I would say they serve their purpose but most of them in KOTOR II feel somewhat flat and forgettable (That is, compared to the first game, anyway). I mean, you have predictable Kriea trying to be mysterious and elusive. Then 'Discount Han Solo' (Atton Rand) trying to fill the shoes of both Carth Onasi and Mission Vao. Oh, and later some Zabrak that sounds suspiciously like Christopher Walken on high doses of xanex. His 'arm' is pretty cool looking, though. But unlike KOTOR, KOTOR II doesn't give me that itch to get to know my party members. And I'm one of those Bioware fanboys that like to lounge around at Base/Camp just talking to my party members about their pasts.
But hey, the gameplay tends to be rather fun even in the midst of what seems like a lot of filler and fluff. I'd even say that the gameplay is so good that it barely makes up for it's generally 'meh' plot and painful stability issues. So this game could honestly walk away with a meh "Thumbs up because nostalgia" like a lot of other reviews.
But just know that it's not without it's share of problems. As I said, it's an old game (that was kind of rushed when it first came out, too).

Bejeweled is a bit of a guilty pleasure.  It is certainly not the kind of 'hardcore' game that makes up the majority of my Steam Library, but it is probably more enjoyable than most of them.  The game's rules are very simple but, like any good game, there is enough subtlety behind these to make things interesting.  While the different game modes provide some interesting alternatives, I found myself mostly playing classic mode.  A good, simple game anyone can enjoy.

First off, I'm disappointed that so many big reviews got this wrong and call it a sport game or basketball or even dodgeball game because this is nothing like a modern sport game.  It's more like a magical style capture the flag game with a isometric perspective.  During the "Rites" an orb appears in the middle, one person on your team can move at a time which is the same for the enemy team, you try to either take out the enemies with your abilities or take the orb to their base to reduce their flame until it goes out.  You can walk it in, fly it in, jump it in, and throw it in from a very short distance.
The rest of the game is a choose your own adventure decision based story that revolves around choices that affect how you power up and what character's stories you focus on.  That part is OK.  If you really like the characters and the story, you'll like that part.  The decisions might make you stop to think for a minute.  But the main story is straightforward and linear.
The gameplay part, the rites, I feel really mixed about.  They started out interesting, but quickly certain strategies become obvious and powering up certain characters can give them very abusive tools.  Luckily there are challenge options by way of Titan stars that open up that make the CPU go from a wet noodle to obnoxiously unfair - but the rewards are fairly meager and it's debatably if it's even worth activating the titan stars as opposed to just moving through the story.
The animation and music are top notch.  I like the "Voice" during the rites, but feel like it was a missed opportunity to not have voice acting for the other characters, the mumble-talk wasn't for me and made the characters seem cartoonish and distant (Tizo is an exception to that).
It's not as good as Bastion or Transistor as far as gameplay but the story is just as intriguing.
For me, this is a solid 8/10 game.  There were several disappointments, but the story, animation, and music make it a worthwhile experience.

The best game Frictional have made!
It builds up from Amnesia's mechanics as a base, but ends up being so much more.
Whereas Amnesia lacked any real storytelling and relied on atmosphere to keep you coming back, Soma has the atmosphere & a surprisingly cogent and thought provoking story. With actual dialogue that brings up some remarkably profound questions about consciousness.
As soon as I started I was hooked. Ended up completing it in 3 short sittings over 2 days.
The puzzles are simple, sometimes they will require lateral thinking in areas. But they never interrupt the flow of the game. The enemy mechanics are similar to what was laid out in Amnesia and seem to paradoxically reward a bolder approach to  confronting them than your character's utter helplessness would suggest. The entire game is about confronting your problems head on.
Any twists to do with the main character are fairly easy to figure out if you're paying attention. And the game doesn't dwell on them. Being more concerned with how the realisations affect the human condition.
Being just slightly over 10 hours for completion (will probably vary depending how you approach the problems), it may be a little short. But it doesn't overstay it's welcome (like isolation did) and leaves you wanting more.
Definitely worth a purchase.

As a fan of both the comics and the first Darkness game, I was looking forward to playing The Darkness II, and for the most part it was worth the wait.
The storyline isn't particularly original - Jackie gets attacked by "The Brotherhood" (original, huh?), unleashes the once-dormant Darkness and goes after The Brotherhood, who are trying to steal The Darkness from him. There's a few interesting scenes where Jackie has visions of his dead girlfriend, Jenny, and the trips to the insane asylum are hilarious - Look out for Adolf!
Gameplay is solid - you can dual-wield guns and use the two Darkness snake-arm things to attack your enemies. This presents some great opportunities to be creative with your kills, which you are rewarded for doing. The powers feel balanced and the gunplay is satisfying. There's a fun co-op campaign too, but it feels a bit out of place.
Overall it's a fun, if a little short, game that'll keep you entertained for at least 8-10 hours.

For those of you out there who enjoy - or rather should I say "love" sniping games (like me), I would definately recommend this game.. HOWEVER! Don't jump into this game and expect everything to be perfect.
Granted, for the most part this game is solid (at least to begin with.) It does degenerate somewhat into a run-and-gun at times, but you can't expect everything to be based around sniping. And even when things do go down the preverbial toilet, you can always rely on your trusty MP40 or PPSH41 to get you out of a tight spot (because lets face it, no enemy in this game carries a Thompson 1928.)
Tripping enemies up by shooting them in the leg, luring them into a tripwire, blasting off their gentlemans parts, masking your sniper fire using distant explosions, bells, thunder etc - all great fun.. BUT!
And there is quite a big, round BUT - towards the end of the game, things start to fall appart somewhat. There comes a point when all of your Hidden & Dangerous 2 tactics fail you, and that point comes when enemies can see you from across the map, can accurately hit you through smoke without a moments hesitation - from a distance that even at full zoom with the time focus down to a pin, you can bearly pinpoint them, and whats worst of all - is when you are hit, take cover and wait for your health to regenerate, poke your beady head out to take a shot, and see a pair of arms holding a rifle through a wall..
Its that facepalm moment when you realise that you will need to restart the whole level (because there is no save game in between checkpoints.)
I played this game through almost continously after I bought it, until I stopped - going back to it today for the first time in over a month made me realise why I stopped playing in the first place.
Sniper Elite V2 is a very good game, and I am sure that there are loads of people out there who can see past these glitches, but I am not one of these people.
After the third time having to restart a level and making progress only by remembering where the enemies are - the game looses its charm. And pretty soon one grows tired, you hit exit and go and do something else.
Towards the beginning - there is a level where you have to clear out a courtyard in order to enter an underground facility, and it was joyfully satisfying to shoot the soldiers in the leg (with the rifle sound masked by ambient noises) - watch them fall to the floor, see their fellow soldiers come to their aid, look around to see where the shot came from, then take cover.. They changed their patrols, focused on the distance to try and find you - and then I picked them off one by one before going down to mow down the rest.
In the level I recently gave up on (russian level towards the end) - the soldiers that get alerted after you take the first shot just ran past me, straight down a slope, and then started searching for "something" down a corridor littered with bodies.. Even firing in their direction didn't get their attention..
Its a great game, but it has all the hallmarks of a project that was being carefully polished off, and then someone in management decided it was time to release it.

Date: 2/13/16
Review Number: 16 (Bank Review #2)
Game: Back to the Future Episode 1
From (Creator Publisher): Telltale Games
Played On: Steambox (Steam Controller)
Steam Price as of Review:
Total Time played: 2+ Hours (Wife observing for all of it)
Review:
For the second review of the vacation, I decided to do something else a bit different.   Now a bit of personal info here, I am married (have been for a decade) and my wife, though not exactly crazy about video games, does enjoy a round or two of some games in my collection.  After she was finished with a round, and since there was nothing on TV, I decided to take over for a round.  Looking through a collection for something we both would enjoy, my choice was quickly overridden when my wife noticed that I had a Back to the Future adventure game.  So we took the time to fire up Telltale Game’s Back to the Future episode 1, a point and click adventure game with so many of the original cast and staff involved that it might as well be considered a sequel of sorts, though granted some thirty years afterwards.
And sequel this very well could be; the writing is superb, the voices so on par, with many of the original characters playing themselves (sans the main character, though Michael J Fox does do some cameo appearances as the non-1985-prime McFly family) this is in many ways a continuation of the Back to the Future series that works well in-canon.  The graphics are pretty, and the animations are fantastic.  The controls are fantastic, and work surprisingly well with the Steam Gamepad.  The only part of the interface that I thought was a little odd was the inventory screen, but even with that, I found that the game parts of the game were so unobtrusive that I could often just ‘go through the motions’ of playing the game and feel like I was just watching a movie.  Indeed, if someone is looking for a more robust ‘adventure’ game, they may find this game somewhat lacking for that reason. Even with a  lot of interactable objects in each area, the game still feels like you only head in one direction, moving along a very specific course with interactable objects proving just a bit of flair.  In the end though, this game is a beautiful continuation of a fantastic movie series, and I fully intend to play this all the way through to it's conclusion. Anyone who loves the movies, or loves point and click adventure games, will eat this up.  Buy buy buy!
Game’s Fate: Kept on the Steambox, will occasionally play it
Buy/No Buy: If you like point and click adventure games, this one isn’t necessarily the most difficult or engaging, but it's enjoyable enough, and fans of the movies will love them.  Buy.

Short story: The game wraps a few basic mechanics into a mildly satisfying gameplay loop with very little replayability or variety and interest to it. You'll probably have a good time for the first few hours as you figure it out, then it turns into a monotonous grind. There's no real challenge.
Long story: Well jeeze, where to begin...
Simply put, the vast majority of the games time will be spent waiting. Waiting for a party to trek across the wasteland, and either reach a lootable location, or have a random encounter. Sometimes you'll have an encounter at a lootable location.
Looting is self explanatory, but encounters are divided into non-combat and combat encounters. I'll cover the combat mechanics later, lets focus on the non combat, the bread and butter of pacifists. You can either attempt to trade, attempt to recruit someone, attempt to bully the person(s) or just start a fight. Some encounters will let the opposing party start the dialog, meaning you'll only be able to trade, or accept/reject a recruit, be offered a fight, or just dropped right into combat. What it boils down to is checking the occasional friendly for a resource you want, refusing hundreds of people with terrible stats shelter, and occassionally having someone ask you if you would like to donate your skin to their collection. Pro tip, don't accept.
Combat is... Not very satisfying, to say the least. While it was much worse during the early access period, and has improved, the improvements have simply made it passable, not really enjoyable. Your presented a few options. You can run away, and attempt a roll of your parties dexterity/agility against the opponents. You are not presented with any chance of success indicator, and if you fail the enemy gets a free round. Rarely worthwhile, to be honest, by the time you've got a high enough stat to get away consistently, you've got high enough stats to pulp the enemy. You can also attempt to subdue an enemy non-lethally. This option is the subject of an achievement, and is otherwise completely useless as it has a roughly 2% success rate against critically injured opponents, and deals negligible damage at the best of times. You can also attempt to disarm or steal from the enemy. Disarm is fairly ineffective as the stats to consistently do that will also consistenly just kill the target outright. Stealing makes very little sense as you will take damage doing this. If you need the items, just kill them and then you don't get damaged.
Regardless of how looting or encounters go, barring death, you'll return to your shelter with your salvaged goods, and progress through a simple tech tree of sorts, gathering increasingly rare components to upgrade your workbench. The upgraded bench permits you to craft fancier items. One of the more unusual decisions that the developers has made is that the game world is littered with damaged objects. broken computers, heaps of scrap metal, old radios, and the like. These items can be salvaged for rare, useful parts. But you cannot salvage them without a recycler, a top tier item requiring a maxed out workbench. By the time you can use it, its mostly useless for its intended purpose. A number of the shelter upgrades are fairly useless as well. While the generator efficiency upgrade is incredibly valuable if your low on fuel, the generator capacity upgrade is a significant resource sink just to reduce busywork of sending someone over every few days for thirty seconds. Crafting only feels like it has one or two viable upgrade paths at any one time. If your wondering about food or water or fuel, its fairly difficult to run out of any of the three. The shelter has a water filtration system, so as long as you spend a pittance on building storage early, your golden. Food is everywhere and is rarely a concern. Fuel burns so slowly that its usually the first thing I ignore and dump once my bags fill up.
The "critical" resources are incredibly available, and you are far more likely to be excited about finding a handful of nails than a pile of fuel canisters. Upgrading the shelter just reduces busywork, makes the abundant critical resources even more abundant, and makes things a bit more fancy looking. Building better beds means they sleep faster, meaning you'll spend less time micromanaging everyones sleep schedule. Not exactly a satisfying upgrade.
But, that shelter you put all your effort into isn't perfectly safe, people on the outside will try to break in and steal your stuff. Maybe the challenge lies there? Well no, not really. Shelter breaches occur very late in the game, well after you have maxed out the tech tree and gotten everything. Once you are breached, your first line of defense is a stationary gun positi- no that would make too much sense. Your first line of defense is home-alone style traps. From paint cans on strings, to spike-dropping plates, to a shotgun stuck on a table, your initial defenses rely on the raiders blindly stumbling into clear, visible danger to be maybe taken out by lucky hit. Its not damage based, its a percentage roll against each trap. A bandit can just up and avoid six shotguns in a row if the game really doesn't like you that particular day. Once your defenses are bypassed, then your survivors can fight. The game will automatically equip them with stuff, no input there. Then, your fighter proceeds to engage the bandits until the bandits are dead, or the bandits kill them. If the bandits win, they move on to the next one. Its possible to build hiding spots to conceal people and prevent them from being attacked, but its of little benefit as the bandits will steal your food, fuel, water, and supplies, break equipment, and generally♥♥♥♥♥♥all over the shelter.
Instead of being a satisfying struggle, it usually ends up with one bandit with a pickaxe giving up halfway through breaching the doors and going home. If they do make it in, they are faced with a line of prepared traps and an army of hardened survivors. They had the potential to be fun, but they just show up so late to the party.
I guess that's my big wrap for this game. It had the potential to be fun, but it shoots itself in the foot in short order. I wouldn't say I regret buying the game, I have had some fun with it, the first hours are fun figuring it out like I said. But it gets old. Fast.
I should also add, since the game is still being updated: The updates have so far brought nonsensicle content that hasn't resolved any issues. The number one complaint is there is no real challenge, people want difficulty levels. What we recieved was the ability to craft metal detectors, lock picks, and portable camping kits. The latter being particularly baffling, as they reduce stat drain during expeditions. The stats which have no effect on the performance of the expedition at all, and the kit takes up a precious equipment slot.
The devs seem to be trying, but they are either blatantly ignoring the communities desires, aren't able to implement the communities desires, or are just throwing in the kitchen sink in an effort to placate us until they either move on, or implement said desires. Much like the game, they have the potential to deliver, but just miss it entirely.

An almost Souls-like experience, Apotheon follows Nikandreos, lead by Hera as he slaughters everyone on Olympus one by one, and sometimes house by house, eventually usurping Zues himself. Refuge or god, none are safe from Nikandreos' primal rage as he fights to avenge a quite literally god-forsaken humanity.  A suprisingly varied experience as brilliant in aesthetic as it is in satisfaction from start to finish. I do reccomend playing on the harder difficulty on your first playthrough to get the most out of this game. The lower difficulty leaves you with far too many resources and breathing room. You are killing gods after all, prove yourself worthy to walk upon the Olympian summit.
One thing to note about this game is that a lot of your learning is done in a heavily autodidactic fashion. Such little tidbits will follow. Semi spoiler alert relating to the specifics of combat.
1: Sweeping an enemies feet out will throw them into the air.
2: Hitting them in the head with your swing will do more damage.
3: When blocking, you need to aim your shield at the point of which the attack will impact with you. This is particularly needed in the final fight.
4: If you get into a fight with guards around the 'non-combat' areas, either run as far as you can and hide. (The top left of the screen shows you portraits of who you are in combat with, and will fade away if they lose you.) But if you choose to fight, make sure you don't let them blow their horns. They will summon more dudes to fight and can do this endlessly.
5: Middle mouse while blocking to do a shield smack, knocking people back and putting their guard down.
6: Stackable weapons durabilities are individual to that weapon. For example, if you have a spear in your hand it's durability isn't shared with the other 4 hidden on your person.
7: When breaking open stuff, if you have the time switch to your fist not to waste durability on weapons.
That's all that comes to mind right now just after finishing the game. I would love to see a similar style game but for Norse mythology instead of Greek. It would be brilliant. Absolutely reccomend this game for fans of souls games type combat.

Rayman Legends is quite possibly the best 2d platformer released in the past 10 years.
It’s the follow up title to Rayman Origins (also a great game) and if you missed it, 40 of the stages from Origins have been included in Legends as additional re-mastered content.
It features over 120 different stages each with varying atmosphere, amazing music, and plenty of hidden collectibles. Each of the levels are hand drawn and beautiful to look at. Despite not being overly impressive on a technical level, Rayman uses a timeless style. While games like Crysis 3 probably won’t look that great 10 years from now, Rayman Legends will no doubt retain its charm.
The game also has multiple characters to choose from along with a host of unlockables. There are underwater stealth missions, time trials, and even musical stages where you jump to the rhythm of remixed popular songs. The inclusion of daily and weekly challenges allows you to compete with your friends, adding tons of re-playability.
If you enjoyed classic 2d platformers like Super Mario World and Donkey Kong Country, you should check out Rayman Legends as it’s the closest thing to them in this day and age.

The long awaited Survarium has finally released on Steam! You know, that spiritual successor to STALKER! But this time it's even better because it's an MMO!
OK.... let's cut the crap.
Originally Survarium was suppose to be an Open World game like STALKER but online. I'm not a very big fan of MMO's (anymore), since you're pretty much doing the same thing over and over again, but if done well I can still enjoy myself for many hours. As it stands now, Survarium is still in Beta (yes, even after all those years) and does not offer an open world, filled with mutated creatures in which you are struggling to survive. No, instead Survarium is a simple PVP game, in which you kill the other people, score points, level up and find new weapons after the match is over.
The gameplay, while being standard, is pretty fun but it's nothing you've never seen before (aside from the post-apocalyptic maps). The graphics are also pretty OK but certainly nothing to brag about.
So the game is a standard but fun shooter? Nothing wrong with that, right?
-Well, I suppose you're right if it weren't for one small problem called: "Free2Play".
I dislike pretty much all free2play games, there are ofcourse a few exceptions like Team Fortress 2, but for the most part I try to stay away as far as possible from these games. Everytime you hit up Survarium, the game (like most free2play games) screams and begs you to spend money on useless crap. The game may be fun for a while but personally, I would not spend that much money on new skins, clothes and faster xp, I simply do not see the point in that.
If you forget about all the promises made by the developers and realise this game is nothing like STALKER, I suppose it can be a fun PVP game for a while but it's not enough for me to fully recommend this game.

If you're a Bejeweled beginner, here's how it works.
Different-colored jewels fill an eight-by-eight board. To wipe them away, you create groups of at least three gems by swapping one gem with one located directly beside, above, or below it. This causes those gems to disappear and the ones above to drop down, allowing for new jewels to appear at the top. Matching four or more gems together creates a special gem that will explode and remove surrounding jewels when it is matched; the more jewels matched, the more powerful the explosion. Matching like-colored gems in a T- or L-shaped pattern creates a Box gem that will zap away all gems of a particular color.

Doom is a household name for good reason. It's a game that brought the gaming industry to it's knees and changed the landscape of video games and software forever. Doom resulted in the widespread adoption of the Windows operating system and later the creation of DirectX. Doom popularized the first person shooter, which is now one of the most popular video game genres. It directly lead to custom maps, modifications, source code releases and online multiplayer being a thing.
Most importantly, Doom is a symbol. It's a symbol of everything good in video games. It is the product of nights spent computer programming, playing Dungeons and Dragons and wishing fervently to make, "That game". That game you fantasize about playing in the back of your mind, that game you think people will judge you for playing, that game that you play 20 years later and find it's still as fresh as the day you bought it.
Doom; "That game"

This is truly one of the great stories ever written, especially now that the restored content mod is in the Steam workshop. With that "extra" content now available, KOTOR II turns from a broken game that could have been so much more into one of the great titles of all time. It's a little strange to think about, because the KOTOR titles are essentially Dungeons and Dragons: Star Wars Edition in terms of gameplay, but the way they're presented, II in particular, turns a simple turn-based RPG into an almost cinematic experience. Watching the dynamics between characters all affect each other, and how the game reflects its own morals and forces you to think about your own in the process becomes a haunting experience. I actually have yet to complete a playthrough of this game because most of my hours were logged before I downloaded the restored content (got all the way through the Academy to the final battle, then realized I done goofed).
I recommend this game to literally anyone, but it brings more to those who want their games to be cerebral. Either way, it's a dollar for every four hours of gameplay if you're speedrunning it without the restored content. Great bang for your buck, and that bang is big, dense, and colorful. Best ten bucks I ever spent, truly.

Rich immersive environment and extreme focus on story with a minimalist approach to gameplay.
SIMILAR GAMES: Bioshock, System Shock, Alien: Isolation, Amnesia, The Last of Us
SIMILAR MOVIES: The Abyss, Sunshine, Gattaca, Dark City
SOMA is an ambitious work of science fiction, fantasy, and mystery all wrapped up into one submerged in sweet honey mustard sauce with a side of bacon and ice cold beer. The game begins following the events of a horrible car accident. The main protagonist, Simon Jarrett, agrees to partake in a new experimental study as a guinea pig in order to improve his chances of recovery from his head injury. After losing consciousness during the study, you wake up in a mysterious underwater facility. If I add anything else to the story, I'll ruin an another amazing adventure you rarely experience in video gaming today. Trust me, it's amazing. The story doesn't cut any corners. The universe so rich and vast, you'll scour every nook and cranny to get the entire story. Something like 60% of the story is delivered through dialogue and 40% through journals and other entries along the way. The script and voice acting is superb - never any cheesy one liners or melodramatic soap opera conversations. Everything that is said is something that the average person would say given the same scenario. The voice actors did a great job at expressing happiness, sadness, fear, and anger and this contributed heavily towards my positive review of the game.
Its formula is sound - explore, interact with characters, evade the enemies, rinse and repeat. SOMA takes a minimalist approach - the same exact gameplay you'd find in Amnesia, Bioshock, or the slightly older point and click adventures - puzzle solving, exploring, not too much backtracking, and the occasional sneaking around and running away from enemies. Yes there are enemies.  Yes they can kill you. No there are no guns. There's also no HUD and its brilliant because of it. This is a survival based game using only your wits and the environment to make it to the next objective. SOMA won't hold your hand and tell you where to go or what you do. So you better take your ADHD medications otherwise you'll might get confused and lost at times. I'll be honest, SOMA is not for everyone. If you can't go longer than 5 minutes without shooting someone, this game is probably not for you. That's okay. There is no perfect game for everyone. SOMA focuses slightly more on storytelling than gameplay to enrich itself. That could be another potential turnoff to some hardcore gamers who just want to game without story. I will say this though SOMA is an experience worth experiencing. It doesn't feel too cheap or repetitive. There are no jump scares but the game is spooky. Not scary, but spooky and creepy. Somewhat unnerving at times. If you want scary, play Outlast. If you want spooky, play SOMA.
If you've seen any of the movies or played any of the games I mentioned at the beginning and found yourself wanting more of that universe, please do yourself a favor and experience SOMA. This game will easily go down in history as top 20 best storylines of all time alongside Metal Gear Solid, Planescape Torment, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, a few others. I highly recommend it you buy it as soon as possible. I did take a few points off for the minimalist gameplay approach as well as the lack of replay value. Once you finish it, you won't really want to play it again. There's no multiplayer or coop. Not much to bring you back. But you will blow your friends up about it and tell them to play it because it's damn so enjoyable.

You create a family of 2 adults and 2 children and these people will be imperative to the game, so choose wisely. These people will need to fight, fix and build their way towards security. Should all 4 of these people die during your game, the game will be over no matter how many survivors you have left.
Your family is very lucky in that they discover a small underground shelter. The place is in dire need of refurbishment, it's food stocks are low and the water supply is completely insufficient. So, get to work! Time is against you in that you must fulfil the needs of these dwellers; their hunger, their thirst, their health, their fatigue - you get it. Your shelter too has needs, it must be routinely repaired and upgraded should you wish to endure the black rain and sandstorms.
You must go into the wasteland. It's hard to leave the kids to fend for themselves but the folks need to roam whatever's left of the towns for supplies. Armed with planks of wood and carrier bags, you send them to explore schools, petrol stations, police stations, factories, scrap-yards and peoples homes. Sometimes you have to fight, a family with a good dog will be able to fend off most things. A family with a horse can travel faster. A family with a pet fish can.... I'll let that one be a surprise.
With a bit of luck and a lot of patience, you should see your dwellers go from radiated, emaciated, half-mad bucket poopers into Kings of the wasteland. Your guys need to be as self sufficient as possible.
Now, go play this game!

This is the first game I was inspired to write any type of review for. Normally I just keep my mouth shut, regardless of the game's quality, but something about this game inspired me to say something.
TLDR: While it's a horribly designed game no where near completion, the core of it is solid and enjoyable for the first 8-14 hours of play and shows a lot of potential. It's worth about $5 in it's current state as I've played many more free (not freemium) mobile games that were far more polished, thought out, developed, and appropriately implemented. This game is clearly not of finished release quality by any stretch of the imagination. It's almost a proof-of-concept prototype that their still hacking things into.
The good: The game's initial play over the first 8-14 hours is overall quite fun. Initially, it is a challenge to keep your family alive, upgrade, craft better items, etc. It is a fun resource management opener in that way. The random interactions, while still repeative are made at least somewhat enjoyable by the writing in the very early game. Oh yeah, and the graphics are--for the most part--pretty nice.
The bad: Sadly, the good ended there. Even before this initial period of play is over, I immediately noticed--and was frustrated--by the increadibly poor UI design (non-existitant keybindings for most things in the game, very inconsistent menus, overall horrible action/party management), badly implemented attribute system (only killing/subding blows count for STR/DEX, telling random people who want to join you to go away does nothing for your INT even though it clearly shows your actual intelligence, etc), and the... atually, I'll save that for the ugly (keep reading). Once past the first 40-60 in-game days (generally, actual game hours countable on two hands), the game turns insanely repetative. The game is backed by what seems to be a primative i.d.d. RNG (think dice rolls)... which--especially for this type of game--was a huge mistake. You can spend hundreds of hours looking for that one last item, only to get the same items you have over, and over, and over again. Insanely boring. There is no end game goal and there is no end game to speak of. There's no reason to even survive. It's just seeking items on a probabilty dice roll.
The ugly: As already strongly hinted at, this game is horribly shallow. After you get settled, the only thing that's a threat is a bug or simply a, "Really? Really? You have got to be kidding me!" moment that's sprinkled so poorly throughout. It's filled with bugs and "what-the-f?!?!?" moments that so near the surface of the game (easy to find without trying just playing for more than a handful of hours) as if they never tried playing their own game for any amount of time. Putting up with "the bad" is pretty easy, but there's really no point to continue when your playthrough is ruined because of some completely arbitrary dice-roll event or bug. The world is tiny, your ability to expore it is pointless, survival is meaningless, and every aspect of doing so results in increasing degrees of boredom and frustration.
Conclusion: This game is--even though the team17 logo comes with the tagline "25 years of gaming excellence" (or something like that)--clearly developed by amateurs. I write that as a 20ish year veteren of software development... not purely as a game enthusiest. However, it shows great promise. Again, the first part of the game is quite a bit of fun and has kept me creating new families over again just to get frustrated or bored enough to do it from scratch again. The very, very basic aspects of this game (it's a game of economic management) are genuinely engrosing. Everything else however, falls horriblely flat. Regardless of the fact that it's been officially released, it's an alpha (pre-beta/think pre-release or dev build) game for sure.
Like many people, I wish that I could somehow tell steam that I "conditionally" recommend this game, but because I can't I'm going to have to say that I don't for the general audience at the asking price ($15 at the time of post).
