Sheltered, a small indie game costing around £10 or around £6 when it’s on sale. But is it worth getting?
Sheltered is a 2D Fallout Shelter-esk survival game in which you start off with 2 adults and 2 children. These people can be modified to look like whatever you want them to look like as well as assigning them traits and stats. For example, it’s good to have one of your adults as a courageous muscleman to go out into the wasteland as they will do more damage to any attackers and won’t curl up into a ball, shaking like a shi*ting dog whenever someone challenges them to a fight. For the children, you are best having them as either optimistic, or small eaters. This means they won’t get depressed as fast and they won’t need a lot of food to survive. You also get to choose a pet. You can choose from a fish in a tank (this calms down your survivors and lowers their stress levels) a Dog (can go out with you on expeditions and fight with you) a snake (catches rats in your bunker you can use for food) or a horse (allows you to travel further using less water in the wasteland but requires a lot of food and a stable). It’s up to you what stats you give your survivors, these are just the most helpful that I’ve found via trial and error.
You slowly but surely expand your bunker and upgrade the different parts (such as your water purifier or your generator) so that fuel doesn’t burn as quickly or you can purify water quicker. You can also upgrade your workbench so you unlock the next level of items you can craft (for example, you start off with a simple bucket for a toilet and a shower that uses A LOT of water, but as you upgrade your workbench, and unlock higher level toilets and showers, they use less water and are more efficient). This isn’t just the case for toilets and showers. This also affects other systems such as starting off with a small water butt to collect water in, and you unlock medium and large ones as you upgrade your workbench, and so on and so on. Crafting relies on having the right resources to make the item. So you need 2 plastic and 2 rubber to craft a gas mask and so on. All the things you need to craft with can be found in the wasteland or from traders.
Your survivors have certain requirements however. These are as follows. Tiredness, stress, hunger, thirst, hygiene, and needing the toilet. If these requirements aren’t met, your survivors will become ill or die. You find food scavenging in the wasteland or you can build a cooker and a freezer and trap animals in traps that you can build to get raw meat which you store in said freezer. You can eat the meat raw, but your survivors WILL get food poisoning, so cuild a cooker and cook it first. You also find tablets such as Anti-Rad tablets if your survivors get radiation poisoning (this can happen by drinking un-purified water or going into the wasteland without a gas mask). Anti-Biotics for curing infections and food poisoning, and first aid kits for stopping bleeding etc if your survivor has been hurt in a fight. You can also trade items with other survivors in the wasteland or they will come to your shelter to trade (them come both by RNG and if you use your radio to signal for traders). Different items are worth different amounts to each trader depending on what they want and what you want. The most expensive items are drugs and the least, springs and wood and common items such as plastic.
The game is very difficult early on as your survivors will always be a second away from death, but as you get used to the game, it becomes easier as you know what to do. If I was you, I’d play the tutorial (which isn’t very good anyway) then set up a test game to get used to everything, then start your proper game. I’m on my third game and have just about got everything down. There is little to worry about late game apart from people breaking in to your bunker, but fear not, as this isn’t RNG and you won’t get attacked until the game thinks you’re ready for it, and you receive little hints that you will be attacked, such as people trying to bully food and other such items off you via the intercom on your bunker door. You can prepair for this by setting traps and hiding spaces for the children. You also get people asking if they can join you in your bunker. These people cannot be controlled like your survivors you start off straight away with and must survive in your bunker for X amount of days before you can control them. If these people don’t feel as though they’re being looked after, they will leave and usually damage things on the way out, such as shi*ting in your water supply and contaminating it to 100%. You know who I’m talking about CHRISTOPHER!
Overall it’s a very good game that is quite challenging throughout until late game. The game can easily take upwards of 20 hours to get to end game so you get a lot for your money. Aesthetically, it uses 8-bit graphics but it is strangely pleasing to look at and reminds you that not all games need to look like Crysis 3 to be enjoyable to play. Well worth buying if you have the money and want a 2D, 8-Bit, bunker survivor game. Top notch stuff.

If you are a fan  of BTTF and have played other Telltale Games and have enjoyed them, then this is a no brainer. I have played through all 3 seasons of Telltale's Sam & Max games, so BTTF: The Game felt like familiar territory. So far, I have completed the first 2 episodes of this point-and-click adventure series, and I have enjoyed them. The story is well written, picking up where the movie triology left off, and feels like it fits quite naturally with the movie story line. The plotline is very much in line with the movies, where time travel inadvertently, and disastrously, messes up the time line, which then needs fixing. This time, Marty and Doc need to visit Prohibition-era Hill Valley to fix history. The voice acting is pretty good and the actor portraying Marty does a pretty good Michael J. Fox impression.
Now on to my gripes...the puzzles are very sensical but they are almost too easy; at times it's almost spelled out for you what you need to do. So far I haven't needed to use the game's built in hint system. Next, the navigation in the game's quasi-3D environments is frustrating. Getting Marty to negotiate his way around the scenery is clunky. This game has the same annoying navigation that was introduced in the last season of the Sam and Max games.
Other than those 2 gripes, these games are enjoyable for BTTF fans who want more stories with the characters they love and who, are interested in exploring more lore about Hill Valley, the McFlys, and the Tannens. Oh, we also get to see Doc when he was much younger.

At this price it's hard to imagine any game that'll fall short of it's worth, and it's not that this game is bad or buggy, it's just that in this day and age, low budget game such as this one really struggle for relevance when there are tons of flash games on site such as
, many of which easily surpass this game, and above all else, free. I got this game on Humble Bundle, while it's on sale (which doesn't save much consider the full price is only 1 dollar CDN), yet somehow, a little part of me still feel that that's roughly one dollar I'll never get back ( and perhaps will be wiser spent tossing into a wishing fountain or something). But I really do admire indie developers trying to put out new content and if the developers of this game sees this, please consider the following advice for your next game:
Graphics: Even though Puzzle games rely most heavily on game mechanics, that doesn't mean your player won't notice how bland your graphics are. Even if you just add a few set of color palette and switch it around would definitely make the game that much more visually interesting and engaging.
Soundtrack: If audio editting isn't your strong suit that's fine, but just like graphics, even if you toss a few simple bell tone on it would make it more interesting than what it is now.
Interface: Maybe the game menu is surprisingly absent because you can't do it, in which case it's high time that you educate yourself to fufill that role. But I can't stress how imporant for a game to have basic fundamental option such as a few graphic setting (resolution, window mode, etc), and maybe a proper exit button.
Length: The game only have 50 levels, really? 50!? There are a lot of puzzle games online that revolves around mechanics just as simple and they could easily churn out hundreds of levels; I think this one just shows a lack of creativity, perhaps spending some time online trying out some other puzzle games might give the developers some inspiration on how to design more levels in their future puzzle games.
TL;DR: as much as I would like to recommend this game, you're probably better off surfing one of those online flash game site if you're budget for entertainment is that low. Only buy this game if you're a serious fan of the puzzle genre.

I found this to be one of the best independent games I've played in a long time.  The artistic style was refreshing, the combat mechanics are pretty advanced (but not complicated), the music set a great tone, and it had a great sense of exploration.  I liked the mood of the game - it's hard to describe, but it's a feeling that most games don't offer.
I only have three major complaints about the game:
1. The British accent of all the characters was off-putting.  It really shouldn't be that hard to do a Greek accent.
2. There were too many items to work with, and it felt clumsy all the way to the end.  I pretty much never used any potions unless I knew I was just about to get into a fight.  The way I see it, being able to throw melee weapons was unnecessary and the controller button for it should have been replaced with either "attack with projectile weapon" or "use potion".
3. The introduction to the story was really lacking.  The story as the game portrays it is decent, but it felt like there were gaps in it.  I suppose it's better if you actually read things like The Odessey.
Anyway, Apotheon is a great game and reminded me a lot of Diablo II, except requires more skill.

Apotheon is as beautiful and rich as you can see from the sceencap images. You're placed into a 2D open-world landscape based on traditional Greek mythology as you travel Olympus confronting each of the Olympians in the hopes of defeating them or convincing them to help you in your quest to challenge Zeus for abandoning humanity. I absolutely love how each of the gods' realms is developed to suit their nature and thematic powers. Each makes you think on your feet for clever solutions on how to beat them or how to use your surroundings to your advantage. You could of course just jab things with spears, but imo the game is much more fun the more thought you put into it.
The voice acting and writing is fantastic; I love how diverse all of the voices sound, and that there are little plaques of information from various Greek writings to set the tone throughout the story. The map is also the perfect size for this game. It's got enough side quests to keep interest, but not so many to deter people from even trying, and the maps are expansive enough to showcase Alientrap's creativity but not enough to overwhelm.
The only criticism I have, that I know is reflected amongst other players, is the unnecessarily difficult fighting system. There's a slight pause between the time you click and the time Nikandreous attacks. I've heard some arguments that it requires you to strategize and time your movements perfectly to attack, but this is hard for me to reason when you have a computer that lags, or the enemies moving faster than you are, or a trackpad (since he attacks in the precise direction your mouse is pointing), or you're simply just less into fighting than you are into the story and world. I feel the combat system as it is would've been better suited for a higher difficulty for players who want to challenge themselves that bit more, because the game is interesting and challenging enough.
But if you can make it through the cumbersome combat or figure out a strategy that works for you, it's worth your $$$. I'm no expert on Greek mythology but even an amateur like me can tell a lot of research, planning, and respect went into every part of this game, up to and including the monsters, gods, history, and overarching symbolic narrative.

If you like Castlevania or Metroid then this will be right up you ally. The game map reminds me of Metroid II: Return of Samus; an overall linear progression from start to finish, but with several deviation areas that you'll need to enter in order to obtain the upgrades. Not all the upgrades are actually necessary to beat the game, but once you move up to either the 'Champion' or 'Olympian' Difficulty Settings, the extra bonuses are certainly worth going out of your way for. Finally, most sections contain at least one secret area which require hidden keys to reach.
You collect 'ingrediants' by killing enemies and then use the pause menu to craft them into useable items like potions, traps, and even summon-able allies. Collect the gold they drop to spend on new crafting recipes, more weapons, better armor, and improved combat training. There are a lot of different weapons to be obtained (both primary and secondary), and selecting the right one for any given circumstance can sometimes be the difference between life and death.
The best aspect of this game is in how well laid-out the 'boss fights' are. The scenarios are generally challenging, but not aggraviatingly so. Each fight is comeplely unique, using setting appropriate material; such as the fight against Pseidon from the deck of your ship; the seas roiling around you while he pummels your tiny vessel. Not to mention the musical scores that accompany each of the fights lends a desperation to the tone of the game not usually seen in side-scrollers.
Do I recommend this game? Yes, it took me almost 18 hours to beat it just on the first Difficulty Setting and I will definately play it through again. Not to mention, once you feel that you're pretty good at the main game, there's Apotheon Arena; the standalone multiplayer portion (which is completely FREE) if you'd like to test you mettle against the best that virtual Greece has to offer!

It's ironic that a game about time travel arrived one year too early before TellTale started to add depth of choice and consequence to their games, as this is just a linear story. You can't blame the game for that, it's just unfortunate that the title that would've benefited most from the modern TellTale treatment just barely missed it.
It definitely has its moments, clever nods to BttF did not go unnoticed, and the voice acting is great. Marty's actor sounds a bit affected in Episode 1, but after that he really nails it. At one point, I was thinking, "Man, Doc's voice actor is spot on too," only to find out that, yeah, it's Christopher Lloyd. That works. I wasn't enraptured by the main direction of the story -- it worked as a "what-if," maybe not BttF IV caliber -- but I really liked a few places they took it.
Ultimately, while there is good, this game didn't add up for me. A lot of the gameplay is tedious and mundane, the mechanics can be wonky, and the narrative is hit-and-miss... and-miss. Hit-and-miss-and-miss is appropriate for much of the game, as it can feel like a dated, drab experience. In a lot of ways, it's a second-rate game.
It's BttF though, so maybe it's worth a try. If you want my advice, a game with real choice-driven narrative is Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, so I recommend that.

A simple Metroidvania game with a relatively unique combat system and an amazing soundtrack. Despite the heavily under-utilized exploration elements, the game nails the rest of its components and was an enjoyable play. Easily recommended for fans of the Metroidvania genre; if you are new to this genre, you can start with this game but there are a few better choices out there (notably Guacamelee).
PROS:
-Amazing soundtrack.
-Solid voice acting.
-Simple metroidvania concept with varied environments, hidden areas, and breakable walls.
-Different weapons feel different.
-Unique artstyle. This style has the possibility of being an eyesore or making certain components difficult to see, but this was not the case at all with Apotheon.
NEUTRALS:
-2 game world hubs. Cannot access the second hub until you clear the first hub which somewhat limits speed run or "alternate path" run throughs. However, within the given hubs, they can be cleared in any order from the start.
-Breakable objects mostly pointless. Only "meaningful" collectible is gold which is used to get damage upgrades but not really needed.
-Enemies are mostly pointless. I found myself simply running past most of them towards the second half of the game, especially after I had level 3 attack upgrades.
-Way too many health/armor drops. I had max inventory almost all game.
CONS:
-No meaningful abilities gained (giving access to new areas).
-No consideration for additional access in level design.
-Heavily under-utilize exploration elements.
**This is especially odd given it is a Metroidvania game, but, aside from armor, you gain no abilities that give you access to new areas. This is quite strange because you DO get the ability to
which could have been used to give access to many new game areas but....the environments/levels are not designed in this way.
-Does not properly support side mouse buttons (not a big deal). 1 of my 2 side buttons did work, but only certain abilities (I ended up using it for throw, but it would not work for roll even though it would bind).

Narratives in video-games have a stigma that their structure is to the detriment of the player’s ability to interact with the world, and if Pyre is to be commended on one thing it has mastered the illusion of structure by taking inspiration from oral storytelling to let the Readers have total influence by how they tell its epic adventure.
After playing games like Moon Hunters and Stories: Path of Destiny which failed to make a story from your choices, Pyre has managed to create one by taking into consideration all the player’s failures and successes. However, like these other games, the problems come in the form of a repetition of simplified gameplay, which does manage better than these other games by raising the stakes each time you begin a new cycle.
As much as I want to enjoy Pyre as much as I love Transistor, which is still my favorite by Supergiant, the imbalance amounts of gameplay with the narrative as well as the concessions made to accommodate this storyline ultimately weaken the experience, yet the moments that can be borne from the player’s actions can be hauntingly memorable when it hits home.
Of all the games that come to mind for a comparison to Pyre in the gameplay inside and outside of combat are the Banner Saga games crossed with an ARPG styled Fantasy Soccer manager.
In-between each competition, the Rites, the Reader and his companions travel across story-book popup landscapes with various choose-your-adventure styled vignettes to apply status effects or debuffs as well as allow more character interactions between you and the rest of the characters. These moments also allow you to train characters, buff your team or forage for supplies to upgrade your equipment. When engaged in the Rites, they consist of three-on-three battles where the player can choose up to eight companions to mix-and-match their strengths into different scenarios when pitied against other teams with unique match-ups. Each faction has their own story-arc and relevance to the team you foster, the Nightwings, as you all are competing for the freedom from a land of purgatory consisting of exiles, convicts and unwanted people from the world above.
As someone who enjoyed the previous games because of the variety of playstyles for the Kid in Bastion and for Red in Transistor, the focus on a “RPG sports” game based on team-play was something I did not initially enjoy. This is why it’s more appropriate to describe it like soccer with various one-on-one battles of offense and defense rather thinking it’s all about dunking basketballs. You can still play most of the game controlling one or two characters in every round; however, in the later challenges the coordination required to win ever increasing odds will tax players to come up with tactics between two or three characters. Combined with the “visual-novel” style of an RPG and the change in narration behind its story, and it’s easy to understand why this game is so polarizing amongst fans.
If, however, you manage to see past its simplistic gameplay elements, which only becomes more difficult the farther you delve into the next tournaments of Rites, then you can begin to appreciate how far Supergiant has come in interweaving the story into a player-driven experience.
Like the name suggests, Pyre is involved with the ceremonious structure of honor to burn the remnants of people lost; however, instead of focusing on death it’s about the path of redemption through adversity to burn away one’s crimes and restore the individual’s glory and rights. When the Rites are performed, the narration that follows are like the whispers during a mourn spoken upon the charred ash of the purifying flames.
Beyond the poetical implications, this style of narration is used by being a narrative told through the victories and defeats you will create to shape the story not only amongst your companions but with every single NPC you come across that can be given freedom or denied it by you. Even in the case that you suffer defeat, it’s not the end; it’s rather another moment for the game to create new conflicts and aspire for their resolutions. The result of such an experience is that the story will be different with every player depending on the choices you make and the failures/victories you accrue.
This is a major shift from Supergiant’s previous games which were entirely linear experiences with some choices made for areas (Bastion) or alternative challenges (Transistor). While choices are available in different manners and there are specialized challenges, they’re in small numbers compared to the journey you undergo. And instead of having one main character that wasn’t the player, Pyre has the player assume the role of a (default: male) Reader that interacts with various major characters. As you might expect from the title, you are going to have to read a lot due to the amount of characters and variables there are to accommodate with only the Voice as the announcer having audio.
Beyond its technical limitations, the lack of vocal narration is also used for themes of knowledge and freedom as you play one of the only literate characters. Literacy amongst non-Scribes are against the law; every character grunts, makes noises, and possesses limitations of their abilities and knowledge until you help them become enlightened; characters have reasons behind their narrowed viewpoints that you can attempt to broaden; and the lore constantly questions powers of authority, knowledge and equality and the struggles they create. Even in the Nightwing’s ultimate Plan, the ultimate goal is to help others by using each races’ abilities to foster growth of knowledge and of true freedom to the world beyond their own. While the tone and consistency of this theme is weaker than their other titles, the narration behind its subtler moments truly shine when the player is given free-will to exercise these ideas through their own means.
This all leads into what is perhaps the greatest issue of Pyre, and that is the story as well as the gameplay becomes repetitive because of how the game is designed. In its structure, you will have to engage in a series of tournaments not once, not thrice, not five times but seven times to complete the game. Each tournament becomes quicker than the last, but the extent of which this game repeats itself can become an issue to some who become tired of the gameplay after the first few runs.
While the game becomes more difficult because they add more challenges by having fewer companions to choose from as well as adding new ones, every following tournament becomes a series of battles with a moment before to prepare, and it’s mainly the narrative that will keep you playing. Encounters can sometimes break the rules with an added difficult spike as well as emphasizing the stat-management system behind the core gameplay as well as added penalties that force you to mix up the gameplay over time. Pyre does all it can to sustain itself with added challenges and higher odds to overcome, but it will inevitably feel tiresome to players who enjoyed how focused Supergiant’s previous games are as well as how formulaic the last six runs will feel outside of the variables you can influence. To the game’s credit, the final showdown was perhaps the hardest fight to overcome that the tension of failing could have impacted this fight was perhaps the best moment from the entire experience when I overcame the odds.
None of these complaints should mean I don’t like Pyre; however, I realize that out of all their previous games it’s perhaps the most bloated with extra content that impacts the pacing and the consistency of it. Like skinning a cat, no matter how many ways there are to achieve the result it all begins to drag after the fifth life.

has far exceeded all of my expectations. The game has wonderfully crafted lore, dialogues, and traditional gameplay all intertwined into one heartfelt and palpable experience. Each character brings a unique personality and skillset to the table, creating great tactical depth and conversations to remember between the various exiles.
The gameplay specifiically takes many different (balanced) forms, on top of the standard difficulties (easy, normal, hard) you will find multiple options later to make the experience even more challenging while recieving extra experience as a reward. In many of the challenges you face, the map or circumstances will change dynamically. It goes without saying that the versus mode is also very smooth, and there is a great deal of fun to be had using your local area network connection; however, I do hope
(or a third party developer) creates an online multiplayer alternative in the future.
There are moments where the characters
will make you laugh, catch you off guard, give you insight into them and your opponents, or truly touch your heart.
. If you spend the time to immerse yourself in the story, you will not regret it. Make sure to speak to your fellow exiles often.
To truly enjoy this game and the depth of its characters, you should not shy away from the prospect of reading,
. The game itself is not a visual novel as some of the negative reviews are suggesting, but there is so much lore. I myself appreciate the game's art direction and pacing, and never found anything to be annoying in that aspect. The color schemes and artwork make the enviroments rich and unique in their own way. Oh and the soundtrack! It brought everything together, and fit whatever task that was at hand quite well.
I give this game high praise, but in light of that I will also voice what I perceive as
cons. As a PC game I was expecting more graphical options, like multisample antialiasing, supersampling, or adjusting FPS. That being said the game plays beautifully in both 1080p and 4k, and I never personally experienced any graphical issues. Secondly I did encounter a bug that caused the game to crash when loading a previous checkpoint (which may have since then been fixed) but this is to be expected from a new release, plus when loading the game again it didn't lose any of my progress so the minor annoyance is forgiven.
It's an incredible game, but certainly not industry changing; however, this is not a bad thing. Unlike many AAA game developers,
is not constantly trying the shove DLC or microtransactions down your throat, or trying the make their games with always-online DRM restrictions. The merit of this studio has no bounds, and if you are looking for a single-player focused experience in a seemingly wasteland of games, this is it. 10/10, IGN (basically)

Out of all the nostalgia that old PC games brought me since Windows 98, one that stood out for me was the Bejeweled Deluxe series. Branching from a trillogy to two extensive games such as Bejeweled Twist and Bejeweled Blitz (a more competitve version of Lightning). Which I'd also recommend playing if you own a facebook account. Bejeweled 2 & 3 are probably my most favorite to play to this day. Part of it brings me back to my younger days when I had a computer all to myself for the first time and I explored all the different games my parents installed and the ones that were set up by default when you purchased the operating system. In Bejeweled 2, you saw a massive installment in comparison to the first immediately. You could do puzzles and explore beautifully designed planets all while using your head to solve complex puzzles throughout your journey. Also it introduced us to the amazing use of the Hyper Cube and the Flame gem. The art alone still is breathtaking to look at if you played B2 today. As a fellow artist. I can appreciate the amount of skill and determination these developers put in to create these beautiful and stunning planetary landscapes. Now for Bejeweled 3, a whole new world is brought before you in a whole new environment instead of outer space. You are surrounded in ancient marble remains of lost cities and temples along side with some olden statues of mighty animals. All with beautiful animations if your computer can handle the highest settings. B3 brings back "Endless" which has been renamed to "Zen" in this version while a bunch more levels to surpass compared to B2. The rest you will have to try out for yourself to see. Lastly, one thing I admire about the Steam version of B3 is that you can compete with your high scores against your fellow Steam friends. Unlike in the original B3, you could only have a sense of competition if more than one person used your computer and liked playing B3 as much as you do. So with that said. I'd give this game a 10/10 for beautiful art, animation, & addictive gameplay!

Supergiant Games continue to impress in Pyre, a story driven by player choice as they face off against others in a 3v3 match to extinguish the opposing team's "Pyre" before they can do the same to you. What appears to be a simple game on the surface however, is so vast in its story telling that it becomes nothing short of amazing. Everything that the player does, from chosing how to interact with allies, right down to whom the player decides should be "liberated" alters the story in a way that makes it feel unique; as if you are carving your own path in this game and not following a preset path laid out by the developers. This goes right down to even losing against your opponent which, unlike most story driven games, does not mean a game-over, but only continues to adjust how the story is written; and this includes if enemy characters are liberated themselves.
As per the usual with Supergiant Game's games, Pyre looks fantastic with its colourful artstyle and the music is nothing short of fantastic; setting the tone perfectly. While the controls can be wonky at times, after a couple hours of play it is easy to ajust yourself to get used to them.
A brilliant game which I would recommend to anyone who loves a good story and interesting gameplay to boot

Although one can't help but notice that Knights of the Old Republic 2 is unfinished, with the TSLRCM mod that restores the content and fixes bugs, it is a great game with a fantastic story (although the end feels rushed even with TSLRCM installed). The gameplay is essentially identical to the first game, but there are new force powers and prestige classes that add more depth to the growth of the player as a Jedi or a Sith.
The game starts off slower story-wise than KOTOR 1; Peragus in my opinion was very slow and tedious and in future playthroughs I have used a skip Peragus mod. I also encountered many bugs on the cutscenes in Peragus too, which gave me another reason to skip it after my first playthrough.
Once the story hits its stride it becomes compelling; Kreia in particular is a magnificently written character with many interesting lines that blur the lines between the Light and Dark Sides of the Force. The story is darker and more complex than KOTOR 1 without a doubt.
The companion influence system is very interesting and it is one reason why I preferred the companions in KOTOR 2. Atton in particular is very clever and witty! HK-47 is back and more entertaining than ever. There's a companion for everyone and it's interesting how your actions can influence the alignment of your companions!
This is a solid 8/8.5 out of 10 game for me; it's a very well written game, but I cannot help but think how much better it could've been if the developers were given a little more time to polish the game. It is one of the greatest Star Wars games and RPGs of all time but it had so much untapped potential, and it is a shame that it was not 100% completed by the developers because of a rushed schedule.

I found this game to be one of those games that teaches you to tolerate a new level of frustration.  Velvet Assassin is a stealth game, plain and simple.  You basically solve puzzle after puzzle on a completely linear path with a half-baked story, set sometime during WWII.  The true objective is never really clear throughout the entire game, all the way to the end.  Even after finishing the game, I felt like I really did nothing special and wished I was never tempted to pick this game up during one of those Steam sales.
The graphics are bland, you spend a lot time in dimly lit environments, and the sound is not good.
There are checkpoints sprinkled throughout the game, which save your progress.  These drove me insane.  You might spend 20 - 30 minutes within a given area scouting, and trying to figure out the best course of action, only to be killed by a rogue soldier, and then you get to start from the beginning of the checkpoint, repeating all of the progress you've just made.  Craziness.  I found myself having to simply walk away from this game many times out of pure frustration, which I rarely do with any game.  I like games that steadily progress, but in this game, I found myself redoing scenes of play, over and over, until I completed each part exactly the way the designers of the game wanted me to.
I would label this a very mediocre game, with a large portion of frustrating mechanics.  I would not wish this game on my worst enemy.  Do not even start playing this game if you value keeping your brain as a single solid mass, and not a skull full of  scrambled mush.

Though I've only played this game for 30+ hours, there is a lot to say on this game overall. This is actually my first review on this game, so to make it easier I'll split it up into the negatives and positives for easy reading.
Positives:
-It's an OPEN WORLD. You're free to do whatever the hell you want, when you want to.
-You get to CHOOSE ANY DINO your heart desires. (Though I think this should be interchanged greatly in the full release)
-The CHARACTERISTICS OF EACH DINO is satisfyingly accurate. What I mean is that raptors have low health and small damage, but the highest speed, whereas a Rex has large health w the most damage of a carnivore, with average speed as it should have.
-CHATTING only amongst your own kind offers organization in chat, which also makes the game even more intense when encountering a herd or pack.
-Considering I'm writing this in early access, this game has brought to us PLENTY OF DINO ACCESSIBILITES, such as different types of roars, hunger, thirst, and the feel of having a dino family that only you can decide to trust. This gives us consumers the feel of being a dinosaur. This makes the game consistently interesting. What more can an early access have to offer?
-The DETAIL OF EACH DINO. Not necessarily just the dinos, but the entire game itself. The texture of each dinosaur provides us with smooth performance of the ability to move, eat, drink and roar, with minimal lag. The minimal but precise details allows us to keep our ping at a low 8-20, which is great for a high population game like "The Isle". The lag factor is dependant upon your Internet.
Negatives:
-There's a CLICHE feeling in this game. Though "The Isle" is one of the highest smooth performing early access games, it does feel a bit cliche to a simple simulator.
-The SPAWNS. This is probably one of my most hated negatives of this game so far. Before I talk about this though you should know there is a large lake called "spawn" on one end of "IslaRegionHQ2" map I believe. Just in case, the closest coordinates are (-40, 140, -20; press insert in-game). This is the place where usually every dino gathers, where carnivores come to kill and eat and where herbivores come to establish territory and a family. With some luck, and this has happened to me before, you would spawn very close to this lake and not have to worry about a 5-15 minute journey. However, it is more likely you will spawn on the OTHER END OF THE MAP on a large pop. server.
-LIMPING, which is now more of a positive. About 2 months ago before there was a patch update, dinos would easily break their leg off of a rock. You'd be forced to rest and heal until it healed, usually taking up to half an hour. Now, after this patch healing only takes 5-10 minutes, which is a drastic improvement. The only thing I'd change is the damn fall distance it takes to break a leg. Perhaps off a 5 foot cliff would be permittable.
-Lastly, SERVER CRASHES. I've played a lot of servers on this game in my 33 hours of gaming, and usually the moment a server opens it will most certainly crash at around 40-50 minutes. I've also figured out that the server crashes when there's a lot of dead bodies around, just a heads up. So sadly you won't be able to recreate that perfect herbivore or carnivore family again unless you add them on steam :( .
-DINOSAUR STABILIZATIONS. What I mean is there would be too many damn herbivores/carnivores at a time. I'm hoping there will soon be a patch to limit different dino spawns.
Overall suggestions for this game:
-Dino Stabilization
-Server crashes
-Spawn
-Fall damage distance
-Add a lot more things to the game (including dinoaurs like Pteranadon, Spinosaurus, Iguanadon, Velociraptor, any dino from the Jurassic Park/World trilogy that makes this game more interesting) that makes it seem unique and different from other dinosaur games. I think this game has the potential to be "THE dinosaur game" everyone's talking about apart from ARK and PRIMAL CARNAGE.

Simple and addictive, but also repetive if you play it 12 hours straight.
You play as a leader of a family of four and you control each member to scavenge, fight, or manage around you base. You can expand your community by recruiting new members and build a bigger shelter. You weapons will also advance from sticks and pipes, to crowbars and knives, and eventually gun. At some point your characters may die, and it may create emotional impact on you, but there is no time to mourn but harvest the body and put the meat in the fridge.
Also, enemies can raid your base, and this is the part where I really dislike the game. You can't arm your members with weapons when you get raided so the fights are quite one sided. You can arm traps that are built inside your base, but you can only start arming when the raid started. Aside from that, the shelter is already cramped with all the other items so traps are just gonna make the shelter even more disorangized. Also, there was no instructions on how to arm traps and I spent 10 mins watching my shelter get rekt wondering when I can't arm a shotgun trap when I have ammo (Turns out I need to craft a trip wire too in order to arm the trap).
It is still a good game though, ate 15 hours straight from me and I am likely to replay it again. This time rushing for police stations and getting all the guns so I can start murdering survivors.
Pros:
-Simple gameplay, low complexity but high depth.
-Customized characters that you grow attach to.
-Crafting, with a large amount of items and materials to fiddle with
-Low graphic entry.
-Base building.
Cons:
-Half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tutorial, quite misleading at late game.
Overall:
A total recommend from me. Though I do find it dull when you start rushing the speed up button to get your survivors finish scavenging, it does get fun when you add some narrative in there by doing some role playing.

Yes, this puzzle game will only cost you 99 cents, but the gameplay experience that it provides to players is unique and definitely worth for a try.
Most of the reviews will tell you about the game's gameplay. There is no meaning to do the same thing here. So, I would like to tell you something different, something about what feelings you will get while playing it.
The game does not hide its simplicity. You can easily understand that by looking at its clean and straightforward art style. It gives me the feeling that Hook's developer is trying to have all my attention focusing on the game's mechanics, and sure the art style does its job very well. You will not only feel none disturbance from it while solving the puzzles; it actually will help you focus.
Like its art style, the gameplay is also simple. There are no other things you can do rather than click your mouse's left button. However, while playing the game, you will constantly find yourself lost in contemplation. Observe, think, and act. The game gives its players plenty of time to consider the problem that they are facing, instead of forcing them to react within low limits. In another way of speaking, this game returns gamers to the rightful place. It let us be the one who make the miracle happen.
After all, I have to point out that, the game is not a long one. I believe that most of the players can solve all the puzzles it in less than an hour. However, this 1 hour of gameplay can rarely be found in the recent game market. No funny graphics, no boring CGs, no suffocating gun shootings. All that 1 hour is about you, about your carefulness, about your intelligence, about your decisions. Hook is the game that allows you to just being you, who is a gamer that really to make some magic happen.

Ok, so I am going to be very honest on how I feel about this game.
For one, it is a GAME! You should be wanting to know about IT, not the people that are making it. Yes I know that they are a big part, but complaining about the Devs will just push people away from The Isle. I, for one, bought it even though so many people told me not to, because of the toxic community and the rude, sometimes harrassing, Devs. 100 hours of gameplay in and I havent had any issues with the Devs. If you are so scared of them, just dont give feedback. Enjoy the game for what it already is, and what it WILL BE.
Two, the servers crash A LOT. But you know what? It doesnt really bother me. If youre on a server that saves, relog when you get to where you want, that way when the server crashes you will be there when you log back in. If not, relog till you get a close spawn. Simple as that. I mean it IS in Alpha guys, this will likely go on for a long time. Just work with it.
Three, yes, there are some people out there that are complete asses and will harrass you for being honest or voicing your opinion on the game. They will harrass you for being what they call a "Carebear" or a "KOSer"(I personally dont like KOSers, but they end up dying quickly anyways.) Just play the game how you want to play it, and deal with the way you are reacted to. Again, IT'S A GAME. You paid for it, you play it how you want.
Four, most of the people I have played with are awesome folks, hell, my friends list has quadrupled since I started playing, don't let a small group of fanatics make you think everyone is "toxic."
Five, the visuals are absolutely STUNNING!
All in all, with all the defects that come with an Alpha Game included, I would still recomend this game. It really is worth it. If you aren't sure, then buy it on sale.

. It is a a bare bones point & click linear adventure game with many mildly infuriating components, but is a faithful 5 episode sequel to the BTTF movies.  You play as Marty McFly in 1985 which starts with an homage to the first movie, but takes place after the 3 movies.
:
One track linear story: Your actions don't affect what happens in the story other than progressing it linearly and definitely do not carry over between episodes.  Choose Your Own Adventure books offer more choice.
Dialog selection not consistent with voice acting: On a regular basis I select a dialog choice, and Marty says something that differs in tone and/or content from what I selected, as if voice script was rewritten after the dialog UI was setup.
Movement limited between areas: In 1st episode movement is limited from the front of the courthouse to either side of the courthouse.
Graphics same as lowest common ported denominator: Aside from antialiasing, I may as well have run the game on a Nintendo Wii.  Low poly counts on characters is a bad choice for such a character & dialog driven game.
Episodes have separate settings and launchers: Ever change any of the game settings? Be prepared to change them for each new episode that you launch.  There is no central UI for accessing each of the episodes.
:
Story and atmosphere: This is a story that fits the franchise well and has a number of nuanced details that fans will appreciate.
Voice acting: Telltale found an impressive Fox soundalike actor and Christopher Lloyd's return is great, along with decent supporting voice acting.
Hint system: Great for casual players.

Back to the Future: The Game does a stunning job of recapturing the feel and flavor of the film trilogy that inspired it. Despite lacking some of the functionality Telltale's become known for in later games, especially regards to consequence, BttF is a solid adventure experience through and through with only a few bits I found frustrating.
Set (initially) in Prohibition-era Hill Valley, the bulk of Back to the Future: The Game is an exploration of Doc Brown's past, and how he became the eccentric genius scientist we know him as in the movies. After tracking down Doc following a journey gone a bit awry, Marty McFly's stuck juggling multiple eras of Doc and eventually having to deal with a much different Doc than he's used to. The consequences of minor changes are even more evident this time around than they were in the films, though the quests to fix those changes show a wide variety of Hill Valleys that were and could have been.
First things first, I need to commend all the performers they got to fill the various roles. Marty McFly's voice actor is a dead ringer for 80's-era Michael J. Fox, and the rest of the familiar cast is well-represented. New characters abound without overwhelming familiar faces, and are all established firmly enough that you care about them, be it out of love or of loathing. It's nice that the game manages to give Marty's history some time in the spotlight as well, despite all the focus on Doc.
Progress in the game is based primarily on conversation, working your way through options to figure out what's going on, what to do next, and how to get people to do what you need. There are several points where this can get tedious and/or unclear as to how to proceed, but those bits are few and far between, especially as you get into the later episodes. There's a bit of item collection and use, but it takes a back seat to the dialogue trees, which makes for a great showcase of Telltale's writing skill. Action sequences pop up from time to time as well, which add to the cinematic feel of the game but are also the weakest, gameplay-wise. Several times, I found myself going in circles trying to figure out how to finish an action sequence, only to find I was missing a single, relatively tiny (visually and figuratively) piece of the puzzle. I guess my best advice for these bits is to look up. Always look up.
Other than that, Back to the Future: The Game is absolutely worth your time. A fitting tribute to the films, these five episodes could easily be considered canon if they aren't already.

I'll be updating this review as I continue through the game.
So far, the game is great. The atmosphere, characters and world created by Supergiant Games are all beautiful as always. The music is atmospheric and well made. The game itself is mostly text-based storytelling with choices spread throughout the game. The dialogue is well-written apart from a few typos, and the world is presented in an interesting way, as you glean little details about it as you progress. There is also a narrator that appears during important parts of the game.
The actual mechanical gameplay comes in the form of a sports/battle hybrid called Rites. The aim is to get the ball into the enemy goal (known as the Pyre) while temporarily eliminating their characters from play with aura-based attacks. The individual characters, both on your side and the enemies', are diverse and have their own skills and stats. They progress and unlock different Masteries, allowing them bonuses in the Rites. The Rites steadily increase in difficulty as the game progresses, and sometimes certain effects in the world have an effect in the Rites themselves. Overall, this mode is fun but not for everyone.
The game so far feels compelling, but nothing like Bastion or Transistor. I applaud for taking risks with their new game, as I feel it really works in an unexpected way.

P2P makes a game about precise fighting and movement boarderline unplayable. Hits don't connect, parrys, guardbreaks or blocks are being flat out ignored due to connectivity issues. This issue should be nothing new to Ubisoft and the fix is simple enough; A dedicated server-system that will host the games players set up automatically. Which is a fix Ubisoft also has done in the past. Why they choose to instead repeat previous mistakes is beyond me. However the class-design is an utter mess aswell. Half of the characters outplay the other half by design due to a few VERY obvious design flaws that wouldn't happen to anyone that actually ever played a game once, and im serious here.
Some of the most defense heavy classes have the strongest attacks for no logical reasons, the fastest characters in the game tend to be to fast or have such a range-advantage that they are atrocious to fight and while almost every class enjoys a variety of abilites, a set of characters comes with that one ultimate move that can be cheesed endlessly and i have no idea how anyone was stupid enough to consider this ready for release. After all, avoiding such ultimate moves is one of the highest rules of beat'em'up game-design. And at its core For Honor really wants to be a Beat'em'up. The worst detail in this is, that these issues HAVE been reported and discussed in BOTH the open AND closed beta, yet nothing was done to fix them.
Which brings me to the last issue, which is the inability of the dev-team to pay attention. They seem utterly incompetent, oblivious or both to fix the issues that matter. Instead they focus on cheaters who - now that they openly stated what they would do - ironically begin to pop up more and more. Maybe they are just unwilling to listen as well. I can understand that a developer has to carefully seperate whining from actual crticism, but when those issues are reported from beta-testers you selected as well as from the open-beta and release players not fixing or commenting on the issue is downright insulting to everyone ever investing time.
And thats For Honor right now. Insulting and infuriating, no matter what quality your playstyle is. And thats a shame, since underneath all the lackluster design choices (that were already present in previous ubisoft games as well) lies a game with huge potential that tries to reach the surface, but will suffocate and die in less then two months if its creators don't pick up the pace...

Warning Spoilers:
Amnesia is a Horror-Puzzle game made by Frictional Games. The game is focused on story and atmosphere, so if what you're expecting is more intense chasing games (Like Outlast or even Slender to a certain extent) this will not suit your taste.
The game puts you in the body of Daniel, a man seeking vengeance in the hopes of killing "Alexander", the story is told by notes, narration and flashbacks and will start making more sense as the game goes by. The voice acting isn't the greatest but it's not bad either.
The puzzles are really fun to solve, they're not the hardest thing in the world and you probrably won't get stuck in any of them, they're also not too easy and boring like some games.The game rewards you for exploring, giving you TinderBoxes (which can be useful sometimes) and Oil for your lantern, it can also give you items that are crucial to your progress like levers or liquids you have to use to progress.
The atmosphere of the game is great, it's not stupidly dark, it gives you a lantern that consumes oil, but you probrably won't run out of it, I finished my game with 4 jars of oil left, just remember to keep exploring the place, not only that but after staying a little bit in the dark you start seeing a little better but your sanity will start to go down. You can grab, rotate and throw a lot of objects, which is a fun gameplay factor and a cool thing to mess around with,
The loading screens are a nice touch as it doesn't take away your attention from the game giving you some story-related quotes, since there are a lot of them it's very unlikly that one will appear twice on the same playtrough. The soundtrack is really good and it really helps you get a feel for the game specially on the chasing parts.
The chasing of the game isn't the best,
Amnesia : Justine is a small Free-DLC, it presents you with some scares and monster hiding along with 3 small puzzles, you will be presented with a person, you can choose to kill it and ignore the puzzle, or you can save them by completing the puzzles. The story and chasing scenes happens a lot faster than the original game making this DLC last for only about 1 hour.
This game has mod support making it last a lot more hours than it would normally, the editor is pretty easy to use, for the people that want to build mods themselves.The community has put out a lot of great mods like Obscurity ; In Lucy's Eyes and many, many others that you can find online. They can also usually be more "intense" than the original game, cutting right to the chase and starting at the running and hiding parts for the people who prefer games like that. It's great to see how big this community once was, even if right now there are not that many people making mods/custom stories for the game. (The game is quite old and it's popularity by YouTube Creators it's drastically lower than it used to be.)
Just like I said on the beggining of the review, if you want chasing and thrill you will be bored by this game really fast, if you want some puzzle slow paced game this will be a great experience.

I'd really like avoid reviewing the game based on its predecessors. Amnesia: TDD is a great game but doesn't have any real bearing on Soma. While there are a lot of similarities, Soma is its own game and deserves to be treated as one. With that being said, there are mechanical similarities and its method of storytelling hasn't strayed too far off. I would strongly recommend you play both games and compair them for yourself.
Soma asks a lot of deap questions about ethics of replacing humans with machines. Can humans continue to exist without a physical presance? I'm woefully unqualified to answer such questions, but it is interesting to at least think about and determine what your own beliefs are. The game asks you to draw a line at what your own ethics are and then asks you to cross the line. It pushes you toward an end that you know is coming and has you decide for yourself based on your own morals. The process of making you cross that line has you questioning weather or not you believe in human consciousness. You know that there can be a better place and going there takes your humanity, but realizing that you already sacrificed it has you thinking if you really want to live anymore. Is it right to end your own life yet allow a simulation of yourself to live as a soulless duplicate? Answering these questions is difficult so don't think you will have a clearly defined threshold, just remember the things discussed in the game might not be science fiction for much longer.
The story has a lot going for it. The confusion of things you don't yet know provides a great platform for learning and horror. It reinforces the mechanical aspects of the game and allows you to be immersed in the world that you are currently questioning. Is anything even real anymore? The way we experience the supporting characters shows us that the boundarys between real and virtual have been smeared. At first you believe that the workers are being controlled by humans, but you quickly realize that there aren't anymore living people. They all exist in a virtual world. The realization that you have the power to destory the last remnant of someone just by turning off the power is horrifying.
Mechanics can set the tone and pace of a game. Soma is a good balance betweek keeping the pace of the game moving forward but slowing you down just enough to think about what you're doing. With that in mind there are some issues. Those of you familiar with Frictional's previous games will feel right at home with the controlls and physics of the game. you will understand how the puzzles are layed out and what you need to do to proceed. This is when the game is at its worst. Part of a horror game is not knowing what to do, how do you move on? Soma lacks the complexity of inventory management. It doesn't ask you to keep track of how much of a light source you have left. Managing these different aspects adds an uncertanty to the game it is sorely missed. Uncertanty can add to the fear of moving forward; not knowing whats ahead and if you will be prepared or not. Pushing forward into the unknown is the most horrifying thing about Frictional's games and some of the seriousness was taken out of those elements by knowing that you are prepared for whatever comes your way.
Overall this game still provides great scares and exploration of its setting and philosophys. It questions your own morals and limits as a player. I would strongly recommend this game to anyone looking to try out this genre and encourage you to try out Amneisa and compair the games for yourself.

It took me a while to come back around to this game because of one particular section, but after finding a way around it I'm in the home stretch, so I felt it was time to write a little bit about the game.
I love the storyline. It's clear that this is where Frictional truly worked their hardest, and the thematic elements of life, death and beyond are captivating. The voice acting is also very good, proving an effective means to immerse the player in the sunken experiment of PATHOS-II. But one thing in particular has been eating at me throughout the course of the game: the monsters. Frictional has done a fantastic job with their creatures prior to this; even A Machine for Pigs, usually noted as a low point in the Frictional canon, impressed me with the placement of the enemies, more of an augmentation to an overall unpleasant atmosphere, and a somewhat frightening unknown in a world that seems to consistently make you question the validity of the shoes you walk in, as well as emphasizing dread over numerous encounters. The Dark Descent did it masterfully as well, creating a hostile environment that felt escapable but purposeful in the way the monsters occupied the world, a manifestation that could be either of the mind or of reality, informed in their grotesque nature by the unstable mind you occupy.
SOMA does not provide the player with obvious conclusions as to why these monsters are there, let alone provide them as a means to convey a horrific situation. Instead they border on busy work, quite frequently causing the player aggravatingly pointless inconvenience. My playthrough has taken much longer than I expected for that reason, and while the creatures are intriguing to look at and clearly designed well, for a player who cannot seem to justify their existence more than for a Frictional touch on the game, I do not see what contribution they make to an otherwise incredibly well thought out story. I did some reading online and uncovered some of the lore related reasons for their presence, but it did little to answer my overarching problem with the gameplay; why create an unnecessary nuisance to inhibit players from progression and reveal the flawed fetch quests the game otherwise had a solid, story centric purpose for?
When the game was announced, the developers said that they wanted any player to be able to finish the game, and to do so at their own pace. But it seems as though the developers have not taken into account that the enemies they ejected so unnaturally into the game do little to explain themselves, and create disinterest in finishing the game thanks to the uneven pace that comes from its irritating hide and seek. Even now I find myself only attempting to finish the game for the lack of other titles that have been released that meet the somewhat uncommon science fiction horror criteria, mostly because of the excellence of the Alien franchise, which finally has an adaptation in video games worth playing, and I will always remember that game fondly.
In short, SOMA is to games as Event Horizon is to film; all of the pieces are in place for something truly amazing, easily outshining many other titles in design and narrative in its ambition. But in the end, poor pacing and badly executed scare tactics prevent it from being a true classic, and I'll only remember it for what flaws prevented it from being the experience that it could have been.
Play it for the story, and leave it at that.

I walked into Breach & Clear hoping for some serious copy of former SWAT series. What I got was a sort of XCOM copy. Although the games tactics may appeal to you, some of the lack of attention to minor details may upset you. I got this game on extreme sale and would recommend you do too.
Plain and simple, this game is no where near the level of what SWAT 3 or 4 was. Still to this day, there hasn't been a SWAT game that has managed to immerse the player as much as those two have. Breach & Clear is a top-down turn based swat action game where your main objective every time is still simply wipe every enemy out on the map. It's fun at first, but the lack of diverse objectives make the game redundant. At the very least, opponents do move about the map when you initiate contact. Meaning, if they are not taken out and you do not having any squad member watching your back, they may sneak up on you. Upon starting a level, the player can scope out what entrances are available and can tell each officer where to start. The game play itself is not bad. You are in control of four units in which you can tell them where to move and how to move. Choosing movement paths was decently done.
Say for instance you would like to go down an open hallway as it can be a little tricky sending one unit at a time to deal with the danger. The system in place lets you choose multiple points on where the unit should go (so broken paths) and additionally, let's you choose which way to face. This latter fact is important in providing the appropriate cover for your units. If your unit is caught off guard due to not looking the right direction, there is a good chance he'll be shot and may go down. The movement itself can be modified as a unit can be told to walk slower to increase his accuracy and allow other units to catch up or overtake. Grenades and flash bangs are available to use upon purchase. Yes you heard me right, this police force has to replenish it's supplies after every run. Every time you use it, you're going to have to replace it if you want to use it again.
There are some units that are able to throw and continue their movement while some units spend their turn throwing the ordinance. This dependence is directly related to the classes you choose. For instance, a fire team leader has the ability to draw fire, a weapons sergeant can use his suppress fire ability to possibly save a comrade in trouble, a breacher can throw a grenade and continue to move along his path instead of ending his turn, a medic (I'll leave this one up to your imagination) and a direct action soldier can go in quietly. Depending on how you want to go in, it's really up to you to choose what's the best combination. I use a fire team leader, a medic and two breachers just because I like making noise. Each individual can upgrade (level wise) as you progress. You can upgrade stats such as accuracy or speed to improve your character. As well, their weapons can be modified with special sights or with fore grips. What drives me extremely mental in the game is the fact there is a pause after every turn to tell you it's the next phase. I believe that could have been done by being a lot more subtle.
The graphics themselves are okay. Their nothing extremely over the top or triple A, but simply okay. The player can maneuver the camera but it can never go exactly where you want it (or if your an explorer don't count on looking around too in-depth). What is nice is that sometimes the camera will go over the shoulder when shooting down suspects or going through a door. The sounds are okay as well. Gun shots sound more or less similar while there is no real dialogue going on.
Honestly, it's an alright game if it's on sale. I'm not recommending it because truth be told, I'd rather play XCOM or UFO when I start playing this. I also don't like the fact it's turn based and how the equipment scheme was set up.

I have played Survarium for a bit of time (12 hours or so?). I am still fairly new to the game, so this review is not as complete as I want it to be. Of course, the game is in Beta, so most of what I state here may change, and I will not go too in depth with stats/balance since the matchmaking places people in games depending on the level of their gear. I will describe the leveling of the game first.
You have your character level, a passive ability tree, and faction levels.
Your character level affects the amount of points you get in your ability tree. Each character level grants you 1 point in this ability tree.
The ability tree at the moment contains passive modifiers including, but not limited to, +% Sprint Speed, or +% Aim Down Sight Speed.
There are 4 factions. The Scavengers, Black Market, Renassaince Army, and the Fringe Settlers. As you complete matches, and missions, you gain reputation for the faction you currently joined. You can switch between factions whenever you would like, without fee. However, The Renaissance Army, and the Fringe Settlers are locked until you completely level one of the starter factions ( The Scavengers, and The Black Market are the starting factions.)
Now, I will describe the gear/equipment/weapons/armor.
There are currently 55 weapons purchasable through the shop. The majority of these weapons are bought with only the in-game-earned currency. Only 14 of these 55 purchasable weapons can only be bought with Gold, the Cash-currency of the game. To unlock certain weapons, you must obtain a certain level within the faction it belongs to.
There are six weapons that you can only obtain as item-drops after a match.
As for armors, there are 20 sets of armor. All are only purchasable with the in-game-earned currency. There are 4 armor sets for each of the starter factions (The Scavengers and The Black Market). The other factions have 6 armor sets each.
There are some notable mechanics Survarium has that I find refreshing, and some of them that I have only seen in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. franchise. I like the fact that if you are shot, you can end up bleeding, although I am not entirely sure of the bleed mechanic's parameters. You have to buy medkits/bandages in the shop to use them in-game, in order to heal yourself or stop the bleeding. The bandages/medkits are very cheap in terms of in-game-earned currency.
The game also has Friendly fire, so shooting through your ally to hit your enemy will not work here. You are punished for Team killing with a negative score, keeping you from earning currency to repair your gear, and progressing.
Anomalies are present in the game, and they can kill. There is also gear which an help keep you alive in anomalies for longer, although not indefinitely (I think).
Something I love is that although rifles/sniper rifles have a very low rate of fire compared to the Submachine guns/Assault rifles/Light Machine guns, most of the time the rifles/sniper rifles will be a one shot kill, or leave your target near death through the bleed mechanic.
I recommend the game as it is, with it's aesthetic most comparable to the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. franchise. Survarium also has some promising features on the way. When I have experienced more of the game, I will try and compose a better review. For now, I will be playing some more.

Before I start with this review I want to point out that this is from my little personal experience with the game and it will be different from yours, so please, keep that in mind.
I honestly didn't want to give this game a bad review (And I'm not a person of doing reviews, much less a bad one) but I have to.
Friday the 13th is a survival horror game where you play as a counselor and try to escape from the map through different ways or you play as the famous killer Jason Voorhees in which you have to kill every counselor in the game. The game itself has a good concept, but some problems holds it back.
-Spawning: As far as I know the places where you spawn are always random and the same thing goes for the items, but there are some times you spawn next to important items or next to Jason (Those two happened to me).  There was this time I started a game and I spawned close to a car battery, some minutes later (3-5) I found some counselors repairing a car and guess what, they were missing a car battery, I helped them and then we escaped, without signs of Jason around. Or the other time where I spawned close to Jason and in which he found me and afterwards killed me, and that was in less than 5 minutes into the match. In short, you either spawn in a good place or a bad place.
-Connection problems: This was often a problem for me, and I have a good connection to the internet. Not to mention the problems that the servers were having at launch.
-The price: I don't think $39.99 is a good price for a game that offers little content:
*10 counselors with so little customization.
*8 different versions of Jason.
*3 maps only.
-Some bugs/glitches.
I still have high hopes that this game will improve with some time because the devs are working hard to fix all the problems right now, but until then, I wouldn't recommend this game in its current state

Move over God of War there is another game based on Greek mythology and it is Apotheon. Sure some Greek Gods show up as personas in Persona 3 or playable gods in Smite, but there aren’t many games entirely set in Greek mythology. With all that said, it is very unfortunate that Apotheon doesn’t do anything much with its’ story. The story is similar to that of God of War without the constant talk of being angry and yearning to have revenge. Zeus being a jerk that he is abandons humanity causing chaos and grief. You play as Nikandreous, a Greek warrior that saves his town from an attack from bandits. He is then greeted by Hera and she explains that the origin of humanity’s suffering is caused by Zeus. The only way Nikandreous can save humanity is by killing gods gaining their power and eventually challenging Zeus.
The visual design is Apotheon’s strongest suit and makes an immediate impact once the game is booted up for the game for the first time. The game looks as if you were playing on ancient Greek pottery. There is a loving attention to detail from how the characters move across the screen as if they were drawn on actual pottery. One striking example is how your character climbs ladders on its’ sides rather than directly in front of it.
The colors match the ancient Greek pottery to a tee, with an emphasis on yellow and red hues. Unfortunately, the game rarely mixes up its’ art style. I found the yellow and red hues especially difficult to look at for gaming sessions longer than an hour. It felt like the equivalent of playing back to back Mario lava levels for one hour straight. There are some some levels that introduce blue and green hues, but they are the exception to the rule.
The gameplay in Apotheon plays like a metroidvania game without the gating element. Once you have access to lockpicks and Greek fire which is gained a little past the tutorial, you’re free navigate to any area within a level. You do gain powers by defeating bosses in Apotheon, but they only serve to advance the story and improve Nikandreous’ combat effectiveness.
Speaking of combat, Nikandreous can wield swords, axes, lances, bows, maces and more. Each weapon has a wind-up time as well as an attack range requiring the player to switch between weapons mid-combat depending on the situation. Attacking an enemy with a spear that’s too close and the spear won’t connect. You can throw your weapon directly at the enemy and pick it back up, offering a stylish alternative to finish off a ranged enemy without resorting to bows or javelins. There is also a stamina bar that prevents you from spamming attacks. Rounding out the list of combat options are shields, a combat roll and craftable utility items like Greek Fire, potions and armor kits.
The combat sounds well designed but is easily abused. Ranged combat works as intended, but become extended affairs especially against shielded foes. There is no enemy collision so you can literally walk into the enemy and swing at him until he dies. In fact you can do this with almost any weapon even spears as long as you have Nikandreous aim directly above or below. Once I was out of stamina, I would roll out the way, let it recharge and redo this process. I was able to repeatedly do this even against late game foes.
The other issue with the combat is its’ physics. There are some enemies that can throw Nikandreous. On one occasion, my character was thrown into a wall and clipped through the other side. On another occasion, my character clipped through a wall and was instakilled. There are also explosions and certain enemies that can knockback Nikandreous. The knockbacks have a tendency to bounce Nikandreous ludicrously high in the air allowing you to skip major portions of a level if timed correctly.
Inventory management is unintuitive and clunky. The weapons and items are arranged vertically as small icons and becomes a mess to go through especially halfway into the game. There is no way to sell items so you’ll often find yourself rummaging through ten to twenty melee and ranged weapons. Adding insult to injury is that some weapons are completely buggy. The discus weapon for example is a boomerang-like weapon, that returns to Nikandreous after being thrown. Once the discus returns to the player, the weapon is automatically equipped. There were occasions when the discus was permanently affixed as my equipped weapon and I was unable to change weapons. In order to fix the issue, I had to throw the discus and have it get stuck in the environment. Also there is no quest log and I wasn’t even aware that there were optional quests until I checked the item section in my inventory.
Technical issues also find its’ way in the audio department. The music was fine, but the sound effects and voice acting were completely silent. After some quick Google searches, I discovered that the game does not work for speakers in surround sound settings and must be set to stereo. I had my speakers set to surround sound for over a year and this is the first game where I’ve encountered such an issue.
Ultimately Apotheon is a satisfactory but flawed metroidvania type game. The game is absolutely gorgeous and nails the ancient Greek pottery art look. But looks are the only thing the game does right, everything else about Apotheon is marred with clunky combat and technical issues. I can’t recommend Apotheon to anyone unless if you’re into Greek Art. If you want to play a metroidvania game that looks great and does its’ combat justice I would recommend playing Guacamelee instead.

You're going to hear a lot of 'buts' in this little review.
As of right now, the game mechanics encourage casual play for maximum enjoyment, so I recommend you play it with friends, or get a party of people going. That's the main reason why I've played this game so much already. It's the social interaction you experience when playing, when a counselor ditches another, when a counselor tries to save someone on their drive out of the camp with Jason hot on their tail, when Jason is taunting his victims, ... THAT is most of the fun in the game right now. And I hope the devs recognize this.
I really wish there was more content right now, more maps, more kills (I know they use motion capture and it's a pain to get them out, but right now the kills are, in my opinion, the best part of the game), more ways that jason can mess with the counselors rather than being a tank that just charges after them, more interactions between counselors, more unique features for specific characters, stuff like that.
Playing this game is absolutely NOT a bad experience despite my complaints, I had fun and I think others will too if they buy it, but... the potential! There's just so much! Luckily, the devs seem to be working on some free updates, with new maps and kills coming, which is exactly what I believe this game needs. Hopefully, they also add more features focused on interaction as well.
tl;dr
It's not bad, but the game could be better and have more content for the price tag they've given it. The game is quite buggy in it's current state but devs seem to be trying to patch it up.

Supergiant Games continue to impress in Pyre, a story driven by player choice as they face off against others in a 3v3 match to extinguish the opposing team's "Pyre" before they can do the same to you. What appears to be a simple game on the surface however, is so vast in its story telling that it becomes nothing short of amazing. Everything that the player does, from chosing how to interact with allies, right down to whom the player decides should be "liberated" alters the story in a way that makes it feel unique; as if you are carving your own path in this game and not following a preset path laid out by the developers. This goes right down to even losing against your opponent which, unlike most story driven games, does not mean a game-over, but only continues to adjust how the story is written; and this includes if enemy characters are liberated themselves.
As per the usual with Supergiant Game's games, Pyre looks fantastic with its colourful artstyle and the music is nothing short of fantastic; setting the tone perfectly. While the controls can be wonky at times, after a couple hours of play it is easy to ajust yourself to get used to them.
A brilliant game which I would recommend to anyone who loves a good story and interesting gameplay to boot
