Doom is a legendary FPS that came out in 1993 on PC and was ported to many other consoles, with ports of various quality. It was released by shareware model and had 3 episodes if your ordered. Later it was released as Ultimate Doom, adding the 4th episode.
Compared to other ports it has full levels and most content. PS1 and Saturn port have it combined with Doom 2 levels and have dark horror atmosphere, with N64 having it's own dark horror atmosphere and was like a new game build from scratch, with it's own levels. The only thing some ports have over PC technically got to be colored lighting. So, you don't miss much, be happy with DOS version.
As old game, we should take a look at how Steam version handles Doom. And well, Id Software once again did a horrible job with handling DOSBox.
First, it wasn't configured probably, thus it lags amazingly in full-screen mode. To fix that you have to go to game's folder and edit line at "output" to "opengl" in "ultimate.conf" and "ultimatem.conf" files.
Second, as you launch game you will notice that you get to choose two control methods: with mouse and classic (Like real man, keyboard only!). And it uses Soundblaster device for Music instead of Midi that everybody is used to. You may think that you can use DOSBox, navigate to game's folder and launch "setup.exe" to configure stuff for yourself, but too bad! Id Software decided not to put it into Steam's version. Your only way to configure controls and music is editing "DEFAULT.CFG" and "MOUSE.CFG" files. Where you have to guess which numbers is related to what keyboard button.
But once you fixed all those issues you will finally get to play Doom. Ultimate edition, yep. Without any plot or cutscenes... Errr, aside from those at the end of episodes. Without much plot and cutscenes, you are going to be immeditly thrown into levels, each one being a compilated maze and a step over the ealier FPS levels, also having buttons to press which can do something else aside from opening doors and keys to collect. Each of 4 episodes has 8 normal levels and 1 secrets, and I gotta say that the secret level of the third episode is brilliant idea. I also should mention that the first, WHOLE first episode is available for free in demo (shareware) version of a game, and that game is easier than Doom 2 in general. Aside form the 4th episode, which was added with Ultimate Doom version and is even harder than Doom 2, especially first few levels, though that episode doesn't have any new content to it.
The presentation of the game is quite good. It's colorful more or less while giving it a dirty darkish feeling. Heck, game was considered scary at release, with usage of sector lighting, it even has has fog-like effect where you can see less clearly in dark places, nice. The resolution isn't big and colors are still quite limited, but with all the maze nacigation and sprite scaling it had to do, the game was at the top of technology cutting edge, especially in FPS genre. At least on PC and consoles, Arcades were still kicking. So, you can say that this was the point where console players got something to envy PCs over, while playing their own awesome platformers.
Gameplay is just plain awesome, pure arcadeish FPS. It's quite a fast-paced game, with many pickups, wide enemy variety, set of weapons, non-regenerating health, map that you can call with Tab so you will not get lost in mazes and, most importantly, instead of being focused on cover-hiding, it was more about projectile avoidance and more out-into-field shooting and running. Well, almost. Zombie enemies still shoot hitscan at you, but those are low-tier enemies, die easily, not used as much as imps. And compared to many other FPS at that time, Doom is more of fair challenge. Once again, Doom is not perfect, it got hitscan zombies with gun and it even forces you to run over damaging acid/lava few times in some levels, it's not Heretic, but compared to games on Build engine, it's better.
Though one of the things that may put people off is that levels are abstract mazes. Looking nice but making no logical sense of place to it.
It has 8 weapons to keep, from useless fist and pistol, up to BFG9000. It's not perfectly balanced, plasmagun outdoes chaingun, while chaingun outdoes pistol while using same ammo pool, but it's a step over Wolf3D, as in some situation some weapons are better. The effective use of BFG9000 also doesn't make common sense, you should read FAQ somewhere over this. But hey, at least it was before SuperShotgun came, with it being best weapon in whole game in Doom 2.
Dissapointing thing got to be bosses. There is only few. Two uncommon dangerous Barons of Hell in Episode 1, which were used later anyway. And then there is Cyberdemon in Episode 2 who's attack can be avoided too easily and Spider Mastermind in Episode 3 who has hitscan attack and you just have to rush him down. Episode 4 also doesn't have anything of it's own.
Multiplayer isn't supported in Steam version, you will have to use Zandronum source port. Or some other mutlipalyer source ports.
So, Ultimate Doom is awesome FPS. Simpler than Doom 2, but less brown and has it's own feel. You get to run over mazes while shooting down enemies in fast-paced manner. It's legendary too, though not perfect game. Highly recommended, none the less.
If you want to get into Doom modding and mods, then instead head toward Doom 2 destination, sir.

I understand this review might seem premature...but I honestly feel as thought I have gained enough of a grasp of what little there is in this game :/ Now do not get me wrong, as an early access game I recognize that there will be more in the future, but I just can't really recommend it at the moment in its current state.
This game requires EXTENSIVE updates and optimizations, the grass itself being the most pixelated, GPU-intensive, framerate dropping, eye sore grass I have ever witnessed @_@. The graphics even on epic are not very impressive at all, and are certainly on the lower end of the spectrum. But in the event you even attempt to run the game on the highest graphical settings without an incredibly powerful setup, you are more than likely to have frame rate dropped to 15 because of the grass, which is ridiculous.
Aside from that, there is just...nothing to do in this game to be honest :/ Pkayers are way too predictable in the sense that they all crowd in a single area of the map around a center lake, hording bodies to consume if their dinosaur gets hungry. Other than though, you rarely see other roaming virtually at all, because there is simply no incentive or reward for doing so, not even in terms of survival. I have seen a few players starve to death from getting lost in the vast expandse of the large map and not being able to find anyone. But other than that, there is simply nothing to do... I really believe that this game needs the implementation of some AI creatures or dinosaurs here and there in order to counteract the sense of void and lifelessness that plagues this game.
Furthermore, there are many issues concerning various bugs:
-Command for eating may not function for herbivores in some instances, leading them to starve to death.
-Broken bones on many occasions will simply not heal for real times hours on end, leading to many players simply killing their dino in order to respawn with a normal status.
-Combat between carnivores and herbivores is insanely bugging and heeds advantages to aggressive herbivores that can one or two shot a carnivore with well placed hits, whereas the carnivores are pretty much required to gang up on the herbivore in order to take one down.
I really would like to enjoy this game for its intentions...but I just can't recommend it as it feels like it is going to become the next "the Hunter: Primal" or "Stomping Lands", etc. :/

Back to the Future: The Game is quite possibly the best movie-based game ever made. If you are at all a fan of the films, you will definitely enjoy this title.
The story picks up after Part III, where Doc Brown has disappeared, and when his DeLorean appears out of nowhere, you must take control of Marty McFly and travel through time to find Doc and prevent the destruction of the space-time continuum. As the story really is this game’s main selling point, I won’t spoil it for you – find out what happens as you play through. At one point Bob Gale, the producer for the films, stated that the game’s story can be essentially considered Back to the Future Part IV.
The gameplay is highly reminiscent of the old LucasArts SCUMM adventure games such as The Secret of Monkey Island and Maniac Mansion, with the only major difference being that you control Marty directly with the WASD keys and not by clicking where you want him to go. To progress, you interact with characters to learn new information, and pick up and use items in appropriate places to complete goals. Those goals are visible in your inventory, and if you get stuck, you can ask for up to 3 optional hints (depending on the puzzle you are on).
The game is divided into 5 episodes, and each one is a separate game that must be downloaded individually. This is fine, but just a heads-up - your play records won’t be combined.
You can save at any time you’d like – IF YOU AREN’T DOING A PUZZLE. If you are in an action sequence of any sort, or doing a multi-step puzzle, you cannot save until it has been completed. This is a slight flaw in that it sometimes forces you to play for extended periods of time if you don’t want to scrap what you’ve been working on.
Each episode will take you 2 to 4 hours to complete, and the game in total will clock in at around 15 hours. It’s a very fun adventure and a surprisingly thoughtful story. The difficulty level isn’t too high, and you won’t be forced to go to the Internet for a walkthrough more than 2 or 3 times if you’re familiar with point-and-click games and have good lateral thinking skills. Unfortunately, the replay value here is very low, simply due to the type of game Back to the Future is. Once you’ve completed the game, there really isn’t a point to going back and playing through it a second time, because it will just be the same story over again. But for a single play-through, it’s a lot of fun.
In conclusion, I would highly recommend Back to the Future: The Game to anyone who is a fan of the films (or the LucasArts games) and is looking for another story featuring the characters they know and love. It’s a true BTTF adventure from start to finish =)

The first thing to really notice about Apotheon is the art: the aesthetic choices for the game are truly superb.  The whole game looks like it's taking place on the side of an ancient Greek vase, and the lines and composition are frequently beautiful. The soundtrack is quite good, and the voice acting is above par to boot, making for a great experience overall.  The game incorporates snippets of Greek mythology, from the writings of Homer to various Orphic hymns, producing an unusual atmosphere for a video game, let alone one of this category.
Mechanically - well, it's a side-scrolling 2-D platformer.  That isn't one of my favorite genres by a long shot (in fact, I usually avoid them).  This category inevitably means a bit of frustration for me with the de rigueur boss fights, the lack of any choice in how the story plays out, and so on.
Apotheon got quite a bit better for me, though, once I moved from keyboard-and-mouse to Steam controller to play, with a minor exception (as I'll explain below).  With mouse and keyboard, it's just too hard to be facing the right direction when fighting, but controller play deals with that considerably better.  Except when you need to, say, aim down a long tunnel to hit a target with an arrow.  Then I pretty much had to go back to mouse and keyboard for that specific trick - no amount of fussing with my Steam controller settings could get the aiming to work with any amount of sensitivity, and there is no way to address sensitivity in-game at all.
(It's worth noting that I have played other 2-D side-scrollers with mouse and keyboard without this problem and I have played other 2-D side-scrollers with the Steam controller without these problems.  These issues seem to be something very particular about how Apotheon works, and it is the worst aspect of the game.)
Many players also complain that the combat is clunky, and I can honestly say that I find it terrible - but that is with the caveat that I frequently find the combat in these sorts of games terrible, so I can't tell if it's genuinely wonky, or I just do not enjoy this sort of thing and since I am only trying to get through the silly boss fights to see where the story actually goes and what the next area looks like.  Just know that in Apotheon, strikes must be aimed and they must be relatively precise; meanwhile enemies will dodge - and will often spring around crazily like mad frogs - which I found to be somewhat disconcerting, and which did not seem to fit well with the game's other artistic choices and tone.  Bottom line though: if you're looking for someone to appreciate unusual or varied combat in game of this genre, it's definitely not me, so take what I say with that grain of salt here.
I got best into the game by floundering through the opening level, mashing buttons until I had (slowly) sublimated attacking, dodging and rolling, and switching weapons, and then I started over in order to pay attention to the story and scenes instead of being focused more on "Oh damn it, I didn't mean to throw that! Bwah! Why am I facing the wrong direction?!?"  That generally provided a better experience for that secondary start and subsequent play.
Otherwise, though, the game is an interesting experience, and looking around provided me a ton of entertainment.  I'd definitely buy and play follow-ups to this game in the vein of Egyptian, Japanese, Sumerian, Aztec, and so on just to see the art and experience the mythology, honestly.  It's worth the admission price for that alone.

is a 2D post-apocalyptic survival game in which your objective is to survive for as long as possible. Manage your own shelter and family as they face resource scarcity, diseases, moral dilemmas, stress and trauma. Your family has established themselves in an old bunker and it’s here where you’ll spend your last days on Earth.
Before going into the game, you get a chance to give your own personal touch to your family, which is constituted by 4 members, 2 adults and 2 children. You can customize their appearance, as well as choose a different trait and set of stats for each. You can also choose to have a pet such as, a snake, a cat or a dog, each one having their own pros and cons. Despite initially choosing a set of stats for your family members, these can be improved by fighting or talking your way out with strangers. You’re also able to recruit more people to your shelter but these will start out by acting automatically in your shelter, you’ll only be able to order them around and send them on expeditions when their loyalty is high enough.
Your initial shelter is pretty basic and lacks most essentials so you’ll need to get your hands to work from the get go. It is vital that you keep an eye on your shelter systems conditions and repair them so that they don’t go bad. Things like the water filter and air filter should always be in good shape in order to prevent disasters. The water filter is particularly important because it allows you to gather water when it rains. However, if it starts raining “black rain”, you have to watch out because your water will get poisoned. There are also other events that might take place on your base, such as dust storms, raids or being approached by traders and people who’re looking for a roof above their heads.
That said, there are other ways for you to gather water and resources necessary to crafting, upgrading and expanding your shelter. You can send a maximum of 2 of your people away on expeditions by using a radio. There is however two things you must, or should, have when preparing these, enough water to endure the trip (otherwise the game won’t let you) and gas maks to protect yourself from radiation poisoning. On the world map, you’ll be able to set a series of waypoints for your party to go through and you’ll also be able to see various different buildings that you can search, each with certain types of items and resources. Still, you can’t just hoard everything you find because your characters have an inventory limit (as does your shelter), so you should know what you’re looking for and craft bags in order to carry more items.
The game is divided into two different styles of play. Combat is turn-based and the management part is in real-time, with the option to speed up time. Combat is pretty simple and it plays like most turn-based RPGs out there, attack, defend or try some other special move on the enemy, rinse and repeat. As for the management side, it plays pretty much like a point and click game, select a character and click what you want to interact with. You’ll need to be able to keep up with your shelter needs early on, which include, cleaning, repairing, fueling the generator, and keep your family needs satisfied. This involves a great deal of micromanagement, so depending on your tastes, you’re either going to find it really addictive or really repetitive.
Overall Sheltered has been a rather amusing and fun experience. From dealing with people trying to force their way into my shelter, to bullying grown ups with my kids, the game has it all. You can even eat your dead family members! Still, I feel like the game could’ve been much more if it focused just a little on story or character interactions.

---A lot of the negative reviews are outdated---
Most of the negative reviews posted  stated that there was only "one game mode" or "the player base is mean". There's 2 game modes now, one a capture the flag, the other basic PvP. Both gametypes are fun to play and easy to understand. Perhaps due to this and the fact the game is freaking FREE, some players that come on arn't the brightest or nicest. But overall most people are quiet and stick to themselves.
PROS:
-The game has easy, intuitive controls combined with great animations. From walking to reloading, the animations and quality of the graphics are great. The controls feel realistic and adds a great "feel" to walking around, gunning people down in irradiated soviet-esque buildings.
-The scenery is breathtaking in almost every map. As a free to play game this is great! A lot of time and effort seems to have been put into textures and scenery with great glowing hazes around military waste barrels, craters filled with glowing blue ooze, and irradiated reactors. One map even has a great mutated tree, twisted and knarled into the various buildings surrounding it, upon which players scramble to climb to drop down on unsuspecting players.
-Textures. Really, REALLY good textures that can look and run great on low platform computers.
-Hardly any lag. I havn't experienced it one bit and I've got an average connection.
-Factions with very specific weapons and armor, from the all rounder bikers, the extreme lightweight fringe settlers, to the heavy weight Renaissance Army. Each factions comes with a specific skill set and brings it to the table (or face) of the other.
-Money shop is decent. Nothing flying in your face saying "BUY OUR SH*T NOW! LOOK AT THESE PINK $25.00 MITTENS. YOU NEED THEM". If you want some cool weapons you can shell out for them, but there isn't anything game breaking or Pay 2 Win like Planet Side 2. A newbie player with the right mindset can easily take down a better equipped character from the store. Just takes more bullets, and a bullet to the head is still a great equalizer.
CONS:
-Many negative reviews. Not that the game is bad, but people were expecting more and took it to heart to bash the game before it's finalized. Might hurt your experience in-game.
-Little help from players. Not many people respond to "HOW DO I BANDAGE" or "BEAR TRAPS. HOW?". The controls are listed but not very descriptive on what does what. Bandages ad Bear traps are one use items that you PRESS 3 TO USE. Sometimes you have to claw players for answers, but it's honestly easy to figure out with a little button pressing.
-2 Game types, both of which arn't the previously advertised "mmo". It's not really that bad, but for the moment if you came looking for that "STALKER MMO THAT EVERYONE'S TALKING ABOUT" you'll be slightly disappointed to know it's not quite here yet.
FINAL: Great Game.
Will be a lot better when freeplay comes out (the open world mmo part), while sparse in diversity atm, this game will grow to be great. The controls, scenery, factions, gametypes, and animations are great and have a lot of hard work put into them. Give the game a try and see for yourself, it's free after all.

To preface this review, allow me to state that I loved the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series, and I love modern-FPS arena shooters; combining them together should make for a fairly good game, then, right?  That would be the case, however, Survarium is bogged down with various "free-to-play, pay-to-win" mechanics, and even then, the actual gameplay isn't exactly the best.  I would like to jump straight into reviewing the gameplay, but said F2P mechanics must be discussed first as they do impact the game in a way.
For starters, there's your obvious generic F2P winnable currency in the form of Silver, and the P2P, real-life money currency in Gold.  Silver's used to buy new equipment, quite obviously, as well as consumables, and to repair and upgrade your equipment.  This is where my first gripe with the game comes in: maintenence costs.  Currently, as still a relative newb to the game, the costs are currently fairly low: I can win a match and gain around 4,000 silver, and ammo, repair, and replenishing consumables would only cost about 120.  However, I can't help but think how would increase later on, with silver gain staying relatively the same, not to mention that end-game gear costs a few thousand to actually buy.  Gold, of course, can be used to skip all that by buying the gold-exclusive gear, which also comes fully modded with game-boosting benefits, including a boost to your silver gain.  It should be noted that said gold weapons aren't exactly cheap: 100 gold = 1 USD, and some of the end-game weapons can cost up to 20 bucks.  Fortunately, it seems that (sans from starter packs), armor can't be bought with gold, albeit I wouldn't be surprised if they added those in later on.
Speaking of mods, there's a modification system in the game which allows you to obtain slight benefits (10% fire rate, 5% movement speed boost) by modifying your equipment.  How this works is by having two of the same item, and consuming one of them (and some currency) in order for a chance to add a mod to the other.  Said chance starts at 50%, and not only decreases with further mods, but you have a chance to actually lose mods.  Of course, you can get a higher chance, and remove the ability to lose mods by paying gold instead of silver when you mod your weapon.  Sensing a pattern here?  You can reroll mods with either silver or gold, but surprise surprise, you can only reroll every 6 hours if you're paying with silver, and the restriction is lifted if you pay gold.
This modification system is another one of my gripes with the game, since, not only does it reinforce the pay-to-win system of the game, in order to have that slight competitive edge which will most likely win you a fair amount of games, you generally have to sink a large amount of silver into buying the weapons to mod your gun, and paying for the mods themselves.  While a small upside seems small, not only is that upside preferable to nothing, but said upsides can stack: 2% movement speed on piece of clothing isn't much, but there're 7 slots for clothes, in addition to your two weapon slots, which means that mods can lead to a significant and noticable upside.
While that's that on the pay-to-win front, there's another system I have gripes with: experience.  There are two types of experience in the game: faction experience, and player experience.  Player experience is straight forward, you level up, you get a skill point, and you can put said skill point into miniscule upgrades.  Aside from getting bonus EXP from buying a premium membership, there doesn't seem to be a way to skip the grind aside from, well, grinding.  Faction experience, however, is interesting, in that you can join a faction in the game, and gain experience within the faction.  Gaining more experience will unlock various equipment for purchase within the faction, most noticeably, better guns.  So for the first few hours of the game, you're going to be stuck with your newb equipment until you grind up enough reputation to buy a singular new gun.  The game doesn't explain this, by the way, but there are only two starter factions within the game, and you need to obtain max reputation with them until you can get to the more advanced factions.
This brings about another gripe with the game for me: grinding.  It took me the entirety of my gameplay hours until I got the rep to actually get to the next faction level to buy a new gun, and it doesn't seem to be speeding up.  After that, I still would need to grind further to get Silver for the new equipment, then more Silver to mod said equipment, and so on and so forth.  It's going to be a grindy game, and gets noticable at faction levels 2-4.
Finally, there's a quest system.  You get three quests a day, with a bronze (character EXP) silver (erm, silver) and gold (faction EXP) ranking for each, and a reward.  Some are "in one game" some are "in one day". Of course, you can use the gold currency to reroll your quests, or make your quests easier.  Considering that some of them are also fairly grindy, or require the usage of consumables (grenades, in my case), I'm not a fan.
For starters, the mission system and PvE stuff they advertised?  Not in.  There's only PvP, and even then, there's only one gamemode: team deathmatch.  Apparently there's supposed to be a capture-point style and a capture-the-flag style map, but I haven't seen them at all, yet.  The gunplay in the game feels horrible: the starter rifle (Mosin-Nagant) is surprisingly inaccurate at long-range, while the starter SMG (PPSh-41) and Black Market SMG (Uzi) feel really bad to use.  Not only do the iron sights take up most of the screen, but the muzzle smoke obscures whoever you're trying to fire at.  There's unneccesary amounts of friendly fire as well, and it doesn't seem to be punishable either, all that seems to happen is a score reduction.  Heck, the Black Market traps (effectively mines) not only trigger on your allies, but trigger on
as well.  There's also a limb damage and bleeding system in the game, like in S.T.A.L.K.E.R.  Unlike in S.T.A.L.K.E.R, however, bandages and medkits in order to heal said damage are locked to a specific faction and even then, medkits are locked at level 3 within said faction.  The only universal medkit available costs 300 silver a pop, far too pricey compared to simply dying and respawning.   An engagement with the enemy will most likely result in both of you dying, one from bullet shots, one from bleeding out.  Limb damage also seems relatively inconsequential, as while there are pretty bad consequences to having a limb crippled, you'll probably be dead before that happens.
Furthermore, the matchmaking is horrible.  My first match was with four premium members armed with Kalashnikovs and the tier 2 SMGs, while my own team was armed with conscripted Nagants and sweaters.  We ended up winning that match, somehow, but the point stands that you're as likely to get matchmade with Gold Premium Spetsnaz as you are with conscripts.
In addition to this, apparently there's a artifact system within the game.  Those equipped can obtain them to obtain passive benefits for their team.  However, I haven't actually seen them, or actually experienced them, which leads me to believe they're not actually in the game.  However, assuming they are in the game, one would need to venture into anomalous areas (usually located in the center of the map) in order to get them.  However, said anomalies aren't actually that big of a deal, unlike in the constantly compared-to S.T.A.L.K.E.R.  There's just one localized anomaly in the middle of the map, and even then it tends to be easily avoided as most of the combat happens on the fringes of the map (think Bombsites and mid in Counter-Strike).
I'm running up to my word limit, so in conclusion: grindy pay-to-win shooter, would not recommend.

I waited a long time before finally deciding to write a review for this game, and I'm still not sure if I can write a fair review that will do The Isle justice. I bought this game in the very month it came out during patch 0.04, via chance by a steam store suggestion. Since then, I've hit over 450hrs of playtime, more than any other videogame has ever held my attention. I love this game, and I definately have the experience to write a review, so why did I wait so long and why do I have such mixed feelings on writing it?
Firstly, it is because unlike most early access games, the Isle's Developers work like people lost in a desert, that haven't been able to drink for 10 years, finally finding an oasis with fresh water. That is to say they are fast. I've seen them update once every day fast, and I'm not talking petty patches, I mean content, Meaningful fixes, bugkilling, gameplay, etc. This game changes so quickly that anything negative I have to say about it could literally be fixed tomorrow, rendering my entire review pointless.
I'm not going to baby my audience by dragging on over the whole Early Access arguement, but in this game's case, it is honestly 100% not fair to write negative reviews for this game based on its minor bugs and technical problems, because they're getting fixed right now, garentueed. So just shut up and be patient 75% of the Isle's community, use the damn bug tracker.
That being said, this game is not all sun and peaches. The Devs may work harder than any devs I've seen before, but they're ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to the community and their own team, to the point where they have needed to give public apologies. 9/10 from what I have seen and experienced personally, if you ask a dev something they'll respond with one of the following:
A: A belittling comment making you out to sound ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
B: Tell you your computer is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥and the problem is your wallet's fault
or C: Talk like you're a threat to their existance and become super defensive and passive-aggressive, or just lock your thread because they didn't like it
(Then D: That lucky 10% that get decent, polite answers/help)
Now I know that sounds bad, but before you start boarding the dev-hate wagon, just know that the community is an even bigger piece of rude ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Most of the time they deserve to be treated that way. Yea, you heard me right defensive readers. The community is nagging, disrespectful, negative, unappreciative, unsatisfiable, childish, the list goes on I could write an entire review just on them and how its highschool 2.0. I wouldn't even bother including them, but the thing is, at this stage the Isle's only functionality as a playable game IS the community. You cannot play this game on singleplayer. In some cases, literally.
This is because the members that join the servers are what fill up the map. There is no AI, there is nothing but you, your survival needs, and the other players getting between them trying to do the exact same thing. If there are no other players and you pick a carnivore, you literally have no foodsource, you are going to starve, period. With herbs you can technically survive just fine, but then I hope you enjoy your goalless, challengeless, walking dinosaur simulator.
However, it is this downfall that makes the Isle so much BETTER than any other survival game I've ever known. You HAVE to kill to survive, either to defend yourself, or to eat, and guess what, that thing attacking you also doesn't want to die, because its another person with the same goals as you. Hunting isnt easy because it means you aren't trying to outsmart AI, you're trying to outsmart another human being, and that's a challenge no AI could ever truly simulate. Ontop of that, each dinosaur has different skills that make it superior and inferior in certian aspects. You could play the mighty rex, but you'll never be as fast as the Galli. This means players need to devise different tactics to deal with certian species, all being pilotted by sentient beings.
For the smaller scale stuff, the graphics are great, and they keep getting nicer and more realistic with every new map. The dinosaur models are the best I have ever seen in a game, and most of them are accurate. Each dinosaur also has unique skins, as well as sounds they can use to communicate, and you'd be surprised how attached you become to the sounds matching the dino. They fit really well, and hearing them sounding different feels weird when you switch to other dino games.
You do need a good computer for this game however, smooth fps is nessisary to do well because if you are operating at 5fps and someone else comes rushing in at 30fps, they're going to have a massive advantage over you. But this is a standard multiplayer demand in my opinion. Its not really something that can be held against this game, especially when its not even fully optimized. You see negative reviews using this as a key point and its really...silly? Look at the operating system requirements and decide if you can run this game well before blaming the game for your ram and graphics card being inadequate and causing you to fall prey.
However, here's what I don't like about the game, that has been established and completed development-wise.
-Fall Damage and Leg Break Counters:
Yea this is a popular one, and while I like the concept, the execution is pisspoor. I don't mind that my character limps if I don't watch my step and go off a sharp incline, what I don't like is that it takes an hour to heal from a fall so pathetic it belongs on the LifeCall: Medic Button Commercial. Your health will have healed in the first 5minutes, yet you will continue to limp for insane amounts of time. The same thing is true for bone crushing dinosaurs, like Trex. Their bites cripple you, and yea they should that's a massive animal, but its not fun to sit around hoping you'll heal soon for an hour or so. That's a long time to drag yourself around, in many cases (especially speedsters) totally defenseless. Its to the point that players prefer dino suicide to playing the game, and crawl up to predators hoping for the sweet release of death. No offense Isle, but if people are trying to kill themselves in a survival game in order to have fun, you're doing it wrong. Any attempts to convince the devs otherwise are always sluffed off with "be more careful nexttime". They have no intentions of changing this horrible gameplay mechanic.
-People Ostrichize you based on how you play:
Remember how I said the community was the reason this game works at all? Welp, a lot of them have very strict and uncalled for trigger-modes where the entire server will gang up on you for playing in a way they don't approve of. For both players that enjoy killing on sight, people that kill their own species for food, people that hang around with the opposite foody (herbs and carns chillin together with rainbows), people playing hero and assuming they know why two dinos are fighting and rushing in to save the day, or protecting random animals being hunted because you're so mean. There's nothing anyone can do about this, but it does suck. People can play how they want to play, when they want to play. The community needs to back off and mind its own buisness.
-The Isle is Really Unqiue....right now:
As more and more information about the final product is released I have realized it doesn't intend to embrace what makes it so amazing. Rather its intended course is to follow the current game trend we all know of every survival game. There will be people, with factions, and crafting, and mythical monsters, and fantasy, and it as aliens/military that put them there...does it sound like ark's plot? Yea. Yea it does.... Many of the realistic models are planned to be replaced with innaccurate and mutated ones, like rex. Much to my displeasure.
Still. This game provides me with endless entertainment, and regardless of what it becomes, I enjoy what it is now.

It's fine and all, fills a niche, but it's stale and lacks obvious features. It's a bit like a 3D version of Doorkickers (worth checking out if you're considering this).
The combat is turn based, let's say you were storming a room with two entrances and lined up 2 guys outside each entrance. You might conceivably want them to storm the room at the same time, but alas, no, the only way to tell if that's going to happen is with a timeline style thing which runs across the characters move path. So on the floor on the otherside of the door might say 2 seconds. Well, on that 2 second mark you might want your other team to storm in. Unbelievably, there's no way to synchronise those events, by say, telling the other guy to pause for a second before proceeding. You could get him to run in circles before going through the door I guess, but then you hardly feel like a SWAT team. Another similarly stupid mechanic is that you cant order someone to go stand where someone else is stood, even if they're going to be 4 seconds down the hall before the other guy gets there. I think the real fun stems from the customisation and the content around that. Lots of maps, lots of guns, and a combat system that is just competent enough to be fun.

This was VERY hard for me to say, because there really is a lot to like about this game (I wish Steam would allow us a third option when voting).  The problem is, overall, the pros don't outway the cons.
As far as the GOOD things: the story feels very much like a BTTF movie.  Fans of the movies will no doubt love the fact that some of the original voice actors returned.  The story is good, some of the new characters are interesting, and overall, it's entertaining.
Now, why don't I recommend this game?  If you take off the nostalgic glasses and look at it for what it is, it's not that great.  While I said the storyline was good, it's not GREAT, which is what you would hope for from a game based off the iconic movies (which I myself love).  The plot is very linear (there's not much in the way of choice), and the story doesn't get really interesting until much later in the game.  Also, the setting of a prohibition-era Hill Valley just isn't very captivating.
In addition, the puzzles vary from being either too easy or too vague to get through without hints (the guitar battle is a good example).  Also, and I know this is minor, but the animation is like something out of a kid's cartoon, which contrasts awkwardly with the adult humor and cussing.  There's more I could say, but that would just be rambling.
Overall, if you're a big fan of the movies and can get this game on sale, then YES, buy this game!  But if you're an average Joe looking for a game as good as their later efforts (The Walking Dead; Wolf Among Us), you'll be disappointed.  You'd be better off spending your money on a different title.

I don't normally like side-scrollers, but I really enjoyed this game.
I was initially enticed by the look of an ancient Greek amphora come to life, and I was pleased to see the mythological research evident in the story, accompanied by an excellent soundtrack.  The levels have just enough variety to keep them interesting, so that it's not just smacking more Greek dudes with a variety of weapons every time.
I'm not sure why some people were unhappy with the combat.  I use keyboard + mouse, and the only problem I had was an occasional inability to hit an enemy because he was standing right on top of me, so that neither facing left or facing right could reach him.  Other than that, I enjoyed the block & attack mechanism that so often resulted in a dramatic *clang* *clang* as I exchanged blows with my foe, each of us using his shield to defend himself.  I also liked the way weapons broke, often forcing me to improvise when I lost the last weapon that was most effective against a particular enemy.
The difficulty ramps up pretty evenly, so that you get more abilities at about the same rate as the enemies get stronger.  One thing I really enjoyed became evident in the boss fights.  In most games nowadays, you have about 5 seconds to figure out the strategy to defeat the boss before it kills you with one or two blows.  Every time in this game, when certain weapons were weak or useless against a boss, I had time to react to this and try something else, because I could still take a fair amount of punishment (even from a god).  Other games would do well to emulate this; it's far more exciting to devise a new strategy while in the middle of a fight than it is to do so while sitting on the Load screen.
The Good:
The Bad:

So I'm just gonna start off by saying, this game has been my life for the past week or so, and I reccomend it HEAVILY. I know right now it only says I have about 6 hours on record, but I usually play offline so in total it should be more like 25 hours on record. Sheltered is an amazing, difficult, strategy game that I can't get enough of. Usually with strategy games, they become boring after you've played them for a long time and it's the same thing over and over, but that is not the case with sheltered. Usually, every single shelter/family you create, you last longer than your last shelter/family. The two bad things I would say about this game is that it is very glitchy, and the controls are kind of weird at first, so it may take some time to get used to.

When I first became aware of the game called Sheltered, I thought to myself: "That seems fun. Yeah, I'd like to play that for a few hours."
Over 60 hours later, I can tell you, Sheltered is fun. A heck of a lot more than it should be, I guess.
Fun, after all, is subjective. I'm not sure how a person would even quantify a game like Sheltered. It is easy, I suppose, to compare Sheltered to other games. But, doing so would be a disservice to Sheltered and the player themself.
Sheltered offers the player a lot of fun in various ways seemingly dumbed down by its simplistic graphical form. That is the allure of Sheltered. And, once you're sucked in, well.... You had better Shelter your family.
I have wondered about the design decision to use 16-8k graphics but, now, after playing the game, I see that it fits the game perfectly. This is not some grim experience about some hollowed out basement in which the survivors eat rats and die. hoping for an end to some war that they had no control over. Sheltered is about family that sticks together inspite of all odds. War or not, the Sheltered family prevails. Unless they don't. That is the draw.
Upon the start of a new game, the player will encounter various situtations where they must choose what to do to protect their family. The family is only as important as the player sees them to be, yet, if the player's entire family dies, the game is over.
Most players will decide to protect their family at all costs. This can lead to some strange and heart-breaking choices. A player might ask themself: Who do I most identify with? Who shall I send out to starve, and who shall I save?
Another reason I enjoy this game is due to what I call the "Memory Aspect". The player must, at least in some part, memorize what materials they are bringing back to the shelter. If the player forgets or overlooks certain needed parts and prioritizes the wrong things, the game can become punishing and unforgiving.
Some might see this as a down-side of Sheltered. I see it as an interesting design choice and conducive to the experience.
While there are still many ways in which Sheltered could become better and more refined, I would rate it at no less than 8/10. The developers are doing a great job improving the game and I would recommend Sheltered highly.

This game gets and deserves much of the praise that it gets.  It's a strategic doorkicking strategy game with enough content featuring 3 modes currently (Terrorist Hunt, Bomb Defusal, and Hostage Rescue/Escape).  You control 4 operatives from the Rangers, SEALs, SpecOps, Speznaz or other such organizations through each area in a series of phases where you issue commands.  The "special" element to this game is it's perspective concept and "owning every corner" by controlling the direction that your guys are looking as they enter and clear each room.  The shooting on it's own is fully automated if the soldiers are looking in the right direction but it does allow you to aim thrown grenades and medkits only work on nearby allies.  The enemies will react to noise and often charge out of rooms so covering doorways is still a concern (or you can use an intelligence soldier to wedge the door)
Certain weapons get unlocked in the store as you achieve a certain number of stars but any completionist out there might want to revist the stages to aim for the 2100 stars achievement.  I found a certain amount of "violence of action" was required to 4 star the missions later on.
The problems with this game lies in it's somewhat hollow customization options when it comes to the marketplace options as outfitting each unit feels more like equipping Stat-sticks rather than anything new an improved (especially when it comes to gear).  The consumables make the game much easier if you're willing to grind out a few of the previous levels to pick up a few defibilators (completely negating permanent death) and UAVs but for hardcore fans/gamers they might choose to avoid those completely to artificially amp the challenge.  The level up perks and stat increase from grinding experience makes the game a snap for anyone playing on harder difficulties but struggling with a particular stage.
The other issue is that the gameplay itself feels tedious as you continue on through it's somewhat repetitive missions of pointing your guys at enemies and watching them do their thing.  The context for the missions is very thinly described on a mission brief but not integrated into the game very well (as you have to escape to the main menu between each mission in order to even read this excerpt).  I found very little keeping me attached to the story or my unit itself without some personal imagination on the "terrorists" we're hunting.
I'll still recommend the title for being a foray into something different but it's not without it's own set of issues.

Having never seen the 'Back to the Future' movie franchise, I was unsure what to expect with this outing from Telltale. However, what "Back to the Future: The Game" delivers is a charming, humorous, and at times, gripping point & click adventure. If you have seen the original movies, then I'm sure the added references and familiar characters will be a bonus. Indeed, some of the original cast provide the voices for the characters, to add further authenticity.
The game sees the player take on the role of the movies' protaganist, Marty McFly, as he and the eccentric, 'Doc' Brown experience misadventures in Marty's home town of Hill Valley, in different times and time-lines.
The gameplay centres on solving multiple 'puzzles', by using the environment, collected items, and dialogue with a variety of in-game characters to progress the story.
If you are a fan of Telltale's most recent 'Monkey Island' release, then you'll certainly be at home. If you are a fan of the movie franchise linked to the game, which is set following the events of the third movie, incidentally, then I can only assume that with excellent voice-acting delivery from some of the movies' original cast at the very least, you will consider this game a welcome addition to the franchise.

I had to wait a bit before posting since I felt on the fence about this game, however I've just had too much fun as both counselors and Jason in this game to NOT recommend it.  It is definitely not without its problems, some of the biggest ones being related to server overloads right now.  There are also some balancing issues on both sides of the aisle: Jason can too easily just appear out of no where with the counselor already in a grab ready to be instantly killed, and the counselors, if they group together in enough numbers, can maul Jason like a pack of wolves.  So even if there are some balancing issues, they go on both sides of the aisle, feel like the cancel each other out usually, and aren't enough to make the game impossible for either side.  There are also a good amount of graphical bugs where counselors are floating next to Jason when they are grabbed, counselors standing straight up like they were afk when killed or hiding, getting stuck in the character select menu, etc.
Those sound major, but you can usually get around them easily enough or happen infrequently enough to be more of an annoyance that needs to get patched rather than something absolutely-gamebreaking.  The good part of the game is all of the experiences you will have.  Having Jason hot on your heels as you dive through a window and then scramble to barricade the door just as his axe makes the first swing to break it down; getting grabbed and knowing you're about to die when some random guy comes up with a stick and hits jason in the back, freeing you; hiding inside a house and watching another player get helplessly murdered while you greedily stay out of sight hoping that Jason didn't see you and will just go away.
My personal favorite so far was finding a gas can, swimming across a river to the boat, filling up the boat with gas and partially fixing it to escape, turning around and seeing another player in a dead sprint holding a propeller with Jason 70 feet behind them, then grabbing a stick to defend them while they fixed the boat, hitting and stunning Jason as he was about to murder my teammate, both of us getting in the boat and pulling away from the dock, and from there on out I acted as look out for my driving-teammate, telling him where Jason was while we escaped.  It was such a rush and so satisfying.  These are the moments that you will have that will make all of the bad things bearable.
At the end of the day, it is $40 dollars.  While this game is great, it definitely has its share of problems that shouldn't have existed on launch.  But, a game like this is best during its initial launch, which is also when it is full price.  Also, most games have problems on their initial launch, from glitches to server problems. For me, it was definitely worth the $40.

In my honest opinion, probably a better game than the first. The Restored Content workshop mod is required to play the game, as a result of it being rushed out. Even with the Restored content here are still quite a few bugs, glitches and missing textures that you find around. From being stuck by nothing when randomly walking around, sections of the ship missing on G0-T0's yacht, and not being allowed to interact with any of the menu's (From Restored Content).
I looked past those problems because the game has much more variety.
The Random loot generator was one of those systems that made me enjoy the game the most, it made every run through of the game entirely unique. It may be kind of weird considering some of the loot does not match the location it was found (Dark Jedi dropping blaster rifles, or Mercenary dropping Jedi robes). But it honestly keeps you guessing and hoping for something new from everything you kill. .
Another great part of the game is the upgrade system. Compared to the first game, this one is a blessing. With the first game you could only change the crystals in your lightsaber, 2 armour upgrades, 4 blaster upgrades, and 3 vibro upgrades. Compared to the second game which has around 40 upgrades for your lightsaber, on top of having your color and upgrade crystals. 55 armour upgrades, 44 blaster upgrades, and 45 vibrosword upgrades.
Not to mention the new variety of weapons and armors added to the game, instead of just choosing Calo Nord's armour and running through the entire game with it (in KOTOR 1). Over time you find better and better sets of armour and equipment which have a larger variety of bonuses. Sometimes that might be ruined by the Random Loot generator, but it isn't that big of a deal.
Overall if you are willing to overlook the graphical impurities , bugs, and glitches in the game. It is worth every dollar that you spend.
PS. you don't need to waste feats on implants in this game(unless you played as scout in the first game, which I didn't).

Not exactly my usual preference of game but being of the WW2 variety I decided to take a chance as the last time I did so (Return to Castle Wolfenstein) my choice was proven a correct one.
Set in WW2 you assume the role of Violette Summer, which was inspired by a real life heroine by the name of Violette Szabo, which is an pretty incredible life story itself for anyone with a passion for history.  The mood of this game is what one would truly expect of war-torn Europe; bleak, fearful, violent and sad.  The opening movie pretty much sums the game up in my opinion, not to spoil it for anyone but it reminds me of that eerie opening to one of my favourite TV series; The World at War were humanity is destroying itself in an unforgiving darkened world.
Now your role as Violette is to infiltrate and end the lives of the darkest and most corrupt seeds in the Third Reich (well you blow stuff up too) in quick and quiet fashion then escape - no charging about like Master Chief, you're an assassin not god with a gun and a green suit because believe me this game can be unforgiving when caught.  Now I very much recommend a Xbox controller or something similar when play this game as the controls are very clunky even on controller, especially when shooting.  The visuals and sound are very satisfying and in-sync with the mood; sombre and eerie would be my quick description.  There is one mechanic that does stand out however and that is the morphine power, to put it simply when injected you enter a slow down mode where you can damn near do anything which does kill the immersion somewhat.  The A.I aren't too bright in the game either, then not many games pull that off but they are not without character.  They have seen war and it has touched them deeply and some of the conversations you hear are truly horrific.

Now this game is certainly not for everyone, but to anyone like me who plays stealthy characters in any game with the option to do so will feel right at home with this game.  You choose the right weapons for your mission, disguise yourself when necessary and gather intelligence when and if you can.
I would give this game a 4/5 for it truly is an enjoyable game with a few flaws.

Velvet Assassin is a much better game in theory than in practice. It has a great premise: a likable female spy who brutally assassinates Nazis to secretly turn the tide of WWII. To be clear, Velvet is a stealth game clearly designed for sneaking, and yet the stealth gameplay can be exceptionally frustrating.
The sneaking system is woefully underdeveloped. There are no visibility indicators or radars or cones of vision. Trial and error is all you have. Then there’s the painfully slow sneaking speed. If you remain undetected, you get rewarded with truly great kill animations. If an enemy spots you, you have to run away or rely on wonky combat and AI exploits.
The game is very linear, with a sort of paint by numbers approach to stealth, resulting in you either going about things the developers’ way or repeatedly dying. The checkpoint system can also be irksome, with some checkpoints quite far apart, making you fearful to fail simply because you don’t want to replay things again.
On the bright side, the story and briefing cutscenes are done very well, building up believability and intrigue. Very strong voice acting by all characters is also a great boon, with humorous enemy dialogue akin to No One Lives Forever being a highlight. Certain mechanics like shadows, whistling, and stat upgrades do help keep things interesting. Graphically the game is bleak, brown, and barren but occasionally looks quite nice.
Overall, Velvet Assassin only takes about 6 hours to finish on Normal, which is good because by the end I was very ready for it to be over. Despite the frustration there’s something charming about its very old school approach, almost daring you to try to survive. The game clearly isn’t great, but it does have some good elements. Most will wish to skip the game, but for those hardcore gamers who find the concept intriguing, Velvet Assassin is worth playing if you pick it up for real cheap.

TL;DR Apotheon has become one of my favorite games in my Steam library.
A lot of reviews call this game a Metroidvania, I however, do not think it quite falls into that category. To me, it was more of a side-scrolling action RPG. Metroidvanias tend to lock advancement through abilities, Apotheon is gated through objectives. While you can earn new equipment and (some) do grant new abilities, you do not gain access to new areas through these assets. Equipment, namely weapons and shields, have durability and you must replace them as you face combat. Armour, on the other hand, acts as a buffer to your health and can be increased permanently by buying/finding new pieces. You can also increase your attack speed and damage with the various weapon types by paying a skill trainer.
The story is well written and, from what I understand, is very accurate to the personality and positions of the gods. It is a unique story, I believe, so just knowing their legends won't spoil the experience for you. It was a very atmospheric game, and I very much felt alone against the gods. While these games won't quite warrant comparison in a gameplay sense, it brought to me memories  reminiscient of Morrowind and Dark Souls, with it's patient yet frantic combat and well-designed atmosphere. The dialogue of even minor characters really grips you, and snipets of the legends of the gods scattered throughout on little statuettes wrap the whole package together quite nicely.
Quests were quite varied, even going so far as to introduce new mechanics temporarily just to mix up the formula and keep the game interesting. This was very refreshing and kept the game from feeling redundant or tedius.
It's not without it's cons. I played through entirely on normal difficulty and, while some battles did present somewhat of a challenge, I found it quite easy because of the abundance of new shields and healing items. I never lacked for protection, and armour upgrades seemed to come quickly. There is the option shortly after the introduction to increase the difficulty and I wish I'd done so right away. It is also worth mentioning that, after game completion, an Olympian difficulty is unlocked.
The physics can, at times, also act a little wonky. This is not a spritegrid-based physics system, and things can act a little rag-dolly. Every once in a while I'd take a hit that would send me flying across the area just because of how it connected. After you get use to the physics of the game this isn't really a hinderance, but worth mentioning. It can make some fights take a little longer than necessary.
I'll end this review with some tips for new players, mechanics the game doesn'tmake obvious:
-Saves DO NOT work by slot! The most recent save is always at the top of the list. Be careful when overriding as your save may not be quite where you expect it to be in the list.
-While you may aim with the mouse/right stick, the direction of the LEFT stick can change the type of melee attack you perform with the weapon.
-Using the throw button IS NOT a quick button for your equipped ranged weapon, but will instead throw your currently equipped melee weapon. Useful for surprising enemies and ditching weapons low on duraility.

The first thing probably everyone will notice is how amazing this game looks. It's certainly a main reason why I've bought it. And what makes it even better is an amazing soundtrack which breathes with mythology and epicness. The one thing that could and should be better visually vise is terrain. At least some parts, like the thin ones designed for vertical traversal. Those are just thin black lines and it looks really weird.
But what about the game mechanics? Well, they are ok.
It's a 2D game and the maps are usually both very horizontal and vertical. The traversing through the map isn't always without problems. Sometimes when you for example jump on a ladder the game won't notice that it's a ladder and you won't be able to climb it. There are these slim terrain parts which are there for you to change your vertical position (I obviously don't know how to explain it), by jumping while holding the Down key. Which isn't really that responsive, especially in combat.
The combat it self is just a click fest, even though you have a stamina which will deplete quickly. I think that they imagined the combat to by more tactical but I don't think that they've managed to do it. Main reason is the problem of the enemy AI with navigation on the map. If there is a vertical traversal or a jump sequence then they'll run around like crazy (especially the animals).
You can block, use different types of attack based on the mouse movement and roll around. It certainly can look good if there isn't too much of a chaos. But more often than not I had to just click attack button like a mad man.
The item progression is a particularly good one. There is a ton of different types of melee and ranged weapons, shields, armor parts, and special items like bombs, creature summons, healing and invisibility potions, the list goes on. There are a lot of special, mythical, weapons.
The way the armor works is kinda weird. You have few armor parts which increase your maximum armor. When enemies are hitting you, the armor goes down and after it reaches zero they'll start to attack your hit points. Then you can either fix your armor with Repair kit or destroy items (boxes, vases, whatever) and find armor points like this.
There are limits for how many of each items you can carry which honestly I don't understand. The main problem with items and combat is that the weapons can break down. And they'll break down really fast. It's not unusual that while you are fighting with few enemies three of your weapons will break down (because all of them were used previously) and you'll just see how every few seconds you have different kind of weapon in your hand. One moment you have short knife so you are right next to the enemy and suddenly you have 5 kilometers long spear in your hand and you can't hit him. I really don't understand reasons for this. And I don't think it fits with the mythology theme. There is a book written about you, great hero fighting gods and every third sentence is about how you have to switch weapon because another one had broken down?

In the few lines of monologues, you can see their different personalities, and that's great. And I have to add that some of those objectives are really creative or at least interesting. So you are just playing around with these average mechanics while looking at a beautiful piece of art.
It's an interesting, beautiful looking game. I would like to see more, but with fleshed out mechanics. The UX could be better, the fighting system should be better, the map traversing should be better, the story telling should be better. Then it could really be an amazing experience. Now, if it would be without its visuals it would be an average game, with those visuals it can't be average but it isn't that much fun to play for a longer time.

I would like to emphazise that this is made by "singleplayer game creators" and it shows. I love that in an era when everything is "E-Sport, E-Sport, E-sport, Bla bla bla, puke" it isnt balanced, because some things are way more powerful than other things, period. But its really great fun. Also, it is clearly an indie game and therefore stupid to compare to any game like COD or BF or CS or something stupid like that, its free and indie, and still the most fun i've had for months.
Pros:
-Kind of unique gameplay. at least the mix of it all.
the people are heavy and can't sprint like dogs. The weapons are hard to master, but really unique. You start out with a choice between a Bolt rifle, very precise and lethal on most of the body but with a slow reload and pull between shots. Or a Medium machingun that sprays terribly and has pretty low damage. And as a side arm you got a very decent gun you easily can fire in controlled bursts. Very quickly you get a shotgun. Either a sawed-off or a longbarreled, and they are equally unique, the sawed-off is lethal in very short range and can hit with a few pellets if lucky, on medium distance, the longbarrel can hit a little longer with a little less spread. both carries 2 shots and can be shot as fast as you can pull the trigger.
-The health system bugged me at first, but got fun and challenging after a short while. You get hit too bad, you start bleeding and probably die. You stand too close to a grenade, your limbs get hit and you cant run for a short duration. I've experienced getting hit in one arm and couldn't ADS, so i threw a grenade and survived.
-The battles last longer then usual FPS. and it feels more immersive.
-The map are very different, and very unique.
-Did you know it's FREE?
-Customization is really fun and challenging, i found a pair of boots after a fight, and they had special attributes, but they were damaged, so i had to repair them first, which took 3 hours. When you buy a jacket you can carry an additional mag, and you can choose from the amount of mags you can carrie, how to divide, if you want 1 mag for the rifle and 3 for the handgun.
-Sounds is really epic, and really unique, except handgrenades, which almost doesn't have a sound.
-Graphics is very nice and definetly has that post-apocalyptic feel to it.
-various game modes already.
-levels and skills on your character makes it personal and longlasting
-It's totally 100% free.
-Great potential with PVE and alot more to come!
Cons:
-It's beta... Nuff said.
-Team damage is a present problem, extremely present. sadly.
-Everyone in the entire game looks the same, and it takes a long time to get a helmet, its actually ugly and annoying.
-It's free, so they really want you buy premium, THOUGH, premium is a greater chance of loot and more money and XP after each fight, you can buy goldbars, but you can also get goldbars in extremely rare loot. So despite the pay-to-win is present, i haven't felt it being pay-to-ruin-others-game.

I'll be honest, I love this game and despite the COUNTLESS issues I still have trouble putting it down (and by putting it down I mean smashing my monitor against the wall). It has great mechanics and a wonderful style to it that Dark Souls fans can fit right at home in. The problem is that it was made by Ubisoft. Due to their "new innovative" peer to peer mesh system that they used for the game, there are no dedicated servers, but instead it connects each player to one another and essentially "meshes" everyone's connection as one. This system makes it so that everyone's IP address is shared to everyone else's in the match. Major secuirty flaw, and that's just for starters. Because this game takes breakneck timing during battle, this system makes it impossible. If one person has a bad connection, then everyone in the match does. The game is already plagued by lag switchers and people disconnecting and reconnecting to the match and it often results in the game attempting to resync and failing. Ubisoft even stated that with their system that there is no host advantage. Bullsh|t. There are still numerous bugs with the game, horrible matchmaking properties and the classes are pretty imbalanced. Seeing as how Ubisoft is in denial about the inner workings of their own system, this potentially amazing title will most likely be left by the wayside and become plagued by hackers and laggers. We've seen this kind of thing happen before and Ubisoft doesn't exactly have the kind of reputation to prove otherwise. Don't buy this game. At least not in the current state it is in. You'll hate yourself for becoming addicted to it and being forced to be subjected to mental masochism.

The game's main character, Violette Summer, is baased on the real life secret agent/saboteur Violette Szabo.  You experience her missions in Europe through her dreams.  In those dreams you become the actor and rely on stealth, wits, and weapons to take out enemies and complete mission objectives.  You'll start with a knife and have to be very careful to get to the first objective.  It gets harder and more interesting as you acquire more talents and weapons.  It is very challenging to  maintain stealth and operate with very limited weapons and ammo, which makes it very satisfying when you get to a mission objective.
Gameplay was engaging, exciting, and sometimes spooky.  The music certainly sets the tone for you secretative missions and dangerious scenarios.  The atmosphere is close to art and can evoke a lot of emotion!
While I thought it was a pretty good game, I have very mixed feelings about recommending it.  So this is a conditional  recommendation subject to some serious "ifs".
The game is old and relies on the outdated checkpoint system instead of real saves and the controls are sometimes clunky.  It probably won't run without some work on your part.  Unless you are willing to download additional drivers, tinker with file names, and maybe edit configuration files in an emergency; this game probably isn't for you.
If on the other hand you are willing to fix a few things on your own, if you have the mettle and patience to stalk and kill quietly, and if you can live with some gameplay bugs; then the game is pretty riveting and exciting. It could be a lot better by today's standards, but was pretty good when it was released.
I enjoyed playing for a short time, but decided to move on because of problems with the controls lagging and getting me killed when I played with an Xbox 360 controller with Steam Overlay running.
.....a.  It works flawlessly with the Xbox 360 controller if you can live without the Steam Overlay.
.....b.  If you want to do screen  shots with the F12 key, then the changes you have to make to get Steam Overlay to work may cause laggy performance with the controller, which makes it harder to play the game successfully.
.....c.  If you play with keyboard and mouse, the controls are flawless with or without the Steam Overlay - definitetly best played with a keyboard/mouse combo.
FIXING GAME PROBLEMS
1.  Game Fails to Launch Issue
....a.  Install the NVidia Legacy PhysX Drivers at
2.  Steam Overlay Fix needed if you want to do screenshots with F12
....a.  Navigate to your Steam\SteamApps\common\velvet assassin folder
....b.  Rename Launcher.exe to Launcher2.exe
....c.  Rename Replay.exe to Launcher.exe
Caution Note:  May cause laggy performance or other game issues
3.  Checkpoint Progress Loop
It is possible to get to a point where you are encountering overwhelming odds and the most recent checkpoint just returns you to the same situation where you inevitable are killed and returned again and again like the movie Groundhog Day.  In
such a case it maybe necessary to edit the values in the follow files at
Steam\SteamApps\common\velvet assassin\aio
....a. difficulty.cfg (NPCDamage and PlayerDamage - decrease the former/increase the latter)
....b. weapons.cfg (Adjust damage  depending on situation)
PROS
*  Very chilling look into a very dark time in history through the eyes of a behind the lines assassin
*  Good story style
*  Edge of your seat encounters
*  Offers around 40 hours of lay time - far more than a lot of other similar assassin type games
CONS
*  Predictable enemies and unrealistic situations with enemies facing away from threat vectors
*  Stealth is inconsistent - in some areas you appear to be hidden, but can be discovered where in another location the same factors would render you invisible to the enemy
*  AI is weak
*  Sometimes gameplay is forced to a linear path and slow
*  Sometimes controller mode controls are non-responsive resulting in you getting killed; e.g. you must be in a precise position to execute a knife kill or you just stand there getting shot
*  Velvet Assassin was released in 2009.  Later that year the developer studio, Replay,  closed its doors due to insolvency.  As a result there is no developer support for this game.

If Steam had a "weak" recommended, that is what this recommendation would be:  There is some fun to be had here, and you may even spend quite a few hours with it, but ultimately, it's just not as good as it could be.  If you are in to the premise, I say buy it -- but not at full price.  Here's why:
Sheltered's strength lies in its base premise and the early game execution.  The early game is decent fun, and the tension is right there with real trade-offs: Do you use your supplies to make a mask, or risk radiation?  Do you use your water for a supply run, or hold off?  Which priority do you build first?  Do you let the new person join, knowing they may eventually pay off, or wait until your supplies are better?  There are some frustrations in execution, but overall, these questions feel right for the theme, and Sheltered has you considering them early in the game.  This is probably all the first two to four hours of gameplay.
Unfortunately, it gets weaker from there.  By mid-game, your trade-offs are more tedious, more a question of "what should I build next?" than any real survival concern.  By the late-game (sometime between Day 50 and Day 100), these tedious trade-offs give way to a simple question: "Where the heck do I find ______ to build ______ (that I don't really need)?"  By this point, scarcity of basic needs is not even a thing.  Day in, day out, repeating the same supply runs to the same places.
Certain types of players will still feel some sense of achievement at this point.  There are a few more things to build, you finally get the camper driving, maybe you find some special end-game content.  A prettier shelter, perhaps?  Sadly, most of us will wonder why we persisted past those early, more challenging but more promising times.
It was hope, I guess.  Somewhat fitting given the theme -- hope of something more kept me going far after Sheltered had any more fun to offer.  It's that same hope that one might imagine kept the Sheltered family going, even after survival became mundane and mechanical.

When it comes to simulation games,  there are two kinds of player; macromanagers and micromanagers.  The former prefers to make generalized decisions and allow the specific details to be handled within the ai.   The latter prefers to manage every detail of the process,  and their gameplay is a collection of their smaller choices aggregated.  Macromanagers for instance leave free will on when playing THE SIMS whereas micromanagers turn it off or override it often.  SHELTERED is a game for the micromanagers.  I am not one of those.
While the premise and depth is great and I can tell the execution here is good,  the biggest flaw I found was a lack of AI in the family members.  They won't do any task unless commanded.   Mom will happily stand outside dying of radiation poisoning while standing next to the damaged air filter with no hazmat suit on,  and will make no effort at all to put on said rad suit and fix the filter unless specifically commanded.  This is true of everyonr;  you must issue commands to get people to do anything,  and they won't grab a gas mask or rad suit unless you walk them through the steps of doing so each time they go outaide.   This sort of play got old with me quickly,  but a micromanager would likely love it.    6/10 but not for all gamers.

I have loved every game that Frictional Games has released, and Soma is no exception.  Although Amnesia was more of a revelation to the genre (despite Penumbra previously introducing many of same mechanics), Soma surpasses its predecessors in almost every way:  world-building, narrative engagement, interface simplicity, that trademark Frictional 'tactility' of interaction, and - of course - raw production values / improvements in tech.
There are some weak points here.  For one, Soma lacks the sense of urgency I remember feeling when playing Amnesia.  In Amnesia, the threat of the pursuing
pushed me to open doors and enter rooms where I knew something horrible was likely waiting for me; in Soma, by contrast, my exploration and progression was usually driven more by curiosity and narrative obligation.  This is not to say that I did not experience a general sense of tension and horror while playing Soma; just that I rarely felt 'forced' into an area before I was mentally ready (not that my nerves complained about this).
The other main weakness was, I suspect, largely caused by the budget constraints of a small studio: enemies, specifically the limitations of their engagement with and integration into the game world due to AI.  The trouble was, despite my abiding unease throughout the game, I typically had at least a decent idea of whether or not I was in an area where I was likely to encounter an enemy.  In light of other recent horror experiences -- especially the ever-stalking xenomorph in Alien: Isolation -- it has become more difficult to forgive encounter predictability (though, again, my nerves appreciated the regular, expected 'breaks' in tension).  Of course, there is more to be feared
than direct attack.
Frictional Games can still scare me better than almost anyone else... at least in the ways that I like to be scared (overdone jump scares are poor-man's horror and simply not enjoyable, in my opinion).  And in Soma, Frictional scared me while also telling their most coherent and interesting story in their most fully-realized world to date.
As always, I look forward expectantly to the next experience they bring to us.
