By far the most bang for my buck I've got from an indie game. Clocked well over 30 hours so far and Im hoping I'll be revisting my saved game in the future (will get to that part). The game runs smooth, never had a glitch throughout and the retro graphics I thought were great.
Gameplay wise I would say it's in similar vein to the sims series, as in you use your customized family to perform tasks and can queue up to 2 actions per person, but in no way is it a carbon copy, the post apocalyptic shelter setting offers a very different experience that can be both humerous and dark. You have to keep your characters fed, watered (rain can be collected and needs to be filtered if its conatminated rain), clean and fresh which offers a more fun challenge being in a post apocalyptic setting. With no mains electricity, water or air (generator pumps air into the shelter) these necessities to your characters need to be well micro managed, especially in the early stages and it offers a very unique gaming experience. The shelter needs to be maintained in lots of areas and can also be expanded to 4 levels. you will end up needing the extra room badly as there's a lot of stuff you're going to need to build.
The game is quite punishing to start with and I recommend going through the tutorial and having a practice run before starting a proper game. As you'd expect with a game like this it has a lot of repetitive elements, you'll be repeating the same tasks a lot, especially with maintaining machinery, but I didn't find this element annoying, in fact I found it very addictive.
AS well as maintaining the shelter and trading with people who visit the shelter, you can go out on expeditions to search or trade for items in a large randomly generated map. You can end up in battles or negotiations with other people in the wasteland and there's a good levelling up system in place to improve your characters stats for both.
The battle system is fairly basic, nothing special with it, it's a very simple rpg type system that can offer a bit of a gambling element. The flee option is avaialable if you get into trouble but I still managed to lose both parents in combat. Not to worry though, I recruited some new people to the shelter to look after the kids and they're still going strong.
The game definitely strikes a good chord with hoarding,  all items are vital to levelling up and maintaining the shelter and your characters. I got completely hooked around half way through and was so hoping it would take the game to another level, but as soon as you get to the stage where your doing well and sending your characters out heavily armed with the van (the van needs to be repaired with parts found on expeditions) the games limitations started to show and there are some major negatives with the game:
First off, the enemies you face are a challenge at early stages, but eventually they're all just too easy when you start using guns. I never once faced another enemy armed with a gun, it was only ever melee weapons so combat became a breeze.
A lot of dialogue gets repetitive, especially when facing enemies or dealing with traders. It's forgivable for an indie game of this type, they got the main things right.
The van whilst great when you get it, speeds the game up exponentially and I actually wouldn't have minded not getting the van till a bit later.
Theres also a recycling machine you can build and all I will say is as soon as you build that, it becomes way too easy to get materials, so if you want to get the most out of the game, build the recycling machine last.
Many have said how they find the attack system on the shelter annoying and whilst I agree that having your usually hard as nails characters cower in fear as opposed to fight off the attackers, it does offer another element by having the need to build booby traps and upgrade the doors to counter these raids. Unfortunately I found that the developers must have taken the criticism of this system on board a bit too much, as I've only been attacked twice and now I've got a fully stacked shelter with lots of traps and I've got bored of keeping the game on fast forward trying to get an attack.
I've explored all the map and there's not much left to do which is a shame, because I didn't want the game to end. Technically there's no end objective but eventually you will reach a point where there's nothing left to build, upgrade or explore and it will be time to call it a day.
BUT I'm really hopeful that some updates will tempt me to re visit my shelter and I think I'll start a new family in the future using a different pet. A top level addictive indie game while it lasts, I had over 30 hours of fun and for the price is a total bargain. Even if you've got a glimmer of intrigue, make sure you give shelter a shot because I was debating it for a while and nearly didn't go for it. I would have been missing out

As a fan of the first 2 Super Giant games, I immediately purchased this one.
It is certainly very different from the other two games they have published, and I agree with others it is not for everyone. However, I still loved this game.
The art work and music is spectacular, the story ingrossing, the characters memorable. All of this is par for the course in a Super Giant game. It is longer than their other two games, Bastion and Transistor, but still only 11 hours long.
The gameplay is likely what will make it or break it for you as a buyer. This game has a very large amount of reading, as much of the game is traveling the world and speaking to your companions and foes. I personally love reading and enjoyed the writing, but this isn't something everyone shares. Along with this, your choices regarding the world and your team makes many small and large changes to the story, which facilitates playing the game multiple times.
The rest of the game is the 'rites', or the 3v3 mode seen in the trailers. This is a large change from Super Giant games, and a novel idea as a whole. I personally liked this mode, but I enjoyed the whole game so understand I have some bias. In the rites you have control over all 3 teammates, but can only move 1 at a time, which lends both the good and bad parts of the gameplay.
As for the good, parts, the rites are unique and intriguing. While others call the gameplay shallow, I see it more as a 'easy to learn, hard to master' type of game. It is very simple to pick up the gameplay of the rites, but through my playthrough I discovered several tactics not at first glance (and many others that the A.I. used on me!). Along with that, it was extremely exciting to be down to the last few hitpoints of my Pyre, only to bring the match around and win a mighty comeback. I look forward to playing the campaign again on a higher difficulty, and to play against my siblings and friends in the Versus mode.
Continuing on about the Versus mode, this is the first Super Giant game to have any sort of multiplayer, though it is local only. However, I was pleased to see the Versus mode has a wide variety of modifiers, choices, and overall robust design.
As I mentioned before, the rites have their downsides. Against the easier A.I foe, the game was very easy (Though this can be increased in difficulty and their are the 'Titan Stars', which increase the power of the enemy teams in a multitude of ways). Against some of the more difficult teams however, I became frustrated by some of the controls (Playing on a gamepad). Sometimes I felt I lost because of controls or input lag This is compounded by the fact that the game becomes lightning fast with late game foes and multiple masteries [skills] on characters. A fast character can dunk the ball into the opponent's pyre within a single second from the start of a match, sometimes leading to no chance of reaction. Some of this may be my lack of ability, however, and it decreased in frustration as I learned some of the knacks of the game.
Pyre describes itself as a role playing game, and has a progression system for your characters. These include talismans, items that give both small and large buffs to your characters, and masteries, skills unqiue to different races ingame. These masteries don't fundamentally change how a character plays but does affect their skills to a point that new combos and tactics can be discovered.
Much of the variety in this game that was found in Bastion through different weapons or Transistor through new skills is the roster of characters you control. Each character has a different move set and list of stats, along with the previously mentioned masteries. Overall I was content with the progression system as a whole.
Again, as a whole I loved Pyre. I am not sure I liked it quite as much as Bastion or Transistor, but it was still gorgeous, fun, and an emotional wild ride at times. It is not a game for everyone, but I would still reccomend it if you don't mind plenty of reading, or get frustrated or uninterested by the rites.

Firstly, my heart aches for not recommending a SGG game whose games I love…
But I did not find in Pyre what I found in Bastion and Transistor.
In Pyre, you are called the reader, and this name is well deserved, because the game is 90% reading, and 10% gameplay. And even then, the gameplay is quite boring and repetitive, even as you
. The AI switch between doing nothing and dying, sometimes being blocked by objects and not picking the orb, and sometimes, it just ruins you, picking the orb, and throwing it at you, banishing you and rushing to the pyre, within seconds.
As for the story, you have very few choices to make, and it doesn't make you feel that they are of any importance (except for the
).
The RPG content, which come as Masteries tree and equipment system is very poor and makes few differences in the gameplay (the talisman are greats, but you can't have many so you are stuck with the ones you upgraded).
You have fought almost any possible team within 2-3 hours, and then you have to do it again, and again, and again, until you finish the game, which is virtually extended by forcing you to roam through all the map, without interest (very few random events, and without any consequence).
As I write this review, I did not find any way to restart the campaign with a new game+ (keeping upgrades), to explore some of the branching/endings quicker.
Let's end with a brief summary of the pros/cons of the game.
Pros : - Beautiful design and graphics, as always
- Good soundtrack, though not as good as the two previous games (just my opinion)
- Characters and their interactions very well developped
- Story rich
Cons : - You like reading? Pick a book.
- Logan Cunningham is not narrating all the story!
- Repetitive gameplay which is quite a feat since it only represents 10% of the game
- Poor RPG content
- Very linear (but as were Bastion and Transistor)
And to clarify, I played Pyre for 10 hours, and I took some pleasure in it. But this is not worth 20€, and it lets a bitter taste in my mouth (maybe because I was expecting much more from Supergiant games).

No game has ever changed an industry like DOOM has, nor has a game delivered so much fun.
STORY
Unfortunately, there's not much to DOOM's plot. All you need to know is that Hell has taken over Mars and it's moons, and you are the last space marine alive on Mars' moon of Phobos. The story hardly progresses and when it does, it only appears through text screens. So, if you're in it for the story, you won't find much here, that's for sure.
GAMEPLAY
This is DOOM's main strength, and the main reason you should play the game. DOOM utilises the old-school mechanics of shooters, with health kits and multiple weapons to carry. Your objective in DOOM is to reach the end of each level whilst eliminating monsters, receiving powerups and activating doors and switches. DOOM's gameplay is very simple and can be understood by any player. Enemy choice and enemy positioning is very creative in DOOM, with there being multiple types of enemy, each one being very cleverly designed. Enemies usually appear in groups of 5-30, which can make the game a real challenge. As you'd expect, there's plenty of ways to dispose with these enemies, with weapons ranging from shotguns to chainsaws. All weapons are very useful and well designed. Level design is another outstanding attribute of DOOM. Levels never feel to maze-like or too linear, which is still a perfect match today. Level design is creative and often gives the player a real challenge. Levels are also scattered with secret areas, which reward the player for exploring the level design and wanting to find new things.
GRAPHICS/VISUALS/EFFECTS
Some will instantly forget about DOOM when they see it's cheap attempts at 3D graphics, but those affect the gameplay in no way whatsoever. However, DOOM's designs are still amazing, everything from box art to level textures are well designed.
CONCLUSION
DOOM is a simple run and gun shooter, however it's sheer fun and enjoyment surpasses any flaw and makes it a game for anyone. 10/10, a game that anyone can enjoy and simply understand.

Have not beaten this game, yet. I'm probably not even close to the halfway point. But I felt the need to share a first-impressions review:
When I first booted up the game and got to the first "combat" session, I wasn't sure I would like this game as much as Bastion or Transistor. But that was most likely due to the fact that I hadn't gotten a hang of it, yet.
A couple hours later, I was marvelling at the new tricks they were giving me access to. It really only took me about two or three matches to start to get a feel for it. I can't really call it combat anymore because, as others have been pointing out, the matches seem very American-football/basketball-esque at their core, so they feel more like games than fights. Regardless, the matches felt a lot less taxing and a lot more rewarding after I started to get a hang of it, though as the opponents are getting tougher all the time, I can tell I'm just starting to scratch the surface of how to play.
Now, this game does lack the open exploration that I enjoyed in both Bastion and Transistor, and I can't say that I don't miss that. Instead, the story is presented in dialogue. You find yourself among a travelling group, and you learn about the world little by little based on what they tell you and what you gleam from their conversations amongst themselves. The game doesn't sit you down with a history book and expect you to memorize it, they let you pick up on things little by little. It feels organic and natural, and they only give you so much at a time.
With all of that said, if you're filled with a deep contempt for textbox dialogue heavy games or visual novels, this might not be the game for you. But if you enjoy visual novels, or even think that there's a time and place where you could, then give this one a chance. It has the same beautiful art and captivating music that I've come to expect from a Supergiant Games release, a similar levelling mechanic, really, a lot of familiarity to what I think made their previous games such hits. But it also has a unique new combat system, and it feels like your decisions hold even more weight in Pyre than they did in Transistor or even in Bastion, and the cast of characters is already finding their way into my heart. Even the one that I didn't like at first.

***Review Update***
This review was made, perhaps irresponsibly, with the trust to the developer that they would remain communicative and continue to pursue excellence through their game. I must admit, as a backer I was biased toward positivity as this is a multiplayer-based game and I felt that the game in a more pure state would have been one of the best asymmetrical multiplayer based games ever made. However as of 7/26/17, the developers and publishers have been radio silent regarding multiple issues with the game (such as melee being currently broken with Jason able to ignore counselor swings, dodging being glitchy, and many many glitches ruining the flow of the game) and have offered no roadmap going forward on how they are going to address these issues that we backers have brought to their attention since Beta.
I still have every belief that, if given enough attention, this game still holds the potential I had mentioned in my review if the problems marring it currently were to be addressed and we see an advent of new content including maps and items. But until then I look at my original review with embarassment thinking that I misunderstood the inexperience that the makers of this game have. This game should have been released under Early Access, and I still have hope that I will be able to delete this blurb from my review and simply return it to the original one.
*** Original Review ***
As of this review, the problems plagueing the connectivity of the game have been 99% removed.
I would like to make something very clear: this is not a competitive multiplayer game. It is an asymmetric multiplayer game in function only. At it's core, this is actually an Immersive Multiplayer Slasher Sim, or otherwise a Friday the 13th Simulator. If you are a fan of slashers, cheesy horror, the tension of being stalked (or stalking), emergent gameplay and drama through crazy situations, thrills n kills, and beating odds that are clearly stacked against you, then you will enjoy this game THOROUGHLY. There is simply nothing like this game on the market, and even its closest peers do not capture the kind of magic that this game captures.
But I want to caution some of you:  if you're in it for leaderboards and metagaming, you may not like this game. This game is best played when trying to play immersively. The situations that arise when people do stupid things out of tension, or the quick witted escapes and jukes, or the Jason who perfectly stalks his prey and fools them into leaving a hiding spot, THIS is what we live for in this game. You're simply not playing for that Win screen because winning or losing in this game simply isn't important - what's important is all the craziness that happens in between.
If this sort of thing sounds appealing to you then there's no need to hesitate in buying this game. There is nothing like it and likely won't be for a long time. It is a unique labor of love created by movie veterans and unabashed horror fans who understand how to make an experience compelling. But if you're still scratching your head on this then I would implore you to atleast wait until it's on sale. This game is certainly not for everyone and I understand that.
Overall however, you will not find a more compelling slasher game.

Well, this is my first serious review and I think I've chosen a good product to review. Incoming wall of text.
First of all, I've been following this game for a long time, since before it was even released and I have to say, this game is going places. The Isle in it's current state shouldn't even be called a pre-alpha. The finished product will be nothing like this current build we have now. However, my review is about the game in its current state, not what it eventually will be. So take that into consideration, and don't base this review on what the game will always be. Dinosaurs won't always be the only factor, the developers have plans for human factions and mythical(more or less made up) creatures too.
Gameplay and Bugs-
The Isle is meant to be a survival-horror multiplayer game. Currently it's more of a survive-as-a-dinosaur simulator. You can choose from a variety of herbivores and carnivores, each with their own special stats and unique niches in the in-game ecosystem.
You can explore different maps and hunt and fight to survive. You can make packs or herds and roam the island fleeing from carnivores or fighting against them. This in and of itself is pretty entertaining, at least for me. Currently it's kind of a choose-your-own-adventure kind of thing and each experience has the chance of being different than the last.
Fighting mechanics are pretty clunky but over time you can get used to this and learn to hunt or fight pretty effectively.
Austroraptor has its pounce, Tyrannosaurus can break its prey's bones.
Now, keeping in mind, it IS an early-access game and it will have it's low-streaks. But if you buy a game that says early-access, that's the kind of stuff you've got to expect. Any major game-breaking bugs are usually fixed in the next few patches.
Maps-
The maps are mostly rolling hills and tall mountains with sections of forest and grassland, dotted by lakes. Pretty basic. Textures aren't so good, but the project lead Dondi has shown off an inbound foliage update and new biomes to come with it, so that's a plus.
Developers and the Community-
Well here's the big section I think everyone wants to see, it's in every review. Well personally, I don't have a problem with how the developers act. That's how they want to behave, so be it. It's their game, not yours. I don't understand why people get so upset that a game developer is acting like an actual human being. Maybe they take it too far to some people, but it really doesn't bother me. Besides, this is about the game, not the developers.
Now the community is a different story. You've got your typicals for every online game. The friendlies, the people who kill you on sight, etc. But honestly, you're looking at people exploiting things that won't really be exploitable in the future. You can typically avoid these kinds of people so long as you stay away from the central "Spawn Lake" hub on any server. If you're looking for a 100% realistic dinosaur simulator, try one of The Isle's several realism servers or wait for a game like Saurian.
Personally I recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of prehistoric animals and/or likes open-world survival games.
If I had to give this game a number rating, I'd say 8/10.

Amnesia. A true classic and the benchmark by which all other horror games are judged. The main selling point of this game is that in other games you would be scared s**tless by what you see, but in Amnesia it is what you can't see that terrifies you more than what you can see.
It keeps you at the edge of madness and terror whilst at the same time keeps you there without ever pushing you to the point where it because mundane.
The story is actually very engaging, with the protagonist being an Englishman named Daniels suffering from amnesia, you find yourself in an old dark castle set deep in the Prussian woods
What Daniels is doing in the castle is up to you to find out, you are searching for answers regarding why you have an Amnesia. But those answer are unlikely to bring you joy.
● There is never a time where you wont be afraid
● Very engaging story
● You have to look after your health and your mental health
● You have to keep an eye on your supplies - eg: Lantern oil
● Very well designed and terrifying game areas/levels - eg: Prison, Sewers, Wine Cellar
● Soundtrack & visuals
● Achievements
● Very immersive
● Very atmospheric
● The darkness will be your best friend and greatest enemy
● Community created stories
● Price range
● Puzzles
● The Lantern runs out of oil pretty fast if you don't conserve it,
● When you die, well. You just die and return to the last saved checkpoint. I wish there was some kind of Survival mode.
● Monsters disappear after a while
● A small amount of bugs and glitches
● Sound stuttering at times
● No Steam Trading Cards
Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a true classic old school horror game where it doesn't rely on jump scares to scare the player, but relies on the soundtrack, levels and the darkness. No game I have ever played has used darkness so effectively. It is both your best friend and greatest enemy at the same time. It will hide you from the terrors, but it will expose you to the insanity brewing in your own mind. Everything about this game works well to produce a true feeling of fear.
If you like horror games this is a must have. And if you have the balls to play it at night with the headphones and curtains closed. Then you are in for rough ride.

KOTOR2 is beloved for many reasons; some memories are more infamous than others. Not only was it the return of Interplay/Black Isle under the new name of Obsidian but it was also the first mainstream Star Wars game to explore the richness of its universe only hinted from the films. Unless you have played an immersive simulator like Tie Fighter, no game since KOTOR 2 has captured the subtleties behind the Force, the political and economic views of a galaxy at war and the childlike sense of wonder into a galaxy far, far away.
However, what I believe is not often considered is how KOTOR 2 was the foundation for modern role-playing games, started by Obsidian here and perfected by BioWare in Dragon Age and Mass Effect. Companions with variable attitudes based on an affinity meter and moral alignments with/against the player along with tons of dialogue, banter and cutscenes; the importance of choice and consequence for companions as well as the player’s expression through dialogue and choices to make each experience distinct; and the vignette storytelling where each area tells the smaller tales of a much grander one with sides to choose to connect with the player’s choices. Although all these aspects are not sacred to KOTOR2 as the original and many RPGs beforehand included these features, the execution, while far from perfection, is so distinctly BioWare you would be forgiven in thinking it was made by them.
(Note: You ABSOLUTELY need to download the Content Restoration Mod via Steam Workshop to get best experience with KOTOR2 as it restores so much great moments the developers were not allowed to add back to the game.)
In my previous review of KOTOR1, I had explained why I felt the sequel was a better BioWare game on reflection of finishing the first game, and after completing the sequel I can understand why even fans of the first game did not enjoy the latter one as much as the first. The debate of which one is better exactly the Coke vs. Pepsi style of debate of Fallout 3 & New Vegas (Nuka Cola or Sunset Sasperella?), and the answer to both dilemmas is which one is more liking to your tastes.
The best comparison I could describe about KOTOR is whether you prefer the Star Wars from the films or the expanded universe from the books. KOTOR 1 was tightly paced its plot focused more on its long-lasting twist than developing characters beyond their quirks in a popcorn-friendly good versus evil story. KOTOR 2, however, deliberately will let you explore nuances of the lore from the simplest of teachings and conflicts for the Jedi and Sith as well as immerse you into a game of Pazaak to understand the thoughts of a character like a chapter from a book. The difference in quality can best be seen by the amount of depth added to returning characters like T3-M4, HK-47 and Canderous and the deviations of similar characters from the original like Atton vs Carth and Kreia vs Bastila.
This difference isn’t limited to the writing but also how much of a different experience each game provides. KOTOR 1 has a lengthy prologue as a non-Jedi character offering you the most role-playing options before boxing you into Sith or Jedi after a montage of becoming a Jedi. Its greatest strengths were the pacing of each world, the few moments of insight into the lore, and its more memorable quests. KOTOR 2 starts you off as an ex-Jedi where you earn your prowess with the Force overtime with role-playing options all throughout as well as letting you decide how much of a Sith or Jedi you want to be. Instead of some exemplary quests, KOTOR2 provides more down-time on the Ebon Hawk as well as relying on set-pieces with choices to make each world distinct in gameplay and story.  I may not remember every quest but I can remember the solo fight with a Wookie, the two-team assault on Dxun and Onderon, and the quiet meanderings and inner battles in the dead Sith Lord tombs.
Even in terms of the core gameplay, there is a refinement behind the sequel that is hard to explain without simply playing for yourself. Perhaps it’s the additional feats, weapons, items and force-powers or the numbers themselves but I found the sequel to be a better challenge, although the moments where you play alone as a companion or yourself feel like sucker punches of difficulty. Where the first game felt more like you had to game the system to win, the sequel manages to add more flair and variable tactics behind the numbers. This is the only aspect I find that KOTOR 2 is undeniably better as a game.
The shorter version of this section is that you should play KOTOR 1 once for its plot, and you should play the sequel many times as a role-playing game.

Unfortunately, as often the case with Obsidian, KOTOR2 was never a finished game. Where KOTOR 1 was a tightly connected story and game, KOTOR 2 had so much trapped in the game files that was brought back thanks to modders with Obsidian’s approval. Even when you restore what was meant to be in the game, the final section of Malachor V is so confusedly put together that it almost risks ruining the whole experience.
What saves KOTOR 2 is that neither the story nor the gameplay was sullied because it was unfinished nor given its conclusion in a sequel. The story and the game’s journey of the Exile is single-handily the best narrative in an RPG that rivals the highest standard of Baldur’s Gate 2. Where BG2 incorporated the game’s morality into the plot, KOTOR 2 integrates the Jedi/Sith conflict as well as the boundaries of what kind of Jedi/Sith you are as the player into the story along with utilizing the Force abilities and the Exile’s unique ability into the raw RPG mechanics. The twist in KOTOR 1, at worst, felt like a cynical retreading of BG2; the twist in KOTOR2 left me spell-bound by how interconnected the journey was up to Malachor V. Even in the game’s climax, the harrowing thoughts of what lies in store for the Exile and Reven as well as the small comforts of knowing the futures of the companions and the result of the player’s choices capitalized what still ends up as one of the greatest stories in an RPG.
However, if you were hoping every question would be provided with an answer or if the journey the game teases you at the end would continue in the nonexistent future, then it can be understood why some absolutely hated the ending. Imagine if the entirety of Mass Effect 3 had never happened, would that ruin the experience of 2 that also ended on a cliffhanger with many unanswered questions? As someone who maintains a level of scope with a story as well as enjoying unsolved mysteries, I do not find the ending, if properly fixed, would had made KOTOR bad. If this is the last we’ll ever see of the Exile or Revan—that isn’t a shoddy novel or bland cameo in The Old Republic—then it was on the best ditch to die on because the journey to get there is compelling enough to replay and evocative enough to imagine what may never come to be.
Perhaps KOTOR 2 should serve as a lesson for pipe-dreams. Disappointment is a fickle to learn to deal with as the expectations you wish only further wound you into finding the smallest of faults borne not out of spite but out of love with what potential lies dormant and yet may never be unearthed. This lasting feeling is something I think is what makes KOTOR 2 as amazing as it is because it will hurt you at what you love about it and yet you will come away feeling as bound to it as much as Sion is to the Force.
Maybe instead of longing for what is unlikely to occur we can heed the same advice from Kreia past down to the Exile, “Perhaps you were expecting some surprise, for me to reveal a secret that had eluded you, something that would change your perspective of events, shatter you to your core. There is no great revelation, no great secret. There is only you."

Sigh. This is one of those games that sounds like such a cool idea on paper, but the way it's done here doesn't really bring it to life.
The basic premise is good. Imagine FTL, but you're trying to stay alive in a bomb shelter. That should be amazing, right? The catch is that the game should be difficult, and Sheltered is not a difficult game by any stretch. In FTL, you have a goal you need to build up for: the flagship. That game would be substantially less interesting if A: the random encounters were all easy, and B: there was no flagship.
In the beginning, there are certain things you have to build for your shelter, mostly for storage, but once you've got those down, the game becomes too easy. Supplies are simply too plentiful, and they replenish in the places you scavenge, so as long as you can hold everything you've found, you're golden. In all my playthroughs, I never ran out of food, and once I learned to build a lot of water storage, I never ran out of water.
You could up the difficulty by getting all the shelter upgrades and then putting 14 people in your shelter, but you don't need them. I didn't need the 7 or 8 that I had as it was, because just keeping up with maintenance and construction only requires 2 or 3 at absolute maximum. The fact that the children you start with can help out so well is kinda broken; basically, just give them a welding torch, and they can fix your water filter.
You would think that going into the post-apocalyptic wasteland would be a dangerous proposition, but it's not. The very hardest encounters will feature people with guns, but for most of the game, the people you fight are a cinch to beat. Frequently, they're unarmed. Here's how: 2 people with 7+ strength, each with handaxes, and kevlar if you feel like being careful. You'll find kevlar and axes all the time, and what you'll get is a two-man death squad that chews up the worst the wasteland can throw at you, and spit it back out like a paper spitball. Then, on top of that, there are guns and grenades. Basically, if you do a bit of scavenging, and then bother to arm your people, you've got it locked down.
For a while, maxing out your shelter will be kinda fun, and there is some satisfaction in getting the best stuff, but the difficulty scales so minimally that it doesn't actually matter. The shelter raids were a source of complaint a while back because your people can't fight back (yes, that death squad I mentioned above can only fight if they're out in the wasteland, not if they're defending their children from murder cultists), so all you could do is set traps. But that was useful at least in presenting a threat to players, something you had to prepare for.
Above all, there's no real end game. You can try and survive as long as you want, but that gets to be boring after about day 10 because it's never actually difficult to begin with, and if you're bothering to get upgrades, nothing you find will set you back.

This game is a must have for fans of the movie trilogy and just fans of these types of point and click games in general. It has quite a few flaws that i will detail below, but the good triumphs over the bad if the game is on sale.
Good aspects:
Detailed and well thought out story that links all five episodes together - Each story has logical and believable writing and execution in relation to the movies. The motives of the characters is similar to that of what was in the movies and it is told well enough.
Great voice acting/dialogue/characters - the person portraying Marty sounds so similar to Mr. Fox in the movies that i kept on actually believing that it really was him doing his best vocal impression of himself at that young age. Christopher Lloyd was also a delight to listen to. As were the other lead characters for the most part.
Nostalgia - The game nails it when it comes to bringing memories back from the movies,  referencing certain aspects of the three movies and just celebrating the most memorable lines, moments and scenes in the movie trilogy without over doing it.
Bad aspects:
Presentation/animation - The character renders and overall presentation is quite bad in comparison to other games that celebrate famous movies (such as Ghostbusters: The Video Game, which came out a year earlier and which looked well detailed and thorogh in its visual appearance snd actually lets you roam around freely with very few issues) Roaming around in the Hill Valley in this game can seem like somewhat of a chore at times with the limitations on where you can walk and the camera angles nearly impossoble to manouvere. That doesn't change whether you use the keyboard controls or your mouse. The design of Hill Valley looks decent enough, but the whole presentation and animations of the chatacters could have been way better if the right time and money was invested. Still, it was still ok and not game breaking for me. Graphically, the game doesn't look as if it reaches its potential.
Choice-based gameplay being limited - The choices that they let your character make are very limiting and don't really add much to your path in the story because whichever options you pick, your character will ultimately go always go in the same path. That is because with the options they provide you during interaction with various characters, you almost always have to pick all of them to move forward in the story. For example, playing as Marty, as you're interacting with Doc Brown you need to find out a specific piece of information and are given four or more choices of questions or phrases you can ask/provide, but you have to ask pretty much all of them to get to where you need to so there isn't really a huge amount of choice involved in actuality.
Overall, it is a very good game for what it is that would be most enjoyed if you're a fan of the movie series that could have been amazing if a little more time and money were invested into this. Probably not worth it for the full price, but is great value when on sale.
However, if they released a sequel to this (whether in episodic format or otherwise), then i would definitely buy it especially if they fixed the flaws that were in this game.

I'm Dayvis2, and this is my review for Telltale's Back to the Future: The Game!
PLOT:
Some may think that this game is just a play through of the three films, but it is actually a completely new story written by Bob Gale. The game is split into 5 episodes - It's About Time, Get Tannen, Citizen Brown, Double Visions and OUTATIME, and they are all about two hours long, assuring about 10 hours of gameplay. The story is based around 1931 Hill Valley, where gangsters rule the streets and a 17 year old Emmet Brown is creating his first scientific experiments. The game parodies the " history repeats itself " theme in the trilogy, with some " Hey Mcfly"s, Marty almost being hit by a moving object and horrible nightmares followed by a sudden realisation. A true tribute to the films.
GAMEPLAY
The game follows the point and click genre, as many other Telltale games do. Unfortunately, as an earlier product, the game does not feature Quick Time Events or the fact that choices affect the story. Quite a few fun puzzles, so you'll need to be ready for some brain twisters!
GRAPHICS
Pretty good graphics. Less comic book style ( as The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us have) and more realistic looking.
SUMMARY
A good product, but you can get it for a fiver on some sales, such as the BTTF day one I bought this on.

Nether is a fun game if you love survival games, but Nether is not a fun game if you have no clue how to play survival games. I've played many games that have a survival concept to them, and the main reason people give bad reviews is because they have no clue how to play these types of games. So with that being said you can trust my review.
Pros:
+Nether has a decent sized map, not too big and not too small. Also it will expand as development continues.
+The survival experience is realistic, you have to scavenge food, meds, and weapons to survive.
+There's little to no hackers in the game, also the servers are VAC secured so hackers are very rare.
+The marketplace is not pay to win, the only things you can buy with gold are cosmetic items, everything else is in game money.
+Nether is very easy to start off in, I recommend not going to a high population server right away, those servers are mainly filled with PVPers, not looters. There are many low population servers that you will be safe to loot in.
+PVP is realistic in the aspect that when you die, you will lose everything except cosmetic items that are equipped. Don't be that guy who runs out with all their stuff.
+The game has a very good crafting system, you can find items and use them to create guns. Also you can kill nether and they drop items you can trade for gun parts, food, ammo, etc.
+There is a Tribe system, which is like a clan system but there is a list of around 8 that you can choose from, you can capture territory around the map for your tribe and you get xp and money for doing so.
+The group system works very well, you can invite players and see them on the map when you are grouped with them.
+There are world events such as: Loot drops, escort missions and Reaper events.
Cons:
-The Nether's AI can be a little buggy, but it's still pretty reasonable.
-Sometimes the servers won't all show up and the cursor will be frozen. They are fixing this right now but the best thing to do is wait, your cursor will get unfrozen eventually. Also the server problem, if you join a server and it kicks you back out to the server list, you want to rejoin until your in game, but you might have to wait for the character menu to show up.
-People with snipers can easily kill someone who just started off, but most likely you won't run into one on a low population server.
-There is a limit to your global inventory, so you can't have an infinite amount of guns and supplies.
-Starting off, Nether are hard to kill, so you have to be extra careful not to attract the stronger variants of them.
So overall, Nether is everything that I would want in a survival game. It's very entertaining and it doesn't have a lot of bugs. If you are into Survival games I would recommend this to you.

Apotheon is the fight of Nikandreos ('Victory of Man') against Zeus & the Gods of Olympus who have decided to destroy humanity once & for all. Nikandreos must travel through the realms of the lesser gods & defeat them, taking their powers & climbing higher up Olympus to battle Zeus. Although the platforming is simplistic & the combat a little clunky, the ambience of the game is beautiful. I love the artstyle, the whole game appearing as if it is wrapped around an ancient Greek vase, the visuals complimented by an excellent music score & voice acting.
Each god's realm has a thought-out, distinctive feel & challenge - Hades is a dark, claustrophic place inhabited by shades clawing at the living, Artemis' glade is serene but full of dangerous beasts & Athena's realm is an ever shifting maze requiring strategy to nagivate. This approach carries over to Nikandreos, who can equip a surprisingly wide variety of weapons and armour to face Zeus (my personal favourites are the weapons & arrows with 'backstab' stats).
Apotheon is beautiful to look at and a pleasure to play.

The good the bad and the ugly - An review of Nether
The Good - Nether is an interesting beast, it has all the elements in place to make it a fantastic game if the developers commited themselves to improvements and not flushing out their microtransaction store they could be on to something. With some alteration to the combat animations (As in more of them so it doesn't feel so static) and a good fleshing out of the NPC quests, weapons, and world events this does have a potential to be a good game.
The skill trees - I've found myself enjoying the hell out of these, building characters for very different things. I've jokingly nicknamed my package runner "The Kenyan" due to a maxed out sprint tree and whooohhh boy does it make a difference. You can actually specalize which is a major improvement over their past games.
Hear me out here, I know its by the same gentleman that did "Infestation survivor stories/The War Z" which was such a catastrophy that steam had to pull it for an extended period of time. It looks like he may be learning. The NPC combat with the teleportation mechanic is actually interesting and outright horifying, this is a massive step in the right direction (Case in point, if running in the subway while a surge is occuring on the surface... the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s warp down into the subway because of the noise you make and they damn well try to kill you). The NPC's are actually pose a threat, they are highly agressive and mechanically they can make life a living nell (pun intended.) - If a dozen + world events and monsters were added to the game, more weapons diversity (and animations) were added, it could be a very good STALKER-esque game.
The Ugly - the luggage - Hammerpoint interactive/Nether/TheWarZ/Infestation Survior stories all operate off of the same engine which has extreme limitations graphically. This by itself is not a bad thing but coupled with the history of the publisher it raises severe concerns. This is the massive problem that almost all gamers are going to have with Nether is the baggage it brings with it and the bitter taste of TheWarZ/Infestation survivor stories.
The Bad - The playerbase (initially) & Repititon - Before clan assignment you really are just some random schlub. Your life has utterly zero meaning or value outside of a of "loot pinyata." The good news is that generally clan members do not attach each other. There is also a problem of "A lack of things to do" at present outside of scavenging and outpost defense/reclimation. This is where the last game also failed. There need to be additional events added that force people to work together to survive the mess that the world became in Nether. It's unfortunate that they might never see the light of day.
Overall Summary
5/10 -
Good - Decent engine, interesting and engaging enemies with their mechanics, decent pvp.
Bad - Can become repetitive, PC's often kill players who've not picked out a clan. Combat animatons need to be fleshed out. Game needs a lot more content to flesh the story.
Ugly - Developer reputation - After The War Z (Infestation Survivor stories) they seriously need to finish this if they want any chance of continuing as a developer. If they do not finish this and make it into something then there is a good chance that too many bridges will have been scorched for them to ever try again.

For a long time, I wanted to play the game that was so important it was deemed a national treasure of the United States. When I finally did, I didn't regret it for an instant.
It goes without saying; Doom is
. You can't crouch, you can't jump, you can't look up or down, and it's not even true 3D - 2.5D, as it was called, unable to stack rooms on top of one another. Pixelated monsters and environments straight out of 1993 look like an absolute mess at the ludicrous speeds the player is capable of and autoaim is a fact of life.
Despite how undeniably and understandably aged Doom is, it's still a fantastic game. It offers a healthy list of useful weapons with unique roles and a good variety of enemies that provide a fair challenge each. Valuable first-person shooter skills saw their rise to prominence in the bloodstained halls of the UAC labs and remain engaging twelve years later. Pacing that satisfies and yet leaves the player wanting for more contributes to an addicting game that gives the player control of how fast and how loose they want to fight their way through each demon-infested level.
Interesting usage of lighting, pleasing level design, detailed sprites and animations - few frames as they had - and a MIDI soundtrack so powerful you'd expect it to take up more than its 800KB in space all drive home Doom's finely aged experience. Even the stock sound effects that Doom relies upon are employed effectively and continue to make their presence heard in video games to this day.
It's no wonder that the first-person shooter genre had the title of "Doom clone" when this classic was released. More than two decades after id Software put shooters on the map, Doom is still an absolute treat to play. To those who have yet to see what all the yelling and screaming is about, my recommendation is to take the plunge and start cooking with gas.

Scratch cards, leader boards, animals, and a currency system based on lums (glowing flies you collect in levels). Couple this together with the dodgy adaptation of Wii U tablet stuff made to work with controllers and you end up with a game that is a bit of a mess. Legends would be a much better game if Ubisoft just trimmed off the fat. But the joy found in Origins is still here under all this pointless flubber. There is still game here that is fun and worth your time, even if you have to wade through the muck to get it.

TL;DR: Fun and faithful despite its bugs, an entertaining game that could be a great game in the making if they’re diligent in addressing player concerns.
Playability issues aside, I see very little to complain about with the new Friday the 13th: The Game.  There may be one caveat, of course, and that is you might have to be a fan of the films to really appreciate the game.
First of all, Jason is STUPIDLY overpowered in this game.  It’s so crazy complicated to kill him that it’s a huge gamble to even attempt it.  He gets stronger and gains more abilities as the game goes on, and by the end of it he can basically walk through walls and doors like they’re made out of paper.  Nearly everything he does, even down to just being near counselors, gives him an advantage as their fear makes them glow bright red on his special radar sense and makes them more likely to trip and fall during chase.
Does any of this sound familiar?  It should.  It sounds exactly like Jason from the movies.  This game isn’t fair.  It’s not balanced.  It’s what Fox News is, not what it claims to be.  Jason plays like he should play and he feels like he should feel when you’re playing a counselor.  You SHOULD feel hopeless when he’s nearby.  After all, encountering Jason in one of the movies is nearly 100% fatal.  There should never ever be a point in playing as a counselor that you should safe, even relatively so.  And I think the game does a great job of that.
Two biggest complaints so far are that Jason can’t climb in through windows and he can’t move or destroy objects.  Jason can move like a torpedo underwater, he can teleport anywhere he wants on the map, and he has a superfast speed walking abilities, but he can’t boost himself up through a window or move a dining room table out of the way?  C’mon!  He should be the one of the most formidable foes you’ve ever encountered in a game, not someone who can be foiled by running around a couch until the Jason player gets bored and goes to find someone a little less cheesy to murder.
Speaking of cheesy players, I was worried that I’d hate the multi-player experience but so far it’s been really positive.  Nobody has made assertions regarding my gender or sexuality and even the worst of the taunting I experienced was followed by some good-natured fun afterwards in the game lobby.  One player who was taunting me and asking, “You mad bro?”  Was actually really nice afterwards and even offered me some genuinely helpful tips, not the, “Get better at the game, button masher!” You sometimes get from these sorts!
I think the camaraderie comes from the fact that it’s better to stick together and try as a group to escape or call in the police to help.  It seems running off on your own in a video game based on a horror movie can be just as bad a choice as it is in the horror movie itself.  Sure, you might last longer than everyone else creeping quietly around the forest, or silently hiding under a bed for the whole round, but that just means you’ll be among the last to die, not the first to survive.  By contrast, in one game as a counselor, I was able to find two others and get a car working in pretty quick order.  Watching each other’s backs and fending off Jason when we had to was enough to get us out of Crystal Lake in about 4 minutes.  It’s way better and much more fun than looking out from underneath a bed seeing only floor for 20 minutes, if you ask me.
When the game really excels, however, is in the emergent gameplay moments.  These little events that just happen in games when the mechanics are just right and the players are interacting in ways the developers could have never anticipated are magical.  And in fact, some of these moments feel the MOST Friday the 13th to me.  In one playthrough, a few players and I got a car repaired and we in the midst of looking for the keys when we were savagely murdered by Jason.  As we all sat in the Dead Room spectating as the remaining players got picked off one by one (which can be as fun as playing the game itself) we watched as one last player was able to find the keys and drive to safety, covered in blood, because we had repaired the car.  We all cheered as she made it out alive, like a true Final Girl from a real horror movie, because we helped.  Sure, Jason killed 6 of the 7 of us, but it still felt like a victory.
Sure, the game is buggy.  Sure, people on 2 of the 3 platforms it was released on are still having trouble getting into games four days after launch.  And yes, some of the animations are just silly looking, but I know how these things go and I have faith that it can only get better, or at worst, stay as it is.  Which, would be fine with me, I have had a LOT of fun with the game over the past few days and already feel like I’ve gotten my money’s worth.  Also, in a couple of months a single player campaign is coming and it’s reportedly going to be all about playing as Jason.

So generally the usual horror games will have a focus more or less on jumpscares and indie like horror.
Amnesia is different.
The game focuses more on its story, suspense/drama, and puzzle solving while using a pretty cheap engine.
The story as you get more into the game feels more complex yet simple due to the very beginning telling you what you did and what to do. As you progress it gives more backstory then at the finale you choose fate.
The suspense is what makes this game great. It uses different sounds from different things whether it be the monster or the environment. The monsters are a little basic not threatening yet giving an ear piercing sound. But using these 2 makes a tingling sensation of unknown and you try to expect it giving more scares from a innocent thing
Last is the puzzle solving. I dont think any of it is hard as long as you look at notes and the area. I think I only managed to get stuck on 1 part and that was it
Overall the game is amazingly put and it is somewhat better when you listen to the discussions of the creators

This is one of the most important games of all time in terms of how much is shaped the industry, this is also one of my favourite game series of all time, and some of the games of my childhood. But how does it hold up today?
DOOM doesn’t really have a story, it’s almost non existent, the only time you ever get any of it is during some text after an intermission screen sometimes. DOOM’s story is that this corporation called UAC has been doing teleportation experiments on mars and its two moons and the UAC accidently opens a gate to hell and demons break out and kill everyone. You play as the DOOM space marine and your goal is to kill ALL of them.
The gameplay is that you go from point A to B: you have to find the exit point, there are locked doors which you need to find various keys to open them, get the to exit point, repeat, as well as relentlessly killing enemies.

The step up from Wolfenstein 3d to DOOM is massive:
In Wolfenstein 3d you only had four weapons being a knife, a pistol, a machinegun, and a minigun. Whereas in DOOM you have a knuckle duster, a chainsaw, a pistol, a shotgun, a minigun, a rocket launcher, a plasma gun, and the BFG (big ♥♥♥♥ing gun).
In Wolfenstein 3d you only had a few enemies ranging from dogs to four different types of soldiers with the only real difference being their reaction times and a slight different damage output. Whereas in DOOM there is quite a variety of enemy types ranging from appearance, reaction time, damage output, movement speed, the amount of health they have, the chances of them getting stunned and just how they behave since some enemies fly in this game, and how they attack; some enemies have hit scanning weapons, some enemies only have melee attacks and most have projectiles as well as the ability of melee attacks.
In Wolfenstein 3d the level design was flat, and it had no structure to it at all, it’s all a group of randomly designed mazes which are extremely confusing (and there’s no map) and all look the same and you end up getting lost all the time. Whereas in DOOM you had lifts, stairs, steps, you have moving parts of levels sometimes, you have wide open areas this time, level design that felt like it had actual structure and not just randomly designed mazes, you also had contact sensitive level design: in DOOM sometimes when you walk past a certain place a hidden room will open which had a horde of enemies inside waiting and this would happen a lot of certain items such as keys, or if a large health item or a gun was in the middle of the room, or if you flicked a switch. You also had toxic pools of waste of blood or lava sometimes as well. You also had different themes with the levels, at the beginning you are going through space stations, then later very nightmarish and hellish environments.
In Wolfenstein 3d the enemies only attack you, whereas in DOOM you can trick the enemies into attacking each other.
Though being considered one of the greatest games of all time there are a few things here and there that can be off putting since this game is very old and dated:
This is before you could jump, crouch and even look up and down in a first person shooter, so your movement is limited to moving forward, back, left, right, and turning, though there is an auto aim system for when an enemy is above or below you.
The weapons in this game just aren’t very fun to use anymore and that is something to be said about a game spent relentlessly killing enemies.
This game is also very much too easy, there are six difficulties other than the last two the game is way too easy since you’ll have fewer enemies who do less damage and there’s more ammo. On the second highest difficulty there are a lot more enemies who do much more damage and items are scarcer however it’s still rather easy if you know what you’re doing since the enemies are very predictable and there attacks can usually be minimised either by breaking their line of sight with the hit scanning enemies, you can just keep your distance with the melee only enemies, and you can dodge the projectiles very easily. However, nightmare mode on the other hand is completely unfair, all of the enemies move much quicker, projectiles move much quicker, the damage output is almost random and very high, but worst of all the enemies respawn a minute later after you’ve killed them.
Despite all this it’s still remains one of my favourite games of all time, and it has quite the lasting appeal, I still go back and play the original DOOM games every now and then, or just in general, people still mod this game today it’s still considered arguably the best shooter of all time, it has been installed more times than windows in the 90s, it’s been ported to nearly every platform in existence, every first person shooter to come out after DOOM in the mid-90s were called DOOM clones even if they aren’t really.
If you like shooters this really is one of those games where you had to have played it and it’s widely agreed “SHAME ON YOU” if you haven’t.

This is one of the best mythology based games Ive ever played, based in a world where the heroes and the monsters are gone. With the fall of the age of bronze and myth comes an age of iron in which zeus loses faith in humanity. The gods abandon the Earth, and only one man can stop them.
Although this may sound "God of War"-ish, the game drops the usual hollywood fluff and special effects for a simpler and more rough myth. It is obvious from the start just how well researched the story was. Although not based on any particular myths, the Gods and other mythic characters are portrayed in a spot-on fashion. The personalities are familiar and correct to the original tales, the places visited such as Hades and the Garden of Artemis feel natural to the legends and impose a vivid and often lasting image. The games aesthetic only furthers these feelings with its use of old Greek art, where the way these ancient people saw the world was immortalized in the only fashion they knew how to use for their time. Even where the game takes liberties in its story, it still rings true to old Greek mythical ideals.
What about the combat you may ask?
From the start, I realized the combat was challenging. Many have complained that its the controls. Personaly, having beaten the game on the hardest difficulty, I can say this is not the case. Although the creators may have not have used the most ideal system for fighting, it still works quite well. Especially in a game about a mortal challenging the divine. Fighting is challenging and often fun, only frustrating in sections of the game where multiple enemies rush you at once. Weapons, armor, and shields all may break if overused. The key is timing, and the system in place feels well balanced and all-around satisfying.
All in all, a must play for anyone who's a fan of mythology. The story, characters, voice-acting, aesthetic, and even combat all wrap up for a very memorable and great work of art. 10/10 imo.

Background: Absolutely fell in love with Bastion (completed 3-5 times, never left Zulf behind once), loved Transistor (completed twice). Completed Pyre once.

Not to mention the art style (as usual) seemed on par with that of Bastion and Transistor.
Fast forward to the day of release, and I dive into the world of Pyre with eagerness and anticipation. Reflecting now, one of the first differences between Pyre and previous SG games is that there's no narrator, which means a lot more reading. In fact, Pyre, in my opinion, plays very much like a visual novel for 80% of the time. That, of course, is a number arbitrarily chosen by me, assuming you read all the conversations and interact with your fellow exiles on every possible occasion. That's not bad in and of itself, however it's something for you to decide whether it floats your boat.
The remaining 20%, whether you call it a mix between basketball and football, a simplified bloodbowl, or any other name, offer a respite from reading. At first the rites felt a little bit slow, but once you get used to it (and get some mastery points in), they feel much more fluid, although I was never able to pull off complex plays involving the whole team. Imagine playing Transistor purely without the time-stopping tactical mode. While I didn't necessarily hate it, it wasn't very rewarding either. Even though at times the freedom of my fellow exiles rested on us winning the rites, it never felt very suspenseful (as it probably should have). Maybe because the rites were relatively easy (though admittedly I did not enable any titan stars and was playing on medium difficulty) or maybe because they went by pretty fast.
I do, however, have to commend the design option to include narrative interactions between characters based on your choice of rites (especially later on in the game). I found myself facing the Tempers, the Fate and the Essence because of the storylines accompanying them. This directly leads me to the characters. SG definitely managed to create a group of entertaining (Ti'Zo and Sir Gilman for me especially) and/or relatable characters. However, somehow, maybe because of being once removed from them (playing as their companion and not as them first-hand, as I did in Bastion and Transistor), I never really felt invested in some of their stories. And the stories that got me involved in them never reached the level of emotional involvement in either the Kid's or the Red's stories. YMMV, obviously. Maybe because of that (you arguably not being the main character and the multitude of your party), upon the conclusion of the story I didn't feel as deeply touched as I was after I completed Bastion and Transistor.
Continuing on, even though, as I've already mentioned, the visuals seemed excellent at first, but when I spent 80% of the time reading text, I never found myself having the time to take it all in. Unlike in Bastion, when the Kid was in the gorgeous environment, trying to not fall off the edge into the abyss, smashing boxes or vases or simply flying through the river on that old ship (Nelly?), you'd have to spend extra time trying to take it in, in a sense separating it from the gameplay. Design of the characters themselves is excellent with the depiction of demons being my favourite. I'd also have to mention that during rites I didn't find visuals to stand out as much as during travelling sections, observing the blackwagon roll.
The soundtrack, something I held in very high regard after completing both Bastion and Transistor, continuing to listen to them on their own merrit years after having completed both games, didn't leave as big of a lasting impression. The few that stood out - the song that Tariq sings during your see voyage and the Dissidents theme  - were neat, but not something I'd consider adding to my daily playlist. The soundtrack itself is sort of a mix between Bastion acoustic guitar chords (which to me felt  like indie, country at times) and Transistor post-rocky sound (do not know how it's called, sorry). In both previous SG games, soundtrack, I'd argue, was an essential element, either because of the moments with which it was associated (Mother I'm here and Zulf choice, Zia's theme and finding Zia, Setting sails, coming home and literally setting sails at the end), or interactions with the game (Red humming, making it feel like it's her songs that are being played, feeling like it's her performance). I found neither of the two in Pyre. Admittedly the Liberation Rite had a song associated with it, but it was never allowed to sink in, like the songs in Bastion.
To conclude, it didn't feel to me, that the type of game that Pyre is, plays to the strengths of Supergiant Games, i.e. their presentation and style (visuals, soundtracks and voice acting) and, to a lesser extent, the ability to create an involving narative. I do not regret buying and completing Pyre, as it gave me ample philosophical thoughts to munch over, however, I don't think it will have as much of a lasting impact on me as Bastion and Transistor did. I wish the best for Supergiant games, for I will certainly follow their next venture, hopefully one that may grip me as Bastion and Transistor once did.
Do I recommend this game universally in its entirety? In all honesty I can't. I do, however, recommend checking it out.
Disclaimer: I'm just a guy playing video games, this review is purely my thoughts on the game and by no means is a claim to any sort of objective truth. As already mentioned, YMMV. Cheers.

A classic Star Wars RPG made by Obsidian, a company formed by refugees from the Black Isle division of Interplay that created Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, Fallout 2, etc. and then as Obisidan went on to make well-received sequels/spinoffs such as Neverwinter Nights 2, Fallout: New Vegas, etc. This game in particular is a follow-up to KotOR 1, which was made by Bioware using a derivative of the Neverwinter Nights engine and a cousin to the engine used by The Witcher 1.
Gameplay and graphics are basically the game as in KotOR 1. This means they're a bit simplistic by today's standards, since that game was from the XBox 1 / PS2 era, but I think it still holds up. It's even a bit ahead of its time for an RPG in that it has a decent crafting system.
One thing you NEED to know about this game is that it was released in a rushed / barely-finished state. I therefore *highly* recommend the fan-created addon "The Sith Lords Restored Content Mod" (TSLRCM). Thanks to Aspyr's updates to the game made in the process of porting it to Linux/SteamOS, you can now install this mod painlessly via Steam Workshop.
Also, the game's graphics can glitch out on modern computers, with weird issues like not being able to exit combat I think? The newest version of this game here on Steam may no longer have these issues, as Aspyr fixed up the game a bit in the process of porting it to Linux/SteamOS. My only issue in Windows 10 on my Alienware 17 R3 is that its use of OpenGL means that I get unavoidable diagonal tearing when playing on my nVidia GTX 980M GPU, but this is a Microsoft/nVidia debacle and not Obsidian/Aspyr's fault.

Holy mother of pearl.
NOTICE: This game is mostly story. And when I say story, think a choose-your-own-adventure book that's a couple hundred pages long with a 3-on-3 basketball game that acts as some of the crossroads for the reader to partake in. If you have seen the trailer, or any other form of gameplay, and wish not for a 3-on-3 basketball-esque game that changes the outcome of the story, or simply don't like story games, please at least get the soundtrack to support these devs. It will be worth your money and your time, you seriously won't regret that.
Alright, so I think i'll start my review on what I love about the game and work my way down to what I don't like about the game. I'll leave my rating of it at the end of the topic's summary on a 1/10 scale.
-Music: Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the music in this game. I love it in it's entirety, simply because there's so much to love about it. It speaks so much volume, not only for the characters, but for the gameplay, the world, for you. Hell (haHAA funee pun for what happens here), the music changes tone when it's a forgotten face's turn for dialogue, and back to that character's, and back again. It gives the characters so much more flavor, and they have a fair bit of flavor in themselves. There is even an entire song that tells what Pyre is about, it's the first song in the ost. Music very rarely gives me any feeling towards it other than enjoyment, but this? This gave me goosebumps, and i'm a frozen hearted individual so something like this is very, very rare. It rightfully deserves a 10/10.
-Art Design: Um ok wow this game is beautiful. From the characters to the world, to the gameplay to, again, the characters. I actually am at a loss for words here. The game looks amazing. I give it a 9/10.
-Story: The story in this game is superb. It doesn't give too much for what happens or what goes on, only enough for you to comprehend what is going on. I will abide by such logic and only tell you that the story is superb. 8/10.
-Characters: I really like the characters that are in this game. No one in this game is truly an antagonist in this game (other than what you're fighting for and against, that's laid clear), they are simply misunderstood and are also wrongly guided in their motives, one of the characters that you receive shows how this is such. This game truly made me feel like a racist towards these characters, simply because of the way that the races are portrayed in this game. They are your simple mythical creatures, but what the devs has done was they made these characters some of my favorite, because these are how sentient creatures with reasonable comprehension and understanding are to be treated, not as their race's sterotype, but instead on that entity's wills and actions themselves. These characters are some of the best that I have seen in game, show, book and movie alike. 8/10.
-Gameplay: The game might look like a fantasty style of basketball with a 3-on-3 team, but unfortunately in the early parts of the game, it'd be best to place a WII in that team, because you only need 1 active character for the Rites. Later on in the game, it certainly gets more challenging to the point where 2-3 is needed, but 3 is a rare number to be in need of. Legit the gameplay is too long and tedious to explain (in even low amount of detail) for me to detail, just imagine it as 3-on-3 basketball with a lot of special additives. But I will give the gameplay credit where it is due, it is a lot of fun and it feels entirely responsive, with each character being unique and actually useful. Along with, it helps progress the story in a lot of ways that I really like. I give the gameplay aspect a 7.5/10.
-World: Ehhhhh. I remember reading in one of the reports from this game, I think the one where they said that they had a hole in their offices that acted as a gladiator ring that granted the victor whatever game they wished to make that Pyre would have the largest world in out of Transistor and Bastion. I guess it is? When we take a look at gameplay aspect, there isn't much to play here with, and neither much to interact with. If we're talking lore-wise, then I guess it is. Unfortunately I do have to rate this a 6/10, but only because that there isn't much in the way of interactability. Seriously though don't get me wrong, the world is beautiful, just not large in the way of gameplay.
-Items: I was debating this being "Items and Events" but the events always reward some mediocre item or some good upgrade materials, so it just fuses back into Items. Where do I begin? Oh right, the items mid-late game suck. That's a pretty good place to start. Early game, items from the shop serve a very good purpose on your quest, but once you get the orb (for your caravan), don't bother spending your Sol on any of the trinkets, it doesn't come to value with what items you can obtain from the orb. Only spend what little Sol you have on upgrade dust. It seriously just doesn't seem right, when Ron is trying his hardest with items that genuinely are really good, but the items you get from the orb (that are character specific mind you, and there is only 1 item per character and one character per race) are beyond amazing. Just seems like wasted coding. 3.5/10.
-Overall: My overall enjoyment with Pyre has been enough where I will come back for the versus. I wish not to spend another 12-16 hours of my time for a story that is still fresh in my mind, and truthfully most dearest to my heart. I will enjoy the versus though, enough for many hours to come of it. My rating of Pyre is a 9/10. This game takes your money, and gives you so much more than what it costs. Sure, it comes from the company behind Transistor and Bastion and people have viewed it as a letdown for them because of the gameplay and the way the story is presented, but damn, give the game a chance, without any expectations, and you'll come to enjoy it like I have.

I picked this up on Steam in the "collection" version when it was on sale for a bit under $20. I've only been playing this for twenty-some odd hours now, but I really like it. I find myself replaying missions over and over chasing that perfect run, and trying out different tactics. Last night I played a mission pretty cleanly, and didn't get shot once so I got the "Hide and Hope" achievement. It felt like I had actually accomplished something!
This game has reminded me of how much I like stealth mechanics, and slow, tactical gameplay. Now I've ordered other similar games for my library that I never played for some reason (Hitman series, Splintercell series). In fact, even though I'm less than half way through this campaign (and haven't played any of the coop), I went ahead and got Sniper Elite 3 and its season pass (together for $35, thanks internet!).
The gameplay is very deliberate, if you like a run-n-gun style, this won't work for you. I really appreciate the tension and atmospherics in this game. Often even when I know I can safely run in a section, I will choose not to just because I hate making so much noise.
Your sniper rifle is your best weapon. Your secondary has very limited range and accuracy, and also limited ammo on the battlefield (though there are strategies to improve this). You have to think like a sniper, don't shoot from a window, shoot from deep within the room, from the shadows (bonus, increased distance points!). Pulling off a perfect mission takes patience and strategy. Pulling it off with style takes experimentation and creativity (I pulled off the final stage of mission 4 using only traps last night). Maneuvering through the maps without ever being spotted is incredibly satisfying, and in some missions, incredibly difficult. Progressing your accuracy from all hits, to all headshots, to all through the eye or through the ear shots (beautifully confirmed by the amazing kill-cam) feels great. Doing that to 3-4 enemies in a row, all in a single breath feels amazing. This is really some kick♥♥♥♥♥sniping. And you can make it even more kick♥♥♥♥♥by tweaking the difficulty in a fairly flexible way.
The in-game collectibles are completely meaningless, getting them all doesn't confer any kind of stat bonus or unlock new equipment, but I still like finding them as it satisfies that inner OCD (especially the bottles).
The lack of a save system could be seen as a down side. It's checkpoint only. So if you screw something up, you may have to repeat a decent chunk, though they are usually pretty close together once you figure out the optimum pattern for a particular map.
