An action/platformer with well thought out gameplay. Feels a bit like an action RPG in the sense that you have a degree of freedom which of your objectives to pursue and a lot of side areas to explore, there's a lot of items to find, weapons, shields, ammunition, crafting items, healing items, buff items... add to that item shops, crafting and there's a lot to do. On the other hand every item is pretty much somehow breakable or consumable meaning you always need more. The secrets themselves are fun to look for but rarely give anything you couldn't just get otherwise. There is a degree of power progression as you get more gear, buy better training and armor over time as well as get permanent buffs for completing quests although it doesn't go into metroidvania territory and upgrades aren't neccesary to open new areas.
Combat itself is fun, varied and has plenty of nuance to it, several types of weapons to use with different ranges, attack types and blind spots when you attack, you can use ranged or melee weapons or even crafted explosives and occassionally items in the enviroment to your advantage.
Enemies are varied although a surprising ammount of them are more annoying than dangerous, such as hit-and-run wolves, skirmishers and archers that do their damnest to keep away from you, skeletons that refuse to permanently die and so on. Even if they're not dangerous landing a hit against some of them can be a chore. Bosses themselves are pretty well done and usually just test your skills in combat, though some get tricky as well and will involve you chasing them around the arena or looking for that one item that can temporarily incapacitate them.
The game features varied enviroments, level design and often has levels distinct by structure or some gimmick that makes it memorable. When you're in Athena's realm, you have to get around through a maze filled with traps, Ares throws you in a bloody pit filled with deathmatch style combat against whoever is present and Hades will see you walking around darkness and fending off the unrelenting dead and that's just a few. This is level design done right and fits in with the personalities of the deities you face against.
The graphics style as you can see is very unique and I understand some people can be turned off by it, but it very much fits the story based on greek myths and makes the game way more stylish than if it just had generic 2D greek style enviroments. The only complaint I have here is the animations look not so well at times and in some cases could do with an overhaul.
Overal, unless you suffer from an irrational hate to the style, definitely try it out. Great and memorable game that could show many other games how to make level design interesting and memorable.

I really thought that this game would be good, everyone said that this game would be way better than the "copy" (these are still different games, dont forget that) of it (alias. dbd). But this game showed me that dbd, a indie game without a huge kickstarter and offical support was better than I thought.
I'm sorry for these devs as it is pretty clear to see that they were forced to launch the game in such a early and buggy state.
So let's make it short:
Pros:
-A dream for everyone who likes Friday the 13th due to the offical support of the creators
-Has a lot of different items and has a great sound design
-A better skill check system than dbd
-Good looking maps
-Interesting ways to escape
Cons:
-Super buggy (All of my games had at least one critical bug in it)
-UI Cluster and too many interactions with objects
-Awful servers (Did they not plan for the "hype"? Having such awful server problems for over 4 days after launch is just sad. I as a dev can understand that a problem such as that one could happen but this problem could have been expected by the devs)
-Weird camera (often overreacts while walking on hiles)
-OP Killer's (Able to teleport, 1 Hit etc. And to the people who say that this is the idea: That's stupid, you feel like you're not able to fight against him, making it a huge con)
-Gets boring very fast
-Feels very slow due to the super slow walk speed and stamina bar
-Way to expensive for it's game scope
I wouldn't recommend buying it as long as the price stays that high or they don't add a lot of new features / fix a lot of problems.

This was a hard game to recommend... I fell that some balancing is necessary. Before everyone freaks out, I do understand the game in it's current state is pretty balanced, and no matter who wins, it can be VERY fun. In my honest opinion, I think the counselors should have buffed stamina. maybe a enegry drink pick up that buffs stamina for a min or two? This would defiantly help movement around the map. Currently you sprint for a few seconds, then crouch in a bush for a minute. I don't think it would be too game breaking, as Jason has his shift ability, which closes any gap between him and prey.
I just feel like some aspects could be changed. Playing as a counselor can feel VERY slow paced at times. Not saying it's a negitive, What makes it a negitive is running around for 10 minutes collecting parts, only to have Jason single you at and track you down, Which can be very disheartening. The solution to this is teamwork, but I found that everytime I'm around someone they attempt to use me as bait as they flee, rarely helping me escape. I don't find these things too demeaning to the game as a whole, because of the few interactions between all players and Jason where everyone is screaming into their mics as Jason says sp00ky things. The times I have enjoyed this game are always when people are talking. When they're not, it can be tremendously grindy, leading up to your death.
Now on to some more pressing issuses. Firstly, the "how to play" is a joke. I understand there are endless amounts of video guideson YT, but I would of really loved to see the devs make a full tutorial, as the game CAN BE sort of complicated. secondly, you can't bind your keys, which is f*cking ludicrous. I end up playing this game on controller because I am left handed and prefer "ijkl" as my move keys. (Crazy right?) But it's not hard to add something like that....

A classic Star Wars RPG made by Obsidian, a company formed by refugees from the Black Isle division of Interplay that created Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, Fallout 2, etc. and then as Obisidan went on to make well-received sequels/spinoffs such as Neverwinter Nights 2, Fallout: New Vegas, etc. This game in particular is a follow-up to KotOR 1, which was made by Bioware using a derivative of the Neverwinter Nights engine and a cousin to the engine used by The Witcher 1.
Gameplay and graphics are basically the game as in KotOR 1. This means they're a bit simplistic by today's standards, since that game was from the XBox 1 / PS2 era, but I think it still holds up. It's even a bit ahead of its time for an RPG in that it has a decent crafting system.
One thing you NEED to know about this game is that it was released in a rushed / barely-finished state. I therefore *highly* recommend the fan-created addon "The Sith Lords Restored Content Mod" (TSLRCM). Thanks to Aspyr's updates to the game made in the process of porting it to Linux/SteamOS, you can now install this mod painlessly via Steam Workshop.
Also, the game's graphics can glitch out on modern computers, with weird issues like not being able to exit combat I think? The newest version of this game here on Steam may no longer have these issues, as Aspyr fixed up the game a bit in the process of porting it to Linux/SteamOS. My only issue in Windows 10 on my Alienware 17 R3 is that its use of OpenGL means that I get unavoidable diagonal tearing when playing on my nVidia GTX 980M GPU, but this is a Microsoft/nVidia debacle and not Obsidian/Aspyr's fault.

At the time of writing, Sheltered is equivalent to The Sims, except it's in 2D and scavenged resources are used instead of money. I'm past day 150, have gone everywhere, built everything and have never been in any real danger. There is not much challenge, it just takes a long time to scavenge enough resources to buy good equipment and furniture. I expected choices like "should we eat John to survive or risk sending him out to steal food?" and not like "should I use these pipes to craft a prettier shower or a prettier toilet?". I've heard that your shelter can be targeted by a raid, but this hasn't happened to me yet. It hasn't caught fire either.
That being said, I like the game design and got quite attached to my group of survivors. The game is charming and somewhat addictive. If you enjoy base building and scavenging games, you might like it once you get the hang of the mechanics. There is great potential, and I'm looking forward to seeing how the game develops. I'm giving it a No plus. It would have been a Yes minus if they didn't call this version 1.0, signalling a finished game.
Some pros:
- The expedition and radio mechanics are nice.
- Many objects can be recycled to useful resources or burned as fuel.
- Psychopaths offer an element of surprise!
- Charming elements like pets, paint, the jukebox and food poisoning puke.
Some of the things that should be worked on:
- Some system upgrades are too expensive and give you almost nothing in return (like durability upgrades).
- Manning the radio is a full-time job of pressing buttons when you have several expeditions going. If you have set a waypoint at a farm, then yes, you want that farm to be looted and don't have to be asked.
- We need more keyboard shortcuts, e.g. for the dialog boxes (Y/N or Enter/Esc) and answering the intercom.
- Perhaps more automation should be allowed, assigning each character specific repeat jobs (fix all furniture, fill pet food, water the planters, etc.).
- The boxing bag and bookshelf works too well. Especially the bookshelf, which many people can use at the same time. All my survivors are rocket scientists by now.
- The "special" furniture obtained by blueprints is just ridiculous. If you have something exciting and new to put there, please do, but drop the magical furniture.
- Stress: Is is ever not zero? (I've got the cat pet, though.) I've seen trauma go up when people die, but that calms down pretty fast anyway.
- Endgame: The game doesn't need an ending, but it should be harder and harder to survive as months go by (less available food, more black rain, more violent factions, etc.).
- Replay value: Starting a new game is unthinkable as I would do exactly the same things again, except choosing a different pet.

• Improved Combat and animation
• New story that is linear with the original KOTOR
• Worth the price
Cons:

It's difficult to know where to begin when reviewing DOOM. For our generation, it's the equivalent of being handed the Bible and asked to give it a score out of ten..... The content isn't so much the important issue here, rather it's the legacy the game left behind.
I don't think many people would argue that gaming (especially PC gaming) could be divided into "Before DOOM" and "After DOOM". No, it wasn't the first to do many of the tricks we now take for granted. No, it wasn't the best FPS around. But.... the iPod wasn't the first portable music player and certainly wasn't the best, but it changed the way we listen to music forever. DOOM did the same thing for the FPS, and that's not an exaggeration.
You only have to look at the timeline of games development to see that it changed both the industry and people's attitudes. Suddenly, corporate networks were being clogged up with data from employees fragging each other when they should have been working. People at home were able to design their own levels and have others play them. The graphic violence drew criticism from various groups and DOOM was talked about in national media. Every games developer in the world was rushing their own FPS to market to try and cream off some of the publicity DOOM was generating. Some were successful (Duke Nukem 3D), some (Nitemare 3D?) less so.
No, it wasn't the first to do any of these things. But at the time it was nothing short of a phenomenon. There was barely a console around which didn't receive some version of DOOM at some point (Even the VIC-20 got one eventually thanks to homebrew).
Is it the best game ever? No. But it's very important if you're even slightly interested in games, and you owe it to yourself to at least play it. The industry was never the same again after DOOM. It kick-started the interest in LAN gaming, and made 3D gaming if not the standard, then at least a target to aspire to.
iD of course managed to make lightning strike twice when Quake was released, but that's another story...

I'd never played a Rayman game before and so I had absolutely no idea what to expect when I started up Rayman Legends for the first time. Man, was I ever pleasantly surprised! It's truly one of the most fun games I've ever played. While not particularly deep from a gameplay perspective, good humor is bursting from every seam and it's impossible not to be swept along.
The level design is perfect and the visuals are utterly spectacular. I find myself playing "just one more level" to see what incredible visual treats the game has in store for me next. I also have to single out the game's remarkable composer, Christophe Héral. Music is as integral to the experience here as it was in classic Warner Bros. cartoons. You may find yourself replaying certain levels again and again just to enjoy the wonderful soundtrack. Of particular note is the fact that many of the tracks were recorded using a full orchestra, something which is very rare in games these days. Huge kudos to Ubisoft for being willing to spend the extra money to get such high quality results!
In conclusion, Rayman Legends is pretty much a must-have game. I think gamers of all skill levels, ages and backgrounds will find plenty to enjoy here.

There is a lot to do in this game, each level has 10 teensies to find (The little blue guys), as well as the challenge to find enough lums (The yellow flying guys) to earn the Gold trophy. There are also unlockable characters as well, collectable creatures, unlockable bonus levels from Rayman Origins (each has teensies and trophies to collect) and Time Trial levels as well. If you're a bit of a completionist like I am with these sorts of things, you'll have lots to keep you occupied. There is also the new music levels, which are very much like the chest chasing missions in Origins, completely timing based where you jump or attack in time with the music. These are excellently thought out and the timing is spot-on. These are a bit more forgiving than Origins' chest chasing missions though, having checkpoints rather than making you restart after each death.
There are downsides though, this game is a console port and at times it shows, making some actions hard to perform using keyboard if you don't have nimble fingers. It is perfectly playable with the keyboard though and supports full key remapping (Which I suggest you do, I set mine to the Origins controls and it saved me a lot of trouble), but it may be easier to play using a controller. I can't say which is better, since I've only played using keyboard, although you can play one handed using keyboard, leaving your other hand free to do other stuff like eat a sandwich or write a book. It also doesn't really have much replayability, apart from the music levels which are awesome just to play occasionally, unless you are a big Rayman fan. Plus it only works through UPlay, which is not a bad piece of software but it does make things frustrating when you just want to get right into the game.
Overall, this game is worth picking up, even at full price and the annoying DRM. Graphics are pretty and there is a lot to do. I'm really looking forward to the next game in the series,

Please read the full review on my personal blog:
Below is an excerpt from that review:
"This narrative is the thing that actually elevates Soma up above Amnesia: the Dark Descent. This narrative explores the mind-body problem in a similar manner to The Swapper, but this time, with a more transhumanist slant. The actual gameplay doesn't incorporate the theme as well as The Swapper does, but the story that is told is still very thought-provoking and offers an interesting dialogue on the concepts of the mind-body problem as they relate to transhumanism. While The Swapper used the mind-body problem as the centerpiece of its core mechanic that you were constantly engaged with, Soma focuses on exploring corridors and evading monsters as its core mechanic, with a thematic transhumanist puzzle or set piece showing up at regular intervals to make you stop and think. It works just fine, but it never reaches the level of ludonarrative harmony that The Swapper excels at.
For anybody who's paying attention to the narrative and actually thinking about the things that you're asked to do in this game, the existential horror of your actions and the events of the game should be screwing with your mind enough that the game doesn't need to throw in deadly monsters. I felt genuinely sad when I had to hurt or kill some of the robots, and the game gives the player some subtle choices as extensions of certain key puzzles that made me pause and think about the repercussions and morality of what I was doing. All the moral choices that you face are presented as "lesser of two evils" options rather than the "paragon or renegade" choices that most other games (including heady games like Fallout) throw at the player.
The game even makes some of these choices for you early in the game (when you don't necessarily comprehend the weight of your actions) by forcing you to make one choice over the other in order to proceed. This just makes the open-ended choices later on feel so much heavier (after the game has explained the sinister nature of the character's previous choices), and they made me stop dead in my tracks and contemplate the weight of what I'm deciding to do. They aren't utilitarian, there's no impression that one path or the other might result in a ludic reward or alternate ending, and even if I did think a choice might affect the game's ending, I was genuinely oblivious as to how. I was left considering what I thought would be the right thing to do based on my own understanding of the subject matter that the game was presenting me with, and that was a genuinely hard decision to make. I sat for a minute or two at some of these choices, moving the mouse cursor over each of the option buttons, as I debated in my head which one was the better choice. And even the word "better" seemed like the wrong term: better for who?"

I did go in the game being aware that it has microtransactions, but I assumed that it was only for the cosmetic items, so I tried to just ignore that they exist. It's just sad that they decided to do this.

TLDR: What you see is what you get. A Horror fan's day pass at an amusement park.
I am a HUGE fan of the Friday the 13th movies, with that said,  the game is a dream come true for a fan but unless you OOZE blood from your hockey mask like me, its going to be a hard sell at that $40 price tag.
3 maps, all with the same escape options
6 different Jasons with varied skills, strengths, and weaknesses
11 Counselers each with unique stats
and more bugs than I can count... lots of bugs.
Thats it. Thats all you get.
HOWEVER.
The gameplay is fun, exciting, and stressful in all the right ways. It can be an exillerating power trip to play as Jason and murder your fellow players, while you aslo feel like an elusive fox when you manage to escape the terrifying grip of Jason's jaws. Its a perfect representation of an 80s slasher in the form of a game, with music ques, gory satisfying deaths, and tension above all else.
If you are a fan of the movies, or a fan of horror in general, and have some money, buy it. I'd recomend waiting either for more content or a cheaper price tag for everyone else.
In conclusion, its still an extremely fun experience, but what you see is what you get.
